# Michel Henry, *L'essence de la manifestation*

# Introduction. The problem of the being of the ego and the fundamental presuppositions of ontology

**Paragraph 1 (epigraph from Heidegger).** Henry opens the entire book not with his own words but with a citation, in German followed by French translation, taken from *Sein und Zeit*: Descartes, with the *cogito sum*, claims to provide philosophy with a new and secure foundation; but what he leaves undetermined in this "radical" beginning is the mode of being (*Seinsart*) of the *res cogitans*, more precisely the meaning of the being (*Seinssinn*) of the *sum*. The choice of epigraph is doubly programmatic. First, it announces the thesis that will structure the entire Introduction: the Cartesian *point de départ* is not radical enough, because it takes for granted what it ought to have interrogated, namely the sense of being ( *Seinssinn*) of the "I am" itself. Second, and more important for what follows, it signals that Henry is taking his departure *from* Heidegger — not from Husserl, and not from Descartes. The specific passage is from §6 and §25 of *Sein und Zeit*, where Heidegger criticizes Descartes for having thematized the *cogito* as a being (*ens*) whose mode of being he never made into a problem, so that the Cartesian beginning is only apparently radical, in truth resting on an unexamined scholastic ontology inherited from Suárez and medieval Aristotelianism. Henry borrows the Heideggerian diagnosis of the Cartesian deficit — the *sum* is left ontologically indeterminate — but, as the book will make clear, he will turn this diagnosis against Heidegger himself: for Henry, Heidegger's own answer to the question of the being of the ego, the Being-in-the-world of Dasein, merely repeats at a deeper level the same mistake (treating the ego's being as a mode of transcendence, of the *Ek-stase* of a horizon). The epigraph thus opens both the agreement (the question is correctly posed: *Seinssinn des "sum"*) and the disagreement (the answer Heidegger gives is, for Henry, still guided by the presuppositions it denounces).

**Paragraph 2\.** Henry states his theme in a single, declarative sentence: the sense of the being of the ego is the theme of the present investigations. He immediately glosses this with the phenomenological *donné*: what the investigations aim to bring "into the light, before the philosophical gaze," is what we understand when we say, on every occasion, and each time we are in question ourselves: *I*, *me*. The formulation is strictly Husserlian in tone — "bringing into the light before the philosophical gaze" echoes the Husserlian *Klärung*, the evidential elucidation that lets the matter appear as it is — but the content (what we mean when we say "I") is Cartesian-Heideggerian. Henry then makes a sociological-methodological observation: philosophy in recent times (i.e., phenomenology) has accustomed us to interrogate radically what most often presents itself as self-evident, as what everyone knows or understands. Does not the ego belong to that domain of the most commonplace and banal in an eminent way? The sentence is deliberately structured to invoke the Heideggerian procedure of *Sein und Zeit* §4: the ontologically remarkable is hidden behind the banally familiar; and just as Heidegger makes a problem of that being which is *je mein*, Henry will make a problem of that ego which everyone claims to know because everyone claims to *be* it. The passage closes with a preemptive move against psychology: psychology has long made the *moi*, or personality, an object of study and a chapter heading. This sets up the next paragraph's critique.

**Paragraph 3\.** Henry concedes to psychology its positive knowledge: on the formation of the idea of the *moi*, on its content, on its role in psychic life, nothing can be taught to psychology that it does not already know in its own positivity. But he immediately asks the philosophical counter-question: what credit can be given to researches that have never thrown light on themselves and whose results they are incapable of evaluating? The formulation is pure Heidegger in tone — the demand that science throw light on its own foundations before claiming positive results is the classical Heideggerian distinction between ontic and ontological research (*Sein und Zeit* §3, on the "regional" foundation of the positive sciences). Henry then drives the point home with a consequential *a fortiori*: if Descartes himself omitted to raise to the rank of a problem what constitutes the sense of being of the *sum*, what help could one expect from psychology, which builds up its positive knowledge on the unexplicated foundation of being, and which treats the *moi* as an object — or, what amounts to the same thing, as a "subject" — without first having interrogated what constitutes the condition of possibility of every object as such? The equation *object \= subject* at the level of ontological indetermination is crucial: it anticipates Henry's later argument (in Section I) that subject and object, so long as they are both held within the single horizon of ontological manifestation, are ontologically isomorphic, because both are determined as what stands-over-against, what is objectified in an *Ek-stase*. Psychology's treatment of the *moi* as an object is not merely a methodological choice but a symptom of a more general ontological presupposition — one that will be named in Section I as "ontological monism."

**Paragraph 4\.** Before claiming any result, every question must seek to become transparent to itself. This is a strictly Husserlian demand — the *Selbstverständlichkeit* of philosophy, the requirement that philosophy be responsible for its own presuppositions — but Henry gives it a Heideggerian inflection: every question must first be able to say whether the problematic it institutes can be considered originary and fundamental, or whether, on the contrary, it is subordinated to a prior research on which it shows itself to be dependent. The vocabulary — "originaire et fondamentale," "subordonnée," "recherche première" — is exactly that of *Sein und Zeit* §§2–4, where Heidegger lays out the formal structure of the question of being and its priority over all regional questions. In the subordinate case, a research necessarily implies presuppositions, uses results it has not itself obtained, or makes use of certain ideas it does not take the trouble to clarify. The passage culminates in a definition of the *Ursprünglich*: independence — and therefore an internal assurance of validity — is given only to a truly originary and, in some sense, absolute problematic, which not only draws its knowledge from itself but has, in addition, already thrown light on what makes possible all knowledge as such. First philosophy has long understood the necessity of instituting such a problematic at the origin of all human research. Henry is here establishing the criterion by which every ontological project — including his own — must be judged: self-transparency, self-grounding, and the prior elucidation of the condition of possibility of cognition in general. This is a formal criterion shared by Husserl's transcendental phenomenology (which grounds itself in the self-givenness of the transcendental ego) and by Heidegger's fundamental ontology (which grounds itself in the being of Dasein as the being that has an understanding of being). The rest of the Introduction will show that Descartes fails this criterion, that Husserl's rationalist interpretation of the *cogito* fails it, and that Heidegger's own alternative only partially succeeds — leading to the necessity of Henry's own re-radicalization.

**Paragraph 5\.** The decisive Heideggerian question is now posed as a rhetorical question: does the problem of the being of the ego belong to first philosophy? Is it not evident, on the contrary, that every question that aims at the ego in its being implies that a response to the problem of the sense of being in general be previously given or at least sought? The argument is almost verbatim from *Sein und Zeit* §2: to ask about a particular being (the *ego*) presupposes that one already has some understanding of what it is to be, since the question "is the ego?" or "how is the ego?" uses the "is" as its guiding thread. Henry gives a concrete illustration: when I say "I am content" or, more simply, "I am," what is aimed at in my affirmation is precisely possible only because being already "shines" (*luit*). The verb *luire* is not a neutral choice — it is Henry's earliest hint of a phenomenological vocabulary (manifestation, light, shining-forth) that will dominate the whole book; being, for philosophy so far, is understood as what appears, what comes into the light, what manifests itself. The conclusion is drawn in the same Heideggerian tenor: the true object of a first research should not be the ego itself, but the being of the ego, or, more precisely, the being in and through which the ego can arise into existence and acquire its own being. Hence the Cartesian commencement is not "radical," because it is possible only on a foundation it has not made explicit, and which is more radical than it. The scare-quotes around "radical" throughout this paragraph repeat Heidegger's own irony in *Sein und Zeit* §6 and §43.

**Paragraph 6\.** Henry now takes the step toward defining "first philosophy": the science that studies the problem of being in general, of being *qua* being, is ontology. This, of course, is the classical Aristotelian definition of *prôtê philosophia* from *Metaphysics* Γ.1 (τὸ ὂν ᾗ ὄν) — and Henry's use of it here places him squarely in the tradition of fundamental ontology, for which ontology is not a branch of philosophy alongside others but philosophy itself in its originary vocation. Ontology is necessarily universal: its object is not this or that thing, nor this or that kind of thing, but what conditions them all equally. First philosophy is universal ontology. With respect to this fundamental discipline every research, and in particular that which concerns the ego, must recognize its inevitable subordination. But this subordination itself must be made the theme of a research. The double move is characteristically Henrian: (i) the question of the ego is subordinated to the question of being in general; but (ii) the nature of that subordination is itself something to be thematized — it is not, as in Heidegger, simply assumed that the ego (or Dasein) is the privileged access-point to the question of being, nor, as in Husserl, simply assumed that the transcendental ego is the ground of the phenomenological reduction. Henry holds both options open because, by the end of the Introduction, he will argue that neither option has correctly understood the structure of the subordination.

**Paragraph 7\.** The Introduction's opening closes with a transitional sentence. The link that attaches the problematic that aims at the ego to universal ontology is particularly complex. The first approximate elucidation of that relation will serve as introduction to the problem of the ego. What Henry announces here is the seven-part structure of the Introduction itself: §§1–7 will progressively elucidate, in increasingly radical form, the relation between the ego-problematic and the problematic of being-in-general. §1 will treat the Cartesian-Husserlian claim that apodictic evidence gives privileged access to the being of the ego; §2 will show why a universal phenomenological ontology must be built up first; §3 will trace the overcoming of intuitionism; §4 will reinsert the *cogito* into the horizon thus liberated; §5 will show the aporia of that reinsertion; §6 will exhibit the difficulties internal to universal phenomenological ontology itself; and §7 will re-pose the ego-problematic, now interpreted as an originary and fundamental problematic in its own right. The Introduction is thus a dialectical ladder: each step refines and partially overturns the previous one, and the whole ladder is erected in order to arrive at the point where, with §7 closing, the real work of the book — the elucidation of the essence of manifestation in Sections I–IV — can begin.

---

## **§ 1\. The idea of an apodictic evidence as privileged pathway of access to the being of the ego**

**Paragraph 1\.** The section opens with a rhetorical question: why did Descartes believe he could dispense with the ontological context inside which alone a question can receive the elucidation it needs, if it does not want to remain a question left hanging in the air, nor arrive at results completely indeterminate in their scope and their meaning? The answer, given immediately, is that this context itself appeared to Descartes as a source of confusion and of sterile discussions. To reject all those presuppositions that always present themselves to us under the form of a historical tradition, to rid oneself at last of all "prejudices" — that, it seemed to him, was the condition to which every research that wants truly and freely to "begin" must submit itself. The scare-quotes around "préjugés" and "commencer" again mark a Heideggerian irony (the Cartesian claim to presuppositionlessness is precisely what Heidegger contests in *Sein und Zeit* §6), but Henry is also tracing a historical genealogy: the Cartesian rejection of scholastic tradition will be repeated in a modified form by Husserl's phenomenological *Voraussetzungslosigkeit* (the "principle of all principles" from *Ideen I* §24), which itself appeals back to Descartes' own *Regulae* and to the First Meditation. Then, Henry writes, a royal road opens for philosophy — the road it follows when it simply abandons itself to its object, the road that leads directly to the result. To turn one's back on all theories and conceptual edifices that mask the real from us, to abandon oneself to the object, to let it be as it is in itself, to return at last to the things themselves: that is a Cartesian teaching. The last phrase, "retourner enfin aux choses mêmes," is of course the famous Husserlian slogan *zu den Sachen selbst* (cf. *Logical Investigations*, Introduction to Vol. II), and Henry's point is genealogical: the Husserlian program is, in its self-understanding, a renewal of a Cartesian vocation. Only — Henry concludes — Descartes had understood very well that what truly gives itself to us does not let itself be so easily recognized, and that most of the things we believe we truly attain in their very being are in reality confused or uncertain. When he decided then to submit to a systematic critique the whole of the given of our experience, he perceived that what offered itself to us under the mode of an irrecusable evidence was nothing other than the *ego cogito*. This is the classical reading of the First and Second Meditations: the methodical doubt is not skepticism but a systematic critique of evidential claims, and its terminus is the one *cogitatio* that cannot be doubted, the *ego cogito*.

**Paragraph 2\.** The central place given to the *ego cogito* by philosophical research, however, implies certain presuppositions on the part of that research. These hold, in truth, to the very nature of such a research, which always obeys the idea of a truth to be attained. What legitimates something like philosophy is that the end which it pursues and which secretly animates it is not proper to it. Evidence is the τέλος of all intentional life. The use of the Greek *télos* here (with deliberate Greek letters) is a Husserlian citation — it recalls the theme of the "teleology of reason" developed especially in *Formal and Transcendental Logic* §§57–59 and in the *Crisis*, where philosophy is understood as the historical self-realization of a teleology immanent to intentional life as such. The point is crucial for what Henry is about to argue: the privilege of the *cogito* is not an arbitrary or a purely historical privilege; it derives from a structural teleology of intentionality itself, which is always aimed at evidence. Henry continues: the problematic concerning evidence is situated in the natural prolongation of life, and it is this problematic that serves at once as context and as frame for the emergence of the *ego cogito* as theme of philosophical meditation. What Henry is placing on the table here is the thesis that the *cogito* is not the beginning of philosophy; rather, the beginning of philosophy is the problematic of evidence, inside which the *cogito* becomes a privileged theme *because* it answers, better than any other being, to the teleological demand for apodicticity. This is already a major rearrangement of the Cartesian order: the *cogito* is not first, evidence is first.

**Paragraph 3\.** The short paragraph that follows situates the problematic of evidence inside phenomenology: it belongs to the phenomenology of reason. It is the radicalization, in conformity with the sense of intentionality, of a problematic of intuition. Intuition is the foundation of every rational assertion. The study of reason demands that this foundation be brought into clarity. Each of these sentences is a precise reference to Husserl. The "phenomenology of reason" (*Phänomenologie der Vernunft*) is the title of the last part of *Ideen I* (§§128–153), where Husserl lays out the theory of evidential positing. The claim that intuition is the foundation of every rational assertion is the "principle of all principles" from *Ideen I* §24: every originarily giving intuition is a source of right for knowledge. And the "radicalization" of a problematic of intuition in conformity with the sense of intentionality is the exact move by which Husserl, in *Ideen I* and in *Formal and Transcendental Logic*, transforms the classical intuition-theory into a theory of the intentional fulfillment (*Erfüllung*) of signifying acts by giving acts. Henry is laying out, in compressed form, the Husserlian doctrine he is about to summarize.

**Paragraph 4\.** This paragraph is a long systematic exposition of the Husserlian theory of regional ontology and of the types of evidence corresponding to the various regions of being. The philosophical analysis of intuition and of its fundamental structure, the systematic examination of the different types of intuition and of their diverse modalities, the correlative elucidation of the field of the intuitive given, of the structures and of the multiple eidetic differentiations it presents — these constitute the first task of phenomenology. In pursuing rigorously this task it gives itself at the origin of its research, phenomenology already puts aside many prejudices. It shows against empiricism that sensible experience realizes only one fundamental type of intuition. The intuition presupposed by empiricism, of the essence of sensible experience, puts us in presence, at least once, of the existence of an eidetic intuition. With the help of this eidetic intuition must be pursued the exhaustive investigation of the different eidetic types of intuition, as well as the examination of their respective value. This is pure Husserl — the argument against empiricism from *Ideen I* §§18–26, which observes that empiricism can only formulate its own thesis (that all knowledge derives from sensible experience) by already presupposing a non-sensible intuition of the *essence* of sensible experience; the self-refutation of empiricism is thus a proof of the reality of *Wesensschau*. Henry then continues with the doctrine of regions: being which gives itself originarily to these intuitive consciousnesses, each distinguished each time by a specific eidetic structure, distributes itself, in conformity with the very manner in which it presents itself, into a plurality of regions to which correspond rigorously determined types of donative intuition. In conformity with these diverse regional types, and correlatively inside each region of being, there is, for that being, a privileged way of giving itself. This is the doctrine of *ontologies régionales* from *Ideen I* §§9–17: each region of being (material thing, animate being, psychic being, ideal objects, values, etc.) has its own eidetic structure, and to each such structure corresponds a mode of evidential givenness proper to it. Within each region there is a privileged mode — the mode of originary givenness, in which the thing itself presents itself "in person" (*leibhaftig*) to an intuitive consciousness. Henry's phrase "en personne" is the direct French calque of Husserl's *leibhaftig*, a technical term of *Ideen I*.

The paragraph continues with the Husserlian theory of *Erfüllung*: this situation is characterized by the fact that the signifying intentions of consciousness find a fulfillment that can go as far as the living presence of the thing itself, so that to the sense aimed at by consciousness is then added in the noema a specific character of corporeality. This is the doctrine of the sixth of the *Logical Investigations*: a signifying act (*Bedeutungsintention*) is fulfilled (*erfüllt*) by an intuitive act that brings the intended object to presence, and the fulfillment can reach the limit where the object itself is given "in the flesh." The French "corporéité" translates *Leiblichkeit* in the Husserlian sense of the "bodily" presence of the object — not the animate body, but the *in-person* presence. Henry continues: the way in which this fulfillment operates defines the degree of the evidence. Consciousness aims at obtaining a perfect evidence. But the perfection of evidence does not depend only on the psychological course and the subjective effort of a determinate consciousness; its type is in reality prescribed by the proper ontological structure of the region considered. It represents an ultimate possibility attached to that region and rigorously defined. It would therefore be absurd to pretend to obtain, for example, an adequate evidence relative to an object to which its eidetic structure, as well as the regional genus to whose empire it belongs, prescribe a manner of giving itself that excludes, and that in principle, the possibility of a presentation in conformity with such a type of evidence. This is the Husserlian doctrine of the impossibility of adequate evidence for transcendent things: a physical thing, in virtue of its regional essence, can never be given in an adequate evidence (never fully, never exhaustively, always in *Abschattungen* or profile-views); to demand adequate evidence of a physical thing would be absurd, because such a demand contradicts the very eidetic structure of the region "physical thing." The point is developed by Husserl especially in *Ideen I* §§41–44 (the analysis of perception and profile). Henry concludes: one can only define for each sphere of being a mode of givenness rigorously characterized — in privileged cases, a mode of originary givenness — which indicates to what genus of evidence, "optima," it is possible to attain in the sphere considered. One will thus be led to circumscribe fundamental types of evidence in correlation with the different regions and with the ultimate modalities of the intuitive donative consciousness, the differentiation of which will have itself been pursued on the eidetic plane. Henry is giving here a schematic description of the Husserlian architecture of regional ontology — the very architecture that §2 will show is insufficient.

**Paragraph 5\.** Because they are rigorously ordered to objective essences in which the *a priori* structures of regions manifest themselves, because for that reason they obey a legality of the eidetic order, the different types of evidence have, in that respect, an equal degree of validity. Each of them proposes to us, in conformity with a determinate category of apprehension, a possibility of experience that corresponds strictly to a sphere of being and that is capable of delivering to us, inside that sphere, being itself, such as it manifests itself there in its essential structure. This is a precise statement of the democracy of regions in Husserlian ontology: the evidence of the material thing is not inferior to the evidence of the *cogito*; each is valid within its region, according to the eidetic norm of that region. But — Henry continues — one cannot rank all types of evidence on the same plane. A discrimination, of an axiological order if one wishes, but which finds its source not in the subjective preferences of a consciousness, but in a teleology of universal signification immanent to intentional life in general, is manifestly established between them. In conformity with this teleology that inhabits it, consciousness turns toward the evidences that present a remarkable degree of perfection. This is again the Husserlian teleology of reason: although regions are formally equal, intentional life is teleologically oriented toward the evidences that best fulfill the idea of truth, that is, toward those evidences which are most perfect. The criterion of perfection, developed in *Ideen I* §§136–141 and in *Formal and Transcendental Logic* §58, is that the evidence be immediate, originary, and adequate — and further, that the object given in it not be able to be submitted to doubt by the ulterior course of experience (the criterion of *Unüberholbarkeit*, insuperability).

Henry continues: at the highest degree of perfection, we find an immediate, originary evidence in which the diverse elements of signifying intention by which consciousness aims at the object are all fulfilled by a corresponding intuition, in such a way that nothing obscure or indistinct remains in such an experience. This experience gives us the absolute certainty that the being seized with evidence exists, such precisely as it presents itself in the evidence. As long, however, as the possibility remains open for the being seized in the evidence to become afterwards an object of doubt, the evidence is not perfect. Perfect evidence must therefore still present a new character, in conformity with which it gives itself as an evidence that cannot be belied by the ulterior course of experience. Only apodictic evidence is capable of offering to philosophical reflection the guarantee that the object it furnishes will not change, that this reflection will always find it identical to itself each time it effectuates anew the act that gives it in evidence. We can then say that the object of apodictic evidence is given to us in an absolute certainty; it plays for that reason, with respect to research, the role of a true commencement. This is the exact Husserlian definition of apodicticity as it appears in the *Cartesian Meditations* §6: apodictic evidence is that evidence whose non-being is unthinkable, an evidence the nullity of which cannot be conceived even in principle. The *cogito*, for Husserl as for Descartes, has this character.

**Paragraph 6\.** The consciousness that aims at obtaining apodictic evidence does not orient itself where it wishes. As there exists a strict relation between the eidetic type of the evidence and the genus of being that this evidence exhibits, it is to a well-determined reality that the reflection which abandons itself to the *télos* of apodicticity has to do. The *ego cogito* necessarily becomes its theme: it was not so at the origin. Henry is making a crucial historical-conceptual point: the *cogito* does not appear first in Descartes' meditation; it appears last, as the terminus of a research that was initially guided not by any interest in the ego but by the rational demand for apodicticity. The ego is the unique reality that satisfies this demand. Neither the ego as such, nor knowledge of self, nor any individualism, nor affective or metaphysical solipsism, have initially the favor of Cartesian consciousness. The latter is a rational consciousness that aims at the universal and the apodictic. The ego arises before it only because it is the sole being capable of furnishing to such a consciousness an adequate intuitive fulfillment. It is the content and, in some sense, the real element that must be grasped and ordered to itself by a philosophy essentially oriented toward the idea of an absolute certainty, if it does not want, at least, to remain in the state of a project and a wish.

This reading of Descartes is a reading through Husserl, and specifically through the *Cartesian Meditations* and *First Philosophy*: Husserl's own interpretation of Descartes strips the *ego cogito* of any content of self-love or self-concern and treats it strictly as the terminus of a methodical search for an apodictic starting-point. The *cogito* is chosen not because Descartes was especially interested in the self but because the self is the only reality capable of satisfying the apodictic criterion. This is in fact one of the most important interpretive moves in Husserl's reading of Descartes, and it is often contrasted with a more existentialist reading (of the sort one finds in the early Sartre or in Jaspers) which takes the Cartesian *cogito* as a proto-existential disclosure of selfhood. Henry stands, at this point in the text, with the Husserlian reading — but, as the following sections will show, he will ultimately criticize it for the same reason he criticizes Descartes: for having interpreted the being of the ego as a correlate of an evidential positing rather than as self-manifestation in its radical immanence.

**Paragraph 7\.** The paradox that binds to the singular reality of the ego, the ego it apprehends in an apodictic evidence and which is always its own, the consciousness whose signification is to attain the universal, does not let itself be easily surmounted. Should it not, at least, be made the object of an explicit problematic? Should this not finally bring to light the link that unites at the origin the problem of truth with that of the ego? Henry is now naming what will later be called, in his mature work, the paradox of the first person: the apodictic evidence of the *cogito* is always *my* apodictic evidence, and yet it is supposed to found a universal science. The tension between the *jemeinig* (mine-ness) of the evidence and the universality of its validity is what Descartes and Husserl, according to Henry, never thematized. But classical philosophy has never raised such a link to the state of a problem, and reason tries to escape from the paradox or to forget it: the consciousness of the *cogito* is not individual but true. The originary intuitive given that manifests itself in the apodictic evidence of the *cogito* is only the motive of a rational positing. The latter finds in the originary content of the intuitive field its originary foundation of validity. Evidence is precisely the unity of the rational positing with the given that motivates it.

The technical vocabulary here is again Husserlian — *Vernunftsetzung* (rational positing), *Motivation*, the unity of positing and given — from *Ideen I* §136. Henry reconstructs the Husserlian response to the paradox: the *cogito*\-consciousness is not individual (mine) but true (valid); the apodictic given is not *this* ego (a particular existent) but the structure of the ego as evidentially given, which is eidetically universal and therefore founds a universal science. In the case of the *cogito*, this unity takes a privileged form because of the specific character of the region of being in which intuition draws its content. In virtue of its eidetic structure, the content renders possible a consciousness of apprehension whose experience is accomplished in conformity with the type of apodictic evidence and reveals itself consequently capable of engendering a rational positing in the strong sense, that is, one whose validity can no longer be put into question. Thus is found a first truth which derives from a thoroughly special mode of positing. What is posited is a true being, a real being, in an absolute sense. The *cogito* is thus the first element of a rational science that realizes first of all in itself its project of apodicticity. It is the point of departure, the commencement; with it a truth is found, consciousness can live in certainty. The passage is pure Husserlian doctrine from *First Philosophy*, where the *cogito* is the "first truth" in a rigorous sense because it is the first positing whose validity cannot be retracted.

**Paragraph 8\.** As philosophical truth, the *cogito* is a rational positing in a privileged sense; it realizes precisely the type of positing that reason aims at in so far as it is faithful to itself. The Cartesian-Husserlian *cogito* is the paradigm of the rational positing because it realizes, in a privileged region, the ideal of apodictic certainty. But — Henry now develops — once the rational positing of the *cogito* is accomplished, two ways open before the meditation of the philosopher. He must decide whether he is going to give himself as task the elucidation of the being of the ego considered as a proper end; the research in which he then engages must present an eminent rational interest, because of the specific character of apodicticity presented by the evidences which govern, as possible experiences, the domain of being to which the *ego cogito* belongs. Such a research, pursued under the title of "rational phenomenology of the ego," could however constitute only a particular research. This is the first way: to take the *cogito* as the theme of a regional phenomenology of the ego, treating the ego as one region of being alongside others. The problematic concerning the being of the ego occupies, in truth, only a strictly delimited place in the ensemble of phenomenological researches. The second way is what Henry will develop next: to take the *cogito* as one region alongside others means recognizing that the task of phenomenology is not exhausted by the ego but must be understood architectonically as the universal elucidation of being in all its regions.

It is with respect to these, however, considered as an architectonic ensemble whose *télos* is the systematic elucidation of being through all its structures and in its ultimate eidetic differentiations, that the task of phenomenological philosophy must be understood, if one wants at least to restore to it its proper amplitude. Reason must be understood in an enlarged sense. Its domain could not be correctly thought if one pretends to limit it by relating it in an exclusive manner to a determinate type of evidence, however privileged this might be. Reason is rather a reflection on the ensemble of the positings that find their foundation, and that in a manner that remains to be specified in each case, in the totality of the fundamental types of evidence and in the empire of the corresponding regions. The vocabulary of "architectonic" is a deliberate allusion to Kant (*Critique of Pure Reason*, Doctrine of Method, chapter 3), but as mediated through Husserl: Husserl speaks of a "systematic architectonic" of phenomenology especially in *Formal and Transcendental Logic* §102 and in later manuscripts from the *Crisis*\-period, where philosophy is understood as a systematic building-up of regional ontologies under the guidance of a formal-universal ontology. Henry is locating the ego-problem inside this Husserlian architectonic and showing that it occupies only one (privileged but delimited) place within it.

A rational type of positing is possible in each case and in each domain; it obeys rigorously defined intuitive and rational modalities. The way in which the truth of this type of positing must confirm or infirm itself, and consequently the mode according to which the rationality concerning the corresponding domain of being is realized, are in turn the object of a study that claims itself to apodicticity. Thus the being of the ego seems to lose its exclusive privilege as the effort of philosophical consciousness accomplishes itself in order to measure up to its own task: to realize in all its amplitude a rational vision of being. The paragraph closes on a decisive thought: the widening of phenomenology from the *cogito* to the universal architectonic of regional ontologies means that the privileged place of the ego, which was won by apodicticity, is lost again as soon as one recognizes that apodicticity belongs equally, *mutatis mutandis*, to the evidences that govern each region. The *cogito* loses its privilege precisely through the Husserlian fidelity to rationalism. This sets the stage for §2, which will argue that this loss of privilege is not an accidental side-effect of Husserl's extension of phenomenology but a necessary consequence of the very logic of regional ontology — and that it makes necessary the construction, prior to any particular ego-phenomenology, of a universal phenomenological ontology.

---

## **§ 2\. The necessity of the prior edification of a universal phenomenological ontology**

**Paragraph 1\.** The section opens by announcing a warning: the overcoming of the *ego cogito* toward a problematic that aims to restore all its forms to the power of intuition, and correlatively to exhibit being in the totality of its fundamental structures and of its ultimate regions, must not create illusion. The research that begins with the *ego cogito* remains conditioned, and that in a decisive way, by the theme it has given itself at the origin. The warning is directed, in historical-philosophical terms, against what one might call the "regional-ontological extension" of Husserlian phenomenology from *Ideen I* onward: Husserl does indeed overcome the exclusive privilege of the *cogito* by developing the theory of regional ontologies, but — Henry claims — this overcoming remains secretly conditioned by the Cartesian starting-point. How must this conditioning be understood? Henry continues by conceding one level of overcoming: the theory of intuition has rejected the pretension of extending to all spheres of being the type of evidence that gives the *cogito*. The attempt to subsume under a monotonous category of apprehension, realizing an ideal type of evidence, the totality of the intuitive field that offers itself to human experience, is absurd in the sense that it contradicts the structure of the given such as it appears in this field with its characters each time different and determined. Descartes was the dupe of his prodigious ambition, both when he wanted to reduce the whole of the real to homogeneous essences submitted to the empire of a unique type of evidence (of which the *cogito* furnished the prototype) and when he undertook to link all these essences together by deductive ties, themselves grasped in intuitive modalities in conformity with this type. This is the standard Husserlian critique of Cartesian *mathesis universalis*: Descartes treats all evidence on the model of the *cogito*'s apodicticity and all cognitive linkage on the model of geometrical deduction; but the real field of experience presents multiple types of evidence, each regional in character, and cannot be homogenized in this way. The critique of Cartesian rationalism is here precisely the Husserlian critique from the *Crisis* and from the *Cartesian Meditations*.

But — and this is the decisive step — the concession does not save phenomenology from being conditioned by its origin. In fact, it is the character to which the problematic of the *ego cogito* obeys that assigns indisputable limits to the ulterior procedures of phenomenological research. Insofar as the latter remains submitted to the *télos* of reason, it continues to aim uniquely at the degree of validity and legitimacy of the positings operated by consciousness. It submits to a minute examination their intuitive sub-structures, it scrutinizes the diverse regions of being, it releases the sense of its most general structures and of their eidetic aspects. It is by taking into consideration such a sense that it says how being can and must present itself inside a determinate region, how the diverse types of presentation differ, how the diverse particular presentations are susceptible of calling each other, of confirming or infirming each other, to what genus of evidence being is susceptible of giving rise in the region considered, how finally the positings of consciousness must operate that want to submit themselves to the universal structures of the regions, in order to be each time in conformity with the being they aim at and to suit it. The whole programmatic summary here is, once again, strictly Husserlian: it is the program of regional ontology as developed in *Ideen I* §§9–17 and in *Formal and Transcendental Logic*. But Henry is characterizing it in a deliberately critical tone: this research "continues to aim uniquely at the degree of validity and legitimacy of the positings operated by consciousness." The word "uniquely" (*uniquement*) is heavy with consequence. The phenomenology of reason — even extended to all regions — remains an evaluative science of consciousness's positings, not an ontology of being itself. And this limitation, Henry will argue, is inherited from the Cartesian origin: the problematic begins from consciousness and its positings and never succeeds in releasing itself from them.

**Paragraph 2\.** Assuredly, the accomplishment of these different tasks, in their strict correlation, is still only an Idea, the practical and regulative Idea of an infinite theoretical work of ontological order. But precisely this Idea dominates the ensemble of the research, and in it lives the *télos* of reason. The term "Idea" capitalized here is deliberately Kantian — the regulative Idea of the *Critique of Pure Reason* — but mediated through Husserl: in *Ideen I* §83 and *Cartesian Meditations* §28, Husserl speaks of the "Idea in the Kantian sense" as the regulative limit-concept that governs the infinite task of intentional analysis. The phenomenology of reason is one such infinite task, oriented by the Idea of complete rational fulfillment of all positings. This means, once again, that the project of consciousness is to arrive at stable, valid positings, whose correlate is "real being," "true being." What is finally attained are therefore truths, realities that one can legitimately posit, with their own contents. The theme of thought is constituted by these particular contents of which one wants to be assured. It is a matter each time of arriving at a certainty concerning something; this something, insofar as it is precisely the correlate of such a certainty, is true being, is a particular truth. The *cogito* has remained a truth of this type, a truth aimed at in a rational consciousness in a specific sense.

It is Cartesian rationalism that confers on the *cogito* its philosophical signification. This rationalism seeks to decide in favor of other analogous truths. This is why it consists first of all in a reflection on the conditions which permit to decide in a rational way. The *cogito* serves as prototype, and in a double sense: on the one hand, because the being it exhibits is a true being, a real being, in an exemplary sense; on the other hand, because the mode according to which such a truth is obtained in the *cogito* serves as model for every apprehension that wants to enjoy rational certainty. If the power of apprehension considered in its own structure is put in relation with the rules to which it must submit in order to attain a "real" being and to be each time conformed to the sense that belongs to the latter, it is because the obtaining of rational truths remains the ultimate end to which the reflection on the conditions of this obtainment is subordinated. The *cogito* is only one of the rational truths, but precisely because it has permitted consciousness to attain, at the heart of its singular being, the order of rationality, it remains the ideal of a research that has been realized in it for the first time and to which it imprints or confirms a defined task: the obtaining of contents that can claim the title of "truths." Henry is showing how the *cogito*, even once its exclusive privilege has been lost, functions as a methodological paradigm (a double paradigm: of *what* is to be attained and of *how* it is to be attained). The phenomenology of regions is still Cartesian in method even when it has ceased to be Cartesian in its exclusive focus.

**Paragraph 3\.** Reason is not a faculty of the universal. The opening sentence is a striking anti-Kantian claim. In Kant, reason (*Vernunft*) is precisely the faculty of principles and of the unconditioned, the faculty that aims at totality — and its Ideas (soul, world, God) are precisely Ideas of the universal. For Henry, by contrast, reason so understood — reason as the phenomenology of reason has reconstructed it — is not in fact the faculty of the universal, because it does not achieve the universal. In determining each time the validity of the positings of consciousness that are accomplished inside a frame of evidence whose eidetic structure is defined in its correlation to the original sense of the being of a given region, reason devotes itself to a task that remains oriented toward the discovery of particular truths. The universal, for Henry, is not the sum or the regulative limit of particular truths; it is the essence of being itself. Reason's task, however, is inescapably particular, region-by-region, truth-by-truth. But the more scrupulous is the effort of reflection in the determination of the contents it is susceptible of legitimating, the more rigorous is this determination, the more numerous are the spheres of being that reason, pursuing its apparently infinite task, has submitted to the methodical work that permits it to operate there the positings it can recognize as its own — the more decisive also and the more fatal is the forgetting (*oubli*) in which philosophy moves. The vocabulary of "forgetting" here is Heideggerian: *Seinsvergessenheit*, the forgetfulness of being, from *Sein und Zeit* §§1–6 and especially from the late Heidegger. The paradox Henry is articulating is that of Heidegger's own history of metaphysics: the more successful the scientific and philosophical elucidation of beings becomes, the more radical is the forgetfulness of being itself.

This forgetting concerns nothing less than the universal itself, considered in its proper essence. The task of philosophy is not to accumulate truths. If science legitimately aims to increase our knowledge by building up the systems in which ever-vaster bodies of knowledge are ordered, it does not for all that avoid the error that always leads it here or there, but rather devotes itself to it in principle. Henry is making a strong claim against the scientistic conception of philosophy as the collation of truths: science is necessary in its own domain but is constitutively marked by error (one could say by partial and provisional validity) precisely because it operates within regions of being, without thematizing their foundation. Philosophy is essentially different; it is not the accumulation of truths but the elucidation of the essence of truth itself — of being itself as the universal. The move is both Husserlian (from the *Logos* essay) and Heideggerian (from *On the Essence of Truth* and from *Vom Wesen des Grundes*, the short 1929 text cited in the bibliography under "WG").

**Paragraph 4\.** One assuredly misses the signification of the phenomenology of reason if one pretends to reduce it to preoccupations of an exclusively ontic order. Henry concedes that the phenomenology of reason is not simply a science of beings; it is already oriented toward the ontological, toward the eidetic structures of regions. It happens that the sciences too come to consider for itself the ontological sub-structure on which they constantly lean, although in a manner that most often remains implicit: this occurs in the shaking of a "crisis of foundations." The reference is clearly to the "*Grundlagenkrise*" — the crisis of the foundations of mathematics and physics around 1900, which had been central to Husserl's own reflections in the *Crisis* and, before that, in the *Philosophy of Arithmetic* and the *Prolegomena*; Henry is here recapitulating Husserl's own diagnosis of how the positive sciences are compelled to turn back toward their ontological foundations. Then, to the reason at work in this or that particular science its proper philosophical destination is abruptly recalled; the sense of being summons it and offers itself to it for a thematic elucidation. The signification of the phenomenology of reason remains however limited, because the sense of being on which it pursues its ontological work remains subordinate, and that in a radical way, to the empire of the regions.

The rhetorical climax of the paragraph consists of two parallel questions: how could regional ontology equal the fundamental task of ontology — it which remains blind with regard to its own foundation? How would it pretend to grasp the sense of being inside a determinate sphere as long as the sense of being in general has not been understood as the proper theme of ontology? The question is pure Heidegger from *Sein und Zeit* §3 ("The ontological priority of the question of being"): regional ontologies presuppose an understanding of being in general; they are therefore not self-grounding; a fundamental ontology that thematizes the sense of being in general must precede them and can alone found them. Henry's argument in §§ 1–2 so far has thus traced a precise trajectory: the Cartesian-Husserlian privilege of the *cogito* yields, under critical pressure, to the doctrine of regional ontologies; but regional ontology itself, though an advance over the Cartesian reduction of evidence to a single type, remains blind to its own foundation, namely to the sense of being in general. Hence the necessity — announced in the section title — of the prior edification of a universal phenomenological ontology.

**Paragraph 5\.** The research that gives itself as theme the sense of being in general, universal phenomenological ontology, does not differ only, in its proper aim, from the diverse regional ontologies that found the ontic sciences; it also departs, for the same reason, from formal ontology. Henry is now demarcating his target from a third possible interpretation of "universal ontology," namely the formal ontology that Husserl develops in *Formal and Transcendental Logic* (especially Part I) and already in the *Prolegomena* to the *Logical Investigations*. Formal ontology is the theory of the most general categories of any object-whatsoever (*Gegenstand überhaupt*): unity, plurality, relation, set, number, whole and part, and so on. Henry's claim is that formal ontology does not constitute the universal ontology he is looking for. Formal ontology dominates only in appearance — or, to be more exact, it dominates in a purely formal way the diverse regional ontologies. By reflecting on the essence of the region considered, not as a region properly speaking, but as the empty form of a region in general which, as such, suits all possible material regions, formal ontology is susceptible only of prescribing to the diverse material ontologies a common legislation of pure form. And as, on the other hand, the analytic categories that correspond to it are incapable of submitting to themselves the synthetic categories of the material regions, it appears clearly that formal ontology can conquer only a purely formal precedence over the empire of being and over the multiple concrete determinations in which the latter expresses its infinite richness.

The distinction between analytic and synthetic categories that Henry is using here is itself Husserlian: in *Ideen I* §16, Husserl distinguishes the formal categories (analytic, empty, valid of any object whatsoever) from the material categories (synthetic, filled, valid only within determinate regions). Henry's point is that the analytic categories of formal ontology cannot found the synthetic categories of regional ontologies because the latter have their own eidetic content that is not contained in the mere form of "object-in-general." Such precedence is not even evident, he adds. On the contrary, it is manifestly in the reign of material essences that formal ontology draws its origin, since the pure essence of a region in general is necessarily relative to something like a concrete region. This is a subtle but important point: the very concept of "region-in-general" is an abstraction from concrete regions and therefore cannot claim to dominate them as their ground. This is Husserl's own position (the formal is an idealizing abstraction from the material) pushed to its logical consequence: formal ontology cannot be the fundamental ontology that philosophy seeks.

**Paragraph 6\.** To the radical dependence of formal ontology, universal phenomenological ontology opposes with éclat its autonomy and its primary sufficiency. Henry now states positively what universal phenomenological ontology is, in contrast both to regional ontologies (which are too particular) and to formal ontology (which is too empty). The universal it exhibits — or at least aims at, seeking to draw it out of the obscurity in which it naturally envelops itself — is a concrete term that each region of being presupposes. It is being itself — not an empty category that would formally suit any region, but rather the very essence of this region, if at least it is a region of being. It is the primordial essence, the essence of every region, but also of every object, of everything that is. The individual being, the genus, the species, are submitted to it, not in virtue of a formal or logical regulation that would remain exterior to them, but in their very being. Being governs all things; over them it extends its reign which traverses them. In every object, being is present, as that which precisely permits this object to be present. It is presence itself; it realizes the essence of presence. This passage is almost pure Heidegger — the doctrine of being as what is "nearest" to beings (from *Sein und Zeit* §§1–2 and from *Brief über den Humanismus*) — combined with the Husserlian vocabulary of "presence" and of essence. "L'essence primordiale" is Henry's coinage for what Heidegger would call *Seyn* or *das Seiende als Seiendes*.

To what does presence reduce? Is it anything other than an empty form that we join each time to a material existence, to the reality of an object, a tool, a culture, a person, a value, as when we say: "this is"? What then is this "is" outside of this thing here, of that person there? Does not the essence of presence signify rather the dissolution of every effective presence? The question is now the central aporia of all fundamental ontology: being is presence itself; but presence-in-general is not any particular present thing; so what can it be? The phenomenon looks like it has no phenomenal content; the "is" is not itself a being; so is the phenomenologist's talk of being not simply empty?

**Paragraph 7\.** It is the essence, nevertheless, that announces itself to us in such a dissolution. "In," this signifies that this dissolution is the aspect that the essence offers us of itself. This is a decisive Henrian move. Rather than treating the apparent emptiness of the concept of being as an objection to fundamental ontology, Henry treats it as a positive phenomenological given: the dissolution of every effective being, the evaporation of every determinate existent, is itself a mode of manifestation — it is the way in which the essence of being shows itself. The disappearance of every effective existent (and the affective tonality that accompanies this disappearance) constitutes the phenomenological given on which every thought that wants to realize the essence in itself must lean. The reference to the "affective tonality" (*tonalité affective*) that accompanies this disappearance is a specific allusion to Heidegger's analysis of *Angst* in *Sein und Zeit* §40 and in *Was ist Metaphysik?*: in anxiety, all beings slip away, and in this slipping-away being itself announces itself — what Heidegger calls the self-disclosure of *das Nichts*, and what his French translators (including Corbin, cited in Henry's bibliography under "WG") render with terms like *néant* and *néantisation*. Henry's whole argument in this paragraph is his initial, still very Heideggerian appropriation of the Heideggerian doctrine of being-as-nothing.

To such a thought the essence certainly proposes itself as what is not the being, as what, in truth, is nothing of all that exists. But the essence is not the simple negation of the existent; it is not a pure privation. Or rather, it is precisely because it is this privation that it is the essence itself. To be indigent and to be, for being, is one and the same thing. Being is being only on the foundation of the Nothingness within it. Nothingness is not nothing; it is the effective operation by which being realizes itself. It is a real nothingness which, in its very nihilating (*néantir*), realizes the essence of being, at the same time that it is the origin of the expulsion out of being by which the being \[*l'étant*\] is promoted to the rank of existent. The doctrine here is essentially the doctrine of *Was ist Metaphysik?* of 1929 and of the subsequent Heideggerian texts on Nothing: the Nothing is not a mere negation but an active *Nichtung*, a nihilating that is simultaneously the self-disclosure of being. The French verb *néantir* is the direct calque of Heidegger's *nichten*. Being is being only on the foundation of this nihilating; and the nihilating is simultaneously the origin of the differentiation between being and beings (what Heidegger calls the *ontologische Differenz*), because the nihilating is what "expels" the being (*l'étant*) out of being — that is, what sets it apart from being as a determinate existent over against the open horizon of being itself.

Being presents itself first to the reflection of the philosopher as a relative nothingness, insofar as it is grasped in its relation to the being as what is not the being; this "not-being" which is still only relative, or if one prefers, this transgression of the being (*étant*) by which being is first characterized, is in reality possible only on the foundation of a real nothingness, which constitutes the very essence of being. The theme of universal phenomenological ontology is therefore not anything that can be assimilated by us to a purely formal essence, or even a completely empty one. The passage operates the distinction Heidegger himself draws in *Vom Wesen des Grundes* between the *relative* nothing (non-being as the merely privative complement of being) and the *absolute* or *real* nothing (nothingness as the active self-disclosure of being itself). Henry appropriates this distinction and draws the conclusion: the theme of universal phenomenological ontology is not the empty form that one might fear; it is, rather, the concrete essence itself, the real nihilating through which being manifests itself.

**Paragraph 8\.** Continuing: it is not an abstract term, the fiction of a hollow metaphysics, the concept whose extension equals all that exists only if its comprehension impoverishes itself gradually to a point that would no longer correspond to a nothingness of comprehension. The reference here is to the classical doctrine of extension and comprehension in scholastic logic (as reworked by Port-Royal and by Kant): the universal concept is extensively maximal only at the price of being intensively minimal, so that the most universal concept (being-in-general) has no content at all. Henry is rejecting this formal-logical understanding of universality, which is exactly the objection he anticipated in the previous paragraph and which he now dispatches. In the indigence in which the thought of being is anguished, what finally rises up before it is the absolute essence, in its highest concretion; it is the identity of being and nothingness. The identity of being and nothingness is of course the dialectical starting-point of Hegel's *Science of Logic* ("Sein, reines Sein, ohne alle weitere Bestimmung... dieses reine Sein ist nun die reine Abstraktion... was es in Wahrheit ist, Nichts"), but Henry's appropriation of it is mediated through Heidegger's own reworking of the Hegelian theme in *Was ist Metaphysik?*. The claim is that the phenomenological essence of being is not emptier than beings but more concrete — concrete in a higher, non-regional sense, because it is the essence in which all regional concretions have their possibility.

Universal phenomenological ontology necessarily clashes, in its very development, with the question of knowing whether it is anything other than a play of words and concepts that correspond strictly to nothing. But when such an objection has succeeded in throwing light on itself, it interprets itself as a progress of thought on the path that leads to the essence, to the understanding of the essence in its very essence. For it is the positive essence of being that is unveiled in the apparently unessential character of the essence. That such an essence be positive, in an ultimate sense, manifests itself in the fact that it is the condition. Everything that is finds in it its foundation. Universal phenomenological ontology, which orients itself deliberately toward the task of an understanding of the essence, is indeed fundamental ontology. The closing sentence is a deliberate identification: "l'ontologie phénoménologique universelle" \= "l'ontologie fondamentale" (Heidegger's *Fundamentalontologie* from *Sein und Zeit* §3). Henry is at this point aligning himself with Heidegger's program: universal phenomenological ontology is fundamental ontology, and fundamental ontology is the elucidation of being as the essence that conditions every region of beings. The alignment is genuine at this stage of the argument; it will begin to fracture in §§3–6 and will be openly broken in Sections I–II. But in the Introduction, Henry is still speaking inside Heidegger's program, using it as the vantage from which to criticize both Descartes and Husserl.

---

## **§ 3\. The overcoming of intuitionism and the liberation of the universal phenomenological horizon**

**Paragraph 1\.** The section opens with a programmatic statement: universal phenomenological ontology supposes, as first condition of a taking-consciousness of its task and of its own possibility, a radical overcoming of intuitionism. It is only in such an overcoming that it can raise itself to the problem of the sense of being in general. "In general" no longer designates here a simple inventory nor even a systematic and coordinated elucidation of the different regions and the different senses that being takes on each time inside these regions. The research is situated, in reality, on another plane than that of the plurality of regional ontologies. Henry is marking a sharp distinction: the "universal" of universal phenomenological ontology is not a generality obtained by inductive or enumerative totalization of regional structures. It does not aim to exhaust the different structures that the ultimate essences prescribe each time to being inside the domains they govern. The generality aimed at by universal ontology does not concern "the explicitation of the sense of every type of being that I, the ego, can imagine." The phrase in quotation marks is taken from Husserl's *Cartesian Meditations* §§59–64, where Husserl describes transcendental phenomenology as the explicitation of every type of being imaginable to the transcendental ego. Henry's point is that Husserl himself still understands the universality of phenomenological ontology in an enumerative, ego-correlative way: universality means "every type," as the ranged-over content of an egological imagination. If such an ontology refers to the "authentic and universal sense of being in general" — again a Husserlian phrase — it is nevertheless in a specific way that does not attach it to the universal structures of being nor to their highest generalities. From such generalities it turns away rather, in order to devote itself to the absolutely original generality that constitutes its proper theme and that deliberately exceeds every genus and every generality pertaining to a genus.

This is a decisive methodological break. Henry is distinguishing two senses of "universality" that he holds Husserl has never distinguished: (i) universality as the highest genus or as the completed enumeration of eidetic structures — which is still essentially regional, since it presupposes and totalizes regions; and (ii) universality as the essence of being itself, which is not a genus at all and which cannot be obtained by any totalization of regional structures. The second universality is what fundamental ontology aims at. This is a properly Heideggerian thesis: being is not a genus (cf. Aristotle, *Metaphysics* B.3 998b22, arguing against Plato that being cannot be a genus; Heidegger makes this the opening of the "three prejudices" in *Sein und Zeit* §1). But Henry here is aiming the thesis specifically against the Husserlian program of universal phenomenological ontology as the systematic elucidation of all regions.

**Paragraph 2\.** Now, orientation toward a determinate structure of being and, inside that structure, toward a being that is itself determinate, which one is to render present with its own characters, is on the contrary characteristic of intuitionism as of the phenomenology of reason that prolongs it and that leans upon it. Intuition aims each time at a particular being (*étant*). Even when it strips this immediate ontic signification to direct itself toward the grasp of an eidetic structure that belongs to a genus of being, such a structure is always a determinate structure, in such a way that the ontological orientation of intuition remains fundamentally limited in its very principle. This limitation or, better, this finitude does not result from the orientation taken by the gaze in this or that intuition; it is rather inherent in intuition as such. Intuition is, in principle, a finite thought. No doubt it determines itself freely by the free orientation of its aim, but this determination is itself a necessity that imposes itself on its freedom, and that in an unsurmountable way. This is why the thought of being cannot be accomplished on the mode of an intuitive realization, but only on that of the mystery.

The argument is subtle: intuition, even when freely directed by the consciousness that intuits, is constitutively determinate, because intuition is always intuition *of* some determinate content. Even eidetic intuition, which strips away the ontic particularity of its object, intuits a determinate eidos, a particular essence. The finitude of intuition is not contingent; it is inherent in the structure of intuition as such. Therefore, if the fundamental task of ontology is the thought of being — of being in general, as what is not determinate, as what is rather the condition of every determination — then this task cannot be accomplished by an intuition. The closing phrase, "mais seulement sur celui du mystère" — but only on that of the mystery — is a deliberate theological-Heideggerian echo. "Mystery" (*Geheimnis*) is a term that appears in late Heidegger (e.g., *Über den Humanismus*, *Vom Wesen der Wahrheit*) to designate the self-withdrawal of being at the very moment of its disclosure. Henry's appropriation of the term here announces, already in the Introduction, that the essence of manifestation will not be reached by any intuition of essence, but only by a thought that respects the withdrawal (the *Verborgenheit*, the hiddenness) of being itself.

**Paragraph 3\.** The project of elucidating the different spheres of being in their proper structure remains submitted, in reality, to the *télos* of intuitive realization. It is precisely to determine the conditions that render possible each time this realization, and in a manner that permits the positings of consciousness which lean upon it to satisfy reason, that reason pursues the infinite task of unveiling the different types of being and their immanent sense. The putting-into-light of the regional eidetic structures that govern the objects belonging to the diverse corresponding regions has no other goal than that of saying how these multiple singular objects can and must be rendered present each time in an adequate intuitive consciousness. The systematic elucidation of the regions is still only a means which remains subordinated to the ideal of obtaining determinate being and particular truths. The signification of the phenomenology of reason cannot be qualified without restriction as "ontological," when the ultimate aim of this reason is the possession of singular and finite being. Such possession remains the ideal of reason in the ontological work it pursues to make this ideal possible. Henry is driving home the critique: Husserlian regional phenomenology claims to be ontology but is in fact a higher-order ontic science — a science of the conditions under which determinate beings can be given to an intuitive consciousness. Its telos is not being itself but rather the possession of determinate beings. The "possession" (*possession*) language is deliberate; it echoes Heidegger's critique of the metaphysical subject as the ground of representation and possession of beings (cf. Heidegger's *Die Zeit des Weltbildes*, in the *Holzwege* volume cited in Henry's bibliography under "H").

The *cogito* represents only a particular and determinate being, grasped in apodictic evidence. One cannot, certainly, forget the manner in which such a being gives itself, the certainty of which the latter is the "real" and "true" correlate, but this experience, privileged in the case of the *cogito*, remains a strictly determinate experience. The consciousness that devotes itself to the finitude and to the determination of being-there (*être-là*, a French equivalent of Heidegger's *Dasein*) is itself, for that reason, only a finite consciousness. However particular and however intense the subjective experience to which the consciousness that equals itself to the object in certainty and truth attains, such experience is still only a mode of an essentially finite life. In the enjoyment of finite being or of the finite experience that gives it, consciousness cannot deliver itself from the mode of existence that it must assume if it wants to live the rational life to which the singular certainty and the determinate being equally belong. In such a mode of existence, which remains essentially marked by finitude, it sinks on the contrary further, turning away from what transcends every finitude. The argument collapses Descartes-Husserl and the whole of rational-intuitionist philosophy into a single verdict: they are all forms of finite consciousness bound to determinate beings, and they therefore all miss the essence of being-as-such, which exceeds every finite determination.

Cartesian consciousness, which rationally aims at determinate being and which gives itself the subjective experience of certainty, is not privileged. It has missed the essence and, by that very fact, the true *Stimmung*. The German *Stimmung* — translated variously as "mood," "attunement," "fundamental tone" — is taken directly from Heidegger, especially from *Sein und Zeit* §29 on *Befindlichkeit* and from *Was ist Metaphysik?* on the fundamental mood of anxiety. Henry is saying that Cartesian rational consciousness, in its complacent certainty, has missed the fundamental tonality in which alone the essence of being announces itself; to the thought of being this tonality is rather given as the coming-into-us of our accord with an essence that can only be realized on the mode of intuitive presence by being destroyed. The paradox is stated sharply: the essence of being is such that to realize it on the mode of intuitive presence — that is, to make it present as a determinate given — is already to destroy it, because its essence is precisely what cannot be given as a determinate intuitive content.

**Paragraph 4\.** The understanding of the finitude inherent to intuition demands that the essence of the latter be brought into clarity. By intuition, one can understand: (1) vision in general, every act that presents or *re-presents* (*présentifie*) in a vision, whatever the nature of the latter; in this sense, every consciousness is intuitive. (2) An intuitive consciousness properly speaking, that is, a consciousness whose signifying intentions are, in part at least, fulfilled by a given that corresponds to them exactly and, if possible, in an adequate way. (3) The fulfillment itself of intuition, understood as the arising of a given to which the signifying intentions of consciousness come to adjoin themselves in a rigorous correspondence. Intuition here designates the intuited reality itself, the particular content that exhibits itself in intuition, in its double opposition to the aim of consciousness and to the content that is itself merely aimed at without being yet given in person nor apprehended in an originary manner. Evidence is produced when this fulfillment is accomplished in a satisfactory way, so that the intuitive consciousness finds itself in presence of the thing itself.

Henry here distinguishes three Husserlian senses of "intuition" that are found distributed across the *Logical Investigations*, *Ideen I*, and the later manuscripts: (i) the broad sense in which every presenting act (including *Vergegenwärtigung*, which Henry's French "présentifie" translates) is "intuitive"; (ii) the proper sense of a consciousness whose signifying intentions are fulfilled; and (iii) the narrowest sense, in which "intuition" names the intuited given itself, i.e., the fulfilling content as opposed to both the aiming intention and the as-yet-unfulfilled content. The three cannot be confused, but they are connected by a profound unity that belongs to the teleology of consciousness. In conformity with this immanent teleology, consciousness tends to make itself intuitive consciousness, because the signifying intention that traverses it aims actively at the determinate content that must come to fulfill it. It is therefore fulfillment — or, to be more exact (for consciousness never aims, in immediate life at least, to transform itself; it aims at a content which it seeks to modify, approaching it for example, and it is in this way that it transforms itself, involuntarily so to speak, and in a non-thematic manner), the content that must give this fulfillment the occasion to be produced — which remains the true goal of intentional life. It is precisely for this reason that intuitive thought and, consequently, rational life remain essentially oriented by the determination of being-there (whether this is an empirical or an ideal being). The Husserlian doctrine of the teleology of intentional life toward fulfillment (from the sixth of the *Logical Investigations*, from *Ideen I* §§135–145, and from *Formal and Transcendental Logic*) is here summarized with great precision — precisely so that Henry can now name its limit.

**Paragraph 5\.** Whatever, however, be the legitimacy of the movement of consciousness toward the transcendent being in whose presence it wishes to live, and that in an ever greater proximity, one cannot forget the conditions that render possible the realization of this ideal, that is, the obtaining of the intuited given. Now, the understanding of these conditions obliges us to traverse, so to speak, an inverse path and to raise ourselves from the intuited given to the intuitive consciousness that gives it and, from the latter, to consciousness in general, that is, to the power of vision as such. The intuited given is only an element of the intuitive consciousness. It belongs to it, in principle, to be surrounded by the horizon that the bundle of signifying intentions not yet fulfilled draws around it. That is to say, a consciousness can never be fully realized as intuitive consciousness. The vocabulary of "horizon" (*horizon*) is here crucial and is strictly Husserlian — the doctrine of the horizon (*Horizont*) as the field of unfulfilled co-intentions that surround every fulfilled intuition is developed especially in *Ideen I* §§44, 83, and in *Erfahrung und Urteil* §§8, 21, and in *Cartesian Meditations* §19. Every intuition of a determinate object is surrounded by a horizon of further possible intuitions that could fulfill the signifying intentions that co-aim the object from other sides, in other modes, etc. A consciousness can never be fully realized as intuitive consciousness because at any given moment it is surrounded by horizons of non-intuitive co-intentions.

The elements of consciousness that must be understood under the title of intuitive consciousness are constituted by the signifying intentions that find themselves effectively fulfilled; they leave, outside of themselves, all the other intentionalities of the same type to which corresponds, as correlate, only a given aimed at but not intuited. One could, it is true, conceive the case of a perfect fulfillment, that is, the possibility of a consciousness all of whose signifying intentions would be realized on the intuitive mode. Such a consciousness is, in truth, the ideal of reason; it constitutes the *télos* that determines consciousness at its foundation as an activity, as an active aiming essentially oriented toward the production of a given received in intuition. But is the rationality immanent to intentional life anything other than an ideal? And although this ideal is precisely what confers on every research the movement by which it surpasses itself ceaselessly and engages in the path of an indefinite progress, is it not, however, in many respects, and despite its practical fecundity, a dangerous ideal? Is it not in this ideal that originary forgetting is engendered, the forgetting of the origin and of the foundation? The problem is to know whether the horizon that belongs to every intuitive consciousness, insofar as it is also and always a non-intuitive consciousness, is a contingent element of the structure of consciousness in general, or whether it belongs to it, on the contrary, in principle.

This is the real hinge of the paragraph. Henry is seizing on a structural feature of Husserlian intentionality — the horizon of unfulfilled co-intentions — and asking whether Husserl has understood its true ontological import. The horizon is not just a practical remainder, the "not-yet-fulfilled" that will in principle be fulfilled someday; if it belonged only contingently to consciousness, then the ideal of perfect fulfillment (total intuition) would make sense as a regulative limit. But if the horizon belongs to consciousness *in principle*, then the horizon is not a deficit of intuition but a positive ontological structure — and the ideal of total intuition is a deceptive, even "dangerous" ideal. The question of this paragraph prepares the argument of the next.

**Paragraph 6\.** The thematic consideration of the horizon in which every intuitive presence bathes is certainly not excluded from the phenomenology of reason. It however shows itself incapable of grasping the true signification that such a "horizon" must receive; it moves rather in the forgetting of this signification, unless it effects a true falsification of it. And this for three reasons. What follows are three numbered points, and they constitute Henry's systematic critique of the Husserlian horizon-doctrine.
