(1) The interest carried to the horizon that surrounds every effective presence finds itself constantly subordinated, in an intuitionist perspective, to the consideration of the determinate content of transcendent effectivity. The analysis of the horizon is only made in order to show how what is aimed at in such a horizon must be susceptible of transforming itself into the corresponding intuitive given, how and in what condition such a transformation can and must each time operate. The content of the horizon has substituted itself as theme of the reflection for the very form of this horizon, that is, for its essence. The pretended taking-into-consideration of the horizon metamorphoses itself surreptitiously into the simple comparison of two specific modes of givenness submitted to elucidation under the title of "originary given" and "merely aimed at," and into the establishment, in conformity with the *télos* of intuitionism, of a priority of the first over the second. The critique is acute: Husserl's horizon-doctrine does not really thematize the horizon as such; it uses the doctrine of the horizon as an auxiliary device to describe how the content *within* the horizon (the not-yet-fulfilled) is supposed to convert itself into the content *at the center* of the horizon (the fulfilled given). The analysis remains content-analysis, not form-analysis; the essence of the horizon as such is missed.

(2) The analysis of the mode according to which the originary given must substitute itself for the simple correlate of the signifying intention implies however a reflection on the structure of the horizon that surrounds in each sphere of being an intuitive presence of that being. To each region, indeed, belongs, in principle, a type of horizon absolutely proper, provided with a determinate eidetic structure. It is in conformity with this eidetic structure of the horizon that the fulfillment of the intentionalities that have not yet given their correlate on the originary mode must each time be operated. The horizon prefigures the path that the intentionality of consciousness must follow if it wants to convert in its intuitive realization what is as yet only aimed at in a void (*vide*) manner. The modification of the given that interests consciousness is therefore accomplished in conformity with a direction prescribed by the structure of the horizon that puts in relation the "merely aimed at" with the "originary," which corresponds to it in a rigorous way in the case of adequate intuition. The thematic elucidation of the *eidos* of each type of horizon therefore constitutes a task for the phenomenology of reason. What is taken into consideration by the latter, however, is never, and in each case, anything but a determinate eidetic structure, the structure of a horizon or of a particular type of horizon. It is therefore particular structures — structures that are themselves put in relation with the singular beings whose intuitive appearance they govern — that such a problematic gives itself, under the form of determinate eidetic contents. What it misses is nothing less than the essence of the horizon as such.

The second point complements the first. Husserl does have a doctrine of different types of horizons corresponding to different regions (the horizon of spatial perception, the horizon of temporal experience, the horizon of intersubjective co-constitution, etc.); this is well developed in *Erfahrung und Urteil*, the *Cartesian Meditations*, and the *Krisis* (all in Henry's bibliography). But each of these horizons is a determinate, regional, eidetic structure. The essence of horizon-in-general — the horizonality of the horizon, one might say — remains unthematized.

(3) Intuitionism is incapable, in reality, of thinking the essence of the horizon. For it seeks to give itself such an essence on the mode of intuitive realization. It thinks to attain it in eidetic intuition. At the very moment, however, when the horizon thus becomes the theme of intuitive thought, it is before an eidetic singularity that the latter finds itself in fact placed. And how can the arising of this singularity before the gaze of the intuitive consciousness be produced, if not inside a horizon of opening that deploys the milieu where it is given to the singular *eidos* to manifest itself as a presence? The horizon is precisely what escapes thought at the very moment when it wants to intuit its essence. This pretended essence is still only the *this* of the singular presence that bathes in the essential milieu of being, in such a manner, however, that it conceals it. Because the horizon is what transcends every determination, the forgetting in which intuitive thought holds itself with regard to it is not due to chance. The essence of the horizon is missed in principle by intuition, and that in such a manner that it is precisely at the moment when the latter takes it as the explicit theme of its thought that it finds itself most far removed from it.

The third point is the decisive one and the most properly Henrian. It operates by a kind of transcendental argument: if one tries to intuit the essence of horizon, then what one intuits is a determinate essence, and this determinate essence can itself be given only *within* a further horizon (because every intuition requires a horizon of opening in which the intuited can appear). So the attempt to intuit the essence of horizon presupposes the very structure (horizonality) that it tried to thematize, and hence the attempt fails in principle. This is the exact structure of Kant's transcendental argument against the claim that the categories themselves can be intuited, adapted by Henry to the Husserlian horizon-doctrine. The forgetting of the essence of horizon is therefore not a contingent lapse of Husserlian phenomenology but a principled impossibility for any intuitionism.

**Paragraph 7\.** To such a difficulty universal phenomenological ontology, which understands as its fundamental task the elucidation of the horizon thought by it as the absolute essence, does not assuredly escape. The candid acknowledgment is important: Henry's own ontology cannot claim to intuit the essence of the horizon; it too encounters the same transcendental limit. It suffices for it, however, to be conscious of the radical obscurity that belongs, in principle, to the essence, not in order to surmount it, it is true, but in order to live it as such in the mystery. But the phenomenology of reason, which searches everywhere and which finds presences whose intuitive realization it wants to assure, could not escape a contradiction that it does not perceive, nor, *a fortiori*, think this contradiction as a positive character of the essence. Henry's universal phenomenological ontology therefore distinguishes itself from Husserlian phenomenology precisely by taking the obscurity of the essence as a positive determination — as the "mystery" — rather than as a defect to be progressively overcome by further intuitive work. Analysis of confused consciousness constitutes, for the thought that does not want to miss the essence, a more sure guiding thread than the systematic examination of the different types of consciousness that each time attain in evidence a strictly determinate content. To the non-intuitive consciousness, for which no rigorously circumscribed given has yet emerged from the indetermination and the obscurity of the horizon in which it bathes, the apperception of this horizon is not masked. The intuitive richness of a singular presence cannot yet divert the attention of a reflection on the horizon that renders possible every presence as such.

The move is methodologically significant: rather than beginning, like Husserl, from the fulfilled intuition and building outward, Henry proposes beginning from the confused, non-intuitive consciousness — the consciousness before fulfillment, still immersed in the horizon as such. Husserl himself, in *Erfahrung und Urteil* §8, gives an analysis of "pre-predicative" passive syntheses and of the "predonated" horizon; Henry's strategy here resembles Husserl's in letter but not in spirit, because Husserl still treats the pre-predicative as the genetic precondition of the predicative, whereas Henry takes it as the privileged site for disclosing the essence of horizonality itself. The task remains assuredly that of grasping this horizon not as a simple psychological horizon, always confused with the contents that fill it or with the marginal objects of consciousness (the characters that psychology attributes to such a horizon — obscurity, indetermination, etc. — are still, precisely, only the psychological characters of these contents), but as the transcendental condition of an object in general, as the pure form of objectivity that prefigures and precedes, by rendering it possible, every object as such.

The distinction here is Kantian-Husserlian: the horizon is not a psychological fact (a mere fuzziness or marginality of consciousness) but a transcendental condition — the condition of possibility of objectivity as such. The "pure form of objectivity" (*forme pure de l'objectivité*) is a calque of the Husserlian *reine Form der Gegenständlichkeit*.

**Paragraph 8\.** What permits every being to manifest itself, to become "phenomenon," is the milieu of visibility in which it can arise as effective presence. The key vocabulary — *milieu de visibilité* — is a French calque of a Heideggerian theme: the "lichtung," the clearing (developed in *Sein und Zeit* §28 and especially in the late essay *Das Ende der Philosophie und die Aufgabe des Denkens*). The deployment of such a milieu, as transcendental horizon of every being in general, is the work of being itself. The taking-into-consideration of this transcendental horizon, or, as we can say, of the universal phenomenological horizon, is not different from the thought of being. The task of understanding such a horizon is that of universal phenomenological ontology, which dominates, as condition, every particular ontology and every ontic science.

Every truth that concerns a determinate being is in effect relative to the manifest state of the latter, to its presence. Every predicative truth susceptible of being formulated supposes first of all the manifestation of the being it aims at, that is, a truth of ontic order. Now such a manifestation is never the simple correlate of a representation or of an intuition; it is produced always, in reality, inside a milieu already open that renders it possible. The opening of this milieu is the *apérité* of being. The word *apérité* is Henry's Gallicization of Heidegger's *Offenheit* (openness) or *Erschlossenheit* (disclosedness), from *Sein und Zeit* §44 on truth. The argumentative sequence that follows is a direct transposition of Heidegger's doctrine in that section: it is only because being is unveiled that the being can manifest itself. Every predicative truth refers to an ontic truth, and the latter, in turn, to the ontological truth. To put into light the necessary and sufficient space for every being to be able to become what it is, is to institute a fundamental problematic with regard to which every determinate research must recognize its necessary subordination. The closing sentence gives the formula of the whole section: universal phenomenological ontology \= elucidation of the phenomenological horizon \= thought of being \= ontological truth as the condition of all ontic and predicative truth.

The doctrine thus established is the doctrine of Heidegger's *Sein und Zeit* §44 almost verbatim, and Henry has arrived at it by following a genealogical path: Descartes-Husserl-Heidegger. §1 gave us the apodictic privilege of the *cogito*; §2 showed the necessity of moving from the regional to the universal; §3 has now shown that the universal cannot be reached by intuition but only by the thought of being as the horizon of every manifestation. The next section (§4) will reinsert the *cogito* into this horizon — and will prepare the crisis that §§5–6 will develop.

---

## **§ 4\. The insertion of the *ego cogito* and of its problematic inside the horizon liberated by universal phenomenological ontology**

**Paragraph 1\.** It is not easy for ontology to preserve the purity of its initial project. The thought of being is difficult. The opening is programmatic and quasi-confessional. Henry is diagnosing a structural weakness of the ontological project as such: even once the project of a universal phenomenological ontology (the thought of being in its opening of the horizon) has been correctly formulated in §§1–3, it is constantly threatened by a "fall" toward determinate beings. We are so profoundly attached to the things of the earth, to the singular contents of our experience, that it does not seem to us that we have elsewhere a proper abode that is reserved for us. Such an abode, it is true, is obtained only by renunciation; in it reigns absolute denudement, the source of our fright. The vocabulary — *séjour* (abode, sojourn), *dénuement* (denudement, nakedness), *effroi* (fright) — is a precise calque of Heideggerian vocabulary, especially from *Sein und Zeit* §§39–40 on anxiety, where Dasein confronts its own groundlessness and is "brought before nothing"; and from the later Heidegger of *Bauen Wohnen Denken* and the *Brief über den Humanismus*, where the "abode" of thinking is being itself.

We cannot rid ourselves of our singular habits, nor of the values that make up the substance of our life. We devote ourselves to the determination that preserves us. From its origin, philosophy succumbs to the temptation of the being (*l'étant*). The hard project that moves ontology in the radical procedure by which it orients itself first toward the origin of everything, toward being, the absolute master, quickly falls into forgetting. To the originary research which, deliberately abandoning the consideration of the being, takes as guiding thread the examination of the categories of being, and which, in its perilous march, advances toward the supreme category, succeeds, as though by the effect of a fatal fall, a movement of attention that turns back on determinate being or, possibly, on a super-being (*super-étant*), thus departing from its first design.

Henry is describing the fall from ontology to onto-theology — the replacement of the question of being in general by the question of the highest being. This is exactly the Heideggerian diagnosis of the history of metaphysics as "onto-theo-logy" (to use the term Heidegger will deploy most explicitly in *Identität und Differenz*, 1957): metaphysics poses the question of being in general, but it always "responds" to this question by positing a highest being (God, the subject, absolute spirit) that is supposed to ground all other beings. The fall from ontology to theology is structural, not accidental.

To the properly ontological analysis which aims, beyond its regional ramifications, at the structure of being considered in its purity, one sees substituted almost inevitably considerations of an ontic order. Philosophy has most often been, as Heidegger says, only a mixture of first philosophy and discussions of God or of the immortality of the soul, which are in fact foreign to its proper domain. The footnote refers to Heidegger directly; this is the classical Heideggerian reading of Aristotle's *Metaphysics* Λ as a slippage from the *prôtê philosophia* of Book Γ into a theology of the first unmoved mover. Saint Thomas Aquinas only pursues the error inaugurated at its apogee by Hellenic philosophy when, in the *scientia divina*, he makes the idea of God intervene paradoxically in the study of the transcendentals. Such a confusion asserts itself with an éclat still greater in Descartes' *Meditations*, where the consideration of the divine occupies, to the detriment of the problem of being, a dominant place. Henry is tracing the lineage: Aristotle (the oscillation between *on hê on* and the *theion*) → Aquinas (the *scientia divina* as science of both being and the transcendentals) → Descartes (the *Meditations*, where the proof of God's existence occupies the center, as condition of all other certainties beyond the *cogito*). The onto-theological fall is continuous.

**Paragraph 2\.** It is true that there is produced in Descartes an oscillation of thought, already visible in Saint Thomas. A competition is instituted between the beings that unduly claim the role of principle. The *ego cogito* obtains in the problematic a precedence whose signification is not only chronological. But the subordination of ontology to egology, implicit or not, in modern philosophy, is no more justified than the ancient primacy of theology. Whether it be envisaged under the title of "subject" or "spirit," "person" or "reason," the *cogito* which undergoes these non-essential transformations remains an existent that one cannot, as such, confound with a foundation of ontological order. This is a crucial passage. Henry is now stating that *modern* philosophy replaces the ancient onto-theological privilege of God with an egological privilege of the ego, and that this substitution — though it appears to be a secularizing break — is structurally identical to what it replaces: the fall from being to a determinate being, from the universal to the singular, from the condition to the conditioned. The subject / spirit / person / reason of modern philosophy is the new super-being, a new stand-in for the ancient God. The diagnosis is again Heideggerian (Heidegger develops it extensively in the 1930s–1940s, in *Die Zeit des Weltbildes* and in *Europäischer Nihilismus*), but Henry gives it a sharper edge by insisting that "ego-ology" is the modern form of onto-theology.

In fact, it is the ontological signification of philosophy that is lost, it is the very possibility of the positing of the problem of being that finds itself put in question. And this in a manner all the more dangerous as the taking-into-consideration of such a problem remains apparently present at the heart of philosophy. Only, the response to it is demanded, in an absurd way, of a determinate existent. Thus one sees the authentic signification of Greek ontology be completely falsified by Hegel, who pretends to reduce such an ontology to a moment in the evolution of consciousness. This is a precise reference to Hegel's *Science of Logic* Book I ("Doctrine of Being"), where Hegel takes up Eleatic and Parmenidean ontology as "the abstract beginning" and reduces it to a stage in the self-development of the concept. For Henry, this reduction of ontology to egology (ultimately, to the subjective-absolute self-knowing of Spirit) is the clearest modern example of the replacement of the ontological by the egological. For idealism, man is first of all a man; the ontological project by which he sketches, in an anticipatory understanding, the being of all things, remains indissolubly attached, as to its foundation, to the preliminary reality of a singular existence. This is Heidegger's critique of Hegelian absolute idealism in the *Wegmarken*\-essays of the 1930s.

**Paragraph 3\.** This — the singular existence of the human — takes on, under the title of consciousness, a double aspect: it designates, on the one hand, the power that deploys the horizon, the very work of the transcendence that originarily constitutes, in the form of such a horizon, the pure fabric of every possible objectivity; on the other hand, it is the singular existent in which this transcendence is rooted. The double aspect of consciousness so identified is the key site of what Henry will call the *equivocation of the Dasein*: consciousness is at once (i) the transcendental opening of the horizon (the transcendence that deploys the milieu of being) and (ii) a singular existent (a man, a psychological subject, a Dasein). These two senses are held together in modern philosophy without being distinguished, and this non-distinction is the source of all the difficulties Henry is about to describe.

Such a transcendence is then nothing other than a particular character of consciousness, the singular property in conformity with which this existent designated under the title of consciousness has received the power to direct itself toward objects and to have access to them. This power to accede to things adds itself to the preliminary existence of the *cogito* as a very remarkable but secondary determination. The ontological or pre-ontological understanding of being is denatured when it becomes the attribute of an ontic determination. Transcendence is not safeguarded in its proper signification if one assimilates it to a character of consciousness. It serves no purpose to say that it is a fundamental, essential character, that consciousness is "wholly" this "movement-toward," this sketch of the world, that such a project is not a predicate that would be added synthetically to the preliminary existence of a subjectivity, that it is transcendence, finally, that makes the very substance, the subjectivity of the subject: as long as the being of the subject has not been elucidated, one does not escape the paradox that makes the condition rest on the conditioned. For whence can the subject hold its substantiality — even if this substantiality is nothing other than the pure act of transcending — if not from being itself? This passage is aimed, with striking precision, at both Husserl and the early Heidegger. The formulations "the subject is *wholly* this movement-toward," "transcendence is not a synthetic predicate added to a prior subjectivity but is the very substance, the subjectivity of the subject" — these are the formulations of Heidegger's *Sein und Zeit* §9 on the *jemeinig*\-structure of Dasein, and of §12 on *In-der-Welt-sein*: Dasein is its transcendence; its being is to be-in-the-world; transcendence is not an added-on relation to the world but the very constitution of Dasein as such. Henry is conceding all of this — and then asking: even granted that transcendence is the very substance of the subject, from where does the subject draw this substantiality, if not from being itself? The question is, in effect: the subject is transcendence, yes — but the subject is also *this* subject, this finite, singular existent who transcends. What accounts for the subject's being-this-subject? The answer cannot be transcendence itself, because transcendence is what the subject *does*, not what makes the subject possible as a doer. The answer must come from being itself, which grounds the subject in a way that is not the subject's transcendence.

**Paragraph 4\.** Transcendence cannot be inserted into a singular existence — it, the bursting-forth (*éclatement*), the pure shaking (*ébranlement*) which breaks and which destroys, in founding them, every existence and every singularity, which is nothingness, the internal work of being, the movement that dissolves every effectivity and that makes it be in this very dissolution. The vocabulary *éclatement*, *ébranlement*, *néant*, *dissolution* is thoroughly Heideggerian, drawn especially from the *Was ist Metaphysik?* of 1929 in Corbin's French translation (cited by Henry under "WG"), and from Heidegger's analysis of anxiety and the "slipping away" of beings in that text. Transcendence, for the early Heidegger, is the bursting-open of the horizon in which beings can appear; but in this very bursting-open, all beings "are dissolved," because they are held, not as things-in-themselves, but as appearances within the horizon opened by transcendence. Henry's point is that this bursting-open (*éclatement*) cannot itself be inserted into a singular existent, because the singular existent is itself one of the beings that is only made possible by the bursting-open.

The nothingness that digs out the opening (what we have called the horizon) where something and everything can emerge into being could not, without absurdity, be enclosed in the limits of this something. It is by negating the existent in the originary and fundamental surpassing (*dépassement*) that is in it the work of nothingness, that being lends, under the form of a horizon of presence, aid and assistance to this existent that wants to be and that demands, hard as it may be, the favor of a protection. Of this protection the "subject" has need as well; it must demand it humbly. Equally well there is not a subject, a single reason, but rather spirits who wait with patience for the work of being, the infinite work of the negative, to accomplish itself. The reference to the "infinite work of the negative" (*le travail infini du négatif*) is a deliberate Hegelian echo — it evokes the famous formulation of the *Phenomenology of Spirit* Preface ("die Kraft des Negativen"). Henry is taking the Hegelian figure of the labor of the negative and situating it at the level of being-itself, not at the level of the self-developing subject. Permission is given to spirits only, leaning on this work that is not theirs and of which they gather the fruit as a blessing, to think things and, if they wish, to hear the strange call that rises from them and that is the call of the origin. Being is an impersonal event. The human existent cannot claim it as its own. Its blasphemy is an absurdity. The subject, spirit, person, subjectivity cannot deploy their existence, however particular or however privileged its structure, except on the ground of being in them. The formulations "being is an impersonal event" and "the call of the origin" place Henry in the lineage of the late Heidegger of *Ereignis* and *der Ruf* (*Der Satz vom Grund*, *Beiträge zur Philosophie*). Being is not the subject's; the subject is being's — and only because being first gives itself to the subject, can the subject be a subject at all.

**Paragraph 5\.** One sinks into contradiction — and at the same time places the problematic in insurmountable confusion — if, while pretending to safeguard the essence in its intimate nature, one nevertheless wishes to insert it into human subjectivity and, in fact, to identify it with the latter. The transposition of the central themes of the ontology of being inside a philosophy of the *cogito* can only in reality end in a deformation. This deformation, so grave that it deserves to be called by us a falsification and a denaturation, has a double consequence. Henry is now in full critical mode: any attempt to combine the ontology of being with a philosophy of the *cogito* (or of the subject) will *distort* (in fact, *falsify*) either the ontology or the philosophy of the subject, because the two are structurally incompatible. The critique is aimed at the Husserl of the *Cartesian Meditations* (who claims to ground universal ontology in the transcendental ego) *and* at the early Heidegger of *Sein und Zeit* (who claims to ground the question of being in the analytic of Dasein).

On one hand, the nothingness which one makes bear the condition of the "subject" deposits, in reality, its nature as essence in order to become a simple subjective operation. The transcendental signification that one tries to maintain in it seems at times to be only an ultimate attempt to escape from psychologism. But how could transcendence avoid indefinitely the confusion with a psychological act, since it appears, in fact, as the property of a determinate being? In any case, one does not avoid the contradiction there is in assigning to the essence whose nihilating deploys the horizon of being, the condition of a particular reality submitted to that horizon. Being which cannot be thought except in the surpassing of the singular existent could not, except paradoxically, take on the nature of such an existent. This is the first horn of the deformation: if the transcendental nothingness of being is installed inside subjectivity, it becomes an operation of the subject — it becomes just another psychological act, and the whole Husserlian anti-psychologism of the *Prolegomena* is undone.

How, on the other hand, could the singular existent, even the human subject, be assimilated with the essence that deploys the horizon and that opens the milieu of being? It is rather inside such a milieu that we, and all things, can manifest ourselves, as "phenomena," in the light of the world. It is because the transcendence that makes the world be radically surpasses us, us humans, in the same way as things, that we can think ourselves as we think things, and grasp ourselves in our relation with them. It is permitted to us only, for our part, to benefit from the work of being and, leaning on the internal operation of transcendence, to accede to things of which it has made for us "phenomena." This is the second horn: if the human subject is assimilated to the essence that opens the horizon, then the human subject is no longer a being in the world; he becomes coextensive with the world itself — which is absurd, because human beings are one class of beings *among others* that appear within the world. The correct position, Henry says, is that we, like things, appear within the world; we are not the condition of the world's appearance but ones who appear in the world.

**Paragraph 6\.** Subjectivity is therefore not the absolute condition, and just as the essence is not safeguarded but undergoes on the contrary a profound alteration when it is thought under the title of a particular determination, one does not respect either the nature of this subjectivity when one pretends to make it play a role to which it cannot measure up. Subjectivity is not the essence; it is a particular life and, as such, profoundly real. The unjustified identification with the essence can only *derealize* such a life or, rather, destroy it. The argument now turns in the other direction. The deformation has a double consequence: (i) the essence is denatured by being inserted into the subject; and (ii) the subject — the real, lived, finite subjectivity — is denatured by being inflated into the condition of all being. Both sides of the transposition lose their proper character.

The discussions relative to spiritual "substantialism" only illustrate the contradiction into which idealism inevitably sinks. Insofar as it holds subjectivity to be an ontological foundation, it makes subjectivity lay down for a time its reality as existent; and if the enterprise reveals itself impossible, it seeks at least to minimize this reality. Subjectivity will therefore not be a substance but only an act — not an act properly speaking, a particular and determinate act, but rather an activity in general, a virtual activity, the pure and by itself empty possibility of accomplishing acts of thought. Insofar as these acts are "real," they belong only to an "empirical subjectivity" that must not be confused with "transcendental subjectivity." Only the latter can claim the role of foundation. Henry is describing, with considerable precision, the Husserlian-Fichtean-Kantian solution: to distinguish empirical subjectivity (which is indeed a particular being in the world) from transcendental subjectivity (which is the condition of possibility of all experience). This distinction is meant to solve the problem by saying that the transcendental subject is not a being-in-the-world but the condition of the world. But Henry denies that this distinction solves the problem — it only displaces it.

Already idealism presages that the ontological signification of such a foundation implies the stripping-away of singular existence, the abandonment of every effective reality. Thus one sees the subjectivity of idealism leave aside all real content in order to be no more than a "pure form," the "empty" form of a thought in general. In order to measure up to the ontological role one claims to have it play, subjectivity deposits every concrete character; it lets all its substance flow out of it and goes to lose itself in the clouds. Subjective thinkers have rightly denounced the dissolution of the interior life in the foggy existence of the "constituting subject." The reference to "subjective thinkers" is to the Kierkegaardian tradition (cited in Henry's bibliography under "D," the *Traité du Désespoir* \= *Sickness unto Death*): Kierkegaard's critique of the Hegelian "System" for having substituted the abstract "I think" for the concrete, existing, anxious individual. For Kierkegaard, the existing subject cannot be absorbed into the abstract universal without being destroyed *qua* existing. Henry is invoking this critique — and turning it against modern transcendental subjectivity in general, Husserlian as well as Hegelian. Such an existence, which precisely no longer is one, is the logical outcome of a thought that obeys this contradictory desire: to identify with a singular reality the condition of every possible reality in general.

**Paragraph 7\.** One cannot, indeed, indefinitely confuse the ontological foundation thought by us under the title of "being" with a singular existent. Every philosophy that pursues this chimerical and contradictory ideal finds itself sooner or later placed before the following dilemma: either to abandon the question of being, and to lose itself then in the consideration of ontic determinations, abstracting from what must play with regard to them the role of a condition of possibility — that is, to renounce finally the philosophical problem of the foundation; or, while remaining subject to the ontological preoccupation that aims at such a foundation capable of opening the horizon inside which existents can manifest themselves for us as phenomena, to subtract at least one unduly privileged existent from this preliminary and ultimate condition. The dilemma is sharply stated: either give up fundamental ontology and descend into the positive sciences of beings, or maintain fundamental ontology but privilege *one* existent (the ego, the subject, Dasein) by exempting it from the condition that applies to all other beings. The latter option is the shape of every modern transcendental philosophy.

But, in this latter case, the contradiction only displaces itself; for either such an existent will effectively strip away its condition of existent, or it will be incapable of in fact holding the role one pretends to have it play. What conceals, at least for an instant, such a contradiction, is that one maintains at the same time the two incompatible terms of the alternative: the existent envisaged in its effective and singular existence, and, on the other hand, the foundation itself, which cannot be correctly thought except in its transgression with regard to every existent. One strives then to attenuate this contradiction by stripping the existent of its nature as existent. One advances as far as one can on this path: after the foggy and "impersonal" subjectivity of idealism, one affirms the identity of subjectivity and nothingness. Absurd affirmation — for if being is nothingness, it is precisely because, in extending its reign over it, it pushes outside of itself every determination, and subjectivity in particular. Subjectivity is thought, whether it be a matter of nineteenth- or twentieth-century idealism, under the title of "transcendental field." One can declare this field "impersonal." But at the moment when one encloses it within the limits of a singular existence, one engages in an analysis that is no longer one.

The reference to the "identity of subjectivity and nothingness" in twentieth-century idealism is clearly to Sartre's *L'Être et le Néant* (cited in the bibliography as "EN"), where consciousness (for-itself) is identified with nothingness. The reference to the "transcendental field" is to Sartre's early essay *La Transcendance de l'ego* (1937), which proposes precisely an "impersonal transcendental field" in place of the Husserlian transcendental ego. Henry's critique: to call this field "impersonal" is already to concede that it is not a subject, because subjectivity is always singular and mine; but if it is not a subject, then the whole project of grounding being in it is still incoherent. The closing sentence — "an analysis that is no longer one" — indicates that the Sartrian attempt to hold together subjectivity and nothingness collapses into incoherence.

The section thus ends in a diagnostic deadlock: the philosophical tradition from Descartes through Hegel, through Husserl, to Sartre has persisted in trying to "insert" the *ego cogito* into the horizon liberated by universal phenomenological ontology, and every form of this insertion has produced the same falsification. The next section (§5) will now formulate directly the problem that this diagnostic has brought to light: what is the "being" (*être*) of the absolute ego?

---

## **§ 5\. The problem of the insertion of the *ego cogito* inside the universal phenomenological horizon: the "being" of the absolute ego**

**Paragraph 1\.** The insertion of the *ego cogito* and of its problematic inside the horizon liberated by universal phenomenological ontology, however, clashes with an objection if the existence of this ego draws its originality elsewhere than in the ontological structure that a determinate region of being prescribes to it *a priori*. This is the hinge sentence of the section and of the whole Introduction. Henry has shown in §4 that the *cogito*, as one existent among others, cannot be inserted into the horizon that it itself is supposed to condition. But now he asks: what if the ego is not an existent-among-others at all, not a being belonging to a determinate region, but precisely the absolute that opens the region-of-regions? The objection Henry is going to examine is the Husserlian-transcendental objection: the ego is not a being-in-a-region, because it is not a being at all in the ordinary sense — it is the transcendental ego, the constituting subject that is the condition of all regions. For this question remains open: can consciousness be assimilated by us, in a correct way, to a region of being? Is it not rather being itself, absolute being, the proto-category of being in general, the *Urregion* in which all other regions find their foundation? The term *Urregion* is borrowed directly from Husserl's *Ideen I* §76, where consciousness is described as the *Urregion* (primordial region) in which all other regions are constituted.

In close connection with such a question, the following possibility then opens before us: the analysis of the *cogito* constitutes by itself an ontological analysis, and that in a decisive and universal sense. It is not at all a particular ontological analysis, the analysis of a determinate ontological structure which, as a region, dominates and rules a determinate category of objects. Certainly, as has been shown, every regional ontology is necessarily subordinated to universal ontology. The elucidation of the sense of being inside a particular domain of objects implies the prior elucidation of the sense of being in general. But the sense of being of the *ego cogito* is not at all a regional sense, if it is true that it is in and through this ego that all possible types of being in general are constituted and, correlatively, all the types of sense immanent in them each time.

The lived experiences of consciousness in which the *cogito* understood in its broadest sense is concretely realized are not, indeed, so many determinate beings enclosed inside a determinate region like dead things or like contents susceptible of being distributed in more or less complex groups or classes. Such lived experiences are, in fact, intentional; they are in all cases "consciousness of"; they aim at an object, precisely the one toward which they transcend themselves, and that in such a way that it is precisely such an act of transcendence that each time confers on the being aimed at a proper sense. Consciousness is constitutive of the sense of being in general; it is consciousness that prescribes to every object and every type of object the sense of being that is its own. The sense of being of the *ego cogito* is precisely to confer a sense on being; it is, more profoundly, to be the source of this sense, the absolute origin whence this sense springs up each time as a free creation.

This is a compressed but precise statement of the Husserlian doctrine of transcendental constitution, as developed especially in *Ideen I* §§35–55 and §§76ff., and in the *Cartesian Meditations* §§30–41. The *cogito* is not a region but the condition of all regions; the *cogitationes* are not dead contents but intentional vectors aimed at their noematic objects; each object-type has the sense it has because consciousness constitutes it with that sense. The final formulation — that the being of the ego is to be the origin of the sense of being — is a precise paraphrase of Husserl's own most mature formulations (e.g., in the late manuscripts of the *Crisis*\-period): the transcendental ego is the *Ursprung* of all sense, the free creativity that constitutes the world.

**Paragraph 2\.** It is only when it is situated in a transcendental frame that the reality of consciousness can be correctly thought. Such a "reality" does not resolve itself into a sum of data whose proper structures a noetic or functional phenomenology could describe exhaustively. Above such a phenomenology, conferring on it its sense and assigning it its limits, is situated a discipline of a higher order, the transcendental phenomenology of absolute consciousness, which consists in the ordered and systematic ensemble of researches aiming to elucidate how this consciousness confers each time, and that in its very life, a specific sense on the being it constitutes in the act by which it transcends itself toward it. Henry is distinguishing a "noetic or functional phenomenology" — a descriptive phenomenology of the types and functions of consciousness, taken as contents — from a "transcendental phenomenology of absolute consciousness," which elucidates consciousness not as content but as constitutive origin. The distinction follows Husserl's own development: the *Logical Investigations* are, for Henry as for the Husserl of the 1913 *Ideen*, a "noetic phenomenology" in this sense; the true transcendental turn is from *Ideen I* onward.

To every object of a possible experience corresponds in the transcendental I a rule of structure, which presides over the constitution of this object. The life of consciousness thus presents typical configurations in which *a priori* every possible form of objectivity is sketched. Whether one takes as guiding thread of research the system of all objects and of all possible forms of objectivity, or whether one describes directly the eidetic structures of all possible constitutive syntheses of experience, nothing is changed in the fundamental situation that transcendental phenomenology aims to elucidate. The doctrine is that of *Ideen I* §§148–153 and of the *Cartesian Meditations* §21: to every type of object there corresponds a type of intentional synthesis that constitutes it, and these two approaches (object-side, noematic; act-side, noetic) are strictly correlative, two guiding threads leading to the same transcendental structure.

What follows from such a situation is that the absolute ego is the origin, the foundation, the *Urstruktur* of all possible structures and of all possible senses of being. Still, this foundation must be correctly understood, in its absolutely concrete signification, for it is not an empty form, the simple by-itself-indeterminate possibility of a thought of objects in general; it reduces, in fact, to rigorously defined configurations that are the very modes of the life of a consciousness, the singular determinations — though of eidetic order — that a real existence necessarily takes on, precisely insofar as it exists. *Urstruktur* is once again a Husserlian term (the "primal structure" of transcendental consciousness). The qualification is important: the absolute ego is not an empty form (against a Kantian-transcendental-idealist reading) but a concrete, life-filled structure, always articulated in specific modes of consciousness. This insistence on the *concreteness* of the transcendental ego is properly Husserlian, especially in the *Cartesian Meditations* §33: the transcendental ego is not the Kantian "I think" that must accompany all representations, but a concrete life whose analysis can be pursued indefinitely.

**Paragraph 3\.** The orientation of the problematic toward the *ego cogito* cannot signify the forgetting of the question of being if the transcendental self-explication of this ego is the very mode according to which thought pursues the realization of its ontological design. The systematic study of the ensemble of constitutional problems is one, indeed, with the phenomenological explicitation of the ego, when this explicitation is pursued in the transcendental frame. The mode according to which such an explicitation must be realized — if at least it wishes to be systematic — is not easy to find. Its accomplishment, which also signifies the completion of all constitutive problems in general, since transcendental life equals the totality of possible forms of objectivity, remains no doubt an ideal for reason. But the ontological signification of this infinite task can no longer be put into question.

Henry is conceding, at this point, the apparent success of the Husserlian program: if the *ego cogito* is not a being-in-a-region but the absolute transcendental source of all constitution, then investigation of the *ego cogito* coincides with the elucidation of being in general; it *is* the ontological task properly understood. The question of being and the question of the ego are not separate; they are one and the same question. "The systematic study of the ensemble of constitutional problems is one, indeed, with the phenomenological explicitation of the ego." This is the thesis of Husserl's *First Philosophy* and of the *Cartesian Meditations*.

**Paragraph 4\.** The restitution of its ontological signification to the problematic of the *ego cogito* is rendered possible by the overcoming that Husserlian phenomenology already operates when it deliberately orients itself toward the constitutive problems that exhibit the relation of the structures of being with consciousness understood henceforth as a power of intuition that gives being and sense to the object it constitutes. When it is the work of a philosophy of the *cogito*, such an overcoming of intuitionism puts us in presence of a radical transformation of the phenomenological situation we are describing. The phrasing is delicate: Henry says that Husserlian phenomenology, *when* it becomes a philosophy of the *cogito* (i.e., when it passes from the *Logical Investigations* to *Ideen I* and beyond), already operates an overcoming of intuitionism — because it moves from describing intuition-contents to describing the constitutive synthesis that makes intuition-contents possible.

The ego no longer appears, indeed, as an intuitive given whose privileged character offered to consciousness the occasion to operate a positing in conformity with the *télos* of reason. That the ego exists, as a constituted reality, as a transcendent being provided with its own sense, which finds its origin in an eidetically defined configuration of transcendental life, must not make us forget that the ego that is at issue now is nothing other in reality than this transcendental life itself considered as the ensemble of possible configurations in and by which are constituted, at the heart of consciousness, all the types of transcendent data and all the senses of being immanent in them. What we are now in presence of is, consequently, the absolute ego, the originary *naturant* \[*naturant originaire*\] that does not belong to a determinate region of being and that could not be correctly thought by us under the title of "region consciousness," since it is, on the contrary, what confers on the ensemble of regions the sense that being takes on each time in them.

The term "naturant" is a striking choice: it is the Spinozist-Scholastic *natura naturans* (nature-naturing, as opposed to *natura naturata*, nature-natured). Henry uses it to designate the absolute ego as *constituting* rather than *constituted* — the pure productive source of sense, as opposed to the constituted reality of the psychological or mundane ego. The distinction between the absolute ego as constituting origin and the ego as constituted transcendent reality is the Husserlian distinction between the *ego pur* (transcendental ego) and the "empirical" or "mundane" ego, developed especially in *Ideen I* §57 and in the *Cartesian Meditations* §11. Consciousness (in the sense of the transcendental ego, the *naturant*) is not a region of being; it is what confers on all regions their being-sense.

**Paragraph 5\.** Is the problem of the being of the absolute ego resolved by the considerations that precede? Do they not rather put us in presence of a situation too easily accepted by classical philosophy, and which can be characterized by the absence of any problematic directed on what makes the subjectivity of the subject, by the forgetting of the problem of the being of the latter? This is the critical pivot of the section. Henry has just conceded that, if one grants the Husserlian transcendental move, the insertion of the *cogito* into the horizon works; but he now turns this concession into a question: has this insertion really solved the problem of the being of the ego, or has it simply displaced it and postponed it? The language — "the forgetting of the problem of the being of the subject" — recalls the Heideggerian critique of Husserl for having thematized consciousness as constitutive source while never thematizing the being of this consciousness itself (a critique developed in *Sein und Zeit* §7 and, more sharply, in Heidegger's 1925 lecture course on the "History of the concept of time," and in Heidegger's marginal notes on Husserl).

Once one has shown, indeed, how the different regions of being refer necessarily to a fundamental power of constitution that is the origin whence the objects they rule draw their being and their sense, one has not for all that resolved the problem of this origin. This problem is posed only with more urgency. The phenomenological explicitation of the transcendental ego, the systematic description of the configurations and sequences of consciousness considered as *a priori* types, as structures of eidetic order to which the lived experiences each time submit — do these not, however, concern such a problem? Do they not constitute, obviously, a thematic elucidation of the foundation? How, however, is such an elucidation possible? How can the origin be brought to the condition of "phenomenon," so as to become the "object" of phenomenological inquiry? Is it not only in the light of transcendence, on the condition of accepting the jurisdiction of the transcendental horizon of being in and by which every thing, and such an "origin" in particular, can become "visible"? The problem of the being of subjectivity sends us back, inevitably, to the problem of the sense of being in general.

This is the decisive argumentative move of the Introduction. Husserl has shown that the absolute ego is the origin of all senses of being. But the absolute ego, insofar as it is elucidated phenomenologically, must itself become a "phenomenon" — it must appear, it must become visible for the phenomenologist. And how can anything become visible? Only inside a horizon of visibility, inside the "light of transcendence" that is the opening of the horizon. So the absolute ego, in order to be phenomenologically investigated, must itself submit to the horizon of transcendence. But then the absolute ego is *not* absolute; it is still subordinated to a more fundamental condition, namely, the horizon itself. Hence the insertion-move of §5, paragraph 1 — the move that elevated the absolute ego to the level of the *Urregion*, the condition of all regions — is overturned: the absolute ego turns out still to be subordinated to the horizon of being in general.

**Paragraph 6\.** The problem of the being of the ego is the same as that of knowing how the ego can accede to the rank of "phenomenon." As it is now a matter of the absolute ego, this problem can be formulated thus: how can the transcendental field understood as the origin of being, of its diverse senses and its diverse structures, arise before us, in the light, in such a way that we can submit it to a systematic investigation? The ontological signification of this investigation is certainly not at issue, since it bears on a constituting consciousness, on the empire of configurations and chains of events that belong to it properly and that prescribe each time to being a determinate sense. It is no longer a matter, however, of describing such configurations as determinate configurations; the minute analysis of the different eidetic types to which they must necessarily conform, the systematic examination of the structures they realize, is no longer what preoccupies us. We ask ourselves, in reality, how such configurations, whatever be their proper eidetic particularizations, are susceptible, in general, of offering themselves to a phenomenological description: it is a question of the being of the absolute ego, not of the diverse modalities of its life as donative and constituting life. The problem of the elucidation of these modalities and of their structures is certainly not abandoned; it remains, perhaps, the very goal of the research. But the research turns itself first toward its own condition of possibility, which is the prior unveiling of the field it wants to explore.

This paragraph formulates precisely the meta-phenomenological question: not what are the structures of transcendental consciousness, but what makes it possible for these structures to become phenomena in the first place, to appear before the phenomenological gaze? Henry is asking for the *transcendental condition of phenomenological description itself*. This is a move that goes beyond Husserl, who generally takes the self-givenness of transcendental consciousness for granted (in *Ideen I* §44–46, where he argues that consciousness is given adequately to itself in immanent perception, and in *Cartesian Meditations* §9, where apodictic self-givenness of the transcendental ego is asserted). Henry is now going to argue that this Husserlian assumption is precisely what requires elucidation: how does the transcendental ego show itself to itself as a phenomenon?

**Paragraph 7\.** The phenomenological reduction necessarily precedes the systematic exploration of the transcendental field. It anticipates, by rendering it possible, the understanding of absolute consciousness in its ontological signification. The *epochê* (ἐποχή, written in Greek) is precisely the "radical" method that permits the grasp of the pure I and of the life that belongs to it as transcendental life, to which the world is immanent as an intentional component. Now the grasp, realized in the *epochê*, of transcendental life is possible only "if I place myself above this whole life" in order to render it present, itself and the multiple *cogitationes* that compose it, in intuition and, finally, in evidence. The cited phrase is from Husserl, as the footnote indicates; the theme of the transcendental reduction as a "placing above" or a "stepping back" from transcendental life in order to intuit it is developed especially in the *Cartesian Meditations* §15 and in the "*Epilogue*" to *Ideen I*. "Transcendental experience," that is, the experience of transcendental life, is no doubt what permits access to it and to its components as "phenomena." Transcendental phenomenology is precisely possible only when the reduction has accomplished its work in showing us the possibility of realizing, each for our own account, transcendental experience — that is, the experience of absolute life and of the ensemble of correlates immanent in it as *cogitata*. But it is clear as well that such an experience implies the prior opening of a field of presence inside which this life and its contents can precisely arise before us as "phenomena." The internal "transcendental" and phenomenological experience to which the *epochê* leads thus remains subordinated to the conditions of evidence and of intuitive realization — that is, in fact, to the transcendental horizon of being in general. Exposing the task of the phenomenological explicitation of the transcendental ego, Husserl writes: one must strictly confine oneself to the pure data of transcendental reflection, take them exactly as they give themselves in the intuition of direct evidence, and put aside from them all interpretations that go beyond this given.

The citation from Husserl is precisely decisive: Husserl explicitly presents the method of transcendental phenomenology as a submission to the criterion of direct intuitive evidence. And Henry has already shown, in §3, that intuitive evidence is constitutively horizon-bound. So the Husserlian method of transcendental reflection, which intuitively grasps the transcendental ego, is *still* operating inside the horizon of being — the very horizon the Husserlian move was supposed to ground.

**Paragraph 8\.** The overcoming of intuitionism toward a transcendental philosophy of constituting and donative consciousness is only apparent. The fundamental difficulty it encounters is not of a methodological order. It does not suffice, for this difficulty to be surmounted, to invite research to exercise itself first of itself, in an unreflective manner, before taking consciousness of its presuppositions and its own procedure. The retro-reference to itself of phenomenology could have an ontological signification only if intuition were to itself its own foundation. But the critique of intuitionism has put into light the transcendental condition of every intuitive realization and every evidence. Of this condition constant use is made — without however taking it for theme — by the explicitation of the transcendental ego insofar as it is a phenomenological explicitation, that is, an elucidation. Every elucidation is a mode of realization of evidence. Such a realization operates, consequently, inside a frame of evidence, and this frame plays, with respect to phenomenology itself, the role of an ultimate foundation, although an implicit one.

This is the decisive argumentative moment. Husserlian transcendental phenomenology wants to ground itself on itself (the "retro-reference" of phenomenology), by turning the transcendental method back upon the constituting life and describing it evidentially. But evidence is horizon-bound; therefore the self-grounding move silently presupposes the horizon it claims to found. The "frame of evidence" (*cadre d'évidence*) is the ontological precondition of phenomenology itself, which phenomenology cannot thematize because to thematize it would be to intuit it, and to intuit it would be to presuppose it. The structure of the argument is strictly analogous to Henry's argument in §3 paragraph 6 against the intuition of the essence of horizon; but it is now applied specifically to the Husserlian transcendental reduction.

**Paragraph 9\.** The necessary subordination of phenomenological description, and consequently of phenomenology itself, to the essence that deploys the transcendental horizon of being in general, is not due — let us note — to the scientific attitude adopted by the phenomenologist, insofar as such an attitude is in principle of reflective order. It is evidence that characterizes already, on the plane of unreflective life, the mode according to which the ego is present to itself. The deployment of the horizon, far from being a simple consequence of scientific reflection, is on the contrary its presupposition. It is because already the ego is present to us as element in the milieu of being, that the project of its systematic elucidation can come into the light. Explicitation does not operate from nothing; it bears on something that must always, in a certain way, be already there.

The point is important: the dependence of phenomenology on the horizon of being is not an artifact of phenomenology's reflective, scientific posture — it is not as though, if phenomenology were more "natural" or less scientific, it could escape the subordination. Already in prereflective life, the ego is present to itself *as an element in the milieu of being*, that is, as surrounded by the horizon, as situated in the ontological opening. The subordination is ontological, not methodological.

It appears, finally, that nothing is changed in such a demand if one takes into account the fact that phenomenological explicitation unfolds inside an attitude of reduction and that, on the other hand, it is pursued on the eidetic mode. In the same way as empirical consciousness, which remains tied to the world and to natural being, the transcendentally-reduced pure ego implies, as condition of possibility of its manifestation — and consequently of every systematic elucidation of its own life — a horizon of presence. This horizon does not lose its role of foundation if the consideration of the *eidos ego*, as well as of the *a priori* possibilities included in the life of the ego, substitutes itself for the analysis of this or that effective determination of a given though reduced subjectivity, for example that of the phenomenologist himself. The manifestation of the *eidos* requires, in the same way as every determinate empirical element, the prior opening of an ontological milieu. The transcendental revelation of the ego is, all in all, only a particular case, though a privileged one, of intuitive realization.

The argumentative net is closed. Neither the transcendental reduction (which supposedly lifts one "above" natural being) nor the eidetic reduction (which supposedly grasps the pure essence of the ego) can escape the condition that the horizon-of-being be presupposed; because in both cases what one does is *manifest* the transcendental ego (under a reduced or eidetic aspect), and all manifestation presupposes the horizon. The "transcendental revelation of the ego" — a technical phrase worth noting, because Henry will develop the concept of "revelation" as a substantive alternative to Husserlian manifestation in the later sections of the book — is "only a particular case, though a privileged one, of intuitive realization." The word "révélation" is used here in a quasi-theological sense that echoes the late Heidegger (*Aletheia*, disclosedness) but will be radicalized by Henry into the concept of *auto-révélation* of life, to be developed in Sections III–IV.

**Paragraph 10\.** The transcendental ego that the phenomenological reduction delivers to us carries within itself, as intentional correlate, a world of objects. This world is not a simple sum of singular existents, of empirical or eidetic order; it is first of all a "universe," the milieu in which all *cogitata* can freely manifest themselves. With regard to such a "universe" and its contents, the pure ego plays the role of a foundation and of an origin. But the ego itself and the *cogitatum* immanent in it as world or as intra-mundane determination cannot themselves take on the condition of phenomena and arise into being except on the ground of being in them.

The final paragraph crystallizes the aporia. The transcendental ego does play the role of foundation for the world; the Husserlian doctrine is correct at one level. But the ego itself, as a "phenomenon" for phenomenological investigation, requires the prior ground of being — and its *cogitatum* (the world it constitutes) also requires this ground. The "ground of being in them" (*le fond de celui-ci en eux*) is the indispensable precondition, internal to both ego and world, of their phenomenalization. The formula anticipates Henry's later thesis: there is a ground "in" the ego and "in" the world that is neither ego nor world, but the essence of manifestation itself — and this essence is what §§6–7 will now try to specify.

---

## **§ 6\. The difficulties relative to the edification of universal phenomenological ontology**

**Paragraph 1\.** If the thought of being implies a decisive overcoming of the existent as of the *eidos* that each time determines the ontological structure to which the existent is submitted, it can appear strange that the accomplishment of this thought throws us back infallibly to a singular existent and to a problematic that makes of this existent its explicit theme. Thus one sees ontology give itself immediately, in the very procedure by which it claims to constitute itself, a foundation of ontic order. The section opens with a precise statement of the scandal to be examined: universal phenomenological ontology, whose whole project is to exceed every particular being and every regional essence in order to think being-in-general, is nonetheless always drawn back to the analysis of one particular being — namely, the being that raises the question of being, the human reality, the Dasein. This seems absurd: an ontology that is supposed to transcend all determinate existents is forced to ground itself in a determinate existent. The effort by which it attempts to arrive at a rigorous understanding of its proper and fundamental task stumbles, at the outset, upon a difficulty: the realization of this task seems to imply the abandonment of the very project by which this task defines itself at the origin. The taking into consideration of the existent imposes itself, on the contrary, to ontology, and that in such a constraining way that the choice of the determination is not even left to it. The freedom of the thought of being is called into question by the interpellation of a singular existent that forcefully claims the character of being a "commencement" and pretends to impose itself as such on research. Fundamental ontology, declares *Sein und Zeit*, must be sought in an analytic of the Dasein. The direct reference is to *Sein und Zeit* §§4–5, where Heidegger famously argues that the question of being must be asked from the vantage of that being for whom its own being is an issue, namely Dasein; and that fundamental ontology therefore takes the form of an existential analytic of Dasein. This is the Heideggerian program; Henry will now submit it to the same critical interrogation he has applied to the Cartesian and Husserlian programs.

**Paragraph 2\.** It is a matter of being itself considered in its radical transcendence with regard to every determinate existent, but the question of being itself must first render itself transparent to itself. The elaboration of the formal structure of this question puts us in presence of three terms: (1) being itself, insofar as it is that about which the question is raised, what is sought for (*Gefragtes*) in the question; (2) a determinate being, the one about which the question is formulated (*Befragtes*); (3) the question itself, finally, which is raised concerning being. Henry is reciting precisely the tripartite formal structure of the *Seinsfrage* as Heidegger lays it out in *Sein und Zeit* §2: every question has (i) a *Gefragtes* (the being-asked-about), (ii) a *Befragtes* (the being-interrogated, the being *at* which the question is addressed), and (iii) an *Erfragtes* (the being-sought-after in the asking). In the question of being, the *Gefragtes* is being itself; the *Befragtes* is a being (specifically Dasein); the *Erfragtes* is the sense of being. Henry retains the first two and collapses the third into the question itself.

The examination of each of these terms sends us back to the being, more exactly to that rigorously determined being which is human reality. The question itself that is raised about being is not nothing; it is a comportment, the comportment of the reality that questions; this reality is a singular reality, a being. Insofar as it questions, however, it takes on a certain manner of being; it makes itself precisely a questioning-reality. The being of this reality is what allows, in principle, that there historializes itself in it, as a proper possibility of eidetic order, something like a question. Such a being, rigorously determined, and that on an eidetic plane, defines this reality as human reality. To this reality is given, as a property that belongs to it properly, the very possibility of raising a question.

The argument follows *Sein und Zeit* §4 carefully: the question of being, as a form of comportment, presupposes a being that comports itself in this way, and this being is Dasein — defined precisely by the fact that its being is an issue for it, that it can historialize (Henry's French *s'historialiser*, translating *sich geschichtlich ereignen*) a questioning relation to its own being and to being in general. The "eidetic" level at which Henry locates this determination is Henry's own gloss — Heidegger himself would reject the eidetic framing, but Henry is still speaking in a quasi-Husserlian register, treating "being-the-questioner-of-being" as an eidetic property of human reality.

**Paragraph 3\.** Being is always the being of a being. It is to the being that the question of being addresses itself, in order to decipher in it the sense of being. Now the being that is chosen as the one starting from which the sense of being must be elucidated is not indifferent. The being that poses the question of being is manifestly a privileged being, the one that will function as the *Befragtes* of the question of being, as the being to whom this question is posed. The being of human reality must first make the theme of the problematic which aims to elucidate the sense of being in general. The paragraph recapitulates the second of Heidegger's theses from *Sein und Zeit* §§2–4: the "ontic priority of the question of being" derives from the fact that the being who asks is a privileged being, the one in whose being the question of being can be raised at all; and therefore, the fundamental-ontological investigation passes through an existential analytic of this privileged being.

**Paragraph 4\.** Being itself, finally, considered in its pure essence, dominates every being, and human reality in particular. To human reality, however, it belongs to be linked to being, and that in a privileged way, insofar as it understands being. The understanding of being by human reality is the fundamental fact that determines human reality in its own essence. Little matters that such an understanding remains in an implicit state, or that — for reasons that must make the theme of a particular problematic — it remains most often submitted to profound alterations. These alterations themselves are possible only as modalities and on the foundation of the relation that links, in the origin, human reality to being itself. If the understanding of being belongs to human reality as what precedes, while guiding them, all the comportments human reality is susceptible of assuming — and in particular, the question it can raise concerning the sense of being in general — it is because this question is nothing other than the radicalization of this ontological or rather pre-ontological understanding of being which is immanent in human reality as its most proper power and as its very essence.

This is the Heideggerian doctrine of the "understanding of being" (*Seinsverständnis*) as the defining mark of Dasein, developed in *Sein und Zeit* §4 and §§31–32 (the analysis of *Verstehen* as an existential of Dasein). Dasein has a pre-ontological understanding of being (it always already operates with some, however implicit, understanding of what it is to be), and the ontological investigation is the radicalization of this pre-ontological understanding into an explicit, thematic one. Henry faithfully reproduces the doctrine — but his faithful reproduction is preparatory to the critique that will follow.

**Paragraph 5\.** Human reality therefore occupies, inside the question of being, a determining place. It can claim, with regard to other beings, a precedence that is at once of ontic order — since the question of being is, all in all, only a determinate mode of this existence that we are ourselves immediately — and of ontological order, if it is true that to such an existence belongs by essence an understanding of being, and that in a double sense, since it is a matter both of its own being and of the being of the being it is not. This is *Sein und Zeit* §4 verbatim: Dasein has an "ontic" priority (it is the being that asks), an "ontological" priority (it has an understanding of being), and a "ontico-ontological" priority (its own being consists precisely in its relation to being). Henry sets all this out cleanly — and then begins to question it.

**Paragraph 6\.** Why, however, is ontology incapable of grounding itself ontologically, and must it place at the center of its problematic a determinate existent, to the point of confusing itself with the existential analysis of this existent? To such a condition ontology can evidently be submitted only in function of the relation that unites, in the essence, being and the being. Now the elaboration of the structure of the question of being constitutes only an entirely external analysis of such a relation. In fact, the link that unites being and the being remains radically obscure; its structure is not homogeneous; its signification is polyvalent.

This is the crux of Henry's critique of the Heideggerian program. The Heideggerian account of the question of being (in terms of *Gefragtes*, *Befragtes*, and the privilege of Dasein) is a formal account of the question's structure; it is an "external analysis" of the relation of being to the being. But the relation itself — the ontological difference, the relation of *Sein* to *Seiendes* — is *not homogeneous*, not univocal. Its "polyvalence" is what Henry now begins to tease apart.

Let us consider human reality. What characterizes the relation it maintains with being is precisely the fact that it is given to it to maintain this relation, to live it. To this privilege is linked that of language: every speech is pronounced only on the background of a more primitive entertaining (*entretien*, conversation) — that of man and of being. The reference is to the late Heidegger, especially to *Unterwegs zur Sprache* (1959) but already present in the 1946 *Brief über den Humanismus* and in *Erläuterungen zu Hölderlins Dichtung*: language is the "house of being," and human speech is made possible by a more primitive "conversation" between being and man. This privilege — which the non-Dasein being cannot claim as its own, and that not by virtue of any ontic deficiency (such as, for example, the absence of an organ of phonation), but on the contrary because of its own ontological reality — confers on human reality the characterized function that it fulfills inside the problematic of being. The parenthetical remark about phonation is a polemical flourish: it is not for biological reasons that a stone cannot ask the question of being; it is for an ontological reason, namely that the stone does not have the comportment of relating itself to being. The critique of reductive biologism (or of reducing Dasein's privilege to ontic features) is Heidegger's own, recurrent throughout the early Freiburg and Marburg lectures (GA 19–21) and consolidated in *Sein und Zeit*.

The precedence of human reality in the question of being is only the methodological equivalent of its own ontological structure — structure in conformity with which an implicit and non-conceptual understanding of being is already given to it. When the relation of human reality to the essence must be defined starting from such an understanding, we call it a transcendental relation. This latter, so understood, does not imply any primacy of "subjectivity" or of the "subject," for its foundation does not reside in human reality itself, but rather in being, which gives to human reality, by ordering it to itself, the possibility of thinking being. The specific character of such a relation is in any case clearly defined.

This paragraph contains a crucial Henrian distinction. A "transcendental relation" between human reality and being means: a relation in which being precedes and grounds the human, making possible the human's understanding of being. So construed, the transcendental relation does not elevate the human to a constituting role (as Husserlian subjectivism does); it maintains the primacy of being, which "gives" itself to the human and "orders" the human toward itself. This is a precise description of the *late* Heideggerian position — being "gives itself" (*es gibt Sein*), the human is "claimed" or "appropriated" (*eignet*) by being — and Henry is taking it as the most charitable reading of *Sein und Zeit*. The critique that follows will ask whether *Sein und Zeit* itself really manages to hold to this position, or whether its analytic of Dasein slides into just the Husserlian subjectivism it tries to avoid.

**Paragraph 7\.** It is in a quite other sense, however, that human reality finds itself submitted to being when being is nothing more for it than what it is for a being whatsoever. The expression "being of human reality" is therefore radically ambiguous, since it designates both the essence of human reality, insofar as human reality maintains with being a transcendental relation, and, on the other hand, the foundation that is in human reality and that makes it be, in the same way as any being whatsoever.

This is the formulation of what, a decade after the publication of *L'essence de la manifestation*, Henry will call simply the "*ambiguïté du Dasein*" (the title of Section I, §13). The phrase "*être de la réalité humaine*" conceals two distinct senses: (i) the transcendental relation, in which the human is ordered to being as that which understands being; and (ii) the ontic-grounding relation, in which the human simply is-a-being, grounded by being in the same sense as any other being. Heidegger's analytic of Dasein oscillates between these two senses: sometimes Dasein is thematized as the privileged opening in which being gives itself (transcendental sense), sometimes Dasein is simply one existent whose essence (existentiality) is being described (ontic sense). Henry's charge is that Heidegger never really clarified which of these two senses is operative, and that the two senses cannot be reconciled: the first raises Dasein above other beings (transcendental privilege); the second demotes Dasein to the level of other beings (it too is grounded by being in the general way).

**Paragraph 8\.** The examination of the relations that exist between the being of human reality and the essence (being considered in its universal essence) leads, on the other hand, to the objection of the circle. Fundamental ontology rests on the analytic of the Dasein. But in the idea of the constitution of human reality, of the "existentiality" that makes the theme of the existential analytic, the idea of being is already implied, as condition of possibility. One wants therefore to bring to light the essence starting from a reality whose study is possible only under the prior condition of a bringing-to-light of the essence.

This is the famous objection of the "hermeneutic circle" that Heidegger himself raises and addresses in *Sein und Zeit* §2 and more extensively in §32.
