The objection is: to analyze Dasein (whose being is its understanding of being) requires already having some grasp of being; but the whole point of the analysis was to arrive at a grasp of being; so the analysis is circular. Heidegger's response is famous: the circle is not vicious but hermeneutic; what matters is the proper way of entering the circle, the proper orientation of the fore-structure of understanding. Henry cites this response:

The presupposition of being ceases, it is true, to be an objection if the research is turned toward this very presupposition in order to elucidate its content. Insofar as it thinks itself as a liberating exhibition of the foundation, fundamental ontology does not reject the idea of a circular progress of its analysis; it welcomes this idea, on the contrary, as in conformity with the nature of things. This is the Heideggerian response correctly summarized. But Henry now introduces a complication: an ambiguity subsists however concerning the mode in conformity with which the foundation operates its work of foundation. When one rests fundamental ontology on the analytic of the Dasein, Dasein manifestly intervenes insofar as it bears within itself the power to relate itself originarily to being; it is the transcendental relation of human reality to the essence that is at issue. When one declares, on the contrary, that the existential analytic can be accomplished only under the implicit presupposition of the essence, the relation of the essence to the being of human reality is identical to the relation the essence maintains with the being of any being whatsoever.

Here is the ambiguity re-articulated: in the circle, Dasein intervenes either as the transcendental opening (as privileged being) or as just any being grounded by being in general. If Dasein is submitted in any case to the power of transcendence, it is still necessary to specify the manner in which transcendence acts: does it ground the being of human reality by ordering it to itself according to a transcendental relation, or is human reality simply immersed in the milieu opened by transcendence, in the same way as the being of any being whatsoever? The ultimate sense of the doctrine is, no doubt, the covering-over and, finally, the identification of the transcendental relation with the simple relation of immanence that each time confers being on the being. But is such an identification possible? Would its paradoxical consequence not be the pure and simple suppression of the privilege of the Dasein? Is this suppression conceivable, if it is true that there are for Dasein two ways of being irreducible to each other: as the being that relates itself to being in general, and consequently to all possible existents, and to itself — and on the other hand, as the being to which it relates itself when it relates itself to itself?

Henry is identifying a structural instability at the very heart of Heidegger's fundamental ontology. Either Dasein's relation to being is *different in kind* from the relation of stones to being, or it is not. If it is different in kind, then Dasein's privileged transcendental role grounds fundamental ontology — but then Dasein is treated as absolute, not as something grounded by being. If it is not different in kind, then Dasein has no privileged role — and fundamental ontology loses its methodological anchor in the existential analytic. The doctrine tries to hold both horns and ends up inviting a "covering-over" of the transcendental relation by the ontic one — that is, Dasein is taken as privileged *methodologically* but as simply one existent *ontologically*. This is, for Henry, the unresolved tension of Heidegger's project.

**Paragraph 9\.** The necessity for ontology to give itself a foundation of ontic order is not, by itself, a difficulty. It conforms to the general sense of the doctrine. The reference of ontology to the reality of a singular existent is only the methodological transposition of the link that unites, in the origin, transcendence and finitude. The understanding of this link is none other than the internal, and no longer simply external, understanding of the relation of being and the being. If being is always the being of a being, it is because being does not have in itself the power to manifest itself. It is rather in the being that it manifests itself, as that *in which* the manifestation of the being becomes possible. By that very fact, however, this manifestation of the being is also what hides being, and that in conformity with a dialectical situation that is not provisional but insurmountable.

This paragraph is a partial concession to Heidegger: yes, the passage through a determinate being (Dasein) is not itself the difficulty — it is rather the methodological expression of the ontological relation between being and the being. Being requires the being as its place of manifestation; there is no "pure" manifestation of being without its concrete appearance in some being. This is the Heideggerian doctrine of the "ontological difference" combined with the doctrine of the "self-concealment" of being in its very revelation (developed in *Vom Wesen der Wahrheit*, *Der Ursprung des Kunstwerks*, and in the late texts on *aletheia*). But Henry locates a *specific* concern: the passage through the being is *insurmountable*, and this means that being is concealed in the very act of its revelation. This concealment, for Henry, is not a provisional lack that further phenomenological work might remedy; it is a structural feature of this conception of manifestation. The claim will become the thesis of Sections I–II: ontological monism (Heidegger's included) is the conception of manifestation as *Ek-stase*, as horizonal disclosure in a being — and this conception structurally entails the concealment of being in its manifestation. Henry's alternative (immanence, self-affection, auto-revelation) will be constructed precisely as the non-ek-static alternative in which revelation does not conceal because it does not pass through the ontological difference.

**Paragraph 10\.** This ultimate reason for the necessary reference of ontology to an ontic foundation does not yet explain, however, the privilege of the Dasein. It is a matter of knowing, finally, whether such a privilege is something decisive or whether, on the contrary, its signification is only of methodological order. Now the subordination of the existential analytic to fundamental ontology is constantly affirmed in *Sein und Zeit*. The existential analytic is in no way the goal of the research. In any case, it remains incomplete; it is pursued only in the direction that interests the problem of being as such. The results to which it arrives constitute, no doubt, a positive moment in the elaboration of the sense of being in general; they remain however provisional. The ultimate signification of the ontological structures that define the fundamental constitution of human reality cannot be considered as acquired until the sense of being in general has been definitively fixed. It is thus that there will impose itself a repetition of the existential analyses, a systematic resumption of their results, when the temporal signification of being has been brought into light.

This is the structure of *Sein und Zeit* as published: the existential analytic of Dasein (Divisions I and II) is meant to culminate in the exposition of temporality as the meaning of the being of Dasein, and then — in the unpublished Division III ("Time and Being") — this would have been repeated "temporally" at the level of being in general. Henry is invoking the announced but never-completed architectonic of the book. This latter, however, will it not send us back to the being of the "Dasein" as to its foundation? If the being of Dasein is essentially constituted by temporality, if temporality is the origin of time, if time is the horizon of being, is not the subordination of the being of Dasein to the sense of being in general, more than ever, ambiguous?

This is a powerful objection. Heidegger's program says: the existential analytic of Dasein is provisional; it will be grounded ultimately in the sense of being, which is time. But time is itself understood starting from the temporality of Dasein (*Sein und Zeit* §65). So the sense of being ultimately refers back to the being of Dasein — which the existential analytic was supposed to be provisional with respect to. The circle is not just "hermeneutic" but vicious: Dasein's being is supposed to be derivative from the sense of being in general, but the sense of being in general is supposed to be derivable only from the temporality of Dasein. Either Dasein is primary (and we are back to transcendental subjectivism) or the sense of being is primary (and we lose the methodological anchor in Dasein). Henry's diagnosis here anticipates the famous objections raised by later Heidegger himself in the so-called *Kehre*, when he acknowledges that the path of *Sein und Zeit* could not be completed as originally planned.

**Paragraph 11\.** The marvelous rebound of the questioned upon the questioner which comes to light in the question of being does not yet permit us to lift the fundamental difficulty that is immanent to this question and that bears on the problem of the homogeneity of being. It is only when a decisive response has been given to this problem that can be defined in a rigorous way the place and role of human reality in the question of being. The closing sentence formulates the real problem that the entire Introduction has been working toward: the question of the "homogeneity of being." Is being *one* — homogeneous, univocal, the same in all its manifestations? Or is being fundamentally *heterogeneous*, irreducibly bifurcated?

This is the decisive question of the whole book. If being is homogeneous — that is, if there is one single structure of manifestation, one single essence of phenomenality — then every being (including Dasein, including the ego, including life, including affectivity) is submitted to that one structure, and the Heideggerian project of finding the "sense of being in general" in the temporality of Dasein's transcendence is, in principle, coherent. This is what §§ 8–16 of the book will call "ontological monism." But if being is heterogeneous — if there are radically distinct modes of manifestation that cannot be unified under a single structure — then there is a domain of being (for Henry, the domain of radical immanence, of self-affective life) whose manifestation is *not* governed by the Heideggerian-Husserlian structure of ek-static transcendence, and the whole monistic program fails. This alternative is the thesis of the book; it is to be developed in Sections I through IV. The Introduction has prepared the ground for it by showing how all previous attempts (Cartesian, Husserlian, Heideggerian) have assumed ontological homogeneity and have thereby missed the being of the ego (or have distorted it beyond recognition). The final section of the Introduction (§7) will now re-pose the question of the being of the ego as the originary and fundamental problematic, whose solution will require the overcoming of ontological monism.

---

## **§ 7\. The problematic concerning the being of the ego interpreted as an originary and fundamental problematic**

**Paragraph 1\.** The necessary insertion of the phenomenology of the ego inside the context constituted by universal ontology can be called into question only if it is solely starting from an elucidation of the central phenomenon of the ego that ontology can acquire its fundamental dimension. The opening sentence formulates the hypothesis that the whole Introduction has been building toward. Until now, Henry has argued: the phenomenology of the ego is one regional investigation among others (§1); it is therefore necessary to erect first a universal phenomenological ontology (§2); this requires overcoming intuitionism (§3); one can try to re-insert the ego into the horizon thus liberated (§4); but this insertion fails, because the absolute ego itself must still submit to the horizon (§5); and the Heideggerian version of the same problem (grounding ontology in the analytic of Dasein) is subject to its own internal ambiguities (§6). The upshot of all this, Henry now says, is that the only way out of the impasse is to reverse the assumed subordination: it is not the ego that must be inserted into universal ontology, but universal ontology that must be derived from the elucidation of the ego. The problematic of the ego, correctly understood, *is* the fundamental problematic.

But — Henry immediately adds — it is still appropriate to understand the precedence of the problematic that phenomenologically aims at the being of the ego in a correct way. Such a precedence in no way signifies that a certain existent (for example, the one who says "I") must be questioned in the first place about its being, if at least the sense of being in general must be able to be released. What is in question, on the contrary, and that in an explicit way, is the solidarity of the sense of being of human reality with that of being in general. If the problematic concerning the being of the ego must be interpreted as a truly originary and fundamental problematic, it is because the being of the ego is not homogeneous with "being in general" — and this not in a restricted sense, as if one meant by that simply that the ego defines another "region of being" different from the one to which belong other beings, diversely constituted, but in an ultimate sense, though one that is still incomprehensible to us. The problem is to know whether the primacy of the analytic of human reality is of methodological order, or whether one must recognize in it an ultimate ontological signification.

Henry carefully distinguishes his thesis from the Heideggerian one. Heidegger also claims that the analytic of Dasein is the privileged access to the sense of being in general; but for Heidegger, this privilege is (at least methodologically) just that — a privileged starting-point, the being whose mode of asking gives access to the question. For Henry, the privilege is much stronger: the being of the ego is *not homogeneous* with the sense of being in general. This is the first explicit statement of the heterogeneity thesis, the thesis of *non-monism*. The being of the ego belongs to a domain of manifestation structurally different from the domain of transcendent beings, and this difference is not regional (which would keep it inside ontological monism) but *ultimate* — that is, it marks a difference within the very structure of manifestation itself. Because this thesis has not yet been established, Henry admits that it is "still incomprehensible to us" at this point. But the sections to follow (Sections I–IV) will establish it.

**Paragraph 2\.** Has philosophy ever been capable of giving a positive interpretation of the fact that it is in the absence of any context that there arises in Descartes the problematic of the *ego cogito*? Has the infinite signification of the Cartesian identification of certainty and truth ever been understood? In Descartes himself, have these fundamental themes been clarified? That the sense of being of the ego remains undetermined in Cartesianism is not exact. Very quickly, on the contrary, it is as *ens creatum* that the being of the ego is interpreted, in the same way as that of every simple nature, and that in the light of the philosophical and theological conceptions of medieval thought, which itself issued from Greek ontology.

Henry here renders much more precisely the claim of the opening Heideggerian epigraph. Heidegger had said that the being of the *sum* is left *unbestimmt* — undetermined — in Descartes. Henry corrects this: the being of the *sum* is in fact determined in Descartes, but it is determined as *ens creatum* (created being, a creature), in the lineage of medieval onto-theology which itself goes back to Greek (Aristotelian, Platonic) ontology. Descartes takes over without question the medieval-Aristotelian ontological category of created substance and applies it to the ego, thereby missing what is properly original in the Cartesian intuition of the *cogito*. The footnote refers to *Sein und Zeit* p. 24 where Heidegger makes essentially this point.

Is such a determination improper because the being of the ego is submitted to an erroneous or insufficient conception of being in general? Is it not rather the very idea of such a subordination that is unacceptable? And is the fact that the horizon of being in general be interpreted as a "transcendental" horizon not merely failing to resolve the difficulty, but on the contrary rendering its solution more urgent? This is the decisive turn. Heidegger's critique of Descartes is that Descartes submitted the being of the ego to an inadequate conception of being in general (the medieval *ens creatum*); the Heideggerian remedy is to submit the being of the ego to a better conception of being in general (the transcendental horizon of *Sein und Zeit*). But Henry now asks: what if the trouble is not with the *conception* of being in general but with the very *idea* of *subordinating* the being of the ego to being in general? What if the being of the ego is not properly understood as subordinate to any horizon of being in general, because it is heterogeneous with every such horizon? To render the horizon "transcendental" only sharpens the problem, because the transcendental horizon still subjects the ego to a single univocal type of manifestation.

**Paragraph 3\.** How can the ego become a "phenomenon"? Is it not on condition of submitting itself to a horizon of visibility in and by which every thing can become "visible"? The power that deploys such a horizon, transcendence, is it not the condition of the being of the ego? The present investigations have been undertaken to show the necessity of responding negatively to these fundamental questions. What they want finally to put into light is that, though it is itself what realizes the condition of possibility of every phenomenon in general, the mode according to which the ego becomes a phenomenon is something so fundamental that it cannot be submitted to any condition.

This is the thesis of the book, stated directly. The ego does not become a phenomenon by submitting itself to a horizon of transcendent visibility; it becomes a phenomenon by a mode of manifestation that is not governed by any external condition at all. This mode Henry will call *auto-révélation* (self-revelation) or *manifestation immanente* (immanent manifestation). The whole book from this point on is, in a sense, the argumentative elaboration of this thesis. The passage also explicitly reverses the direction of conditioning: the ego is *itself* what realizes the condition of possibility of every phenomenon — and so cannot itself be conditioned by anything else. The ego is the absolute, but in a sense different from Husserl's "absolute ego": it is absolute because it is self-revealing, not because it is the constituting source of objective sense.

The problem of philosophy is the problem of truth. Truth is nothing other than what in general renders possible something like phenomena. The problem of truth is more originary than that of reason. The being, "real" and "true," that reason each time arrives at positing on the foundation of a determinate intuitive given implies, as condition, what precisely renders possible the realization of such a given. Insofar as it is the object of a rational positing, the *ego cogito* is subordinated to a horizon of truth. Its privilege has only a limited signification; it is relative to the *télos* of reason. How and why, however, the being of the ego is what must conduct, and that in an originary way, the problematic of truth — this can be understood only if such a being is interpreted as that which realizes in its very accomplishment every truth as such. The being of the ego is truth. Not, it is true, that truth which is possible only by transcendence and as the very work of transcendence, but a truth higher in origin, more ancient, and without which transcendence itself would not be. To such a truth, which is not different from the ego itself and which constitutes its very being, we give the name of *originary truth* (*vérité originaire*). It is only when the problematic of truth is capable of going back to the origin that it reveals itself as identical to that of the ego.

The passage is philosophically dense. Henry distinguishes three levels: (i) the truth of the rational positing (the evidence of particular truths in regions of being); (ii) the truth of transcendence (the disclosure of being in the horizon of *Sein und Zeit*, Heideggerian *aletheia*); (iii) a more originary truth — truth as the self-revelation of the ego — which is the condition of possibility of both of the preceding. The "being of the ego is truth" — this is a startling formulation, and Henry intends it as a substantive thesis: the mode in which the ego is present to itself is the primordial mode of truth, the self-revelation that makes possible all derivative modes of disclosure (the horizonal, the predicative, the evidential). The thesis directly inverts Heidegger's doctrine: for Heidegger, *aletheia* is the *Offenheit* of being in the horizon, and Dasein's truth is derivative from this disclosive openness; for Henry, the self-revelation of the ego is primary, and every horizonal opening is derivative from it. "Plus originaire que la vérité de l'être est la vérité de l'homme" — more originary than the truth of being is the truth of man. The whole book is a defense of this sentence.

**Paragraph 4\.** Is it not losing the proper sense of the essence to identify this essence with a real and determinate being? The essence can be correctly thought by us only as the ultimate condition of possibility of every existence. It is the foundation, and that in an ontological sense. It could not, consequently, be identified with a particular existence, even if the latter plays a privileged role in an ontic sequence. The first truth cannot signify the truth of a singular content starting from which one could claim to deduce other truths. The realization (however problematic) of such a deduction would leave intact the problem of the foundation. The first truth is an ontological condition of possibility whose signification is absolutely universal. Possibility, understood as the transcendental condition that precedes, while grounding it, every effectivity of whatever order, is not by itself, however, a pure possibility. The passage works through a possible objection — one Heidegger himself might raise — namely, that by making the ego into the fundamental principle, Henry would be confusing a determinate existent with the ontological foundation, thus repeating exactly the error Heidegger diagnosed in Descartes. Henry concedes the objection *so long as* the ego is understood as a determinate existent; but he will argue that the ego (in the sense of the being that realizes self-revelation in radical immanence) is not a determinate existent but precisely the *mode of being of the foundation*. It is not one existent elevated to foundational status; it is the foundational structure itself, which happens to coincide with the subjectivity of the ego.

One leaves the problematic incorrectly suspended at an entirely undetermined term when, in the manner of Kant, one does not concern oneself with defining in a rigorous way the status of the "condition of possibility of experience." To institute a reflective analysis in the hope of obtaining, by this indirect path, a more pressing determination of such a "condition," is a method entirely insufficient. The term at which thought thus arrives in its regressive march is only a pure possibility which has no right to the title of foundation. It is a pure possibility because it is still only the condition of a possible experience and not of a real experience. It is an "empty" possibility because such a condition reduces itself to a purely formal structure, deprived of all content. It is finally a possibility that is strictly nothing because the problem of the being of this possibility, of its status, is just never posed. In reality, the condition of experience is only a term posited by reflective thought, something that floats freely like the simple correlate of a consciousness searching for an explanatory principle — it is finally no more than a hypothesis. That such a condition be most often presented under the title of "subjectivity" or "transcendental subjectivity" is a mysterious affirmation, without any foundation in the doctrine, and which, in the absence of any problematic concerning the being of this subjectivity, has strictly speaking no sense.

The Kantian critique here is sustained and sharp. Kant's method in the Transcendental Deduction of the First *Critique* is to argue regressively from the fact of experience to its conditions of possibility, locating these conditions in the structures of the transcendental subject. But, Henry objects, this regressive reflection gives only a formal skeleton of a "condition of possibility" — it is empty because it is only a condition of a *possible* (not an actual) experience, and its ontological status is never questioned. The transcendental subject of the First *Critique* is, in Henry's view, a *hypothesis* — a reflective construction, not a real foundation. Similarly for all post-Kantian transcendental philosophy (including Husserl's, which still operates within the Kantian framework of "conditions of possibility"). The critique foreshadows, in modified form, Fichte's own critique of Kant (which Henry treats at length in his book on Marx, and indirectly in *L'essence de la manifestation* itself, where Fichte figures as the philosopher who most clearly grasped the *need* for a real — not merely reflective — principle of the I). A transcendental subjectivity whose *being* is never posed as a problem is, Henry says, strictly senseless.

**Paragraph 5\.** Is the reality of the essence not safeguarded, on the contrary, by the thought that thinks the essence as being? The transcendental condition that plays with regard to every being the role of an ontological foundation is not a pure and simple possibility, something virtual which, by itself, is still nothing. If being is identical to nothingness, it is only with regard to the being that this nothingness is "nothing." Considered in itself, nothingness is a real nothingness. Being is not an abstract universal. Ontological possibility is absolute reality. Henry now considers the Heideggerian alternative to Kantian transcendentalism: Heidegger tried to escape the emptiness of Kantian "conditions of possibility" precisely by thinking the foundation as *being* (nothing-ness in the concrete, positive sense of *Was ist Metaphysik?*, the productive *Nichtung* of the essence of being). So Heidegger's move goes further than Kant's. But Henry's argument is now going to press Heidegger too. Is the affirmation of the reality of the essence anything other, however, than the pure and simple *realization* of the essence? Is such a realization not suspended on an act of thought by the philosopher? Must it not be held to be a pure and simple "theory"? The foundation, if it is anything other than a simple metaphysical hypothesis, must still make proof of its reality — and that without appeal being made to mediate considerations or theories whose entanglement is always supposed to obey a logical link. Being must be able to show itself. The method of ontology is phenomenological. It is precisely when it brings its aid to ontology that the phenomenological method acquires its decisive philosophical signification.

Here is a new move. Heidegger's ontology needs to be phenomenological — it cannot rest on theoretical construction but must produce the phenomenon of being itself, must let being show itself. What can, indeed, claim for itself — and that in an imperative and urgent way — a mode of explicit presentation and the title of "phenomenon," if not that which does not first show itself but remains most often hidden, namely being itself, the object of ontology? Philosophy is then in embarrassment. The difficulty it encounters can be formulated as follows: how can the condition of possibility of every manifestation become itself something manifest? "Ontology," says Heidegger, "is possible only as phenomenology." But can being ever truly and in itself become a "phenomenon"? The citation is from *Sein und Zeit* §7, where Heidegger famously declares that ontology is possible only as phenomenology. Henry accepts this as a formal requirement, but then presses the question: how can *being* itself, which is not a being, become a phenomenon? This is the question that structures the remaining paragraphs.

**Paragraph 6\.** Many equivocations will be set aside if one keeps present in mind the idea that the theme of phenomenological ontology is in no way constituted by the determinate and in some sense material content of some manifestation, but bears, on the contrary, on the "how" of that manifestation and of every possible manifestation in general. What, in a phenomenon, precisely makes it something susceptible of appearing — whatever be this something in its determinate content — is what is in question. Now being, the condition of possibility of every manifestation in general, cannot become a "phenomenon" if by this one understands the singular content of a determinate manifestation. What can the project of a phenomenological ontology then signify? What does one mean exactly when one declares that being must be able to "become a phenomenon"?

This is a major methodological clarification. The "phenomenon" that the ontologist aims at is not a phenomenal *content* (this determinate being, that property) but the *how*, the mode, the *Weise der Gegebenheit* (to use Husserl's term) — the manner in which appearing happens. Phenomenology understands being not as an object to be described but as the way-of-appearing. But this only sharpens the difficulty: being cannot be given as a content-phenomenon; so how can it be phenomenologically disclosed at all?

**Paragraph 7\.** Is the question of the reality of the foundation linked to that of the possibility for being to become a phenomenon? Must we not recognize, on the contrary, the rights of a thought which, in conceiving the originary work of unveiling as a dissimulation of that from which this work can each time be accomplished, is not for all that dialectical, but rests, on the contrary, on an effective experience whose sense is to reveal the antinomic structure of the foundation? If the essence of the foundation dissimulates itself in the very act by which it opens a horizon of light, it is because to this essence it belongs, in principle, not to show itself. The essence is real, insofar as it grounds truth — nevertheless it is not itself the truth, but rather a more originary non-truth. To this non-truth, however, the phenomenon always refers, insofar as it shines on the foundation of an obscure relation. Ontology is still possible on a phenomenological basis. What is put into question is only — but that in an essential way — the possibility of an absolute knowledge.

Henry is recapitulating the Heideggerian position, which tries to solve the difficulty by saying that being is *phenomenalized* through the very concealment by which it retreats in its disclosure. *Aletheia* involves *lêthê*: truth (disclosure) involves a withdrawal (concealment). This is the late Heideggerian position of *Vom Wesen der Wahrheit* and *Der Ursprung des Kunstwerks*. Being becomes a phenomenon precisely as the hiddenness at the heart of every disclosure. Henry concedes that this is a real phenomenological position — not a dialectical sleight-of-hand — but he notes its price: on this view, the foundation does not fully reveal itself, and therefore absolute knowledge (in the Hegelian sense, but also in any sense of fully transparent self-understanding) is impossible. The essence is always only a "more originary non-truth," a concealment at the bottom of every disclosure. If this is the final word, then philosophy must accept a kind of permanent epistemic modesty — which Heidegger, by the 1930s, indeed accepts (*Gelassenheit*, *Unterwegs*, etc.).

**Paragraph 8\.** That the foundation be, in fact, from top to bottom "phenomenon," that it be the truth — and that in an ultimate and originary sense — is what can be understood only when a radical elucidation of the concept of phenomenon has guided the problematic to the idea of a revelation that owes nothing to the work of transcendence. The elucidation of the concept of phenomenon will be the first task of the present investigations. Its result will be to make understood that the determination of the "phenomenon" as something that shows itself in the horizon of light inside which every thing can become visible in itself, remains in fact unilateral. Now the radical insufficiency of such a determination has commanded almost the whole history of human thought. It is on a new basis that philosophy will rise up when it is capable of circumscribing a "phenomenon" absolutely original in that the very mode in conformity with which it reveals itself is irreducible to the "how" of the manifestation of transcendent phenomena.

Henry now directly names his alternative to the Heideggerian position. The Heideggerian view treats phenomenality itself as irreducibly bound to the structure of horizonal disclosure (being shows itself by concealing itself in the horizon of the ontological difference). This determination of phenomenality, Henry says, is "unilateral" — it identifies one mode of phenomenality (the horizonal-transcendent) with phenomenality as such. But there is another mode of phenomenality, *absolutely original*, whose "how" is irreducible to the horizonal. This other mode is immanent self-revelation, the self-manifestation of the ego in radical interiority. The recognition of this other mode of phenomenality — overcoming the unilateral determination that has dominated "almost the whole history of human thought" — will inaugurate a new basis for philosophy. The historical claim is striking: the entire history of Western philosophy, from Parmenides and Plato through Descartes, Kant, Hegel, Husserl, and Heidegger, has operated under a single, unilateral conception of phenomenality — the conception of phenomenality as disclosure-in-a-horizon. Henry's book proposes to break this dominance by exhibiting an originary phenomenality that is not horizonal. This break is what §§ 8–70 of the book will argue for.

Now it so happens that this mode which designates the "how" of a revelation, the manner in which this revelation is accomplished — abstraction made of every consideration concerning content — has also, and that in a paradoxical way, a material signification. Originary revelation is to itself its own content. The "how" of this revelation is a real being. This phenomenon, or rather this manner of being a phenomenon that does not shine in the universal light, this "manner" that is a concrete being — this is what will be designated under the title of "ego." The paradox is that, in the case of originary revelation, the "how" and the "what" coincide: there is no distance between the mode of revelation and what is revealed, because what is revealed is the very self-revelation. The ego is not a content that is given in self-revelation; the ego just *is* the self-revealing as such. This is the thesis of the identity of self-manifestation and selfhood that will be worked out in Sections III–IV of the book, especially in the analyses of affectivity, pathos, and self-affection.

**Paragraph 9\.** What permits something to be by manifesting itself is what we call a foundation. This foundation concerns, obviously, the mode of manifestation of the something that manifests itself. Now this mode of manifestation refers (insofar as by "manifestation" one designates the work or the product of transcendence) to a mode of revelation more originary. Transcendence rests on immanence. Originary truth is the true foundation. It is the ontological condition of possibility of all transcendent phenomena which it grounds insofar as it is the origin of transcendence. It is itself, however, a phenomenon, but in an irreducible sense, insofar as it is an immanent revelation. The fact that the foundation be a "phenomenon" in the sense of a "revelation" is what confers on this foundation its reality by giving it the moment of presence.

This paragraph crystallizes Henry's thesis. Transcendence (ek-static manifestation in a horizon) rests on immanence (self-revelation in radical interiority). Immanent revelation is the true foundation — it is the condition of possibility of all transcendent phenomena, because it is the origin of transcendence itself. And crucially, this immanent revelation is itself a phenomenon — but in an *irreducible* sense, that is, in a sense not governed by the structure of horizonal disclosure. It is phenomenon because it is self-revealing; it is not transcendent phenomenon because its self-revealing is not an ek-static exposure in a horizon. The "moment of presence" it possesses is not the presence of a being-given-in-the-light but the presence of self-affection, of self-feeling, of self-immanent coincidence. This presence is such, when it concerns the origin, that it is not submitted to a horizon of presence and is not either the being — in truth never present — of the horizon itself. This originary ontological presence, which escapes the general conditions of being, is that of the ego itself. The phenomenological being of the ego is one with the originary revelation that accomplishes itself in a sphere of radical immanence. The reality of the foundation rests on its phenomenal character. But insofar as this character follows from a strictly determinate mode of revelation, the reality of the foundation is, at the same stroke, perfectly defined. The reality of ontological possibility is the being of the ego.

This is the thesis, fully stated: the condition of possibility of all manifestation (of all transcendent phenomena) is a reality — a real foundation — that is itself manifest, but in an irreducible mode (immanent self-revelation). This reality is identical with the ego. The being of the ego is therefore not a regional being alongside others; it is the ontological foundation as such, realized in the mode of self-immanent revelation. The formula "*La réalité de la possibilité ontologique est l'être de l'ego*" is the single condensed statement of the book's thesis.

**Paragraph 10\.** If the foundation is itself a phenomenon, and that in an originary sense, it appears that the way of access to the foundation is no other than the foundation itself. What remains, however, in this fundamental identity of its reality and of an "arriving" at this reality, is life itself, the transcendental life of the absolute ego insofar as it is the ultimate foundation. The foundation is not something obscure; it is neither light (which becomes perceptible only on the thing that shines in it) nor the thing itself (as "transcendent phenomenon"), but an immanent revelation that is a presence-to-itself, though such a presence remains "invisible." An immanent revelation is an interior experience; it necessarily takes on a monadic form. It is in the eidetic structure of originary truth that is rooted the ipseity of the ego. An interior experience understood in the sense of an originary revelation that accomplishes itself in a sphere of radical immanence, exists by itself, without any context, without the support of any exterior and "real" being; it is itself precisely an "existence" or, to say it better, existence itself, the existence that it is fitting to think under the title of "human reality." Such an existence owes nothing to transcendence; it precedes it, on the contrary, and renders it possible. More originary than the truth of being is the truth of man.

Several major themes are here introduced: (i) *Life* (*la vie*) is named as the transcendental life of the absolute ego, understood as the ultimate foundation. This is the first appearance of "life" as a technical term in the book — and it will become central, especially in Sections III–IV, where "auto-révélation de la vie" (self-revelation of life) will be the thematic center of Henry's positive construction. (ii) The *invisibility* of the foundation: it is neither light nor the thing-that-shines, but a self-presence that remains invisible. This is Henry's famous inversion of the metaphor of phenomenality: classical phenomenology is a phenomenology of the visible (of what can be seen, intuited, brought into the light); Henry proposes a phenomenology of the invisible, of what is revealed precisely without being made visible in any horizon. This inversion will be worked out in the opening sections of the book (§§ 11–31), where Henry argues that the "essence of manifestation" is not *Sichzeigen* (showing-itself) but *Sichempfinden* (self-feeling). (iii) The *monadic* form of immanent revelation: Henry invokes the Leibnizian monad (cited in the bibliography) to indicate that immanent revelation is self-contained, "without window" on the exterior, because its reality coincides with its self-revelation. This is not a cosmological thesis (there is not a plurality of substances-without-windows arranged in a hierarchy); it is a structural thesis about the mode of being of the self-revealing ego. (iv) The *ipseity* of the ego: the selfhood of the ego (its *ipséité*) is rooted in the structure of originary truth, which is to say, in the structure of immanent self-revelation. Selfhood is not a formal identity ("I \= I") but a phenomenological-ontological structure: to be a self is to be self-revealing in immanence. (v) *Existence* is redefined: it is not the existence of Dasein (which is ek-static, horizonal, transcending) but the interior experience of immanent revelation. This is a direct polemic against Heidegger's existential analytic. The "human reality" of Corbin's French translation of *Dasein* is here reappropriated by Henry in a non-Heideggerian sense: "human reality" properly means not the being that is thrown into a world-horizon but the self-revealing life that is the ultimate foundation. (vi) *More originary than the truth of being is the truth of man*. This is a striking reversal of the late Heideggerian dictum that the truth of being is more originary than the truth of man (as Heidegger argues in the *Brief über den Humanismus*). Henry turns the dictum around: the self-revelation of the ego (the truth of man) is the origin from which the truth of being (the horizon of transcendence) derives, not the other way around. This is the most compressed formulation of the book's anti-Heideggerian thesis.

**Paragraph 11\.** The interpretation of the essence of the foundation as immanent originary revelation leads us to rethink the essential connection that unites ontology and phenomenology. The phenomenological mode of treatment that ontology rightly wants to apply to the problem of the foundation remains in fact totally indeterminate as long as the signification of the concept of phenomenon has not been fixed in a decisive way. More still, this mode of treatment shows itself to be essentially dangerous as long as the problematic continues to progress in the light of a unilateral conception of the "phenomenon." Insofar as it interprets itself as "phenomenological," ontology understands its task as an "elucidation." To elucidate — does this not mean to render manifest, to bring into the light? Elucidation receives the signification of an intuitive realization, of a progress in evidence. What has need of such an elucidation can effectively be determined, on the other hand, only as "what does not first show itself" but remains most often "hidden." In fact, the methodological work of phenomenology is already interpreted in the light of a philosophy of transcendence. Phenomenology receives a radically different signification when it understands that its task is not to submit the reality to be elucidated — for example, the foundation — to a univocal type of manifestation conceived as the universal transcendental truth, but to ask itself whether there does not exist another mode of revelation, the taking into consideration of which can alone introduce us to the problem of the foundation. The ultimate signification of phenomenology holds in this, that it is finally the discovery of a "phenomenon" which is the foundation itself.

This paragraph presents the methodological consequence of the thesis. If the foundation is immanent self-revelation, then phenomenology must not simply "elucidate" it in the classical sense (bringing into the light of intuitive evidence), because such elucidation presupposes already the horizonal-transcendent conception of phenomenality. Phenomenology must rather *discover* or *recognize* a mode of phenomenality — the immanent — that is not governed by the elucidation-into-light paradigm. The double citation from *Sein und Zeit* §7 on phenomenology as making manifest what is hidden registers Heidegger's own classical formulation; Henry's point is that this formulation assumes that phenomenality \= showing-itself-in-the-light, an assumption that the thesis of immanent revelation overturns. Still, this "discovery" must be correctly understood, for it does not signify a "bringing to light" of something primitively "hidden." If there is a sense to saying that the foundation is an originary revelation, it is because the ontological condition of possibility of every effective transcendent presence is itself present to itself at the heart of an internal transcendental experience which can, strictly speaking, neither be "obtained" nor "lost." To want to "bring to light" the foundation is the ultimate ontological absurdity. The ego has not to manifest itself in the milieu of transcendent being, one day or another, sooner or later, in the course of a history, individual or universal, or at the heart of the progress of philosophy, if it is true that it is already present to itself at the heart of a revelation that owes nothing to time or to transcendence, but accomplishes itself in the sphere of radical immanence of absolute subjectivity.

A crucial point: immanent self-revelation is not something that needs to be brought to light — it is always already present to itself. Philosophy does not *discover* the foundation in the sense of revealing something that was hidden; it recognizes the foundation as what has always been present in the very act of philosophizing (and in every act of consciousness, of feeling, of life). The ego is not at the end of a phenomenological history; it is the always-accomplished self-presence in every phenomenological moment. The rejection of a *historical* progressive disclosure of the foundation is here a direct swipe at the Hegelian and Heideggerian historicities (whether the history of Spirit or the *Seinsgeschichte*): the self-revelation of the ego is *not* historical, it is not acquired over time, it is not "progress." It is the always-already of life.

**Paragraph 12\.** One can ask oneself whether it is not on the sole condition of losing all methodological interest that phenomenology is susceptible of taking on this ultimate ontological signification. Why must the foundation undergo the treatment of a method that aims essentially to draw from obscurity, to "clarify," if it belongs to the foundation, in principle, to reveal itself? Where can the progression of a research that takes as its theme what has already revealed itself, such as it is in itself, indeed be? In what can the necessity of such a research — which is nothing other than philosophy itself — legitimate itself? In truth, the goal of this work is to show that there exists an absolute knowledge and that this knowledge is not solidary with any progression whatsoever. Such knowledge is not linked, indeed, to a determinate mode of existence; it is not the privilege of a moment. It is rather the very milieu of existence, the essence of life. The "utility" of philosophy is not put into question by the thought that thinks the essence of life as originary immanent revelation. What there is of the simplest and the most "evident," we know of old that it is also what there is of the most "difficult." It is precisely because the foundation is a revelation that philosophy is possible, and that in a well-determined sense, as phenomenological philosophy. There is no need, no doubt, to "elucidate" the being of the foundation, but the phenomenological method does not reduce to the process of elucidation; this must cease to be understood in a unilateral sense. Phenomenology is rather a critique of every revelation, of its different forms and of its fundamental conditions. It is in this sense that it has a universal signification.

The paragraph answers a self-posed objection. If immanent self-revelation is always already accomplished, why do philosophy at all? Why does the philosopher need to say anything? Henry's answer has two parts. First, what is simplest and most evident is also most difficult (the formula recalls the *axiôma* of Aristotle and Heidegger's quotation of Aristotle on the obviousness and obscurity of being, from *Sein und Zeit* §1). Second, phenomenology is not merely the elucidation of what is hidden but the critique of revelation itself — of its different forms (transcendent/immanent) and of its fundamental conditions. So conceived, phenomenology has the task of distinguishing modes of manifestation, of exhibiting their respective structures and their relations. It is not a work of bringing-to-light but a work of discrimination and of grounding. *This* is how phenomenology has universal signification: not as the universal clarification of everything (Husserlian ideal) but as the universal critique of manifestation as such.

**Paragraph 13\.** When it is correctly understood, the task of phenomenology appears in all its complexity. The problem of knowing what mode of phenomenological treatment it is fitting to make the foundation undergo is none other than that of the relations between philosophy and life. The deepening of this problem, in which is decided, indeed, the foundation of philosophy, puts us in presence of extraordinary difficulties, all of which converge toward the question of the possibility of an "absolutely subjective science" — a science of which Husserl thought himself the possessor. The understanding of these difficulties leads reflection to the idea that if philosophy is second with respect to life, there must however exist a mode of philosophizing that does not harm the essence.

This is a statement of profound philosophical humility, and of the distinction between philosophy and life that will structure Henry's entire subsequent oeuvre. Life is primary; philosophy is always secondary to life (because life is the self-revelation that precedes every philosophizing). But this does not mean that philosophy is impossible or worthless; there must exist a mode of philosophizing *that does not harm the essence* — that does not distort or reduce the self-revelation of life by treating it with the wrong methodological apparatus. Husserl thought he had found this mode in the phenomenological reduction and the transcendental ego; Henry thinks Husserl was mistaken (for the reasons §5 exhibited). The proper mode of philosophizing that respects life is what Henry's whole philosophy will try to articulate. The phrase "absolutely subjective science" is Husserl's (from the late manuscripts); Henry takes it up as the shared aspiration of phenomenology but argues that it cannot be realized within the Husserlian framework.

**Paragraph 14\.** To such a mode of philosophizing, thought raises itself only when it is capable of accomplishing, and that in a decisive way, an overcoming of intuitionism. Now the overcoming of intuitionism is not effective as long as it presents itself as a reflection on the transcendental conditions that render possible the realization of a presence in intuition or in evidence — that is, as a liberation of the universal phenomenological horizon. It is no more so when it consists in the integration of a philosophy of intuition into a transcendental philosophy of constitution. In both cases, and however different the paths on which philosophical reflection engages, this reflection remains in fact exclusively conditioned by the preoccupations of a problematic of the object. Despite essential transformations, research remains in fact incapable of crossing the limits that were its own when Kant gave it that ontological signification that we so admire.

A decisive methodological statement. The "overcoming of intuitionism" that §3 announced is not truly accomplished by either of the two Husserlian or Heideggerian strategies: (i) reflecting on the transcendental conditions of evidence (Husserl's move in *Ideen I* and after) — which is still intuitionism, because it still treats the intuited given as what must be conditioned; (ii) integrating a philosophy of intuition into a transcendental philosophy of constitution (which is just a more sophisticated version of the same). Both remain trapped in what Henry calls the "problematic of the object" — the thought-structure according to which manifestation is always manifestation-of-an-object-for-a-subject. Kant is named as the patron of this structure: the First *Critique*'s ontological signification, which Henry ironically says "we so admire," consists precisely in making the condition of possibility of objects into the fundamental ontological problem. This is what Henry wants to overcome: the idea that ontology is about conditions of possibility of objects. Real overcoming of intuitionism requires moving to a domain in which there are neither objects nor subjects but only immanent self-revelation — which is life.

If the "critique of the paralogism of rational psychology" has been chosen to make the object of an ontological destruction that brings into light the absence of any ontology of subjectivity at the heart of a problematic that claims to make the ego its explicit theme, it is because the signification of this destruction interests, we believe, the whole of modern philosophy. The metaphysical themes of modern philosophy result, despite their apparent novelty, from the fundamental imperfections that become particularly visible in Kantian philosophy but that corrupt, in fact, philosophical thought since its Hellenic origin. Henry announces (and the footnote, note 12, confirms he has not been able to include this in the present book) a separate work devoted to a destruction of Kant's Paralogisms: the point of this destruction would be to show that at the very place where Kant explicitly addresses the being of the thinking subject (the Paralogisms of the First *Critique*, A341/B399 ff.), there is no ontology of subjectivity at all — Kant's treatment of the "I think" is purely formal and misses the being of the subject. The scandal is that this deficiency characterizes not only Kant but the whole of modern philosophy — and indeed, Henry claims, philosophy since its Hellenic origin. The historical reach of Henry's thesis is maximal.

The *cogito* of Descartes or the philosophy of existence of Kierkegaard do not play, with respect to modern "culture," the role of a commencement. They correspond, at most, to historical moments at which there "manifests" itself paradoxically in the history of philosophy a current of thought which remains most often underlying, and that for essential reasons. Henry names his own lineage — the *cogito* of Descartes (insofar as it can be disentangled from its onto-theological wrapping) and the philosophy of existence of Kierkegaard — as isolated "manifestations" of a subterranean tradition. This tradition (which also includes Maine de Biran, Fichte, and, in ways Henry treats elsewhere, Marx, Nietzsche, and certain religious thinkers) is the tradition of *radical subjectivity* or of *interior experience*, which has always existed in Western philosophy but has always been marginalized by the dominant (horizonal-ek-static) tradition that runs from Plato through Heidegger.

**Paragraph 15\.** These reasons become precisely comprehensible to the thought which, in operating the radical overcoming of intuitionism, reveals itself capable of calling into question the ontological primacy of transcendence. To such a thought is given to advance into a new region and, in that, also to confer on ontology a new dimension. The universal light is not the abode of all phenomena. The "invisible" is the mode of a positive, and in truth, fundamental revelation. The ambiguity of a philosophy of the Night dissolves before the gaze of the reflection that distinguishes from the obscurity, which is the lot of transcendence, the first interior tremor of knowing in which, this side of light, knowing first reveals itself to itself.

This is a culminating moment of the Introduction. The positive thesis: *the universal light is not the abode of all phenomena*. Some phenomena — and the most fundamental ones, the ones that concern life and selfhood — are not phenomena of the light at all; their mode of revelation is the "invisible." The "invisible" (*l'invisible*) is Henry's name for the phenomenality of immanence: what is revealed not by being exposed to a horizon of visibility but by being given to itself in self-affection. The reference to a "philosophy of the Night" is a deliberate allusion to German Romanticism (Novalis's *Hymnen an die Nacht*) and to certain mystical-theological traditions (John of the Cross, the Eckhartian *Abgrund*). Henry wants to distinguish his own "invisible" — which is a positive fundamental revelation — from Romantic obscurantism or mystical ineffability. "The obscurity that is the lot of transcendence" (the Heideggerian *Verborgenheit*) is one thing; the "interior tremor of knowing" in which knowing reveals itself to itself before the advent of light is quite another. The second is not obscure; it is invisibly clear, clear to itself in its immanence, without requiring the element of light.

Now if the mode in conformity with which the manifestation of any phenomenon is accomplished is always transcendent with respect to the material content of this phenomenon, it is no longer the same in the case of the originary phenomenon of revelation. This phenomenon, understood in the sense of a manner of revealing itself, in the sense of a "how," is, on the foundation of its essential identity with itself, coextensive with its content. Every manifestation is in principle inadequate. But where there is no transcendence, there is no finitude either.

The concluding formulation is luminous. In all horizonal manifestation, the "how" (the mode of appearing) is transcendent to (distinct from) the "what" (the content appearing); this is why horizonal manifestation is always inadequate — the phenomenon is given "in person" but never exhaustively, always by *Abschattungen*, always with a horizon of unfulfilled co-intentions. In the case of immanent self-revelation, by contrast, the "how" and the "what" coincide: the mode of self-revealing just is the content self-revealed. Therefore self-revelation is *adequate* — not in the Husserlian sense of an exhausted intuitive presence, but in a stronger sense: the structure of self-revelation involves no distance between mode and content, no horizon of co-intentions, no fundamental inadequacy. And *where there is no transcendence, there is no finitude either*. The finitude of all intuitive manifestation, which §3 diagnosed, is rooted in the ek-static structure of transcendence. In immanent self-revelation, there is no such structure, and therefore no such finitude. This is one of the most radical claims in the book: life's self-revelation is *infinite*, not because it comprehends everything but because its structure is free of the finitude that marks every horizonal manifestation.

**Paragraph 16\.** The sphere of absolute knowledge is rigorously defined. The ontological work that arrives at the determination of this sphere is none other than that which permits reflection to pose the problem of self-knowledge on a correct basis. As long as philosophy remains prisoner to the idea of a transcendent horizon of human knowledge, the relation of the ego to itself cannot be understood except as a particular case of the transcendental relation of being-in-the-world. Once fallacious interpretations of being that most often command the existential understanding of oneself are set aside, it remains that, on the ontological plane, the problem of the being of the ego is legitimately subordinated to that of the sense of being in general — that is, to the problematic of transcendence. Relation to self can only be produced in errancy. The problem of self-knowledge is posed on a completely new basis when, in the light of the problematic of immanence, this knowledge ceases to be envisaged as a "relation."

The final paragraphs rapidly draw consequences from the thesis. First: self-knowledge. Traditional philosophy thinks self-knowledge as a *relation* — the ego relates to itself as to an object (Kant's "I think"), or via a reflective act (Fichte's *Tathandlung*, in one reading), or via a horizonal return through the world (Heidegger's analytic of Dasein's self-understanding through its possibilities). In all these cases, self-knowledge requires the mediation of a horizon, a distance, an ek-static movement — and therefore, Henry says, self-knowledge "can only be produced in errancy" (*errance*, a Heideggerian term for the drift of Dasein in the history of being, from *Vom Wesen der Wahrheit*). But in the problematic of immanence, self-knowledge is not a relation at all; it is the primordial self-presence of the ego to itself in its self-revelation. The ego does not *know* itself by stepping back and representing itself; it *is* itself as self-revealed, and this being is already knowing. The dissolution of the relational structure of self-knowledge is one of the major consequences of Henry's thesis.

The refutation of the transcendence of the ego plays, with regard to the ensemble of ontological theses advanced in these investigations, the role of a demonstration by the absurd. The concept of alienation loses all ontological signification when the problematic has brought into light the transcendental immanence of the ego and when the relations of absolute subjectivity and time have been defined in conformity with the *eidos* of this immanence. The understanding of the existential signification of human alienation requires that a rigorous distinction be established between the plane of existence and that of ontology. This same distinction, understood in its relation with the problem of alienation, permits reflection to prepare the paths to an understanding of the essence of freedom.

The "refutation of the transcendence of the ego" is a direct reference to Sartre's 1937 essay of the same title (*La Transcendance de l'ego*); Henry has already criticized Sartre's thesis in §4. Here Henry announces that the *refutation* of Sartre's thesis — that is, the demonstration that the ego is *not* transcendent but immanent — functions as a "demonstration by the absurd" for the rest of the book's theses. The concept of alienation (Hegelian-Marxian-Sartrian) loses ontological signification when the ego is understood as transcendentally immanent: there is no ontological alienation of the ego from itself because the ego cannot be external to itself. The distinction between "existence" (where alienation can occur, as a matter of historical-cultural condition) and "ontology" (where alienation is impossible, as a matter of the structure of the ego's self-revelation) is crucial and must be rigorously maintained. This distinction also prepares an understanding of freedom: freedom, for Henry, is not the freedom of the transcendent subject (the Sartrian for-itself that surpasses its facticity) but the freedom rooted in the immanent self-possession of life.

**Paragraph 17\.** In tearing existence away from the absolute milieu of exteriority, the present investigations wish to draw attention to the "subjective" character of this existence; they invite us to ask ourselves whether it is not fitting, today, to give back a sense to the concept of "interior life."

The Introduction closes with a single, final sentence that is both programmatic and polemical. Against all philosophies of exteriority (whether Husserlian-egological, Heideggerian-existential, Sartrian-nihilating, Marxist-materialist, structuralist-linguistic), Henry wants to reclaim the concept of "interior life" (*vie intérieure*). The scare-quotes acknowledge that the phrase has become, by the mid-twentieth century, almost unusable — the preserve of devotional literature or psychological introspection, looked down upon by academic philosophy. But Henry proposes to give it back a philosophically rigorous sense: "interior life" names the sphere of radical immanence in which the self-revelation of life is accomplished, the sphere whose phenomenological-ontological structure is what the book sets out to elucidate. The whole work that follows — Section I on the ontological horizon of being, Section II on phenomenality as manifestation, Section III on affectivity and immanence, Section IV on life as the essence of manifestation — is the working-out of this final sentence. The Introduction has built, through the dialectical ladder of §§1–7, the philosophical situation in which the thesis of interior life becomes intelligible and necessary. What follows in the body of the book is the positive phenomenological-ontological elaboration of this thesis.

---

## **Closing synoptic observations**

The Introduction accomplishes several distinct but interlocking tasks. First, it traces a historical genealogy: Descartes → Husserl → Heidegger → Sartre, showing how each successive step in modern phenomenological thought inherits and refines, but fails to overcome, a single unilateral conception of phenomenality (manifestation as horizonal transcendence). Second, it argues the negative thesis: every attempt to reach the fundamental from within this unilateral conception fails — whether by Cartesian apodicticity, Husserlian regional ontology, or Heideggerian fundamental ontology. Third, it introduces the positive thesis: there exists another mode of phenomenality — immanent self-revelation — whose structure is irreducible to the horizonal, and this mode is what constitutes the being of the ego (or of life, or of interior experience). Fourth, it sketches the architectonic of the book: Section I will formulate explicitly the problem of "ontological monism" (the doctrine that all manifestation has one single structure); Sections II and III will work out the phenomenological-ontological structure of immanent revelation; Section IV will name this structure as the self-affection of life and derive its consequences.

The seven sections of the Introduction form a genuine dialectical sequence. §§1–2 establish the need to move from the Cartesian *cogito* through regional ontology to universal phenomenological ontology. §3 overcomes intuitionism and liberates the phenomenological horizon. §§4–5 try to reinsert the *cogito* in the liberated horizon and diagnose the aporia of this insertion. §6 transposes the aporia into Heideggerian fundamental ontology and exhibits the ambiguity of Dasein. §7 draws the conclusion: the aporia cannot be resolved within the framework of ontological monism; a different mode of phenomenality must be recognized; this mode is immanent self-revelation; and this self-revelation is the being of the ego.

Several themes, introduced here in the Introduction, will be developed at length in the body of the book:

* *Ontological monism* (the thesis of the homogeneity of being), diagnosed here in §6 and §7, will be explicitly named and argued against in Section I.  
* *The essence of manifestation*, invoked here as the absolute essence whose elucidation is the task of universal phenomenological ontology, will be analyzed throughout Section II as the structure of phenomenality as such.  
* *Immanence*, introduced here in §7 as the sphere of the self-revelation of the ego, will be developed in Section III as the structure of *Leben*, *pathos*, and self-affection.  
* *Auto-révélation* and the phenomenality of the invisible will be the explicit theme of Section IV, the culmination of the book.

Henry's engagement with the phenomenological tradition is thus not dialectical in the Hegelian sense (an *Aufhebung* that preserves what it negates) but rather destructive-foundational in a sense closer to Heidegger's own *Destruktion*: an overturning of the reigning conception of phenomenality in order to make visible a more originary structure that has always been operative but has never been thematized. The figures who preside over this destructive-foundational project — Descartes (in his most radical, Cartesian moment), Maine de Biran (not named but implicit throughout), Fichte (cited in the bibliography as "F"), Kierkegaard ("D"), Nietzsche, and Husserl (in his most radical, *First Philosophy* and *Cartesian Meditations* moments) — constitute Henry's subterranean tradition of radical subjectivity. Against the reigning tradition (Plato-Aristotle-Kant-Hegel-Heidegger, a tradition of horizonal transcendence), this subterranean tradition is what the book means to recover and radicalize.

The single most condensed formulation of the book's thesis, given in §7 paragraph 9, bears repeating: "*La réalité de la possibilité ontologique est l'être de l'ego*" — the reality of ontological possibility is the being of the ego. The possibility of anything manifesting itself at all is grounded in the actual, self-revelatory presence-to-itself of life in its radical immanence. This is the thesis the book sets out to defend; and the Introduction has prepared the stage on which the defense can be mounted.

# Section I. Elucidation of the concept of phenomenon: ontological monism

## **§ 8\. The elucidation of the essence of the phenomenon, central task of phenomenology**

**Paragraph 1\.** Phenomenology is the science of phenomena. The opening sentence of Section I — and indeed of the body of the entire book — picks up the thread that the Introduction broke off at §7 paragraph 17\. The whole Introduction was preparatory: it established the *necessity* of recognizing a non-horizonal mode of phenomenality (immanent self-revelation) and the *insufficiency* of all attempts to derive the being of the ego from the structure of the horizon. The body of the book now begins by returning to the most apparently humble and disciplinary question — *what is phenomenology?* — and works it through to the same conclusion at the level of methodological principle. This means that phenomenology is a description, anterior to every theory and independent of every presupposition, of all that is proposed to us, in the quality of existent, in whatever order or whatever domain. Understood as a description, phenomenology implies the rejection of every hypothesis, of every principle that has a unifying value (real or supposed) with regard to a group of knowledges and, finally, with regard to a sector of reality which would find in such a principle a rule of intelligibility, even a necessary condition of its existence.

The opening definition is strictly Husserlian: phenomenology is *Beschreibung*, descriptive science, anti-theoretical, anti-explanatory, anti-hypothetical. This is the methodological program that Husserl announces in the Foreword to the *Logical Investigations* (Halle, 1900\) and recapitulates in *Ideen I* §§18–26 and §24 (the "principle of all principles"): phenomenology presupposes nothing, accepts only what gives itself in the manner in which it gives itself, and brackets every theoretical construction. Henry takes this Husserlian definition as the starting-point because it is the *received self-understanding* of phenomenology — and it is precisely this self-understanding that the section will progressively unfold and complicate.

Science, it is true, is concerned to go beyond the facts and to coordinate them in systems of explanation. But, in all cases, the scientific element and the ensemble in which it enters refer necessarily to a phenomenological given without which they would, strictly speaking, have no sense. More still, these elements and these systems exist for us themselves only as givens. They juxtapose themselves in the phenomenological milieu with the very reality they claim to explain. This reality, consequently, could not be totally reduced — no more, indeed, than scientific reality itself, in all its forms, could be reduced. Their explanatory value once put between brackets (but subsisting under that title), theories penetrate into our environment as data. As such, they require also the attention of the phenomenologist who is capable of describing the structures of their own configurations.

This is the Husserlian doctrine of the *Lebenswelt*: scientific theories and their products do not float free of the phenomenological field; they are themselves *givens* within that field, with their own modes of presentation, their own configurations. Husserl develops this most fully in the *Crisis* (especially Part III), but it is already present in *Ideen I* and in *Formal and Transcendental Logic*. The phenomenologist's task is not to compete with science by giving rival explanations, nor simply to dismiss science, but to describe the structures of how scientific objects, theories, and procedures appear within the phenomenological milieu. The mistrust that phenomenology shows with regard to philosophical or scientific conceptions holds only to the fact that these most often mask from us a reality whose characters and proper sense they forget or travesty in claiming to explain it. But, on closer view, this mistrust is not discernible from a taking-into-consideration; it is the index of a positive work. What is, in the first place and most often, altered by theories, is the very sense of theoretical work and of its products. It is with regard to the signification of ensembles constituted as explanatory principles that phenomenology accomplishes first its work of preservation; it is the being of scientific objects and of the groups they constitute that it restitutes in its integrity in conferring on it a status. It is phenomenology that defends science against the temptation of being a new metaphysics by interdicting it from constituting itself as an absolute reality, and by operating on the contrary the insertion of edifices and abstract principles into the context of human experience. If the scientific object is the same as the object of this experience, it is not only because it refers necessarily to an object of experience (sensible or not), but because it is itself an object of experience.

This is the opening polemic against scientism in the Husserlian sense: science misunderstands itself when it treats its own constructed objects as the absolute reality (the temptation Husserl diagnosed in the natural sciences and especially in the Galilean mathematization of nature, *Crisis* §9). Phenomenology preserves science precisely by reinserting it in the experiential field from which it abstracts. Henry endorses the program — but, as the section will develop, he will press it further than Husserl did, asking what conception of "experience" and what conception of "phenomenon" governs Husserl's own program.

**Paragraph 2\.** If the concept of phenomenology is easy to grasp in its negative signification — insofar as it implies the bracketing of all the interpretations and constructions that theoretical thought superposes on the real, to the point of taking its own products for reality and hypostatizing them under an absolute form — its positive determination, precisely because it aims to introduce us into the kingdom of positivity, demands an analysis. This must be centered on the idea of phenomenon, since, as the science of phenomena, phenomenology claims to confine itself exclusively to what manifests itself, precisely as it manifests itself. *It is we*, said Husserl, *who are the true positivists.* It is assuredly a matter here of refusing empiricism and of recognizing as a source of right for knowledge "not only empirical vision, but vision in general, as originarily donative consciousness in all its forms." The citation is from *Ideen I* §24 — the famous "principle of all principles." Henry endorses Husserl's reformulation of "positivism": the true positivism is not the empiricist restriction of evidence to sensible intuition, but the broader phenomenological positivism that recognizes every mode of originary giving as a legitimate source of knowledge (sensible, eidetic, categorial, etc.).

It is when the properly theoretical element of knowledge confines itself to expressing the intuitive given in significations that correspond rigorously to it that it can serve, as foundation, for the ulterior development of knowledge and be thus what Husserl calls an "absolute commencement," or again a "principle." Because it rests exactly on what shows itself in itself such as it is, the phenomenological statement claims to have an absolute value. Absolute is indeed the appearance to which it refers, insofar precisely as it is an appearance. What appears is what one cannot refuse, what escapes reduction. A truly positive science is then possible insofar as it constantly refers to such an appearance. Because it wants to entrust itself to this appearance and restitute to it all its dimensions, phenomenology liberates the foundation on which can be re-established "in their old right metaphysics and, at the same time, being and life, as absolute givens." And elsewhere, Scheler adds: "A philosophy founded on the phenomenological intuition of the essence must affirm that absolute being is knowable, in an evident and adequate way, in every sphere of the exterior and interior world."

The two citations are from Max Scheler's early phenomenological essays (in *Vom Umsturz der Werte* and elsewhere). Scheler's appearance here is significant: he is, with the early Heidegger, one of the German phenomenologists who pushed Husserlian phenomenology furthest in the direction of an ontology of being, life, and the absolute. By citing Scheler, Henry signals that he reads phenomenology not narrowly as an epistemology of evidence (the "logical-positivist" reading of Husserl one might caricature) but as the discipline that opens onto an ontology of the absolute. The phenomenological method, properly understood, restores being and life to their philosophical dignity by showing that they can be apodictically given in evident intuition. This is the maximalist phenomenological program — and Henry's whole project will be both to honor it and to show that it has been mis-realized by Husserl himself, because Husserl's conception of "appearance" is too narrow.

**Paragraph 3\.** A philosophy that leans on the given does not however elude the problem of non-truth.
