But it has the means to substitute, for the traditional problematic of error, that, more radical, of illusion, which justifies in fact appearance, whose "content" is always "true," illusion resulting from the inadequate transport of a *Sachverhalt* into another stratum of being than its own. As for error, which is, all in all, only a particular case of illusion, it consists in the establishment of an inadequate relation between a *Sachverhalt* thought in the judgment and the corresponding *Sachverhalt* present in intuition.

The vocabulary is Husserlian-Schelerian: *Sachverhalt* is "state-of-affairs," the categorial unity given in a categorial intuition (developed in Husserl's sixth *Logical Investigation*, especially §§40–48). Henry's point is that phenomenology, by treating appearance as the ultimate datum, transforms the classical problem of error: error is no longer the discrepancy between a representation and a thing-in-itself (the realist conception) but the discrepancy between two phenomenological strata — the *Sachverhalt* as judged and the *Sachverhalt* as intuited. Even illusion has a content that is always "true" *qua* appearance; the illusion lies not in the appearance as such but in the wrong inference about what stratum of being the appearance belongs to. (One thinks here of the classic example of the Müller-Lyer illusion: the lines do truly *appear* to be of unequal length; the illusion is only the inference that they *are* of unequal length.) But the phenomenon of knowledge always and in all cases refers to a given, to an appearance which plays the role of ultimate foundation and which it is only a question of understanding in its own sense and of situating on the plane of being which is its own. For that, it suffices to let the appearance appear such as it appears and simply to read in it what is indicated.

The methodological optimism here is fully Husserlian: every phenomenological problem can in principle be resolved by *letting the appearance appear* and by *reading off* its sense and its proper plane of being. This optimism will be put under pressure in the next paragraphs.

**Paragraph 4\.** The absolute signification of phenomenology is thus founded on the presence of the thing — that is, on its appearance. When one interprets phenomenology in a philosophy of consciousness, this absolute signification is translated by a dogmatism of intentionality which, because it attains being itself, is susceptible of furnishing to the "ontological argument" a real foundation. But if the relation of the thing to consciousness makes of the thing — insofar as it is a phenomenological given — an absolute, the signification of this absolute appears very quickly to be relative.

Here begins the critical pivot of §8. Husserlian phenomenology, when interpreted as a philosophy of consciousness (i.e., when the *cogitatum* is taken as a phenomenological absolute given to the *cogitatio*), produces a peculiar structure: the appearance is absolute (it cannot be denied, cannot be reduced), but its absoluteness is *relative* — relative to the consciousness for which it is an appearance. The reference to the "ontological argument" is sly: Husserl himself in *Ideen I* §49 explicitly draws the parallel between phenomenology's claim that consciousness is the "absolute being" and the Anselmian-Cartesian ontological argument; and the late Husserl (especially in unpublished manuscripts) was preoccupied with the problem of the relation between transcendental subjectivity and "God." Henry signals that this peculiar absoluteness of the phenomenon-for-consciousness is not really absolute at all, because absoluteness here means "indubitably given to consciousness," not "self-grounded as such."

This is because every appearance as such surrounds itself with a zone of shadow. The phenomenological given encloses within itself implications whose sense is, each time, to refer back to something that is *not there*. Is not the signification of phenomenology envisaged as method, however, precisely to pursue the elucidation of "what is 'implied' by the sense of the *cogitatum* without being intuitively given," to extend thus the reign of appearance — that is, of light and of reality, and of rationality also, which finds in appearance its foundation? But the accomplishment of phenomenological work cannot, despite its positive signification, totally dissipate the shadow that surrounds the appearance and comes to call into question its absolute character. There is no intuitive totality, because the elucidation of what is implied in the apparent given can be pursued only if this given makes the sacrifice of its presence to the ulterior unfolding of the phenomenological process.

The argument is acute. The phenomenological given is *absolute* (it is the indubitable foundation), but it is also surrounded by a "zone of shadow" — by horizonal implications that refer beyond what is given. The phenomenological method, as Husserl conceives it, is precisely the elucidation of these implications: the method works by progressively unfolding what is co-aimed but not yet presently given (the doctrine of horizons in *Cartesian Meditations* §19, and the doctrine of the infinite tasks of intentional analysis). But this method has a paradoxical structure: in order to unfold the implications, the originally given appearance must itself "sacrifice its presence" — that is, the phenomenological gaze must move from the present given to the unfolded implications, losing the original presence in the process. There is no "intuitive totality": no moment at which the entire field of phenomenological implications could be intuitively present together. The "absolute" given is therefore always surrounded by a non-given "shadow," and the absolute is thereby relativized.

And this interrogation rises before us as well: that to which appearance refers — is it susceptible of giving itself to us, in its turn, as appearance? Or does the finitude in virtue of which an appearance always demands to be elucidated not refer back to a more essential finitude in virtue of which this elucidation is, in fact, never possible? The questions are framed as open — but they are leading questions, and Henry's answer will be: yes, finitude is essential, the elucidation can never be completed, and therefore the Husserlian interpretation of the phenomenon as the absolute given to consciousness is fundamentally flawed.

**Paragraph 5\.** The law, in any case, that prescribes the putting-into-relation of appearance with a phenomenological process of explication remains foreign to natural consciousness, for which appearances simply succeed each other; foreign also to phenomenology so long as the latter does not understand itself otherwise than as a positivism — even in that enlarged sense which restitutes to the power of vision the plurality of its fundamental dimensions. This law, indeed, is that of the essence, which is not taken into consideration as long as thought confines itself to what appears as to the absolute. But such a thought remains at the level of a naïve and in some sense pre-critical interpretation of phenomenology; it makes use of a concept of phenomenon that remains in fact non-elaborated. What then makes phenomena possible in the sense of positivism? What founds for us the presence of what appears, if not the very act of appearing, the essence of phenomenon and of presence as such?

This is the decisive question of the section. Phenomenological positivism (which lets appearance appear and reads off what is given) takes the *fact of appearing* as its starting-point; but it does not interrogate the *act of appearing*, the essence of phenomenality as such. Phenomena are the products; phenomenality is the producing. Husserlian phenomenology — for all its sophistication about regions, horizons, and intentional analyses — remains, in Henry's reading, naïvely positivist insofar as it never asks what phenomenality itself is. The whole rest of Section I (and indeed Sections II–IV) will be devoted to this question. And while natural consciousness laments before the temporal destiny of being which befalls it, the thought that concerns itself with the essence understands the necessity of going back to the law that commands this destiny. For the content that appears to us each time is not responsible for this destiny; it rather undergoes it as a foreign law. But the reason that posits it in appearance escapes it just as does the one that tears it from existence. It is, in truth, only one and the same reason, only one and the same law, that founds and that suppresses, and the content does not contain it.

The Heideggerian background here is unmistakable: the "destiny of being" (*Schicksal*, *Geschick*), the "law" that is hidden from natural consciousness, the temporal arising and disappearing of beings — all this is the language of the late Heidegger of *Holzwege* and *Vorträge und Aufsätze*. Henry borrows the language to indicate that the law of phenomenality is not a content within phenomenality but a structural condition that exceeds every content. The natural consciousness, like the positivist phenomenologist, sees the contents but misses the law; the philosopher of essence sees that the contents are governed by a law that they do not themselves contain.

**Paragraph 6\.** The fundamental dependence of what appears with regard to the act of appearing demands that the latter henceforth make the theme of the problematic. This problematic aims at the presence of what is present; it refers to the essence on the foundation of which everything that is given to us can precisely be there for us. Its object is the mode of manifestation of what manifests itself; it is, as Hegel already said in commenting on the religions of light, "simple manifestation." The reference to Hegel is to the *Phenomenology of Spirit*, "Religion in the form of art" (or to the corresponding analyses in the *Lectures on the Philosophy of Religion*), where Hegel discusses the "religions of light" (Zoroastrianism) as religions in which the divine is grasped as pure manifestation, light as such, before any determinate content. Henry takes up the Hegelian formulation to indicate the level at which his own analysis operates: not this or that determinate manifestation, but manifestation as such, the light of phenomenality before any phenomenon-content.

To such an object thought arrives only when it is capable of overcoming the consideration of the singular existent that is proposed to us, in order to raise itself to the being of this existent — that is, to the act of appearing as such. The critique of positivism signifies that phenomenology could not be confused with a description of an ontic order, however extended its field, but that it acquires its properly philosophical signification only when it understands itself in its ontological design, in conformity with which it operates this overcoming of the existent toward the essence that founds it in its being. Phenomenology is the science of phenomena in their reality. Its object is not the ensemble of phenomena, with their structures and consequently their specific domains, but the essence of phenomenon as such. The phenomenological reduction does not seek to save certain contents considered as "certain" while others would be struck or suspended. The reality it releases as an irreducible foundation is not a privileged phenomenon; it is the omnipresent and universal essence of every phenomenon as such. For this reason, the phenomenological reduction is one with the eidetic reduction understood in an ultimate sense.

This is a powerful re-reading of the Husserlian doctrine of the reductions. In Husserl, the phenomenological (or transcendental) reduction is one operation (bracketing the natural attitude) and the eidetic reduction is another (passing from fact to essence). They are typically presented as separable. Henry collapses them into one when both are understood "in an ultimate sense": the true phenomenological-eidetic reduction is the move from contents (phenomena) to the essence of phenomenality (essence-of-phenomenon-as-such). This is no longer a regional eidetics (eidos of physical thing, eidos of psychic being, etc.) but a *fundamental* eidetics: the eidos of manifestation itself.

The reduction is the liberation of the essence which could not be reduced and which alone subsists, as condition. The reduction then introduces us into the sphere of the absolute. That the condition is the absolute follows from the fact that it is not posited by analysis and thought only as necessary. The condition is the essence of phenomenon, appearance as such, in its act of appearing. The transcendental truth to which the phenomenological reduction introduces us is not a mysterious reality \= x; it is truth itself, identified with being, insofar as "being" and "truth" designate nothing other than appearance as such. *Being and truth are contemporary*, says Heidegger. This means that the act of appearing is what confers being on every thing, and that truth, understood in a primary sense, is itself nothing other than this act of appearing considered in and for itself. This truth, insofar as it is transcendental, we can also call the *Form*. It is the formal element, properly ontological, to which every phenomenon belongs precisely insofar as it is a "phenomenon."

The cited phrase "being and truth are contemporary" (*Sein und Wahrheit sind gleichursprünglich*) is from Heidegger's *Sein und Zeit* §44, where Heidegger argues that truth is not a property of judgments or representations but the very disclosedness (*Erschlossenheit*) of being. Henry adopts this Heideggerian thesis as the formal expression of his own program: the essence of phenomenon \= appearance as such \= being \= truth \= the Form of phenomenality. All four terms designate the same structure: the act of manifesting that makes possible everything that manifests itself. The use of "Form" (capitalized) is striking — it signals that this is not a content, not a thing, but a pure structural condition, the condition of every content. The insufficiency of positivism holds to the fact that it does not give an account of the positivity it constantly presupposes in describing phenomena without having previously interrogated the phenomenal-being as such.

**Paragraph 7\.** Insofar as it attaches itself to the essence of phenomenon, the problematic that phenomenology institutes must be understood in its absolutely universal and fundamental signification. While error or, more exactly, illusion is — at least for phenomenological positivism — a problem, the reflection that aims at the essence of phenomenon finds in the examination of "simple appearance" a confirmation of its absolute character. For the essence is "the act of appearing of which even appearance has need to be a simple appearance." Error, illusion, truth (in a rational sense) are co-determined by a common foundation. It is the absolute truth that allows illusion to manifest itself and thus founds it in its being. Error is not for an instant separated from the absolute. The immanence of absolute knowledge at the heart of non-true knowledge is what permits us to respond to the question of Hegel: how can true knowledge make the proof of its truth against non-true knowledge? Will it simply affirm that it is the true knowledge? "By such an assurance," remarks Hegel, "it would in effect declare that its force resides in its being; but the non-true knowledge equally appeals to this same fact that it is."

The Hegelian reference is to the Introduction of the *Phenomenology of Spirit*, where Hegel asks how true knowledge can demonstrate its truth in the face of competing claims — and answers that the proof can lie only in the *Selbstbewegung* of consciousness through experience. Henry repurposes the Hegelian question to make a different point: any claim to knowledge — true or false, real or illusory — appeals to the same condition, namely, the act of appearing, the manifesting that makes anything claimable at all. Just as Hegel notes that the appeal to bare *being* is shared by true and false knowledge alike, so Henry notes that the appeal to bare *appearing* is shared by true and false phenomena alike. There is missing, however, in non-true knowledge only the understanding of the sense of its affirmation for it to be also a true and real knowledge. For the fact that non-true knowledge be — that is precisely what makes it a true knowledge, in an absolute sense. Knowledge is manifestation and, as such, the essence. Because it is a knowledge, non-true knowledge is also something that manifests itself; it bears within itself, as its condition, the act of manifesting itself — that is, the essence. In reflecting on the act of appearing, on the fact that knowledge — even apparent — appears, the problematic that aims at the essence reduces to itself and subordinates the secondary problems that concern "truth" or "error," "appearance" or "reality," each understood in a particular sense. It has, for its part, a universal sense, in this: that it shows that reality is precisely the reality of appearance, in all its forms, and consequently an absolute reality. It rises therefore to the idea of the equality of true knowledge and non-true knowledge in the regard of absolute knowledge. True knowledge, by opposition to non-true knowledge, is true only in a second sense — for, as the sun shines on the just and the unjust, truth understood in an absolute sense makes no distinction and, in its ontological power, equally promotes to existence and protects illusion and "reality." It is the absolute reality, the truth of the true and of the non-true, the origin that illuminates every thing, the universal foundation.

The biblical allusion (*the sun shines on the just and the unjust*, Matthew 5:45) is a deliberate flourish — it suggests the radical neutrality of phenomenality with respect to the distinction true/false. The act of appearing is a condition prior to any evaluation of what appears; even illusions are made possible by the same essence as truths. "Absolute truth" is thus not the truth of true judgments but the very *light* in which both true and false judgments can be formed. The thesis is austere: phenomenology, properly understood, takes its theme not from any particular content but from the universal structure of phenomenality that equalizes all contents *qua* appearances.

**Paragraph 8\.** It is true that natural consciousness most often forgets the essence that gives it the gift of presence; and that, by opposition to its apparent knowledge, one can call true or real knowledge that which recognizes the work of the essence. Phenomenology is precisely true knowledge so understood, insofar as — understood in its universal signification — it aims to be the knowledge of the essence. *Phenomenology is the science of the essence of the phenomenon.* It is because he understands being as the essence of phenomenon that Heidegger can say that phenomenology is the science of being and, as such, ontology. For phenomenology in no way consists in the application of a monotonous method to diverse problems. It is fitting to distinguish here the ultimate problems of phenomenology, which define the field of a *phenomenology of the first order*, from a *phenomenology of the second order* that aims to elucidate the sense of being in the different regions. Expressions like "phenomenology of being," "phenomenology of the ego," "phenomenology of time" are by themselves essentially ambiguous, for the disciplines they indicate risk finding themselves juxtaposed in our mind with a phenomenology of social forms or of the mathematical object, for example. Now, while these latter researches manifestly belong to the domain of a second-order phenomenology, the problem is posed on the contrary of knowing whether the phenomenology of the ego or of time does not derive from phenomenology understood in a primary sense.

Henry introduces a key distinction between *phenomenology of the first order* (the elucidation of the essence of phenomenon as such) and *phenomenology of the second order* (the elucidation of the being-sense of particular regions). The distinction is not Husserlian — Husserl operates with the distinction between formal ontology and material/regional ontology, and with the distinction between phenomenological psychology and transcendental phenomenology, but he does not hierarchize "first" and "second" order phenomenologies in this sense. The distinction is rather Heideggerian in spirit — it corresponds to Heidegger's distinction between fundamental ontology (the elucidation of the sense of being in general) and regional ontologies (the elucidation of the being of specific regions of beings), which Heidegger draws in *Sein und Zeit* §3. But Henry sharpens the distinction further: among the apparent "regional" phenomenologies, some — specifically the phenomenology of the ego and of time — may not be regional at all, but may belong to first-order phenomenology because they enter constitutively into the essence of phenomenon itself.

In which case, the ego and time would not be realities of the same order as society or mathematics in this sense, that, far from being submitted to the essence, they would on the contrary belong to its internal structure, and would enter thus, as constitutive elements, into the immanent definition of absolute truth. But if such a question can receive its answer only when the essence of phenomenon has been clarified, what appears very clearly already now is that the object of first-order phenomenology cannot be exterior to it. It is on the contrary so interior to it that it is founded on this object and finds in it its principle. This object is the essence of phenomenon, and phenomenology is nothing other than the putting-to-work of this essence insofar as, on the foundation of this essence, it aims at an "elucidation" — that is, at a promotion and a realization in presence.

The whole thrust of the section is now in view: first-order phenomenology is the discipline whose object is the essence of phenomenon, and this object is *internal* to the discipline — that is, the elucidation of the essence of phenomenon is itself an exercise of the essence of phenomenon. (Phenomenology that elucidates manifestation is itself a manifestation, governed by the same essence it tries to elucidate.) This circular constitution is a structural feature of first-order phenomenology, not an objection to it.

The understanding of the link that unites phenomenology (insofar as it is first-order phenomenology) and its object reveals itself however to be difficult. Phenomenology is, indeed, the mode of treatment that we want to make the reality — that is, the essence — undergo. It is the "how" that indicates to us the manner of treating what must be debated by it. What must be debated, however, is nothing other than the "how"; it is the manner in which reality manifests itself and must manifest itself to us. The reality of the real is in effect only the manner in which the real manifests itself. "Ontology and phenomenology," says Heidegger, "are not two disciplines belonging next to each other in philosophy. The two titles characterize philosophy itself as to its object and its mode of treatment." The cited phrase is from *Sein und Zeit* §7: phenomenology is the *Methodenbegriff* (method-concept) of philosophy, ontology is the *Sachbegriff* (object-concept), and they coincide because the proper object of philosophy (being) demands precisely this method (letting be seen what shows itself).

But, in the case that occupies us, the object is the mode of treatment itself. Phenomenology is what gives us access to the phenomenon understood in its reality, that is, to the phenomenon as such. But the way of access to the phenomenon is the phenomenon itself. Phenomenology proposes itself to us as a means, the means of bringing near to us the concrete and true essence, the essence of presence, the absolute insofar as it is the *Parousia*. But the means is the absolute itself, since the act of bringing near to us is the work of the essence, insofar as it is the essence of presence, the *Parousia* and the absolute. Phenomenology seeks the *Parousia* of the absolute on the foundation of the absolute understood as the *Parousia*.

The Greek *Parousia* (παρουσία) is theologically charged: in the New Testament, it is the second coming, the eschatological arrival; in Plato (e.g., *Phaedo* 100d), it is the presence of the Form in the participating particular. Henry uses it to designate the fully realized presence, the absolute as the very event of presencing. Heidegger had already mobilized *Parousia* in his early Freiburg lectures (especially the 1920–21 *Phänomenologie des religiösen Lebens*) as a name for the eschatological structure of factical Christian life, and in later writings as a name for the Greek understanding of being as constant presence. Henry combines these resonances: the absolute is the *Parousia* — not a timeless presence behind appearances, but the very *act* of presencing that is appearance itself.

**Paragraph 9\.** Insofar as it is the application of the phenomenological method to the problem of the essence of phenomenon, phenomenology moves in a circle. This is the sign of its absolute character. This absolute character of the problematic that it institutes does not signify that phenomenology be without presupposition. It admits on the contrary a fundamental presupposition, insofar as this presupposition is the foundation itself, the absolute. Phenomenology is a research that aims to elucidate its own foundation; it is a reflection on itself. Phenomenology is its own object.

Henry now openly declares that first-order phenomenology is *circular* — it presupposes the essence of phenomenon in order to elucidate the essence of phenomenon. But this circularity is not vicious; it is the index of phenomenology's absolute character (a reality is absolute when it presupposes nothing other than itself). Phenomenology's only presupposition is the essence of phenomenon, which is identical to the foundation it seeks to elucidate — so the presupposition is internal, not external; structural, not contingent. This is again broadly Heideggerian (the hermeneutic circle of *Sein und Zeit* §32) but radicalized: not just any circle, but the circle in which the discipline coincides with its object.

The ultimate problems of phenomenology relate to phenomenology's reflection on itself and on its foundation. It is in the response brought to these ultimate problems that the sense of phenomenology is decided. This sense depends, indeed, on the nature of the foundation. How phenomenology can enter into relation with the essence — that is, with the fundamental *How* in conformity with which reality realizes itself by making itself "phenomenon" — depends evidently on the nature of the "How." The problem of the essence of phenomenon is primary with respect to that of elucidation. Phenomenology lets itself be guided by its object. The How of its approach is subordinated to the How of the reality it approaches, reality which is the "How" itself. It is finally this reality that comes toward us and that illuminates us. The manner in which this reality comes toward us — must it not command the manner in which we receive it and open ourselves to it? Or rather: must not the how of our reception be — and is it not necessarily — the same as the how of the coming-into-us of the absolute? The eye by which the absolute regards us is the same as the one by which we regard the absolute. But how must this eye that is the absolute itself be understood? What is the nature of vision? What is the essence of phenomenon?

The penultimate question adapts the famous Eckhartian formula that will be cited later in the book (§39 on Eckhart): "the eye in which I see God is the same eye in which God sees me." The Eckhartian appearance here is anticipatory and signals the late-medieval mystical tradition that Henry will mobilize to articulate the structure of immanent self-revelation. The question — "what is the essence of phenomenon?" — is the question of the entire book.

**Paragraph 10\.** To this question are suspended all the problems, already formulated or only glimpsed, that pertain to first-order phenomenology. The understanding of the link that unites ontology and phenomenology remains undetermined as long as thought has not arrived inside the structure of the essence. Because it remains subordinated to a non-elucidated essence, the very project of an elucidation of the essence — which defines first the methodological work of phenomenology — remains uncertain with regard to itself, to its sense, and to its foundation. One assuredly does not let oneself be stopped by the objection of the circle: the work of elucidation engages itself and pursues itself without fear of departing from the essence, since on the contrary it entrusts itself to the essence, and thus the essence will end up rendering itself transparent to itself at the heart of this work. Unless it be a will of the essence to refuse this final transparency and to maintain itself definitively in the mystery. In any case, this will shall be brought into clarity, and the essence brought before itself.

The hesitation on whether the essence will achieve transparency or remain in mystery is not a stylistic equivocation but a substantive openness: it is one of the major problems of the section — and indeed of the book — to determine whether the essence of phenomenon, when it is finally elucidated, reveals itself as a structure of full transparency (as Husserl assumed for the absolute consciousness) or as a structure that essentially involves withdrawal and concealment (as Heidegger argued for the truth of being) or as something else again (as Henry will argue: the immanent self-revelation of life, which is invisible without being mysterious in the Heideggerian sense). The hesitation is the open horizon of what remains to be determined.

How must this putting-of-the-essence-into-presence-with-itself be operated, however? The essence understood as the ontological power that grounds every presence is certainly not foreign to natural consciousness. Insofar as natural consciousness is a consciousness, a being-there (*être-là*), absolute knowledge is immanent in it. But the thematic grasp of the essence, the true and real knowledge — that is, the knowledge of absolute knowledge understood in its absoluteness — does it consist in the representation of the essence? This could only be if the essence itself consists in representation. And how should one interpret the nature of the latter? Thus the understanding of the relation of the essence to itself depends finally on the determination of the structure of the essence. This determination alone can say if, finally, such a "relation" has a sense.

This paragraph names a crucial methodological-substantive entanglement. The "putting-of-the-essence-into-presence-with-itself" — that is, the phenomenological elucidation of the essence — depends on what *kind* of essence it is. If the essence consists in representation (i.e., if manifestation is essentially representational), then phenomenology can elucidate it by representing it. But if the essence does not consist in representation (e.g., if it is immanent self-affection, as Henry will argue), then phenomenological elucidation must take a different form — it cannot be representation of the essence but must be itself a mode of the essence's self-revelation. The whole methodological question of phenomenology depends on the substantive question of the structure of the essence.

**Paragraph 11\.** "In the sphere of the psychic," says Husserl, "there is no difference between being and appearing." The citation is from *Ideen I* §44: in the immanent perception of consciousness's own acts, what appears coincides exactly with what is, because there are no profile-views (*Abschattungen*) for inner perception, no horizon of further sides to be presented. This Husserlian claim is the foundation of the apodicticity of immanent perception and of the special status of the *cogitationes* in transcendental phenomenology. But this affirmation, on which one has thought one could found the absolute character of the phenomenological problematic insofar as it aims at the immanent sphere of consciousness, remains in fact an extremely vague indication so long as one has not defined what is fitting to understand by the fact of appearing. Likewise, if one says that there is in the essence itself something that does not appear, what does not appear — or, to be more exact, the fact of not appearing — remains as undetermined in its being as the pure and simple manifestation, so long as the latter is not grasped in a rigorous way in its essence.

This is a sharp double critique, applied symmetrically to Husserl and Heidegger. (i) Husserl's "no difference between being and appearing in the psychic sphere" is empty until "appearing" has been determined in its essence. (ii) Heidegger's claim that there is "in the essence itself something that does not appear" (the *Verborgenheit* internal to *Aletheia*) is equally empty until "appearing" and "not-appearing" have been determined in their essence. Both Husserl's affirmation of full self-transparency in immanence and Heidegger's affirmation of withdrawal-in-the-disclosing presuppose a determination of what manifestation as such is — and neither has provided this determination. The whole argument of the section turns on this point: the *positive* substantive content of any phenomenological doctrine depends on the prior elucidation of the essence of manifestation, which neither Husserl nor Heidegger has accomplished.

More still: the fact of not appearing perhaps has only a limited, purely negative signification if it remains in relation with a non-elaborated concept of phenomenal essence — for it could be that what is given as not-appearing be such only with regard to a unilateral and, as such, abstract conception of the essence. To push to the end the determination of the essence so as to recognize it in its fully concrete character — perhaps this is to bring into light a Form, a more fundamental How, whose law confers a presence (though of another order) to what was primitively thought as "not appearing."

This sentence anticipates the central thesis of the whole book. What Heidegger calls the *Verborgenheit* of being (the not-appearing internal to appearing) may be such *only because* Heidegger operates with a unilateral conception of phenomenality (the horizonal-ek-static conception). If one moves to a more fundamental conception of phenomenality — one that recognizes a non-horizonal mode of manifestation, namely immanent self-revelation — then what was unmanifestable for the horizonal conception (selfhood, life, affectivity) turns out to be perfectly manifest, but in a different mode (the invisible, the immanently self-affecting). Heidegger's "withdrawal" is, on this reading, an artifact of his unilateral conception of manifestation, not a structural feature of phenomenality as such.

**Paragraph 12\.** The determination of the essence must also furnish us with the ontological frame for a discussion of the relation of this essence to the existent that finds in it its foundation. This determination alone can say, indeed, whether the overcoming of positivism is, from the ontological point of view, definitive and without appeal; whether the transgression of the existent operates without return; and whether the essence acquired in such a transgression can close upon itself, abstract itself from the ontic determination, absolutize itself in this abstraction, and yet subsist thus, preserving its absoluteness in its autonomy. It is the way of understanding the concrete character of the essence and, finally, its absoluteness, that is in question.

This paragraph announces the second major task: not just *what* the essence of phenomenon is, but *how* it relates to the existents that depend on it. Is the essence radically autonomous, capable of being grasped in complete abstraction from existents? Or is the essence essentially bound to existents (e.g., to Dasein, to the human, to the body, to time)? This question will be developed especially in §§14–16 (the relation of essence to ontic determination) and forms one of the major axes of the section's argument.

**Paragraph 13\.** The determination of the internal structure of the essence is alone susceptible, finally, of delimiting the field of the ultimate problems of phenomenology. It alone can say whether the phenomenology of the ego belongs to this field of first-order problems, and in what sense. The task of a determination of the essence of phenomenon thus appears as the central task of phenomenology; it imposes itself on us in a manner all the more urgent in that it is on the foundation of an unexplicated conception of the phenomenon that philosophy has, since always, posited and resolved its problems. The elucidation of the essence of phenomenon will show that, when this essence has finally made the theme of an explicit problematic, this problematic has done nothing but ratify — by carrying them to the absolute — the ontological presuppositions which have, since the origin and in an almost uninterrupted way, guided but also, and rather, led astray philosophical research and thought.

This is the closing programmatic sentence of §8. Three theses are announced: (i) the determination of the essence of phenomenon is the central task of phenomenology; (ii) the elucidation of this essence will show that previous explicit treatments of it have only ratified an unconscious presupposition; (iii) this presupposition, which has dominated almost all of philosophy since its origin, is what §11 will name "ontological monism." The remaining sections (§§9–16) will develop this argument in detail: §9 will exhibit the unilateral determination of the essence in the form of the concept of "phenomenological distance"; §10 will analyze the doubling of being that this concept implies; §11 will name and define ontological monism; §12 will critique the philosophy of consciousness as one form of monism; §13 will exhibit the ambiguity of the Heideggerian Dasein as another form; §§14–15 will analyze the relation of essence to ontic determination; §16 will formulate the idea of the autonomy of the essence and prepare the transition to Section II.

---

## **§ 9\. The unilateral determination of the essence of phenomenon and the concept of "phenomenological distance"**

**Paragraph 1\.** Henry begins this critical section with a long citation from Pierre Gassendi's *Objections* to Descartes's *Meditations* — specifically from the Fifth Set of Objections, on the impossibility of self-knowledge. Gassendi argues, against Descartes's claim that the mind knows itself directly, that nothing can act on itself (the hand cannot strike itself, the foot cannot kick itself, the eye cannot see itself); since knowledge requires that the thing known act on the knowing faculty (sending its species or image into the faculty), the faculty itself cannot transmit its own species into itself and therefore cannot form a notion of itself. Why does the eye that cannot see itself see itself nonetheless in a mirror? Because there is space between eye and mirror; the eye sends its image to the mirror, which then reflects it back. Provide a mirror against which the mind can act in the same way, Gassendi concludes, and you can know yourself — but only by reflected, never by direct knowledge.

The choice of citation is precisely strategic. Gassendi's argument is, on its surface, an empiricist-scholastic position: it relies on the medieval theory of *species* (intelligible forms transmitted from object to faculty), on the metaphor of the mirror as the model of reflective knowledge, and on the principle that nothing acts on itself. But Henry will argue that what is *really* going on in Gassendi's argument is something deeper than its scholastic-empiricist surface. The empiricism of Gassendi appears in this text overdetermined by conceptions inherited from scholastic philosophy and, through the latter, from ancient thought. These conceptions do not however constitute the foundation of the argument here directed against Descartes; and empiricism, in its turn, is only one possible expression of the *fundamental ontological presupposition* which — though neither stated nor even clearly perceived — is nonetheless at the center of this argument. To this ontological presupposition, the theory of species, the idea of action at distance on things and on oneself, and finally the idea of the "mirror," are however not foreign; they constitute rather diverse ways for a thought that has not yet known how to raise to an ontological plane the problematic it institutes — and that lives by "theories" — to express, through these theories precisely, the ultimate ontological presuppositions from which the theories are, in truth, never entirely separated. That a single and same presupposition expresses itself through these diverse theories attests to the persistence across history of a *common ontological horizon* under variable philosophical material.

This is the methodological premise of the entire section. Particular philosophical theories (Gassendi's empiricist scholasticism, Descartes's rationalism, Husserl's transcendental phenomenology, Heidegger's fundamental ontology) are surface formulations; underneath them lies a *common ontological horizon* that constitutes what Henry will call (§11) "ontological monism." The philosophical task is not to refute Gassendi's theory of species (which is easily done) but to identify the ontological presupposition that *underwrites* Gassendi's theory and that survives all the surface refutations because it is shared by Gassendi's opponents.

That such a horizon could remain intact down to our day in spite of so many revolutions of thought — and in particular in spite of the Cartesian revolution, for the reason that these upheavals always took place inside and on the foundation of this horizon, far from putting it in question — is what appears with evidence if one is willing to compare Gassendi's text to one in which a contemporary author, commenting on modern ontology, expresses himself in these terms: "To see something one needs what one calls field \[*champ*\]. I see this inkwell, this book, distinctly only because a certain distance separates me from them. If I bring them close to my eye, I perceive them less and less as the distance diminishes. At the limit, I no longer see anything. As for my cornea, it is forever forbidden to me to see it. I can perceive its image in a glass and its structure in an anatomy treatise. But it is no longer it that I see. Certainly, it can still be seen. But only by another than me, and because he has field. In short, immediate knowledge is in reality always mediate. It operates by the intermediary of a minimum distance. Now, it is a fact that being knows itself, by man or by any consciousness. It is therefore necessary that being be at a distance from itself."

The footnote attributes this citation to "Malverne" — actually a contemporary French commentator on Heideggerian-existentialist ontology whom Henry takes as illustrative of how the ancient ontological presupposition survives, intact, in mid-twentieth-century philosophy. The structure is identical with Gassendi's: knowledge requires distance; the eye cannot see itself because there is no distance between eye and itself; therefore being, in order to know itself, must put itself at a distance from itself. The vocabulary has changed (we no longer speak of *species* or of mirrors but of *field* and of *consciousness*); the underlying ontological presupposition has not.

**Paragraph 2\.** The presupposition, underlying Gassendi's text, that comes more clearly to the fore here, is certainly only rather vaguely sketched. The ontological signification of this presupposition is put in question at the very moment when it seems affirmed, since the only precision brought to the nature of the distance that is posited as the condition of knowledge of being tends to confuse this distance with a real distance, assimilable to an ontic characteristic of the existent. It is the cornea of the eye, indeed, that is understood as the zero-point of this distance, and one furthermore admits that the distance can be greater or smaller. There remains that "distance" intervenes as a universal condition of knowledge; it imposes itself on knowledge, in its accomplishment, with an eidetic necessity: "immediate knowledge is in reality always mediate." That of which distance is the condition is still thought, it is true, only under the title of knowledge. There is however no restriction here, in the author's thought, brought to the universal and eidetic signification of the condition so defined; this condition is in no way limited to the sole phenomenon of knowledge. What it aims to define is rather the very possibility of a "phenomenon" in general. That this phenomenon, understood in its universal ontological structure, be falsely identified with knowledge understood in a classical sense — this is precisely a heritage of classical thought.

The diagnosis is precise. Even though Malverne (and Gassendi before him) confuses the structural presupposition with an empirical-physical fact about distances, the real meaning of his claim is structural: the condition of every "phenomenon" — of anything's being-given to consciousness, of anything's appearing — is *distance*. Not spatial distance, not psychological distance, but a structural-ontological distance that is the condition of phenomenality as such. This is what Henry will call "*la distance phénoménologique*" — phenomenological distance.

What is finally aimed at, despite the imperfections and imprecisions of the analysis, is therefore the ontological and universal possibility of a phenomenon in general; it is the essence of the phenomenon. Insofar as it is thought as the condition of the phenomenon as such — that is, identified with its essence — the distance in question deserves to be called by us "phenomenological distance." It is only with the concept of "phenomenological distance" that we raise ourselves to the ultimate ontological presupposition that is underlying the texts that have just been evoked.

**Paragraph 3\.** Understood in its ontological signification as the condition for something like a "phenomenon" to offer itself to us — or, more exactly, as the very structure of phenomenality — the concept of phenomenological distance must evidently be distinguished from that of spatial or "real" distance. The distance that separates things, or that separates us from them, is a distance that we can measure objectively but that exists already prior to every measure of this sort, as distance immediately experienced, belonging to the surrounding world. However, this distance lived in originary perceptual experience rests in turn — just like the space which it comes to structure and to which it belongs — on a more originary spatiality which is none other than the phenomenological milieu primitively opened so that something like a space can first manifest itself. This originary spatiality is the phenomenon of the world, the phenomenon of all phenomena, their visibility as such. The world, understood in its pure worldhood, is precisely this visibility itself, from which every thing borrows the possibility of manifesting itself and of being thus a "phenomenon." The world is the transcendental condition of space, for, as Heidegger has shown, far from the world resting in space, it is on the contrary space that rests in the world. Now the concept of phenomenological distance is in no way linked to space, and in this it differs fundamentally from our ordinary concept of distance. "Fundamentally" — that is, insofar as it belongs to the foundation, to the worldhood of the world.

Henry distinguishes three layers: (i) measurable, objective spatial distance (the distance one can measure with a ruler); (ii) the distance lived in perceptual experience prior to any measurement (the immediately experienced "near" and "far" of phenomenal space); and (iii) the more originary, non-spatial "phenomenological distance" that is the very structure of the worldhood of the world, the visibility-as-such within which everything can become visible. The reference to Heidegger is to *Sein und Zeit* §§22–24, where Heidegger develops the worldhood of the world (*Weltlichkeit der Welt*) and shows that space is grounded in the worldhood of Dasein's being-in-the-world, not the other way around (the famous polemic against the Cartesian *res extensa* as the ontological model of the world). Henry endorses this Heideggerian thesis and uses it to articulate his concept of phenomenological distance.

**Paragraph 4\.** The concept of phenomenological distance is not only "linked" to that of "world"; the deployment of this distance is one, in reality, with the arising of the world in its purity. Understood in its radical ontological signification, the concept of phenomenological distance functions as a title for the essence. But this ontological signification is safeguarded — and first thought — only if the concept of distance receives, by opposition to every idea of a spatial distance, the originary signification of *a power*. The distances on which we lean the concept that habitually corresponds to them in our mind are *found* distances. They are found, it is true, inside a field that, before being spatial, is a phenomenological field. But the distance, insofar as it now characterizes the originary and non-spatial phenomenological extension of this pure field, is not in turn found. It is rather *the power that permits us to find*, the originary work of the transcendence that deploys the horizon. It is "distancing" (*éloignement*), but understood — as Heidegger wishes — "in an active and transitive sense." Before concerning the being-distant, distance is what *distances*. It is what distances, not as a particular and determinate comportment, the one by which we push an object on the table or throw a stone in the field. Such a comportment, material or not, is still only a process of an ontic order. It presupposes, as condition of the act of distancing it accomplishes each time, a more originary distancing — namely, the ontological event that makes the horizon arise toward which and inside which concrete acts of approaching or distancing can in fact take place. The phenomenological distance fashions the originary distances; it deploys the ultimate horizon of visibility inside which every thing can become visible for us. Every presence is a presence starting from the horizon and on the foundation of it. The horizon precisely deploys the milieu of presence; it opens the ontological dimension of existence. The phenomenological distance is the ontological power that gives us access to things; it is this access itself, an access in and through the distance.

The vocabulary of "distancing" (*éloignement*) read in an "active and transitive" sense is taken directly from Heidegger's *Sein und Zeit* §23, where Heidegger develops the existential of *Ent-fernung* (de-distancing, dis-stancing) as the spatial structure of Dasein. *Ent-fernung* is not the distance of one object from another but the active comportment by which Dasein opens up the field within which distances can be measured. Henry takes Heidegger's term and intensifies it: *éloignement*, understood actively, is the very work of phenomenality, the *power* that opens the horizon of visibility. This is what phenomenological distance means: not a distance between two things, but the distancing-as-such that is the condition for there being any "between," any "things," any visibility at all.

**Paragraph 5\.** We say of things that they are distant or near to us, and this determination varies correlatively with the modalities of the real or virtual ontic comportment that links us to them. But this relation, with its each-time determinate characters, leans on a more originary relation, which is the work of the distant. Proximity and distance are two modalities inside a more fundamental distancing that belongs, as condition, to the very structure of phenomenality. The essence of phenomenon is distancing itself, as transcendental distancing. It is this distancing that is the condition of every presence; it is what constitutes the proximity — variable, moreover — of things, a proximity of which the distance we ordinarily speak of is only one modality. Proximity, understood no longer as an ontic characterization but in its ontological possibility — that is, in its very essence — is one with the originary distancing that is the work of the essence. Proximity and distance are equivalent titles for the essence of phenomenon considered in its purity; taken together they signify that the essence of presence harbors in some way an internal antinomy — but this antinomy is precisely what confers on the essence its proper ontological power. Distancing is the condition of every presence, presence as such. The distant is the essence of proximity. "Thus," Heidegger can say, "the human being… is a being of the distant. It is uniquely by these originary distances that he fashions himself in his transcendence with regard to all the existent that grows in man the true proximity of things."

The cited passage is from Heidegger's 1929 *Vom Wesen des Grundes* (On the Essence of Ground), part III, in Henri Corbin's French translation (cited as "WG" in Henry's bibliography). Heidegger's thought there is precisely that Dasein is a being whose essence is to deploy distances — not because Dasein is far from things, but because Dasein is the very opening of the dimension within which "near" and "far" can be ontologically distinguished. Henry adopts Heidegger's vocabulary and pushes it: the essence of phenomenon harbors an "internal antinomy" between distance and proximity. This is not a contradiction but a structural duality: phenomenon-as-such is the *distancing* that *grants* presence; the same essence that distances is the essence that brings near. The "antinomy" is the essence's mode of self-realization.

The understanding of the transcendental status of distancing invites us to reflect on the non-originary character of the signification of the concepts of "near" and "far" already in use in classical philosophy and taken up by Husserl in the phenomenology of reason. When he studies, in the *Ideen* for example, the "proximity" and "distance" of the given, or, in *Erfahrung und Urteil*, the differences of appearance of objects according to "near" or "far" (as well as, for each object, its way of passing from "far" to "near"), the phenomenological characters that are then aimed at refer evidently only to the diverse contents of thought. It is each time a content — whether an empirical or ideal object — that is said to be near or far, in conformity with the way it gives itself according to a series of degrees of clarity or indistinctness, while consciousness, obeying the *télos* of evidence, seeks to traverse this series of degrees in the sense that ends in the greatest possible clarity for a determinate content. When this degree of maximum clarity is attained, one says that the object finds itself in an "absolute proximity." On the ontological plane, however, this concept of absolute proximity has, strictly speaking, no sense. Proximity as such is always absolute, just as the distancing that is one with it is always absolute. There are degrees in proximity only at the moment when proximity ceases to be considered in its ontological signification — insofar as it belongs as constitutive structure to the essence of phenomenality — to become a phenomenological characteristic of the existent itself.

The references are to Husserl's *Ideen I* §27 and *Erfahrung und Urteil* §22 (and in fact across many texts), where Husserl develops the doctrine of the "near-sphere" (*Nahsphäre*) and "far-sphere" (*Fernsphäre*) of perception. Husserl's "absolute proximity" is the limit-case in which the object is given in maximum clarity (typically in the immanent perception of consciousness's own acts). Henry's polemic: Husserl's "proximity" and "distance" are characteristics of *contents* given to consciousness, not characteristics of the structure of phenomenality. They are degrees within an already-deployed phenomenological field; they presuppose the very phenomenological distance whose ontological structure they fail to thematize. "Absolute proximity" is, for Henry, ontologically meaningless because at the ontological level proximity is *always* absolute (every present thing is fully present *qua* present, even if it is given in a partial profile); the degrees come in only at the ontic-content level.

**Paragraph 6\.** Considered as the ontological power that gives us access to "phenomena" and thus founds "knowledge" in its possibility, the phenomenological distance could not be said to be greater or smaller, and there is no sense in speaking of "minimum distance." When the distance between my eye and the object diminishes progressively, it is evidently only a matter of a spatial distance. When this distance becomes nil, I no longer see anything, Malverne tells us. But when I say that I no longer see anything, this proposition — if it has a sense — comments on an experience. That I no longer see anything: this is a positive fact, a "phenomenon." For it, the essence has already accomplished its work; a distance has deployed itself which is certainly neither spatial nor "real" but constitutes rather the very reality of the real, the possibility of every presence as such. This transcendental phenomenological distance distinguishes itself thus, in the most clear way, from every spatial distance, since it subsists in its absoluteness even there where spatial distance becomes nil — there as well where the structure of being is such that there is no longer any sense in speaking of spatial distance.

The argument is acute: even the experience of "I see nothing" presupposes a phenomenological field within which "nothing" is given as a phenomenological content. The phenomenological distance has done its work even in the limit-case where empirical-spatial distance reaches zero. So phenomenological distance cannot be reduced to or measured by spatial distance; it is a structurally different kind of distance, ontologically prior to all spatial distances.

In the case of the distances that structure the objective world — and first that of life — it is clear that they belong to the intra-mundane existent as ontic determinations. It is precisely insofar as distance appears as a "categorial" determination, to speak as Heidegger does — that is, as relative to the non-Dasein existent — that distance is susceptible of differentiation; insofar as it is on the contrary an "existential," that is, co-belongs to the ontological structure of the essence, it bears within itself this eidetic characteristic that it is always an absolute distance. The technical Heideggerian distinction between *categorial* (the determinations of non-Dasein beings — substance, quality, quantity, etc., the Aristotelian categories) and *existential* (the determinations of Dasein — *Befindlichkeit*, *Verstehen*, *Rede*, *Sorge*, etc.) is from *Sein und Zeit* §9. Spatial distance is a categorial determination of intra-worldly beings; phenomenological distance, insofar as it is part of the structure of phenomenality, is an existential, and as such is always absolute.

**Paragraph 7\.** As absolute and transcendental distance, phenomenological distance must also be distinguished in its concept from that of "existential distance," which characterizes the more or less great proximity in which things hold themselves for us according to the interest we carry to them. This proximity has no relation with spatial proximity. Things very distant from us in space can be very "close" to us, and we can make ourselves the "contemporaries" of an event that took place twenty centuries ago. Existential distance is linked to *Care* (*Souci*, Heidegger's *Sorge*). Care lives in the surrounding world, in such a way however that it is never about the world as such, but only about what arrives inside the world, that it cares. There is in Dasein, says Heidegger, a fundamental tendency toward the near. But what is near to us is always such or such determinate content; it is never proximity as such. Proximity is on the contrary what is most far from us, and this not because it is in itself identical to the originary essence of the distant, but because it is never for us the object of our Care. The object each time determinate of our Care dissimulates from our eyes the ontological milieu where it appears. The careful (*soucieuse*) orientation toward being-distant hides from us distancing as such.

The reference is to *Sein und Zeit* §23, where Heidegger develops the existential structure of *Sorge* (Care) and its tendency toward what is *zuhanden* (ready-to-hand) and "near." Henry adapts the analysis: Care is a third kind of distance (alongside spatial and phenomenological-transcendental), a *life*\-distance in which things are nearer or farther according to our concern. But Care, like spatial distance, is *ontic* in its determinations; it never thematizes the structural-phenomenological distance that is the condition of all caring orientation. The very fact that Care orients itself toward intra-worldly contents *hides* from it the ontological distancing that opened the world in which those contents can appear. This is a perfectly Heideggerian point — the forgetfulness of being is partly built into the structure of Care, which always orients itself toward beings rather than toward being.

**Paragraph 8\.** Being-distant however finds its foundation in distancing itself. The lived distances — existential or spatial — that mark out our world delineate themselves on the very foundation of the world as such and rest in it. They can well characterize the intra-mundane existent and belong to it; the being of this existent is the very being of the world. Categorial determinations rest on existential structures. Transcendent being, if it masks from us each time the work of transcendence, nonetheless takes from transcendence all its ontological characters. These are assuredly only derivative characters, but they must be linked, and that in principle, to the essence from which they derive. One can falsely interpret the essence by understanding it from what arrives thanks to it, confuse the transcendental concept of distancing with that of being-distant which arises for us at the heart of the originary distant. It is to originary distancing nonetheless that being-distant owes being what it is. The non-elaborated concept of distance is still only the way in which natural and pre-philosophical consciousness represents to itself the condition of phenomenon — and this representation is not yet a thought. It is nonetheless with the help of elements that suppose the essence and that find in it their foundation that natural consciousness figures the essence to itself. However improper this figure may be, it is no less significant. Action at distance, the theory of species, the concepts of "reflection" and "image," the presupposition of distance — these still refer only to realities or processes of an ontic order. But they are valid only as symbols, and what they symbolize is not homogeneous with them; it is their own foundation. It is in fact a matter of circumscribing the essence of phenomenon — and if traditional philosophical thought has shown itself incapable of situating and maintaining its problematic on an ontological plane, its profound design nonetheless had to burst forth one day. *Heidegger thinks the same thing as Gassendi, but this thing he thinks in its ontological truth.*

The closing sentence is the most important sentence of the section. Heidegger and Gassendi (and a fortiori Husserl and Descartes) are united by a common ontological presupposition — that phenomenality is constituted by a distancing-structure, a horizon, an ek-static opening within which beings can be given. Gassendi expressed this presupposition in the theory of *species* and the metaphor of the mirror; Heidegger expresses it in the existential analytic of Dasein and the theory of the ontological horizon; but the underlying structure is the same. The whole tradition — empiricist as well as rationalist, classical as well as contemporary — is unified by what §11 will name *ontological monism*: the doctrine that phenomenality has one and only one structure, that of distancing-into-a-horizon. The next section will analyze this distancing more closely as the "doubling of being," and §11 will name the resulting doctrine.

---

## **§ 10\. Phenomenological distance and the doubling of being: presence and alienation**

**Paragraph 1\.** Being is a phenomenon only if it is at a distance from itself. The opening sentence states the thesis the section will develop: phenomenological distance, identified in §9 as the structure of phenomenality, when applied to being itself entails that being can become phenomenal — can manifest itself, can appear — only by being-at-a-distance from itself. Phenomenality is thus an internal *self-distantiation* of being. The work of phenomenological distance understood as an ontological power, as a *naturing* (*naturante*) and not simply *natured* distance, is precisely to institute the interval thanks to which being will be able to appear to itself. The Spinozist-Scholastic distinction *natura naturans* / *natura naturata* (already deployed by Henry in Introduction §5 to characterize the absolute ego as constituting source rather than constituted reality) is here applied to phenomenological distance: distance is not a fact (a *natured* distance, a distance-as-product) but a productive operation (a *naturing* distance, a distance-as-act).

The appearing, on the foundation of phenomenological distance, of the being that appears, the manifestation of this being is identical with its existence. Because it is founded on distance, the existence of being is different from being itself. It differs from being itself precisely as that which is at a distance from itself; it is being itself, if you will, but at a distance from itself, in its non-coincidence with itself; it is being in difference. Henry now articulates a precise structure: existence \= being-at-distance-from-itself \= being-in-non-coincidence-with-itself \= being-in-difference. Existence is not something added to being from outside; existence *is* being insofar as being puts itself at a distance from itself in order to manifest itself. This *self-distantiation* is what existence is.

Let us consider with Fichte the wall of which we say that it "is." What is aimed at in the "is" — namely, the being of the wall — "is not identical with the wall... but distinguishes itself from this wall as something independent." What distinguishes the being of the wall from the wall itself, what differentiates them in a fundamental way, is precisely the difference understood as the essence that allows the wall to be. The being of the wall is the wall itself in the infinity of the distance that confers on it, with the phenomenal condition, existence itself.

The Fichtean reference is decisive. The citation is from J.G. Fichte's late lectures *Die Anweisung zum seligen Leben* (1806) — *The Way Towards the Blessed Life*, which Henry refers to in the bibliography as "F" along with the *Wissenschaftslehre* of 1804\. (Henry has worked on Fichte at length elsewhere, particularly in his commentary on the 1804 *Wissenschaftslehre*.) The example of the wall is Fichte's: when I say "the wall is," what I mean by "is" is something distinct from the wall itself — it is the *being* of the wall, which stands over against the wall as something independent. The "is" is not the wall; it is the being-condition of the wall, which is articulated only by being differentiated from what it makes possible. This Fichtean analysis of the predicative "is" is here read by Henry as a phenomenological-ontological doctrine: the "is" is the very phenomenological distance that constitutes the wall as a phenomenon. Fichte, in the late lectures Henry is reading, was working out a structure of the absolute as Image (*Bild*) — the absolute manifests itself only by producing an image of itself that is distinct from yet identical to itself.

The existence of the wall is the being of the wall insofar as this being is posited in a radical exteriority with respect to itself; it is, to take up Fichte's strong expression, "its being outside its being." It is true that natural consciousness "does not have the time to contemplate the 'is' which entirely escapes it"; to aim at this "is" on the contrary in a thematic way in philosophical consciousness is to be led to posit that "the 'is' with respect to being is immediately existence." Being must exist; it exists necessarily. The ontological argument is not a proof in the ordinary sense of the word; it consists in the *reading* of the phenomenal condition of being. This phenomenal condition is precisely the existence of being; it is, as being-outside-its-being, the very being of being.

The reference to the ontological argument is striking. Henry's claim is that the Anselmian-Cartesian-Hegelian argument from the concept of the absolute to its existence is not a proof in the deductive sense but a *reading*: a reading of the structure of being itself, which entails that being-as-such must exist (that is, must put itself at a distance from itself in order to manifest itself). This is essentially the Hegelian reading of the ontological argument (cf. *Encyclopaedia* §51 and the *Lectures on the Philosophy of Religion*): the ontological argument is not a syllogism but the explicit articulation of the self-positing of the absolute. Henry adopts this reading and gives it a phenomenological inflection: being must exist because being is essentially phenomenal, and phenomenality is essentially self-distantiation.

**Paragraph 2\.** Existence which thus makes the very being of being does not coincide with pure and simple being, with stable and absolute being. It coincides so little with this being that it rather distinguishes itself from it; it stands with respect to it in an absolute exteriority and, having withdrawn itself from being into this exteriority, it posits being in face of itself as a stable being. Existence is nothing by itself, except the act of withdrawing itself from being and, in annihilating itself before being, of positing being in face of itself as another absolute existence. *"Existence,"* says Fichte, *"must seize itself, recognize itself and form itself as simple existence and posit and form in face of itself an absolute being of which it is itself only the simple existence: it must by its own being annihilate itself in face of another absolute existence; which precisely gives it the character of simple image, of representation… of being."*

The Fichtean doctrine here is the doctrine of *Bildlichkeit* (image-character) developed in the *Anweisung* (lectures 3 and 5, cited by Henry). Existence (= phenomenality, \= the manifesting) and being (= the manifested) stand over against each other: existence has the structure of *being-an-image-of* being, and in this structure it "annihilates itself" in face of being — that is, it presents itself as merely the image, while being is given as the substantive original. But the substantive original is itself only constituted as substantive by the work of the image-existence that posits it as such. The doctrine prefigures the entire Hegelian-Sartrian dialectic of the in-itself and the for-itself.

Existence is thus thought as the simple image of being or, if you prefer, as its concept; for what is designated under the title of image is, regarding being, nothing other than its own exteriority with respect to itself. The image is the name of existence considered as the manifestation of being; it is the form of being, what Fichte also calls knowledge (*savoir*, Fichte's *Wissen*). The Fifth Lecture envisages the "character of knowledge in general which is only a simple image of a being given and subsisting independently of it." Already in the Third Lecture, Fichte had characterized knowledge as "absolute existence or… the manifestation and revelation of being in its only possible form."

Henry's purpose in displaying these Fichtean formulations is to show that Fichte, in his late phase, articulated with great clarity the same ontological presupposition that Gassendi expressed in his theory of species: phenomenality requires a distance, a doubling, an exteriority — being and its image, being and its existence, being and its knowledge. The presupposition operates whether one is doing scholastic empiricism (Gassendi), German idealism (Fichte), Husserlian transcendental phenomenology, Heideggerian fundamental ontology, or Sartrean phenomenological ontology. The doubling of being is the underlying ontological structure that all these positions share.

**Paragraph 3\.** The dualism of being and of its own image, which has just been thought as the phenomenal condition of being, could not be limited in its scope; it belongs on the contrary to the very definition of the internal structure of phenomenality and appears as an eidetic prescription, as an absolutely universal condition, identical with the essence of manifestation as such. To such a condition is submitted, consequently, not only the wall of which we have spoken, but everything that claims the title of phenomenon, everything that can and wants to manifest itself — being itself insofar as its most intimate vocation is precisely the revelation of self. The being of God would be nothing but the *Ungrund* — not only the most obscure but the most abstract and, as such, something entirely unreal — if it did not in turn submit itself to the conditions that open and define the field of phenomenal existence and of true spirituality. Or, to be more exact, God is not himself something that would submit itself to such conditions; if he is the very essence of spirituality, he is one with these conditions; he is confused with them; it is he who is not only the vocation to manifest himself and to realize himself in this manifestation, but the very movement that actualizes this vocation, the power that makes of it something real. The essence of divinity is identical, consequently, with that of this power; what is thought, in both cases, is the internal structure of the absolute; it is the essence of manifestation as such.

The reference to the *Ungrund* is to Jakob Böhme, the early-modern German mystic whose doctrine of the "ungrounded ground" (*Ungrund*) — the dark, undifferentiated abyss out of which God comes to manifestation — was fundamental to Schelling's late philosophy and, through Schelling, to Hegel and to existentialism. Böhme is named explicitly in the next paragraph. The point Henry is making is that the dualistic structure of being-and-its-image, which Fichte articulates philosophically, is also articulated theologically in the German mystical tradition: God-as-*Ungrund* (pure being, undifferentiated abyss) is "nothing" until it manifests itself; manifestation requires the doubling of being into Father and Son (or being and Word, or being and image). The structure of phenomenality is identical with the structure of divine self-manifestation, because in both cases what is at stake is the internal structure of the absolute.

Thus the conditions of phenomenality find in the description of the divine essence not the particular though privileged example of a reality they would submit and that would be subsumed under them as under a general rule, but their own reality, insofar precisely as they are not abstract conditions but the very conditions of reality — and, as such, the absolute ontological reality itself.

**Paragraph 4\.** The Fichtean commentary on the beginning of the Gospel of Saint John is situated in this perspective; it counts as a *repetition* of the ontological presuppositions that have been evoked — a repetition which, because it situates itself decidedly this time on the plane of the absolute, confers on these presuppositions a decisive character. The reference is to the central theme of Fichte's *Anweisung*: the meditation on the Johannine Prologue ("In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God"). Fichte reads the *Logos* (Word) as the primordial *image* of God, the existence-of-God that stands over against God and constitutes God's manifestation. The definition of God as Word signifies the understanding of divine being as existence. The being of God exists, manifests itself, in conformity with the conditions that constitute the essence of manifestation — that is, in fact, the essence of divinity itself. That the being of God exists signifies, in conformity with these conditions which constitute his being, that God divides himself in virtue of the dualism of being and existence — that the divine being can be posited in appearance only insofar as there is produced in face of him, in annihilating itself before him, his own image, which is the existence and the knowledge of his being itself. The existence of God, produced from him as that which makes him exist, thus constitutes the reality of divine being; it is, as being-outside-its-being, as image and as existence, the very being of this being. *The being of God is existence.*

The thesis is structurally Hegelian (the absolute must alienate itself in order to be itself, must produce an other of itself — the *Logos*, the Son — in which it manifests itself), but Henry is locating the structure pre-Hegelianly in Fichte and Böhme. The continuity is what matters: from late-medieval mysticism (Eckhart, Böhme) through German idealism (Fichte, Hegel) to existentialism (Sartre), the structure of self-distantiating manifestation persists. It is, Henry will argue, the dominant ontological structure of Western philosophy — what §11 will name *ontological monism*.

**Paragraph 5\.** How must the relation in God of being and existence be understood, in a more precise way? The existence of God is neither exterior nor posterior to his being. This "existence which we distinguish… is not distinct from being," says Fichte; it is "primordial," just as primordial as his being. Thus, for Fichte as already before him for Böhme, one cannot consider divine being apart from the process by which it emerges into the light; the Father is not dissociable from the Son whom he eternally engenders, and his being is one with this engendering in which it is realized. The Word, said Saint John, is in God, or rather it is God himself. What is advanced, however, in the affirmation of the unity of being and existence is only the dwelling of the latter under the form of the *Logos* in the originary being of the Father; it is its belonging to the internal structure of the absolute. But it is not said by this that this structure be — on the foundation of the immanence of existence in being — a unitary structure.
