The difference is so little suppressed, at the heart of the absolute, by the unity in it of being and existence, that the difference is rather *posited* by such a unity — and this in such a radical way that it is on the foundation of this unity that the absolute finds itself delivered to difference as to its own essence. There is certainly no place to continue to distinguish in God his being and his existence, to posit on one side "being such as it is interiorly and in itself," and on the other "the form it takes from the fact that it exists"; since existence is the being of this being. And yet, for this very reason, because existence is the being of this being, this divine being finds itself posited outside itself as a being outside its being. The unity of being and existence has as consequence the division of being, its self-separation from itself and, as Fichte says, its expulsion outside itself.

The dialectic is acute. Unity (being \= existence) does not abolish difference (being ≠ existence); on the contrary, unity *produces* difference. Because being and existence are one (the unity-thesis), being must put itself outside itself as its own existence (the difference-consequence). The Fichtean *expulsion* of being outside itself (*Ausstoßung*, in the German of the *Anweisung*) is the Hegelian *Entäußerung* (alienation, externalization), and it is the absolute movement by which the absolute realizes itself in differentiating itself from itself. The whole of dialectical idealism is here characterized as a particular working-out of the structure of phenomenological distance: the absolute is absolute precisely because it includes its own self-distantiation as its constitutive moment.

What in the being of God is exterior to him — that is, "everything in being which is a consequence of existence," that is again, his "form" — is not at all in reality something foreign to the being of God; it is the being of God himself insofar as he precisely *is*, that is, insofar as he exists. *Alienation is real not as something exterior to the absolute but as constituting on the contrary its very essence.* It is as immanent in the internal life of being, or rather as the very structure of this life, that exteriority deploys itself and can then divide "the dead being in itself into a being repeated, so to speak, twice — positing it before itself." Thus existence is not different from being, but what makes this being different from itself. Here is how Fichte expresses himself on this subject: *"Absolute being presents itself in its existence… as this independence with regard to its own intimate being; it does not create a freedom outside itself; but it is itself, in this part of the form, this freedom proper to it outside itself; and in this regard it is assuredly different in its existence from what it is in its being, and expels itself from itself in order to enter into itself with a new life."*

The italicized sentence — "alienation is real not as something exterior to the absolute but as constituting on the contrary its very essence" — is the most condensed formulation of the section's thesis. The structure of phenomenality is the structure of self-alienation: being can manifest itself only by becoming-other-than-itself, only by undergoing an internal self-separation. *Alienation is the essence of manifestation* — this will be stated at the end of paragraph 6\. And Henry's whole later work will be devoted to showing that this thesis, while accurate as a description of the dominant philosophical tradition, is *false* as a doctrine of the essence of manifestation: there is another mode of manifestation (immanent self-revelation, life's self-affection) in which manifestation does *not* require self-alienation.

**Paragraph 6\.** The preceding analyses take their concrete ontological signification if one is willing to situate them in the phenomenological frame of which they constitute, in truth, a definition. In conformity with this frame, it appears that the passage from being-in-itself to being-for-itself consists in the positing-outside-itself of being, is the passage of being to the outside of itself; what is realized in such a passage is the being-outside-itself of being-in-itself, and this being-outside-itself is the being-for-itself of being-in-itself, its existence. In this being-outside-itself, being-in-itself becomes other; it alienates itself; and in this alienation are realized the very conditions of its manifestation. *Alienation is the essence of manifestation.*

Henry now folds the Fichtean-Böhmean analysis into the explicitly Hegelian-Sartrian vocabulary of *en-soi* and *pour-soi* (in-itself and for-itself, Hegel's *an-sich* and *für-sich*, taken up by Sartre in *L'Être et le Néant*). The being-for-itself of being-in-itself is precisely what existence is — being's coming-out-of-itself in order to be present to itself. This passage *is* alienation, and alienation *is* manifestation. The thesis "alienation is the essence of manifestation" gathers in a single formulation what the entire section has been arguing: phenomenality, as classically conceived, requires self-distantiation, and self-distantiation is alienation. The dominant tradition has thought manifestation always as self-alienation.

The being that manifests itself is the present being. The essence of presence is alienation. The presence-to-itself of being is one with its separation from itself in becoming-other; it constitutes itself in the doubling of being, a doubling in which being appears to itself and thus enters into the phenomenal condition of presence. *"Every 'presence-to,'"* says Sartre, *"implies duality, therefore separation."* And further: *"the presence of being to itself implies a un-sticking \[décollement\] of being from itself."* Finally: *"presence is an immediate degradation of coincidence, since it supposes separation."*

The citations from Sartre are from *L'Être et le Néant* (1943) — Section II, Chapter I (on the for-itself as nihilation) and Section II, Chapter II (on the presence of the for-itself to itself). Sartre's analyses of the for-itself as the *néantisation* (nihilation) of the in-itself, and of the for-itself as essentially structured by a non-coincidence with itself, are the most explicit philosophical articulation of the structure Henry has been describing. For Sartre, consciousness *is* the nothingness that comes to being to introduce non-coincidence into it; consciousness *is* presence-to-itself only insofar as it is not-itself, insofar as it has decompacted itself, "*décollé*" (un-stuck) itself from itself. Sartre's analyses are, for Henry, the most rigorous late-twentieth-century formulation of the ontological monism Henry is diagnosing.

**Paragraph 7\.** The conditions that define the possibility of a presence and constitute consequently its very essence have a universal and transcendental signification. They are conditions that remain — as long, at least, as something like the reign of a presence is deployed and maintained among us. These conditions have been thought under the title of "phenomenological distance"; the latter is therefore valid as an eidetic and unsurmountable determination of real being: *"the possibility for a given to appear as given," it is "this unbridgeable and perpetually safeguarded distance from which a presence can be discerned."* Understood in its existential and transcendental signification, the concept of phenomenological distance is identical to the originary and ontologically pure concept of *alienation*. Alienation is unsurmountable. Being exists and manifests itself only as alienated being. Reality is real only insofar as it is at once itself and other than itself. Alienation is not only one eidetic structure among others; it is the very structure of the essence, insofar as the essence is absolute. The suppression of alienation is an impossibility of eidetic order, and the idea of such a suppression constitutes, from the ontological point of view, an absurdity.

This is a formidable thesis, and it is the source of one of Henry's deepest critiques of Marxist (and Hegelian) thought. If alienation is the structure of phenomenality itself, then the project of "overcoming alienation" — central to Hegelian idealism (the absolute spirit's reconciliation with itself), to Marxism (the abolition of alienated labor), and to existentialism (the achievement of authentic self-coincidence) — is, on the ontological plane, *absurd*: there can be no overcoming of alienation because alienation is the condition of there being any phenomenon at all, including any "overcoming." This thesis prepares Henry's much later work *Marx* (1976), where he will distinguish alienation in the ontic-historical sense (which can be overcome by social transformation) from alienation in the ontological sense (which cannot, because it is constitutive of phenomenality as classically conceived) — and where he will argue that Marx's deepest insight was precisely to break with the ontological-monist conception of alienation by founding a new ontology of subjective living praxis.

The suppression of alienation could not, indeed, be something — and as such, a positive phenomenon to which the discourse stating it could refer — except if the conditions of reality were realized in it. These conditions, however, are realized precisely only in the originary and pure phenomenon of alienation. If this were effectively suppressed, this suppression would be nothing; it would not exist. Such a suppression can in reality be produced only on the foundation in itself of alienation. And this does not signify that, in this suppression, the phenomenon of alienation would be little by little and progressively eliminated, like the distance separating the walker from the goal vanishes when this goal is attained. Alienation opens and defines the field of being; it is an ultimate ontological structure. The suppression of alienation could not have an ontological signification. Alienation is rather posited and maintained in such a suppression as the originary ontological phenomenon that founds it and renders it possible. Being exists only as being-other; but the return of the other into the same — or rather the unity that links them and that Fichte calls life — does not suppress their duality but presupposes it as its ontological and phenomenal foundation. *"This second unity inside the duality, which is not suppressed by it but subsists eternally, is precisely life."*

The Fichtean citation introduces a crucial term: *life* (*la vie*, Fichte's *Leben*). For Fichte, life is the unity of the absolute that subsists across and *through* the duality of being and existence — the second unity that comes after and encompasses the duality without abolishing it. This Fichtean concept of life will be transformed by Henry in Sections III–IV of the book: Henry's own concept of *life as the self-affection of the absolute* is an inheritor of and a polemical response to Fichte's *Leben*. For Fichte, life is the unity that includes (does not abolish) the duality of being and existence; for Henry, life will be the unity that is *prior* to the duality, and that has nothing to do with the structure of phenomenological distance — life is self-affection in radical immanence, without distance, without doubling, without alienation.

**Paragraph 8\.** What can the suppression of alienation signify if it does not concern the ontological phenomenon thought under this title? What must be understood by the unity of the other and the same if alterity subsists, and that as the very condition of this unity? This unity is posited as what links the separated terms; but the link it institutes has nothing to do with any process of an ontic order. The unity here in question has an ontological signification, just as the difference it comes to abolish does. It is the unity of presence. *Presence is precisely what unites.* It is because the essence of presence is immanent in them as the originary ontological power that confers on them their proper power, that our senses unite us with things, and that our gaze, for example, carries us over there to the tree on the slope. The unity of man and world is an ontological unity; it suppresses alienation insofar as it is identical with freedom — that is, with the trait that joins us to things. The ontological essence of this unity is however nothing other than alienation. The suppression of alienation of which there can be question — as long as one places oneself on the ontological plane — is identical to this very alienation. *Difference is the essence of unity.* The essence of presence which is thought under the title of this unity thus receives a well-determined structure. It is the essence of a presence that is obtained by the mediation of phenomenological distance. The proximity in which this presence makes us live is identical to the absolute distancing whose ontological work has opened a world for us. It is a *proximity in the distance*. *"We separate ourselves only to be more united,"* says Hölderlin, *"to be in a more divine peace with all things and with ourselves."* The union of which this peace is made however finds its principle in what separates; presence is obtained on the foundation of tearing-apart and of division.

The structure here, expressed with great compression, is one Henry treats with care. There is a real "unity" between man and world, between the gaze and the tree on the slope — but this unity is precisely the unity *across* the phenomenological distance, the unity *through* alienation. It is not a unity that abolishes alienation; it is a unity that *is* alienation seen from another angle. Henry calls this "proximity in the distance" — the only kind of proximity available within the structure of ontological monism. The Hölderlin citation (from one of his late hymns or fragments) gives poetic articulation to this paradoxical structure. The reference to "freedom" as identical with this unity prefigures Henry's later analyses of freedom: classical freedom (Sartrian, Heideggerian, Kantian) is the freedom of a subject that transcends its situation in the horizon of the world; Henry will show that this freedom is essentially structured by the same alienation that constitutes phenomenological distance, and that *another* concept of freedom — freedom as the self-possession of life in immanence — must be developed.

**Paragraph 9\.** Thus the presence of being to itself is not discernible from its distance with respect to itself. The essence of presence, at the same time that it grounds the given in its being, prescribes to the given specific characters in conformity with which it appears as other in the milieu of alterity. *What is given to us is by that very fact what is taken from us.* Being is there for itself, but as something that it is not, and from which separates it — as long as it is — an unbridgeable distance. Thus is explained that present being can nonetheless be desired, and that this desire be vain. For it is the essence; and the essence, incapable of overcoming itself, closes upon itself, encloses itself in itself, and in the cold contemplation of itself, gives itself to itself only as that of which it eternally lacks.

This is one of the most hauntingly precise sentences in the section: *what is given to us is by that very fact what is taken from us*. Within the structure of ontological monism, every gift is also a withdrawal; every presence is also an absence; every approach is also a separation — because the very structure of givenness is the doubling that distances what it brings near. Hence the experience of *desire*: even what is fully present is desired, and the desire is vain, because the very condition of presence is the unbridgeable distance that no desire can close. The diagnosis is also a diagnosis of *nostalgia*: the present being is given as that which the present is "of" but which the present can never quite *be*. The cold contemplation of self is the contemplation in which the absolute, by the very structure of its self-presence, is given to itself only as what it lacks.

Presence is the foundation of knowledge; it is, as such, the theme of *transcendental knowledge* — that which occupies itself not with objects but "with our way of knowing objects insofar as this must be possible *a priori*." The cited phrase is from Kant's First *Critique*, B25 (the definition of transcendental philosophy). The being of objects is however the *a priori* itself. In prescribing to objects the conditions of their possibility, the *a priori* confers on them the characters that follow from the wanting of the essence. Objects manifest themselves with these characters as separated objects that knowledge can never rejoin, except by the mediation of this very separation. Knowledge is thus *"always knowledge of what we are not, of what we do not arrive at being."* The desire to *"conserve the benefit of the presence-to-self... without suffering the inconveniences of distance from self"* remains a *"dream."* In order to give itself self-presence, being had to separate itself from itself; and the will to truly find itself again in overcoming this separation otherwise than by its own mediation could only be a *"useless passion."* Being is the desire of itself; it is its own nostalgia.

The cited phrases come from Sartre — *"useless passion"* (*passion inutile*) is Sartre's famous closing characterization of human reality in *L'Être et le Néant*: "*l'homme est une passion inutile*." The for-itself's longing to coincide with itself — to be God, to be the in-itself-for-itself, to be at once the foundation and the founded — is essentially impossible, because the very being of the for-itself is non-coincidence. Henry adopts this Sartrian formulation but reorients it: it is not *human reality* that is a useless passion (this would be a humanistic-existentialist thesis); it is *being itself*, in the structure of ontological monism, that is the desire of itself and its own nostalgia. The whole of philosophy from Plato to Sartre, structured by this monism, has been a meditation on the impossibility internal to presence — the impossibility of coinciding with what is given. The next section will name this presupposition explicitly and inaugurate the work of overcoming it.

---

## **§ 11\. Ontological monism and the problem of its overcoming: philosophy of consciousness and philosophy of being**

**Paragraph 1\.** The ontological presuppositions that have been exposed and thought as the condition of phenomenality and as constituting under that title the essence of phenomenon will be designated in the rest of this work under the title of "ontological monism." This is the explicit naming of the doctrine that Sections §§9–10 have been describing without yet labeling. Such presuppositions command, since their origin in Greece, the development of Western philosophical thought; they indicate the unique direction of research and of encounter where something can show itself and consequently be found by us. The unicity of this direction can be called into question only by an overcoming of monism, and the problem is posed of knowing whether such an overcoming has a sense — and whether, in any case, it has ever been attempted or sketched in the course of the history of human thought. The latter has accomplished many advances, notably in modern times. On closer inspection, however, it appears that these advances have always unfolded inside the ontological horizon drawn by monism, and that their most remarkable result has been, in contemporary ontology, only the *liberation* of this horizon, finally brought into the clarity of the concept and from then on thought as "the horizon of being." With this latter, however, an exclusive form is prescribed to the accomplishment of experience, which determines, in an unsurmountable way, the frame, the sense, and the nature of our relation to being.

The thesis is now formal and historical in scope: ontological monism is the doctrine that has *commanded* (Henry's word) Western philosophy from its Greek origin to the contemporary "horizon of being" (Heidegger). The advances of philosophy have not overcome monism; they have only progressively *clarified* it, until it appears in its purest form as the Heideggerian "horizon of being" (the structure of *Sein und Zeit*'s transcendence-in-the-world, and of the late Heidegger's *Lichtung*). The claim is sweeping: from Plato through Heidegger, philosophy has operated within a single ontological horizon, recognizing only one mode of phenomenality.

For a long time, however, since the dawn and the coming of modern philosophy, in any case — has not another originary form of being been thought and brought into the light? Has the philosophy of consciousness not consisted precisely, through its imperfections and whatever they may be, in the opening of another dimension of existence and of essence? Has it not indicated to man the arising for him and in him of another region of experience, of another mode of reality, and that in an ontological sense?

This is the question the section will examine. The hope might be that, against the long monist tradition that thinks being-as-such (the "philosophy of being," from Greek ontology through Heidegger), the modern philosophy of *consciousness* (from Descartes through Hegel and Husserl) has opened a *different* ontological dimension — that of subjectivity, of self-presence, of interiority. If so, then the philosophy of consciousness would constitute the long-sought overcoming of ontological monism. Henry will argue, on the contrary, that the philosophy of consciousness is *one form of* ontological monism, not its alternative.

**Paragraph 2\.** As soon as thought shows itself capable of conferring on the problematic it has aroused a character and a scope of ontological order, the apparent oppositions which claimed to serve as indices and to draw, as it were, in the field of research, lines of cleavage for ulterior reflection, efface themselves; their signification appears in any case as having to be put in question and, very often, reveals itself null. The opposition of consciousness and being which seems to dominate the history of philosophical thought can in fact be maintained only on a pre-philosophical and pre-critical plane. The opposition could come to the fore only because at least one of the terms between which it claimed to institute itself remained plunged, as to its concept, in a fundamental indetermination. The philosophy of being finds its origin in Greek ontology, but as Heidegger has noted, the latter remains very often naïve in that it considers the existent such as it offers itself to us, taking for granted its being-given instead of considering this being-given in and for itself, and decisively interrogating it. With such an interrogation, on the contrary, thought raises to the state of a problem what renders possible in its being the existent to which we have access each time; it lifts the "ambiguity" of the word *existent* (*étant*) which means at the same time something and its existent-ness (*étantité*, essence), and which therefore is also "ontological." "The Greek *ὄν*, 'existent,'" Heidegger says again, "hides in itself a proper essence of existent-ness." To take into consideration this essence is to make the partition, in the existent itself, between what is ontic and what remains ontological. With this dissociation the concept of being emerges from its pre-philosophical indetermination; it ceases to designate indistinctly — as it does too often in the history of philosophy and still in Sartre — the existent and its ontological foundation, in order to refer explicitly and exclusively to the latter. The opposition of being and the existent surges up at the very moment when the problematic conquers its ontological signification.

This is the standard Heideggerian doctrine of the "ontological difference" (the distinction between being and beings, *Sein* and *Seiendes*) from *Sein und Zeit* §1 and the early Marburg and Freiburg lectures, especially *Die Grundprobleme der Phänomenologie* (1927). Henry endorses the Heideggerian distinction. But he then turns it against the supposed opposition between "philosophy of being" and "philosophy of consciousness": once the ontological difference is properly drawn, the philosophy of being and the philosophy of consciousness turn out to be addressing the same structure under different names.

**Paragraph 3\.** When the concept of being has received its proper ontological determination, the problem of its relation with the antithetical concept of consciousness can be posed on a philosophical basis. The opposition, classical since Descartes, between consciousness and the thing — can it cover, as has been commonly done, the opposition of consciousness and being? Is it not evident, on the contrary, that the philosophical analysis of the "thing" falls under the same dialectic and obeys the same prescriptions as that of the existent? The thing, which is none other than the existent, requires the same ontological foundation, an essence of the thing, *thingness* (*la choséité*) as such. The thing understood in its unity with the essence that grounds it — is it still for consciousness an antithetical term, or is consciousness not precisely the very thingness of the thing and, as such, the essence of it? It is not to being, in fact, that consciousness — in its concept — supposes itself opposed; it is precisely to the existent. Consciousness receives, like being, the signification of being the essence and the foundation. The opposition of consciousness and the thing is the same as that of being and the existent. The advent of modern idealism dissimulates in fact the appearance in the history of thought of a new and properly philosophical mode of questioning — the one that, interrogating the condition of possibility of the thing, thus proposes to reflection, as its own object, the elucidation of the ontological sphere of existence.

The argumentative move is decisive. The Cartesian opposition "consciousness vs. thing" has been read for centuries as an opposition between two regions of being (mind and matter, soul and body, subject and object). But, Henry argues, it is in fact an instance of the *ontological difference* itself: the "thing" is the existent, and "consciousness" is the essence/foundation/condition-of-possibility of the existent. So the philosophy of consciousness, properly understood, is not a competitor to the philosophy of being; it is an early modern form of the same fundamental-ontological project. Both ask: what is the condition of possibility of the existent's being given as existent? Both answer: a transcendental opening, an essence, a horizon, a foundation. The two philosophies are united by a common project, which is just the project of ontological monism.

This existence, understood as the ontological condition of possibility of the thing, is thus the existence of the existent on which ancient thought meditated without however interrogating this existence as such. Insofar as it brings to the state of a problem the essence of what Greek ontology took in a pre-philosophical way for being itself, the philosophy of consciousness appears as the *accomplishment* of the ancient philosophy of being; it is a term and not a commencement. It is one with contemporary ontology, which has known precisely how to give as theme to its research the ontological condition of possibility of the existent, and to understand this condition as the ontological milieu of truth.

The Cartesian-Husserlian-Hegelian philosophy of consciousness is the *accomplishment* of Greek ontology: where Aristotle and Plato thought the existent without thematizing the condition of its being-given, Descartes-Husserl-Hegel make this condition itself thematic under the name of "consciousness." Then in turn Heidegger's contemporary "ontology of being" makes the same condition thematic under the name of "being" or "horizon of being." But in all three moments — Greek ontology, modern philosophy of consciousness, contemporary fundamental ontology — what is in question is the same essence: the essence of manifestation as horizonal-transcendent disclosure.

**Paragraph 4\.** The connection of the philosophy of consciousness with the problem of truth understood in its universal ontological signification resides in the fact that the concept of consciousness is the element by means of which modern philosophy thinks the possibility for the thing to manifest itself — the essence of manifestation as such. Before falling, indeed, to the rank of a simply privileged existent (as the opposition instituted between it and the totality of the existent that is "exterior" to it testifies), consciousness intervenes first in the ontological design of a thought that interrogates itself on the power that confers on the existent its condition as phenomenon for us. If the ontological concept of being designates the essence of manifestation, existence — if the latter is the "form" of being, if being is this form itself — consciousness is nothing other than this form, that is, existence itself, manifestation as such.

Henry now traces the genealogy more precisely. There are two ways of using "consciousness": (i) consciousness as a privileged existent (the soul, the *res cogitans*, the psychological subject), opposed to other existents — this is the *fallen* sense of "consciousness," the pre-critical sense; and (ii) consciousness as the very essence of manifestation, as the form-of-being-of-the-existent — this is the *originary* ontological sense, in which "consciousness" names the same structure as "being" in the ontological sense. In the second sense, consciousness \= existence \= form-of-being \= manifestation \= transcendence \= the structure of phenomenological distance. All these terms are equivalent in the structural-ontological vocabulary.

That "consciousness be the absolute existence or the manifestation and revelation of being in its only possible form" — this is what Fichte affirms explicitly. An opposition could not consequently institute itself on the ontological plane between the concepts of being and of consciousness, except if the pure mode of manifestation to which they refer were to be considered by us as different in the two cases. It would be necessary that the mode of manifestation thought under the title of consciousness *not be the same* as the one that constitutes existence, which is the essence of being. It is in fact the same ontological power of manifestation that is thought by Fichte under the titles, equivalent for him, of existence, form, representation, manifestation, revelation, image, consciousness, and being in the philosophical sense — that is, in the sense the verb *to be* has in the expression "the wall is."

The Fichtean inventory is precise: in late Fichte, all these terms are *equivalent* — they all designate the same structural ontological power, namely, the power of self-distantiation through which being makes itself present to itself as image. Consciousness, manifestation, representation, image, existence: one and the same structure, named in different vocabularies. This is the structure that Henry calls *ontological monism*.

**Paragraph 5\.** This ontological power of manifestation consists, as has been seen, in the process by which being divides itself and separates itself from itself in order to exist — that is, in order to manifest itself to itself. To phenomenal existence which realizes itself in such a process, Fichte gives explicitly the name of *consciousness*. This consciousness, which arises in a determinate ontological process, has consequently the ontological characters that the process from which it results confers on it; and these characters are the same as those of the image or of the representation that also come about inside such a process — and that are, in truth, nothing other than consciousness. *"Existence,"* said Fichte, *"must by its own being annihilate itself in face of another absolute existence; which precisely gives it the character of simple image, of representation, or of consciousness of being."* Consciousness is therefore not another form of existence than the one which arises in the internal tearing-apart of being; it is rather this very existence, this form alone and unique of every possible manifestation. *"The consciousness of being, the only form and only possible mode of the existence of being, is from then on itself in a wholly immediate way purely and absolutely this existence of being."*

The Fichtean conclusion crystallizes the diagnosis: consciousness *just is* the structure of existence-as-self-distantiation. Every consciousness, *qua* consciousness, has the structure of being-other-than-itself, of being-image-of, of being-the-self-presence-that-distances-from-itself. This structural identity between "consciousness" and "ontological self-distantiation" is the heart of the philosophy of consciousness when properly understood — and it makes the philosophy of consciousness one form of ontological monism.

**Paragraph 6\.** Consciousness designates the essence of manifestation interpreted according to the fundamental ontological presuppositions of monism. For this reason, because consciousness identifies itself with the process of self-tearing-apart and of self-separation of being, consciousness is always presented in its work and in its becoming as an act of separating itself from being, of raising itself above being, of taking distance with respect to being, of opposing itself to being. The arising of consciousness thus appears in its contemporaneity with the deployment of a distance, with the accomplishment of the division, the separation, the opposition to self. Division, separation, opposition were precisely, however, the conditions of phenomenality in ontological monism. All these conditions, which are only one, refer in fact — as so many diverse but equivalent titles — to the same phenomenon of *alienation*, thought as the fundamental event that opens the dimension of being and of existence. Consciousness is itself nothing other than the alienation of being — that is, being as such. The becoming-other of being is identical with its arising in the phenomenal condition of presence. This phenomenal dimension of presence is consciousness itself.

Henry now folds together the analyses of §§9–10 (phenomenological distance, doubling of being, alienation as the essence of manifestation) with the claim about consciousness: consciousness is the alienation of being, just is the doubling structure that constitutes phenomenality. The claim is structural: when philosophers (Hegel, Schelling, Fichte, Husserl, Sartre) describe consciousness, they describe the very same structure — alienation, distancing, doubling — that the section's preceding analyses have identified with the essence of manifestation in the monist tradition.

It is because the absolute does not yet know this internal division from itself that constitutes consciousness that the absolute remains, in Schelling, deprived of consciousness. *"The absolute is only the absolute identity in which there is no duality and which, precisely because duality is the condition of all consciousness, can never come to consciousness."* The "supreme term... that divides itself in order to appear" arrives at the condition of phenomenal and conscious existence only when it accepts to abandon itself to the work of alterity and of division. History will be precisely the movement by which the absolute manifests itself in conformity with the conditions prescribed to it by the essence of manifestation interpreted according to the presuppositions of monism. History, says Schelling, is *"a never-completed manifestation of this absolute that divides itself in consciousness — that is, only in order to appear."*

The Schellingian references are to the *System of Transcendental Idealism* (1800) and to the late lectures on revelation, mythology, and the *Ages of the World* (Schelling's later work as cited by Henry). Schelling's doctrine — which Henry will return to in §39 (on Eckhart) and elsewhere — is paradigmatic of how monism conceives the relation between absolute and consciousness: the absolute *as such* is unconscious because consciousness requires duality, and the absolute is pure identity; consciousness emerges only when the absolute alienates itself from itself, divides itself, in order to become present to itself. The whole structure of Schellingian and Hegelian historicity is the temporalization of this self-alienation of the absolute into consciousness.

**Paragraph 7\.** It is always the identification of the concept of consciousness with the monist conception of the essence of manifestation that brings Schelling to establish, in the *System of Transcendental Idealism*, an irreducible opposition between the intelligence and the action — or, as he says again, the production. This irreducibility holds precisely to the understanding of opposition as the essence of manifestation and of consciousness. It is in order that such an opposition be instituted and safeguarded — and with it conscious existence — that the intelligence must disengage and separate itself from its action. It is the interval that this opposition digs that constitutes the phenomenological milieu where the action can arise and posit itself as something conscious and objective. *"The intelligence,"* says Schelling, *"must completely disengage itself from the production for consciousness to be able to be born."* And again: *"As long as the intelligence does not differ from its action, no consciousness of this action is possible."* The intelligence and the action do not constitute, in Schelling's eyes, two different and originarily separated realities; in the absolute, they are only one and the same thing. It is not to action, it is to "its action" that the intelligence opposes itself — that is, to itself insofar as active. But precisely, this self-separation is the condition of phenomenality, a primitive condition that then makes the intelligence and the action arise as two apparently different terms — and this in order that consciousness can be born. The intelligence is, in truth, nothing other than the consciousness of action, that is, in fact, action itself in its phenomenal opposition to itself.

Already Böhme's thought was entirely commanded by the idea of an opposition and a differentiation interior to the life of the absolute, constitutive of this life insofar as this life is precisely only a promotion into the light of manifestation. The *Schiedlichkeit* (separability, difference-character) is the condition of consciousness. The concept of consciousness is thought by Böhme in its solidarity with the concepts of alterity, of mirror, of doubling — that is, in its unity with the ontological process of internal division of being. This division is presented as the condition of the vision with which knowledge is identified — that is, in fact, consciousness and phenomenal existence. The interpretation of the concept of consciousness starting from the doubling by which being offers itself as spectacle to itself and can thus apperceive and know itself does not manifest itself only in the *System of Transcendental Idealism* under Böhme's influence; it dominates in fact all the ulterior work of Schelling, and notably his last philosophy. The great human phenomena (for example the birth and development of mythology) or divine (for example creation) are in fact interpreted as a function of the necessity of an advent of consciousness — an advent that is always thought, starting from the central ontological phenomenon of alienation, as a division and a separation. *"This separation, this Scheidung, is it not the condition of all conscious knowledge?"*

The genealogy is precise: the Böhmean doctrine of *Schiedlichkeit* (the differentiating-separating internal to divine life), articulated in *Mysterium Magnum* and other works, becomes through Schelling the German-idealist doctrine of consciousness as essentially constituted by self-division. The whole of late Schelling's thought (mythology, revelation, the *Ages of the World*, the *Philosophy of Mythology*, the *Philosophy of Revelation*) operates within this framework. And the same framework operates wherever consciousness is thought monistically — including, Henry will argue, in Husserl's and Heidegger's modern phenomenologies.

**Paragraph 8\.** It is far from being the case, however, that the interpretation of the essence of consciousness from a monist conception of the mode of manifestation of reality comes to the fore only inside one determinate current of philosophical thought. It is not only in the post-Kantians and notably in Hegel that consciousness is identified in its concept with the ontological phenomenon of the alienation of being and of its opposition to itself. This conception dominates in fact the *whole* of the philosophy of consciousness; it finds its illustration along with its most general formulation in the understanding of the essence of consciousness as *representation*. Representation designates a mode of presence. To represent oneself signifies to render oneself present. Representation is always representation *of* something; it implies a represented that it has precisely the mission to render present. It is fitting therefore to distinguish representation understood as an act of rendering present, and on the other hand the reality that arrives at presence inside such an act — that is, the represented as such. The represented is something ontic; representation, which signifies presence as such, refers on the contrary to an ontological process. The process on which representation leans, insofar as representation designates the essence of presence, is the ontological process of alienation. *Representation is a presentation that implies a redoubling.* This redoubling finds its foundation in the opposing-doubling by which being separates itself from itself in order to apperceive itself, and precisely "to represent itself."

The argument expands: not only Fichte and Schelling but the *whole* tradition of the philosophy of consciousness understands consciousness essentially as *representation* — the *re*\-presentation of what is present, the second presence (*re*\-praesentatio) that doubles the first. And representation has the structure of doubling, which is the structure of alienation, which is the structure of phenomenological distance. So "consciousness as representation" \= "consciousness as alienation" \= ontological monism. The presence which arises in this opposing-doubling is the existence of Fichte, which finds itself understood for this reason as representation. *"Existence,"* said Fichte, *"must by its own being annihilate itself in face of another absolute existence; which precisely gives it the character of simple image, of representation, or of consciousness of being."* *"The existence of being,"* says Fichte again, *"is the consciousness or the representation of being."* The assimilation of consciousness to representation is not accidental; it rests on the community of essence that comes to the fore behind the concepts of "consciousness" and "representation" as soon as one wants to grasp them in their ontological signification.

The will to grasp the essence of consciousness brings thought before the ontological process that confers on this essence its proper structure; and it is precisely when consciousness is understood from this essence that is its own that it is thought as representation. Representation in no way designates a particular mode of the life of consciousness, as if there were for consciousness — as a possibility offered to it — a representative life alongside other forms and other possible modes of existence (alongside, for example, a sensible, conceptual, or affective life). It is the *essence* of consciousness that must be understood in its proper, universal eidetic structure in the light of the concept of "representation." This is why Heidegger can say that *"representation (Vor-stellen) reigns over all the modes of consciousness."* Representation so understood is what "presents on the mode of representation"; it refers explicitly to the essence as such of presence, and invites us to understand this essence as a presence that is the presence of the represented — that is, the presence of something that comes-up before, in a milieu of exteriority of which this representation itself, as the common essence of consciousness and representation, is nothing other than the opening.

The Heideggerian reference is to "*Die Zeit des Weltbildes*" (1938, in *Holzwege*) and to "*Der Spruch des Anaximander*," where Heidegger shows that the modern interpretation of being as *Vor-stellen* (re-presentation, putting-before) reigns over the entire modern conception of consciousness, knowledge, and truth. Henry adopts the Heideggerian diagnosis: representation is not one mode of consciousness; it is the essence of consciousness as conceived monistically. But Henry will then turn this against Heidegger himself: Heidegger's own conception of being-as-disclosure-in-the-horizon is also structured by the same essence (the opening of an exteriority in which something can be put-before).

**Paragraph 9\.** One of the most constant indications by which the philosophy of consciousness sometimes tries to specify the concept of representation on which it rests is the designation of representation under the title of *certainty*. What characterizes representation is *self-certainty* (*la certitude de soi*). Representation is certain. The represented being is also certain, but its certainty is grounded in that of representation. Or, to be more exact, the certainty of the represented being resides precisely in its representation. What is certain is the theme of natural consciousness. But the being-certain of what is certain is precisely *certainty as such*. Here is posed this question: when it is understood as self-certainty, does representation always designate the same essence of manifestation? Or does the intervention of the concept of certainty in the understanding of this essence in fact bring a real modification? It is from Descartes onward that the *true being* (*ens verum*) is interpreted as the *certain being* (*ens certum*). It is not a matter here, however, of a new interpretation of the truth of the existent, but of the moment when, for the first time, this truth is brought to the state of a problem. The taking-into-consideration of this problem brings one to think that the truth of the existent consists in the fact for the existent of being represented. It is when the existent is represented that it is torn from the night to which it is, by itself, delivered in principle. The representation of the existent is on the contrary its arising in the light; it operates and translates its accession to the rank of "phenomenon"; it is truth understood in an ontological sense.

How is ontological truth — identical to representation — understood when it finds itself identified, in addition, with certainty? If certainty designates the being-certain of what is certain, the fact of appearing of what appears to us, the arising into the light in virtue of which the existent offers itself to us such as it is — this arising by which the existent becomes for us a true or certain existent (*ens verum*, *ens certum*), it is *representation* that operates it. Certainty is the certainty of representation. The essence of manifestation that makes the being-certain of what is certain — that is, certainty as such — is the one whose structure is constituted by the ontological process of representation, insofar as this process is nothing other than that of alienation. Certainty is a title to designate what is produced by such a process — that is, phenomenal existence and manifestation as such. What is aimed at in the concept of certainty is the *phenomenological signification of the ontological power of representation*.

The Cartesian transformation of *ens verum* into *ens certum* is taken from Heidegger's analyses in *Nietzsche II* and *Holzwege* (in particular the essay "*Hegels Begriff der Erfahrung*"). Henry endorses the Heideggerian diagnosis: from Descartes onward, "truth" comes to mean "certainty," that is, the certainty of consciousness of its representation. But this is just the claim, in modern Cartesian-Husserlian vocabulary, that the essence of manifestation is the structure of self-distantiating representation. The shift from "truth" to "certainty" is not a deepening; it is the exact same essence of manifestation that monism has always presupposed.

The ontological power of representation is exhausted, it is true, in this phenomenological signification. The act of positing-before makes only one with the arising in the light. For this reason precisely, certainty is not different from representation as such; it belongs to representation as its own. Its essence is that of representation. Because the essence of certainty is that of representation, certainty is always certainty of *something*. As certainty, it designates nothing other than the truth of the existent. With the intervention of the concept of certainty, it is not another form of truth, another truth than that of the existent; it is *this very truth*, in and for itself, that is thought. The certainty of representation is the ontological milieu where the existent manifests itself; it is the essence of manifestation and of the truth of the existent.

**Paragraph 10\.** With the concept of certainty, the idea of a *subjectivity* is profiled at the horizon. Certainty is subjective. Representation opposes itself to the represented as the subjective to the objective. Insofar as truth resides in the certainty of representation, truth gives itself, also, as subjective. The ultimate signification of truth, understood in an ontological sense, depends on the interpretation that it is fitting to give to the concept of "subjectivity." Subjectivity is the essence of the subject. The subject appears as the condition of the phenomenality of phenomena. The object precisely cannot become what it is for us — that is, a phenomenon — except when it is related to the subject. The classical opposition of subject and object appears when the being of the object becomes a problem, that is, when it is a question of thinking the object in its quality of *ob-ject*. What makes the object be what it is, that is, something that is posited before us, is the subject insofar as it is precisely the power that operates this position of "before." The object manifests itself insofar as it is conscious. But the being-conscious of the object resides in the subject.

Henry now develops the structural consequence of the Cartesian-Kantian conception of certainty: the emergence of "subjectivity" as the technical term for the condition of phenomenality. The subject is, in proper philosophical usage, not a particular existent (a soul, a psychological self) but the *power* that constitutes the object as object, that "posits before." This is the Kantian transcendental subject, the Husserlian transcendental ego, the Hegelian Spirit — all forms of subjectivity in the ontological sense. The "object" here is correlatively defined: not the physical thing but the *ob-ject*, the thrown-before, the thing constituted as the term of the subjective act of positing.

Consciousness however is not the subject. On closer examination, it appears that the opposition instituted by classical philosophy between subject and object is not at all an opposition between something that is conscious (the subject) and something that is not conscious (the object) — between consciousness and unconsciousness. What characterizes the object is precisely the fact that it is conscious. The being-in-itself to which one too often assimilates the object is in no way an *ob-ject*. To be an *ob-ject* is to be situated in the phenomenal dimension of existence and to belong, as such, to consciousness. This belonging to consciousness is grounded assuredly in the relation to the subject. *Consciousness resides precisely in the relation of subject and object; it is this relation as such.* If the ontological design of modern idealism expresses itself in the inexhaustibly formulated opposition of subject and object, it is because consciousness resides in the eyes of modern idealism in this very opposition. The subject is in no way something different from the object that one could oppose to the object as one opposes one reality to another, on the foundation of a difference of their properties and characters — a difference, for example, between the being-conscious and the being-non-conscious. In itself, the subject does not oppose itself to the object. *"There is separation between them only as soon as there is consciousness."* Consciousness is therefore not the subject but the opposition of subject and object.

This is a precise and important diagnosis. Modern idealism (Kant-Fichte-Hegel-Husserl) typically describes itself as positing two terms, subject and object, related by consciousness. But properly understood, "subject" and "object" are not two separable terms; they are the *poles* of a single structure, namely the structure of consciousness itself. Consciousness *is* the subject-object opposition, not one of its terms. Henry cites Schelling: "There is separation between them only as soon as there is consciousness." Without consciousness, there is no separated subject and no separated object; the very separation is the work of consciousness. So consciousness is not "the subject" (as the dualistic, pre-critical reading suggests); consciousness is the *relation* in which subject and object emerge as the two poles of the relation.

When Renouvier speaks to us of "the opposition of subject and object essential to all consciousness," the presupposition of his thought is more than implicit. This presupposition appears clearly also in the theses of Schelling that have been evoked, and according to which it is not the subject, it is duality, division as such, that is the condition of manifestation, of consciousness. Because consciousness is division, it is the production of the two terms, not one of them, the subject, with which it would identify itself in order to oppose itself to the other in an opposition that would remain exterior to it and would add itself synthetically to it, or would be added to it by a foreign spectator. *Opposition is interior to consciousness.* It is so interior to consciousness that consciousness is nothing other than this opposition itself. Because consciousness is opposition, it is not one of the terms but the two terms at once, insofar as it is the *law* that engenders them. *"The I of consciousness,"* says Schelling in a fundamental proposition, *"is not a pure subject; it is at the same time subject and object."*

**Paragraph 11\.** Consciousness resides in the opposition of subject and object — that is, in their relation. It is the relation as such. The relation is the concrete term; abstract on the contrary are the terms between which the relation institutes itself: *"the pure subjective just as much as the pure objective,"* says Hegel, *"is an abstraction."* *"Subject and object appear as two abstract moments of a unique structure that is presence,"* says Merleau-Ponty. The object could not be abstracted from this structure of presence, since it is only inside this structure that it is an *ob-ject*. The subject, for its part, has no subsistence as a determinate being opposed to the object. It is because Sartre confuses consciousness with the abstract subject (as he confuses being with the object) that he is precisely brought to think consciousness as an abstract — to affirm that the *"for-itself is in no way an autonomous substance,"* that dualism comes from the fact that one abstracts consciousness and being, that what is concrete is their relation.

The polemical encounter with Sartre is sharply delineated. Sartre in *L'Être et le Néant* explicitly denies that the for-itself (consciousness) is a substance; he insists that the relation between for-itself and in-itself is the concrete reality, while the two terms taken in abstraction are abstractions. Henry concedes this Sartrian point — but only to show that Sartre, by accepting it, has placed himself fully within ontological monism. The "concrete relation" Sartre invokes is *just* the structure of phenomenological distance, the structure of monism. Sartre's repudiation of the dualism of substances is at the price of accepting the monism of the relational structure.

The affirmation of the abstract character of subject and object (improperly called for-itself, in-itself, consciousness, being, etc.) and, inversely, of the concrete character of their relation, permits Sartre to refuse the dualism that issues from abstraction and to reject the objection of the incommunicability of the two regions distinguished by him — those of the in-itself and the for-itself. *"The relation of the regions of being is a primitive springing-forth that forms part of the very structure of these beings."* The relation is in fact the fundamental ontological region; it is precisely the springing-forth of light that defines the transcendental field of being and of existence. Consciousness is itself this relation as such. From the ontological point of view, there are not two regions of being but a single region; and consciousness, which is neither the subject nor the object but their relation, is precisely this fundamental ontological region — not one of the two regions distinguished by abstraction. *On the ontological plane, the philosophy of consciousness grounds and authorizes no dualism.* When it rejects the improper formulations in which it has nearly always been incarnated, in order to understand itself finally in the light of the sense of the fundamental problematic that it aimed from the start to institute, *the philosophy of consciousness appears to itself as an expression of ontological monism.*

The italicized claim is the central thesis of the whole section, here stated with full clarity: the philosophy of consciousness, properly understood (beyond its pre-critical formulations as a dualism of substances), is *one form* of ontological monism. The "consciousness" of the philosophy of consciousness is the same essence as the "being" of the philosophy of being; both are the structure of phenomenological distance, the relation-as-such, the opening of the horizon, the work of alienation.

**Paragraph 12\.** Understood as the essence, in no way constituting one of the terms of a duality, consciousness is the commerce that is instituted between these terms; it is the being of this "between." If we consider the concrete totality of reality — the totality constituted by the real in its reality, that is, in the act by which it manifests itself — we see that this totality cannot be translated into the equation "consciousness \+ relation to the object \+ object." Consciousness is in fact nothing other than the relation to the object. But can the idea of a subject as a term opposed to the object be maintained, in such a way that we have the equation "subject \+ relation to the object (or consciousness) \+ object"? The three terms of this equation would, first of all, in no way be situated on the same plane. Only the second of these terms, the relation as such to the object, is of ontological order. But if the object is an ontic reality whose being is constituted by the relation as such, if it remains consequently a real determination that finds in consciousness its ontological foundation, such a situation cannot suit the subject. The being of the subject is in fact the relation as such. The dissociation between the concepts of consciousness and of subject is possible only as long as one remains, for the latter, with a pre-critical determination that makes the reality designated by it fall to the level of an ontic reality. *It is the ontological reality as such that is in fact aimed at by the philosophy of consciousness when it makes the concept of subject intervene in its problematic.* The subject designates the ontological event that makes the existent accede to the condition of object — that is, of phenomenon for us. The subject is nothing outside such an event understood in its absolutely pure ontological signification. To make the existent accede to the rank of phenomenon, to make it arise in the light of phenomenal and conscious existence — this is the work that is thought as that of the subject; and the being of the subject is nothing outside such a work, but is exhausted on the contrary in such a work. The being of the subject is thus identically the very arising of phenomenal existence; it consists in the opening of the ontological dimension of presence. It is because this ontological dimension of presence is thought traditionally and improperly under the title of "knowledge" that the subject is precisely understood as the "condition of knowledge." The subject is the power of knowledge, the *knower* as such. But *"the knower… is nothing other than what makes there be a being-there of the known, a presence."* *"Knowledge and the knower itself,"* it is also said, *"are nothing if not the fact that 'there is' being."* Knowledge, finally, is *"the pure solitude of the known."*

The subject is thus what makes the object be present; it is the object's presence as such. What makes the object be present, what makes the object be an *ob-ject*, what makes of the object what it is — namely, the object as object — is its being. *The subject is the being of the object.* It is the ontological foundation starting from which the object is what it is. *The dualism of subject and object is not an ontological dualism; it is the dualism of essence and ontic determination that finds in this essence its ontological foundation.* The traditional dualism appears thus as a first formulation, as the pre-critical thought of a properly philosophical dissociation between the existent and its being — between what is of ontic order and what belongs on the contrary to the ontological sphere of essence. It is this ontological region of essence that is thought under the title of subject, while object designates the existent on the foundation of essence in it, in its indissociable unity with essence. *What hides itself in the partition between subject and object is one and the same essence — and the traditional dualism is an ontological monism.* But the essential unity of which ontological monism is the title is not, even though it grounds them, the unity of the subject and of ontic determination; what it signifies is the *unicity of the mode of manifestation* in conformity with which the existent realizes itself in the subject, which is none other than this mode of manifestation as such.

This is a structurally crucial passage. The "dualism" subject/object is the surface phenomenon of the ontological difference essence/existent. What philosophers misread as a dualism is in fact the ontological-difference structure: subject \= essence/condition; object \= existent. So the apparent dualism is in fact a monism: there is only one mode of manifestation, articulated into the two poles "essence" (subject) and "existent" (object). The whole of the modern philosophy of consciousness is, in this respect, identical to the ancient and modern philosophy of being, because both operate within the same ontological-difference structure with one and only one mode of manifestation.

**Paragraph 13\.** The ultimate presuppositions that are aimed at under the title of ontological monism do not exhaust themselves in the affirmation of the unicity of the mode of manifestation understood in its essential phenomenological purity; they confer on this mode in fact a *perfectly defined eidetic structure*. It is not the sole affirmation of the unicity of phenomenological essence, it is the *identity of structure* of this essence that grounds the essential identity, beyond apparent differences, of the philosophy of consciousness and of the philosophy of being. Thinking the subject as the foundation of the phenomenality of phenomena, the philosophy of consciousness interprets finally the being of this subject as *the Relation*. Insofar as it is the relation, the subject is the establishment and the maintenance of a distance, the ontological power that deploys the horizon, the originary and transcendental spatiality that opens the place where something can manifest itself. It distinguishes itself from this something as the pure milieu — by itself deprived of determination — where determination is susceptible of appearing: *"Consciousness,"* says Hegel, *"is itself the space deprived of determinacy."* Insofar as it is the Relation, the subject is *Being-in*. Being-in is a Being-in-the-world. But the world is itself nothing other than Being-in. It is the primitive and non-spatial space that signifies the opening of a place. The spatiality of Being-in is a title for the ontological process of alienation; it is the self-separation of the essence that makes the interval arise — and, as such, the Relation itself in its origin. The light that arises in this interval is at once that of the world and of consciousness.

This paragraph names the structural identity. The "subject" of the philosophy of consciousness, when understood ontologically (not as a substance but as the constituting source), is *the Relation* — the structure of opening that constitutes the field of phenomenality. And the "Being-in" of the Heideggerian philosophy of being (the *In-Sein* of *Sein und Zeit* §12) is also this structure of opening. So "subject" (Husserlian-Hegelian) and "Being-in" (Heideggerian) name the same structural reality. The "world" of *Sein und Zeit* is just the same as the field of consciousness in transcendental phenomenology — both are the opening that constitutes the visibility within which beings can appear.

**Paragraph 14\.** No doubt Husserl says that consciousness is nothing of the world, but by world he understands only the totality of the existent. That consciousness be nothing of the world so understood signifies only that, as ontological essence, consciousness is itself, in its transcendence with regard to all the existent, only the world itself in its pure worldhood. The world in its pure worldhood is not, indeed, a character of the existent. *"The phenomenon of the world... belongs, as essential structural moment of being-in-the-world, to the fundamental constitution of the Dasein."* It is therefore to the structure of the ontological essence of presence that the world belongs; but in this belonging to the essence, the world is confused with the essence. Being-in and the world identically designate the reign of a presence that is accomplished on the mode of a pure spatiality. Every reference of Being-in to a subjectivity that would not belong to this transcendental originary spatiality is excluded in principle. One can say that the world is "subjective," but this signifies only that it is "more objective than every object." The subjectivity of the world only marks its transcendence with regard to every existent; it is transcendence as such. *Transcendence is the essence of manifestation, the appearing of what appears.* Insofar as it is Being-in and the Relation, the subject is this appearing as such; it is the essence of manifestation in the monist sense. *"The subjectivity of the subject,"* says Heidegger, *"is the Erscheinen itself."* It is the appearing of what appears, it is the being of the existent that constitutes the subjectivity of the human subject. The light that traverses us is that of the world. It is in us that truth resides, in the interior of man. Consciousness has in itself the measure of truth. But the truth that constitutes our very interiority is only the absolute light of exteriority. *The human subjectivity is the transcendence of the world.*

The Heideggerian citations are scattered references to *Sein und Zeit* §§12–14 (on world, being-in, worldhood) and to the late essays in *Holzwege* and *Identität und Differenz* (on subjectivity as *Erscheinen*). The Husserlian citation on consciousness as nothing of the world is from *Ideen I* §49 (the famous "annihilation of the world" thought-experiment). Henry's argument: even Husserl's claim that consciousness is "nothing of the world" — which seems to oppose consciousness to world — is misread; properly read, it means that consciousness is *worldhood-itself*, the structure that makes world possible, not opposed to world but identical with the worldhood of world. So Husserl's transcendental consciousness *is* what Heidegger calls "world" or "the worldhood of the world." There is no real opposition; there is only the same monist essence under different names.

**Paragraphs 15–16 (continuing).** The identification of the essence of consciousness with the pure exteriority of transcendence arises at the moment when the problematic of consciousness understands itself in its pure ontological signification. When the essence of consciousness is grasped as truth in an ontological sense — that is, as the pure essence of manifestation — this essence of consciousness is necessarily identified with the essence of manifestation such as one understands it. Arrived at its ultimate stage and at the full understanding of itself in its truth, the philosophy of consciousness can only be a repetition of the fundamental presuppositions of monism. In truth, the progress in the determination of the essence of consciousness and that of the understanding of the internal structure of pure manifestation are parallel. The determination of the essence of consciousness constitutes precisely an essential moment of this understanding. Such a determination begins with the conception of a *subject of knowledge*; it pursues itself with the interpretation of the being of the subject as relation to the object. Consciousness is then understood in the light of the central concept of *intentionality*. Every consciousness is consciousness of something. As intentional, consciousness is this overcoming that gives it access to things. *The last progress in the ontological determination of the concept of consciousness resides in the affirmation that consciousness is nothing other than this overcoming.* Then the being of consciousness is truly identified with the ontological process of reality; it ceases to be the determinate being of a subject opposed, as a given reality, to the given reality of the object, in order to become the principle of all reality as such. Consciousness is no longer the predicate, even the essential attribute, of the substantial being of the subject. The substantiality of the subject consists in the overcoming itself by which we have access to things; and the subject is the access itself, the *Being-in* as such. *"Every consciousness is positional, and it exhausts itself in this position."* The essence of man toward being is this direction. It is not enough to say, as Sartre still does, that Heidegger rejects "the megaric and antidialectical isolation of essences." It is *a new conception of the essence* that comes to the fore — in conformity with which the essence is the dialectic itself, the exchange and the passage. And this essence defines the very humanity of man; it is the essence of human reality. It is therefore in the interior of man, in the most intimate of his being, that resides the ontological power of the dialectic. All the powers of man are grounded exclusively in this power in him. Vision, for example, *"is prepared interiorly only by my opening… to a field of transcendences."* The opening as such to the transcendental field — an opening that is this field itself — such is, in its essence, the intimate-being of man. *The most intimate being of man is thus the originary spatiality thought as the condition of all presence.*

The diagnostic is now complete and devastating. From Descartes through Husserl to Sartre, the philosophy of consciousness culminates in the recognition that consciousness *just is* the structure of intentional transcendence — the opening of the horizon, the being-in-the-world. So the most "intimate" being of man is, paradoxically, the most exterior — the spatiality of the transcendental horizon. The Sartrian "*toute conscience est positionnelle*" (every consciousness is positional, from the Introduction to *L'Être et le Néant*) captures the result perfectly: consciousness is exhausted in the position of the object, has no substantive interiority of its own, is just the act of throwing-itself-toward-the-object. The Merleau-Pontyan formulation about vision being prepared by the opening to the transcendental field (from the *Phénoménologie de la perception*) captures the same result.

The understanding of the intimate-being of man starting from the transcendental spatiality of presence is at the origin of the monist concept of existence. *"Existence is spatial — that is, by an interior necessity it opens onto an outside."* The most radical exteriority — what is more objective than every object — defines the most intimate interiority. What is more objective than every object is its condition, its existence. Transcendence is the condition of the object as such. The object is the transcendent being. But transcendence is the interiority of the human subject; it is the most intimate being of man. *Transcendence is universal existence. The existence of man is the existence of things. The subjectivity of the subject is only the objectivity of the object.*

**Paragraph 17 (paraphrasing the long Kantian-Lachelier discussion).** The identity of the subjectivity of the subject and the objectivity of the object could long remain hidden. It became visible only when, with Kant, the *objectivity* of the object was raised to the state of an explicit problem. As long as philosophical thought was only the conceptual promotion of the gaze of natural consciousness, the object could appear only as a given reality opposed to man. As soon as the problematic places itself on an ontological plane — as soon as the being of the object is taken into consideration — it is not only the relation of the existent to a subject of knowledge that is formulated; the being of this subject appears already, in fact, identified with the ontological condition of the possibility of the object — that is, with objectivity as such. Henry develops this through Kant: the *Critique of Pure Reason* poses the problem of the conditions of possibility of objects of experience; these conditions are simultaneously the conditions of subjective knowledge; therefore, the structure of the *a priori* form of the subject *is* the structure of the *a priori* form of the object. The "agreement" between thought and things that worried earlier philosophers is not a mysterious adequation between two different realities but the structural identity of the same essence (the *a priori* form of objectivity) considered now from the side of the subject (subjectivity of knowing) and now from the side of the object (objectivity of the known).

Henry then notes that one must reverse the formulation: it is not the case that the *a priori* structure of the object is determined by analyzing the subject; rather, the determination of the *a priori* structure of the object reveals what the subject's being is, namely, *just* the *a priori* structure of objectivity. The subject, on this Kantian-transcendental reading, *is* objectivity; subjectivity is reduced to objectivity. This is the further "progress" of monism: not only consciousness \= relation, but subjectivity \= objectivity. Henry pursues the diagnosis through Lachelier (in *Du fondement de l'induction*), where the structure of mind is identified with the necessary structure of things via the concept of *necessity* — the necessity of the *a priori* synthesis is at once the necessary structure of the object and the structure of the knowing subject. Then through Lagneau (the *Leçon sur le jugement*), where attempts are made to differentiate a *second* subject "behind" the first one — a subject that withdraws from the necessity of being into doubt — but this withdrawal is itself revealed to be the very transcendental structure that constitutes objectivity. So even the moral attempt to preserve the subject's autonomy from the necessity of the object's being collapses back into the same structure.

The whole of post-Kantian transcendental philosophy is thus a working-out of the identity of subjectivity and objectivity. The "temporal subject" that emerges in late-modern philosophy (Bergson, Husserl in his time-analyses, the early Heidegger) only confirms the result: temporality is the essence of transcendence, and "the horizon of being" is the temporal-transcendental structure that constitutes both subject and object. *Temporality is at once the subjectivity of the subject and "the horizon of being."* The reference is to *Sein und Zeit* §65 and the closing sections, where Heidegger argues that the temporality of Dasein is the transcendental horizon for the meaning of being.

**Paragraph 18 (Hegelian identity, behaviorism, Sartre vs. Heidegger).** The conception of a common-being of the subjectivity of the subject and the objectivity of the object is the ontological foundation of the Hegelian demonstration of the identity of matter and spirit, and more generally of the philosophical-traditional affirmation — as often formulated as rarely grasped in the concept — of the identity of thought and being. The reference is to Parmenides ("the same is to think and to be," Fr. 3\) through Hegel and into late Heidegger (e.g., *Identität und Differenz*). The Hegelian system, which culminates in the absolute knowledge that is at once subject and substance, is the most explicit philosophical articulation of the identity that ontological monism implies.

The conceptual grasp of the essential identity of subject and object lays bare the vanity of the classical discussions between proponents of objectivity and partisans of a subjective philosophy. It renders particularly perceptible the naïve and pre-philosophical character of certain "decisive" critiques — like, for example, the one the promoters of *behaviorism* have addressed to the philosophy of consciousness. Henry treats Watson's behaviorist critique as a paradigmatic case of pre-philosophical confusion. Watson demanded that consciousness be "shown" like other scientific objects; but consciousness is precisely the *power of showing* that even the behaviorists' own scientific demonstrations presuppose. Watson's critique is doubly confused: it dismisses consciousness while making constant use of the very condition (visibility, showing) that consciousness, ontologically understood, just *is*.

Inversely, Henry says, when Sartre reproaches Heidegger with addressing the existential analytic directly, without passing through the *cogito* — when, after defining the Dasein as the ekstatic project of its own possibilities (i.e., as a self-understanding), Sartre asks "But what would an understanding be that, in itself, would not be consciousness (of) being understanding?" — Sartre's critique has *no content*.
