For Sartre, consciousness is the position of the object; it is exhausted in this position; it is therefore the ekstase of transcendence — which is precisely what Heidegger means by the ontological understanding (*Verstehen*) of being. Sartre and Heidegger are saying the same thing; Sartre's claim that Heidegger has "missed" consciousness misses the fact that Heideggerian *Verstehen* and Sartrian "consciousness (of) being understanding" are structurally identical. Both are forms of the same ontological monism.

**Paragraph 19 (closing).** *"Subjectivity,"* declares Heidegger, commenting on classical philosophy, *"is presence on the mode of representation."* Representation finds its foundation in the ontological phenomenon of alienation that opens the transcendental horizon of being — that is, finally, in the transcendence of the world. *The world is my representation.* (The Schopenhauerian-Heideggerian formula crystallizes the diagnosis: Schopenhauer's famous opening of *Die Welt als Wille und Vorstellung*, and Heidegger's analysis of the modern conception of being in *Die Zeit des Weltbildes*, articulate the same fundamental result.) The reversal of the doctrine that comes to the fore in the last works of Heidegger — where the principle of phenomenality is sought in the radical exteriority of being (rather than in subjectivity) — finds its premises in *Sein und Zeit* and in traditional philosophical thought, where it is in fact already included. The problem of knowing whether the access to the transcendental must be made in the light of a philosophy of being or of a philosophy of consciousness *is of little importance if the essence of manifestation that is finally aimed at — and which constitutes this transcendental — is the same in both cases.* The determination of the transcendental remains conditioned, and that in an essential way, as long as the transcendental is nothing other than the principle of the object. *There is no difference between the philosophy of consciousness and the philosophy of being.*

The closing sentence is the explicit, summary thesis of the section and one of the most consequential philosophical claims in twentieth-century French phenomenology: there is no difference, on the ontological plane, between the philosophy of consciousness (Descartes through Husserl and Sartre) and the philosophy of being (the Greeks through Heidegger). Both are forms of ontological monism, because both think the essence of manifestation as the structure of horizonal-transcendent disclosure that produces phenomena by a doubling of being. The shift from "consciousness" to "being" as the name of the absolute transcendental structure is a shift in vocabulary, not in essence. The whole of Western philosophy, from Plato to Heidegger, operates within this single monist horizon. Henry's program in the rest of the book will be to show that there exists *another* mode of manifestation — the immanent self-revelation of life — that is not horizonal, not ekstatic, not representational, not transcendent, and that is therefore radically heterogeneous with the structure of ontological monism. Sections III and IV will work out this alternative; the immediately following sections (§§12–16) will further analyze and deepen the diagnosis of monism by examining particular philosophical positions (philosophy of consciousness in §12, Heideggerian Dasein in §13) and by reflecting on the relation of essence to ontic determination (§§14–15) and the autonomy of the essence (§16).

---

## **§ 12\. The critique of the philosophy of consciousness**

**Paragraph 1\.** If there is no difference between the philosophy of being and the philosophy of consciousness, why has Heidegger thought it good to direct against the latter a radical and ceaselessly resumed critique? The opening question is sharp. §11 ended on the thesis that the philosophy of consciousness and the philosophy of being are identical at the level of their ontological essence. But Heidegger's critique of the philosophy of consciousness — his repeated attacks on the Cartesian-Kantian-Husserlian tradition — is one of the most prominent features of his work, especially in *Sein und Zeit*. If the two philosophies are essentially identical, what is Heidegger criticizing? The motive of this critique has been indicated: it resides in the will not to let the essence fall to the rank of the determination that finds in this essence its foundation. The rejection of the traditional concepts of subject, subjectivity, consciousness, reason, even of "person" — the objection ceaselessly formulated against the legitimacy of their use, in conformity with which the reality these concepts designate remains always in fact unquestioned in its being — signifies the *transcendence* of being with regard to the elements that are thought as the principle of phenomenality (or, more narrowly, of knowledge). For being finds itself beyond the determination posited as the principle, and it is in this beyond that the determination finds in fact the foundation of its being.

The diagnosis is precise. Heidegger's critique of the philosophy of consciousness is not a critique of its essential thesis (the thesis of the monist structure of manifestation, which Heidegger shares); it is a critique of its tendency to *fall* — to let the essence (which is the structure of transcendence) be confused with a particular determinate existent (a "subject," a "consciousness," a "person") that, in being so designated, gets treated as one being among others. Heidegger insists that what gets called "subject" or "consciousness" is not a being in the world but the *transcendence* that constitutes the world. The critique aims at preserving the *purity* of the ontological from contamination by the ontic — but it does not (and Henry will insist this is the crucial point) propose an *alternative* mode of manifestation. Heidegger's critique is internal to ontological monism; it is the monism's self-purification.

**Paragraph 2\.** Why can the essence not be maintained in the originary distance where it resides? Why can the Dasein not be grasped in the purity of its radical ontological signification as the very essence of transcendence? Because the being of transcendence is inevitably understood from the foundation of what comes about in transcendence. *"In-Sein,"* which signifies the originary ekstasis of being, *"is denatured"* because the Dasein understands it in the light of the existent that is produced thanks to this *In-Sein*. The cited passage is from *Sein und Zeit* §12. Understanding *In-Sein* in the light of what is produced in it, it is itself that the Dasein understands in this manner. It understands itself as an existent, and the originary structure of Being-in-the-world becomes the relation that exists between this existent-Dasein and the existent that is not it. These two existents — whose being is understood from the intramundane existent — are called *the subject and the object*; and it is in their "relation" that the "theory of knowledge" looks for its foundation. This relation itself, which institutes itself between two given realities, is in turn understood as a given reality. *It is the degradation of the essence of manifestation into a reality of ontic order, it is the understanding of the formal ontological element of knowledge in the light of such a reality, that is rejected by Heidegger.*

This is a clean diagnosis of the Heideggerian critique. The trajectory is: (1) The essence of manifestation is *In-Sein*, the originary structure of transcendence. (2) Dasein, in its everyday existence, falls into a misunderstanding: it interprets *In-Sein* on the basis of what appears within it (intramundane existents); it takes the structural-ontological *In-Sein* and reads it as a relation between two given things — itself (the subject) and the world (the object). (3) On this misreading, the theory of knowledge takes the subject-object relation as a given empirical fact and tries to explain knowledge in terms of it. (4) Heidegger's critique of the philosophy of consciousness is the rejection of step 3 (and of its presupposition in step 2): the philosophy of consciousness mistakes the ontological structure (transcendence) for an ontic relation (between subject-things and object-things).

*"Natural consciousness could be called an ontic consciousness insofar as it directs itself directly upon the object as upon an existent and upon its knowledge of this object as upon something that is also an existent."* The philosophy of consciousness is recused insofar as it is a thesis of natural consciousness. As such it accomplishes a fundamental omission. As soon as it is posited as an existent, knowledge presupposes being. *"Natural consciousness immediately posits before itself its represented and its act of representing-itself as existent, without considering the being which, in doing this, it also already represents."* This is why this knowledge posited as an existent (and that is precisely called consciousness, subject, subjectivity, reason, or person) must be questioned about its being. As long as this question of being has not been raised concerning knowledge — assimilated without further ado to something that is — the pretension of this knowledge to play the role of a principle in the problematic attests only to the forgetting of the ontological problem. Solidary with this forgetting is the fall of the essence into the determination that substitutes itself for it, while in fact it (the determination) refers back to it. Existence from then on is confused with something that exists. To think existence in its truth is to understand existence on the contrary as truth. *"The truth of existence"* is obtained in the effort by which thought ceases to understand existence from anything other than itself. *"The Dasein,"* says Heidegger, *"can understand itself… from the 'world' or from others or from its most proper power-to-be."* The understanding of the Dasein from its most proper power-to-be signifies for the Dasein an understanding of itself from itself — it is the self-understanding of the essence as essence.

The references are to *Sein und Zeit* §§9, 12, 31 and Heidegger's analyses of *Verfallen* and authentic self-understanding. The Heideggerian analysis is precise: Dasein has a tendency to misunderstand itself by interpreting itself from the world or from others (i.e., from the ontic existents it encounters); the antidote is to interpret itself from its "most proper power-to-be" — from its existential structure as the essence of transcendence, not from any particular existent. The critique of the philosophy of consciousness is thus a *purification* of the conception of consciousness: the proper concept of consciousness is the structure of transcendence-as-such, not the determinate-existent of "the subject."

**Paragraph 3\.** The preservation of the truth of existence is the ultimate aim of the great critiques of Heideggerianism, and notably of the critiques directed against Cartesian ontology and against the traditional conception of truth. Cartesian ontology results in an alteration — indeed in a complete forgetting — of the essence, on the foundation of the understanding of the essence from the existent that is produced in and by it. Yet the existent whose being unduly guides the understanding of the ontological phenomenon of the world is not even the existent that arises in the first place for us inside this world. From the existent, in fact, Descartes retains, as constituting its being, only what in it is accessible through mathematical knowledge. Mathematical knowledge has as correlate a being given in permanence. The being-given-in-permanence (*ständige Vorhandenheit*) is the character of being of the mathematical existent. What has the trait of being-given-in-permanence is the *substance*. The idea of substance thus finds its origin in the determinate structure of a determinate existent.

Henry now reproduces in compressed form Heidegger's critique of Cartesian ontology from *Sein und Zeit* §§19–21. Descartes, says Heidegger, understands the being of beings on the model of the *ens creatum*, the substance, the *Vorhandenes* (present-at-hand) — and indeed on the model of the mathematical *Vorhandenes*, the geometrical extended thing. Descartes thus takes one regional ontological structure (the structure of mathematical objects) and generalizes it into the ontological structure of beings as such. This is the deepest reason for the Cartesian failure to ask the question of being: Descartes already operates with a *determinate* (and unexamined) ontology, derived from the mathematical-geometrical region.

It is from this determinate structure, thought under the title of substance, that Descartes interprets — not only and rightly the being of the mathematical existent, but again and unduly the being of the intramundane existent in general (and it is thus that the idea of a *mathematical nature* comes to the fore, which will reign henceforth over the Western conception of nature and definitively veil the originary being of nature). And finally, the being of the world itself: the latter is not only confused, as the milieu of the intramundane existent, with space; but the being of this space is again interpreted as substance. The doctrine of the *res extensa*, which counts as a philosophical interpretation of the originary being of the world — that is, of the essence — is thus constructed from the determinate being of the existent that offers itself to mathematical knowledge. Mathematical knowledge, as the prototype of the *intellectio*, is not only privileged in an arbitrary way insofar as it is given as the only valid mode of access to the being of the existent (the *sensatio* does not attain this being); its being in turn is interpreted from the determinate ontological structure of the mathematical existent — that is, from the substantial permanence of a given reality. *"Descartes,"* writes Heidegger, *"understands the being of the Dasein, to whose fundamental constitution belongs the being-in-the-world, in the same way as the being of the res extensa, as substance."* The Dasein, however, is nothing other than the world in its pure worldhood. The "*res cogitans*" and the "*res extensa*" are two equivalent titles in which expresses itself the same fall (in the light of the idea of substance, that is, from mathematical being) of the same essence (the ontological essence of presence). *The Cartesian dualism is an alteration of ontological monism.*

The closing thesis is striking. Cartesian dualism — the famous opposition of *res cogitans* and *res extensa*, of mind and body — is not a true ontological dualism (which would mean two genuinely heterogeneous modes of being). It is the application of *one* ontological structure (substance) to two regional domains (the mental and the corporeal). Both are interpreted as substance; both are *ständig vorhanden* (constantly-present-at-hand) in the same sense; both share the same essential structure of being. The "dualism" is a regional dualism within a unified ontological monism. And this monism is precisely defective, because it imports into the *cogito* (which should have been interrogated as the ontological essence of the world) an ontology derived from a regional analysis of mathematical objects. The critique is Heidegger's; Henry endorses it precisely so that he can, in due course, turn the same critique against Heidegger himself: Heidegger too imports into the analysis of Dasein an ontological structure (that of horizonal transcendence) that derives from a regional analysis (of intramundane comportment).

**Paragraph 4\.** The critique of the traditional conception of truth as agreement between the representation and the object has the same sense. The representation enounces itself in a proposition. The proposition is a given-reality, or a tool, that comports within itself, it is true, a relation to the existent of which it enounces something. When this relation is adequate — when there is agreement between the proposition (example: the rose is fragrant) and the existent (the perfume of the rose) — there is truth; error in the contrary case (if the rose has no smell, is an artificial rose, etc.). Thus the representation, which as opening and discovery of the existent is the essence, falls to the rank of the proposition; the proposition, as proposition expressed, is an intramundane reality (ideal or not). The transcendental relation that is the originary opening of representation and of existence is preserved in the proposition, as expressed proposition, in the form of the relation that the proposition entertains with the existent to which it corresponds. This relation of conformity or non-conformity between two given realities is itself understood — because it is inserted in one of them, the proposition — as a given reality. The nature of this relation, as a given being, results thus from the interpretation of the being of the originary transcendental relation of transcendence in the light of the given being of the proposition as expressed proposition. *The agreement that defines "truth" in classical philosophy is only the fall of the originary ontological truth of existence, insofar as this truth resides in the opening and the discovery of the existent.*

This is precisely the Heideggerian critique of the *adaequatio* theory of truth, developed in *Sein und Zeit* §44. Truth as *adaequatio rei et intellectus* — agreement between representation and thing — presupposes truth in a more originary sense: namely, the *aletheia*, the disclosure of beings that makes them available to be matched (or not matched) by propositions. The propositional theory of truth is a "fall" from the originary ontological theory of truth-as-disclosure. Henry endorses the Heideggerian critique while again reading it as internal to ontological monism: both the propositional theory and the Heideggerian disclosure-theory of truth presuppose the structure of representation/transcendence as the essence of manifestation. The critique purifies but does not overcome.

It is the same fall that comes to the fore again in the Kantian theses relative to the critique of *problematic idealism*. The very idea of a demonstration of the reality of the external world implies the misrecognition of the originary essence of the world as such. This essence is confused with the totality of intramundane reality. It is this latter that one in fact tries to ground, by showing that the psychological and interior life of consciousness is possible only in its connection with exterior objects, whose objective order constitutes the only assignable foundation for the unity (as well as the distinction) of interior events. The subjective representations — identified with these events — receive, like them, the signification of forming a reality juxtaposed to the exterior ontic reality. As for the relation that unites these two given realities and confers on the subjective series its unity, it is in turn only a given relation.

The reference is to Heidegger's analysis of Kant's "Refutation of Idealism" (Critique of Pure Reason, B274–B279) in *Sein und Zeit* §43. Kant's attempt to refute Cartesian "problematic idealism" by demonstrating the reality of the external world from the inner experience of time presupposes the very ontological misunderstanding it tries to refute: that there is an "interior" world (consciousness) and an "exterior" world (the things), and that the philosophical task is to bridge them. But this presupposes that the world has been confused with the totality of intramundane existents — and thus the *worldhood* of the world (the ontological essence) has been missed. Kant's "refutation" remains within the ontic dualism it tries to overcome.

**Paragraph 5\.** The signification of the Heideggerian critique of the philosophy of consciousness is thus to refuse the fall of the essence into ontic reality — a fall that is accomplished with the understanding of the being of the essence from the determinate being of the existent. It is because the ontological problem must be grasped in its purity that the question is not "how the subject goes outside up to an object," but: "what makes ontologically possible that the existent can occur intramundanely and be objectified as occurring." The answer, says Heidegger, is found in the *"ekstatically, horizontally founded transcendence of the world."* It is *transcendence*, it is not *the subject*, that is the essence. The essence that was thought — or at least aimed at — by the philosophy of consciousness under the title of subject was, however, the very essence of *transcendence*. The Heideggerian critique has an ontological signification insofar as it aims to think the essence in its purity. *For this very reason, one can also say that it has in fact no ontological signification.* It is not placed, indeed, on the ontological plane properly speaking, but on its frontier — a frontier it works to define and strives to situate rigorously. *It is not the internal structure of the essence of manifestation that is called into question; it is an understanding (improper because of ontic origin) of this one and only essence of manifestation that is rejected.* The ontological element must only be preserved against every external contribution of ontic order; in itself it remains what it was when it found itself covered and hidden under this contribution.

The diagnosis is now complete. The Heideggerian critique of the philosophy of consciousness is a *purification*, not an overcoming. It does not call the structure of monism into question; it only purifies that structure from contamination by ontic readings. The essence of manifestation — transcendence, the horizon, the opening — remains exactly the same in Heidegger's purified version as it was in the impure traditional versions. Heidegger has cleansed the structure of the philosophical impurities that obscured it; he has not displaced the structure itself.

The philosophy of being elaborates the essence underlying anterior philosophies; it makes this essence the theme of a research that understands itself finally in the rigor of its ontological design. It is a matter of thinking exteriority in its purity, instead of inserting it in a "subject" of which it becomes the interior property. But the essence of manifestation resides in all cases in this exteriority as such. The ontological purification of the principles that were still thought as ontic realities or processes — such is the sense of the critique of the philosophy of consciousness. The purificatory elucidation of the essence however does nothing but show the *presence* of the essence under the very principles that must be rejected.

**Paragraph 6\.** It is on the foundation of this common essence and of the identity of its ultimate internal structure that the exchange of themes between the philosophy of consciousness and the philosophy of being operates. The insertion of the eidetic components of being and of its most essential foundation into the subjective principle of consciousness would not have been possible if this subjective principle had not been thought for a long time as the condition of objectivity. *The identification of nothingness with consciousness or with man is no doubt absurd* — since nothingness, which is the origin and the power of transcendence, could not as such be enclosed in any reality — but it attests the permanence of the ultimate ontological presuppositions that are those of monism. For this reason, it must be understood that the illegitimate insertion of the essential foundation of being into consciousness — realized as a "*sui generis*" region of being — cannot in any way be called a "*subjectivation*."

The reference to "the identification of nothingness with consciousness or with man" is to Sartre (in *L'Être et le Néant*), where consciousness/the-for-itself is identified with nothingness. Henry's claim is sharp: this identification is *absurd*, but the absurdity reveals the persistence of monist presuppositions. Sartre attempts to give nothingness a determinate ontic locus (in human consciousness), but nothingness — as the structure of transcendence — cannot be locally housed in any particular existent. The Sartrian formulation is incoherent. But its incoherence is not a departure from monism; it is monism's continuing pull, even when it leads to contradictions.

For one to be able to speak of a "subjectivation," it would be necessary that this subjectivation be *something*, that one could indicate in what it consists. More precisely, it would be necessary that this subjectivation have an ontological signification — and for that, it would be necessary that subjectivity be *an essence*. The transformation brought to the directing themes of Heideggerian ontology when these themes are taken up inside a philosophy of the cogito is *not essential* as long as the being of consciousness remains *Being itself* identified in its foundation with Nothingness. As long as the alteration suffered by the essence consists in a fall into what remains in fact a reality of ontic order, this alteration constitutes an "*existentialization*" (*étantisation*) of the essence — not a radical modification of the intimate being of the essence, and even less the position of *another* essence. If the existentialization, unduly taken or given as a "subjectivation," is only the insertion of the essence of objectivity inside the frame-without-status, or the "carcass," of a subjectivity whose being consists precisely in this very essence — such an existentialization is only attributable to natural consciousness; it does not promote, in fact, in its result, any new mode of manifestation or revelation; and as such it has *no ontological signification* in the strong sense.

The argument is acute. To say that the insertion of being's structure into consciousness "subjectivizes" being would be a substantive claim — it would mean that a different essence of manifestation (a *subjective* essence) had emerged. But subjectivity, as the philosophy of consciousness has understood it, is just the same essence as objectivity (the structure of transcendence). So the insertion is not really a "subjectivization"; it is a mere mislabeling, a "*existentialization*" (treating an ontological essence as if it were an ontic existent). The mistake is verbal-conceptual, not substantive — the same essence is operative under both names, just with different (sometimes contradictory) labels. There is no genuine alternative essence at stake.

**Paragraph 7\.** It is not nothing, assuredly, to maintain the essence in its radical transcendence with regard to every existent — if it is precisely in this transcendence that the essence resides. *The more rigorous, however, is the internal understanding of the essence as nihilating foundation of being — the more pressing the demand to maintain this essence, on the foundation of this nihilating in it, in its radical transcendence with regard to every existent — the more incomprehensible also is the explicit assimilation of the essence to an ontic reality in the paradoxical but ceaselessly formulated affirmation according to which the "Dasein" is an existent.*

The closing sentence formulates the great paradox internal to Heideggerian fundamental ontology, which §13 will analyze in detail. Heidegger insists that the essence (the structure of transcendence) is utterly heterogeneous from any existent — it is the *nihilating foundation* of being, not a being. And yet Heidegger constantly affirms that the Dasein "is an existent" (cf. *Sein und Zeit* §9: "Das Dasein ist ein Seiendes...") — the privileged existent, but still an existent. This is the unresolved tension at the heart of *Sein und Zeit*: Dasein is supposed to be the place where the structure of transcendence is most purely manifest, and yet Dasein is itself counted as a being, indeed as the privileged starting-point of fundamental ontology. The paradox is what §13 ("The Ambiguity of the Dasein") will analyze in detail. It is the same paradox identified already in Introduction §6 — the *équivoque* of "the being of human reality" — and it is the central structural problem of ontological monism when it tries to maintain the rigor of the ontological difference while still anchoring fundamental ontology in a privileged existent.

## **§ 13\. The ambiguity of "Dasein": essence and ontic determination**

**Paragraph 1\.** Does the fundamental ambiguity of the Heideggerian Dasein signify that — no more than that of consciousness — the philosophy of being has not been able to remain faithful to the rigor of its ontological design? Is the thought of essence subject, in all cases, to a defection such that it must lose along the way that very thing which was its goal? Must an *inevitable fall* decisively forbid us access to the kingdom of presence understood in its purity? Or is the inevitable character of this fall not — if precisely we say it inevitable — inscribed in the essence itself, and must it not be understood, from then on, as an eidetic character, as a property of the essence itself, that historializes itself in the essence in conformity with its own will?

The opening question is the diagnostic problem of the section. §12 closed on the paradox: Heidegger demands that the essence be radically distinguished from every existent, yet Heidegger constantly affirms that "Dasein is an existent." This is the *ambiguity of the Dasein*. The question now is: is this ambiguity merely a symptom of Heidegger's failure to maintain the rigor of his own program (a "fall" akin to the Cartesian fall into substance ontology)? Or is the ambiguity *necessary*, structurally inevitable, inscribed in the essence itself? The latter is the deeper hypothesis: if the essence — the structure of transcendence — *intrinsically* requires the privileged ontic anchoring in a particular existent (Dasein), then the ambiguity is not a defect of Heidegger's exposition but the necessary working-out of monism's own structure.

**Paragraph 2\.** Transcendence is the act in which is instituted a radical overcoming of every existent — an overcoming such that it is precisely in transcendence that the existent finds its being. In such an overcoming, however, in transgressing every existent, the essence also obtains the abode that is proper to it. *The abode of the essence is precisely that of the existent.* Being is the being of the existent. To the question of knowing whether the transgression of the existent is without return, the response is given if such a transgression does not lead in reality beyond the existent but constitutes on the contrary the very place where the existent stands. *Why can the essence not be maintained in the originary distance where it resides — beyond the existent — if not because this beyond is the very being of every existent as such?*

The argumentative pivot is decisive. Transcendence — the act of overcoming every existent — does indeed go beyond the existent; but the *beyond* it reaches is precisely the *being* of the existent. So transcendence does not arrive at a region separate from existents; it arrives at *the being of existents*. This is what "the ontological difference" means structurally: the difference between being and beings is not a difference between two regions but the difference *internal* to the ontological structure that includes both. So the essence cannot be maintained in a "purity" separate from existents; the essence's "abode" is precisely where existents are.

The affirmation according to which being is the being of the existent must be understood. What is enounced in such an affirmation is the *essential unity of being and the existent*. The thought that opposes being to the existent does not yet penetrate into the content. To penetrate the content is to go in it as far as what constitutes its most essential foundation — to grasp being at the very heart of the existent. The immanence of being to the existent does not signify, no doubt, the suppression of their opposition — or rather, of opposition as such. But the opposition that makes the existent always arise as the *opposed* results precisely from the immanence in it of being, that is, of the nothing. The ontological power of the nothing is immanent to the existent as its most essential foundation. It is on the foundation of the nothing in it that the existent is. On the foundation of the nothing in it, the existent is *negated*. Being negated, the existent is held at distance; it appears, it is. The negation of the existent — which is the work of the nothing — is identically its promotion in the dimension of phenomenal presence, its ontological advent as such. *It is in the existent itself, however, that this work is accomplished.*

The dialectic is intricate. (i) The essence (the nihilating, the work of the *néant*) is "in" the existent — immanent to it — as what makes the existent be. (ii) The work of the nihilating *negates* the existent (puts it at distance, distinguishes it from itself), and this negation is what allows the existent to *appear*. (iii) But this whole work happens *in* the existent. So the structure is: the essence requires the existent as the place of its work; the existent requires the essence as the power of its appearing; the two are inseparably bound. Henry is here giving a precise reading of the late Heideggerian doctrine of being-and-beings — being is not above or beyond beings but *in* them as the nihilating that makes them be. The reference to Hegel ("the concrete life of determinacy is the operation of dissolving itself") situates this in the dialectical tradition: being and the negative are co-immanent in determinate beings.

Because the nothing is immanent to the ontic determination as that which makes it be, one can say with Hegel that *"the concrete life of determinacy is… the operation of dissolving itself."* The nothing does not so much negate singular determination as make it exist; it preserves it and conserves it. By negating it, no doubt, it preserves it. This signifies only that being is identical to the nothing. But the nothing *is* being. It is the being of the determination. The nothing is not opposed to the existent; it is constitutive of its being. This is why also negation is not exterior to the content; it is so interior to the content, on the contrary, that it is only in negation that the content manifests itself in itself and such as it is. *The content is exterior because negation is interior to it, because its being is the nothing.*

**Paragraph 3\.** To the vain thought that would believe itself able to wander freely above the content, one must recall the sense of every transcendence as such — that of constituting the being of the existent. In its radical overcoming with regard to every existent, it is to the existent that, no less radically, this transcendence is ordered and bound. Bound to the existent in the very act by which it gives the existent being and conserves the existent, transcendence — because it constitutes precisely the essence of ontic determination as such — is *essentially finite*. Such a finitude — more originary than the finitude of the determination that results from it — does it not inevitably affect transcendence, since transcendence develops itself beyond the existent — that is, in fact and always, *from the existent*? Is the link that unites in the origin finitude and transcendence not the one which, in the very overcoming, links the overcoming inexorably to what is overcome by it? Does the signification of such an overcoming, from then on, not reverse itself? *Is the "élan toward the beyond" of transcendence not rather, in reality, a "return upon" — if it is true that the overcoming of the existent is only what opens a place for the existent?* In this "opening for," the "élan beyond" finds in fact its goal. The existent is that beyond which transcendence, in its radical overcoming, deploys the horizon, only because the existent is first that *in view of which* this horizon is, as such, opened. The movement beyond-the-existent of transcendence finds its *télos* in the existent. *Every transcendence is as such essentially receptive.* In the receptivity of transcendence resides its most essential finitude.

This paragraph is one of the most important in the section. Henry argues that the Heideggerian "transcendence" — the going-beyond beings that opens the horizon of being — is not really a free-floating "elsewhere" but is structurally *bound to* and *for* the beings it transcends. Transcendence opens a horizon; the horizon is opened *so that* beings can appear in it; therefore transcendence is *for* beings, *in view of* beings — and this *in-view-of* is what Henry calls *receptivity*. Transcendence is essentially receptive because it opens itself toward the beings it must receive. This receptivity is the deepest form of finitude: the essence of transcendence is *needy* — it has *need of* beings to fulfill its work.

This finitude results from the fact that, in the very accomplishment of transcendence — which composes the possibility of a reception — is inscribed *a need*: the need of what will be received in this reception as such. What finds the possibility of its reception in the deployment of transcendence — is it not, evidently, the existent itself? *Transcendence is the need of the existent.* Insofar as it is transcendence, the essence realizes itself only when this need that it bears within itself is satisfied. The essence obtains its concretion only in this realization. But the essence is, as such, concrete. The need of transcendence has already realized itself, if the transgression of the existent is identically the return upon the existent — and as such, the very act by which the existent is posited. This is why being is, in virtue of its very structure, always and necessarily the being of the existent. In virtue of its structure, being is always this act of "going beyond" and "returning upon" — which is an act of going beyond the existent and returning upon the existent. To this act the existent is as essential as the transcendence that constitutes it. Transcendence is finite insofar as the existent is implicated in it as that of which it has need.

The thesis is forcefully stated: *transcendence is the need of the existent*. Heideggerian transcendence does not stand alone; it is essentially needy, oriented toward beings, open *to* receive them. This is the deepest meaning of the famous Heideggerian doctrine that "being is finite" — not because it is limited in some quantitative sense, but because its very structure includes the receptive opening to beings.

**Paragraph 4\.** Is it by chance that it is in Kant — where the essence of the ontological power is grasped for itself and understood from the idea of transcendence — that this finitude finds itself affirmed for the first time, and that with the greatest force? *"Kant,"* says Heidegger, *"had to look for finitude in the rational being itself."* It is because the rational being is understood in its ontological structure as transcendence that finitude can and must be looked for in the rational being first. The rational being is finite as having to find outside of it the existent that it must for this reason receive — and this in such a manner that it is only in this reception that the essence realizes itself, or, as Kant says, that reason arrives at a *cognition*. Thus finitude is not bound in man to the fact that to the pure rationality which defines him as a metaphysical being is bound synthetically (and that in a way incomprehensible to us) a sensibility; *it is pure rationality itself, in fact, that is finite*, and that insofar as, as transcendence, it is and remains essentially receptive — that is, fundamentally oriented toward the existent that it is not. As receptive, transcendence thus constitutes in itself sensibility as such and in its possibility. Sensibility with regard to the existent — that is, the possibility of receiving the existent — is thus founded as the very possibility of any effective cognition whatsoever in general.

The reference is to Heidegger's *Kant und das Problem der Metaphysik* (1929), where Heidegger reads the *Critique of Pure Reason* as a fundamental ontology of finite human knowledge. Kant's central thesis (according to Heidegger): all human cognition is finite because it is essentially receptive — it must receive its content from a sensibility that is given to it. Heidegger generalizes: the receptivity is not an accidental feature of human cognition (something added to a pure rationality that, in itself, would be infinite); it is the very structure of finite transcendence as such. Even the pure understanding (Kant's intellect) is finite because its very mode of being is receptive — oriented toward what it does not produce but must receive. Henry endorses Heidegger's reading and uses it to characterize the structure of monism: in *all* monist conceptions of phenomenality, transcendence is essentially receptive, essentially bound to the existent it requires.

**Paragraph 5\.** The overcoming of the existent is identically the act that maintains the existent in being. Thus the world that is constituted in such an overcoming is transcendent to "phenomena" only insofar as it is, in fact, related back to phenomena. If the totality is never dissociable from what manifests itself in it, it is because the transcendence of the world is finitude itself. The task that ontology gives itself of thinking the essence in its purity cannot signify the rupture of the link that relates transcendence as such to the phenomena to which transcendence relates itself. It resides rather in the *understanding* of this link. *"In the reversal,"* says Heidegger, *"consciousness must not… abandon the abode at the heart of the existent; it must assume this abode expressly in its truth."* To think this abode in its truth is to understand how and why this abode is always in reality for us an abode *near* the existent.

The Heideggerian reference is from *Holzwege* — the essay on Hegel's "Erfahrung." The point: the philosophical task is not to escape from existents into a purified region of the essence; it is to *understand* the essential relation that binds the essence to existents. To "abide near the existent" is the proper mode of philosophical thought — not despite but because of the essence's structure.

The character of the task that ontology gives itself in the project by which it defines itself — does it not, from then on, sufficiently illuminate the manner in which ontology must go about realizing itself? If, in conformity with its most proper character, the task of thinking the essence cannot be accomplished outside of the fundamental relation by which transcendence (in the indissociable return of its surge) finds itself related to phenomena, *the necessity for ontology to give itself an ontic foundation does it not, from then on, begin to clarify and understand itself?* It is because being is the being of the existent — because the nothing is always the nothing of what it nihilates — that the interrogation about being that ontology promotes is always necessarily and first an interrogation about the existent that finds itself questioned in its being. Thus the finitude that affects, in its accomplishment, the procedure by which ontology constructs itself is one in reality with the finitude of being itself — that is, with the finitude of transcendence insofar as transcendence finds itself related to phenomena in the very act by which it transgresses them. The necessity for ontology to give itself an ontic foundation is only the expression — on the plane where philosophy is constituted — of the indissoluble link in conformity with which being is always the being of the existent.

This is the resolution of the paradox raised in §6 of the Introduction (and reformulated at §12 paragraph 7). Why does ontology need to anchor itself in a particular existent (Dasein)? Not because of methodological or pedagogical convenience, but because the very structure of the essence — the structure of monist transcendence — requires being's being-for-and-of-beings. Transcendence is essentially receptive; therefore ontology, which is the elucidation of transcendence, is essentially anchored in the existent that receives. The anchor in Dasein is not external to the structure but internal to it — it expresses the structural finitude of monist transcendence.

**Paragraph 6\.** What does it mean, from the phenomenological point of view, the affirmation according to which being is always in reality the being of the existent? Being designates the essence of manifestation. That being be always the being of the existent — does this not signify, from then on, that manifestation as such, and in its purity, is always however and only the *manifestation of something* that manifests itself? And how must one understand phenomenologically this necessary reference of the essence of manifestation to the determination that manifests itself? If the essence of phenomenon refers necessarily to the phenomenon itself, is this not because this work that defines the essence — the act of making arise into presence — is accomplished by the essence not vis-à-vis itself, but only with regard to the determination that comes about by the essence as a "phenomenon"? *The essence is the essence of manifestation, but manifestation is not a manifestation of-self that illuminates itself and suffices to itself in the appearance it gives of itself, with which appearance it is confused.* The essence of manifestation is not the *manifestation of self*. It is not the essence that manifests itself; it is the existent. *Manifestation is the manifestation of the existent.* A manifestation, Böhme already thought, can manifest only something other. Insofar as it is necessarily, in its very structure, the manifestation of something other, manifestation is essentially finite.

This paragraph crystallizes the key consequence of the analysis. *The essence of manifestation, in monism, is not the manifestation of itself.* Manifestation is always manifestation-of-other; it shows the existent, not itself. The essence is the *power* that makes existents manifest, but the essence itself does not manifest — it withdraws, conceals itself, in the very work of letting beings manifest. This is the structure of the late Heideggerian *Aletheia/Lethe*: in disclosure, what is disclosed is the being, not the disclosing as such; the disclosing-itself withdraws into the disclosed. Henry endorses this analysis as the proper articulation of monism — and now positions himself for his own counter-thesis: the essence of manifestation as Henry will articulate it (in Sections III–IV) *is* manifestation-of-self; immanent self-revelation has the structure of manifestation that *is* its own content, that *is* what it manifests. This is the heterogeneity that monism cannot grasp because monism takes "manifestation-of-other" as the universal structure of all manifestation.

**Paragraph 7\.** The essence is what makes being not only being-in-itself but also being that exists for itself, being-for-itself. The essence is the for-itself itself as such; but insofar as in its act of appearing it is not this act of appearing that appears, the for-itself is not the manifestation of self — it is not a *selbst-ständig* (self-standing) essence. *It is being-in-itself that becomes for-itself*; it is being-in-itself that appears. It is precisely because, according to Sartre, it is being-in-itself that becomes for-itself, that the for-itself bears within itself an unsurmountable contingency, insofar as the for-itself is never anything but the being-for-itself of the in-itself — that is, the appearance of the contingent determination. It is also for this reason — because the for-itself is only being-in-itself become for-itself, that is, appearing — that *"we have no occasion to interrogate ourselves on the manner in which the for-itself can unite itself to the in-itself."* Commenting on Heidegger, Sartre had already written in the introduction to *L'Être et le Néant*: *"Being is simply the condition of every disclosing: it is being-for-disclosure and not being-disclosed."* And, further: *"The being of the phenomenon, although coextensive to the phenomenon, must escape the phenomenal condition… and consequently, it overflows and grounds the cognition that one takes of it."*

The reading of Sartre is precise. Sartre's for-itself is *not* an autonomous essence; it is the appearing-of-the-in-itself, the becoming-conscious of the in-itself. Hence Sartre's claim that there is no problem about how the for-itself "joins" the in-itself — they are not two separable realities but two structural moments of the same manifestation. The for-itself is constitutively *of* the in-itself; the in-itself is what manifests through the for-itself's appearing. This is the structure of monist manifestation perfectly stated: phenomenality is the appearance of beings (the in-itself), not the appearance of the appearing-itself (the for-itself, which "is" the appearing but does not itself appear in any positive way).

The conception according to which the for-itself would constitute an autonomous essence can in reality come to the fore only when its signification of being the essence is precisely lost. It is at the moment when the for-itself is considered as an existent opposed to the in-itself that it can seem to have, as an opposed and independent term, an autonomy and a sufficiency at least relative. As soon as the sense of the essence is no longer travestied and the for-itself is considered as the pure manifestation, its necessary reference to the existent comes to the fore as well — insofar as the for-itself is no longer anything but the appearance of the existent itself. When Sartre's thought arrives at avoiding this fall of the essence into ontic determination (a fall characterized by us not as a "subjectivization" but as an "*existentialization*"), the signification of the for-itself as nothing other than the simple presence of the known finds itself inevitably affirmed: *"Knowledge is nothing other,"* says Sartre, *"than the presence of being to the for-itself, and the for-itself is only the nothing that realizes this presence."* If by "being" one wants to understand, as is fitting to do, the existent itself, one sees that the "knowledge" that finds its foundation in the for-itself is in no way the act of a determinate reality opposed to the in-itself, but the pure and simple manifestation of being-in-itself itself and as such. *It is therefore at the very moment when the essence is understood in its purity that is also understood the indissoluble link that attaches the essence to the existent.*

**Paragraph 8\.** Insofar as the being of the phenomenon evades the phenomenal condition into which the phenomenon alone arrives, the essence of manifestation dissimulates itself in the very time when it accomplishes its work. *This dissimulation-of-self of the essence of phenomenality is the manifestation-of-self of the existent.* It is to the extent that the essence is this dissimulation that it links itself necessarily to what manifests itself — that is, to the existent. *The non-truth of the essence is the truth of the existent.* The existent therefore bears within itself, in its truth, the non-truth of the essence of manifestation. It is precisely because the essence is non-truth that the essence does not manifest itself otherwise than in the truth of the existent — that is, in the phenomenon itself and as such. The essence is only there where the determination is, although the essence is and because the essence is this "there," this "where," this "is" as such. The phenomenological signification of the link that unites indissolubly being and the existent consists in the fact that the light of manifestation does not shine elsewhere and not otherwise than on the existent that manifests itself. It is not, in truth, the light of being that shines on the existent; it is the existent itself in fact that shines in this light, in this light which is nothing other than the existent's own brilliance. *"Light,"* says Hegel in the *Philosophy of History*, *"is enlivening only if it applies itself to what is different from itself, acting upon it and making it bear fruit."* It is what is different from itself that permits the light to be enlivening — that is, to accomplish its work, that is, to be the light. In acting upon the existent that it is not and in making the existent bear fruit, it is to itself first that the light gives the possibility of historializing — though not otherwise than in the act by which it applies itself to what is different from itself. *What is different from itself alone permits the light to manifest itself; the existent is what manifests the essence of manifestation.*

This is a crucial structural point. In monism, the essence of manifestation cannot manifest itself directly; it can only manifest itself indirectly, through what is other than itself (the existent). The existent is the *necessary mediator* of the essence's self-manifestation. The light shines, but it is visible only as it shines on the things; without the things, the light would be invisible. Heidegger draws the same conclusion in his analyses of *Lichtung* (clearing): the clearing as such cannot be seen; it is only seen as the place where things appear. Hegel's formulation in the *Philosophy of History* (in the chapter on Persia and the religion of light) names the structural necessity: the absolute (light) is enlivening only as it applies itself to its other (matter, things). Without the other, the absolute is inert, indeterminate, "nothing." This is the dialectical formulation of the same monist structure.

**Paragraphs 9–10 (work of art, the chthonian element, the determination as enigma).** Insofar as the existent permits the essence of manifestation to manifest itself, the indissoluble link that unites being and the existent becomes phenomenologically clear. In conformity with such a link, it appears that only the totality constituted by the existent and being is concrete. Being is bound to the existent as light is to the thing on which it becomes visible. It is because the appearing appears only in the appearing-of which it is the being, that the ontological element is united indissolubly with the ontic determination. Thus one sees in the work of art the light join itself to the earth — and that in such a manner that the light is nothing other than the chthonian element itself, which tears itself away from the night and shines for an instant for us, as if this tearing-away of the existent from the obscurity of its originary milieu were not different from the tearing-away of the light from a reign that is not in itself a less profound night than that of the marble or of the column. Thus the artist has need of the stone, not only as a matter for his chisel, but first as a solid surface where manifestation reflects itself and can shine. *It is in the chthonian and recondite element of ontic determination that the essence finds its abode. The earth is the place of light.*

The reference to the work of art, to the earth, to the chthonian, and to the marble column draws on Heidegger's *Der Ursprung des Kunstwerks* (1935–36, in *Holzwege*) — Heidegger's famous essay on the work of art, where the work is described as the strife (*Streit*) of *Welt* (world, the openness of meaning) and *Erde* (earth, the self-closing materiality from which the work emerges). Heidegger's formula: the work of art *sets up* the world by *setting forth* the earth. Henry reads this as an exemplary illustration of the structural necessity of monism: the essence (the world as openness, the light) is bound to and made visible only through the determinate ontic material (the earth, the marble, the chthonian element). The artist's relation to stone exemplifies the philosophical relation of essence to existent: the essence requires the existent as the "solid surface" on which it can shine.

The luminous abode of which Aeschylus speaks — and which Marx wanted to give to the workers — is constituted by stones, thick blocks, and soulless rocks. Hegel reports the propositions of Herodotus, according to which the Persians had no idols and laughed at the anthropomorphic representations of the gods. These mockeries have a limited signification if the essence refers necessarily to the phenomenon — if it is on the figure alone that the pure manifestation shines, if, finally, the image is always *this* image. The classical-mythological references continue the theme: the essence of manifestation is necessarily incarnated in the figure (the idol, the column, the work). To mock the anthropomorphic idol on the grounds that the divine essence is purer than any figure is to misunderstand the structural necessity that the essence can manifest itself only *in* and *through* a figure.

Thus the essence of manifestation is susceptible of showing itself only on the ontic determination and *through* it. It is in the effective being of the determination that the essence of pure phenomenality finds the condition of its reality; it is in the phenomenon itself that pure phenomenality arrives at the phenomenal condition. *The essence however is not the determination, nor is it the phenomenon.* If phenomenality finds its immediate effectivity in the determination where it appears, the determination has no less immediately the signification of *not being* the essence. *The essence of pure phenomenality is other than its effectivity.* Insofar as the essence of phenomenality is other than its effectivity, the essence finds rather in its effectivity *its own suppression*. The determination manifests the essence, but in such a way that the essence dissimulates itself in this manifestation. Insofar as the determination manifests the essence, the determination is the essence's truth. Insofar as the essence dissimulates itself in this manifestation — insofar as it does not coincide with the effective phenomenological content of the determination — the truth of this content is foreign to the essence; the truth of this content is rather, with respect to the essence, the *non-truth*. *It is this non-truth of the essence, finally, that dissimulates itself in the truth of effective phenomenality.* The latter (the truth of effective phenomenality) gives itself for the truth of the essence. But the truth of the essence is the *non-truth of its non-truth*.

This compressed dialectical formulation captures the hidden structure of monist truth. Effective phenomenality (the manifestation of beings) is the "truth" — but it is a truth that *conceals* the essence (because the essence as such does not appear in it). So the truth of effective phenomenality is, with respect to the essence itself, *non-truth* (concealment). And the truth of the essence is *non-truth-of-this-non-truth*: the recognition that the apparent "truth" (manifest beings) conceals the essence. Heidegger's *Vom Wesen der Wahrheit* (1930–43) develops exactly this structure: truth (*aletheia*) involves *Verbergung* (concealment) — and the truth of the essence (*Wesen der Wahrheit*) is the recognition of this concealment internal to truth itself.

**Paragraph 11 (alienation and the death of the determination).** To arrive at effectivity, the essence had to alienate itself. The essence alienates itself not only because it is the becoming-other in which it realizes itself, but more originarily because it loses itself in this realization, where it dissimulates itself by manifesting itself. Because the essence cannot manifest itself in the determination except by dissimulating itself, what manifests the essence has the signification of being also what hides the essence. *The determination is the enigma.* It is the appearance (*Schein*) — but an appearance such (*Erscheinung*) that in it what appears refers inevitably to what does not appear.

The German technical vocabulary — *Schein* (mere semblance, illusion) and *Erscheinung* (appearance, that which shows itself) — is borrowed from Kant and Hegel. The *Erscheinung* is what appears; but as Kant already showed, every *Erscheinung* refers to a "noumenon" or "thing in itself" that does not appear. Hegel transformed this Kantian structure: the appearance refers, not to a hidden noumenon, but to the essence that *appears in* the appearance and yet *withdraws* in the appearance. Heidegger continues this Hegelian-phenomenological analysis: every appearance is also a concealment. Henry inscribes this whole analytic of appearance/concealment as the proper structure of monist phenomenality.

Insofar as the effective determination manifests the essence by dissimulating it, the determination can manifest this dissimulation only by *disappearing*. The dissimulation of the essence in the effective entity signifies an inequality of the entity with respect to the essence. The suppression of this inequality is the suppression of the entity. *The death of the determination is the manifestation of pure manifestation.* Or rather, since with this disappearance of the entity also disappears the element where the essence finds its effectivity and its truth, this essence cannot be anything other than nothing — except with the apparition of a *new* entity. The essence arrives among us only through the time of things; and the consciousness that seeks to grasp the essence — led astray in fact by the essence and constantly distracted from the object of its search — can only wander, from experiences to experiences, from objects to objects, without finding repose.

The closing paragraph of §13 is haunting and structurally decisive. Within monism, the essence of manifestation can manifest *itself* (its own essence) only through the *death* of the determinate beings that conceal it — for as long as a determinate being shines, the essence is concealed in it; only the disappearance of the being would let the pure essence shine. But the disappearance of the being is also the disappearance of the very element through which the essence can shine; so the manifestation of the pure essence requires the immediate apparition of new beings. This is the structure of *time*: the perpetual passing of beings, the constant succession of determinations, is the only mode in which the essence can "shine" — in the very flux that conceals each successive being in the next. Consciousness's pursuit of the essence is therefore essentially an *errancy* (*errance*, Heidegger's *Irre*), a wandering through experiences and objects without ever arriving at the essence as such. The Hegelian *Phenomenology of Spirit* — with its succession of figures of consciousness, each suppressed and replaced by the next — is the classical philosophical articulation of this temporal-errant structure of monist truth.

This is, for Henry, the structural diagnosis of why all monist philosophies (from Plato through Hegel through Heidegger) inevitably culminate in some form of *historical* or *temporal* finitude: the essence, on the monist conception, can only be approached through the temporal succession of beings, never directly. The "errancy" of consciousness is built into the structure of monism itself. Henry's alternative (in Sections III–IV) will be precisely that there *is* a mode of manifestation — immanent self-revelation — in which the essence manifests itself directly, without temporal mediation, without the death-of-the-determination, without errancy. Life's self-affection knows no such temporal succession because it knows no distance between the manifesting and the manifested.

---

## **§ 14\. The relation of essence and ontic determination in the philosophy of consciousness**

**Paragraph 1\.** As the philosophy of being and the philosophy of consciousness exchange their themes, they exchange also their problems. The link of being and the existent — whose phenomenological foundation has just been recalled (in §13) — becomes in the philosophy of consciousness the link of consciousness and the thing, or again that of the subject and the object. The subject relates itself necessarily to the object because the essence of consciousness — identical to the essence of manifestation understood according to the fundamental presuppositions of monism — refers itself inevitably to the determination as to its truth. The phenomenological signification of the indissoluble link that unites consciousness and the thing is perceived by classical philosophy when it declares that *the subject knows itself only on the object*. The object intervenes, from then on, in the problematic of the philosophy of consciousness — not as a synthetic and contingent contribution with regard to the philosophy of consciousness understood as the essence of manifestation, but as a reality implicated in fact in this essence as that which alone allows the essence to realize itself. This realization — that is, the essence of manifestation's own promotion into the phenomenal condition — the essence of manifestation obtains consequently only in and through the object. *Thus the determination appears finally as belonging to the internal structure of the essence*, insofar as the essence of manifestation can find its effectivity only in the phenomenal condition that it must ground. The object is essential to consciousness as that which permits consciousness to be what it is. This is why the thought that thinks consciousness in its possibility must recognize the necessity of the element that belongs to the definition of this possibility as such.

§13 established the structural necessity, in monism, that being be the being of an existent — that is, that the essence of manifestation be inseparably bound to ontic determination. §14 now applies this same structural necessity to the *philosophy of consciousness*: the parallel link in this philosophical vocabulary is the link of consciousness and object. The philosophy of consciousness inherits the structure of monism: just as Heidegger's Dasein is structurally bound to ontic existents, so Husserl's consciousness is structurally bound to its objects. Husserl's "every consciousness is consciousness of something" (the principle of intentionality from *Ideen I* §84) is the philosophy-of-consciousness articulation of the same monist necessity that Heidegger articulates as "being is the being of the existent." The thesis of §14 is that the philosophy of consciousness, when it correctly understands itself, recognizes that the object is *internal* to the structure of consciousness — not an addition to consciousness but a constituent moment of consciousness's possibility.

**Paragraph 2\.** The link of essence and determination is visible in the philosophy of Jacob Böhme, which (as has been seen, in §11) is dominated by the problem of conscious manifestation that Böhme understands as constituting the very structure of the absolute. It is on the foundation in itself of the opposition that the absolute manifests itself; but the opposition as such draws only the pure space for a possible manifestation in general. In such a space, which is an undifferentiated milieu, there is yet no real manifestation. In it there reigns only a diffuse clarity — a light so indeterminate that in fact it is not light at all, because it is not conscious of itself. As in its primitive indetermination, the pure phenomenological milieu has no consciousness of itself, there is in it no effective consciousness — at least as long as there is in it nothing other than itself. Opposition will signify the arising of light only if opposition posits the element opposed to light. What opposes itself to the pure milieu of manifestation, in such a manner that manifestation finds in it the condition of its realization, is not in itself, as opposed to this milieu, something *ontological*. The element opposed in the opposition is the *ontic determination*. Real differentiation supposes a *nature*. The revelation of opposition — that is, the manifestation of the essence of manifestation — is therefore possible only by the mediation of what, with respect to this essence (that is, with respect to opposition as such), is *radically other*.

The Böhmean doctrine — central to the German mystical tradition that informed Schelling and Hegel — articulates the structural point with mythological vividness. The "*Ungrund*" of the divine is pure undifferentiated absolute; pure opposition (as the structure of self-distantiation) is opened in the divine, but this opposition is itself empty — it provides only the *space* for manifestation, not manifestation itself. Real manifestation requires that something *opaque*, something *radically other*, be opposed within the opposition — and this opaque other is what Böhme calls "nature" or the "chthonian" element. The metaphor of the mirror: the divine cannot see itself in a transparent surface; it needs an opaque mirror that reflects. The opacity of the mirror is what allows reflection. So manifestation requires not just the formal structure of opposition (essence of manifestation as such) but also the *material* of ontic determination (the opaque other) on which opposition can be enacted as visibility.

Thus one sees in Böhme that the divine *Sagesse* (Wisdom), which consists in pure objectivation, cannot tear the absolute from the primitive night of the *Ungrund*, although it adds to it opposition as such — that is, the essence of manifestation. In opposing itself to itself, the absolute wants to give itself a mirror in order to see itself; but as long as the element opposed in this mirror is only the absolute itself, it is not a mirror but something transparent that reflects nothing. The opacity of ontic determination is in opposition itself the radically other element by which opposition realizes itself. This realization of opposition in the determination as effective being-opposed, Böhme affirms in the conception of a *nature interior to the absolute* — that is, constitutive of the very process by which manifestation is produced. The immanence of determination to the effective becoming of manifestation is also expressed in the opposition (to the idea of light) of the idea of *fire*, which implies in itself the presence of a "matter." For on close inspection, it appears that this opposition is not really an opposition: light realizes itself only in fire, and thus becomes effective only in its indissoluble union with the opaque and radically other being to which it opposes itself. Fire is the phenomenal condition of light — a condition that light obtains only on the foundation in light of opaque and brute determination. The whole of Böhmean philosophy of the body attests the necessity of the presence of the ontic element at the heart of phenomenal essence and as a condition of the realization of phenomenal essence.

The Böhmean doctrine of *fire* (developed especially in *Mysterium Magnum* and *De Signatura Rerum*) — fire as the unity of light and matter, as the phenomenon in which the absolute makes itself manifest — is for Henry exemplary of the monist necessity. The structural conclusion: the essence of manifestation requires the ontic determination as its constitutive other; without the ontic, the essence would be a transparent nothing.

It is because the ontic determination is essential to the realization of the essence that the determination is not, in truth, posited *in* the essence at a given moment of time. It is by *abstraction* that we distinguish in the absolute the moment of the *Ungrund*. As soon as the absolute *is*, in fact it is real. This is why the determination is as ancient as the absolute — because the determination defines a condition of phenomenality, that is, of the absolute itself. *God bears within himself an eternal body, because he is the originary and pure essence of manifestation in its effective accomplishment.* In such an accomplishment is included the determination as its condition. Insofar as it constitutes the condition of possibility of the effective becoming of phenomenality, the existent belongs to the internal structure of phenomenality. *The ontic element is an eidetic structure of the ontological and pure essence of manifestation.*

The conclusion is structurally radical: the ontic is not opposed to the ontological as something external; the ontic is *internal to* the structure of the ontological, an "eidetic structure" of the essence of manifestation itself. The fact that monism cannot maintain a pure essence apart from ontic determination is not an accident or a defect; it is internal to the essence's structure. In Böhme this is expressed as: God's body is eternal; the absolute's relation to the determinate is co-original with the absolute itself. There is no "moment" in which the absolute is prior to or apart from determination; only abstract analysis can isolate such a moment.

**Paragraph 3\.** The belonging of the ontic element to the internal structure of the essence of phenomenality, as condition of possibility of the effective becoming of phenomenality, is visible also in Schelling's philosophy of consciousness. The object is thought by Schelling as the condition of effective consciousness, insofar as *"consciousness is the act by which the thinking subject becomes immediately object to itself."* The theme according to which objectivation is the becoming of consciousness under the form of the becoming of the object — that is, objectivation is the realization of consciousness, insofar as consciousness must objectify itself in order to appear — belongs to the philosophy of consciousness in general. But the objectivation that is the realization of consciousness is not pure objectivation. It is *effective* objectivation, in which determination is present. It is therefore in a real object — in the effectivity of a transcendent and (as such) limited entity — that consciousness manifests itself. *What enters into the phenomenal condition in the effective becoming of phenomenality is the finite determination.* "*To arrive at consciousness and to be limited is one and the same thing.*" The pure essence of manifestation manifests itself only under a finite form. Schelling conceives this pure essence as a primitive and infinite activity. This is why he writes: *"It is the condition of consciousness that this primitive and infinite activity, this essence of all reality, become its object to itself, become consequently defined and limited."* Thus the concrete entity (by itself non-conscious) is, as conscious, the only possible realization of the phenomenal essence of pure consciousness.

The Schellingian doctrine, from the *System of Transcendental Idealism* (1800), is exemplary. Consciousness is "infinite activity" (the pure essence of manifestation), but it can become *conscious* only by limiting itself, by objectifying itself as a determinate (finite) entity. Without this self-limitation, the activity would not appear; with it, the activity appears but in the diminished form of the determinate. Henry's diagnosis: this is the precise structure of monism — the pure essence cannot manifest without limiting itself in determination, but in limiting itself it loses its purity. Phenomenality, on this conception, is intrinsically the *finitization* of the infinite essence.

If, in the *Investigations on Human Freedom* (1809), the nocturnal element which serves as "reactive" to revelation and constitutes as such the condition of revelation's possibility can be interpreted as a pure ontological element — insofar as the causal Ground is not the determination on which light reflects but what, in the very essence of light, dissimulates itself (and that not anteriorly to its effective becoming but at the heart of it) — the element different from consciousness, in the late philosophy, is clearly posited in its heterogeneity with respect to the essence. It is a real being in the sense of determination, and not the essence itself, that the essence opposes itself in the alienation where it seeks conscious existence. The reference is to Schelling's later work (the *Philosophy of Mythology*, the *Philosophy of Revelation*), where the "real" element opposed to divine consciousness is no longer interpreted as a still-ontological dark Ground (as in 1809\) but as the genuinely created, ontic other that the divine produces in order to manifest itself.

The opposition to the simple thought-of-self of the idea of an effective creation — terminating in a real and (as such) foreign-to-the-pure-self-objectivation-of-thought term — has the same signification as the critique directed by Böhme against divine Wisdom. This phenomenological signification is that pure objectivation can accomplish its work only if what comes about in objectivation is *foreign* to it. The effective separation of the creature from God in the phenomenon of creation, and the constitutive rejection of pantheism in favor of an "*autonomy of the progeny*," thus find their motive in the conditions that render possible the effective becoming of phenomenality.

The argument: the late Schelling's break with pantheism (in which God and creation are identified) is not an arbitrary theological choice but a structural-ontological necessity of the monist-phenomenological project. Pantheism keeps creation within the divine self-objectivation, so creation remains transparent — and the divine cannot really manifest itself. To manifest itself, the divine needs a *real* other, an autonomously created being, against which the divine can become visible. So the "autonomy of the progeny" (the doctrine that creation is genuinely independent from the creator) is the ontological condition of the divine's manifestation.

**Paragraph 4\.** These conditions, which postulate the effectivity of alienation, Hegel had to understand in turn as the conditions of the realization of the essence — that is, of the absolute. The essence realizes itself at the heart of the effective becoming of phenomenality, which is the concrete spirit, only if, in the ontological process of alienation that constitutes the essence, the *non-ontological* is included — the radically other term, the being different from this alienation itself. As long as alienation does not signify the existence of this radically other being, as long as alienation does not envisage this being independently of its relation to alienation, *"this alienation is still imperfect; it expresses the relation of the certainty of self with the object that, precisely because it is in the relation, has not yet gained its full freedom."* Thus the being-other that comes about in the pure self-objectivation of thought is still only the *concept* of being-other — that is, the pure possibility and not the effectivity of real and concrete appearance. The "nostalgic need of a reality" of which the early writings already speak signifies that pure appearance can arrive at the effectivity of concrete appearance only through "the intrusion" in it of "a real historical element." Alienation is the essence of objectivity, but objectivity realizes itself phenomenally only in objective determination. *This is why the alienation constitutive of the Logos becomes effective only in nature.* In this effectivity, which is that of consciousness, is posited the indissoluble link that unites pure concept and ineffable determination.
