The Hegelian references are to the *Phenomenology of Spirit* — both the early sections on consciousness, and the late sections on the unhappy consciousness and revealed religion. The core doctrine: pure thought (the Logos) cannot remain merely conceptual; it must alienate itself into nature (the *Naturphilosophie*) and into history (the *Philosophy of Spirit*) in order to become effective and realized. Without the "intrusion" of a real historical element, the Logos remains pure possibility. So the entire architecture of the Hegelian system — Logic → Nature → Spirit — is the working-out of the structural necessity that the essence (pure thought) realize itself through alienation into determinate being. This is the same structure as Böhme and Schelling, articulated in fully systematic dialectical form.

**Paragraph 5\.** The link that unites essence and determination is implicated in the effective becoming of phenomenality. The pure essence of manifestation realizes itself only by the mediation of being-in-itself. *Consciousness is always consciousness of something.* The consciousness of something is the exterior consciousness of the object — what Hegel calls "consciousness." Insofar as the essence of phenomenality manifests itself only in the phenomenon, the phenomenon is the appearance of this essence. The object is the becoming-conscious of the essence of consciousness; it is what permits this essence to take consciousness of itself. *The consciousness of self is identical to consciousness.* It is because consciousness is identical to the consciousness of self that being-there has, in a general way, "the signification of pure thought." Being-there is the appearance of thought. The determination is the realization of the essence insofar as it is the becoming-conscious of the essence.

The structural identification is precise: in monism, "consciousness of self" (the supposed inner self-presence of consciousness) is identical with "consciousness of object" (the outer presence of the object) — because both are realizations of the same essence (the essence of manifestation as opposing-doubling). There is no special inner self-consciousness over and above object-consciousness; self-consciousness *is* the consciousness of objects, because the only way for consciousness to become conscious of itself is to objectify itself, to make itself an object for itself. This is the Hegelian doctrine of the *Phenomenology of Spirit* (especially the Self-Consciousness chapter): self-consciousness arrives at its "for-itself" only through the mediation of an other. Henry will of course reject this thesis in Sections III–IV: there is a self-consciousness (life's self-affection) that is *not* mediated by any object, that is *not* the object's consciousness — but this requires breaking with monism altogether.

**Paragraph 6\.** The problem of the manifestation of the pure essence of phenomenality was already posed in Fichte, who understood it in the *Conferences* as the problem of the manifestation of "existence." Because the solution of this problem was demanded by Fichte from the ontological process of objectivation, the solution consisted equally — for this reason — in the arising of determination as appearance and consequently as the only effective reality of the pure essence of the concept. Interrogating himself on this effective reality — that is, on the becoming-conscious of pure existence — Fichte asks of pure existence: *"What happens to it when it grasps itself thus?"* What happens to existence when it grasps itself thus (that is, in objectivation) is the becoming under the form of conscious determination. *Existence exists effectively only as this or that.* "*In this vigorous return upon itself,"* says Fichte, *"it (existence) sees directly that it is this and that, that it bears such a character."* And further: *"In the reflection upon itself, knowledge — by virtue of itself and of its own nature — divides itself by the fact that it is not only evident to itself (which would give only one term), but by the fact that it is at the same time evident to itself as this and that."* Because the pure essence of manifestation realizes itself in objectivation only under the form of finite determination, Fichte could understand such a realization as the very advent of the world in its diversity. The pretension of grasping the reason of empirical diversity in the concept itself finds its legitimation in the understanding of the internal structure of the concept — that is, in the definition of the conditions of effective phenomenality.

The Fichtean doctrine, from the *Anweisung zum seligen Leben* (1806) — Fichte's late "religious" philosophy already treated in §10 — is exemplary. Pure existence cannot remain pure; it must, in becoming-conscious, become determinate as "this" and "that." The diversity of the world is therefore not contingent but flows from the internal structure of the essence of manifestation: the essence requires concrete determination in order to be effective, and concrete determination is necessarily diverse, plural, finite. The essence's manifestation \= the world's diversity.

What is produced, however, when this phenomenality becomes effective? *"What does consciousness then enclose in this state?…"* Fichte asks. *"The world,"* says Fichte, *"and nothing but the world."* By "world," it is fitting to understand the sum of the existent. Nothing other is produced in the effective becoming of phenomenality than ontic determination, and it alone: *effective consciousness is the transcendent entity.* The conclusion is striking: in the becoming-effective of phenomenality, what we have is only the world of ontic existents — the essence of manifestation as such has *vanished* into the existents that manifest themselves. Effective consciousness is identical with the totality of objects.

Or is the pure essence of phenomenality not present as such in the real content of appearance? Does not the absolute manifest itself in itself in this effective consciousness? *"Or,"* asks Fichte, *"is the divine life not found immediately in this consciousness?… No, for consciousness can only transform this immediate life into a world; and as soon as one posits this consciousness, this transformation is posited as effected."* The effective becoming of the essence of phenomenality in real consciousness is its *transformation* into the determinate appearance of the transcendent entity: in this transformation that realizes the essence, the essence has equally lost itself. The pure essence of phenomenality is objectivation itself, transformation as such. In its accomplishment, however, this transformation does not show itself. *"The absolute consciousness is precisely by itself the immediate accomplishment — and for this reason no longer conscious — of this transformation."* The pure consciousness does not arrive at the phenomenal condition. *The absolute consciousness is unconscious.* The fundamental ontological process of objectivation, which defines the essence of manifestation, lets this essence escape in the very accomplishment of objectivation — insofar as in this accomplishment, objectivation does not itself arrive at the phenomenal condition of appearance. The thought that thinks the essence of manifestation as objectivation runs up against a contradiction included in the very essence it thinks. *Thus one sees the philosophy of consciousness inevitably constrained to posit the unconsciousness of the absolute consciousness under which it strives to think the essence of phenomenality.*

This is one of the most striking diagnoses of the section. The philosophy of consciousness, which sets out to understand the essence of manifestation as consciousness, is forced by the structure of its own analysis to conclude that the pure essence of consciousness is *unconscious*. This paradoxical result has classical philosophical resonance: it is the doctrine of the "unconscious absolute" that runs from Schelling through Schopenhauer through Nietzsche. The diagnosis: the philosophy of consciousness collapses, on its own terms, into a philosophy of the unconscious — because the very structure of monist phenomenality requires that the essence of phenomenality not itself appear as a phenomenon. The pure consciousness, which would be the essence of all manifestation, cannot itself be conscious — because for it to be conscious would require its objectivation, which would destroy its purity.

Just as in Fichte the pure existence that defines the essence does not enter into the phenomenal condition except under the condition of objective determination — without however being able to maintain in this form the purity of its originary essence (so that *"the form always veils the essence from us"*) — likewise in Schelling the pure consciousness that realizes itself phenomenally in the object is no longer, in fact, in this realization, anything but the object itself. *Pure consciousness is the process that makes the finite entity arise; it is "the activity that limits."* But *"the limiting activity never arrives at consciousness,"* and that because it *"does not become an object."* The originary essence of manifestation can therefore only remain in the night of its originary unconsciousness, or lose itself in the object. In the object, the essence of manifestation realizes itself but precisely by losing itself. *The appearing of consciousness in objectivation is its own disappearing.*

The diagnosis is now complete. In monist philosophy of consciousness (as in monist philosophy of being), the essence of manifestation has *no* mode of self-manifestation: either it remains unconscious (pure but invisible) or it becomes object (visible but no longer pure). There is no third option within monism. The essence cannot be both pure and conscious. This is the deepest impossibility internal to ontological monism: monism cannot account for the self-manifestation of the essence of manifestation.

**Paragraph 7\.** What however of the manifestation of consciousness in its purity? Must such a manifestation not be exhibitable, if the philosophy of consciousness pretends to speak with any right of the pure concept on which it is founded? Schelling cannot lift the paradox of a consciousness that knows itself only when it becomes object, nor maintain the validity of the pure concept of consciousness, otherwise than by making consciousness the condition of the effective phenomenal appearance of the object. As objectivation, consciousness is the primordial act that renders the object possible. *"But how does the philosopher assure himself of the existence of this primitive act?… Evidently he does not have its assurance immediately; he arrives at knowing it only by induction."* The originary essence of manifestation is the *non-objective*, and as such it does not belong to the effective sphere of phenomenality. It is only from this effective sphere — that is, from the objective element — that one can posit reflexively the reality of the act that is thought as the condition of the object. *Reflexive analysis is the methodological expression of the paradox constituted by the non-phenomenal condition of the essence of phenomenality.* This paradox seems lifted by the opposition instituted by Schelling between "the transcendental point of view" and that of common consciousness. While common consciousness knows only the objective (because *"the objective alone arrives by intuition at common consciousness"* and because *"intuition itself loses itself in the object"*), *"from the transcendental point of view,"* on the contrary, *"one considers the object only through the act of intuition."* Thus the transcendental point of view directs itself explicitly upon the act that renders the effective phenomenological entity possible — that is, upon the transcendental element of pure consciousness. This pure consciousness, however, is it reached in itself? Does it arrive in itself at the phenomenal condition? It seems yes: *"the property of the transcendental point of view is to bring back to consciousness and to render objective what, in every other order of thought, of knowledge, or of action, is absolutely non-objective — that is, escapes consciousness."* Does the essence of phenomenality, which does not enter into the phenomenal condition, not enter into this condition in the transcendental point of view? But how? To "bring back to consciousness" what is "absolutely non-objective," the transcendental point of view can only "render it objective." *The transcendental can appear to itself only under the form of the object of inner sense.* Unless one confuses the two, as Schelling does, it must be recognized that here again the phenomenal becoming of the essence of phenomenality is the *self-suppression* of this pure essence. Buffeted between psychologism and the reflexive method, the transcendental philosophy of consciousness cannot, in any case, give itself the reality of the essence by which it defines itself.

The diagnosis of Schelling's transcendental philosophy is sharp. Schelling tries to thematize the pure non-objective essence by introducing the "transcendental point of view" — the point of view that focuses not on the object but on the act of objectivation. But this very thematization requires that the act of objectivation be itself made into a kind of object (an "object of inner sense"). So the transcendental thematization is a *self-suppression* of the essence: in trying to make the pure essence of manifestation into a phenomenon, the transcendental method actually destroys the essence's purity by treating it as just another object. The transcendental philosophy of consciousness oscillates between two unacceptable options: (i) psychologism (treating the essence as a psychological phenomenon) and (ii) reflexive analysis (positing the essence as a logical condition that is never given). Neither option grants the essence its proper reality. This is the structural failure of modern transcendental philosophy from Kant through Schelling to Husserl: the transcendental is always either psychologically reduced or logically posited; never *given* in its proper mode of manifestation.

**Paragraph 8\.** In the eidetic structure of the essence of manifestation as classical philosophy conceives it is inscribed a *double demand*. On the one hand, the obligation for consciousness to objectify itself and thus to arrive at effectivity. The consciousness of self is identical to the exterior consciousness of the object. Thus comes to the fore a philosophy of effectivity that situates the concrete essence in the being-there of objective determination. On the other hand, the necessity of preserving the essence in its purity brings the recognition of the inadequate character of the manifestation of this essence in the entity where it appears to itself. The essence realizes itself in determination, but this realization does not contain the essence. Like the God of Böhme who, *"manifesting himself eternally in being, remains eternally outside \[it\],"* the essence in its phenomenological realization is *"something else again."* The determination can well be understood as the manifestation of the absolute, as the document that bears witness to its eternal source — but this document is the ambiguous cipher, the simple appearance that refers to something other. *Finitude is the form that veils the essence.* The freedom that is nothing "outside of nature" is however in its essence other than nature. This is why one sees in Fichte freedom ceaselessly displace the limit it opposes to itself in order to realize itself — that is, in order to appear. Because freedom alienates itself in fact in the element where it realizes itself, the essence must as well reject as posit such an element. The element, consequently, enters into history. But at each moment the problem is the same. *It is in vain that the philosophy of consciousness mutates into a philosophy of becoming.* Its contradiction remains what it was in Kant when it was said that *"we know only phenomena."* The effective reality of the essence is the *contrary* of what the essence is at bottom. One can speculate as much as one wishes on this contradiction, affirm for example the determinism of phenomena and transcendental freedom — but transcendental freedom is only the freedom of the transcendental object \= x. *The philosophy of consciousness has been able to save the absolute only by rejecting it into a hinter-world.*

This paragraph crystallizes the diagnostic. The double demand of monist philosophy is incompatible: (i) effective phenomenality requires that the essence realize itself in determination; (ii) preservation of the essence requires that the essence remain *other* than determination. Both demands cannot be satisfied simultaneously, and so monism oscillates eternally between a philosophy of pure essence (which loses effectivity) and a philosophy of effective determination (which loses the essence). The philosophical history of trying to escape this dilemma — the German idealist philosophies of becoming, the Hegelian history-of-spirit, the Kantian transcendental object \= x, the Heideggerian *Seinsgeschichte* — is in vain because the dilemma is structural. The "absolute" of the philosophy of consciousness is "saved" only by being *exiled* into a hinter-world (an *Hinterwelt*, in Nietzschean vocabulary) — into the unreachable transcendental, the unknowable thing-in-itself, the absolute that never appears.

**Paragraph 9\.** Do the difficulties common to the philosophy of consciousness and the philosophy of being not lose their signification of being an *obstacle* to the progress of the thought that wants to circumscribe the concrete essence of phenomenality, if this thought understands precisely such an essence in its concrete character — that is, in the effectivity of its being-realized? For it is *not* the inevitable reference of the essence to determination; it is the pretension of grasping the essence outside of this reference and in a so-called purity that must be put in question — if the being-there of effective determination is the phenomenal becoming and, as such, the realization of the essence of phenomenality. That the pure essence vanish into the night of the transcendental origin signifies only that it cannot be understood outside the ontic element where it finds the moment of phenomenal presence. *The pure essence is the abstraction of being-present.* Being is present only as the being of the determination that is there, and that not only in the sense that it is always and inevitably the appearance of an existent, but more originally because this appearance becomes precisely what it is — an appearance — only by the mediation of what appears in it. *It is the existent that appears.* The link of being and the existent, the inevitable reference of transcendence to what is by it transcended, has this ultimate phenomenological signification. What expresses itself in this signification is the indissoluble unity of the ontic element and the ontological element in the effective becoming of phenomenality. *The effective being-there is ontic and ontological at the same time.* If the *Dasein* does not designate only the abstraction of a presence but this presence itself in its real accomplishment, is it not legitimately, then, that transcendence is qualified in Dasein not as "the property of a given subject," but as *"the essential mode of being of this existent"* that the Dasein is also? Is the right to speak of an *"ontic possibility of the understanding of being"* not founded? Does the fundamental ambiguity of the Dasein not find its reason in the internal structure of effective phenomenality?

The closing paragraph performs a careful reversal. After the long diagnosis of the difficulty (that monism oscillates inevitably between pure essence and effective determination), Henry now considers an alternative reading: perhaps the difficulty is not really a difficulty but the proper structure of phenomenality itself. If "effective being-there" *is* both ontic and ontological at the same time (because phenomenality requires this dual structure), then the apparent ambiguity of the Dasein (which §13 diagnosed as a structural problem) is actually the *proper expression* of the structure of effective phenomenality. The Heideggerian formulations Henry cites — Dasein as "the essential mode of being" of an existent, the "ontic possibility of the understanding of being" — would then be vindicated as faithful to the structure of phenomenality, not as ambiguous lapses.

The question is left open. The closing question of §14 — "Does the fundamental ambiguity of the Dasein not find its reason in the internal structure of effective phenomenality?" — frames the program of §15: to determine the ontological signification of the problematic that aims at the essence apart from its concrete realization. If the essence cannot be grasped apart from determination (which is what §14 has just established), then the program of "thinking the essence in its purity" is illegitimate; what must be thought is the *concrete unity* of essence and determination. But this concession would make the philosophy of being and the philosophy of consciousness — which both pursue precisely this concrete unity — fully vindicated. §15 will examine whether the program of pure-essence-thinking has any ontological signification, or whether it is a philosophical phantom.

---

## **§ 15\. The ontological signification of the problematic that aims at the essence and the originary concept of finitude**

**Paragraph 1\.** It is here that it is fitting to recall with force the signification of a problematic that aims at the essence. The ontological character of such a problematic signifies that the essence constitutes by itself the condition of possibility of appearance as such. If the ontic element defines a condition of this possibility — if it belongs to the internal structure of the act of appearing considered in and for itself — then it belongs also to the essence; it is *ontological*. *It is the very definition of such an element as ontic that must be put in question.* It is the distinction operated in the real between what is ontic and what is ontological that must be rethought. For one can no longer dissociate what appears and the act of appearing if the concrete content of what appears belongs as a constitutive element to the very structure of the act of appearing as such.

The opening of §15 reverses the apparent concession of the closing paragraph of §14. §14 ended on a question: does the structural necessity of the essence-determination link mean that "Dasein is an existent" is not a defect but the proper expression of the structure of phenomenality? §15 now refuses this concession in the form of a methodological purification: if the ontic element really were a constituent of the essence of phenomenality, then it would not be ontic at all (since the very definition of "ontic" excludes it from the structure of essence). The distinction ontic/ontological is foundational; it cannot itself be put in question by the concession that the ontic enters into the constitution of the essence. So the apparent paradox of §13–§14 must be resolved otherwise: the ontic does *not* enter into the essence; what does enter is something that has been *confused* with the ontic but is in fact ontological. The whole section will work to identify what has been so confused.

*Is the existent yes or no a condition of manifestation?* The question is sharply posed. The remainder of the section will answer: *no*. What functions as the apparent "condition" is not the existent (the determinate content) but the ontological *place* of the existent (the horizon of being, the field of objectivity). The existent itself contributes nothing to phenomenality; it is the *form* of objectivity (the horizon, the field, the "before" of representation) that is the genuine condition.

**Paragraph 2\.** The thesis according to which the existent must be understood — as an element belonging to the phenomenal becoming of the essence of phenomenality — as a condition of the being-effective of phenomenality, is *absurd*. How could the existent be that on which the pure essence of manifestation becomes visible to itself, if the existent were not first and already there? And how could the existent precisely be there, that is, *appear*, if the act of appearing considered in and for itself had not already accomplished its work? *It is the accomplished work of the originary and pure essence of manifestation that permits the existent to be there.* The essence has therefore realized itself as concrete essence (which grounds the phenomenal becoming of the existent) when the existent finally appears. *To realize the effective becoming of the essence, the existent always comes too late, because the existent presupposes this becoming.*

The argument is rigorous. If the essence required the existent as a condition of its becoming-phenomenal, this would presuppose that the existent is "already there" — but the existent's being-there is precisely what depends on the essence's accomplished work. So the existent cannot be a condition of the essence's accomplishment; rather, the existent is the *result* of this accomplishment. The structure-of-priority is one-way: essence → existent, not existent → essence. The misreading that puts the existent as a condition of the essence has the structure backwards.

When one says that it is the *in-itself* that *becomes* for-itself, one formulates an ambiguous proposition. For the being-in-itself has in itself nothing in common with the for-itself. The for-itself designates the phenomenal dimension of existence — to which the in-itself, as such, is fundamentally foreign. That the being-in-itself penetrates into this dimension of phenomenality does not signify that the in-itself is in itself this light of pure manifestation. It is so little this light, in truth, that scarcely entered into the dimension of phenomenality, the in-itself withdraws from it and returns to its night. Such a return into the night of its originary condition, the existent could surely not accomplish if it were in itself identical to the being of light. The existent is always *this* one or *that* one. By the singularity of its concrete content, the existent is *the different*. But the ontological power that manifests the existent is always *the same*. *To the particular nature of the existent, the light that illuminates it is indifferent.* It is one and always the same work that promotes the determination — whatever it may be and despite its contingency — into the open dimension of existence. *It is not the determinate character of the object, it is its objective character that grounds its phenomenal character.* The fact of manifesting itself is foreign to the determinate character of the determination. The universal being does not find its foundation in the contingency of ontic determination.

The argument refines the diagnosis. The Sartrian formulation "the in-itself becomes for-itself" (the in-itself comes to be conscious through the work of the for-itself) is structurally misleading. The in-itself does not "become" the light of phenomenality (it is foreign to this light); what happens is that the in-itself enters into the *dimension* of light (the for-itself, the field of objectivity), and this dimension is provided by the essence of manifestation, not by the in-itself. The light that illuminates objects is *indifferent* to which particular objects it illuminates: the same light makes possible an infinity of different existents. So the determinate content (this particular existent) is *contingent* with respect to the structure of phenomenality; what is *necessary* is the *objective character* (the form of objectivity, the horizon).

**Paragraph 3\.** Does the indifference of the act of appearing to the content of what each time appears in fact necessarily imply an *independence* of the effective becoming of apparition with regard to the ontic element that shows itself in apparition — does it signify the *Selbständigkeit* (self-standingness) of the essence? The contingency of the content of the determination that is there — is it not rather the sign of a *necessity* and, as such, implicated in the accomplishment of the being-effective of phenomenality? For the contingency of the content does not exclude but presupposes perhaps the existence of the content, whatever it may be. Thus one sees that any empirical diversity is however thought by Kant as what is required in every real cognition — and that as a condition. The universal and pure character of the category does not prevent that the category find its effective use only by the mediation of empirical intuition. Thus the contingent character of the ontic determination does not exclude its *necessary* belonging to the accomplished being of the essence.

The argument now adds nuance. To say that the content is "contingent" is *not* to say that the content is "dispensable." The Kantian model: the categories of the understanding are universal (they apply equally to whatever empirical content), but they cannot operate without *some* empirical content; the *that* of empirical intuition is necessary even though *what* particular content is given is contingent. So with the essence of phenomenality: the essence is indifferent to which particular existents it manifests, but it requires *some* existents to manifest. The essence's necessary linkage to determination is a necessity for *some* determinate-content-or-other, not for any particular content. This formal-Kantian point preserves the structural necessity of the link without making the essence depend on the contingent specificity of any particular existent.

**Paragraph 4\.** The phenomenological signification of the belonging of determination to the accomplished being of the essence finds its origin in the understanding of the internal structure of the essence. The essence of manifestation is thought — by the philosophy of being as well as by that of consciousness — as the *opposition*. In the ontological process of opposition arises the phenomenon as that which is found posited *before*. *The fundamental ambiguity of the term that is thus posited before must finally be denounced.* What arises by the mediation of the essence of opposition into a foreground of light, and as the condition of the effective becoming of manifestation, is *not the existent*; it is *this foreground itself and as such* — it is the *transcendental horizon of being*. In the deployment of the transcendental horizon of being, the work of the essence is exhausted; with this deployment, the effective becoming of phenomenality realizes itself. It is when this horizon has deployed itself, when the field of transcendental visibility has opened, that the existent — *then and only then* — can be there. *Far from the existent being a condition of the phenomenal becoming of this originary and pure phenomenological field, it is in the becoming-visible of this field, and only in it, that the existent can be seen.*

This is the decisive disambiguation. What is "posited before" in the essence's work of opposition is *not* an existent; it is the *space*, the *foreground*, the *horizon*, in which an existent will become possible. The "before" of representation is a structural place, not a thing. The Heideggerian "horizon of being" (*Sein und Zeit* §65) and Husserlian "horizon of givenness" (*Cartesian Meditations* §19, *Erfahrung und Urteil* §22) name precisely this space. The essence's work creates this space; only in this space can existents subsequently appear. So the *existent* is a result, not a condition; what is the condition is the *horizon* (the foreground of light), which is fully ontological.

The being-there of the existent is produced in *ontic knowledge*. But ontic knowledge presupposes — as a condition of this being-there, or rather as this being-there itself and as such — the accomplishment of *ontological knowledge*: the opening of the horizon of being. The *contrarium* (the opposite term) which, on the foundation of the understanding of the essence of manifestation as opposition, is thought (since Böhme) as the condition of the phenomenal becoming of phenomenality, must be grasped not as an *ontic* element but in the nudity of its pure ontological signification. The progress realized by the philosophy of being has consisted precisely in the bringing-into-light of this pure signification — out of the representations in which the ontological process of opposition was grasped in a confused way and still interpreted as a process of ontic order.

The structural correction is elegant. The whole tradition — Böhme, Schelling, Hegel, Fichte — thought the essence of manifestation as requiring an "opposite term" (the *contrarium*, the opaque other, the chthonian element). They took this opposite term to be an *ontic* reality (matter, nature, the in-itself). But properly understood, the opposite term is the *ontological place* of objectivity (the horizon of being, the field of representation), not any ontic content. Heidegger's contribution is precisely to have purified the conception by making explicit that the "opposed" is the horizon as such, not any particular existent within the horizon. So the philosophy of being has clarified what was confused in the philosophy of consciousness; both, however, operate within the same monist structure.

**Paragraph 5\.** One has seen how the distance instituted by opposition (and which defines the open field of phenomenality) was first thought as a "real" distance. To the concept of this distance — which functions as a category of the existent — is bound that of being-distant, understood on the foundation of this link as an ontic reality. Being-distant as such, however, is not the existent; it is what permits the existent to manifest itself. *What finds itself thus distanced in the originary work of the essence — and as the condition of the manifestation of the existent — is so little this existent itself that it is, in truth, nothing.* What holds itself at distance in the originary accomplishment of transcendence is the *horizon of nothingness*. *It is the nothing, not the existent, that finds itself objected (objectified) in objectivation, and that — under the form of a horizon — realizes the phenomenal becoming of the essence of phenomenality.*

This is a striking formulation. What is "objectified" in the work of objectivation is not any existent, not any thing — it is *nothingness* under the form of a horizon. The horizon of being is the "horizon of nothingness" because it is, as horizon, *nothing* (no determinate content); it is purely the *form* of the place where determinations can appear. The Heideggerian-Sartrian doctrine of the *Nichts* (the nothing as the horizon of being's manifestation) is here precisely articulated in its proper ontological function: nothingness is not a being; nothingness is the structural emptiness of the horizon that makes beings visible. (Compare *Was ist Metaphysik?* — Heidegger's 1929 lecture, where the *Nichts* is identified with the horizon of being's revealing.)

The ambiguity of the stable being that, for example in Fichte, existence posits in face of itself by withdrawing from it, holds therefore to the old confusion of being and the existent. *It is the nothing of being, not the singularity of the existent, that existence posits in face of itself in the movement by which it realizes itself — that is, in the effective becoming of phenomenality.* The being posited in opposition is therefore not the transcendent being in the sense of determination; it is the *pure milieu* where this determination is susceptible of showing itself. *Transcendence does not object the existent to itself; it objects the existent's place.* This pure place is what is instituted in the internal process of the essence insofar as this process accomplishes itself; this pure place is, as such, the effective becoming of the essence of phenomenality.

The Fichtean (and more broadly idealist) doctrine of "stable being" posited by existence as its other is reread: what is posited is not an ontic stable being (a *res*, a *Ding*), but the *place* of stability, the structural form of "being-stably-there." This place is purely ontological (it is "nothing" insofar as it is no particular content), but it is the necessary structural correlate of the work of the essence.

**Paragraph 6\.** With the understanding of the pure ontological structure of the essence, the pretension of defining the existent as a condition of the effective becoming of the essence is set aside. It is because the philosophy of consciousness has not yet raised itself to such an understanding that it falls into equivocation as soon as it is a question of defining the effective conditions of phenomenality. This equivocation becomes visible in the description of the process the philosophy of consciousness conceives as the one in which the phenomenal becoming realizes itself — a process designated under the general title of "*objectivation*" and by which there comes about precisely the "phenomenon," the "object." The fundamental obscurity of this latter concept consists in this: that the partition is not made *in the object* between what is ontic and what is ontological. *The content of the object is the ontic determination, but its condition as object depends on the essence.* What makes the object an *ob-ject* — and as such a phenomenon — is the ontological power of objectivation. *Objectivation creates the objective character of the object*; or, to say it better, objectivation identifies itself with this objective character. The objective character of the object is its phenomenal character. *The effective becoming of phenomenality in the objective being of the object is the doing of the essence and of the essence alone. To this effective becoming the existent is totally foreign: the existent contributes to it no more than the existent results from it.* It is therefore well in the object that the effective becoming of phenomenality realizes itself, although in this becoming the existent takes by itself no part.

The structural point is now made decisively. The "object" is an ambiguous term: it has both an *ontic* aspect (its content, what it is — this stone, this tree, this sound) and an *ontological* aspect (its objective character, its being-an-object, its being-posited-before). The whole work of phenomenality concerns only the *ontological* aspect: what the essence of manifestation does is constitute objectivity-as-such (the form of being-an-object), not produce or modify the ontic content (the determinate stone or tree). So the philosophy of consciousness is right that "consciousness creates the object" — but only in the sense that consciousness creates the *objective character* of the object, not in the sense that consciousness produces the ontic content. The confusion of these two senses is the source of all the equivocations of idealism.

**Paragraph 7\.** As long as the distinction is not made between the existent itself and, on the other hand, the ontological power that confers on the existent the quality of *ob-ject*, the affirmation of the philosophy of consciousness — according to which consciousness creates the object — remains as inevitable as it is paradoxical. For it is true that consciousness creates the object — that is, the being-posited-before as such. More exactly, consciousness is identical in its being with the being-posited-before considered in itself, since — according to the fundamental presuppositions of ontological monism that are those of the philosophy of consciousness — the essence of consciousness resides in objectivity. Because the philosophy of consciousness sees in the object as such the condition of the effective becoming of phenomenality, the condition of the becoming-conscious, it posits this object at the same time as it posits consciousness — and as identical to consciousness. The becoming of the object is the becoming-conscious. *Consciousness is the ob-ject as such.* In positing the object, the philosophy of consciousness adds nothing to the pure essence of consciousness; it posits rather the very condition of consciousness — that is, this pure essence.

*Absolute idealism confuses only the existent with the effective conditions of phenomenality.* Because absolute idealism operates no discrimination between the existent and the object as such, the position of this object — identical with the becoming-conscious — signifies for absolute idealism also the position of the existent. *The act of positing-before — constitutive of the effective becoming of phenomenality — being confused with the position of the existent itself, absolute idealism believes itself able to deduce the existent.* The becoming-other in which the essence opposes itself to itself, so that the pure appearance of ideality may realize itself, takes on the signification of being the becoming of the existent. The action of thought — which exhausts itself in the ontological process of objectivation — paradoxically becomes a modification that affects the existent as such, either by positing the existent or by suppressing it. Finally, because the position of the object — where the becoming-conscious realizes itself — has been confused with the position of the existent itself, thought (which finds only its realization in this becoming, that is, in the object) believes in fact to find its realization in the existent itself. The existent is understood as the *affirmation of ideality*, as an *ideal element*. *"Because thought,"* writes Marx, *"imagines itself to be immediately other than itself, sensible reality, and that its action takes therefore for it the value of a real sensible action — the ideal suppression which leaves its object existing in reality believes to have really vanquished it; and on the other hand, because the object has now become for thought an ideal element, thought equally considers the object in its reality as the affirmation of itself, of self-consciousness, of abstraction."*

This is a remarkable analysis, with the Marxian critique of Hegelian idealism (from the *Paris Manuscripts of 1844* — *Economic-Philosophical Manuscripts*) cited at the climax. Marx had argued that Hegel's deduction of nature from the *Logic* — the move by which the absolute idea "alienates itself" into the natural world — is a confusion: Hegel takes the *ideal* operations of conceptual thought (abstraction, position, suppression) and treats them as if they were *real* operations on real existents. The result is that Hegel treats existents as if they were just the externalizations of thought, and treats thought-operations as if they had genuine external effect. Henry adopts the Marxian critique and folds it into his own diagnosis: the Hegelian "deduction" of the existent is an artifact of the failure to distinguish between (i) the ontological positing of objectivity (which is a real phenomenological event) and (ii) the ontic existence of the existent (which is independent of the ontological positing). This is the source of all idealist over-reaches, from Fichte's deduction of nature to Hegel's *Naturphilosophie*. The structural correction: ontological positing creates only the *form* of objectivity, not the existent.

**Paragraph 8\.** The non-belonging of the existent to the effective becoming of phenomenality — insofar as what is found posited in the process of this becoming is not the existent itself but its *being-object* as such — brings us to repose the problem of finitude in its relation to the essence of phenomenality, that is, to *being as such*. It is precisely in its relation to being as such that finitude must be understood. The idea of finitude presents itself first to the thought that considers the *receptivity* of ontic knowledge. It is to the extent that ontic knowledge is not creative with respect to the existent but only receptive that this knowledge is said to be finite. Finite, knowledge is, because its content does not come from it, because its content is not what knowledge objects to itself. The content of knowledge however presupposes what knowledge objects to itself. It is only as object that the existent is susceptible of forming the content of a knowledge — that is, of being known. The receptivity of finite knowledge with regard to the existent presupposes its receptivity with regard to the *object*. More exactly, the problem of the receptivity of knowledge with regard to the existent is that of its receptivity with regard to the *object*, since it is precisely as object that the existent is received. The finitude of ontic knowledge is identically *something else*. It is the finitude of a knowledge that has *need* of the *object* for the reception of the existent. *It is the finitude of ontological knowledge.*

The argument now extends to finitude. The "finitude of human knowledge" (Kant's celebrated theme) is typically thought as the dependence of human knowledge on what is *given* to it (rather than what it itself produces) — i.e., on sensible existents. But Henry refines: the existent is received by knowledge only *as object*; what is received is not the bare existent but the existent *qua object* (i.e., the existent under the form of the horizon of objectivity). So receptivity to the existent presupposes a more fundamental receptivity, namely, the receptivity to the *form of objectivity itself* (the horizon). And this latter receptivity is the *finitude of ontological knowledge*: the knowledge that *opens* the horizon of being is itself finite, because its very work of opening is dependent on what it opens for (the existent that will appear in the horizon). The finitude is structural, internal to the very work of opening the horizon.

**Paragraph 9\.** What ontic knowledge has need of for the reception of the existent, ontological knowledge creates itself. It is in the proper act of transcendence that arises the transcendental horizon of being. Why is ontological knowledge — creator of its own object — said to be finite? *Because the horizon of transcendence is itself finite.* The finitude of the horizon signifies the finitude of effective phenomenality. It is the place where light arises — it is the place itself as such — that is finite. *The light is this finitude of a place.* Finitude has an ontological signification. It concerns the internal structure of the originary and pure essence of phenomenality, insofar as this essence realizes itself only in the process by which it objectifies itself under the form of a finite horizon. The phenomenality that becomes effective in the objectivation of this horizon is itself a finite phenomenality. *Manifestation is finite insofar as it is produced.* The finitude of manifestation insofar as it is produced signifies the finitude of manifestation as such. *Finitude is an eidetic structure of the essence of phenomenality.*

The paragraph completes the radicalization of finitude. Finitude is not (i) a contingent feature of human cognition (the Cartesian-Kantian view) nor (ii) a feature of the receptive relation to existents (the Heideggerian view as Henry has just analyzed it); finitude is (iii) an *eidetic structure* of the essence of phenomenality itself — a structural feature of *manifestation as such* in the monist conception. The horizon of being is finite because it is a horizon (a delimited place); it is delimited because it must be the place *for* something (the existent that will appear). So the horizon's very being-a-horizon-for is its finitude. Manifestation is finite *because* it is manifestation-of-other (the structure §13 already analyzed): the manifestation that requires an other for its realization is essentially finite.

**Paragraph 10\.** *"What it is fundamentally a question of,"* says Heidegger, *"is to bring into light the essential imbrication of being (not of the existent) as such and of finitude in man."* Finitude must be understood in its relation to being, because what is finite is *being itself*. The link that unites in the origin transcendence and finitude is not the link of being and the existent. It is *not* because being is always and necessarily the being of the existent that being is finite. The finitude of being results so little from the indissoluble link uniting being to the existent that the existent, by itself, is not finite. The thought that seeks the origin and the essence of finitude in the finitude of ontic determination *goes astray*. The determination is finite only insofar as it manifests itself. *It is not the existent, it is the object that is finite.* Considered in itself, the existent is as well the noumenon, the *Enstand* of infinite intuition, as the *Gegenstand* of receptive knowledge. The existent is finite insofar as it is the *Gegenstand* of receptive knowledge — insofar as it is encountered by a being constrained, in order to receive it, to deploy the finite horizon of being. It is inside this horizon — which renders the existent accessible to us by manifesting it (that is, consequently, as object) — that the existent is finite. *The existent is finite on the foundation of the finitude of being in it.* The most essential finitude concerns being itself, insofar as being is the need of being so that, in the finite field of its horizon, the place be opened for something to be.

The Kantian-Heideggerian distinction between *Enstand* (the object as it might be intuited by an infinite intellect — the "noumenon") and *Gegenstand* (the object as it is given to finite human receptivity — the "phenomenon") is from Heidegger's *Kant und das Problem der Metaphysik*. Henry adopts this distinction to make a precise structural point: the existent in itself is *not* finite (it could in principle be intuited by an infinite intellect, in which case it would be a noumenon, an *Enstand*); the existent is finite only insofar as it is given as *Gegenstand* — that is, only insofar as it appears within the finite horizon of receptive ontological knowledge. So finitude is *not* a property of the existent as such; finitude is the structure of the *horizon* (the form of objectivity) that makes the existent appear *as object*. The finitude is fully ontological.

**Paragraph 11\.** The thesis according to which transcendence is finite in itself must therefore be understood. The finitude of transcendence results no doubt from the fact that transcendence is, as such, essentially receptive. As receptive, transcendence finds itself inexorably bound to what it receives. What transcendence receives, however, is nothing other than what transcendence *itself forms*. Freedom, says Heidegger, *"cannot evade what thus takes its birth from it."* What freedom cannot evade is therefore what takes birth in freedom. What takes birth in the ontological freedom of transcendence is the transcendental horizon of being — the world itself in its pure worldhood. *It is therefore to the world as such, not to the existent, that freedom cannot evade itself; it is to the horizon that freedom deploys that transcendence is bound.* Transcendence is bound to the world insofar as transcendence is nothing other than the arising of this world as such. Far from escaping the world by its freedom, it is *as free*, on the contrary, that transcendence is *delivered* to the world. Delivered to the world, transcendence is also, more precisely, delivered to a *finite* world. The limit of transcendence is therefore not the existent. It is *not* the existent that — as "limit," "obstacle," and "stop" — permits freedom to take consciousness of itself by colliding with the existent. For freedom can, strictly speaking, collide with an obstacle only if this obstacle exists. *It is existence itself that is limited*, and that because the transcendence which constitutes its essence bears within itself this limit *as what it produces*.

This paragraph contains a precise polemic against existentialist conceptions of freedom (especially Sartre's, but also Jaspers's). Sartre had argued that freedom takes consciousness of itself only by colliding with the *coefficient of adversity* — the resistance of the world (the in-itself) that limits and shapes the for-itself's projects. Henry's critique: the resistance offered by existents presupposes that those existents *exist* — that is, presupposes the prior accomplishment of the work of phenomenality (which makes the existent be-there in the horizon). So the limit on freedom is not the contingent encounter with this or that existent but the *structural* limit of the horizon itself, which is finite. Freedom is bound to the *horizon*, not to particular existents; the horizon is finite as the very condition of phenomenality. The limit is internal to freedom (the freedom of transcendence), not external to it.

**Paragraph 12\.** That finitude finds its ultimate foundation not in the ontic content of representation but in the very structure of representation, Husserl had already understood. Studying in *Erfahrung und Urteil* the problem of absolute substrates, Husserl shows that the only absolute substrate is *nature*; but nature, he says, is never *"the theme of a simple grasping."* The finitude of knowledge seems here introduced from the consideration of the infinite diversity of the existent — a diversity such that it can never be grasped in its entirety inside a single act of intuition and consequently in an absolute certainty. *It is the finitude of the act of intuition itself, however, that is responsible for the impotence of the spirit to know the existent otherwise than under a fragmentary and successive form.* What prevents us from absolutely grasping something is not finally the fact that this something can present an infinity of always new aspects; *even if these aspects were limited, if the existent bore in itself only a determinate number of properties, the global grasp of these properties would be impossible because such a grasp is finite in itself, insofar as it always produces itself inside a finite horizon.* *"Certainly,"* says Husserl, *"one cannot say a priori that any determinate object can exhibit of itself proper determinations in infinite number… Yet its horizon of indeterminate determinability is always essentially given with it."* The finitude of knowledge does not result from the fact that the existent possesses properties in infinite number; it resides in the *mode of givenness* of the existent — that is, in the existent insofar as it is an *object*. Far from being the principle of the finitude of knowledge, the infinite diversity of the existent is its simple consequence. It is because the existent is grasped inside the finite horizon of being, as object, that the existent is said to be finite. The "finitude" of the existent signifies rather the *infinitude* of the existent, originally, with respect to the finitude of its objective condition. It signifies that — in entering the finite place of its phenomenal existence — the existent eludes also the light of this place, which the existent overflows on every side. *As the horizon is beyond the existent, the existent is beyond the horizon.* The idea of a horizon of co-given and non-given ontic properties can seem to bring thought back to the exclusive consideration of content. But the existent has a horizon of potential or virtual properties only because it is an *object*. *The horizon of ontic determinations finds its foundation in the transcendental horizon of being.*

The Husserlian reference is to *Erfahrung und Urteil* §29 (on absolute substrates) and the chapters on the horizon-structure of perceptual experience (especially §§8, 22). Husserl's analyses of perception had shown that any perceptual object is given through a horizon of co-given determinations (the unseen sides, the implicit properties, etc.) that can never be fully made explicit. The ordinary reading of these analyses takes the inexhaustible horizon as a feature of the object's *infinity* (the object has infinitely many aspects). Henry's reading is structural: the inexhaustibility is not a feature of the object's infinity but of the *finite horizon's structure* — the horizon, as horizon, is necessarily a finite delimitation that always leaves a beyond. So the horizon-structure is the source of finitude, not the object's content. This is the most rigorous form of the analysis: finitude is a structural-ontological feature of the horizon (the form of objectivity), not a contingent feature of either knowledge or its objects.

**Paragraph 13\.** The bringing-into-light of the ontological character of finitude replaces thought before the signification of the problematic that aims at the essence. It repeats the result of the analyses that have shown how the existent is foreign to the work of the essence. *The effective becoming of phenomenality, which is the work of the essence, is accomplished without the mediation of the existent.* That the finitude affecting this becoming as its most proper and most remarkable phenomenological character does not find its principle in the existent either — this confirms the radical independence of this becoming (that is, of the essence in its effective reality) with regard to every ontic determination.

The closing paragraph summarizes the result. The essence of phenomenality (in the monist conception) is fully *ontological* — it does not require the existent for its accomplishment, even though it culminates in making existents appear. Finitude, which has been thought traditionally as a feature of human cognition's dependence on existents, is in fact also fully *ontological* — it is the structural delimitation of the horizon, not the contingent encounter with finite things. So the program of "thinking the essence in its purity" is *vindicated*: the essence is independent of the existent, the essence has its own structure, and the analyses of the essence are not contaminated by ontic considerations. The essence is autonomous.

This conclusion sets the stage for §16, which will formulate the *idea of the formal structure of the autonomy of the essence* — that is, the idea that the essence has its own internal structure, independent of the existent, and that this structure can be the proper theme of philosophical thought. The whole Section I has been the diagnostic of monism; §16 will close Section I by formulating the formal idea of an essence-thinking that is free from the contamination by the ontic — an idea which, as Henry will show in Sections II and following, monism is itself unable to realize, but which provides the formal program for what Henry's own positive phenomenology will accomplish in a non-monist way (immanent self-revelation as the truly autonomous essence).

---

## **§ 16\. The idea of the formal structure of the autonomy of the essence and the task of a repetition of the ontological elucidation of the concept of phenomenon**

**Paragraph 1\.** What is implicated in the radical independence of the effective reality of the essence with regard to ontic determination must now be thought. The essence is the essence of manifestation. The effective becoming of the essence signifies the effective becoming of manifestation; it is *the manifestation that manifests itself*, its reality. That this effective reality cannot find its condition in the existent results from the fact that the existent can manifest manifestation only if the existent itself manifests itself. Whatever the manner in which determination manifests the essence — by dissimulating the essence or by indicating it, in its essential or inessential signification — the determination must first *be there*; for the determination to be, the essence must have accomplished its work in the effective becoming of phenomenality. The effective becoming of phenomenality resides in the opening of the transcendental horizon of being. *If the opening of the transcendental horizon of being realizes the effective becoming of phenomenality, it is because this horizon shows itself.* The horizon of being considered in its purity must be perceptible in and for itself. *Being must be able to show itself.* The independence of the effective reality of the essence with regard to determination results from the fact that the phenomenal becoming realizes itself *in* the essence and *by* it. What realizes itself in the essence and by it is no doubt not the "phenomenon" in the sense of something that manifests itself; it is *pure and yet effective phenomenality*. Effective phenomenality arises in the very bosom of the essence, because the essence objectifies itself under the form of a horizon that *shows itself*. For this reason — because the essence of phenomenality comprehends in itself the phenomenal becoming — *the essence is autonomous*.

The opening paragraph crystallizes the result of §15 and announces the program of §16. The essence of phenomenality has been shown to be independent of the existent. But this independence has a positive content: the phenomenal becoming (the deployment of the horizon) takes place *in* the essence itself, not in any external relation to existents. The essence is therefore *self-realizing*: it accomplishes its own becoming by its own work. This self-realizing character is what Henry calls the *Selbständigkeit* (self-standingness, autonomy) of the essence. The crucial structural condition for this autonomy is that the essence be able *to show itself* — that is, the horizon of being must be itself a phenomenon, must itself be perceptible, otherwise the essence's becoming would not be effective. So the essence's autonomy depends on the *self-manifestation* of the essence — and this is the question that will dominate the remaining sections of the book.

**Paragraph 2\.** The autonomy of the essence signifies the *Selbständigkeit* of ontological knowledge. Ontological knowledge, however, is the condition of possibility of ontic knowledge. *Being is the being of the existent.* That being be always the being of the existent — the *Selbständigkeit* of the essence does not exclude this; at least we cannot say so now. The essence of manifestation that realizes the effective manifestation may well — for reasons unknown to us — only ever realize the effective manifestation of the existent. Inversely, and for reasons here evident, the manifestation of the existent always presupposes — as its condition — the effective becoming of manifestation in the pure work of the essence: the *Selbständigkeit* of the essence. *If the existent can manifest itself on the foundation of the nothing, it is only and first because the nothing manifests itself.* *"Because the nothing is revealed,"* says Heidegger, *"science can make of the existent itself the object of its research."* It is therefore the experience of the nothing that permits us to grasp the existent. In permitting us to grasp the existent, the nothing determines the ontological structure of the existent. But the nothing of being determines the ontological structure of the existent in the act by which the nothing manifests the existent as an object only because the nothing is as such a "phenomenon." *The determination of the existent by being presupposes the manifestation of the determining element itself in its purity.* *"In order that one can understand the essential determination of the existent by being, it will be necessary,"* says Heidegger, *"that the determining element itself show itself with a certain clarity."* The finitude of the existent in its objective condition therefore could not dissimulate the essence. Quite on the contrary: this finitude of the existent presupposes as its condition the effective manifestation of the essence in its purity.

The Heideggerian citations are from *Was ist Metaphysik?* (1929) — Heidegger's lecture on the experience of nothingness as the foundation of the encounter with beings. Heidegger had argued that we encounter beings as beings (rather than just as functional tools or scientific objects) only on the foundation of the experience of *Nichts* (in anxiety, in the sense of "the nothing nothings," *das Nichts nichtet*). The nothing is the disclosure of being as such, against which beings stand out as beings. Henry takes up this Heideggerian doctrine and uses it for his own structural argument: the existent appears against the foundation of the nothing (the horizon of being); the nothing is therefore the *condition* of the existent's appearance; but for the nothing to function as this condition, the nothing must itself be in some sense *manifest* — must show itself, must be a phenomenon. So the structure requires: (i) the essence (= the horizon of being \= the nothing) shows itself; (ii) on the foundation of this self-showing, existents become manifest. The autonomy of the essence consists in this: that the essence's showing is internal to the essence itself, not derivative on the existents whose appearance the essence makes possible.

**Paragraph 3\.** The understanding of ontological knowledge as condition of the possibility of ontic knowledge does not impair the *Selbständigkeit* of the essence, if the manifestation of the existent presupposes that of the horizon in the pure work of the essence. *The manifestation of the horizon in the pure work of the essence signifies the immanence of phenomenal becoming to the essence of phenomenality.* *In this immanence resides the Selbständigkeit of the essence.* The *Selbständigkeit* of the essence grounds the right that we have to call it an essence. But the origin of this right must be drawn into clarity. The autonomy of the essence must be understood in its signification and in its possibility.

The signification of the autonomy of the essence is first to render *more incomprehensible* the designation of the Dasein as an existent. If the Dasein designates the effective reality of manifestation, the belonging of the ontic element to this reality understood in its pure ontological signification has been excluded. *The effective becoming of manifestation is being-there.* To this effective becoming — which is produced without the existent and before it — the existent has no part. The existent is foreign to being-there as such. *The Dasein as such is ontological.*

Henry now returns to the unresolved problem of §13: the ambiguity of the Dasein. §14 had suggested that this ambiguity might find its reason in the structural necessity of the essence-determination link. §15 had then refused this concession by showing that the essence is in fact autonomous from the existent. So the closing of §15 returns the problem in sharper form: if the essence is fully ontological and autonomous from the existent, then the ambiguity of the Dasein (as both existent and non-existent) is *more* incomprehensible, not less. The Heideggerian designation of Dasein as "an existent" is now revealed as a residual contamination of his thought by the ontic — a contamination that the rigorous understanding of the essence's autonomy makes impossible to maintain. *The Dasein as such is ontological*: it is the very work of the essence, the structure of transcendence, not any particular being. The existent has no part in being-there as such.

**Paragraph 4\.** The interdiction to understand the Dasein as an existent is only a *negative* consequence of the autonomy of the essence. The *positive* signification of this autonomy expresses itself in the *impossibility of separating* the essence understood in its purity and, on the other hand, the phenomenal becoming where it realizes itself. Insofar as it constitutes effective phenomenality, the phenomenal becoming is the reality of the essence of phenomenality. Insofar as the phenomenal becoming is included in the essence of phenomenality, the latter finds in itself its reality.

The negative consequence is: Dasein cannot be an existent. The positive consequence is: the essence and the phenomenal becoming are inseparable — not because the essence depends on the existent, but because the phenomenal becoming (the becoming-effective of manifestation) is internal to the essence. The essence is not a static structure that needs to "go out" to become real; the essence is *intrinsically* a becoming-real-in-itself. This is the formal idea of self-grounding self-realizing essence — what the German idealists tried to think under the name of the "absolute" or the "concrete universal," but which Henry will argue they could not really achieve within monism.

**Paragraph 5\.** The positive signification of the *Selbständigkeit* refers to the problem of its possibility. The *Selbständigkeit* signifies that phenomenal becoming is *immanent* to the originary and pure essence of phenomenality. The immanence of phenomenal becoming to the essence of phenomenality understood according to the fundamental ontological presuppositions of monism expresses itself in the affirmation that the horizon opened by this essence manifests itself as such and in its purity. With the manifestation of the horizon, *being shows itself*. The problem is that of the *possibility* of the manifestation of the horizon. This possibility resides in the essence of manifestation. The immanence of phenomenal becoming to the originary and pure essence of phenomenality has a *foundation*. This foundation is the essence itself. *The problem of the phenomenal becoming of the essence of phenomenality is precisely the problem of the internal structure of phenomenality.*

The decisive structural reformulation is now made. The essence of phenomenality is autonomous because the phenomenal becoming is *immanent* in it — that is, the becoming-effective of manifestation takes place within the essence itself, not by some external addition. But this immanence requires that the *foundation* of the immanence be located within the essence — the essence must contain within itself the resources for its own becoming-effective. And this foundation is just the *internal structure* of the essence: the essence has, within itself, the structure that allows it to manifest itself. So the program of phenomenology (Henry's program) becomes: to elucidate the *internal structure* of the essence of phenomenality such that the essence can manifest itself, can be effective, can ground its own becoming. This is the program of the rest of the book — and it will require, Henry will argue, breaking with the monist conception (which makes the essence's self-manifestation impossible, as §14 and §15 have shown) and articulating a different conception in which the essence's self-manifestation is structurally possible.

The essence of phenomenality finds in itself its reality, insofar as it is in itself that phenomenality is produced. Such is the positive signification of the *Selbständigkeit*. That the effective phenomenality be produced in the essence is possible, however, only *by* the essence. The signification of the *Selbständigkeit* finds its possibility in the essence. *It is in this ultimate sense that the essence is autonomous.* The essence of manifestation finds in itself its reality, insofar as the effective reality of manifestation that produces itself in it finds also in it its own foundation.

**Paragraph 6\.** The elucidation of the foundation of the immanence of phenomenal becoming to the essence of phenomenality alone permits us to say whether this becoming totally coincides with the essence that grounds it — whether the originary and pure essence is the truth or whether it is also the non-truth. Once the existent is set aside in its pretension of manifesting or of hiding the essence, it is to the essence that this double possibility must be addressed.

The closing of the central argument now opens the question that will haunt the next sections (and indeed the whole book): is the essence of manifestation, in its self-manifestation, fully transparent to itself (truth) or does it also involve a structural concealment (non-truth)? Section §13 had already raised this question in the form of the Heideggerian *aletheia/lethe* doctrine: in monism, the essence's self-manifestation is necessarily also a self-concealment because the essence can manifest only by becoming-other and this becoming-other is the alienation that conceals the essence. But once the existent is set aside (once it is recognized that the existent contributes nothing to manifestation), the question becomes purely internal to the essence: does the essence contain within itself the structure of self-concealment, or does it contain only the structure of self-revelation?

Henry's eventual answer (in Sections III–IV) will be: monism's essence does necessarily involve self-concealment (because monist manifestation is *manifestation-of-other* — the essence manifests beings, not itself); but there is *another* essence of manifestation (the immanent self-revelation of life) in which manifestation *is* manifestation-of-self, and which therefore does *not* involve self-concealment but is full self-transparency. The "double possibility" Henry leaves open here is the seed of his entire positive doctrine: there are two essences of manifestation, the monist (alienating, manifesting-other, partially self-concealing) and the immanent (non-alienating, manifesting-self, fully self-revealing). The first is the essence that classical philosophy has thought; the second is what Henry will articulate.

**Paragraph 7\.** The task of phenomenology has been defined as the *ontological elucidation of the essence of phenomenon*. It has been shown how this elucidation finds its possibility in the essence itself. What finds its possibility in the essence itself, however, is not only this elucidation — it is *manifestation in general*. The first elucidation of the essence of phenomenon, pursued according to the fundamental ontological presuppositions of monism, has at least shown that — to accomplish its work — the essence of manifestation must be able to *manifest itself*. *"Being must be able to show itself."* The understanding of this possibility demands that the ontological elucidation of the essence of phenomenon be *repeated*. *The task of the repetition of the ontological elucidation of the essence of phenomenon is the bringing-into-light of the possibility of the manifestation of the essence.* The bringing-into-light of the possibility of the manifestation of the essence puts in question the fundamental ontological presuppositions of monism *and introduces us to the originary essence of revelation*.

The closing paragraph of Section I formulates the program of Section II — the program of *repeating* the ontological elucidation of the essence of phenomenon. The result of Section I has been: the essence of manifestation in its monist conception cannot manifest itself (as §14 demonstrated through the analyses of Fichte, Schelling, Hegel — the absolute consciousness is unconscious, the pure essence remains hidden, the essence is veiled by the form). But the essence's accomplishing of its work *requires* that the essence be able to manifest itself (the *Selbständigkeit* requires the self-showing of the horizon). Therefore: monism is incoherent on its own terms. It posits an essence that must be able to manifest itself, while also showing that this essence cannot manifest itself within the monist structure.

The resolution requires *repeating* the elucidation — going through the same analysis again, but this time questioning the monist presuppositions themselves. Section II ("Repetition of the elucidation of the concept of phenomenon") will perform this repetition, working through the same problems but with a different starting-point. The result of the repetition will be the discovery of *the originary essence of revelation* — Henry's name for the non-monist essence of manifestation, the essence that *can* manifest itself because it has the structure of immanent self-affection rather than horizonal-ekstatic transcendence.

The Heideggerian term "*repetition*" (*Wiederholung*) is technical: in *Sein und Zeit* §74, Heidegger defines authentic historicity as the *repetition* of an inherited possibility — not as a mechanical copying but as a creative resumption that rediscovers and transforms the inheritance. Henry adopts the term: the second elucidation will not abandon the results of the first; it will *retrieve* them and rework them at a deeper level, so that what was implicit in the first elucidation becomes explicit in the second, and the limits of the first conception become visible in the second. The repetition is the fundamental philosophical movement that opens the path from the diagnostic of monism (Section I) to the discovery of immanent self-revelation (Sections III–IV) by way of a renewed ontological elucidation (Section II).

The closing sentence — "The bringing-into-light of the possibility of the manifestation of the essence puts in question the fundamental ontological presuppositions of monism and introduces us to the originary essence of revelation" — names the title of Section IV, the architectural climax of the book: the *fundamental ontological interpretation of the essence of revelation*. The whole long path from §8 to §16 has been the diagnostic preparation for this discovery; the path from §17 to the end of the book will be its constructive elaboration. Section I closes by pointing forward to a non-monist phenomenology that will be neither the philosophy of consciousness (Husserl) nor the philosophy of being (Heidegger) but a phenomenology of immanent self-revelation — a phenomenology of *life* in the sense that Henry's mature work will give to that word.

# Section II. Repetition of the elucidation of the concept of phenomenon: transcendence and immanence

## **§ 17\. The originary character of the manifestation of being and the problem of natural consciousness**

**Paragraph 1\.** The affirmation according to which being must be able to show itself is *ambiguous*. The opening sentence of Section II picks up the closing thesis of §16. The whole motive for "repeating" the ontological elucidation of the concept of phenomenon was that, on its own monist terms, the essence of manifestation must be able to manifest itself — but this requirement now turns out to be ambiguous, and this ambiguity is what the repetition will work to resolve. This ambiguity grows to the point of leading the research astray and travestying the signification of the problematic that aims at the essence — when the possibility for being to show itself is put in relation with the methodological work of phenomenology. The methodological work of phenomenology is understood as one of *elucidation*. To elucidate signifies to show, to make arrive into the light what is not primitively in the ray of light. What must be elucidated is what first hides itself. When it is put in relation with the work of elucidation of phenomenology, the possibility for being to show itself appears as a possibility that by itself is not effective — a possibility that finds its realization precisely only in and by phenomenological work. It is only when phenomenology has accomplished its work that the essence it elucidates arrives in the light — that is, that being shows itself.

The ambiguity Henry identifies is decisive.
