There are two senses in which "being must be able to show itself" can be taken: (i) as a *methodological* requirement on phenomenology — phenomenology must be able to bring being into manifestation through its work of elucidation, in which case being's manifestation is the *product* of phenomenology's accomplishment; (ii) as a *structural* fact about being itself — being must be able to manifest itself prior to and independently of any philosophical elucidation, in which case phenomenology presupposes (rather than produces) being's self-manifestation. The whole of Section II will work to show that only (ii) is the correct reading; (i) is the source of all the misunderstandings that have plagued phenomenology from Hegel through Husserl.

The first result of the elucidation of the concept of phenomenon has however been to render evident the necessity of operating a *dissociation* between this work of elucidation that defines the task of phenomenology and, on the other hand, the reality of the concept that forms its object — namely, the arising of the essence in the effectivity of its phenomenal condition. *The manifestation of being, far from being able to be a simple consequence of the methodological work of elucidation of phenomenology, is on the contrary the condition of phenomenology, just as it is the condition of every possible manifestation of any existent in general.* The manifestation of being therefore does not realize itself in the "*at last*" of the accomplished work of phenomenology but in the "*already*" of its primitive condition — which is, as such (as this *already* of the pure effective manifestation that renders possible every comportment and every ulterior procedure), *the absolute*. *Being manifests itself already, anteriorly to every work of elucidation.* Already: not only as presupposition of this work itself, but as an absolutely universal condition of every activity of natural consciousness in general.

The temporal-logical contrast — the *already* (*déjà*) of being's self-manifestation versus the *at last* (*enfin*) of phenomenology's accomplishment — is structural. Phenomenology comes *after*; being's self-manifestation has *always already* taken place. Phenomenology's work of elucidation is possible only because being has already manifested itself; phenomenology does not accomplish or produce being's manifestation but only renders it explicit, brings it into the clarity of the concept. This is the central insight of the section: the originary character of being's manifestation. The essence of manifestation is *originary* — it has always already happened, prior to any reflection, prior to any philosophical work, as the very condition of natural consciousness's existence. Heidegger's vocabulary of the "always already" (*immer schon*) of Dasein's being-in-the-world (*Sein und Zeit* §12 ff.) is here generalized into the structural thesis of the originary character of manifestation.

**Paragraph 2\.** No less ambiguous is the proposition previously cited, according to which "in order that one can understand the essential determination of the existent by being, it will be necessary that the determining element itself show itself with a certain clarity." The cited Heideggerian formulation (from §16, paragraph 2\) is here reread. The manifestation of being — understood as the element determining the existent (insofar as it is constitutive of the latter's ontological structure) — is here interpreted as having to be produced *in the future*: it is referred consequently to a work of elucidation that being's manifestation calls for, and that precisely so that it (being's manifestation) may be produced "with a certain clarity." But the determination of the existent by being realizes itself *anteriorly* to the comprehension of this determination by the philosopher; and this determination, anterior to every philosophical comprehension, presupposes nonetheless the manifestation of being — insofar as this determination is in fact nothing other than this manifestation itself. For it is on the foundation of this manifestation that the existent is what it is. To natural consciousness — which grasps each time the existent with its proper characters — being is *already given*: *the manifestation of being is originary*.

The Heideggerian formulation Henry cited at §16 paragraph 2 — that "in order to understand... it will be necessary that the determining element itself show itself" — has the future-oriented structure of (i) above: it makes being's self-showing depend on philosophical understanding. Henry now critiques even this Heideggerian formulation, showing that it falls into the same ambiguity. The correct reading is the opposite: being's self-showing is the *prior* condition of every philosophical understanding (and indeed of every natural-consciousness understanding); philosophy comes *after* being has shown itself, not before. This rereading sets up Section II's central polemic: even Heidegger's "fundamental ontology" — for all its virtues — has misunderstood the radical priority of being's self-manifestation.

The determination of the existent by being expresses the dependence of what appears with regard to the act of appearing considered in and for itself. In pure appearance the determination finds the origin of its destiny: this destiny which is its own is foreign to it. That its own destiny be foreign to the content of the determination does not signify that it (the destiny) be foreign also to natural consciousness, which lives in the presence of this content. To devote itself to the exclusive consideration of the existent, consciousness must have *access* to being. Being manifests itself to natural consciousness as that which permits natural consciousness to be what it is — namely, a consciousness that aims at the existent. Consciousness therefore lives *in the presence of being*, which is this presence itself. The presence of being in which natural consciousness lives is not a *supposed* presence — a condition disengaged by philosophical reflection and thought by it as the presupposition of every possible relation to the existent. The presence of being which renders this relation possible (that is, consciousness itself) is rather *present in itself*. It is because the relation is present, because being manifests itself, that natural consciousness has effectively a relation with the existent. *The reality of the relation is its manifestation.* The manifestation of the relation is the manifestation of being which is given to natural consciousness as soon as natural consciousness relates itself to the existent. *The manifestation of being is the manifestation of the absolute. The manifestation of the absolute is its absoluity.* The absoluity of the absolute is the *Parousia*. As soon as it relates itself to the existent, natural consciousness must hold itself in the *Parousia*; it is already *absolute knowledge*, the science that *"at its first step arrives in the Parousia of the absolute, that is, is near its absoluity."*

The Hegelian citation is from the introduction to the *Phenomenology of Spirit* and from related early texts. Henry cites here Hegel's celebrated formulation that science (philosophical knowledge) does not need to be "introduced" to the absolute because it is already in the absolute from the start — its first step is already a step in the *Parousia* (presence) of the absolute. The vocabulary of *Parousia* — already mobilized in §8 to designate the absolute as the very event of presencing — is here applied directly to natural consciousness: even natural consciousness, in its everyday relation to existents, *is* in the *Parousia* of the absolute, because its very capacity to relate to existents presupposes the prior manifestation of being.

**Paragraph 3\.** That, to be able to relate itself to the existent, natural consciousness lives in the *Parousia* of the absolute — this signifies that *being manifests itself to natural consciousness*. Being does not manifest itself to consciousness from time to time, in virtue of a will that would be its own and (as such) separated from the essence of consciousness. *From its first step* — in reality, as soon as it exists, and that as natural consciousness which is concerned only with the existent — consciousness lives in the presence of being which manifests itself to it, in the *Parousia* of the absolute. *Consciousness is itself as such the manifestation of being.* For this reason consciousness has not to be brought from elsewhere into the place where this manifestation is produced. In relating itself to the existent, natural consciousness already holds itself in the place where the manifestation of being is produced; consciousness is itself this place. *"Natural consciousness cannot be introduced into where it already is."* This is why there is no *introduction* to phenomenology. Phenomenology is the phenomenology of spirit. The phenomenology of spirit is consciousness itself. Consciousness is in itself — and consequently also as natural consciousness — the phenomenology of spirit, because it is the manifestation of being, the *Parousia* of the absolute. *"How are we in the Parousia of the absolute? We are in it according to the habit of natural consciousness."*

The Hegelian readings are dense and culminate in a startling identification: *consciousness itself is the manifestation of being*. Not "consciousness has access to the manifestation of being," not "consciousness is the place where being manifests itself" — but *consciousness is the manifestation of being*. Consciousness *is* itself, in its very being, the act of being's self-manifestation. This is a strong reading of Hegel: the *Phenomenology of Spirit* is not a propaedeutic that leads consciousness to the absolute (the prevailing reading); rather, the *Phenomenology of Spirit* exhibits how consciousness *already is* the absolute's self-manifestation, even at the level of natural (sense-certainty) consciousness. The famous Hegelian thesis that there can be no "introduction" to absolute knowledge (because absolute knowledge is already operative even in the most naïve consciousness) is read by Henry as the structural recognition that being's manifestation is *originary* — coextensive with the very being of consciousness, not a result added to it from outside.

**Paragraph 4\.** That natural consciousness always and already holds itself in the *Parousia* of the absolute signifies that the manifestation of being — which is this *Parousia* — is *originary*. The *habit* in virtue of which natural consciousness holds itself in the *Parousia* is not an *acquired* habit; it designates on the contrary the *immediate condition* of consciousness. The condition in virtue of which consciousness holds itself in the *Parousia* is immediate because it constitutes the very essence of this consciousness. *The essence of consciousness is the Parousia* — that is, the presence in its presence, the being-present as such insofar as it is itself present. The immediate manifestation of the existent presupposes this immediate presence of presence — the presence of being-present itself and as such. It presupposes this immediate presence because the immediate manifestation of the existent is itself, as manifestation, this *Parousia*. For this reason one can only call into question the affirmation of Hegel according to which "the immediate manifestation of truth is the abstraction of its being-present." By "immediate manifestation of truth" Hegel means the manifestation of the existent. This manifestation is said to be immediate because in it consciousness directs itself immediately upon its object, namely, the existent. This immediate manifestation of truth — that is, the manifestation of the existent — is so little the abstraction of its being-present that being-present (namely, the absolute concept) constitutes rather the essence of this manifestation as such. In the manifestation of the existent the concept is present, and that in an absolute sense. The presence of the concept in the manifestation of the existent signifies that being-present itself and as such is present in this manifestation, signifies the immediate presence of presence in the immediate manifestation of the existent. Because being-present constitutes the essence of the immediate manifestation of truth, it (being-present) cannot be abstracted from this manifestation. *The immediate manifestation of truth is identically its being-present, is the absolute concept.*

This is a precise local critique of Hegel that is also a structural advance. Hegel had spoken of the "abstraction" of immediate manifestation from being-present (the concept), as if the concept were something *added* to natural consciousness by philosophical work. Henry corrects: the concept is not added to natural consciousness by philosophy; the concept *is* the very essence of natural consciousness's manifestation of the existent. The "absolute concept" (*absoluter Begriff*) — which Hegel saved for the culmination of speculative philosophy — is, on Henry's reading, already operative in the most ordinary perception of the most ordinary thing. There is no possibility of "abstracting" presence from manifestation; presence is the very work of manifestation, present in every act of consciousness's relation to existents.

**Paragraph 5\.** That being must be able to show itself signifies therefore finally that *it shows itself*, and that not at the term of a process or of a history, but *originarily*. The originary manifestation of being alone renders possible the manifestation of the existent, and that because it constitutes the very essence of the latter. The originary character of the manifestation of being signifies that what is first present is *not the existent*, but *being-present itself and as such*. That being-present itself and as such be what is first present — this attests the *ontological character* of the origin. That being-present which constitutes the origin be precisely present, that is, manifest itself — this attests the *phenomenological character* of the origin. The understanding of the ontological and phenomenological character of the origin permits us to grasp the signification of the proposition according to which the manifestation of being is originary. It shows us what sense it is fitting to give to the affirmation according to which "being must be able to show itself."

The "origin" (*l'origine*) here named has a twofold character: (i) ontological — what is first is being itself, not any existent; (ii) phenomenological — being is, in being first, *manifest*, not hidden. The combination is striking: the origin is at once ontological and manifest. This is precisely the opposite of the pre-Socratic Greek conception that Heidegger had highlighted (in *Holzwege*, in *Vorträge und Aufsätze*) — namely, the conception that the origin (*physis*, *aletheia*) is the *concealing* power that lets beings emerge while withdrawing itself. For Henry, the origin is rather the *manifesting* — the very event of presencing that is itself present in its presencing. This is the structural pivot of Section II: against the late-Heideggerian ontology of withdrawal-in-disclosure, Henry will articulate an ontology of immanent self-manifestation in which the origin is itself fully manifest.

Speaking of the primitive religious community and its desire turned toward the past, Hegel says that "*at the foundation of this turning-back is certainly the instinct to go up to the concept; but it confuses the origin — as the immediate being-there of the first manifestation — with the simplicity of the concept.*" The origin is certainly *not* the existent that manifested itself in the past. To the first manifestation of this existent — to its immediate being-there — the concept is however immanent as that which constitutes this manifestation itself, this being-there as such. From this immediate being-there the concept therefore could not be abstracted. It is the concept that is the immediate; it is the concept that is the origin; it shows itself in the origin as this *first act of showing* that constitutes the very essence of every origin as such.

The Hegelian critique of religious nostalgia (the desire for the lost original event) is repurposed: the "origin" is not a past historical event but the *ontological* origin — the very act of being-present that is operative in every act of manifestation. The primitive religious community's confusion is to look for the origin behind in time, in the historical past, when the origin is in fact in front of and within every present manifestation as its essential condition. Henry generalizes: every search for the origin in some prior historical or logical moment is the same confusion. The origin is the *concept itself* — the ontological structure of being-present that is always already operative.

**Paragraph 6\.** Because the manifestation of being is originary, because natural consciousness holds itself (in conformity with its essence) in the truth, natural consciousness could not be said to *turn away* from the truth. *Consciousness cannot forget the being which constitutes its very essence.* When one affirms however that this consciousness lives, as natural consciousness, in the *forgetting* of being, one wants to say that consciousness holds itself with the existent and, in doing so, holds for nothing what is not of this nature — that is, being, the appearing of the appearing. Natural consciousness, indeed, directs itself toward the existent; and in its exclusive preoccupation with the existent, it does not concern itself with being. Natural consciousness can however preoccupy itself with the existent only if the existent shows itself to it. But the manifestation of the existent is, as such, the manifestation of being. *Not for an instant has being ceased to show itself to natural consciousness*, in the very moment when natural consciousness is said to "forget" being.

This is one of the most consequential paragraphs of the section. Henry critiques the entire Heideggerian doctrine of the "forgetting of being" (*Seinsvergessenheit*) — the doctrine that the West has forgotten being, that natural consciousness lives in the forgetting of being, that the philosophical task is to retrieve being from forgetting. Henry's critique: the forgetting of being is impossible at the level of consciousness's essence. Consciousness *just is* the manifestation of being; consciousness cannot forget being any more than vision can forget light. What Heidegger calls the "forgetting of being" is only the *thematic* non-attention of natural consciousness to the structure that is operative in it. But this non-attention is not a forgetting in the strong sense; being continues to manifest itself even (and necessarily) in the moment when natural consciousness is "forgetting" it. There is no recovery to be made; there is only a thematization. The Heideggerian project of the *retrieval* of being from forgetting is, on this reading, structurally misconceived: there is nothing to retrieve, because being has never withdrawn.

This is also a precise philosophical liberation. The melancholy that pervades late Heidegger — the sense of a great forgetting, a primordial loss, a withdrawal to be mourned and perhaps recovered through patient meditation — is, on Henry's diagnosis, a confusion. Being has not withdrawn, has not forgotten, has not abandoned us; being has always already manifested itself, is manifesting itself now, and will continue to manifest itself, as the very condition of every act of consciousness. The recognition is properly *liberating*: phenomenology is not a desperate quest for what is lost but the patient explication of what is always already given.

**Paragraph 7\.** Because natural consciousness — in conformity with the essence of consciousness in it — lives in the presence of being which manifests itself to it, the manifestation of being to consciousness requires *no radical modification* in the life of this consciousness. The manifestation of being is produced constantly, habitually, in the life of natural consciousness, insofar as it is identical with the essence of this life. The life of consciousness is certainly not monotonous; it is susceptible of modification. A radical modification intervenes in its life when, ceasing to direct itself toward the existent that until then constituted the object of its exclusive preoccupation, consciousness takes into consideration not this existent itself but the *act of appearing* in virtue of which the existent appears. Such a modification is the *reversal* (*Umkehrung*) of consciousness. In such a reversal consciousness directs itself toward the appearing of the appearing; it represents to itself "the appearing as appearing." Directing itself upon the appearing as such, consciousness grasps what reigns in the appearing — that is, its appearing. *The reversal is the act by which consciousness represents to itself the act of appearing itself*, the pure manifestation as such. In the reversal the appearing of the appearing arrives at *representation*. Arriving at representation, the act of appearing *appears*. The representation of manifestation in the reversal of consciousness is the manifestation of pure manifestation as such.

The Hegelian *Umkehrung* (reversal, conversion) is the technical term, from the introduction to the *Phenomenology of Spirit*: the philosophical movement is not a transition to a different content but a *reversal* of consciousness's gaze — from looking at objects to looking at the act of looking. This is what Husserl will later call the *phenomenological reduction* (the bracketing of the natural attitude). Henry adopts the Hegelian-Husserlian gesture but interprets it carefully: the reversal does *not* produce being's manifestation (which is always already given); the reversal *brings into representation* the manifestation that was already operative non-thematically. The reversal is a *thematization*, not a creation. What it brings into representation is the *act of appearing* itself.

**Paragraph 8\.** In representing the manifestation, the reversal realizes the *appearing of the appearing*. The appearing is the essence of consciousness. The reversal is the doing of consciousness. The appearing of the appearing in the reversal of consciousness is the act by which consciousness represents itself in its essence — *"by which consciousness represents itself in its appearing."* The reversal of consciousness is the *self-appearing* (*s'apparaître*) of the appearing. *The self-appearing of the appearing is the presence-to-itself of the absolute, the Parousia.* The manifestation of the absolute to itself in the *Parousia* demands the reversal.

The structure articulated here is precise and crucial. (i) The appearing (the act of manifestation) is the essence of consciousness — always operative, always already there. (ii) The reversal is what brings the appearing into representation — what makes the appearing itself appear. (iii) When the appearing thus appears (in the reversal), what we have is the *self-appearing of the appearing*, which Henry identifies with the absolute's *Parousia*. So the absolute is not behind or above natural consciousness; the absolute is what natural consciousness *is* in its essence (the appearing); and the absolute's *Parousia* (its presence-to-itself) is what the reversal makes manifest. The *Parousia* is the appearing-of-the-appearing-to-itself.

The representation of the act of appearing in the reversal introduces consciousness into *philosophical knowledge*, into *true knowledge*. Philosophical knowledge is true knowledge because — in representing to itself the appearing and no longer the appearing-thing — it is the knowledge of *truth*, not of the existent. The knowledge of truth is the presence of the absolute to itself, its *Parousia*. The *Parousia* of the absolute is the *doing of true knowledge*.

In representing to itself the appearing of the appearing, true knowledge represents to itself the condition of the knowledge of the existent — or rather, it represents this knowledge of the existent itself. The representation of manifestation in the reversal by which consciousness arrives at true knowledge is the *self-knowledge of the knowledge of the existent*. The self-knowledge of the knowledge of the existent is — as Fichte and Schelling already understood — *transcendental knowledge*. *Transcendental knowledge is true knowledge.*

The structural-historical claim is bold. The whole modern tradition of "transcendental knowledge" (from Kant through Fichte and Schelling) is, on Henry's reading, the same project: to bring the act of knowing into representation, to make consciousness's structure thematic to itself. This project is "true knowledge" because it makes the appearing itself appear. But — and here is the crucial point — this true knowledge does *not* produce the appearing of the appearing; it only thematizes what is always already operative. The transcendental subject (Kant), the *Wissenschaftslehre* (Fichte), the system of transcendental idealism (Schelling), and the phenomenology of spirit (Hegel) all attempt the same thematization. They all succeed at the level of representation. But they all share a common limitation, which Henry will analyze in §18: they all conceive the appearing of the appearing on the model of *representation*, and representation is the structure of horizonal-monist phenomenality, which (as Section I has shown) cannot account for the self-manifestation of the essence.

**Paragraph 9\.** That transcendental knowledge *not be* true knowledge — this results from the fact that transcendental knowledge is the knowledge of natural consciousness which has not yet arrived at true knowledge in the reversal. This results from the fact that *the manifestation of being is originary*. Being, as has been sufficiently shown, manifests itself already to natural consciousness which relates itself to the existent — insofar as the manifestation of the existent is, as such, the manifestation of being. But transcendental knowledge is nothing other than the manifestation of being. *Natural consciousness is transcendental consciousness.*

The thesis is striking. There are two ways of taking "transcendental knowledge": (i) as the philosophical-thematic knowledge that makes the appearing appear (the reversal); (ii) as the *originary* manifestation of being that is already operative in natural consciousness, prior to any reversal. The second is the *truer* sense, because it is the more originary. So transcendental knowledge in the philosophical sense (Kant, Fichte, Schelling, Hegel, Husserl) is just the *thematization* of what natural consciousness already accomplishes non-thematically. Transcendental philosophy adds nothing essential to natural consciousness; it only represents what natural consciousness already is. Hence the paradoxical-sounding identification: "natural consciousness is transcendental consciousness." Both are the manifestation of being; the first does it pre-thematically, the second thematically.

This identification has powerful consequences. Transcendental philosophy is not, as Kant and Husserl thought, a *higher* form of knowledge that is normative for natural consciousness; it is only the thematic explication of what natural consciousness always already is. The "two attitudes" — natural and phenomenological — are not two regions of consciousness; they are two *modes* of one and the same essence (the manifestation of being). Phenomenology does not transcend or replace natural consciousness; it only thematizes it.

**Paragraph 10\.** Being is the pure manifestation. The manifestation of being is the *manifestation-of-self of pure manifestation*. The manifestation-of-self of the pure essence of manifestation is so little the doing of the reversal that it belongs on the contrary to the pure essence of manifestation itself. That being must be able to manifest itself does not signify that the manifestation-of-self of being can or must add itself to the essence of being in the course or at the term of a process that would permit this essence to realize itself; it signifies that *the essence of being is the manifestation-of-self*. *The manifestation-of-self is the essence of manifestation.* It is still fitting to understand how this manifestation-of-self of manifestation is produced: *it is originary*. Originary means: it is not the doing of philosophical knowledge but of the essence itself. The manifestation-of-self of the essence is so little the doing of philosophical knowledge that the latter (philosophical knowledge) presupposes it constantly as the very condition of its accomplishment.

The closing paragraph crystallizes the central thesis of the section, which is also the central thesis of the entire book in its constructive aspect: *the manifestation-of-self is the essence of manifestation*. This is not a tautology. It says: what makes manifestation be what it is (its essence) is precisely the *self-manifestation* — manifestation's relation to itself, its showing itself to itself. So manifestation is essentially *reflexive*: not in the sense of a logical or methodological reflection performed by some reflecting subject, but in the sense of an ontological self-relation internal to manifestation itself. Manifestation manifests itself; that is what makes it manifestation.

This formal thesis is fully developed only in Sections III–IV, where Henry articulates the structure of *immanent self-revelation* that satisfies the formal requirement here stated. But the thesis is already announced here, at the threshold of Section II, as the proper goal of the *repetition* announced at the close of §16. Section I had shown that monism cannot account for the manifestation-of-self of the essence (because monist manifestation is essentially manifestation-of-other, requiring distance, doubling, alienation); Section II repeats the elucidation by showing that what monism cannot account for is in fact the *originary* phenomenon — the very condition of every philosophical and natural-conscious act. The originary character of being's self-manifestation is the structural fact that monism has missed, and that the repetition will progressively bring into clarity.

The structural pivot is that the manifestation-of-self does *not* require the reversal, *not* require philosophical work, *not* require any distancing or doubling — it is just the *essence* of manifestation itself, operative as soon as anything appears. This breaks decisively with the monist tradition (for which manifestation requires self-alienation, doubling, distancing) and prepares the ground for the immanent phenomenology that Sections III–IV will articulate: a phenomenology in which manifestation is *immediate* self-presence, without distance, without alienation, without the structure of horizonal opening.

---

## **§ 18\. The concept of representation: ontological structure and existential understanding**

**Paragraph 1\.** The manifestation of being belongs to the essence of consciousness as constituting this very essence — and consequently to natural consciousness. That the manifestation of being belongs to natural consciousness assuredly does not signify that natural consciousness *represents* it to itself. Or rather: it is the *ambiguity of the very concept of representation* that it is fitting finally to denounce. When one declares that natural consciousness does not represent being to itself but only the existent, this signifies that, in its exclusive concern with the existent, natural consciousness does not preoccupy itself with being itself and "holds being for nothing." That natural consciousness does not represent being to itself thus means that being is not the object of its aim — the theme of its thought. "Representation" here designates the thematic object that consciousness aims at, as well as this aim itself in its particularity. Representation so understood is a *determinate mode of the life of consciousness*; and it includes within itself, as irreal noematic correlate, the "object" in the presence of which this life holds itself in this determinate mode of existence which is then its own. In the case of natural consciousness, this correlate is the existent. Natural consciousness itself is this determinate mode of the life of consciousness in which this consciousness aims precisely at the existent, holding for nothing all that is not it.

The opening paragraph identifies the central ambiguity that has to be resolved in §18: the word "representation" has two structurally different senses. Sense (i) — the *narrow*, Husserlian sense: representation is a particular noetic act in which consciousness thematically intends an object; the object is given as a noematic correlate of the noetic aim. This is the sense Husserl analyzes throughout the *Logical Investigations* and *Ideen I*. Sense (ii) — the *broad*, ontological sense: representation is the very structure of consciousness as such, the essence of manifestation in the monist conception. This is the sense in which Heidegger uses "*Vor-stellen*" (in the late texts on the modern conception of being). Henry's task: to show that these two senses must be carefully distinguished, and that the failure to distinguish them has produced systematic confusions in the phenomenological tradition.

Philosophical knowledge or true knowledge is also a determinate mode of the life of consciousness, a particular determination of its existence. In the philosophical or true knowledge to which it arrives in the reversal, consciousness "represents" being itself to itself; it makes being the theme of its thought, the "object" with which it concerns itself. *Because true knowledge is a determinate mode of the life of consciousness, it has nothing to do with absolute knowledge.* Absolute knowledge designates the existence of consciousness in its universal essence — not a determination of this existence, a particular mode of its life. The existence of consciousness in its universal essence is absolute knowledge because the essence of consciousness is existence — the manifestation-of-self of being, the *Parousia*. Far from arising only in a determinate mode of the life of consciousness, the *Parousia* constitutes the very essence of this life and, as such, the condition of all the determinations this life is susceptible of giving itself. *The Parousia is not the doing of true knowledge; it is its presupposition, just as it is the presupposition of the non-true knowledge of natural consciousness which holds itself with the existent.*

The argument carefully distinguishes three levels: (i) natural consciousness — a determinate mode in which consciousness aims at existents; (ii) philosophical (true) knowledge — a determinate mode in which consciousness aims at being thematically; (iii) absolute knowledge — the universal essence of consciousness as such, which is *not* a determinate mode but the very *Parousia* (manifestation-of-self of being) that constitutes the essence of every mode. The crucial structural point: levels (i) and (ii) are equally on the side of "determinate modes" — neither is closer to absolute knowledge than the other. Both presuppose the same universal essence (the *Parousia*); both differ from each other only in their thematic focus (existent vs. being). Absolute knowledge is *not* the philosopher's privileged possession; it is the universal essence operative equally in natural and in philosophical consciousness.

Because the presupposition of the true knowledge of philosophical consciousness and of the non-true knowledge of natural consciousness is the *Parousia*, this presupposition is not a foundation hidden behind the life of consciousness; it is the conscious life itself as such — the life of philosophical consciousness as well as that of natural consciousness. Because the life of consciousness in general is the *Parousia*, *the Parousia does not demand the reversal*. The self-appearing of the appearing, the manifestation-of-self of pure manifestation, are not produced in "representation."

This is the decisive point. Henry now corrects the apparent suggestion at the end of §17 that the *Parousia* requires the reversal. Strictly speaking, the reversal is only the *thematization* (in philosophical consciousness) of what is already operative non-thematically in natural consciousness. The *Parousia* itself does not depend on the reversal — it is operative *whether or not* the reversal has occurred. So the "manifestation-of-self" of manifestation is *not* produced in the act of representation (in either sense): it is the very essence of consciousness, prior to and presupposed by every representational act.

**Paragraph 2\.** It is true that by "representation" one can also understand — in conformity with the fundamental presuppositions of ontological monism — the essence of manifestation itself, the manifestation-of-self of being. Representation now designates the essence of consciousness. The object of representation so understood is being itself. The representation of being is the manifestation-of-self of being, the manifestation of pure manifestation, the *Parousia*. The representation of being is consciousness itself in its universal essence. The object that consciousness represents to itself as such, in its universal essence, is *neither* the object that natural consciousness represents to itself, *nor* the one that philosophical consciousness represents to itself. The object of natural consciousness is the existent. But, while natural consciousness represents the existent to itself, it also represents the *being* of the existent. Only it does not represent being and the existent to itself in the same manner; the object that it attains each time in its representation has only the name in common.

The double sense of representation now extends to a double sense of "object." There is the *thematic object* (the existent for natural consciousness, being for philosophical consciousness) — the object given to a particular noetic act. And there is the *non-thematic object* of the universal essence of consciousness — being itself as the horizon, the field, the very condition of every thematic act. The "object" of consciousness in its universal essence is *not* an object in the thematic sense; it is the *form of objectivity itself*, the horizon within which thematic objects can appear.

That natural consciousness represents the existent to itself signifies that its gaze directs itself upon the existent — that it aims at the existent, that the existent is the theme of its thought. More exactly, consciousness represents the existent to itself in the sense that the existent is accessible to it inside the aim that it directs upon the existent. A particular modification of the life of consciousness is here necessary so that consciousness can attain what does not give itself to it except inside this modification which is then its own. This modification is the representation. The representation of consciousness is here heard in the *first sense* of the word representation, in conformity with which "representation" designates the aim of consciousness and refers thus to a *particular mode of its life*.

That natural consciousness, *now*, represents being to itself — this means that being manifests itself to it and is accessible to it *outside* of every modification of its life that would have being for theme, *outside* of every position-taking and every particular aim. *Natural consciousness represents being to itself without making being the theme of its aim, because the representation of being is the essence of consciousness in general.* Representation now designates the essence of consciousness, the manifestation-of-self of being, the *Parousia*. It is in a *radically different* sense that philosophical consciousness represents being to itself in true knowledge. Philosophical consciousness represents being to itself *as natural consciousness represents the existent to itself* — by making being the theme of its aim, inside a determinate modification of the life of consciousness in general. Although it is being and no longer the existent, *the object of philosophical consciousness is an object in the same sense as the object of natural consciousness*: it is something that gives itself to consciousness through the mediation of a determinate act of consciousness, inside a specific aim and as its strict and itself-determinate correlate.

The structural diagnosis is precise. Philosophical consciousness, when it makes being its theme, treats being *in the same way* that natural consciousness treats existents — that is, as a *thematic object*. So even philosophical consciousness "objectifies" being, makes being into a Gegenstand, treats being as something *given to* a thematic act. But this is precisely what being is *not*, in its originary structure: being is not a thematic object given to an act; being is the universal essence of consciousness, the *non-thematic* form of objectivity that makes thematic objects possible. So even philosophical consciousness, in its very attempt to think being, distorts being by treating it as just another object. This is the structural failure of all representational philosophies of being — including, Henry will argue, Husserl's transcendental phenomenology and Heidegger's fundamental ontology insofar as they remain within the structure of representational thinking.

**Paragraph 3\.** To the radical division of the concept of representation corresponds a radical division of the concept of *object*. The object toward which consciousness turns to "represent" it to itself is a *determinate object*. Determinate, this object is by the act that directs itself upon it — and as that which gives itself to this act. The object of philosophical consciousness is an object in the ordinary sense of the word. But the object of consciousness in its universal essence is determined by no act of consciousness; it is solidary with no particular determination of its life. Insofar as the object of consciousness in its universal essence gives itself to consciousness in the absence of every particular aim directing itself upon it, it is not "something" that consciousness can attain in an act; it is not an "object" in the ordinary sense of the word. *The object of universal consciousness is rather the condition of possibility of every "object,"* as the representation of universal consciousness is the condition of every particular "representation," of every specific act each time aiming at an "object." *The object of consciousness in its universal essence is objectivity, being itself under the form of a horizon. The representation of consciousness in its universal essence is the representation of the horizon.* The representation of the horizon is the manifestation-of-self of this horizon in the absence of every singular act of grasping directing itself upon it. *To the essence of the horizon it belongs not to let itself be thematized.* The object of the representation of universal consciousness is independent of every particular "representation" and, as such, it is never the "object" of the latter.

The structural distinction is now made fully precise. The "object" in the universal sense is *the horizon itself* — being as the form of objectivity, the field of givenness, the structural place in which determinate objects can appear. This horizon is *not* a determinate object; it cannot be thematized; it does not give itself to a particular noetic act. Its mode of givenness is precisely that of a non-thematic background, a horizon-of-givenness, an originary openness. The "representation" in the universal sense is the manifestation-of-self of this horizon — the originary self-disclosure of being-as-horizon, which is operative whether or not any particular thematic act takes place.

This is a precise reading of the Husserlian doctrine of horizon (from *Cartesian Meditations* §19, *Erfahrung und Urteil* §8, etc.), reinterpreted in Heideggerian terms. The horizon is structurally what "cannot be thematized" — every attempt to thematize the horizon converts it into a thematized object and thereby destroys its character as horizon. The only proper "knowledge" of the horizon is the non-thematic knowledge that is operative in every consciousness — what Heidegger calls *vorontologisches Seinsverständnis* (pre-ontological understanding of being) in *Sein und Zeit* §4. Henry endorses this Heideggerian doctrine but radicalizes it: even philosophical thematization of being misses being-as-horizon; the only proper "representation" of the horizon is its own self-manifestation, which is operative independently of any philosophical act.

**Paragraph 4\.** The bringing-into-light of the ambiguity of the concepts of "representation" and of "object" permits one to lift the equivocation that weighs on the formulas by which one tries to define the knowledge of natural consciousness. What characterizes such knowledge, says Heidegger, is the contradiction it bears within itself. This contradiction of natural knowledge holds to the fact that *"in its representation of the existent it does not take care of being and yet must take care of being."* It is because natural knowledge does not take care of being that natural knowledge is only — according to Hegel's word — *"the concept of knowledge"*: a concept here designating the simple "representation of something in general," by opposition to the *absolute concept* in which knowledge grasps itself in its own essence — in which the absolute is present to itself in its absoluity. It is not in the same way, in truth, that natural knowledge "takes care" of being and "does not take care" of being. *To take care does not signify the same thing in the two cases.* Used affirmatively, to take care designates the *representation that constitutes the essence of consciousness in general*. The being to which this consciousness takes care is the *transcendental horizon*, whose originary manifestation belongs to the very essence of being and is, as such, radically independent of every grasping in an act of consciousness directing itself upon it. It is this grasping in an act of consciousness that is in question, on the contrary, when one says that natural knowledge "does not take care of being": one observes that such a grasping having being for object is not included in natural knowledge, insofar as what natural knowledge aims at is precisely not being but only the existent. The object of which natural knowledge does not take care could not be being itself in its originary nature — insofar as being manifests itself to consciousness in conformity with its own essence, in conformity with the essence of this consciousness, whether this consciousness be natural or philosophical, whether it "takes care of being" or "does not take care of being." But the originary manifestation of being in consciousness is *the absolute concept*. *It is therefore false to say that natural knowledge is only the "concept of knowledge"; it is knowledge itself in an absolute sense*, the presence of the absolute to itself in its absoluity, and as such, the *Parousia*.

Henry now applies the disambiguation to clear up what he diagnoses as a confusion in the Hegelian-Heideggerian characterization of natural knowledge. Heidegger (and behind him Hegel) had said that natural consciousness "doesn't take care of being but must take care of being" — making natural consciousness essentially contradictory and inadequate. But the apparent contradiction dissolves once the two senses of "take care of being" are distinguished. (i) *Thematic* taking-care: natural consciousness does *not* thematically take care of being (it aims at existents, not at being). (ii) *Ontological* taking-care: natural consciousness *does* "take care of being" in the structural sense — being manifests itself to natural consciousness as the condition of its very being-a-consciousness-of-existents. So there is no contradiction; there are only two different senses of "taking care," each of which has its own truth. Natural consciousness is thematically existent-directed but ontologically being-disclosing.

The consequence is that natural knowledge is not, *pace* Hegel, merely "the concept of knowledge" (the abstract structural form of knowledge that lacks its content). Natural knowledge is *itself absolute knowledge*, in the structural-ontological sense — because natural consciousness *is* the manifestation of being, the *Parousia* of the absolute. The Hegelian denigration of natural consciousness as merely abstract is misplaced: natural consciousness is fully concrete *qua* manifestation, even if it is not thematically reflective.

That natural knowledge does not take care of being signifies therefore not that being does not manifest itself to natural consciousness in this originary manifestation-of-self that is the *Parousia* itself, but simply that being does not manifest itself to this consciousness *under the form of an object given in an act of grasping*. It is only of such an act of grasping, in reality — that is, of a determinate mode of the life of consciousness — that one can say that it is only the "concept of knowledge," insofar precisely as "it does not take care of being." True knowledge, on the contrary, will take care of being by grasping it. The taking-care of true knowledge is precisely the one that is not the doing of natural consciousness. But natural consciousness has *already* taken care of being — in a quite different sense, it is true — insofar as it is a consciousness and the representation of being belongs to it as the originary manifestation-of-self of being, as the *Parousia*. Taking care of being or not taking care of being in an act of grasping has *no relation* with the taking-care of being inherent in the essence of consciousness — that is, with being itself. *The opposition of natural consciousness and true knowledge is inessential.*

This is a consequential thesis. The opposition philosophy/natural-consciousness — which has been the very motor of the philosophical tradition from Socrates onward (philosophy as that which *transcends* common opinion, the natural attitude, the cave) — is, on Henry's reading, *inessential*. Both modes have the same essential structure (the manifestation-of-self of being); they differ only in the thematic focus of their respective acts. The privilege of philosophy is greatly diminished: philosophy adds nothing essential to natural consciousness; it only thematizes what is already there. The proper task of phenomenology is therefore *not* to overcome natural consciousness but to render explicit what natural consciousness already accomplishes.

**Paragraph 5\.** Let us make here an important distinction for the rest of our researches: a distinction between what is *ontological* and what is *existential*. The "taking care of being" of true knowledge and the "not taking care of being" of natural consciousness are *modes of the life of consciousness*, *determinations of its existence*. We will call these determinations *existential determinations*. The "taking care of being" inherent in the essence of consciousness — and as such indifferent to the "taking care of being" of true knowledge as well as to the "not taking care of being" of natural consciousness — is on the contrary, as this originary manifestation-of-self of being which constitutes consciousness itself in its universal essence, *an ontological structure*. The relation between the ontological structure of consciousness and the existential determinations that it is susceptible of taking on in its life is easy to understand, at least as far as what is said here: *the ontological structure of consciousness is at once indifferent and immanent to the existential determinations of consciousness*. Indifferent, because this structure does not prescribe that this or that existential determination of consciousness be produced and, for example, that consciousness — turning back upon its own essence — direct itself upon its essence to grasp it in true knowledge. In conformity with this indifference, consciousness can exist without true knowledge being produced in it. *Existential determinations are inessential*; they are, with respect to the essence, contingent and variable predicates. But the inessential character of these determinations does not signify that they be separated from the essence: quite on the contrary, the essence is *immanent* to them as that which renders them possible — as their very essence. *This is why natural knowledge is ontological.*

Henry now introduces a fundamental distinction that will structure the rest of the book: *ontological structure* vs. *existential determination*. The ontological structure is the universal essence of consciousness (the manifestation-of-self of being); the existential determinations are the various particular modes in which consciousness can live (natural, philosophical, scientific, religious, artistic, etc.). The ontological structure is *immanent* to every existential determination (no existential determination can occur without it); but the ontological structure does *not prescribe* any particular existential determination (the same ontological structure can be lived in many different ways). The relation is one of *indifferent immanence*: the essence is fully present in every mode, but the essence is indifferent to which particular mode obtains.

This distinction is structurally similar to the Kantian distinction between transcendental form and empirical content, or to the Husserlian distinction between essence and fact. But Henry uses it to make a precise philosophical point: *the essence is not normative*. Philosophical consciousness is not *better* than natural consciousness on the side of the essence; both are equally manifestations of the essence. The choice between modes of life is contingent, not determined by the essence. This breaks with the entire tradition of philosophical valorization of the contemplative life over the practical life, of the philosophical reflection over the natural attitude — these valorizations are, on Henry's reading, illegitimate impositions on what is in fact an indifferent equality of modes.

**Paragraph 6\.** The distinction in consciousness between its existential determinations and its ontological structure lays bare the ambiguity of a proposition like the one by which Heidegger still tries to characterize natural knowledge and to underline its contradiction: *"natural consciousness is and is not… ontological."* Natural consciousness *is* ontological insofar as the essence of consciousness in its universal structure is present in it. It is improper to say that natural consciousness *is not* ontological. Considered as an existential determination, natural consciousness is no less ontological insofar as it is precisely a mode of the life of consciousness, a mode of existence in its universal ontological structure — insofar as, in general, the universal ontological structure of existence is immanent to every existential determination as constituting its very essence.

What brings one to say improperly that natural consciousness is not ontological is that — if one considers the content aimed at by it, precisely as it aims at this content, as it understands this content — one must recognize that this content is *not being*, is not "ontological." One can qualify a consciousness by its "object" — that is, by the particular content it attains each time in a determinate act of grasping — more precisely, by the *sense* this content has for it in this act. What a consciousness has to do with, what it retains in the content it has before it (not these clumsy strokes on a chalkboard, but a "triangle"), more precisely, the sense it confers on this content (that of being an ideal figure formed by the intersection of three lines on a plane) — this is what qualifies the life of this consciousness, what determines this consciousness from the existential point of view. One will call *mathematical* a consciousness whose object is mathematical. One can say in the same way that natural consciousness is not "ontological" because being is not the particular signification it aims at. The right to qualify a consciousness by the signification it aims at finds its foundation in the correlation that exists between this signification and consciousness — more precisely, in the *determination of this signification by consciousness itself*. For the determination of the signification is identically that of the aim that constitutes it. The noetic-noematic structure of consciousness is a unitary structure. The unity of this structure assures the existential unity between a determinate mode of the life of consciousness and the signification it constitutes and in the presence of which it holds itself. *An existential determination is therefore a determination of the life of consciousness and, solidarily, a determination of its transcendent signification.*

Henry now uses the distinction to clarify the famous Husserlian-Heideggerian doctrine of intentional correlation (the noetic-noematic structure). Consciousness has, at each moment, a determinate noetic act (its mode of intending) and a corresponding determinate noematic correlate (its intended object as intended). The two are one structure; they are determined together. This is the unity of the existential determination. So when we call natural consciousness "non-ontological" because its object is the existent (not being), we are correctly characterizing its *existential determination*; but this characterization concerns only the surface level (the noetic-noematic correlation of the particular act), not the ontological-structural level that underlies all existential determinations. The mistake is to confuse the existential characterization with an ontological characterization.

**Paragraph 7\.** To live in the presence of a signification is to *understand*. Every existential determination is an *existential understanding*. Existential, this understanding is, because it realizes itself in a determinate mode of existence. One can also call existential understanding an understanding that makes existence itself its object and that confers on existence a sense. Every existential understanding in general is also, in reality, an existential understanding in this particular sense, because — in understanding its object in a certain way — it is in this way also that this existence understands itself. No doubt this existential self-understanding is rarely produced under a thematic form; existence is not habitually the theme of its aim. But an *implicit* existential self-understanding always accompanies the explicit existential understanding of its object by consciousness; more, this implicit self-understanding regulates itself on the explicit understanding. The foundation of the implicit existential self-understanding and of its link with the explicit existential understanding of the "object" resides in the fact that the latter (the explicit understanding) is identically a determinate mode of the life of consciousness — and, as such, an existential determination. Every existential understanding bearing on an objective signification consists therefore in an existential determination: on this is grafted an existential understanding (most often implicit) of existence itself, or more precisely, of this existential determination considered in its particularity. Every existential understanding in general, now, presupposes existence itself, as every transcendent signification in general presupposes the transcendental horizon of being. These two presuppositions, in truth, make only one; they consist in the manifestation-of-self of being — that is, in the universal ontological structure of the absolute essence. *The existential understanding finds its foundation in the ontological understanding of being.* This latter is the understanding, no longer of a determinate signification, but of being itself as foundation of all possible significations. *The ontological understanding of being is the originary manifestation of being to itself in consciousness in general.* As such, ontological understanding is identically the universal structure of the absolute essence. *The ontological understanding differs from the existential understanding in this: that the being which it understands is not understood in an act of grasping of consciousness but precedes on the contrary every act of grasping as that which renders the latter possible.*

The key distinction is now made fully explicit. *Ontological understanding* (*compréhension ontologique*) — the understanding of being itself as the universal foundation of all significations — is the originary manifestation-of-self of being in consciousness. This is the structural-essential level. *Existential understanding* (*compréhension existentielle*) — the understanding of any determinate signification, including the signification of one's own existence as such-and-such — is the level of particular modes of life. The two relate as universal essence to particular determinations: every existential understanding presupposes the ontological understanding (because no determinate signification can be understood without the prior horizon of being); but no particular existential understanding determines the ontological understanding, which is invariant.

The distinction parallels — but radicalizes — Heidegger's distinction in *Sein und Zeit* §31 between *Verstehen* (the existential understanding that is one of the modes of Dasein's being-in-the-world) and *vorontologisches Seinsverständnis* (the pre-ontological understanding of being that grounds all of Dasein's modes of comportment). Henry's contribution is to identify the pre-ontological understanding of being with the originary self-manifestation of being — that is, with the *Parousia* of the absolute. The pre-ontological understanding is not a vague "implicit grasp" that needs to be developed; it is the absolute concept itself, fully operative in every consciousness.

**Paragraph 8\.** In the ontological understanding of being resides absolute knowledge. True or philosophical knowledge is an *existential* (or, better said, *existentiell*) understanding of the ontological understanding. But every existential understanding of the ontological understanding is not necessarily true and not necessarily philosophical. If it does not limit itself to the understanding of an existential determination considered in its particularity, the implicit existential self-understanding of existence is an existential understanding of the ontological understanding — the implicit and most often improper sketch of an existentiell understanding. In truth — and precisely because an existential determination is a determination of existence — the implicit existential self-understanding of existence is always implicitly an existential understanding of the *essence* of existence in its universal ontological structure — that is, an existential understanding of the ontological understanding. *Philosophical knowledge is only a thematization, conducted with the conceptual material required and elaborated to this end, of this implicit existential self-understanding of existence — that is, of the ontological understanding itself.*

This recasting of the philosophical task is precise. Philosophy does *not* discover anything new; it does *not* reach a level of being that is closed to natural consciousness; it does *not* possess an exclusive epistemic privilege. Philosophy is only a *thematization* of what natural consciousness already implicitly understands. The conceptual machinery of philosophy (categories, terms, distinctions, arguments) is a tool for explicating the implicit pre-ontological understanding that is operative in every consciousness. The philosopher and the non-philosopher have the same access to being; they differ only in the degree of explicitness with which they thematize this access.

The Heideggerian terminology Henry uses ("existential" \= *existenziell*, concerning the ontic-existential particulars of Dasein; "existentiell" \= *existenzial*, concerning the ontological structures of Dasein) is taken from *Sein und Zeit* §4. Henry applies it: philosophical knowledge is an *existenzial* understanding (it concerns the ontological structures of existence), but it is itself a particular *existenziell* mode of life (the philosopher's mode of life). So philosophy itself is doubly characterized: existentially as a particular mode of consciousness; existentielly as a thematization of the ontological structures.

**Paragraph 9\.** *The ontological understanding of being is radically independent of every existential understanding.* That the existential self-understanding of existence be true or false, that it accomplish itself in an "authentic" or "inauthentic" mode of existence — this changes nothing in the originary nature of existence, in the ontological understanding of being in its universal structure. The radical independence of the ontological understanding with regard to every existential self-understanding of existence brings us to establish an *absolute opposition* between what existence is in itself and the way in which this existence represents or understands itself. *"Just as,"* says Marx in the preface to the *Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy*, *"one cannot judge an individual on the idea he has of himself, one cannot judge a… period… on its consciousness."* Showing elsewhere how *"the social structure and the State emerge continually from the vital process of determinate individuals,"* Marx takes care to add: *"but of these individuals not as they may appear in their own representation or in that of others, but as they really are."* The distinction between what existence is in itself and the way in which this existence understands itself is a distinction it is important to have constantly present in the mind because terms like "representation," "understanding," and even "consciousness" are too often used indifferently to designate realities that are however *radically* different. It is thus that by *consciousness* Marx understands the way in which existence represents or understands itself — the "consciousness" of an individual or of an epoch characterizing the way this individual or this epoch understand the world in which they live and consequently understand themselves. It is in this sense that Marx says one cannot judge an epoch by its "self-consciousness." It is in this sense that one will speak of a "bourgeois consciousness" or of a "proletarian consciousness." *The critique directed by Marx against the concept of consciousness can only be understood as a function of this signification attributed by him to the word consciousness.* This critique consists in saying that consciousness (so understood) cannot change anything in reality — and that, far from playing with respect to reality the role of a principle, consciousness is at most an effect of reality.

The Marxian interlude is highly significant. Marx's famous critique of consciousness — that consciousness does not determine social being but is determined by it — is here framed by Henry in a precise philosophical reading. Marx, on Henry's reading, was using "consciousness" in a particular sense: the *existential* sense (how individuals and epochs *understand* themselves and their world). And Marx's critique was correct in that sense: existential self-understanding is *epiphenomenal* with respect to the ontological reality of existence; changing how people *understand* themselves does not change what they *are*. But this critique does *not* apply to consciousness in the *ontological* sense (as the universal essence of manifestation, the *Parousia* of being); the ontological consciousness is the very *reality* of existence, not an interpretation of it. Marx's critique of "consciousness" is therefore compatible with — indeed presupposes — the deeper recognition that there is an ontological consciousness (the manifestation-of-self of being) that is the reality of existence itself.

This passage is a preview of Henry's later book *Marx* (1976), where he argues at length that Marx's critique of Hegelian-idealist consciousness is the discovery of a *new* ontology — an ontology of subjective living praxis, of life as immanent self-realization — that breaks with the entire tradition of representational consciousness. The Marxian "real individuals" (the individuals "as they really are," not as they appear in representation) are, on Henry's reading, the precursors of the immanent self-affecting life that Henry's own phenomenology will articulate.

That consciousness so understood cannot change anything in the reality of existence results from the absolute opposition existing between existence in itself and the way existence understands itself — results, more profoundly, from the radical independence of existence in its originary nature with regard to every existential self-understanding of this existence. A change of "consciousness" therefore signifies a modification of the existential self-understanding of existence and *affects in nothing* the reality of existence. *"This postulate of modifying consciousness,"* says Marx, *"comes back to demanding that one interpret what exists differently — that is, that one recognize it by means of another interpretation."* Recognizing what exists, and for example existence, by means of another interpretation — representing existence to oneself as something that exists, as natural consciousness does (which understands itself from the "world" understood as the sum of the existent), or on the contrary as the pure ontological element that is in itself nothing ontic — this changes nothing in the originary reality of this pure ontological element in its radical anteriority with respect to every act of understanding (implicit or explicit, philosophical or not) directed upon it. *It is uniquely — is it necessary to underline it here — of this pure ontological element in its originary reality anterior to every act of understanding directed upon it, that the present researches occupy themselves.* The distinction between the originary reality of the pure ontological element and, on the other hand, the existential understanding of this element can appear simple. Respect for such a distinction would however bring us, we believe, to reject from most works said to be of philosophy a good part — when not the near totality — of their content.

The closing sentence is striking and polemical. The whole tradition of "philosophy of consciousness" — as Henry has been describing — has confused the ontological structure with the existential understanding, has treated being as if being were just another determinate object thematizable by a particular act, has missed the radical anteriority and indifference of the ontological essence to all existential modes. The result is that "most works said to be of philosophy" are in fact analyses of *existential understandings* (of how consciousness understands itself in this or that mode), not of the ontological structure proper. Henry is announcing that *The Essence of Manifestation* will rigorously confine itself to the ontological structure — to the originary self-manifestation of being prior to and independent of every existential understanding of it.

This methodological declaration sets the tone for the rest of the book. Henry's whole positive phenomenology (in Sections III–IV) will articulate the ontological structure of self-manifestation in a way that does not depend on any particular existential mode (not on the phenomenologist's reflective gaze, not on the religious mystic's contemplation, not on any privileged human comportment). The structure is universal-essential, operative in every consciousness equally, prior to all existential differentiation.

---

## **§ 19\. Being-for-itself from the ontological point of view and from the existential point of view: consciousness and truth**

**Paragraph 1\.** The distinction between the universal ontological structure of existence and the existential understanding of this existence by itself lifts the equivocation that ceaselessly weighs — within philosophy — on the problematic of the *for-itself*. This equivocation holds precisely to the fact that, under the term *for-itself*, one designates *as well* the essence of existence (insofar as this essence — and consequently existence itself, understood in the reality of its universal ontological structure — consists in the manifestation-of-self) *as* a particular determination of this existence in which it understands itself, in a thematic or only implicit way, inside an "authentic" or "inauthentic" mode of understanding. It is clear, however, that the analysis of the for-itself can receive an ontological signification (in the eyes of philosophical thought) only if the object of this analysis is constituted, in an unequivocal way, by *existence such as it is in itself* and not such as it understands itself. Everything one can say from this latter point of view — that is, by considering the manner in which existence understands itself — remains *radically foreign* to the project of first philosophy, if by first philosophy one understands (as it is fitting to do) ontology itself.

The opening paragraph applies the distinction of §18 (ontological structure vs. existential understanding) to one of the most consequential terms in modern philosophy: the *for-itself* (*pour-soi*, *für sich*, German idealist *Fürsichsein*). The term has been used in *two* radically different senses: (i) the *ontological* sense — the for-itself as the essence of existence, the very structure of self-manifestation, the *Parousia*; (ii) the *existential* sense — the for-itself as the determinate mode in which existence thematically understands itself (in any of its many possible modes, "authentic" or "inauthentic," philosophical or mystical or religious or everyday). The whole tradition from Hegel through Heidegger and Sartre has equivocated between these two senses, and the equivocation has produced systematic confusions.

The manner in which existence understands itself is variable. One can call "*experience*" this self-understanding of existence, because, in understanding itself in this way, existence makes the experience of what it is itself in its own eyes. The different ways for existence to understand itself constitute thus so many "experiences" of consciousness. But what consciousness attains each time in its experience — the signification it gives to the content of this experience and gives to itself — is something that holds only "for itself"; it is existence such as it represents existence to itself; *it is not existence such as it is in itself*. Thus the *unhappy consciousness* of Judaism understands itself as something inessential, as an existence that leaves the essence outside of itself — an essence of which it is radically deprived and which remains forever transcendent to it. The essence, however, is *immanent* to existence as constituting its very essence. What is defined, however, in this immanence of essence to existence, is *existence itself in its universal eidetic structure* — not the variable representation in which this existence understands itself. For existence can very well understand itself, and effectively understands itself in Judaism (according to Hegel), as inessential. Existence is in itself the essence; existence is not the essence "for itself." But the essence is the for-itself. Existence which is the essence is existence-for-itself. *How can existence which is the for-itself not be "for itself"?*

The reference is to Hegel's *Phenomenology of Spirit*, "The Unhappy Consciousness" (Part B, Self-Consciousness, the third moment) and to Hegel's analyses of Judaism in the *Lectures on the Philosophy of Religion* and elsewhere. For Hegel, Judaism (like the Stoic-Skeptic-unhappy-consciousness sequence) is an existential mode in which consciousness understands itself as separated from the essence (God), the latter being conceived as transcendent and absolute, the former as inessential and abandoned. Henry uses this Hegelian analysis to make a structural point: the unhappy consciousness *understands itself* as inessential, but this self-understanding is *false* — at the structural-ontological level, this existence (like every existence) *is* the essence. The self-understanding (*how* existence represents itself to itself) and the structure (*what* existence is in itself) can come apart radically.

The closing paradoxical question — "How can existence which is the for-itself not be 'for itself'?" — names the structural paradox precisely. There are two answers, corresponding to the two senses of "for-itself": the existence is the for-itself in the *ontological* sense (it just is, in its essence, the manifestation-of-self); but the existence may not be "for itself" in the *existential* sense (it may not thematically understand itself as the for-itself). The paradox dissolves once the two senses are distinguished.

**Paragraph 2\.** Existence is the for-itself insofar as it is the essence — insofar as its ontological structure is the manifestation-of-self of the essence of pure manifestation, the presence-to-itself of the absolute in its absoluity, the *Parousia*. Existence which is the for-itself is *not* "for-itself" insofar as it does not direct itself upon its own essence to grasp it in an act, insofar as it does not understand itself as being the essence. To the being-for-itself which belongs to the essence of existence (insofar as this essence is the manifestation-of-self) is thus opposed *radically* the being-for-itself which designates the existential self-understanding of existence inside a determinate act of grasping and representation. This opposition signifies — here again — *the radical independence of the ontological for-itself with regard to the existential for-itself*. That existence understand itself as not being the essence does not prevent that existence be this essence — from which existence is separated only in the illusory representation that existence gives of itself. *The separation of essence and existence in representation is an irreal separation.* Irreal, however, this separation is not because it is *false*, but because it is produced *inside representation* — that is, as a signification aimed at by consciousness in a determinate mode of its life. *The unity of essence and existence such as we can understand it in true knowledge is no less irreal*, insofar precisely as it is a unity *understood by us* — a unity that belongs to the existential self-understanding of existence, such as it accomplishes itself at least inside philosophical knowledge.

The structural distinction is sharply drawn. Both the *separation* (proclaimed by the unhappy consciousness) and the *unity* (proclaimed by philosophical consciousness) of essence and existence are *irreal* — they exist only "in representation," only as significations aimed at by determinate modes of consciousness. The *real* relation of essence and existence is neither separation nor unity but the structural-ontological identity that is operative independently of any representational understanding.
