So the contrast is not between the unhappy consciousness's *false* representation and the philosopher's *true* representation; both are equally representations, equally irreal at the ontological level. The real is the manifestation-of-self that is operative in both consciousnesses without being thematized by either.

This is a remarkable diagnostic. The Hegelian system, which culminates in the philosopher's grasp of the unity of essence and existence in absolute knowledge, is itself, on Henry's reading, only a *representation* — a thematization of what is in fact already operative without any representation. The Hegelian "absolute knowledge" is not the achievement of the absolute (which has always already been operative); it is only the philosophical representation of this achievement. Hegel mistook the philosopher's representation for the achievement itself.

**Paragraph 3\.** The unhappy consciousness of Judaism does not represent to itself the unity of essence and existence; this unity is not *for it* (*für es*); the unity is on the contrary *for us* (*für uns*) who understand existence in its truth — that is, as the essence. When natural consciousness has raised itself, through the whole series of its experiences, through the experience of the unhappy consciousness, to philosophical knowledge which is ours, the unity of essence and existence (which constitutes the essence of this consciousness) will become present to it; this unity will no longer be only a unity *for us*. Consciousness will be brought before its truth. Its truth — namely, the unity in it of essence and existence — will be a truth *for it* (*für sich*). However — and as one has just seen — the unity of essence and existence which is for the consciousness that arrives at the understanding of its essence (*für sich*), as it is for us (*für uns*) who move within philosophical knowledge, is *no less irreal* than the separation of existence and essence which is for the unhappy consciousness, for natural consciousness in general (*für es*). What is for consciousness — "for it," "for itself," "for us" — what consciousness represents to itself in understanding itself in a determinate mode of its life is always (and that whatever this mode may be) something *irreal*. To the irreal separation of essence and existence which is for natural consciousness (*für es*) is opposed, *not* the (itself irreal) unity of essence and existence which is for us (*für uns*) or for the consciousness that understands itself in its essence (*für sich*), *but only* the *real* unity of existence and essence. *It matters little finally whether existence understands itself or does not understand itself as being the essence; existence is the essence — that is, the reality.* It is the manifestation-of-self of the essence of manifestation, the originary being-for-itself of being itself.

The schema is now articulated with precision. There are three "ways" the unity of essence and existence can be: (i) *für es* (for the natural/unhappy consciousness — as separation, falsely representated); (ii) *für sich* (for the consciousness that has come to philosophical self-understanding — as unity, correctly represented); (iii) *für uns* (for the philosopher who watches consciousness's ascent — as unity grasped from outside). Henry argues that all three are equally *irreal*, because all three are *representations*. The *real* unity is none of these; it is the structural identity operative *prior to* and *independent of* every representation, including the philosopher's. The Hegelian trick of moving from *für es* to *für sich* through *für uns* (which is the very motor of the *Phenomenology of Spirit*'s dialectic) does not move from irreality to reality; it only moves from one irreal representation to another irreal representation. The reality is *not* in any of these representations.

**Paragraph 4\.** Although it seems to introduce the problematic into the originary dimension of the being-for-itself, the distinction instituted by Hegel between what is *for consciousness* and what is *for us* in fact remains *radically foreign* to this originary dimension; it does not concern the ontological structure of being-for-itself. *The Phenomenology of Spirit* — which holds itself to the description of existence such as it is for the consciousness that represents existence to itself, whether this consciousness be natural or philosophical — therefore at no moment has to do with reality. The examination of the diverse modalities inside which existence understands itself pursues itself in *abstraction*, because (as Hegel himself says) *"abstraction is precisely what is not authentically — what only is for consciousness."* It is true that by "what only is for consciousness" Hegel understands what holds for the *non-philosophical* consciousness which has not yet arrived at self-knowledge. But (as has been seen) what is for *philosophical* consciousness (*für sich*, *für uns*) is no less irreal: the unity of existence and essence that this consciousness represents to itself in understanding itself in its truth is still only an *abstract* unity. One sees, more precisely, the fundamental ambiguity that there is in the obligation laid on the in-itself to *become for-itself* — when, as is constantly the case in the *Phenomenology of Spirit*, the in-itself designates the reality of consciousness, that is, in fact, the originary ontological structure of being-for-itself. *The becoming-for-itself of the being-in-itself of consciousness has, strictly speaking, no ontological signification.* The essence is wholly contained in the being-in-itself of consciousness, where the essence has already accomplished itself. The becoming-for-itself of the being-in-itself of consciousness concerns only the manner in which this consciousness understands itself and has, as such, only an *existential* signification.

The Hegelian critique is now devastating. The whole motor of the *Phenomenology of Spirit* — the becoming-for-itself of what is initially merely in-itself, the long ascent of consciousness through its experiences toward absolute knowledge — has, on Henry's reading, *no ontological signification*. It is purely an existential narrative — the story of how a consciousness comes to thematize what it already is. The "in-itself" of consciousness is *already* the for-itself in the ontological sense (it is already the manifestation-of-self of being); the "becoming for-itself" only adds the thematic representation, which is a contingent, dispensable, irreal supplement. Hegel mistook the existential ascent for an ontological event; he mistook the thematization for the realization.

This devastating critique has consequences that propagate through the whole modern tradition. Every philosophy that takes the form of a *path* — a Bildungsroman of consciousness, a journey to self-knowledge, an ascent to absolute knowledge — operates under the same misunderstanding: it takes the existential narrative for an ontological event. This includes not only Hegel but also the philosophical tradition that derives from him: Marx (in his Hegelian moments), Sartre (in *L'Être et le Néant*), and even Heidegger insofar as *Sein und Zeit* presents Dasein's authenticity as a kind of achievement to be reached through resolute decision. All these are mistaken in the same way: they treat what is in fact a contingent existential modulation as if it had ontological weight. Henry's diagnosis is severe: the *real* essence is already there, fully accomplished, in every consciousness; the philosophical task is not to *reach* it but to *recognize* it.

Far from being able to contribute to the realization of the spirit, true knowledge is in fact *totally foreign* to spirit, because true knowledge is situated on a quite different plane than that of reality. *The becoming-for-itself of the being-in-itself of consciousness is not the phenomenology of spirit.* The phenomenology of spirit, the manifestation of pure manifestation, resides in the being-in-itself of consciousness — which is the originary being-for-itself of being and, as such, the manifestation of pure manifestation, the manifestation of spirit. The "manifestation of spirit" in true knowledge — what Hegel improperly calls the phenomenology of spirit — is *not* the manifestation of spirit which constitutes the very essence of spirit (the essence of consciousness and of existence in general); it is *not* reality, but only a *representation* of reality inside a determinate act of consciousness. The expression "manifestation of spirit" is therefore fundamentally ambiguous: spirit is *as such* manifestation. The "manifestation of spirit" is therefore the essence itself; it is the originary and pure ontological element such as it is in itself. The "manifestation of spirit" in true knowledge does *not* belong, on the contrary, to the internal structure of the essence; it is not something ontological. The "manifestation of spirit" in true knowledge is the strict correlate of a determinate representation of consciousness; it is only a "manifestation" among others which, far from constituting the essence, presupposes on the contrary the universal and pure essence of manifestation in general. The becoming-for-itself of the being-in-itself of consciousness is a modality of the existential self-understanding of existence. *But manifestation as such is not the doing of this understanding; it is the doing of the essence. The phenomenology of spirit is an ontological structure.*

The polemic with Hegel reaches its sharpest formulation. The very title "phenomenology of spirit" has the same ambiguity as the term "for-itself": it can name (i) the ontological structure of spirit-as-manifestation (the essence itself), or (ii) the existential narrative of spirit's coming-to-self-knowledge (Hegel's book). Henry insists that only sense (i) has ontological signification; sense (ii) is a contingent existential narrative without ontological weight. The "real" phenomenology of spirit is *the ontological structure of consciousness as the manifestation-of-self of being* — not Hegel's Bildungsroman of consciousness's experiences. So Hegel's masterwork is, on Henry's reading, *not* the phenomenology of spirit (despite its title); it is only one existential thematization, contingently chosen, of what the *real* phenomenology of spirit consists in.

**Paragraph 5\.** The distinction between the ontological for-itself and the existential for-itself permits us to understand the relation that unites *consciousness and truth*. *Consciousness is in itself the truth.* When consciousness understands itself in its truth, it understands that *it is* the truth. The truth that it held until then to be the existent appears to it now as constituted in reality by its knowledge of the existent — that is, by itself. That truth is not the existent but the knowledge of the existent — this is not only, however, *for the consciousness* that aims at this "truth." As long as the identity of truth and knowledge is only *for the consciousness* that aims at this identity, the "truth" constituted by this identity remains *transcendent* with respect to consciousness — and that in a double sense. It is transcendent with respect to philosophical consciousness (*für uns*) as the signification this consciousness attains in surpassing itself toward this signification. It is transcendent with respect to natural consciousness (*für es*) as a signification this consciousness does not attain and which remains radically foreign to it. But, in all cases, the "truth" that consciousness attains or does not attain — according to whether it has or has not arrived at true knowledge — is a *signification*, the strict correlate of a determinate act of understanding. *Truth so understood refers to the manner in which existence understands itself*; it designates what this existence represents as being the truth, "its truth": *it is an existential truth*. But the truth that consciousness *is in itself* — and which is independent of what this consciousness represents as being the truth — is the *ontological truth*.

The relation of consciousness to truth is now disambiguated according to the same schema. (i) *Existential truth*: the truth that consciousness represents as truth in a determinate act of understanding (whether the determinate act is natural-consciousness's "the existent is the truth" or philosophical-consciousness's "the knowing is the truth"). (ii) *Ontological truth*: the truth that consciousness *is* in its very essence — the manifestation-of-self of being, which is operative independently of any representation of truth. The two are radically different: existential truth is a signification correlate of an act; ontological truth is the structural-essential reality of consciousness itself.

The contrast is absolute. Existential truths can be true or false; they vary across individuals, epochs, philosophical positions; they belong to the order of representations and significations. Ontological truth is invariant; it is operative in every consciousness equally; it is not subject to the categories of "true" and "false" because it is the very condition of every assertion of truth. The ontological truth is what natural consciousness *is*, what philosophical consciousness *is*, what the unhappy consciousness *is* — equally, regardless of how each represents itself.

**Paragraph 6\.** We say with regard to this ontological truth: "truth that consciousness *is* in itself" and not "in itself," because the ontological truth which constitutes the essence of consciousness is precisely the truth, the manifestation-of-self of being, the being-for-itself itself and as such, in its originary ontological structure. *The being-in-itself of the truth is the being-for-itself.* The truth is the truth-for-itself. *The being-for-itself of the truth is precisely consciousness.* That consciousness be the being-for-itself of the truth — this is precisely *its life*. The life of consciousness is a life *in the truth*; it is the life of truth itself. Because the life of truth is the very life of consciousness, *consciousness is at no moment separated from the truth*. The truth is not transcendent to consciousness; it is never exterior to consciousness, never "unknown." The truth that is not for consciousness — that, at least, may not be for consciousness — is only an *existential truth*; it is a truth that consciousness represents or does not represent to itself when it understands itself. In truth, existence always understands itself in some way; existence always represents to itself a "truth." Simply, in representing this "truth," existence does not represent another "truth." It is only of this "truth" that existence does not represent — of an *existential* truth — that one can say that consciousness is separated from it. With the dissociation between the ontological truth (which constitutes the essence of consciousness and of existence) and the existential truth (which concerns the manner in which existence understands itself), is lifted the ambiguity that weighs on an expression like "the truth of existence." To "the truth of existence" which varies according to the manner in which existence understands every thing and itself, is opposed *radically* "the truth of existence" which designates the very essence of existence — insofar as this essence is the originary manifestation of being and, as such, the truth.

The closing paragraph of §19 articulates the full structure: consciousness *is* the for-itself of truth — that is, consciousness is the very being-for-itself in which truth, as the manifestation-of-self of being, is realized. This is consciousness's *life* (*la vie de la conscience*) — a key term that prefigures the late Henry's mature thought. The "life of consciousness" is not consciousness's biological life or its temporal succession; it is the continuous, immanent, self-affecting realization of truth in the very being-for-itself of consciousness. This is the structural ontological core of consciousness, prior to and independent of any existential mode.

The thesis that "consciousness is at no moment separated from the truth" is a powerful philosophical liberation. The traditional anxiety about truth — am I in error? do I see things as they are? — is, on Henry's reading, an existential anxiety that arises *only at the level of representation*. At the ontological level, consciousness *is* truth; consciousness *is* the for-itself of being's manifestation; there is no possibility of separation from truth at this level. The existential anxiety remains real (consciousness can have false existential representations of itself and of the world), but it does not touch the ontological reality.

The closing distinction between two senses of "the truth of existence" sets up a polemic that will continue through the rest of the book. Heidegger's celebrated formulation "*Wahrheit der Existenz*" (truth of existence, in *Sein und Zeit* §44 and *Brief über den Humanismus*) is, on Henry's reading, fundamentally ambiguous: it can mean (i) the ontological essence of existence as manifestation, or (ii) the existential thematization in which existence comes to its "authentic" understanding. The two are radically different. Henry's program is to develop only sense (i) — the ontological essence of existence as the originary manifestation of being.

---

## **§ 20\. Critique of the Hegelian concept of experience**

**Paragraph 1\.** The dissociation between ontological truth and existential truth puts in question the Hegelian conception of *experience*. Experience is, according to Hegel, the experience that consciousness makes of the *truth*. This truth is first for consciousness the existent to which consciousness relates itself. It is to the existent that consciousness measures its knowledge; consciousness asks itself whether its knowledge corresponds to the existent or does not correspond. The existent is the measure of truth. *Consciousness has thus its measure outside itself.* But the existent is the object of consciousness's knowledge; the existent is, in reality, only an existent *for it*. The being-for-the-consciousness of the existent is its truth. *Consciousness has the measure in itself.* It is in two very different ways, in truth, that consciousness is the truth of the existent. Consciousness is the truth of the existent insofar as it is the originary manifestation of being and, as such, the ontological structure of absolute truth. The originary manifestation of being, however, is the doing of consciousness in general; it is the doing of natural consciousness which nonetheless posits the truth outside itself. What one opposes — as having its measure in itself — to natural consciousness which has its measure outside itself, is therefore not consciousness itself in its universal ontological structure; it is not the consciousness which *is* the truth of the existent. It is the determinate representation of an itself-determinate consciousness which understands itself precisely as the truth of the existent — as having the measure in itself. Consciousness is here the truth of the existent in the sense that *it understands itself as this truth*. How can such a consciousness be born? How and why does consciousness so represent itself?

The opening paragraph deploys the distinction of §§18–19 against the central concept of Hegel's *Phenomenology of Spirit*: the concept of *experience* (*Erfahrung*) developed in the Introduction. Hegel's account of experience: (i) consciousness initially takes the existent as the truth (it measures its knowledge against external reality); (ii) consciousness discovers that this "external reality" is only what reality is *for it* (a representation given to consciousness); (iii) consciousness therefore comes to understand that *it itself* is the truth (the criterion of truth is internal). This is the Hegelian dialectic of consciousness's self-discovery. Henry's critique: this whole movement equivocates between the two senses of "consciousness is the truth" — the *ontological* sense (consciousness *is* the manifestation-of-self of being, structurally) and the *existential* sense (consciousness *understands itself as* the truth, in its representation). Hegel uses sense (ii) — the existential representational sense — and pretends it has ontological weight.

The questions Henry poses at the end — "How can such a consciousness be born? How and why does consciousness so represent itself?" — are pointed. Hegel takes the consciousness-that-represents-itself-as-truth as a starting-point of the dialectic; but this representational self-understanding cannot be a *principle* (it is itself a result, requiring explanation in terms of something prior).

**Paragraph 2\.** No doubt consciousness becomes for itself, in its representation, the truth of the existent only because *it is in itself this truth* — only because the truth that consciousness is in itself is the being-for-itself. *Far from resulting from the representation of truth in consciousness, the being-for-itself of truth is on the contrary its presupposition.* The consciousness that is the truth of the existent in the sense that it represents itself as such is therefore the *result*, not a *principle* of experience. Yet this is what Hegel makes it. Explaining how experience resides — in his eyes — in the comparison consciousness institutes between its object and its knowledge, Hegel justifies his point of view thus: *"For consciousness is on the one hand consciousness of the object; on the other hand, consciousness of itself: it is consciousness of what is the true for it, and consciousness of its knowledge of this truth. Since both are for it, consciousness is itself their comparison; it is for consciousness that its knowledge of the object corresponds to this object or does not correspond."* The possibility for consciousness to compare its knowledge and the object — and to make of the object first, of the knowledge second, the measure of truth — finds its foundation in the affirmation that knowledge and object are both "for it," and that in the same way, as what consciousness represents to itself. Knowledge of the existent is not presented here as something that is only an object *for us*; it is *for natural consciousness* that this knowledge is an object — and that precisely so that natural consciousness can compare it to the existent. The movement of consciousness in experience finds its principle, according to Hegel, in *what this consciousness represents to itself* — and that not only on the subject of the object, but also with regard to itself. *This movement of consciousness is however considered by Hegel as constitutive of reality.* Thus reality explains itself finally by the play of representations of consciousness, by the dialectic of significations in the light of which consciousness thinks the object and thinks itself. *Our history is the product of what we think.*

The critique is sharp. Hegel's central methodological move in the Introduction to the *Phenomenology* — that consciousness has within itself both knowledge and the object, so that consciousness is itself the comparison between them — *requires* that knowledge be a representation given to consciousness on the same plane as the object. But this is a representational reading: knowledge is treated as a thematized object, as something that is "for" consciousness in the existential sense. And then this *representational* movement — consciousness comparing two representations — is taken to be *constitutive of reality*. The Hegelian system is, on this reading, a vast intellectualism in which reality is reduced to the dialectic of consciousness's representations. The closing punch — "Our history is the product of what we think" — captures Hegel's idealism in its most extreme form: history (the real, the concrete) is reduced to what consciousness represents.

This is a polemic that anticipates, by structural-philosophical means, the Marxian critique of Hegelianism (cited at the end of §18). The Hegelian system reduces reality to representation; Marx's critique recovers the priority of real material life over consciousness's representations of it. Henry's reading aligns with Marx in critiquing Hegelian intellectualism, but Henry articulates the critique at a more fundamental ontological level: not just the social-historical priority of real life over its representations, but the universal-ontological priority of the manifestation-of-self over every existential thematization of it.

**Paragraph 3\.** To this history of the experience of consciousness, however, Hegel assigns a *goal*: that of consciousness understanding itself such as it is in itself. This self-understanding of consciousness in its essence, Hegel attributes however to the consciousness that makes the experience — and that as a *condition*, as a principle that renders this experience possible. *The self-understanding of consciousness in its essence cannot however result from experience and at the same time precede experience as its own condition of possibility.* It is in an ambiguous way, in truth, that one declares that "consciousness is on the one hand consciousness of the object; on the other hand, consciousness of itself." It is *not in the same way*, in reality, that consciousness is consciousness of the object and consciousness of itself; the object and consciousness itself are not "for it" in the same manner. The object is for consciousness insofar as consciousness represents it to itself. *Consciousness is for itself insofar as it is in itself the truth* and, as such, the being-for-itself in its originary ontological structure. Self-consciousness does not therefore oppose itself to consciousness of the object and cannot be compared to it; self-consciousness rather constitutes the very essence of consciousness of the object. To institute a dialectic that rests on the comparison of self-consciousness and consciousness of the object, it is necessary to treat *surreptitiously* this self-consciousness as a self-representation — to confuse the ontological signification of being-for-itself with its existential signification.

The argument now turns precise. Hegel's "consciousness is consciousness of object and consciousness of itself" treats both sides as equivalent — both are objects given to a comparing consciousness. But consciousness of the object is *thematic representation* (the object is what consciousness aims at); whereas self-consciousness *in the ontological sense* is not a thematic representation at all (it is the structural self-presence of consciousness, the manifestation-of-self of being). To compare them as if they were both representations on the same plane is to treat self-consciousness *as if* it were a representation — that is, to confuse the ontological sense with the existential sense. Hegel's whole methodology requires this confusion (otherwise the dialectic cannot get started); but the confusion is precisely the philosophical error that underlies the entire Hegelian system.

Hegel, however, *needs* such a confusion: it alone permits him to treat the being-for-itself at once as something that is at the *origin* of experience (which belongs to consciousness in virtue of its very essence) and, on the other hand, as a *knowledge* that consciousness represents to itself in the same way as it represents an object to itself — and that in such a way that there can be instituted between them (as between two terms situated on the same plane) a comparison, whatever the way this comparison establishes itself, whether the knowledge or the object serves as measure.

**Paragraph 4\.** In confusing it with the being-for-itself which constitutes the originary ontological structure of consciousness, Hegel does not only obtain the advantage of placing the representation of its knowledge by consciousness at the beginning of experience — and of being able consequently to make of it (this representation) a spring of experience. Or rather, this advantage can also be expressed otherwise by saying (as Hegel does) that not only the two moments — the object and the knowledge — are for consciousness, but also that *the comparison itself is its doing*: "*so that, when consciousness examines itself, there remains for us from this point of view only the pure act of seeing what happens*" without intervening ourselves. And certainly the movement of the experience of consciousness finds its principle in consciousness itself (since such a movement is produced even if we are not there to examine it and to understand it). This immanence to consciousness of the principle of the movement of its experience, Hegel however interprets as *an explicit presentation to consciousness of the elements it examines, as a presentation in representation*. Experience is precisely for Hegel an examination by consciousness of objects that consciousness represents to itself. *Thus one sees the being-for-itself fall from its primitive ontological condition in order to become one of these objects.*

The Hegelian methodological gain Henry now identifies: by confusing ontological for-itself with existential for-itself, Hegel can claim that the dialectical movement is purely *immanent* to consciousness (consciousness alone is the agent of its own movement; the philosopher only watches). But this immanence is purchased at the price of treating the ontological for-itself as itself a representation — as an object-on-the-same-plane-as-other-objects that consciousness can examine and compare. This is the *fall* of the ontological structure into the rank of just another existential representation.

In such a fall, however, resides the passage *from reality to the representation of this reality* — the passage from reality to *irreality*. But in the sphere of the irreal, something can *not be* for consciousness; the represented knowledge is never an absolute knowledge. *Here comes to the fore the paradox of every intellectualism.* After saying that everything is for consciousness, Hegel must say — precisely because this being-for-consciousness is only a being for and in its representation — that *something also however is not for consciousness*. What then is it that is *not* for consciousness but only for *us*?

The deep paradox of intellectualism is now exposed. Once you have reduced reality to representation (as Hegel does), you must distinguish two kinds of representations: those that are "for consciousness" (its current thematic representations) and those that are only "for us" (the philosopher's external view, what consciousness will eventually come to represent but does not yet). But this second kind of representation — the "for us" — is also a representation; it cannot escape the irreal sphere of representations. So the dialectic moves entirely within the sphere of the irreal, never touching the real. Reality has been excluded by the very methodological move that purported to ground the system.

**Paragraph 5\.** The movement of experience is, according to Hegel, that by which consciousness perceives that the object it took until then for the in-itself (the truth) is in reality only an in-itself *for it* — and that consequently it is the *being-for-it* of this in-itself that is, in fact, the truth. In such a movement consciousness passes from one object to another: the first is the in-itself, the existent; the second is the being-for-it of this existent. The second object is simply the truth of the first object, its essence — but *"this consideration of the thing is our doing."* The consciousness that makes the experience and for which the second object now holds as the truth sees in this second object only a new object that purely and simply replaces the first. *Consciousness does not understand whence this new object comes to it*; the suppression of the first is for it a simple loss that it experiences in suffering. The birth of the new object from the first (as the simple truth of the first), the movement of its being-become — this is what is *not* for consciousness, what *"happens, as it were, behind its back,"* what is only for us. But (as we have seen) what is for us is *as irreal* as what is only for it. The movement of the birth of the new object — if it is real — is not only for us. The reality of the movement of experience is, in truth, *neither for it nor for us*. Real experience is not produced before consciousness, nor behind consciousness; it is produced *in the originary ontological dimension of being-for-itself*. The understanding of the movement of experience in the representation of the becoming of the new object — this is what is only for us, what may not be for it. The "moment that is not present for the consciousness which is itself sunk in experience" is an *abstract* moment. *Far from constituting reality, the being-for-us is the simple representation of reality.*

The Hegelian "behind the back" formulation (from the Introduction to the *Phenomenology*) is famous: consciousness experiences only the change of objects (loses the old, gains the new) without understanding that the new object is the *truth* of the old. The understanding happens "behind consciousness's back" — that is, only the philosopher (who watches from outside) sees the necessary connection between the old and the new objects. Henry's critique is structural: the philosopher's "behind the back" view is itself only a representation, no less irreal than the consciousness's own representations. The *real* movement of experience does not happen in the representational sphere at all (neither in front of consciousness nor behind it); it happens in the ontological dimension of being-for-itself, which is the manifestation-of-self of being.

The confusion of reality with representation is heavy with consequences: what does not display itself before consciousness must — if it is real — find itself *somewhere else*, in such a way however that it is *also* a representation, a content displayed for a possible consciousness. Of what is not produced before consciousness, one will say therefore that it happens "behind it." *Intellectualism, whether that of Hegel or that of Freud, is a doctrine of the unconscious.*

This is a striking — and sweeping — diagnostic. The "unconscious" — that vast philosophical category that surfaces in Schelling, Schopenhauer, Hartmann, Nietzsche, and especially Freud — is, on Henry's reading, an artifact of intellectualism. Once you have reduced reality to consciousness's representations, anything that is real but not currently represented must be put "somewhere else" — namely, in a sphere of *non-current representations*, the *unconscious*. So the unconscious is not an alternative to intellectualism; it is intellectualism's necessary corollary. The unconscious is a sphere of *as-yet-unrepresented representations* — still representations, not yet reality. Henry's diagnosis: the proper alternative to intellectualism is not the unconscious but the recognition that reality is *not* in the sphere of representation at all (whether conscious or unconscious); reality is in the *ontological* dimension of self-manifestation that is structurally prior to the entire sphere of representation.

This anticipates Henry's later, more developed critiques of psychoanalysis (especially in *Genealogy of Psychoanalysis*, 1985), where he argues at length that Freudian unconscious is a representational concept that misses the structure of immanent affective life. Already here in §20, the diagnostic is in place.

**Paragraph 6\.** What happens behind consciousness is however *that toward which consciousness tends*, what consciousness aspires to represent to itself. When consciousness will represent to itself what happens behind the back of natural consciousness, what is only for us will be also for it (*für sich*); consciousness will have arrived at true knowledge. *The movement of consciousness toward true knowledge is the movement of experience.* The movement of experience finds its origin, according to Hegel, in the *inequality* that exists between consciousness of the object and self-consciousness — in the *difference*, says Heidegger, between natural knowledge and real knowledge. When this difference will be suppressed — when consciousness will be equal to its object, because this object will be consciousness itself — then experience will stop. In what however does the inequality between consciousness of the object and self-consciousness consist (the difference between natural knowledge and real knowledge — the difference that is at the origin of the movement of experience)? Natural knowledge is the knowledge of consciousness which aims at the existent. *Real knowledge is the knowledge that permits natural knowledge*; it is the originary manifestation of being which renders possible the manifestation of the existent. *Real knowledge is immanent in natural knowledge as constituting its very essence.* The difference between natural knowledge and real knowledge is the difference that exists between *a modality of the life of consciousness* and *this consciousness itself in its universal ontological structure*. *Such a difference is not susceptible of being suppressed*: it subsists in true knowledge. The existential truth that comes to the fore in true knowledge is not the ontological truth that constitutes the essence of real knowledge.

The structural argument now reaches its climax. The Hegelian-Heideggerian doctrine of the experience-as-overcoming-of-difference (consciousness moves toward knowledge by suppressing the inequality between its current grasp and the truth) confuses two different kinds of difference:

* (a) the difference between *natural knowledge* and *true knowledge* (both are existential modes of consciousness — one focused on existents, one focused on being); this difference *can* be suppressed, when natural consciousness becomes thematically philosophical;  
* (b) the difference between any *existential mode* (whether natural or true) and the *ontological structure* (real knowledge, the manifestation-of-self of being); this difference *cannot* be suppressed, because it is the structural relation between universal essence and particular determination — the essence is always immanent in the determinations without being identical to any of them.

Hegel and Heidegger conflate (a) and (b). They take (a) — the suppressible inequality between two modes of representation — as if it were the same as (b) — the structural ontological difference. So they take the achievement of true knowledge (the philosopher's reflective grasp) as if it were the achievement of *real* knowledge (the ontological structure), as if the philosopher's thematization were itself the realization of the absolute. This is the fundamental error.

The difference that *can* be suppressed at the end of experience is only the difference that exists between natural knowledge and true knowledge — when precisely natural knowledge has become true knowledge. But this difference, abolished in true knowledge, between what is "for us" and what is "for it" is precisely *not* the difference that is at the origin of experience. The difference that is at the origin of experience is *not a difference between two representations*; it is *a difference between what consciousness represents to itself and, on the other hand, what consciousness is in itself*. How can this difference between two terms (only one of which is "for it") nonetheless enter into the life of consciousness in such a way as to become acting in it and to determine in it a movement? Hegel did not conceive this possibility otherwise than by making the *other* term — the being-in-itself of consciousness — *something that is also, in some way, "for it."* In confusing thus the ontological signification and the existential signification of the being-for-itself, Hegel made of *real knowledge* a representation. The confusion of the ontological signification and the existential signification of the being-for-itself is identically that of *real knowledge and true knowledge*. Because real knowledge was confused with true knowledge, it became something one could compare with natural knowledge. Because the difference (immanent in consciousness) between real knowledge and natural knowledge was understood as a difference between two representations, it was also understood as a difference that *can* be surmounted. The difference that is surmounted at the end of the course of experience became thus the very same difference that was at its origin. Surmounted at the end of the course of experience, this difference risked, it is true, being so from the beginning — since the real knowledge immanent in natural consciousness (the self-knowledge of the knowledge of the object) was precisely understood as a representation of this knowledge, as true knowledge. No doubt this representation could be improper — and natural consciousness understand its knowledge of the object, for example, as something ontic. *This false knowledge was at least a true knowledge, a knowledge bearing on the truth.* The truth had been, from the start, *replaced by its own representation*.

The closing of §20 articulates the deepest critique of Hegel: the *Phenomenology of Spirit*'s entire dialectical structure rests on a confusion that, once exposed, dissolves the apparent necessity of the system. The "experience of consciousness" is not the path by which consciousness *attains* truth (because consciousness is *already* the truth, ontologically, from the start); it is only the existential narrative by which consciousness comes to *thematically represent* itself as the truth. The achievement of "absolute knowledge" at the end of the *Phenomenology* is not the realization of the absolute (which has been there from the start) but only the philosopher's representation of this realization. The philosophical question — what is the proper way to think about the absolute, given that the absolute is structurally already present in every consciousness? — is not addressed by Hegelian dialectic; Hegel's dialectic operates entirely in the irreal sphere of representations, while the real (the manifestation-of-self of being) is presupposed throughout but never properly thematized. Henry's task in the rest of *The Essence of Manifestation* will be to thematize precisely what Hegel could not thematize — the immanent structure of self-affecting life that is operative in every consciousness as its ontological essence.

---

## **§ 21\. The reaffirmation of the originary character of the manifestation of being in the bringing-into-light of its non-historical character**

**Paragraph 1\.** The confusion of true knowledge and real knowledge brings the problematic to situate the latter (real knowledge) at the *end* of the course of experience. Real knowledge is the absolute. *"The absolute,"* says Hegel, *"is essentially Result."* What results from the history of the experience of consciousness, in fact, is not the absolute, but only its representation in true knowledge. No doubt this representation differs from the one in which natural consciousness represents to itself its own knowledge in order to compare it to the object. This difference between natural knowledge and true knowledge does not exclude their *homogeneity*. It is this homogeneity that permits Hegel to *go from one to the other* — to depart from phenomenal knowledge in order to rise to "the absolute." In rising to "the absolute" from phenomenal knowledge, Hegel believes himself able to oppose Schelling, who cannot explain how consciousness arrives at absolute knowledge or, inversely, how consciousness separates itself from absolute knowledge. *The problem of knowing how consciousness arrives at absolute knowledge can however not be resolved at the term of the history of consciousness; it must be resolved at its beginning.* Consciousness, in truth, no more arrives at absolute knowledge than it separates itself from absolute knowledge. The absolute is being itself; absolute knowledge is the manifestation-of-self of being. *Insofar as it is the manifestation-of-self of being, consciousness is itself absolute knowledge.* The problem of absolute knowledge is the problem of the *internal structure of consciousness in general*.

The opening paragraph identifies the structural error of Hegel's celebrated dialectic. Hegel famously claimed (against Schelling's "absolute" given immediately at the start, "shot from a pistol") that the absolute must be reached by a dialectical labor, that it is "essentially Result." The implicit assumption: phenomenal knowledge and absolute knowledge are *homogeneous*, on a continuum, so that one can move from one to the other through a series of dialectical mediations. Henry's correction: phenomenal knowledge and absolute knowledge are *not* homogeneous in the way Hegel supposes. Phenomenal knowledge is an existential mode of consciousness; absolute knowledge is the ontological essence of consciousness. The two are related as universal essence to particular mode — *immanently*, not *transitively*. So one does not "arrive at" absolute knowledge through a sequence of mediations; one is *already* in absolute knowledge from the start, because consciousness *is* the manifestation-of-self of being.

The Hegelian-Schellingian dispute is here resolved at a level neither party recognized. Schelling was right to insist that the absolute is given immediately (not as the result of a dialectical labor), but he could not articulate the structure of this immediate giving. Hegel was right to insist that an immediately-given absolute remains abstract and undeveloped, but he wrongly inferred that the absolute must be the *result* of a dialectical labor. Henry's resolution: the absolute is given immediately as the ontological essence of consciousness, but this essence has its own internal structure (which Sections III–IV will articulate as immanent self-affection); the philosophical task is not to *reach* the absolute through dialectic but to *thematize* its internal structure, which is operative from the start.

**Paragraph 2\.** That consciousness must be arrived at absolute knowledge — and that from the beginning of its history — does not signify that absolute knowledge is *equivalent* to natural knowledge. Absolute knowledge is not the natural knowledge by which the history of consciousness begins; it is *its essence*. In what is at the beginning, it is fitting therefore to distinguish *a modality of the life of consciousness* (a modality in which this consciousness begins the history of its life) and, on the other hand, *what renders such a beginning possible* — namely, the beginning itself. Absolute knowledge is this absolute beginning; it is the *origin*, and that in an *ontological* and not only existential sense — the origin which is the arising of the effective dimension of phenomenality where something in general (and natural knowledge first) can be produced, that is, can manifest itself. As it is the essence of natural knowledge, absolute knowledge is also the essence of true knowledge. By difference from natural knowledge, true knowledge represents to itself the very act by which it arises, and thus renders present to itself its own origin. But this manifestation of the origin in the representation of true knowledge is *not the origin itself*; it presupposes the origin insofar as — like every other knowledge — true knowledge first manifests itself, on the foundation in itself of the essence of manifestation. *Precisely because it is the common essence of natural knowledge and true knowledge, absolute knowledge is foreign to their history; the passage from natural knowledge to true knowledge does not concern absolute knowledge.* The relation of absolute knowledge to natural knowledge and to true knowledge is the one (previously studied) that exists between the essence of consciousness and its existential determinations.

The structural articulation is now precise. Three terms must be distinguished:

* *Natural knowledge*: existential mode of consciousness aiming at existents.  
* *True (philosophical) knowledge*: existential mode of consciousness aiming at being.  
* *Absolute (real) knowledge*: the ontological essence of consciousness as such, the manifestation-of-self of being, operative in every existential mode.

The Hegelian dialectic operates at the level of the first two — it describes the passage from natural knowledge to true knowledge through dialectical experience. But it confuses true knowledge with absolute knowledge — treats the philosophical achievement as if it were the realization of the absolute. Henry's correction: absolute knowledge is *not* the result of any dialectical movement; it is the structural essence presupposed by every dialectical movement (and by every consciousness, philosophical or not).

**Paragraph 3\.** The dissociation between *ontological truth* (which constitutes the essence of consciousness) and *existential truth* (which appears to consciousness through the determinate acts of representation by which consciousness understands itself) permits us to fix the partition between *what is historical and what is not historical*. What is historical is the truth that existence represents to itself with regard to itself; it is *the representation of truth*. It is only of this representation of truth that one can say that it has a history and that it becomes — at the term of this history only — "equal" to its object, that is, to the truth, to the concept. *But the truth is present before the accomplishment of this history, before consciousness represents it.* The concept is there before its becoming in time; the essence of manifestation is effective before the work by which consciousness arrives at giving itself a representation of this essence (that is, of itself) that is conformed to it. It is with these restrictions — in truth essential — that it is fitting to understand this text of Hegel: *"but as concerns the being-there of this concept in time and in effectivity… as the spirit that knows what it is, it does not exist otherwise and it exists only after the accomplishment of the work by which… it creates for its consciousness the figure of its essence and in this way equalizes its self-consciousness with its consciousness."* What comes about in the work accomplished by consciousness in the course of its history is only the "figure of its essence" — it is *not* this essence itself. *The essence of consciousness is however the effective being-there of the concept.* To the concept it belongs *to be effectively there otherwise than by the work of consciousness — elsewhere than in history*.

The non-historical character of essence is now made explicit. History is the realm of *representations* — what consciousness comes to thematize, the shifting figures it gives to itself across its experiences. The essence is *not* in this realm; the essence is the *condition* of every historical movement, operative independently of any thematization, operative *before* and *outside* the historical labor of consciousness. The closing claim — "the concept is there before its becoming in time" — is a strong anti-Hegelian thesis. Hegel had insisted that the absolute *becomes* itself through history (the absolute spirit reaches its full self-consciousness only through the temporal labor of human history). Henry insists that the absolute is *already* itself, structurally, ontologically, before any history; history is only the existential thematization of what is structurally already real.

This thesis has powerful philosophical-religious resonances. The classical theological doctrine of God as eternal — as not subject to time, not "becoming" but always already what He is — is here defended in a phenomenological key against the historicizing-dialectical theology of Hegel and his successors. The "essence of manifestation" is, structurally, what theology has called the eternal God — not in any anthropomorphic sense, but in the structural sense that the manifestation-of-self of being is operative *prior to* and *independently of* every temporal history. Henry's later religious phenomenology (in *Words of Christ*, *I Am the Truth*, etc.) will develop this convergence between the phenomenological essence and the theological eternal.

**Paragraph 4\.** It is in an improper way, on the other hand, that one speaks of an *equality* between "consciousness" and its essence. With the essence which constitutes the ontological structure of being-for-itself and of absolute truth, the "consciousness" which designates the representation of this essence cannot coincide — even in philosophical knowledge — for, as has been seen, the difference between *reality and its representation* cannot be suppressed. The self-consciousness — of which Hegel says (against Fichte) that it arises only after a preliminary process — has therefore *strictly speaking no ontological signification*; it could not designate the structure of the essence nor belong to it. The absolute, if one wishes to understand by it the originary being-for-itself of the essence which makes the essence the reality, *is not produced in history*. It is therefore, again, the simple representation of the essence that one can refuse to "*that enthusiasm which, like a pistol shot, begins immediately with absolute knowledge and gets rid of different positions by declaring that it wishes to know nothing of them.*" The absolute that this enthusiasm posits is, indeed, only *a position*; another position from then on opposes itself to it — the one in particular at which this enthusiasm will arrive only after having changed itself into its contrary, and that on the path of despair which is the path of consciousness. Absolute knowledge however *is* the doing of this enthusiasm — and that as what permits it to be: as that first act of appearing of the originary and pure essence of manifestation which has *already* accomplished its work for it (for the enthusiasm), in order at least to permit the enthusiasm to manifest itself. *History is therefore not the "movement by which the appearing comes about,"* for the appearing has already come near us; the self-appearing of the appearing has *already* been produced — and that as the originary arising of an effective dimension of phenomenality where this history can accomplish itself and first begin. *Transcendental knowledge is not to be acquired; it is a priori.* What is at the beginning is not the modesty of an obscure *Grund*; it is the *Verbe* (Word). The reality of the absolute is presupposed as the condition of every possible reality in general, as the condition of a history. But the reality of the absolute is its absoluity, *its originary presence to itself in the Parousia*. The presence of the absolute to itself, the reunion of its essence in its unity with itself — such is the strong nature of the origin itself. The *Parousia* is produced at the origin because it constitutes the essence of the origin. Because the *Parousia* constitutes the essence of the origin, the *Parousia* results from no progress; it is the presupposition of progress. *In the Parousia resides the reality of the absolute.* Because the absolute finds its reality in the *Parousia*, the absolute finds it in the origin. *The destiny of the absolute is not played out in history.*

The Hegelian "pistol shot" — Hegel's polemical image (in the Preface to the *Phenomenology*) for Schelling's immediate positing of the absolute — is here vindicated, against Hegel's own intent. Henry argues that Schelling's "enthusiasm" was structurally correct: the absolute *is* given immediately, prior to all dialectical labor. What Schelling could not provide (and what Hegel rightly criticized) was the structural articulation of this immediate giving. But Hegel's alternative — making the absolute the result of dialectical labor — was the worse error: it lost the immediacy in trying to articulate it.

The reference to *Verbe* (Word, *Logos*) is theological-Johannine — recalling the Prologue to the Gospel of John ("In the beginning was the Word..."). The contrast Henry draws is striking: classical philosophy posits at the beginning either an *obscure ground* (Schelling's *Ungrund*, the German mystical tradition) or a *modest origin* (Hegel's "pure being" at the start of the Logic) that needs to develop into the absolute. Henry insists: at the beginning is the *Word* — that is, the fully articulated, fully self-manifesting essence. The origin is not modest; the origin is the absolute in its full self-presence (the *Parousia*). The whole structural-philosophical liberation of the section consists in this: the absolute is not poor or obscure or undeveloped at the start, requiring history to enrich it; the absolute is rich, manifest, and self-present from the start, and history adds nothing essential to it.

**Paragraph 5\.** Because the absolute finds its reality in the origin, the historical representation of truth is foreign to it — does not enter into the structural definition of absolute reality. Because it is foreign to the structural definition of absolute reality, the historical representation of truth does not constitute the moment in which this reality realizes itself; it is in no way its condition. To the question posed of knowing "*how a knowledge in itself atemporal — an absolute knowledge — can have temporal conditions in the existence and the becoming of a humanity,*" it must be responded that such a knowledge — if it is the absolute — has in fact no historical condition. Such a "condition" would itself presuppose absolute knowledge (and that not as a *virtual* absolute that would realize itself only in the condition, but as an absolute that has *already* realized itself — as the effective and concrete act of accomplished manifestation). *The accomplished essence of manifestation is the condition of possibility of experience, the essence of experience and of truth.* Because this accomplished essence does not enter as a condition into the definition of the internal structure of this essence, *representation does not belong to it*. It is therefore false to say (as Heidegger does, following Hegel) that *"representation belongs to the essence of experience,"* or again that *"the representation of experience is willed from the essence of experience as belonging to it."*

The paragraph extends the critique from Hegel to Heidegger. Heidegger, in his late essay on Hegel's concept of experience (in *Holzwege*), follows Hegel in making representation essential to experience and to the self-disclosure of the absolute. Henry's critique: this is to mistake the existential representation for the ontological reality. The essence of experience (= the manifestation-of-self of being) is independent of representation; representation is a contingent existential supplement, not a structural component. So Heidegger, despite his powerful critiques of Hegel elsewhere, follows Hegel in this fundamental error.

**Paragraph 6\.** Why, however, would representation belong to the essence of experience — why would it be willed from this essence as belonging to it? The essence is the essence of manifestation. Representation signifies the *reversal* and *history*. That representation belong to the essence — this means that the reversal and history are *necessary* for the essence to realize itself, for manifestation to become effective. But effective manifestation has been shown to be the *condition* of the reversal and of history. That the character in virtue of which the essence is the *presupposition* be however *forgotten* at the very moment when the essence is thought as realizing itself only in the reversal and in history — this attests that this character is not clear. The character in virtue of which the essence is the presupposition is nothing other, however, than the *originary character of revelation*. *It is because this character is not for us, it is because representation represents to itself badly the originary essence of revelation, that representation inserts the originary essence of revelation in the process that belongs properly to representation — in a history that is the history proper to representation.* The reason for which (confusing their power with that of the origin) the reversal and history substitute themselves for the origin to identify themselves with the essence (which assures the promotion of effective phenomenality) resides thus in the *incapacity of thought to grasp in itself its own foundation*. The task of grasping such a foundation is however that of ontology. To this task that is its own ontology equals itself only in the *respect for the origin*. If, as Hegel himself says, a pure thought is *"the one that turns toward the beginning of things,"* ontology will be this pure thought — ontology will preserve its purity — only in the clear consciousness of *what was before it*. What was before ontology was already *the spirit*, for, as Hegel says again, *"what spirit is, it always was in itself."* But the in-itself of spirit is the originary being-for-itself of the essence of manifestation — and this being-for-itself of the essence is *not* the doing of representation but its *condition*.

The structural diagnosis is now complete. The very fact that representation (Hegel's reversal, Heidegger's hermeneutic disclosure, Husserl's transcendental reduction) has been thought as essential to the realization of the absolute is itself a *symptom* of the philosophical incapacity to grasp the originary character of revelation. If philosophy could properly grasp the originary self-manifestation of being, it would not need to make representation essential to it. The mistake is to *substitute* the philosophical-thematic act for the originary ontological event. This is what Henry calls "the incapacity of thought to grasp in itself its own foundation."

The closing reference to Hegel — "what spirit is, it always was in itself" — is a beautiful hermeneutic recovery. Hegel himself, in this saying, recognizes the structural priority of the in-itself of spirit over its development. But Hegel did not draw the proper consequence: the development *adds nothing essential* to the in-itself; the in-itself is already the full reality of spirit. Henry draws the consequence Hegel could not: ontology must be the patient elucidation of *what spirit always already was*, not the dialectical narrative of its becoming.

In rejecting representation outside the essence, the distinction of ontological truth and existential truth interdicts us from considering this essence as *unfinished* as long as representation does not understand it. It rejects the affirmation according to which consciousness is "*something it is not yet.*" *What consciousness is not yet is not consciousness*, does not belong to the sphere of reality. What consciousness is not yet is only the *science* — the ideal element that has need of reality but does not produce it. The identification of what consciousness is not with what consciousness is is the temptation of science — the illusion science has, in understanding itself, of understanding reality.

The closing thesis is striking: science (here understood as the philosophical-systematic discourse, including the Hegelian *Wissenschaft*) has the temptation to confuse *what it represents* with *what is*. To say "consciousness is what it is not yet" (Hegel) is to identify the philosophical ideal (the represented goal of consciousness's development) with the philosophical reality (the actual being of consciousness). Henry's critique: the philosophical ideal is *not* the reality; it is only an existential representation; the reality (the manifestation-of-self of being) is operative independently of every philosophical representation, including the representation of "what consciousness is not yet."

**Paragraph 7 (closing).** *Philosophical knowledge misses its goal when it interrogates itself.* Or else, it must push this interrogation far enough that the interrogation be identically an interrogation about the essence of every knowledge as such. *It is not philosophical knowledge that matters.* *Philosophy comes always too late, for what it says was at the beginning.*

The closing aphorism is one of the most striking in the whole book. Philosophy has tendency to interrogate itself, to make philosophical reflection the proper object of philosophical reflection. But this interrogation is misguided unless it is pushed all the way to the *essence of every knowledge as such* — that is, to the originary self-manifestation of being. Otherwise, philosophy's self-interrogation only produces another existential representation. The proper philosophical task is to recognize what is *prior to* philosophy: the originary essence of revelation that operates in every consciousness, including the philosopher's own. Philosophy's vocation is not to *create* the truth but to *recognize* the truth that has always already been there.

The closing aphorism — "*Philosophy comes always too late, for what it says was at the beginning*" — recalls Hegel's own famous formulation in the Preface to the *Philosophy of Right* ("the owl of Minerva spreads its wings only with the falling of the dusk"). But Hegel meant this in a quite different sense (philosophy understands a historical epoch only after it has run its course). Henry repurposes the formula in an ontological sense: philosophy's articulations of the essence of manifestation always come after the essence has already accomplished its work. There is no philosophical labor that produces the essence; the essence is the structural condition of every philosophical labor (and of every consciousness whatsoever).

This closing positions the program of the rest of the book. Sections III–IV will work out, in patient and rigorous detail, what was always at the beginning — the structure of immanent self-affection that is the originary essence of manifestation. The philosophical labor will not *create* this structure but *recognize* it; not *establish* it but *exhibit* it. The repetition (announced at §16) of the elucidation of the essence of phenomenon thus prepares the way for the constructive task of Sections III–IV.

---

## **§ 22\. The interpretation of the essence of phenomenality within the fundamental presuppositions of monism and the problem of receptivity. Ontological signification of this problem**

**Paragraph 1\.** The analyses that precede (§§ 17 to 21\) have brought into light the *originary character of manifestation*. Such a character signifies that the essence of manifestation manifests itself *in itself and by itself* — and that in an originary manner, as that which must already have manifested itself in order that something else (namely, the existent) can — *then and only then*, in the milieu thus opened of effective phenomenality — manifest itself in turn. The essence of manifestation, however, has been interpreted *within the fundamental ontological presuppositions of monism*. The originary character of the essence of manifestation so understood signifies the manifestation in and for itself of the *pure horizon* in which the essence objectifies itself in order to realize its work.

The opening paragraph recapitulates the result of §§17–21 with precision: the essence of manifestation has been shown to be *originary* — to manifest itself in itself, by itself, prior to and independently of every existential representation, prior to and independently of any external condition. But — and this is the critical pivot of §22 — this whole demonstration has taken place *within the fundamental ontological presuppositions of monism*. That is: the entire repetition of the elucidation has remained within the conception of phenomenality as horizonal-transcendent self-distantiation. The "originary self-manifestation" of the essence has been articulated as the manifestation of the *horizon* — the field of objectivity opened by the essence's self-objectivation. So even though Section II has corrected many errors of the philosophical tradition (Hegel's, Heidegger's, Husserl's), it has done so within the same monist framework that Section I diagnosed. The deepest question — *whether monism itself can really account for the originary self-manifestation* — has not yet been faced.

The essence realizes its work by itself; in this resides its *Selbständigkeit*. But the problem (as has been shown) is that of the *possibility* of this *Selbständigkeit*. It is a question of knowing how the manifestation of the pure horizon of being is possible. The horizon is what the essence — as transcendence — opposes to itself. To the essence, however, in order to be real, *it does not suffice to oppose to itself the horizon in which it objectifies itself*. Or rather, this opposition is truly an opposition (an opposition that *persists* and that is thus possible in and by this persistence) only if what the essence opposes to itself is *maintained near it* — and that in the very act of opposition. *How, however, can what the essence opposes to itself be maintained near the essence, if not on the condition of being received by it?* The opposition and the *reception* of what (in the opposition) finds itself opposed to the essence constitute together the possibility of objectivation. The ontological possibility resides in the phenomenological power of the foundation. *In the indissoluble unity of the opposition and the reception of the horizon appears the fundamental character of reception, which assures in fact the possibility of this unity.* To be received means: to give oneself to, to appear, to manifest oneself. *The receptivity of the horizon is identically its manifestation.* If — as has been shown — the phenomenal becoming of the pure essence of phenomenality resides in the manifestation of the horizon, the question of the internal possibility of this becoming (which confers on the essence its reality) *concentrates itself in the problem of receptivity*. The response to this problem alone renders comprehensible (in its internal structure) the *Selbständigkeit* of the essence.

The argument is now precise. The essence's self-manifestation, on the monist conception, requires that the essence *opposes to itself* the horizon (the field of objectivity). But mere opposition is not yet manifestation: the opposed horizon, to be a horizon (and not just an absence), must be *maintained* in some way near the essence — must be *received* by the essence as the very content of its self-manifestation. So the essence's self-manifestation requires not just the act of *opposing* (the work of transcendence) but also the act of *receiving* (the work of receptivity). And the receiving is what *makes* the opposition into a manifestation: the horizon is *present* (manifest) only insofar as it is received; receptivity *is* the manifestation of the horizon.

The structural problem is now visible: the essence must *be receptive* to its own opposed horizon, in order for the horizon to be actually manifest. So the essence must contain, within its own internal structure, a *receptive* power. The whole question of the essence's *Selbständigkeit* (autonomy) reduces to the question of the *internal possibility of receptivity*: how does the essence have the power to receive what it itself opposes to itself? This is the problem of §22.

**Paragraph 2\.** *The problem of receptivity has a pure ontological signification.* The ontological character of receptivity results from the *belonging to the essence* of what is to be received. What is to be received, indeed, is not the existent but the pure phenomenological milieu in which the existent can manifest itself — that is, can be received in turn. Such a pure milieu (in which the existent is susceptible of showing itself) cannot, in truth, be called by us a "phenomenological" milieu except insofar precisely as it is received. But receptivity is not only ontological because the content it receives is a pure ontological content. *Insofar as it receives this content precisely (that is, in its very nature), receptivity is ontological as constituting what is most essential in the essence itself.* What is most essential in the essence is what assures the possibility of its internal coherence. What assures the possibility of the internal coherence of the essence (which objectifies itself under the form of the pure ontological horizon it opposes to itself) is the act that *maintains near the essence* what is thus posited before it — the act by which the essence receives this opposed content. *Insofar as it grounds the self-reception of the essence and, solidarily, the manifestation of the horizon, receptivity is what is most essential in the pure essence of manifestation. Receptivity is ontological.*

The thesis is fundamental: receptivity is not an external addition to the essence; receptivity is *what is most essential in the essence itself*. Without the receptivity that maintains the opposed horizon near the essence, the essence's act of opposing would issue in nothing — would be a mere abstract negation, not a manifestation. The receptive act is what *holds together* the essence's self-positing — what makes the structure of self-distantiation actually a structure of self-manifestation. So the ontological essence (in its monist conception) requires receptivity at its very heart.

This is a profound restatement of the Kantian-Heideggerian doctrine of receptivity (which Henry analyzed in §13 and §15). For Kant, receptivity is the necessary mark of finite human cognition — the cognition that must receive its content from sensibility. Heidegger, in *Kant und das Problem der Metaphysik*, generalized this: receptivity is the structural mark of every transcendence. Henry now further radicalizes: receptivity is the structural mark of the essence of manifestation *itself*, in its monist conception. Without receptivity, the essence cannot be self-realizing.

**Paragraph 3\.** The ontological character of receptivity has been able to be masked insofar as receptivity is first thought in the light of *the problem of the reception of the existent* — and finds itself bound, for this reason, to the concept of *finitude*, such at least as finitude presents itself in the first place. As the reception of the existent is grounded on the essence, this reception presupposes (anteriorly to itself, anteriorly to the receptive act itself) a knowledge of *another order*: an *ontological knowledge* which — by opposition to this receptive knowledge — is at first interpreted as a knowledge no longer receptive but on the contrary *creative*. *"If the finite knowledge of the existent is possible,"* says Heidegger, *"it must be grounded on a knowing of the being of the existent that precedes every receptive act. The finite knowledge of the existent therefore demands — to be possible — a non-receptive knowing… a kind of 'creative' intuition."* In what, however, does the ontological knowledge consist that renders possible the reception of the existent? If such a knowledge — no longer concerning the existent — cannot be receptive with regard to the existent, *is it not, and that essentially, receptive with regard to being itself*, insofar as it finds itself determined as the process by which the essence objectifies itself under the form of a horizon that does not manifest itself to the essence except insofar precisely as the essence receives it? To show that the problem of the reception of the existent refers to a problem of ontological order is *not to resolve* the problem of receptivity, but only to pose it on the plane that is originally its own. And this is all the more urgent in that *in the essence of ontological receptivity reside the foundation and, finally, the essence of ontic receptivity itself*. That receptivity have an essentially ontological character does not signify that it be foreign to the reception of the existent — since, quite on the contrary, it is only as object that the existent is susceptible of being received. Objectivation must be possible for the reception of the existent to accomplish itself. *But the possibility of objectivation resides in the ontological essence of receptivity.* Far from suppressing it, the reference of ontic knowledge to ontological knowledge makes the problem of receptivity *arise in all its acuity*.

The argument is intricate and deserves close attention. The classical conception treats receptivity as the mark of *finite* (existent-receiving) knowledge — and contrasts it with *creative* (object-creating) ontological knowledge. The classical contrast: ontological knowledge is creative (it creates the horizon of being); ontic knowledge is receptive (it receives the existents that appear in the horizon). Heidegger inherits this contrast in *Kant und das Problem der Metaphysik*. But Henry argues that this contrast is *misleading*: even ontological knowledge is *receptive* in a deeper sense — receptive to the horizon it itself produces. The horizon is not just *created* by the essence's act of opposing; the horizon must also be *received* by the essence in order to be a manifest horizon. So even ontological knowledge has a receptive moment — and this receptive moment is the deepest, most fundamental form of receptivity, on which all other receptivity (including ontic receptivity) depends.

**Paragraph 4\.** The understanding of the ontological character of receptivity *lifts the ambiguity* that weighs on the opposition instituted by traditional philosophical thought between a "creative" knowledge, on the one hand, and a "receptive" knowledge, on the other hand. Such an opposition holds, in fact, only relatively to *the existent*. Knowledge will be said to be creative or receptive (in its relation to the existent) according to whether the existent springs forth from the very act by which knowledge intuits it, or whether on the contrary knowledge is constrained to *find* the existent as an existent it does not create but that exists independently of it. *But the ontological knowledge — which forms the horizon of being at the same time as it receives this horizon — is creative and receptive at the same time*, and that in the indissoluble unity of its very essence. *Thus appears the inessential character of the Kantian distinction between Entstand and Gegenstand.* In truth, this distinction is not only inessential; it reveals itself fundamentally obscure.

The Kantian distinction (further developed by Heidegger in *Kant und das Problem der Metaphysik*) is the technical contrast between *Entstand* (the object as it would be intuited by an infinite, creative intellect — what would be there *as it is in itself*, the noumenon) and *Gegenstand* (the object as it is given to finite, receptive intuition — what stands *over against* the finite knower, the phenomenon). The contrast supposes that there could be a non-receptive, purely creative intuition — and that this would be the divine, infinite mode of cognition. Henry's critique: the very contrast is incoherent, because *every* intuition (including any "creative" intuition) is structurally receptive — it must receive what it intuits as the content of its intuition. So the "infinite creative intuition" that Kant and Heidegger imagine as the contrast to finite receptive intuition is itself, structurally, also receptive. The Kantian distinction collapses.
