In opposing the *creative intuition* — of which we have at least the idea — and on the other hand an *intuition constrained to receive a foreign existent*, Kant pretends to hold the foundation of the metaphysical opposition between a *finite* knowledge and an *infinite* knowledge. But the true problem is not whether the existent does or does not proceed from the knowing power itself; the true problem is to understand *how this existent — that knowledge creates or does not create — can however manifest itself* to knowledge. Even were the existent posited in existence by the very act of the power that knows it, it would still be necessary — if precisely this power is that of a *knowledge* — that the existent *manifest itself* to it. And how could it do so if not through the mediation of the originary and pure essence of manifestation? *But finitude is, as has been shown, an ontological category; it finds its foundation in the essence, insofar as what arises in the work of the essence is the finite horizon of being.* That the existent be created changes nothing in the finitude of its manifestation, in the essential finitude that concerns the existent in its very being. It is no doubt as object that the existent is finite. But the existent is not an *ob-ject* because it exists prior to a knowledge that does not create it. Intuition is not finite because it receives an existent that does not emanate from it. *Intuition is finite in itself, as intuition.* It is the ontological power — constrained to receive the finite place (which it itself forms) of being — that is finite. And that abstraction made of every consideration concerning the *nature* of the existent that arises in this place (whether this existent is produced or not by the ontological power of manifestation).

The argument has consequential structural implications. Finitude is *not* a property derived from the relation to existents (the standard Kantian-Heideggerian account); finitude is a structural-ontological property of the *essence of manifestation* in its monist conception — namely, the property that the essence's self-manifestation always takes the form of a *finite horizon*. So even an "infinite creative intuition" (if we could give sense to the term) would still be finite *as intuition*, because intuition (in the monist sense) just is the manifestation of a finite horizon. Henry is dismantling the classical infinite/finite contrast at the structural level: in monism, *all* intuition is finite, because all intuition operates within the horizonal structure that is intrinsically finite.

This sets up a profound structural conclusion: if there is to be an *infinite* manifestation — a manifestation that is not finite — it must operate by a *different* structure than the horizonal one. It must not be intuition in the monist sense; it must not deploy a horizon. It must be a different essence of manifestation. This is exactly what Henry will argue in Sections III–IV: the immanent self-revelation of life is non-horizonal, non-intuitive, non-finite — it is structurally heterogeneous from monist manifestation, and hence does not suffer from monism's structural finitude.

**Paragraph 5\.** That the existent is finite as object means: the existent is finite insofar as it is intuited. For intuition finds its foundation in the process by which the essence opposes to itself the pure field of phenomenality under the form of a finite horizon. It is clear then that the antithetical concept of an *originary infinite intuition* arises in the problematic *without any context*. That such an intuition be said to be originary and infinite because it is creative of the existent changes nothing in the finite nature of intuition in it. Or else, with this idea of an infinite intuition, *another mode of manifestation* is thought — *another manner of appearing and of giving itself* that wants to make its concept count before philosophical reflection. *But by what right is this other mode of revelation still called an intuition? In what title can philosophy welcome it in the absence of every veritable and explicit problematic directed upon it?* Such a mode of revelation — which constitutes a pure ontological formal element — could not, in any case, be defined by its relation to an ontic content, by the fact that this content is supposed to emanate from it. *It is of the internal ontological structure of the essence of manifestation considered in itself and understood in its purity that it is a question.* As long as this essence is interpreted as that of *transcendence*, the effective pure phenomenality it promotes must — as such — be *finite*. The existent that manifests itself through the mediation of this essence is finite as well — and that whether it be created or not by the power of knowledge (that is, by this essence itself). It is in all cases an existent that manifests itself *inside the finite horizon of being*. The "*Entstand*" is also an *ob-ject*, at least as long as it is intuited. Only a *confusion* permits one to oppose it (from this ontological point of view) to the existent that intuition does not create but simply finds before it. This confusion Heidegger commits when he writes: *"to finite knowledge alone can be given a reality of the type 'object' (Gegenstand). It alone must expose itself to the existent that already is."* The character in virtue of which the existent is anterior to the exercise of a knowing power that does not create it is *an ontic character*. The character in virtue of which the existent is the *ob-ject* is an *ontological* character that determines a priori the structure of the being of every possible existent insofar as it is an intuited existent. *The confusion of these two characters brings one to give an ultimate sense to the opposition of a "creative" intuition and a "receptive" intuition.* But this opposition loses every ontological signification — and perhaps every kind of possible signification in general — for the thought that thinks the *object*. To such a thought it is given to understand that the *ob-ject* is not *before* (*ob*, *gegen*) because the existent it represents is found and not created by the power of knowledge, but because the existent *manifests itself in an intuition* — and that this is also why it is *finite*.

The structural argument is now devastating. Heidegger had distinguished the existent given to *finite* knowledge (the *Gegenstand*, the ob-ject standing-against) from the existent that would be available to *infinite* knowledge (the *Entstand*, the in-itself). Henry shows: the very being-an-ob-ject of an existent (its *Gegenständigkeit*) is determined by its being-intuited-within-a-horizon. Whether the existent existed prior to the intuition or was created by the intuition, *as intuited* it stands over against in the same way — it is a *Gegenstand*. So the supposed contrast Heidegger wants to draw (finite knowledge gets *Gegenstände*; infinite knowledge would get *Entstände*) collapses: as long as we are within the structure of intuition (the horizonal monist structure), what is given is always an ob-ject, regardless of whether it is created or found.

The deeper consequence: the very idea of an "infinite intuition" — if it is to be a genuine concept, not just a verbal placeholder — must designate a *different mode of manifestation*, not a different species of intuition. It must be a non-intuitive, non-horizonal mode of giving — a mode whose structure has not been articulated by classical philosophy. This is precisely what Henry promises to articulate. The "infinite" in the proper sense will not be the infinitely productive intuition (which is structurally still finite); it will be the *immanent self-revelation of life*, which is non-horizonal and therefore non-finite — but which is also no longer "intuition" in any classical sense. Section III–IV will articulate this.

**Paragraph 6\.** In interdicting one from binding the receptive signification of knowledge to a *character of the existent*, the critique of the distinction instituted by Kant between the *Entstand* and the *Gegenstand* renders more evident *the ontological character of receptivity*. Receptivity concerns no doubt the existent insofar as it renders possible the reception of the existent. *It is not the existent, however, that is received, but its being.* More exactly, *the being of the existent resides in its receptivity*. Receptivity is not a category of the existent; receptivity is ontological insofar as it constitutes the very essence of being.

The closing thesis is fully crystallized. Receptivity is not (i) a property of finite human cognition (the Cartesian-Kantian view); not (ii) a feature of how existents are encountered (a neutral feature of the encounter); but (iii) a structural-ontological property of the essence of being itself, in its monist conception. The essence's self-manifestation requires receptivity at its very heart — receptivity is *what is most essential in the essence*. So the question of the possibility of the essence's autonomy (*Selbständigkeit*) reduces to the question of the *possibility of ontological receptivity*: how does the essence have the structural capacity to receive its own opposed horizon, in order for that horizon to be actually manifest?

**Paragraph 7\.** The understanding of the ontological character of the problem of receptivity renders more urgent its solution. For if the reception of the existent is grounded on the receptivity of being, it does not suffice to ascertain (constate) the latter. *This question, from then on, arises inevitably before us: what is it then that renders ontologically possible the receptivity of being — that is, the manifestation of the pure horizon that the originary essence of objectivation opposes to itself?*

The closing question of §22 — and of Section II — names the program of Section III. The whole movement of Section II has been the *repetition* of the elucidation, which has reaffirmed the originary character of the manifestation of being but has also identified a new and deeper problem: the *internal possibility of ontological receptivity*. The essence (in the monist conception) requires receptivity at its heart; but how is this receptivity itself possible? What structural feature of the essence makes the reception of the horizon possible?

Section III ("The internal structure of immanence and the problem of its determination") will address this question by articulating the *internal structure of immanence* — that is, by showing that the receptivity required by the essence's self-manifestation cannot be a horizonal-transcendent receptivity (which would only repeat the structure that needs to be grounded), but must be an *immanent* receptivity — a self-receptivity that is not mediated by any horizon. This will be the structural breakthrough that makes Henry's whole positive phenomenology possible. The receptivity that monism requires but cannot account for will be revealed as *immanent self-affection* — the direct, non-horizonal, non-distantiated self-reception of life by itself. With this discovery, the whole monist framework will be left behind, and the immanent essence of life as the originary essence of revelation will be articulated.

The whole of Section II has thus performed a precise philosophical function. It has *worked through* the monist conception of the essence of manifestation to its limit — pushing the conception to articulate its own deepest structural requirements (the originary character of self-manifestation, the internal *Selbständigkeit* of the essence, the necessity of internal receptivity). At this limit, the conception encounters a problem (the possibility of internal receptivity) that it cannot solve within its own structural framework. The solution — which Section III will provide — will require a *displacement* to a different ontological framework: from the horizonal monism of "the essence of manifestation as transcendence" to the immanent ontology of "the essence of revelation as self-affection." The repetition of Section II has prepared this displacement; Section III will accomplish it.

## **§ 23\. The internal possibility of the receptivity of being and the problem of schematism**

Henry begins by fixing what has to be received. It is the pure horizon of being, and since it contains nothing of the order of beings, it is equally the horizon of nothingness. But this nothingness is not nothing. Only a thought that has silently taken beings as its measure of reality concludes that the pure horizon is empty and that the power making intuition possible is a form void of content. Likewise it is called "unknown" only if knowledge is reserved for the thematic grasp of beings — and that grasp already presupposes the horizon's manifestation. The horizon can leave room for thematic seizure only by not itself being thematized. This yields a purely negative determination, and Henry says so: to deny that the horizon is a being, or that it appears thematically, settles neither its reality nor its manner of appearing. Since for the horizon these two are the same, the question is whether a phenomenology of nothingness is possible at all.

Determining what is set over against the essence cannot explain how being is received, because any such determination already draws on reception as its condition. The horizon's reality lies in the power that manifests it, so the question of that reality has to be addressed to receptivity itself. Still, the indeterminate content yields one indication about the power that posits it: since what is posited is not a being but nothingness, the power in question is the power of positing something other than a being — imagination, and transcendental imagination, since it belongs constitutively to the pure essence of objectivation. Heidegger's formula, that imagination is the original and uncompounded unity of receptivity and spontaneity, does not answer the question but restates it. Imagination is spontaneous as the free invention of a horizon beyond beings; the problem is how it can be receptive toward what it itself forms.

A second negative solution has to be cleared away: that imagination receives the horizon *because* it forms it. Heidegger appears to offer this when he says of the pure intuitions that their reception is itself a formative act giving itself what offers itself. That the pure ontological content is formed by the essence explains nothing about its being received by the essence. The dependence runs the other way. Forming the horizon has phenomenological sense only insofar as what is formed shows itself — that is, is received. So imagination's capacity to produce the content it sets over against itself rests on its capacity to receive it. Henry states the reversal flatly: the essence of spontaneity lies in receptivity. Showing that pure intuition is formative, hence imagination, is a real result; it does not touch the ultimate possibility of objectivation, which always receives what it forms, and receives it as the very condition of forming it.

The solution actually offered runs in the opposite direction from the one just examined: not that intuition is imagination but that imagination is intuition. Heidegger calls imagination a faculty of intuition and cites Kant's remark that it is constantly sensible. The reversal is not arbitrary. It occurs exactly where the horizon's perceptibility, and thus its receptivity, can no longer be deferred. For beings to offer themselves, the horizon within which they are encountered must itself offer itself; if the horizon of objectivation is to do its work, this offering requires a certain perceptibility; and what is perceptible is what can be immediately received in intuition. Intuition renders the horizon perceptible by receiving it — and because it renders it perceptible, receiving the horizon coincides with forming it. Intuition therefore turns out to be the essence of the power that forms the horizon: imagination belongs to the faculty of intuition.

Then what makes intuition itself possible? The essence of intuition lies in objectivation: what makes an encounter possible has already been defined as the process by which the essence proposes itself to itself as object in the form of a horizon. Henry's earlier critique of intuitionism established that intuition is possible only through the opening of the transcendental field of being. But once reflection on the conditions of actual phenomenality shows that the horizon can render beings accessible only by manifesting itself, it is intuition that is charged with manifesting the horizon. Intuition thus finds its condition in a horizon that becomes real only insofar as it is intuited; it is grounded in transcendence, yet transcendence, Heidegger says, must in objectivation render the horizon it forms intuitable. The thought that asks intuition to realize what it conceives as intuition's own condition is moving in a circle.

An obvious defence is that the intuition grounded in the transcendental horizon was intuition *of beings*, whereas intuition of the horizon is pure, not empirical — so the claim would simply be that pure intuition conditions empirical intuition. Henry blocks this by pressing what "condition" means here: pure intuition conditions empirical intuition by constituting its essence. Empirical intuition is pure precisely insofar as it is intuition, since what makes it intuition is its power to render manifest, and whether what it manifests happens to be a being is external to that power. So the topic all along is the ontological power of intuition taken in itself, and that power is understood as objectivation. The circle is untouched by the distinction: the intuition interpreted as grounded in objectivation is then brought in to make objectivation possible, so the conditioned presents itself as the condition of its own condition.

Henry pauses to state the purpose of Heidegger's argument, which is offered as a reading of Kant: to exhibit the essential affinity of thought and intuition and thereby clarify schematism. The affinity holds because both are grounded in one common essence, imagination. The thesis that intuition is imagination thus belongs to a dialectic aimed at showing thought and intuition to be identical, and it is paralleled by a demonstration of the imaginative essence of thought. Both demonstrations work the same way, against the traditional distribution of spontaneity to thought and receptivity to intuition: each of the two is spontaneous and receptive at once. Since classical philosophy grants the spontaneity of thought and the receptivity of intuition, the work falls on the other two halves. Intuition's spontaneity is established by showing it to be original — formative with respect to a pure ontological content, since pure space and time are what intuition gives itself. Thought's receptivity follows from the understanding's being the faculty of rules: rules function only in the act by which they impose themselves on the mind, that is, are received by it.

What makes intuition and thought imagination in their essence is that spontaneity and receptivity define imagination's own essence. Imagination is transcendence itself: it forms the pure horizon of being and secures its reception in one act, and that is why it is the uncompounded unity of receptivity and spontaneity. To present a horizon whose presentation one secures by forming and receiving it is to *represent*. Representation is the process by which the essence sets over against itself the horizon it receives. So exhibiting the imaginative essence of thought and intuition is the same as defining both as representation — thought and intuition are distinct, but not separate like things of wholly different natures; both belong, as species, to the common genus of representation. Knowledge as representation is intuition or concept. Because thought is representation it must receive what it represents, so the understanding is intuitive; because intuition is representation it must be able to project freely what it offers, so it is spontaneous.

Receptivity and spontaneity therefore do not belong to intuition and thought in their specificity at all; they belong to imagination. Thought's spontaneity is grounded in imagination's spontaneity; far from grounding receptivity, intuition is made possible by it. Imagination alone forms and receives the transcendental horizon of being whose actual emergence makes both thought and intuition possible, and its immanence within each confers on each its power of representation while founding their affinity and so making schematism possible. Intuition, on this account, is subordinate to imagination. But the real problem is imagination's internal structure — how it holds near itself, by receiving it and so letting it appear, the horizon it has itself formed. The answer given is: by intuiting it. Which means that intuition, itself grounded in receptivity, is charged with making receptivity possible.

The equivocation in the concept of intuition can now be named. On one side, intuition is one of two specific and differentiated powers whose cooperation yields knowledge; in that role it is, like thought, subject to transcendence, which makes it a representation. On the other side, intuition presents itself as the very essence of transcendence, grounding it by securing the original reception of what transcendence sets over against itself. Henry's question is how intuition in the first sense — what relates immediately to its object and is singular — could possibly play the second role, since as an act of relating-to it manifestly presupposes what it is supposed to found. The double role does not conceal the absence of a solution but exposes it. Appealing to intuition to ground the internal structure of transcendence explains intuition by itself; more broadly, it falls back on a way of thinking whose presuppositions are Greek. For Greek philosophy, to know is to intuit. There intuition had only the grasp of beings in view; but once the possibility of intuiting beings becomes a problem and the manifestation of the pure horizon of being appears as its ground, that manifestation is in turn interpreted as a knowing accomplished in intuition. The transcendental philosophy of being has therefore not surpassed intuitionism: it has raised intuition's conditions to the absolute, and then resolved the ultimate questions about those conditions by falling back on intuition.

Henry now separates two problems that "schematism" conflates. The first is the possibility of the union of thought and intuition, solved by exhibiting their common essence. The second — the real one — arises only once the first is solved: how is that common essence, transcendence itself, internally possible? Its possibility lies in the original manifestation of the pure horizon of being, since only this lets transcendence keep and hold near itself what it has formed; in that act of holding lies transcendence's internal possibility, its actual accomplishment. Heidegger assigns exactly this ultimate grounding to schematism: the accomplishment of transcendence must at bottom be schematism, and Kant necessarily comes upon transcendental schematism as soon as he seeks the ground of transcendence's intrinsic possibility, so that transcendental schematism is what explicates original, transcendental truth in its essence. Schematism thus stands as the proposed solution to the problem of the manifestation of being. But how does it manifest the horizon? By sensibilizing it: the horizon shows itself insofar as it is brought into relation with sensibility, that is, intuited. The perceptibility credited to schematism is therefore grounded in intuition after all. The pure view or image-schema schematism supplies is an open place within the milieu of transcendence, and this place is visible, is genuinely an image, only through its intuitive character — the image-schema arises from a possible presentation, and what it presents can be brought within the sphere of a possible intuition. Because intuition is the bottom of schematism, the two problems Henry distinguished collapse into one another. Looked at closely, it is not thought but thought's *essence* that gets shown to be identical with intuition. Thought proceeds by rules it posits itself, and these rules are concepts; but the essence of thought is representation, and concepts are something for the mind only insofar as they are represented — the concept is nothing outside the representation of the regulative unity. So the problem of the concept reduces to the problem of representing the unity contained in it. That unity is represented when the concept is given an image, becomes image; this becoming-image is its sensible transposition, which consists in the concept's pure content being intuited. Intuition alone lets the concept's content appear, and so lets the concept be something rather than nothing: what the concept intends becomes accessible only through this intuitive character, which is why all conceptual representation is essentially schematism. Henry's correction is precise: it is not as *conceptual* but as *representation* that conceptual representation is schematism. Of the concept in itself we know nothing so long as it does not appear; hence its reality lies wholly in its manifestation, and its only possible use lies there. But that manifestation is interpreted, in conformity with monism, as representation — and representation implies intuition as the power securing the perceptibility of what it sets before itself. Thought is intuition insofar as it is representation: the pure concepts of the understanding, thought in the pure "I think", need an essentially pure intuitiveness if what is opposed in pure objectivation is to be perceptible as opposed.

Schematism therefore amounts to showing that thought and intuition are identical not in their specificity but in their essence — that is, insofar as they appear. Insofar as they appear they are both representation, and representation implies intuition as what secures the perceptibility of the represented. The intuition invoked here is admittedly not a specific power set against thought; it is a wholly general power, indeterminate in its ground, the power of rendering the pure horizon of being perceptible. But the manifestation of that horizon was itself posited as intuition's condition. Does noting that this intuition is not the specific cognitive faculty dissolve the circle? No: insofar as the intuition grounding schematism is given any determination at all, it is assigned to sensibility, and it manifests the horizon by rendering it intuitable, so that the perceptibility it founds is a sensible transposition. One and the same intuition appears alternately as condition and as conditioned.

The circle must be broken, but it has a use: it keeps returning the problematic to the real problem it both discloses and hides. That problem is receptivity, for which the intuition that is schematism's last word is merely a name — or, when it is more than a name, an unclarified and mysterious power borrowed outright from a tradition that Henry has shown stands in need of grounding. His note here is pointed: Heidegger himself observes in *Sein und Zeit* that the idea of intuition has governed every interpretation of knowledge from the beginning of Greek ontology to the present, and Kant opens the Transcendental Aesthetic by declaring intuition the mode in which knowledge relates immediately to objects and the end to which all thought is a means. The tradition's primacy of intuition is thus acknowledged by the very thinkers who inherit it unexamined.

Because it concerns thought and intuition in their essence rather than their specificity, the schematism problem belongs to the book's central question, the essence of manifestation. Clarifying that essence's internal structure has made receptivity appear as what grounds it in its ultimate possibility. The problem of the essence of manifestation now contracts into the problem of receptivity, whose essence alone could ground the "intuition" by which schematism claims to settle the question. Before clarifying receptivity — which must resolve the problem of the essence's internal structure, posed as the problem of its self-subsistence — Henry proposes to reaffirm that receptivity is ontologically central. He will do so by way of time.

## **§ 24\. Reaffirming the central place of the problem of receptivity, and the ontological interpretation of time as auto-affection**

Time is not an arbitrary place to make this point. Since Kant, time is understood as what makes manifestation possible in general — as the universal condition of all appearances, hence as the essence of phenomenality. Henry sharpens the overlap. Once the essence of phenomenality was finally raised to a problem, it was interpreted as the ontological process in which the essence sets a horizon over against itself; and that process is thought as time. The ego can be credited with performing objectivation only on condition of being understood in turn as time: in originally forming time, that is, as time, the ego forms the nature of objectivation and its horizon. Time is not merely another name for the essence of manifestation but is said to ground the act of objectivation in its ultimate possibility — time is implicated in the intrinsic possibility of that act. On this claim, the problematic of time ought not to repeat the general problematic of manifestation but to solve the central problem that emerged within it. Henry's question is how time is supposed to be so implicated.

The possibility of objectivation lies finally in the manifestation of the horizon the essence sets over against itself. Time can therefore be implicated in objectivation as its intrinsic possibility only insofar as it lets what is formed in that act appear — only insofar as the horizon of being is rendered perceptible by it. Heidegger says exactly this: time lends the horizon of transcendence, from the outset, the character of a perceptible offering, and renders the "opposedness" of objectivity perceptible to a finite being. But the horizon's perceptibility rests in turn on the essence's capacity to receive what it has itself formed, that is, to affect itself. That time is understood, after Kant, as auto-affection is what allows it to be presented as the intrinsic possibility of objectivation, Kant's universal condition of all appearances. So: how is time auto-affection?

Henry now makes the distinction on which everything after this turns. Auto-affection has a double sense. It means, first, affection *by* itself: what affects time is time and nothing else — above all, not beings. Time is affected outside experience, where experience means the determination of the subject by something ontic. Such ontic determination exists, but it presupposes a pure, ontological affection. What affects time is then time itself in the form of the pure horizon of being, since time is essentially horizon. Until thought rises to this conception of time as the transcendental horizon of being, time's nature stays unintelligible to it, because the intuition of time keeps getting confused with the intuition of what is in time. Defining the instant from the being that is present fails: what is present was awaited and will soon have passed, and a pure place had to be opened in advance for it, along with the pure dimension in which it will be retained; a being that is not yet there cannot constitute that place. Nor can beings define the present, since the present is a vanishing instant that would be nothing at all if it did not consist in seeing the thing come and seeing it pass. The now therefore includes in its own structure the acts of fore-seeing and of holding in view — the pure horizon that makes any presence possible.

What affects time is thus the pure horizon of being. But affection-by-itself is not the horizon's doing, since the horizon has to be formed before it can affect anything, and that forming is time's own work. Affection of time by a horizon that time has itself formed is what makes this an affection *by itself*. What affects, in the end, is not the horizon of pure time but the original power that deploys it: original time affects itself through the mediation of pure time, and in doing so solicits itself in the form of the horizon — which is why time forms the essence of all self-solicitation. As producer of pure time, capable of raising a transcendental horizon of being, original time is the power of positing something other than beings, so it is imagination: transcendental imagination is original time. As imagination, time is an intuition able to bring forth from itself the content it supplies. That content is the three-dimensional horizon of pure time, which, because it issues from intuition itself, is rooted in imagination as the originally formative act that is at once seeing, fore-seeing, and re-seeing. The threefold synthesis conditioning transcendence thus belongs to time only insofar as time is in essence imagination. Time also constitutes the essence of inner sense, of which Heidegger says that it receives nothing from outside. How can inner sense, which as time constitutes the pure milieu of objectivity and so the most radical exteriority, receive nothing from outside? Because the milieu of exteriority it receives is what it has itself formed: it takes what it receives from itself, and as a pure formative activity it holds everything from itself. Time is affected by nothing but itself because it is imagination — this is affection by itself. But auto-affection is not exhausted by this. More fundamentally it is affection *of* itself. Time is not only what affects; as what affects, it presupposes what is affected by it, and what is affected by time is time. Affection by itself is grounded in affection of itself.

Henry raises the obvious objection. If the power by which time affects were also the power by which time posits what is to be affected, then affection of itself would result from self-positing: the affecting time would posit itself as the reality about to be affected by it. This is the classical idealist move, offered here as a rival account of the priority Henry has just asserted.

He refuses to settle it speculatively. Questions of that form stay speculative so long as the answer is asked of speculation. The demand is phenomenological: what is the link between the time that affects and the time that is affected, and what does the claim that affection by itself is grounded in affection of itself mean *phenomenologically*?

The time that affects is the pure imaginative power deploying the transcendental horizon of being, the pure succession in which beings can be present. But that horizon cannot render beings manifest, and the pure succession from future to past cannot make a being present now, unless the horizon first manifests itself, unless the pure succession is visible in its purity. Kant says pure time cannot be perceived. Despite the context of the first two Analogies, Henry reads this as denying only that the horizon of pure time can be thematically grasped like a being; far from excluding its apprehension in its pure ontological content, this requires it. And apprehending that content is time's own task — this is what affection of itself means. As the essence of transcendence, time names the process by which the essence objectivates itself as a horizon; but the horizon of transcendence exists only insofar as it affects transcendence. To affect the pure act of objectivation, which is pure orientation-toward, means to raise some opposition against it. Raising that opposition is not the work of the act insofar as it *forms* the horizon of pure time but insofar as it *receives* it: the emergence of the opposition, its phenomenological manifestation, belongs to the essence's receptivity. The horizon's manifestation is grounded not in the time that forms it but in the time that receives it, and to receive the horizon of opposition is to be affected by it. Yet the manifestation of pure time is identical with its formation, if formation is to have phenomenological sense at all. Affection by itself — original time's opening of the horizon of pure time — is therefore possible only insofar as that horizon is received by original time, that is, affects it. Hence affection by itself is grounded in affection of itself, and affection of itself is the ultimate possibility of the auto-affection that defines time's internal structure. Heidegger's own formulations are conscripted: time is by nature pure affection of itself; pure inner sense is pure affection of itself, that is, original time; and pure affection of itself determines the deepest essence of transcendence.

Understanding time's essence as affection of itself forces a radical distinction between pure time and original time. Pure time is the horizon of succession formed by the pure places of future, past, and present; it is what is formed in transcendence, its pure object, and as pure object it is roughly comparable to space, the ontological content of an intuition. But pure time is not real time. It has no reality in itself because it neither forms nor manifests itself, and so refers necessarily to the original essence of time, which forms the horizon of succession by receiving it — to transcendence itself insofar as it can receive that horizon, insofar as the original time determining it is in essence affection of itself. Time is thus not only what transcendence sets over against itself but what makes transcendence possible. And since affection of itself conditions everything presupposing transcendence, spatial representation is grounded in it too. Henry uses this to expose a familiar comparison as superficial: contrasting the intuitions of space and time by their extension — everything spatial is temporal, not everything temporal is spatial — records a fact without grounding it. Time has the wider extension not because the temporal form of succession happens to subsume all representations, but because original time, in which that form is itself grounded, secures as affection of itself the internal coherence of the essence of manifestation and so makes any manifestation possible, space included. Heidegger's own text says as much: space is in a certain sense always identical with time when time is understood as what is formed in pure intuition, as pure object — but it is not in that form that time is the original ground of transcendence, rather as pure affection of itself, and as such it is the condition of possibility of every formative act of representation and renders pure space manifest.

Henry returns to the self-positing objection and now shows it to be abstract. Suppose the affecting time posited the time to be affected by it. That posited time would either float in the air, collapsing into the fictional entities of speculation and dragging down with it the time it is charged with receiving, or it would have to be received in turn by yet another time capable of being affected by it — in which the ultimate possibility of affection of itself would then reside. Given phenomenological precision, the point is this: for the affecting time, to posit the time that is to be affected means to posit it outside itself. But the milieu of exteriority in which the posited time would then be situated is not something capable of being affected by anything; it is rather what demands to be received in order to appear at all. In truth the time posited by the affecting time is not situated in the pure milieu of exteriority — it *is* that milieu. Self-posited time is pure time. And being pure time, it is not the affected time but presupposes it as the condition of its manifestation and so of its reality. The affected time, the condition of the manifestation of the horizon of pure time, is therefore nothing exterior to original time but coincides with it. The time that is affected is the same as the time that affects: original time is the time of affection, at once affecting and affected, in such a way that the affected side, which makes the actual phenomenological formation of pure time possible, constitutes affection's ultimate possibility and thereby what is most essential in the essence of transcendence.

If time as affection of itself constitutes the ultimate possibility of transcendence, it does so by securing reception of the horizon transcendence has formed. How does time secure that reception, and what in time's nature finally makes it possible as affection of itself? The answer given is: by intuiting the pure ontological content transcendence sets over against itself as that horizon. Time is possible as affection of itself insofar as it is by nature intuition. Henry draws the conclusion that guts the whole construction: what matters in the time that ultimately grounds the essence of manifestation is not its temporal character but its intuitive character. Time is the pure succession of the series of nows, and as such has a pure ontological content with determinate properties distinguishing it from space's. But the time of succession can no more be called an intuition than space can. Space and pure time are both only the *content* of an intuition; calling such a content intuitive means precisely that it gives itself only to the intuition that receives it. Intuition is neither pure time nor pure space but the power that receives them, and as such what confers phenomenological significance on them and constitutes their essence. As the power to receive the horizon of pure time, within which space too appears on the basis of that reception, intuition is what secures the internal possibility of the original essence of manifestation — the possibility of transcendence. Original time plays its central role as intuition, not as time.

Schematism makes the reason for time's centrality visible. Schematism forms a pure view prior to all objects of experience and making their manifestation possible; the possibility of that view or pure image lies in the reception of the pure place it develops. Time constitutes the essence of schematism because time is intuition and as such secures that reception. When Kant says the pure image of all objects of the senses in general is time, the reason is not that time, as pure form of succession, is the universal horizon of being — the horizon of all understanding and explication of being — but that time, as intuition, makes the reception of that horizon possible. The pure image formed in schematism is conditioned by time because time intuits the pure content of that image; because such a content must ask the time that intuits it for the condition of its phenomenal reality, what is formed in schematism necessarily gives itself intuitively in the pure image of time. Since what schematism forms is an image, its formation falls to imagination — but the decisive thing in the act of imagination is that it forms, that is, procures an image by an act of intuition. Forming the image therefore belongs to the power of intuition that receives its pure ontological content. And the intuition enabling imagination to perform its originally presentative function is again time: in transcendental schematism, imagination has an originally presentative function exercised through the pure form of time. So the ultimate possibility of the actual formation of the transcendental horizon of being — the realization of the essence of phenomenality in that essence's becoming-phenomenal — lies in time understood as intuition.

Which forces the question back one more step: what is intuition? Speaking of the pure succession of nows, Heidegger says pure intuition intuits this succession without objectifying it. To intuit without objectifying means to apprehend without grasping thematically in the manner of a being. But the critique of thematism, as already shown, is only a negative determination of the act that intends a pure ontological content. Heidegger does supply a positive one: to intuit means to receive what offers itself. Henry's verdict follows immediately. Intuition is only a name for the receptivity that secures the manifestation of the pure horizon of being. Determining time's essence as intuition does not solve the problem of the essence's receptivity; it poses it more urgently.

Bringing time into the problematic of the essence of manifestation therefore leads, despite time's claim to constitute the intrinsic possibility of objectivation, to a simple repetition of that problematic and its difficulties. Because time plays its central role in schematism as intuition, and because the intuition constituting the essence of original time as affection of itself is thought as the condition of the transcendence in which it nonetheless finds its own ground, the circularity of schematism is not removed by the appeal to time but only made more conspicuous. The repetition has its value: precisely as repetition, it confirms the problematic in the task that is properly its own, clarifying the essence of receptivity.

## **§ 25\. Clarifying the essence of receptivity and the problem of determining phenomenologically the original reality of transcendence**

Under monism's ultimate presuppositions, the essence appears only by objectivating itself in the pure horizon it sets against itself; and that horizon realizes the essence's manifestation only insofar as it manifests itself; and its manifestation is identically the act in which the essence receives it. Everything therefore turns on determining the essence of that receiving act. Its reality lies in its manifestation, so determining the essence of receptivity means determining its phenomenological status. But the act that receives the horizon is the essence itself, so the manifestation of the receiving act is the manifestation of the essence. Henry poses the resulting question as a temptation rather than a thesis: is the manifestation of the receiving act, then, nothing other than the process by which the essence objectivates itself as a horizon?

To answer yes would mean locating the receiving act's phenomenological reality in what that act produces. Only in what it produces — the opening of the pure horizon of being — would phenomenality actually come about; and the act would occur precisely because phenomenality comes about only there. Transcendence hurls itself forward because in going out toward the outside it creates, along with that outside, the foreground of light that constitutes the actual dimension of phenomenality. The milieu of exteriority that animates the act as its *telos* would then also contain that act's reality, since it secures the act's becoming-phenomenal. But the milieu of exteriority is *produced*: transcendence deploys the transcendental horizon of being. Transferring the reality of the act that opens the milieu of being onto the opened milieu means, in the absence of any explicit inquiry into that act's own original mode of manifestation, assigning to the act the phenomenological status of what it produces — a status the product holds only in and through the act. If determining the milieu's phenomenological status requires clarifying what makes its phenomenality possible, the determination refers inescapably back to the original act of transcendence. Thought that sees in the horizon's perceptibility the manifestation of transcendence forgets that this perceptibility is not the horizon's doing but transcendence's; more exactly, it lies in transcendence's ultimate capacity to be affected by the horizon. To help oneself to the horizon's perceptibility is to help oneself to the whole concrete essence, which includes not only the pure horizon but its perceptibility, identical with its essence. Since receptivity grounds that perceptibility and so constitutes the horizon's essence, reality is to be sought in receptivity and not in the horizon taken separately. Cut off from the power that secures its phenomenological formation in the act of receiving it, the horizon loses its capacity to offer itself and with it its reality. The pure horizon of being taken by itself is an abstraction. Pure time, as shown, is not real time — and the radical separation instituted between original and pure time implies their non-separation, the absolute impossibility of grasping the horizon of pure time apart from the act by which original time, affecting itself, forms it. To circumscribe the reality of the receiving act within the opened horizon is to ground the reality of original time in pure time. Or else, if the claim is well founded, it amounts to saying that the essence's essential being lies in the manifestation of the horizon — which is exactly the problem whose first clarification produced the task of understanding what makes receptivity possible. Far from grounding the reality of the act that receives the horizon, the manifestation of that horizon finds its own condition in it.

Once the horizon is ruled out as the source of transcendence's reality, thought turns to the act of transcendence taken in itself, whose essence has been understood as receptivity. That determination arises at the point where transcendence must be grasped in its essence, in what secures its internal coherence — and receptivity secures it as the power to hold near itself, by receiving it, the horizon the essence has formed. Henry then asks what holding-near more precisely consists in, and floats the answer that will occupy the next paragraphs: is holding the horizon near not identically opposing it and maintaining it before oneself, and so the very act by which transcendence, in its free surge, deploys the transcendental horizon of being?

The thesis that the horizon is received because the essence formed it was already criticized in § 23\. Henry distinguishes it from the position just rejected. Locating the receiving act's reality in the horizon merely forgets the power that opens the horizon; the present position, by contrast, explicitly thinks that power as the act of opening, as transcendence itself. Transcendence taken in itself, the actual opening of the horizon, was understood as the act of forming and receiving it, and that act was shown to be one — as the time that affects, positing the horizon of pure succession by which it will affect itself, proved to be the same as the time that is affected. Yet this unity cannot be taken as simply cancelling the duality of powers that together constitute transcendence's possibility, if analysis of the ultimate structure of original time's affection of itself in fact discloses that duality. Grasping the unity means grasping the identity of the act that forms the horizon with the act that receives it — and what announces itself in that identity is that the horizon becomes perceptible in the very act by which the essence posits it before itself. To form the horizon is to posit it before, so that what is posited before is, for that reason, seen by the act; and to be seen means to be received. Because positing-before is identically seeing, the possibility of vision — of receiving what is to be received — is immediately included in it. The horizon's actual phenomenological formation therefore lies in the act by which the essence posits it before itself, and it is by this act that perception of the horizon is made possible. Henry lets the consequence stand as a question aimed at his own earlier result: should the thesis that the horizon's actual formation lies in receptivity be reversed? Reception of the horizon presupposes its formation, not merely because the essence cannot receive what it has not formed, but more deeply because that reception consists in the act by which the essence posits the horizon before itself. And if so, was the claim that the essence of spontaneity lies in receptivity not premature?

The reversal is granted, then undercut. Reception of the horizon lies in the act by which the essence forms it by positing it before itself. But for that act to be real, it lacks self-manifestation. Henry presses for where the transcendence-act's own phenomenality shines. What manifests itself, when the emergence of phenomenality is entrusted to a transcendence that creates the milieu of being by positing it before itself, is not the act taken in itself but the original distance it fashions in giving it the form of a horizon. Phenomenality shines *over there*, in the free space transcendence has opened; that opened milieu is what becomes phenomenal and is visible as such. Transcendence's reality is not defined by the phenomenality of the horizon — it is presupposed by it. But a presupposition that never manifests itself leaves the claim to have grasped the ultimate structure of the essence of manifestation groundless, since transcendence's reality does not lie in the phenomenological milieu of being. So when the moment comes to make good on that reality and confer a phenomenological status on the originally imaginative act, secret appeal is made to the horizon's phenomenality after all. The thesis that reception of the horizon is conditioned by the movement of transcendence forming it does not coincide with the thesis locating the receiving act's reality in the opened horizon — but it borrows all its force from it.

Henry now takes up the remaining escape route: if the horizon's phenomenality does not contain the reality of the act it presupposes, perhaps that reality must be sought outside the ontological milieu of truth altogether. Might the philosophy of transcendence claim its inability to grasp the originally formative act as evidence of fidelity to the real, on the ground that truth is conditioned by an untruth older than itself? When Heidegger says that laying the ground of metaphysics leads not to the absolute and clear evidence of a first thesis or principle but deliberately directs us toward the unknown, is that not because taking the originally formative act as its ultimate theme concentrates such an inquiry on what cannot in principle be exhibited? With transcendental imagination thought stands before the abyss of metaphysics, and what it moves toward escapes it and shows itself as the unknown because it conceals itself essentially in thought's very movement toward it — as constituting that movement's essence.

The claim that the accomplished being of actual phenomenality has a non-phenomenal ground was already put in question when Henry exposed the paradox of a philosophy of consciousness forced to seek consciousness's principle in the non-conscious. That difficulty was never peculiar to it: the philosophy of being shared it as long as it sought a condition of actual manifestation in beings. The evidence that emerged was that the emergence of phenomenality is the essence's work and the essence's alone; far from enabling the ontological milieu to become phenomenal, the manifestation of the ontic is constituted by it. Once beings are set aside, the essence itself comes into view — and it was the essence that both philosophies were aiming at even while paradoxically enlisting beings within the structure of actual phenomenality. What was thought to realize phenomenality was not beings but the *object*; and if phenomenality is realized in the object, it is grounded in the power making the object possible, the ontological process of objectivation taken in and for itself. It is therefore no longer enough to oppose to beings the original manifestation of the horizon in which they appear: the real problem is the relation between that actual manifestation and the power grounding it. That relation becomes unintelligible when the production of the object's phenomenality leaves the producing itself in shadow; it ceases to be a relation at all when horizon and originating act fall apart, one into the light of the milieu it constitutes, the other into the night of its original condition. Ontological truth and the untruth grounding it become two juxtaposed essences, and in mere juxtaposition their character as essences is lost and the founding link between them goes dark. Henry then presses a series of questions at the doctrine of untruth as non-essence. Is defining untruth as an essence anything more than the ontological hypostasis of what remains wholly indeterminate? Does the determination it receives as the non-essence of truth amount to anything but passing off the absence of any real phenomenological character as a positive ontological one? What does the *non* of the non-essence of untruth negate — every actual phenomenological property, or only the one defining the horizon? And absent any inquiry into this essence's specific phenomenality, where would its positive determination come from, if not from hypostatizing the negation of the horizon's phenomenality? Can the philosophy of being then avoid the recourse that the philosophy of consciousness took when its own ground proved groundless, namely the reflexive method, which Henry has shown to be merely the methodological expression of that groundlessness? The indeterminacy does not stay confined to the non-essence: it infects what is grounded in it, the ontological essence of truth, since truth is what it is only through the action of its own ground within it. As the hypostasis of non-phenomenality in the non-essence of untruth is arbitrary, so is the hypostasis of phenomenality in the opened milieu of pure exteriority. That milieu cannot constitute the essence of truth if essence means the set of conditions making truth possible; those conditions exist, and they belong to the ontologically indeterminate milieu of the non-essence. The indeterminacy blocks any view of how the non-essence makes the horizon's phenomenality possible. And characterizing the non-essence as untruth, a purely negative phenomenological determination, only makes plainer the isolation of the two essences and their inability to constitute together the reality of manifestation's actual becoming. That the ground is merely non-phenomenal, in the sense of lacking the phenomenality proper to the horizon, says nothing about how such a ground could produce that phenomenality; introducing a ground defined solely by privation of what it must produce makes the production less intelligible, not more. Yet it is in that production that the link between the essences, and their reality, lies: the ground's reality is its power to produce what it grounds, as the reality of the grounded is in the ground. When reality has not been grasped where it is, in the ground's essential being, it must be realized outside it in the abstraction of truth's separated being, and the ground in turn realized in the abstraction of the non-essence of untruth. Dividing reality between what shows itself and what simply does not only appears to satisfy phenomenology's demands; it expresses the impossibility of penetrating what makes manifestation possible, and is nothing but the dismemberment of the concrete unity of the real, scattered into the lifeless and unconnected essences of abstraction.

## **§ 26\. The intrusion of man into the problematic of receptivity, and the fact that the original conditions of truth do not belong to the absolute milieu of exteriority**

Realizing the essence of truth outside the ground's essential being, in the abstraction of the horizon's separated being, is bound up with a dialectical reversal: by placing the principle of intelligibility squarely in the absolute milieu of exteriority, the philosophy of being deliberately forbids itself to look for that principle in the interiority of a human subjectivity. The radical exteriority of the ontological milieu is interpreted as an exteriority of truth, and so of being itself, *with respect to man*. This is how the philosophy of being takes itself to oppose the philosophy of consciousness, which locates the principle of phenomenality in man. If phenomenality lies instead in the original spatiality opened by the horizon, if that pure transcendental space is not found in the subject but constitutes the subject's being, its very subjectivity, then subjectivity is no longer enclosed in human "consciousness" — man does not possess it, it possesses him, and as the free milieu unfolding beyond every existent it alone lets man and humanity relate to any existent at all, themselves included. Once man is understood not as the origin of the light but only as what is lit by it, the philosophy of being can fairly regard itself as rejecting the idealism that credits human consciousness with producing, if not beings, at least the milieu in which they are intuited.

Whether phenomenality has its principle in the essence of man cannot be settled while we do not know what man is, and while the problematic lacks the ontological substructure needed to decide how a phenomenology of the ego stands to fundamental ontology. For the present purpose — clarifying receptivity — less is required. If placing the conditions of intelligibility in the milieu of exteriority realizes truth outside man, then the question arises of how man *receives* that truth. That man no longer carries the light of being within him does not remove but sharpens the problem of his being enlightened by it. Realizing truth outside man means nothing less than his non-belonging to the ontological milieu of being; separated from it, man is a merely ontic reality. Beings are indeed lit by the being that surpasses them in the horizon where it lets them appear. But being does not enlighten man as it enlightens the tree or the flower. For man, to be enlightened by being means to receive its light in such a way that he becomes that light himself and can in turn enlighten other beings and himself. Heidegger's own formulation concedes the point: it belongs to the truth of being to bind the essence of man to itself in a privileged way.

That privileged binding is what needs explaining. Insofar as man's essence is bound to the truth of being in a privileged way, it is nothing other than what can receive the light of that truth, enter it, reach it, and so become that truth itself. Beings are incapable of this arriving-within-truth. Light shines on them but does not penetrate them; they never become it, and it stays forever foreign to them. So it is not as a being that man can receive truth. How then does he receive it, if not on the basis, in him, of the original and pure essence of manifestation? The essence of truth cannot be realized outside man without immediately raising the problem of its reception by man, that is, of its presence in him. But more essential than how man receives the truth of the essence is how the essence receives *itself*. Man can receive truth only through the action in him of the pure ontological power that secures its reception — the essence's power to receive itself.

Bringing man into the problematic of the essence of manifestation only deflects it from its real problem and hides what is most essential in the possibility it seeks. That possibility lies wholly in the essence, not in man: it is the essence that secures in man the reception of truth, a reception in which truth conquers itself and becomes what it is, the actual essence of phenomenality. That truth resides in the essence and not in man does not mean it coincides with the absolute milieu of pure exteriority, or that the actual phenomenality of that milieu is grounded in it. Yet that is the implicit presupposition of the philosophy of being when, opposing truth to man, it realizes truth outside him in exteriority as such. Bound up with this is the forgetting of what secures in the essence, by receiving it, the possibility of its actual manifestation and so of its reality. The essence, however, is constraining: it unfolds the chain of its requirements inexorably and always adds one more term to whatever has been abstracted. The abstraction of exterior being becomes visible when man, whom truth binds to itself, has to be added back to the truth of the pure milieu. What hides in this possibility of man's being bound to the milieu of exterior being is nothing less than the possibility of that exteriority itself, the possibility of the essence of truth. The essence's own power — receiving itself — is surreptitiously handed to man.

Man's intrusion therefore has a double significance. It first masks the essence's ultimate possibility by realizing the conditions of truth in the milieu of pure exteriority; and contemporaneous with that realization is the positing, facing it, of a man stripped of the ontological power just placed outside him. But what must then be given back to this stripped man does not exactly coincide with what was placed outside him. What secures in man the possibility of opening onto the milieu of exteriority is not that milieu but the very possibility of opening onto it — receptivity as such. Receptivity is the ultimate possibility of truth: this is the second significance of man's intrusion, letting appear what the intrusion had itself first concealed.

If this second significance does not emerge more readily, it is because it stays hidden behind the prestige of the themes that habitually accompany the realization of truth in the abstract being of pure exteriority. What accompanies it is the stripping of man, now separated from the ontological power that produces phenomenality. Human finitude is the evidence seized upon by thought that locates truth in the spatiality of pure exteriority. But what does this finitude mean? For a man who no longer carries the principle of phenomenality within him, to be finite means to be separated from truth. What is separated from truth, and truth means the light of phenomenality, is in itself dark. The intrinsic obscurity of human nature is the sense of its finitude. Realizing truth in the opened milieu of exteriority casts into shadow whatever lies short of that foreground of light — and when what lies short of it is man, abandons him to the misery of his night. In Malebranche, where the conditions of truth are explicitly realized in intelligible extension, the human soul is accordingly consigned to the wholly obscure and confused sphere of feeling. Henry's note makes the structural point: for Malebranche, intelligible extension is not God himself but the face of his being that he turns toward us, our means of access in him — so that extension, exteriority, defines the conditions under which the absolute becomes phenomenal. That is monism's ultimate presupposition operating in a seventeenth-century theological register, and Henry defers to § 48 his account of Malebranche's remarkable presentiment of its insufficiency, and of the failure of that presentiment. The soul's obscurity is tied to the religious theme of the nothingness of finite, sinful man, while extension's intelligibility identifies truth with the transcendental spatiality of exteriority as such.

That the human understanding has no ideas in it, that intelligibility lies outside it in exteriority itself, still does not solve the problem of that understanding's internal possibility — its capacity to receive the ideas and be enlightened by them. This possibility becomes unintelligible when what it consists in is defined only by its radical heterogeneity from an intelligibility it is nonetheless supposed to receive. Henry cites Guéroult's question about Malebranche's understanding: what becomes of it if everything that is clarity and reason is higher than it and outside it, if it is reduced to a passive, affective faculty? Henry's response redirects the challenge. The understanding's passivity is not what should be indicted as making the reception of truth impossible; passivity is precisely what needs grounding. The conditions grounding the understanding's passive character — its essence, insofar as that lies in its capacity to *hear* truth, that is, the conditions constituting receptivity itself — are simply not contained in the essence of a humanity defined as nothing but what is not truth, and hence as constitutively incapable of any relation to it.

But man is not really what is at issue here, and man is not what is dark. The obscurity attributed to man by the existential and religious theme of finitude is the obscurity of the power that secures in him the reception of truth. That obscurity means nothing but the absence of any clarification of what constitutes, in the essence of manifestation, its most fundamental possibility. And when the obscurity claims a positive sense, the non-phenomenality by which it then defines itself is again only the hypostasis of the negation of the phenomenality proper to the pure milieu of exteriority. The obscurity of the human soul conceals within it the ontological essence of untruth: the impossibility for finite, sinful man to receive truth covers over the impossibility for the essence of untruth to unite itself with the essence of truth — that is, to ground it.

## **§ 27\. Grasping the central place of the problematic of receptivity and putting in question the ultimate ontological presuppositions of monism**

The centrality of receptivity emerges once its essence stops being interpreted first and exclusively by reference to the transcendental horizon it has to receive. Taken in that relation, receptivity turned out to be nothing but the original act by which transcendence forms the view of the horizon by positing it before itself. If the horizon's perceptibility — being itself, understood as the horizon's manifestation — is grounded in that act, then the act is the ground: in it lies the essence of manifestation, the essence of being. Receptivity is central because, understood radically, the problem of receptivity concerns the act of transcendence itself, and so manifestation in its ultimate ground. For receptivity to concern the act of transcendence is for it to define no longer the possibility of receiving the horizon transcendence opposes to itself, but the possibility of receiving *transcendence itself*. Receptivity becomes central when its essence, no longer grasped first through its relation to the horizon, is grasped in its original link with what grounds that horizon's phenomenality. For what must originally be received is not what is formed in the essence's imaginative act but what makes that forming possible — the imaginative power itself, identical at bottom with the essence.

Since to be received means to appear, the receptivity that names the possibility of receiving the original act of transcendence is identically the possibility of that act's manifestation. What is put in question, once the problematic of receptivity takes on this radical sense, is the phenomenological status of the act of transcendence — the reality of what constitutes the essence's ultimate possibility. Determining that reality is what makes receptivity, radically understood, central to the problematic of the essence of manifestation.

Radically understood, receptivity is still only the title of a problem. Receptivity means manifestation in general: the receptivity of the horizon is its perceptibility. How does the horizon become perceptible? Through transcendence. Transcendence is the *how* of the horizon's perceptibility; it states in what the horizon's receptivity, identical with its manifestation, consists. That transcendence counts as an essence rests precisely on its being this "how" — it is the essence of manifestation because the ontological power that brings phenomenality forth resides in it. More exactly, the phenomenality whose "how" lies in transcendence is the phenomenality of the *horizon*. And transcendence brings that phenomenality forth in the very act by which it posits the horizon before itself.

The decisive question follows by symmetry. As the problem of the horizon's receptivity refers back to the "how" that makes it possible, namely transcendence, so the problem of receptivity radically understood — the receptivity of transcendence itself — refers back to the "how" of that last and fundamental receptivity. Is that "how" the same as the one making the horizon's receptivity possible? Since the latter is transcendence, the question amounts to asking whether transcendence secures the possibility of its own receptivity — whether transcendence is the essence. Henry spells out the phenomenological sense. If transcendence is the "how" of the horizon's receptivity, that is because it forms the view of the horizon in positing it before itself, so that the horizon's exteriority, identical with its being seen, means the horizon's manifestation; and as manifestation, exteriority defines a dimension of phenomenality. Whether what becomes phenomenal in that dimension, as constituting that very phenomenality, is transcendence — the question in which the sense of being is decided — has already been answered: transcendence's reality does not lie in the opened milieu of pure exteriority. Which means that what becomes phenomenal in that milieu is not transcendence; that the original manifestation of transcendence is not the original manifestation of the horizon; and finally that the "how" making transcendence's receptivity possible, and so constituting its manifestation, is not the "how" making the horizon's receptivity possible. But that latter "how" is transcendence itself. Therefore transcendence does not secure the possibility of its own receptivity: the original manifestation of transcendence is not transcendence's own work. Exhibiting transcendence's incapacity to secure the possibility of its own manifestation is identically putting monism's fundamental ontological presuppositions in question, because with that incapacity comes the impossibility for transcendence to ground itself and so to constitute the essence of a ground. In that impossibility lies the abstractness of the essence of manifestation within monism's presuppositions — and that abstractness explains the failure of the problematic to determine the being of such a ground and to grasp, in its reality, the ultimate possibility of manifestation.

## **§ 28\. The abstractness of the essence of manifestation within monism's ontological presuppositions, and the problem of constructing a phenomenology of the ground**

The essence's autonomy was first thought as the non-belonging of beings to its internal structure: its concreteness, its *Selbständigkeit* (self-subsistence), lies in its power to abstract from ontic determination and hold itself in that abstraction. On this reckoning it is absurd to call the for-itself *unselbständig*, to deny that it is a self-subsistent substance — and Sartre's is Henry's example. The absurdity sharpens when the for-itself's alleged ontological insufficiency is explicitly construed as a lack of the in-itself, that is, of something non-ontological in principle: consciousness, Sartre says, is an abstraction because it harbours within itself an ontological origin toward the in-itself. If "ontological" means anything, what it names is so far from tending toward the in-itself that it is foreign to it in principle. Henry indicts the whole cluster of Sartrean themes built on this — consciousness's "ontological" deficiency, man identified with the ontological element and defined as lack, need, and desire, the vanity of that desire, and the existential descriptions of how the project fails. The vanity belongs not to man but to a thought that assigns the ontological element the project of turning itself into something ontic. The analyses fail because the concepts they rest on are confused.

The confusion deepens, and simultaneously becomes legible, in Sartre's claim that the cogito leads necessarily outside itself, that consciousness is a slippery slope on which one cannot install oneself without at once being tipped out onto being-in-itself, because as absolute subjectivity it has no sufficiency of being and refers first of all to the thing. Henry recovers the ontological presupposition beneath it. That the cogito leads outside itself does not mean that the in-itself must be added to the pure ontological element to make up the concrete reality of actual phenomenality; that reality is contained in the ontological element itself. What is really at issue, appearances notwithstanding, is the internal structure of the for-itself. Consciousness's necessary reference to something else is a reference to *alterity itself*: the cogito's movement outward is not originally movement toward beings but movement toward the outside as such, toward pure exteriority. Because phenomenality is tacitly identified with exteriority, consciousness is thought to realize itself only by going outside itself — that is, in and through exteriority. It is by being confused with exteriority that the in-itself illegitimately passes for a condition of the ontological element's own reality.

The same confusion runs through the claim that the concrete is the synthetic totality of which consciousness and the phenomenon are only articulations. Here it is no longer the in-itself but the "phenomenon" that supposedly forms, with consciousness, the concrete totality in which phenomenality is realized. But what is thought behind the concept of phenomenon is not the in-itself; it is what makes the in-itself a phenomenon — the objectivity of the object, exteriority. Stripped of its confusions, then, the appeal to the in-itself amounts to identifying actual phenomenality with exteriority as such, which is to say that a conception of the pure ontological element is at work behind it: ontological monism. Measured against that conception, one can finally say in what sense consciousness has no sufficiency of being and is "abstract". Consciousness is abstract insofar as it is separated from phenomenality — and it is separated from phenomenality insofar as it has not yet realized itself in exteriority, insofar as it remains "in itself". Consciousness is abstract in itself and real outside itself. Hence the cogito necessarily leads outside itself; hence the slippery slope. In going outside, consciousness does not go toward something else: it goes toward itself, toward its own reality. So long as it has not made that movement, it is abstract.

What, then, of consciousness taken "in itself"? If it is abstract because separated from actual phenomenality, what does it become in that state — absolutely nothing? And if nothing, why does it figure at all as one of the two terms composing the concrete synthetic totality of the real? Henry answers by pointing at what the doctrine cannot do without: the phenomenality residing in exteriority is conditioned by exteriority's *becoming*, and that becoming, the original act by which consciousness goes outward, is consciousness itself. The opposition between consciousness in itself and consciousness outside itself is therefore not the opposition of an empty, indeterminate interiority to the phenomenological milieu of exteriority. It is the opposition of that milieu to the power that engenders it. Consciousness in itself is transcendence, and the abstraction of consciousness is the abstraction of transcendence.

How can transcendence be abstract? The original ontological power that deploys the transcendental horizon of being and grounds its phenomenality in positing it before itself is precisely what grounds that phenomenality, hence its essence. Taken in itself, in the pure act of its transcendence, consciousness is the *concrete* term.
