It is rather of the horizon's manifestation that one should say what Hegel says of immediate truth: that it is the abstraction of its being-present, whose essence and being-in-itself are the absolute concept, the movement of its having-become. As the movement in which the horizon's exteriority has come to be, transcendence is the being-in-itself of the present and so the essence of truth. Why then is this essence designated as the *unselbständig* term, why does consciousness taken in itself have no sufficiency of being? Because it is separated from actual phenomenality — because in itself it does not appear. The abstraction of transcendence means its non-phenomenality. Henry then names the paradox that governs the whole chapter: the ground is stripped of its reality at exactly the moment its reality is to be phenomenologically determined, that is, at the moment such determination proves impossible. Transcendence appears alternately as the concrete term and the abstract term, and not by accident. It is concrete as long as the condition of the phenomenality realized in exteriority must be thought as exteriority's becoming; it ceases to be concrete, ceases to be a condition, as soon as one has to say what it *is*. Then it is nothing but something "abstract" without sufficiency of being. Being is withdrawn from the ground at the very moment the being of the ground is asked after. In consenting to the absurdity of placing reality outside the ground, the problematic is still obeying the great law of being: it looks for being where being appears. Because manifestation resides in exteriority, being is placed outside the ground, in exteriority as such. Reality shifts as manifestation shifts.

Determining the being of the ground as "being outside its being" is in conformity with monism. What stays wholly indeterminate in such a determination is the ground itself in what makes it a ground, its being — since the ground's being-outside-itself is possible only on the basis of the ground insofar as it grounds its own being-outside-itself. Being cannot be placed outside the ground, reality cannot be situated in exteriority, without raising the question of the ultimate ground of that reality: the being of the ground, not as being-outside-itself, but as what grounds that. So a problematic that thinks the possibility of phenomenality under the title "consciousness" must come back to what consciousness is "in itself". This abstract consciousness, which can only be criticized yet cannot be dispensed with, which re-enters the analysis at the very moment it is pronounced abstract, testifies that thought locating reality in exteriority cannot altogether forget what is implied in the idea of a ground.

But consciousness is necessarily abstract precisely insofar as reality lies outside it, in exteriority — so one must return to exteriority, to which consciousness refers. The problematic then falls into a dialectical predicament, ceaselessly referred from the essence to the essence's being-outside-itself and back. And is what gets legitimated in that shuttle not the master idea of dialectic — that only the totality, as synthesis, is concrete? Was the concrete not defined precisely as the synthetic totality of which consciousness and the phenomenon (that is, exteriority) are only articulations? Henry's objection is structural: can what has the character of a ground enter a synthesis as one element? Must not what makes it a ground already have been lost for it to become the abstract term that needs the other? The recourse to the dialectical schema comes exactly when the problematic proves unable to determine the ground's reality. Unable to determine reality in the ground, it posits reality outside the ground, in the grounded; but the grounded refers back to the ground. Faced with its own inability to grasp reality in either of its two terms, each referring to the other, thought imagines it escapes by hypostatizing the reality that eludes it in the total being of the synthesis — as if *Selbständigkeit* could result from joining two *unselbständig* elements. The synthesis would first have to be possible. But incessant passage from one term to the other is no real link; it is the panic of a thought spinning between them without finding what it seeks, which sees no way out of the vortex except to declare that the movement — that is, its own inability to grasp reality — is reality itself.

The dialectical predicament is not removed but brought to its highest tension when the shuttle is stopped by identifying the two terms, flattening essence and exteriority onto one another. That identification is performed when it is said that the field in which *Erscheinen* (appearing) comes to intuit itself is made of appearing itself and by it. Taken in indeterminate generality the proposition is true: it announces the essence's decisive character, being the ground of its own manifestation, which is exactly what it is for the essence of manifestation to *be* a ground. But this character cannot simply be asserted; it has to be grasped in its possibility, and that possibility lies in the manifestation of the ground itself, of transcendence as such. Henry credits the formula with not evading this: the manifestation of the act of appearing is included in the claim that what becomes phenomenal in the pure field of phenomenality is that act itself. The field is where appearing comes to intuit itself precisely because the field is made of appearing. But the field is also said to be made *by* it — which invites reflection on appearing insofar as it is not merely what becomes phenomenal in the field, not merely the field itself, but what creates it. And what creates the phenomenological field is not the field but transcendence. The evidence that then presents itself is that the whole formula rests on a confusion, more exactly on the ambiguity of "appearing", which designates at once the phenomenality of the transcendental horizon and transcendence itself. The sense of the confusion is clear: it is the attempt to determine the ground's reality by conferring a phenomenological status on it. But the phenomenological identification of transcendence with the horizon performs that determination badly. Far from removing the ground's phenomenological indeterminacy, the identification is *made possible* by it — transcendence can be identified with a horizon it is not only insofar as its own original mode of revelation stays wholly unclarified. Because that mode is unclarified, or rather wholly unknown, the horizon's mode of manifestation is simply substituted for it. The identification therefore implies an ontological identity that the whole context of the problematic denies, and it turns out illusory on phenomenological grounds too: in the manifestation of the horizon the problematic seeks in vain the principle of a phenomenology of transcendence, helping itself to something it does not have, since the horizon's manifestation is possible only through transcendence — that is, precisely on the basis of what escapes it.

That the being of the ground escapes the problematic just where it tries to grasp it in the horizon's manifestation shows in another way: transcendence is rather what does *not* show itself in the truth of that field, and so is the ontological essence of untruth, older than the field. As soon as transcendence is understood in its ontological character as ground, it withdraws from the horizon's phenomenality. And that at the moment of withdrawing it is simply hypostatized in the night of untruth attests the failure, in both directions it takes, of the attempt to assign transcendence a positive phenomenological status and thereby determine the being of the ground.

## **§ 29\. Exhibiting the ontological motive behind the problematic's inability to construct a phenomenology of the ground and to give content to the idea of the formal structure of autonomy**

The failure occurs precisely where the problematic faces its most proper task, so the failure itself calls for explanation. Excluding beings from the internal structure of the essence of manifestation means that this essence itself appears — and it can do its work and be what it is only because it appears. The essence acts if it shows itself; because it shows itself, it is the essence of manifestation. But being the essence of manifestation also implies that this self-manifestation is accomplished *by* the essence: the possibility of the self-manifestation of the essence of manifestation lies in that essence, which is therefore the ground of its own manifestation, and so autonomous. The concept of the essence's autonomy thus carries a double presupposition, both members of which the earlier elaboration of autonomy's formal structure brought out: that the manifestation accomplished through the essence of manifestation is the manifestation of that very essence, and that the essence grounds it. The first was thought as the positive sense of *Selbständigkeit* — the immanence of phenomenal becoming to the essence of phenomenality designates that essence as what becomes phenomenal within that becoming, which in turn is conditioned by the essence. The possibility of *Selbständigkeit* must be exhibited if the essence's manifestation is to be more than a pious wish. The claim that the field in which appearing comes to intuit itself is made of appearing and by it satisfies both requirements: that the act of appearing appears means the essence of manifestation shows itself and so can act; that this manifestation is appearing's own doing means the act grounds its own manifestation.

A further and genuinely essential presupposition belongs to the determination of appearing. If the appearing that comes to intuit itself in the phenomenological field is appearing taken as what creates that field's phenomenality, then the act that grounds its own manifestation shows itself *as* that ground. It appears qua ground of its own manifestation. And in this determination of the ground's being as what shows itself, does the positive sense of *Selbständigkeit* — the essence's manifestation — not simply coincide with what makes it possible? That possibility stops being abstract, stops being a condition \= x, if it exhibits itself in the field it grounds as that which grounds it. The problematic that seeks to clarify the essence of the phenomenon is equal to its task, and reaches its goal, when what makes the manifestation of the essence of manifestation possible — the being of the ground — is determined in its reality. That determination is what a phenomenology of the ground would be, and with it the essence's *Selbständigkeit* would no longer be a presupposition but something exhibited in its possibility.

The elaboration of autonomy's formal structure nevertheless stays formal, and the conditions it enumerates remain empty presuppositions, so long as one question goes unanswered: what is appearing? That the act of appearing appears, grounds its own appearing, and appears as that ground, suggests it is self-sufficient — but says nothing while the word "appearing" remains, each time, wholly indeterminate. Henry presses the point into a series of objections against his own schema. Can the distinction between appearing and its manifestation, between the act as what becomes phenomenal in the field of being and the same act as what grounds that field's phenomenality, be maintained if what is to be understood by "appearing" is not only indeterminate but consequently undifferentiated? Can the division, within the work of manifestation, between what accomplishes the work and what is accomplished by it claim any legitimacy, despite its logical appearance, if what is to be thought under each of the separated terms is in fact the same thing, "appearing"? Is such a division not merely logical? Is the effort to identify the visibility of the open field of phenomenality with the power that opens it and renders it visible not idle, if the unity being promoted is nothing but the empty identity of a tautology? Behind the coincidence of appearing and the field in which appearing comes to intuit itself, if that field is made of appearing and indeed *is* appearing, what remains but the bare, wholly indeterminate act of appearing, which one has merely seen fit to name twice? And if the distinctions prove illusory, does the very idea of a formal structure of the essence's *Selbständigkeit* not look needlessly complicated, or rather empty and groundless?

Looked at closely, the elaboration is not formal in itself; it is caught up in the advance of the problematic aiming at the essence of manifestation, and it proceeded as a clarification. The idea of autonomy emerged *within* that work. Far from being a presupposition of the analysis, it is its result — or if it is a presupposition, only in the derived sense that what it points to is, in the order of reality, the absolute presupposition. The problematic meets the idea of autonomy, in which the conditions of reality are defined, precisely when it comes into contact with that absolute presupposition, the essence of all reality. Autonomy's formal structure is the expression of the essence's internal structure, and for that reason the idea is neither formal nor empty. Henry insists on the direction of travel: thought did not move from the idea, as a heuristic guide, to the reality the inquiry explicates. The idea of autonomy was born from the clarification of what has been understood as reality, the essence of manifestation, gathering in its concept the conditions the analysis had itself disengaged. For thought sunk in its ontological work, the idea of autonomy is *a posteriori*. Yet at the point where thought is brought before what makes the essence of manifestation an essence — before its own object — the idea presents itself as a concept retaining everything acquired so far, in such a way that this content, suddenly synthesized and illuminated, also defines rigorously the task it must now match. The idea of autonomy is still only a question, but a question elaborated by the phenomenological advance of the analysis: a question that is a result, a philosophical question. With it the problematic becomes transparent to itself and understands itself in its aim. The idea of autonomy is now a guiding idea.

That the essence's autonomy is still only an idea shows that although the goal is now clearly defined, the means to reach it are lacking. The idea is not empty but the index of concrete ontological work: it lets the problematic recognize its own insufficiency in being unable to supply the idea with effective content. And it is no accident that the problematic turns against the idea sprung from its own advance, questioning whether it means anything at all, at exactly the moment it cannot fill it. When does that moment come? When the being of the ground must be determined in its reality. The idea of autonomy is nothing but the idea of that necessary determination. Because the determination fails — because it turns out to be a fundamental ontological indeterminacy — the idea of autonomy looks formal and empty.

Wherein does that formality and emptiness consist? In giving appearance itself as the ground of appearance. But the context lends this empty tautology a particular sense. Within it, appearance is rigorously defined: it means the visibility of the transcendental horizon of being. Because the idea of the essence's autonomy arises within the phenomenological advance of the analysis, the elements composing its formal structure are not originally indeterminate or uncertain. No more than the concept of appearance (which is the horizon's), is the idea of the ground originally a mere logical presupposition: the ground is transcendence itself. Originally — that is, within the movement of clarification in which they figure — the elements composing autonomy's formal structure are *different*, and understanding that difference is identically understanding their unity. Only when the ground's own being is determined can what it grounds be understood from it, in its unity with it. To determine the ground's own being is to exhibit transcendence's original mode of revelation. Lacking any idea of that mode, the problematic can determine transcendence's being only by conferring on it the phenomenological status of the horizon. Poverty of means is what drives a thought moving within monism to identify the structural elements it had itself distinguished in the essence. Once the ground coincides with the appearance it grounds and *is* that appearance, distinguishing them is indeed a useless complication and their identity is the empty identity of tautology. But is the identical term, needlessly named twice, anything but an empty word? It is the appearing that says everything and says nothing: the appearing that appears, grounds its appearing, and appears as such — as if the formalism of all these relations could say what the act of appearing consists in and how it is genuinely possible.

Or else, if that act has a sense, it is the one it has in the problematic's context, where it designates the manifestation of being in the form of a horizon. That this manifestation is possible only in and through transcendence sets the problematic its task, determining the being of transcendence itself; and the project of that determination is precisely what the idea of autonomy's formal structure elaborates. That the idea loses its sense when the problematic proves unable to carry out that task brings the problematic at last before the question of *why* the determination always and inevitably fails. Why does a problematic to which transcendence supplies the idea of a ground prove unable to determine that ground's being? Why does transcendence withdraw from thought at the moment thought would seize it? Henry breaks this into two: from what thought does transcendence withdraw, such that grasping the being of the ground becomes impossible for it, and what does "withdraw" mean? To withdraw means not to show oneself. The thought to which transcendence does not show itself is the thought that thinks manifestation as the manifestation of the horizon — which means that transcendence does not manifest itself in the form of that horizon, is not what becomes phenomenal in the field the horizon constitutes. Understanding this impotence repeats, in its sense, its course, and its results, the problematic of receptivity at the point where that problematic grasped its own centrality. What the repetition brings to light is the radical insufficiency of the presuppositions gathered under the title of ontological monism.

That insufficiency puts the problematic in a paradoxical position. How can it miss the ground when the idea of the ground presents itself to it — and not as the formal idea of a ground in general, but as the determinate idea of transcendence? Is it so destitute if it is in possession of the very power that secures the manifestation of being? Henry's answer is that philosophy often helps itself to what it does not have. The idea of a ground containing the ultimate possibility of manifestation may well present itself under the determinate idea of transcendence; but is the problematic in possession of that ground so long as it has not clarified the origin of its knowledge of it, the origin of the idea of transcendence itself? With that idea something is given to the problematic which does not belong to the presuppositions it acknowledges as its own — if transcendence's manifestation is not transcendence's work. And that is exactly what illuminates the paradox: the problematic cannot ground the idea of the ground on which it claims to rest. But what remains groundless is not merely the idea of the ground; it is the ground itself. The problematic's inability to determine the being of the ground originates in the ground's own inability to produce itself in and by itself in the actual dimension of phenomenality — which is identically transcendence's inability to secure its own manifestation. Does the manifestation of the horizon opened by transcendence not at least give the problematic one real dimension of phenomenality? No: because that horizon is opened by transcendence, it is nothing so long as transcendence's being is not given. Not containing the conditions of the horizon's actual manifestation, the philosophy of transcendence cannot ground the manifestation of transcendence either, cannot say what it consists in or how it comes about. Strictly, the totality of the conditions of any manifestation whatever escapes it. Manifestation as monism understands it is not merely one-sided; it is abstract in the sense that, on those presuppositions alone, it does not occur.

And yet the horizon does manifest itself, being does show itself — so the transcendence making that manifestation possible is something rather than nothing. The reality of transcendence is constantly presupposed by ontological monism without that ultimate presupposition figuring among the presuppositions by which monism defines itself. How can the reality of transcendence fail to be given to a thought that consciously and explicitly makes transcendence its ground? How can transcendence be a presupposition foreign to the philosophy of transcendence? Only if transcendence presupposes something other than itself — if, paradoxically, transcendence's reality is not constituted by transcendence. For transcendence, to be real means to be given, to be received; its reality is identically its manifestation. Because its manifestation is not its own work, its reality does not reside in it but in the power that secures that manifestation, in the essence that receives it. The essence securing transcendence's receptivity is the original essence of revelation.

An ontological determination of the original essence of revelation is now required, and it will exhibit that essence as immanence.

## **§ 30\. The ontological determination of the original essence of revelation as immanence. Immanent content and transcendent content**

Recognizing that it cannot fill the idea of autonomy it has itself produced brings the problematic before the poverty of its means and the insecurity of its ultimate ontological horizons: its own ontological deficiency is what it now has, while the ground it claimed to assign to all manifestation escapes it. But exhibiting monism's insufficiency stops being merely negative once the insufficiency is *understood*. Understanding the failure in its origin and its deep ontological motive already contains elements belonging to a positive determination of the reality that eludes it. What positive elements? Henry's answer: the reason the ground's being conceals itself is now available to the problematic — and that reason is contained in the ground, indeed is the ground itself.

The reason is that transcendence's manifestation is not transcendence's work, and what this implies must now be thought as a positive determination. What does it mean for a manifestation not to be transcendence's work? Transcendence's work is to open a horizon: the phenomenological formation of the transcendental horizon of being in the act that creates exteriority. So not to be transcendence's work means to arise, be accomplished, and be maintained independently of the movement by which the essence hurls itself forward as a horizon — independently of objectivation, in the absence of all transcendence. Yet the manifestation in question is the manifestation of transcendence itself. So the original act of transcendence is revealed independently of its own forward surge, independently of the movement by which it projects itself outside itself; it is revealed *in itself*, where "in itself" means without surpassing itself, without going outside itself. What does not surpass itself, does not hurl itself outside itself, but remains in itself without leaving or quitting itself, is in its essence immanence. Immanence is the original mode in which the revelation of transcendence is accomplished, and as such the original essence of revelation.

Understanding monism's inability to fill the idea of autonomy repeated the problematic of receptivity, and that problematic, once it understood itself, yielded a positive result too: the concept of receptivity splits in two, according to whether it refers to the horizon in which the essence objectivates itself or to the original power that deploys that horizon. What differs in the two cases is not only the reality to be received but, more essentially, the *mode* of reception considered in itself. Indeed the realities differ only in virtue of the mode of reception proper to each; more exactly, where ontological reality is concerned, reality is not discernible from the mode of reception in and by which it is defined. Transcendence and the horizon are different ontological realities precisely because the mode in which each is originally received is different. The mode in which the horizon is received is transcendence, and because that receptivity is constituted by transcendence it is determinate in its own nature — which is why the reality it receives is determinate too, is a horizon. But the mode in which the horizon is received is not what grounds transcendence's own receptivity. Since this latter mode is not the power that forms the horizon by hurling itself outside itself, it is not merely "different" from that power; its characterization is positive, and Henry states it as follows: in the internal structure of this original mode of receptivity, transcendence is not included. What gets defined is the internal structure of an essence, if it is true that transcendence does not operate in it. An essence in which transcendence does not operate is an essence that does not divide, does not separate from itself, but remains in itself. The essence of the original receptivity securing the reception of transcendence is immanence. And determining the essence of original receptivity is identically determining its *content*: constituted by immanence, the original mode of receptivity reaches its content without moving or surpassing itself toward it, so that the ontological reality constituted by that pure content is in no way transcendent to it and is not posited before it as a horizon. A content that is neither exterior nor foreign to the essence of receptivity in its original accomplishment is an *immanent content*.

Henry immediately blocks the loose sense of the term. Calling this content immanent does not merely say that it is given to the power whose office is to receive it. That is the too-general and ontologically indeterminate use, indicating only that a content is "given in fact" and so actually apprehended — as when one speaks of a content "immanent to consciousness", meaning that it effectively enters that sphere and is really reached. What stays wholly indeterminate in this use is nothing less than the mode in which the reception occurs, that is, "consciousness" itself. And the ontological indeterminacy of the mode of reception is identically the ontological indeterminacy of the content received. One and the same indeterminacy afflicts the act of appearing in its form and in its pure ontological content — that is, the essence of manifestation, which the problematic was supposed to clarify.

Or else, when the indeterminacy is lifted and the problematic does take up its task, the determination is not free: it proceeds under presuppositions that forbid any rigorous ontological grasp of a content's immanence. Once "immanent" means more than "received by consciousness", that is, more than an indeterminate "appearing", and once the mode of reception itself becomes a problem, the structure of that mode is always and inevitably understood — explicitly or not — in the light of a philosophy of transcendence. The content received and thereby "actually given" then means: reached by consciousness in the act by which consciousness transcends itself toward it. Immanence paradoxically takes on the sense of objectivity.

Does calling a content immanent not nonetheless determine it more precisely, by opposing it to the "transcendent" content of consciousness? If the opposition has a sense, if experience really does divide into contents belonging to it as immanent and contents still transcendent to it, must the mode in which each is received not differ in each case? And if immanence names precisely that mode, must it not be determined as such and so constitute the essence of a specific kind of receptivity? Henry's answer is that Husserl's distinction between immanent and transcendent contents of experience is *inessential*, because the essence of those contents is the same: the ontological power ultimately making them possible by securing their reception is in every case transcendence. The content first improperly called immanent shows up as transcendent to consciousness as soon as the problematic stops recording that the content belongs as given to consciousness's real experience and asks instead after the condition of possibility of that givenness — the ontological power that originally secures its reception. Then the content immanent to consciousness insofar as it enters the sphere of its actual experience appears as transcendent, since what lets it enter that sphere is the ontological power projecting it into the foreground of light where it can appear: transcendence itself.

Where, then, does a principle of distinction lie, if not in the essence securing reception? Contents are called immanent or transcendent according to whether they are merely intended without being given (the unseen faces of a cube) or are given and reached in person in the act by which consciousness orients itself toward them. Henry notes in passing that Husserl's immanence–transcendence distinction has further aspects whose analysis he cannot undertake here, and which would confirm the book's general theses. Whether or not it finds adequate intuitive fulfilment, this act of orientation-toward is the ontological condition of "immanent" and transcendent contents alike, and so their common essence. Because they are conditioned by consciousness's act of orientation, that is, by transcendence, these contents belong to one and the same milieu, the transcendent ontological milieu of the horizon. The distinction is internal to that milieu and cannot set another ontological milieu, another dimension of existence and revelation, against it. Its inessentiality shows in the fact that the contents it sorts can trade places: a transcendent content can become immanent and conversely. So immanence is a contingent character of such a content, since the content can equally take on the opposite one. That contingency has its reason in the essence: the finitude inherent in the horizon of transcendence means the various contents that can appear in it can do so only successively, so that any actual manifestation in an originary mode of presentation is, for each content, a passing and hence contingent determination.

Which contents are these, for which immanence and transcendence are contingent determinations? Contents capable of appearing *within* the horizon of transcendence — ontic contents. The distinction between immanent and transcendent contents taken as ontic contents really given or merely intended is not only inessential; it is fundamentally inadequate to a problematic aiming at the essence of manifestation and its pure ontological content. For while the particular mode in which an ontic content is given is contingent and variable with respect to it, it is a law of essence that the content proper to an essence is not contingent but rigorously determined by it. Because it originates in the essence of transcendence, the pure ontological content of that essence is radically determined by it: transcendence, being transcendent, names the essential mode of being of that content. In the same way, for a pure ontological content to be immanent is to be radically determined in its being by a specific mode of appearing and revelation — by the original essence of revelation insofar as that essence resides in immanence.

What does this determination consist in? In the mode in which the revelation occurs. Determined by immanence, that is, by an original mode of receptivity in possession of its content without moving or surpassing itself toward it, such a content was understood as what offers itself without pro-posing itself as a horizon, what reveals itself otherwise than in the form of an outside and without becoming one. This suffices to rule out, as radically improper, subsuming under immanence any content really given to consciousness where being given means offering itself as a transcendent content, through the mediation of a horizon. The impropriety is not only that thought thereby forgets its ontological design and reverts to ontic contents and their variable characters; more gravely, on the ontological plane itself it assigns to the essence of a fundamental ontological structure what is excluded from it in principle. To give the concept of immanence a rigorous ontological sense is, on the contrary, to understand the internal structure of the essence it names as defined by that exclusion of all transcendence. Without such a sense the problematic loses its way entirely and permanently bars itself from grasping the ultimate possibility of the essence it aims at. But defining immanence by the exclusion of transcendence does more than make it impossible to call any ontologically transcendent content immanent, whether ontic or the pure ontological content constituted by the horizon: it yields the positive determination of an immanent content in the strict sense. That determination requires recalling that a content proper to the ontological power securing its reception is radically determined in its being by the essence that receives it. To belong to the essence means to enter as a constitutive element into its internal structure — and how a pure ontological content does so depends on the nature of that structure. Since transcendence is excluded from the internal structure of the essence of immanence, immanence's own ontological content is not exterior to it: the essence of immanence is not separated from its content. Not to be separated from its content means, for immanence, not to hold that content before itself, not to receive it as something other in the milieu of alterity, as something different. Where then does the reality of such a content lie, if it is neither separate from nor different from the ontological reality of the essence? Henry's conclusion is that the pure ontological content of the essence of immanence is constituted by that essence. To give the concept of an immanent content a rigorous ontological sense is to understand it in its ontological identity with the essence that receives it — to understand it as that essence itself. The ontological reality of a content immanent to the essence is identically the ontological reality of the essence.

Immanence enters the problematic as the mode in which the reception of a content is accomplished — more precisely, as the internal structure of the possibility of an original reception in general. Since the original essence of receptivity is defined in its internal structure by immanence, it itself constitutes the pure content it receives. What the original essence of receptivity receives is itself.

To receive a content is to be affected by it. Since the content received by the original essence of receptivity is constituted by that essence, it is by itself that the essence is affected when it receives what belongs to it, when it receives itself. To be affected by oneself, to affect oneself, is to constitute oneself as auto-affection. Auto-affection is the constitutive structure of the original essence of receptivity.

An objection arises at once, and Henry states it in its full force. Does auto-affection not rather name the mode in which the essence affects itself according to monism's presuppositions? Was it not understood as the ontological process by which the essence sets itself over against itself and pro-poses itself as a horizon? Is pro-posing oneself as a horizon not exactly how the essence affects itself, and so the essence of auto-affection? Does the auto-affection of time in schematism not exhibit this ultimate ontological structure as the very possibility of auto-affection in general? If original time as affection of itself affects itself through the mediation of the horizon of pure time, in which it projects itself as the threefold unity of succession, is that not because affection mediated by a horizon is the only way for the essence to affect itself, that is, to manifest itself?

The evidence emerging under this pressure defines the next task: to bring to light, and thereby dispel, the fundamental ambiguity in the concept of auto-affection.

## **§ 31\. The fundamental ambiguity in the concept of auto-affection. Auto-affection and affection by itself**

From the moment the problematic set out to think the first condition of the essence's being operative — the manifestation of the essence — it understood that manifestation not as manifestation plain and simple but, spontaneously, as manifestation *to itself*. The appearing of the act of appearing was read as appearing's appearing-to-itself. Henry endorses the spontaneous reading: the ontological possibility of the essence's manifestation lies in the essence's referral back to itself. This means that the essence manifests itself *to itself*, and only because it does so can it be what it is, an operative essence, an essence that appears. Nor is appearing a contingent property added to the act of appearing: that the act of appearing appears is what makes it appearing as such. Because the appearing of the act is conditioned by its appearing to itself, what ultimately makes such an act possible lies in this relation to self. Referral back to itself is what determines the act of appearing in its essence.

The entry of auto-affection into the problematic is therefore not contingent. If the essence's manifestation is itself made possible by appearing's referral back to itself, the concept of auto-affection is neither formal nor empty: its content is what secures the ultimate possibility of that manifestation. Auto-affection names the essence of manifestation grasped in what makes its own manifestation ontologically possible. The essence affects itself because it is operative only if it appears, and appears only if its own manifestation is not lost to it but gathered into it and held there, so that, retained by the essence, that manifestation shows itself to the essence and reaches actual phenomenal condition. Or rather, the essence manifests itself to itself, manifests itself at all, only because it can affect itself. Its power to take hold of itself rather than let itself go into the abandonment where it would be given over to the night of non-phenomenality, its capacity to hold itself out of that abandonment and stay near itself, is exactly what lets it, while remaining with itself, appear to itself, be for itself. So the manifestation of the essence of manifestation is made actual by the ontological process in which the essence can affect itself. And since that manifestation was thought as the condition making the essence actual — letting it be the act of appearing insofar as it appears — auto-affection determines the essence of manifestation as what makes it possible.

The more decisive auto-affection's work appears, the more urgent it becomes to clarify auto-affection's own internal ontological structure. If that structure is constituted by the essence's relation to itself, nothing further has been said about it so long as that relation is not itself grasped in its intrinsic possibility. Determined as having for its content the ontological necessity by which the essence enters into relation with itself in the phenomenal becoming where it is realized, the concept of auto-affection is in fact indeterminate, and stays in fundamental ontological obscurity, until the problematic settles the nature of the power that lets the essence enter into relation with itself — that is, manifest itself. The nature of that power, the internal structure of auto-affection, is now what is at issue.

And at the very moment it asks after that structure, the problematic finds it already has the elements to define it rigorously. The essence's power to affect itself is identically its power to receive itself. Auto-affection names the essence of receptivity insofar as that receptivity is both the essence's doing and about the essence. Insofar as the receptivity is the essence's doing — the essence is what receives — the essence is affected. Insofar as the receptivity is about the essence — the essence is the ontological content received — the essence is affected by itself. Auto-affection is the internal structure of an essence whose property is to receive itself. Understanding that structure therefore depends on the link between the essence and its content when the content is constituted by the essence — and the nature of that link, the manner in which the essence receives a content constituted by it, is precisely what the problematic of receptivity has clarified.

What was first taken to ground the essence's power to receive itself, that is, to manifest itself to itself, was the ontological process by which the essence objectivates itself and pro-poses itself as a horizon; the horizon then constitutes the pure ontological content the essence receives. But the most important result of the problematic of receptivity was that the ontological power securing the horizon's reception, and having the horizon for content, itself constitutes a content: *transcendence is received*. The decisive advance came when the problematic represented to itself the implicit presuppositions under which the problem of receptivity had always — by Henry's own analysis too, at first — been interpreted as the reception of an *exterior* content. Those presuppositions govern the spontaneous, pre-critical understanding of the essence of manifestation as representation. Because representation essentially pro-jects before itself what it represents, the question arises how it can receive the content so projected. The interpretation of receptivity as the reception of an exterior content therefore originates in monism, and specifically in the understanding of manifestation as representation. Its most immediate effect was to make the very idea of a reception that is not the reception of an exterior and foreign content inaccessible to philosophy. Henry then complicates the charge in a way worth marking. Can that incapacity really be imputed to thought moving within monism, if the pure ontological content the essence represents is constituted by that essence itself? The reproach of failing to rise to the conception of an essence that receives itself can be levelled only against a thought that takes receptivity to be the reception of an *ontic* content. Once the content whose reception is to be grounded is interpreted not as a being but as the pure ontological element letting beings appear, it is manifestly the essence that constitutes the content it receives. By what right could such a content be called exterior to the essence if it is nothing but the essence? A problematic that understands the pure ontological content into which the essence projects itself in order to represent itself to itself as constituted by that essence therefore does possess the idea of a receptivity whose content is not foreign to it.

How, though, does the essence receive a content that is not different from it — how does it represent that content to itself, not as a foreign reality, but as the reality it itself is? Precisely because receiving such a content means, for the essence, representing it, and because representation is the ontological act that posits its content before itself, the essence's reception of itself in representation is still the reception of an exterior content, a reception operating in and through exteriority. The ambiguity of "exterior content" now surfaces. The represented content is certainly not exterior to the essence in the sense of being different from it, and this non-difference is identically its pure ontological character, which follows from the content's entering the unitary structure of the essence, the process of objectivation taken as a whole. Because it is the essence that objectivates itself in the pure ontological content it represents, that content belongs to it in two senses: as an element of the process constituting it, and because this element, interior to the essence, is the essence's own representation. But the *mode* of that belonging is what has to be ontologically determined — and exteriority is precisely the ontological character of this belonging, the mode in which the essence receives the pure content that it is. To give "exterior content" a rigorous ontological sense is to extend it to every represented reality whatever, and first of all to the ontological reality of the essence itself insofar as it projects itself as a horizon in the pure milieu of exteriority. Because it is constituted by that horizon, by a milieu of pure exteriority, the content the essence represents in objectivating itself is an exterior content in a radical sense: exteriority is no added property but determines that content in its own ontological reality. So when a problematic working within monism claims a mode of receptivity whose content is not exterior to it, all it has in view is the content's purely ontological character, the fact that it is constituted by nothing other than the essence and is in that sense identical with it. Yet it is in the ontological milieu of exteriority that this content is what it is, a content that manifests itself to the essence. That the content is the essence changes nothing in the mode of manifestation that determines it essentially as exterior. The essence manifests itself to itself *as a horizon*. The identity of the essence with its content is an identity in difference, since the milieu of exteriority is also the milieu of a radical alterity: if it is the essence that manifests itself to itself, it manifests itself as other than itself, as precisely what is other.

This appears to threaten the foundations of a phenomenological ontology, which rest on the identity of ontological reality with appearance as such. What becomes of that identity if the manifestation of a content radically other than the essence is nonetheless interpreted as the manifestation of the essence? That it is the essence that manifests itself in the horizon of alterity is an empty presupposition if the look of that horizon is the only phenomenological element the problematic has. On what does it rest in going beyond the given appearance to the metaphysical claim that this appearance is the essence's? Or does the claim have no metaphysical character at all, and mean simply to identify the essence with the phenomenological appearance available — the appearance of the horizon as such? But then the character of alterity in that appearance can no longer be accounted for, if the essence really is identical with such a content. And the whole context of the problematic has shown that it is not. How, though, can a pure ontological content fail to be identical with the essence, if it is the essence that objectivates itself as the horizon it proposes and into which it projects itself in order to manifest itself to itself?

The way out is to hold strictly to results already obtained. The transcendental horizon of being is not the essence but the product of its imagination; and in its imaginative act, as creative intuition, the essence can produce nothing but nothingness, since what it creates is nothing ontic. Far from implying ontological identity with the essence, the horizon's purely ontological character marks it only as created by the essence — and in a creative relation the created does not merge with what creates it. The pure ontological content of the essence of representation has an origin in the essence with which it does not coincide. This makes the ambiguity of "the essence manifests itself to itself as a horizon" plain. What manifests itself as the transcendental horizon of being is the phenomenological form of that horizon, not the essence. Or, if the horizon manifests the essence, it does so in a quite different sense — where to manifest means to be the appearance *of* something, in such a way that what manifests itself in the appearance is not the thing whose appearance it is but merely refers to that thing as to what does not show itself in the appearance's actual phenomenological content. In this sense manifesting equally means concealing: indicating something as different in essence from the appearance that indicates it. The appearance is then a "mere appearance", not the essence hiding "beneath" it. In "the essence manifests itself to itself as a horizon", the form of the horizon is the mere appearance beneath which the essence hides. So the claim inevitably takes back its metaphysical sense, in which reality transgresses the appearance where it was supposed to manifest itself; and correlative to that sense is the thesis that every appearance as such is inadequate. The "critical" force this thesis carries throughout classical philosophy testifies only to that philosophy's inability to build a phenomenology of the ground. What should be called inadequate is the manifestation of the essence *as a horizon* — the form of the horizon alone, that is, the form of every actual manifestation as monism understands it. Of that one may say with Fichte that the form always veils the essence from us. Even this is not quite right. Dissociating appearance from reality always betrays a confusion: the form of the horizon can be understood as veiling the essence only on the presupposition that it is the essence that manifests itself in that form, so that the horizon's phenomenological content would be the essence under a certain form, merely an inadequate one. With that presupposition the relation between the essence and the horizon's content is misconstrued. Rigorous understanding requires holding strictly to what appears. What appears as the horizon is the phenomenological content of the horizon and nothing more: the essence that creates it does not show itself there. And because it does not, one cannot say the horizon is nonetheless the essence under a certain form — for ontological reality is not separable from the form in which it shows itself, being that form as such. The ontological reality of the transcendental horizon is identically that horizon's phenomenological content, just as the ontological reality of the essence is the pure phenomenological content in which the essence shows itself as such.

Dissociating the essence from the pure content it opposes to itself in representation yields the decisive result: in receiving the pure ontological content it represents, the essence does *not* receive itself. But receiving itself was thought to constitute the essence's power to manifest itself to itself, to be what it is. That power is therefore not constituted by the act in which the essence receives the horizon it projects: the internal ontological possibility of the essence of manifestation does not lie in representation. Understanding the essence's internal structure as ultimately constituted by its power to receive itself lays bare the radical insufficiency of monism and the impossibility of continuing to interpret the essence of manifestation on the model of representation. The result is not merely negative. The essence's power to receive itself lies in the original essence of receptivity, a receptivity whose property is to receive itself — for it is not the horizon of being that the essence receives in its original work. The horizon is indeed received, and the essence performs that reception; original receptivity is the receptivity that receives the essence itself insofar as the essence secures the horizon's reception. There are therefore two receptivities: one that receives the horizon, one that receives itself. The first is a receptivity in representation, the second a receptivity in immanence, and both are the essence's doing. Under the first mode, receptivity is representation itself — positing before oneself, and so pro-posing to oneself, a content whose ontological origin lies exclusively in that projection and which therefore coincides with exteriority as such. Under the second, receptivity is the power of receiving itself. To receive in the first sense is to create the content one receives, so that creating it is identically receiving it. To receive in the second sense is not to create the content but to *be* it, so that it is nothing exterior to the being that receives it — and so that this being is no longer free with respect to it but receives it passively, as something that does not depend on it and that it has not created, as the uncreated something that it itself is.

The doubling of receptivity clarifies the relation between receptivity's form and its content. In the receptivity of representation, form and content differ. The form lies in the essence, is the essence in the reality of the imaginative act by which it sketches a horizon. The horizon itself is a purely imaginary product; its ontological reality is not the essence's, is not reality. What the essence creates is only an image, and the transcendental horizon of being defines the ontological milieu of *unreality*. Form and content in representation therefore differ ontologically as reality and unreality. In the original mode of receptivity, by contrast, what the essence receives is its own reality, not the product of its imagination — and because the content is constituted by the essence, it is identical with the form. Only exhibiting the original essence of receptivity puts the problematic before a receptivity whose form and content are ontologically identical, and that identity defines the structure of an essence whose property is to receive itself. Since the identity is realized only in the original form of receptivity, that form alone makes self-reception possible. There are two ways for the essence to receive; there is only one way for it to receive *itself*. The duality of powers securing receptivity in general can no longer conceal the uniqueness of the mode in which the essence receives itself — the sole ontological dimension of access to the original reality of the essence, that is, of being itself.

The essence's power to receive itself is its power to affect itself, auto-affection, and this was shown to be identically its power to manifest itself to itself, to be the essence of manifestation. But this ultimate possibility was itself indeterminate: auto-affection remained a mere presupposition until it was grasped in what constitutes its own possibility, its essence. That essence is now determined: the possibility of auto-affection lies in the original essence of receptivity, in immanence.

Determining that possibility lifts the ambiguity weighing on the concept — which means rejecting the sense the problematic is first tempted to give it. Corresponding to the doubling of receptivity is a doubling of affection. Insofar as receptivity is objectivation and receiving means pro-posing to oneself the pure ontological content of a horizon, the essence is affected first of all by the horizon: to affect the act of objectivation purely, Heidegger said, means to raise some opposition against it. But under the original mode of receptivity, the act of objectivation receives *itself* before receiving the content it opposes to itself, and is affected by itself first. Transcendence's affection by itself is more original than its affection by the horizon. As regards the projective opening of the horizon this means: in the original act by which it projects the horizon that solicits it and by which it affects itself, transcendence is *already* affected. And that it is already affected in the act of forming the horizon means its original affection is independent of that horizon and of the forming act as such — independent, that is, of objectivation, hence of transcendence itself. The original essence of affection lies in immanence.

Does exhibiting an original affection in radical ontological opposition to transcendence's affection by the horizon not give the ambiguity in the concept of affection a positive, even decisive, role? Should it be lifted or deepened? Henry's answer distinguishes two ambiguities. Deepening the one disclosed by the analysis is identically exposing another, purely negative one: monism has constantly confused affection with auto-affection. Transcendence's affection by the horizon it projects is not an affection of transcendence by itself, if the ontological dissociation of the essence from the pure content it represents holds — if, in receiving that content, the essence does not receive itself. Not being an affection of transcendence by itself, it cannot rigorously be called auto-affection. Auto-affection lies neither in transcendence nor in representation. It is therefore false to say that pure affection of itself determines the deep essence of transcendence, if by pure affection of itself one means, as Heidegger does, auto-affection. And for the same reason auto-affection cannot be interpreted, as Heidegger also has it, as constituting the essence of time insofar as time is implicated in the intrinsic possibility of objectivation — that is, as transcendence.

The interpretation of auto-affection as transcendence is not accidental. Once auto-affection was understood as the ultimate possibility of the essence of manifestation, its own structure and possibility had in turn to be determined; and for that, transcendence is the only essence a thought moving within monism has. Precisely because transcendence creates an affection, that affection is taken to supply content to a concept of auto-affection whose formal structure is identically that of the essence of manifestation. The confusion is thus between affection in general and the rigorously determined concept of auto-affection — between the affection of the act of objectivation by the content it sets over against itself and the original affection of that act by itself. Because the original affection has its possibility in immanence, the concept of auto-affection is clearly defined and univocal. Henry's verdict on the ambiguity is severe: it does not mean there are two ways for the essence to affect itself; it means nothing at all. It is merely the product of a problematic that, lacking the ontological substructure and the categorial means, moves in equivocation.

Might auto-affection nonetheless take a second sense bearing on the affection of the act of objectivation by the content it represents? What is peculiar to that affection is that the content affecting the act is also produced by it: transcendence creates the horizon by which it is affected, and so creates its own affection. Since the affection originates in transcendence, is it not transcendence that affects itself through the horizon, and is transcendence's affection by itself not therefore an auto-affection?

What does it mean for transcendence to be affected "by itself"? The sense is double. On one side, transcendence affects itself insofar as it creates the horizon by which it is affected: being affected by itself means being affected by a content originating in it. This is a metaphysical claim about the affection's ultimate origin. But the problem is the ground of that claim, since the phenomenological content of transcendence's affection by the horizon contains nothing but that affection — the pure appearance of the horizon — and does not include the power that raises it. That the appearance is transcendence's doing can be asserted only if the problematic has available an affection whose actual phenomenological content is constituted by transcendence itself. Such an affection exists: it is what has been thought under the concept of auto-affection. Far from coinciding with transcendence's affection by itself in the horizon, auto-affection is that affection's presupposition.

Auto-affection gives "affection by itself" its second sense: transcendence affects itself insofar as it *constitutes* the pure ontological content by which it is affected. Being affected by itself now means not creating the content that affects it but being that content. Only in this second sense can transcendence's affection by itself be rigorously called auto-affection. Yet the identification remains doubtful in the other direction: understanding transcendence's original auto-affection as "affection by itself" threatens to reintroduce the ambiguity, and dispelling it means bringing out a further sense of "affection by itself". Applied to transcendence, must the phrase not necessarily designate the affection that is transcendence's *work*, an affection whose mode of accomplishment is constituted by transcendence? That mode is objectivation. To affect in this way is to raise a horizon; to be affected by itself is, for transcendence, to submit to the horizon it raises and pro-poses to itself, by receiving it. But when the affection of transcendence is transcendence's own work, the *content* of that affection is no longer constituted by transcendence. The relation between the two concepts therefore inverts: not their identity but their mutual exclusion is what imposes itself, once affection by itself is thought as finding its mode of accomplishment in transcendence. The resulting paradox is that transcendence cannot be affected by itself *by way of itself* — cannot, that is, be affected in conformity with the ontological process defining it in such a way that the affecting content is constituted by its own essence. In that paradox the ambiguity of "affection by itself" reappears, according to whether the phrase names the affection whose mode of accomplishment lies in transcendence or the affection whose content does. Depending on which, affection by itself coincides or fails to coincide with auto-affection, whose rigorous determination was to make possible the determination of the essence of manifestation. Merely flagging the ambiguity is not enough. Clearing up the paradox requires understanding the nature and the relation of the two modes of affection — and understanding the relation between the affection whose mode of accomplishment lies in transcendence and the affection which, as auto-affection, has transcendence for content, is identically understanding the relation between transcendence and immanence.

## **§ 32\. Immanence and transcendence**

That transcendence's auto-affection excludes rather than coincides with the affection whose mode of accomplishment lies in transcendence is not a paradox but the problematic's most proper assertion. Repeating the results of the problematic of receptivity in determining the original essence of revelation showed that reality is subordinate to the internal structure of the modes in which it is received — decisively so when the reality to be received is ontological reality itself. For an affection whose mode of accomplishment is constituted by transcendence, it belongs to the essence of the case that the reality affecting it necessarily takes the form of a horizon and is defined by it. But the ontological reality of the horizon does not coincide with the reality of transcendence. So the condition for an affection's pure ontological content to be constituted by the reality of transcendence is that the original mode of receptivity in which the affection has its essence *not* be transcendence. Excluding transcendence from the internal structure of the essence that receives it is no paradox but the evidence that emerges as soon as the subordination of ontological reality to the receptive power determining it is made perceptible. If transcendence's belonging to the internal structure of a receptive power inevitably makes that power's pure ontological content something transcendent, a horizon — which transcendence precisely is not — then transcendence's power to be what it is depends on the existence of a mode of receptivity other than transcendence: one that reaches its content without surpassing itself toward it and without receiving it as something transcendent.

This is how the subordination of reality to the essence of the receiving power now works. When transcendence is not present in the internal structure of that essence, the reality received does not take the form of a horizon before it; it is no longer anything standing before, and in this absence of all distance it is identical with the essence itself. Such a mode of receptivity exists, since the exclusion of transcendence from original receptivity turned out to have a positive sense, expressed in a specific mode of receptivity whose internal structure is immanence. The subordination of reality to this original receptive power means the possibility of a pure ontological reality no longer defined in its essence by exteriority — the possibility of a reality other than the horizon, the original ontological possibility of transcendence itself. And what makes something possible is properly called its essence. Henry states the thesis: immanence is the essence of transcendence.

Is this a positive determination of transcendence's reality, or a purely negative one that leaves indeterminate what it claims to determine? That the ontological reality given to a receptive power whose internal structure does not enclose transcendence is nothing exterior or transcendent certainly leaves room for a pure ontological content essentially different from anything that could offer itself as a horizon. Transcendence does differ essentially from such a horizon, since the purely imaginative product of the imaginative act does not coincide with the ontological reality of that act. But what follows so far from the eidetic determination of the pure content of original receptivity, on the one hand, and of the reality of transcendence taken in itself, on the other, is only the *similarity* of their formal ontological structure. On that basis the problematic can assert a priori the bare possibility that transcendence constitutes the ontological content of original receptivity and so finds in immanence the ultimate condition of its reality. That this possibility is actual — that transcendence's reality is precisely that content — still has to be shown.

Henry answers by recalling what receptivity means: to receive is to render manifest, to reveal. A receptivity that receives a pure ontological content does not leave it in indeterminacy; the content's reality is neither mysterious nor hidden to it, since it manifests itself to it, and what is exhibited in that manifestation is precisely the content's ontological reality. The concept of receptivity belongs to phenomenology, and this must not be forgotten in the ontological work of clarification. Distinguishing modes of receptivity is distinguishing fundamental modes of *revelation* of a content — and where the content is ontological, fundamental modes of revelation of ontological reality itself. Ontological reality is revealed as the receptive power is accomplished according to its modes; the differentiation of reality that follows from the differentiation of those modes is a real differentiation only because it is phenomenological. Just as the reality of the pure content of receptivity in representation is the original phenomenological reality of the transcendental horizon, so the reality of the content given to the original receptive power cannot be defined speculatively and negatively: it is a phenomenological reality, exhibiting itself as it is. For that reason the content it constitutes is not a something \= x of which we would know only that it is not the horizon and might therefore *guess* to be transcendence. The reality of the pure ontological content of original receptivity is the phenomenological reality of transcendence itself. That is why the immanence constituting the internal structure of this original mode of receptivity turns out to be the essence of transcendence: because it reveals transcendence and so makes it possible in its very being. The coincidence between the formal structure of that content and the structure of the reality of the act of transcendence is no coincidence at all — it is one and the same structure. The reality lit up in receptivity as originally exercised turns out to be identically the reality of transcendence and, in conformity with the structure of this revelation, a reality that is nothing transcendent. That the original reality of transcendence can be subsumed under this fundamental phenomenological character looks like a coincidence only because the problematic is bringing together elements it had itself distinguished in the course of its analysis. The analysis ran in two directions — one toward transcendence's original phenomenological status, the other toward the formal ontological (hence equally phenomenological) structure of the pure content of original receptivity. One and the same reality, transcendence's original reality, was at issue in both, and the subsumption is only the recognition, at the level of discursive thought, of that ontological identity.

The double labour is not idle. The phenomenological significance of the receptive power that renders the original act of transcendence manifest in its own reality is not recognized outside the movement of analysis in which the nature of that power is clarified. It is not enough to record the content of the revelation accomplished in original receptivity; *how* it is accomplished must be understood — and the revelation is not separable from that "how", being that "how" as such. It is within a specific mode of receptivity that transcendence shows itself as it is. Transcendence's ultimate possibility of being what it is does not lie in the bare revelation of its own reality. Rather, that revelation is possible as revelation of the original act of transcendence only insofar as it occurs not freely or indeterminately but in such a way that the reality it reveals — the revealed reality of the originally formative act, the original phenomenological reality of transcendence — is in itself nothing transcendent. Immanence is the essence of transcendence because it reveals transcendence, and more precisely because it reveals it in the determinate manner that makes transcendence possible in its essence.

The identity of formal structure between transcendence's reality and the pure ontological content of original receptivity now takes its full sense. It rests not merely on the essence's phenomenological power but on that power's internal structure, the mode in which it accomplishes revelation. Because the essence of receptivity is the power of rendering manifest, its content shows itself to us, and in that showing — as accomplished in the original mode of receptivity — it reveals itself to be transcendence's own reality and at the same time a reality that is nothing transcendent. The identity of transcendence with the essence's immanent content is what we *see*. But it is not merely recorded; it is understood. What announces itself in that understanding is the eidetic necessity by which the original presentation of transcendence occurs with the formal structure of an immanent content. And this understanding is not our doing: it is nothing exterior or foreign to the immediate revelation of transcendence's original reality but belongs to it essentially, or rather is identical with it. Understanding transcendence's immanent character is not superimposed on our vision; it defines what that vision is. The immanence of transcendence *is* its revelation. For this reason the word "understanding", used here for the original grasp of transcendence in its ontological structure, is fundamentally inadequate: such a grasp does not occur in the mode of an understanding, that is, on the basis of transcendence within it. In this exclusion of transcendence from the internal structure of the power that reveals transcendence in itself lies the eidetic necessity by which the revelation of transcendence is an immanent revelation. That necessity is not different from the essence of revelation; it constitutes it, is included in it, and manifests itself. The reason for the formal structure of the pure ontological content of the original essence of revelation is identically that essence itself. The structure of reason is the structure of phenomenality, and therefore a phenomenological structure. The structure of reason — the determinate mode in which revelation occurs — is the structure of revelation itself, is that revelation in the concrete mode of its actual accomplishment. In the concrete accomplishment of the original revelation of transcendence's ontological reality, the structure of that revelation is revealed. The revelation of this structure is revelation itself in the revealed "how" of its revelation, and that revealed "how" is our vision as it is. Because we *live* this vision as it is, because revelation is revealed in the "how" of its concrete accomplishment, the determination of the revealed reality by that "how" is included in it — not as an unknown law or a mysterious prescription of the essence, but as what is itself revealed within that revelation, in phenomenological identity with it. Transcendence's immanent character is not posited a priori by an analysis clarifying the conditions of objectivation by its own methods; that character, which constitutes the formal ontological structure of the original act of transcendence, arises together with the reality of that act and is essentially identical with its arising. The immanent character of the essence is therefore phenomenological in a radical sense: immanence constitutes the original phenomenological milieu of the revelation of transcendence. And since transcendence's own reality lies in its revelation, immanence is not a character — not even a phenomenological character — superadded to that reality; it constitutes its essence. Determining transcendence's formal ontological structure as immanent content stops being merely negative when it is nothing other than the revelation of transcendence's original reality in the positivity of its concrete phenomenological accomplishment. That the "how" of this revelation reveals itself within the revelation as what determines it in its essence is exactly what determines the original essence of transcendence, phenomenologically and ultimately, as immanence.

## **§ 33\. The ontological interpretation of the essence of transcendence as immanence and the internal possibility of surpassing**

Interpreting transcendence's essence as immanence clarifies and determines the internal possibility of the transcendental relation of being-in-the-world. That possibility lies in the fact that this is not a relation in the ordinary sense but a *relating-itself-to*, such that in and through this relating, the relation itself relates to what it relates to. Where does the essence of such a relation lie? Henry uses Heidegger's own examples negatively. The sides of a geometrical figure stand in relations of magnitude and position, yet no side *relates itself* to the others; the table stands in a certain relation to the wall — against it, beside it — yet the table does not relate itself to the wall, cannot, as Heidegger puts it, touch the wall. Why? Because neither can surpass itself toward what it might then stand in relation to. But the possibility of relation in the transcendental sense cannot simply be described as having its essence in transcendence; the description must at the same time exhibit the possibility of transcendence's own internal structure. Understanding being-in-the-world as essentially including a relating-itself-to accomplishes exactly that, and reverses the order of grounding: the relating-itself-to is not conditioned by transcendence but is what makes transcendence possible.

What is relating-itself-to? Henry unpacks it as *bringing itself alongside*. For a movement that bears toward something, bringing itself alongside means not separating from itself, staying near itself, remaining in itself, so that this "self", maintained and preserved throughout the movement, is carried with it to whatever the movement bears toward. And the self so maintained is the movement itself. That the movement has a self means that the movement of bearing-toward holds itself near itself in its very accomplishment — and this holding-near-itself is identically its original revelation to itself. Wherever a relation exists, it exists *for itself*. But the being-for-itself that makes it possible as a relation is determinate: included in the essence of the original revelation of the movement that brings itself alongside is that movement's capacity to remain near itself in its accomplishment and so to be possible as an act of relating-itself-to. The original self-revelation that determines this movement in its intrinsic possibility — the ultimate possibility of transcendence, constituting it in its essence as relating-itself-to — is immanence.

Here Henry clears away confusions that arise inevitably when transcendence is to be grasped in its essence. Transcendence is indeed described as the act of relating-itself-to, of surpassing-itself-toward. But what is that surpassing? Henry notes that it is usually interpreted first and negatively, starting from beings: transcendence's internal possibility is defined from what beings are deprived of. Why can the table not touch the wall? Because it cannot surpass itself toward it. Unable to do so, it remains "in itself", imprisoned and closed, without relation to what surrounds it. To surpass itself toward the wall would mean going out of itself, being outside itself, and in that exteriority being *alongside* — more precisely, creating in that exit a neighbourhood, a pure milieu of exchange in which it could find all things and find itself among them in the light. Being-outside-itself-alongside is the fundamental possibility of which the table is deprived.

This possibility, denied to the table, is then taken to constitute the essence of relation, the essence of transcendence. Understood in this purely negative way from beings, the account stays fundamentally obscure despite its apparent clarity: it leaves room for equivocation and ends by passing over transcendence's essence in silence — decisively so for the philosophy of transcendence as a whole. The equivocation concerns what kind of reality is surpassed in the "going out of itself", and hence what kind of surpassing is in play. With the table, the reality surpassed is the table. It is on condition of surpassing *itself*, of being outside itself, that the table could relate to the wall. So surpassing-toward, in the sense of being-outside-itself-alongside, would mean, for the table, itself constituting the reality surpassed in the surpassing. Is this then a mere eidetic analysis moving in fiction, or does a surpassing in which a being constitutes the reality surpassed actually exist? Henry's answer: the surpassing of beings *is the world*. So phenomenality can seem enclosed in the concept of a surpassing whose agent is also what it surpasses.
