That reality is admittedly not reducible to any particular being — the table does not touch the wall. But man? We do not yet know what man is: might he not be just that being capable of surpassing himself and so finding himself out in the light, man among men, thing among things?

That possibility is remarkable and worth noting, but one would still have to show what it consists in and how it is itself possible — and here the problematic falls into embarrassment. Of the possibility of accomplishing any surpassing, including self-surpassing, man *as a being* is as fundamentally deprived as any other. No more than the table can man's hand, considered as an ontic reality, touch the wall; it stands beside it in the world. Is the world, which unfolds its horizon beyond every being, not itself the surpassing? Does surpassing not lie in being-beyond-beings, in that radical exteriority which is more objective than any object and which is also the light? But objectivity relates to nothing; in objectivity there is no relation, and nothing within it relates to anything else. It is not the hand's particular nature but its *objective* nature that prevents it from relating to the wall. So a manifestation, even granting it were actual, does not suffice to ground the possibility of a relation; it can on the contrary make it impossible. If the hand cannot touch the wall although their spatial contiguity manifests itself in the world, that particular but in itself pure manifestation does not yet constitute a relation in the transcendental sense — because the phenomenological reality of such a relation is not the phenomenality of the world.

The formal identity of structure between the surpassing of beings in the world and the essence of transcendence — an identity expressed in a monotonous ontological understanding of surpassing as surpassing-itself-toward — is therefore illusory. For the human being, to surpass itself toward the world is to be itself the reality surpassed in the surpassing, that is, to manifest itself as a being; and in that manifestation there is no relation: man among men, thing among things, man relates to nothing. To surpass-toward in the sense of transcendence, to relate to, is to *be* the surpassing — a surpassing that does not surpass itself and is possible precisely as what does not surpass itself but remains in itself, as immanence. The act of surpassing-toward that defines transcendental relation is thus conditioned by the *not-surpassing-itself* that qualifies transcendence in its essence. In conformity with this, transcendence never goes beyond itself and never stays short of its own surpassing. Not going beyond itself means, for transcendence, not manifesting itself in a world; never staying short of its own surpassing means never being a being. Doing neither, transcendence does not leave its essence outside itself in some foreign spirit but preserves it within: it is the surpassing in itself, and so possible as surpassing.

Understanding transcendence from the surpassing of beings in the world therefore only silences transcendence's internal structure. That structure is not exhibited but *dismembered* between beings and world when surpassing-itself-toward is read as the being-beyond-itself of a being, so that the reality that surpasses turns out to be the very one surpassed, and the surpassing is understood as the world. Nor is the structure merely broken between the two: reuniting them, the synthetic unity of the being-beyond-itself-of-beings, would not contain it. Transcendence is neither beings nor world. Interpreting it as the being-beyond-itself of beings does not merely omit its essence but travesties it. The confusion becomes visible in the phrase "transcendence of the world": the real content of that concept is the surpassing of beings in the transcendental horizon of being, and its only phenomenological reference is the phenomenality of the world. Because that reference at least seems available, the internal possibility of surpassing is sought in the world, which then coincides with transcendence — and the living bond of a relating-itself-to and a surpassing-itself-toward, in the sense of bringing-itself-alongside, is lost in the indifferent relation of light to things.

Because the interpretation of transcendence from the surpassing of beings misses its target, it also gives the antithetical concept of immanence a spurious and empty sense. If transcendence means the being-outside-itself of beings, where would immanence lie but in beings themselves, in their being-inside-themselves? And since beings cannot go out of themselves, being-inside-itself is no superadded property or one determination among others but the being's most proper qualification. Immanence thereby becomes an *ontic category* — and it is precisely as an ontic category that it counts as transcendence's antithesis. To transcendence's going-out-of-itself is opposed the staying-in-itself that falls to immanent being. And just as transcendence's being-outside-itself was understood from beings as the possibility they lack, so beings' staying-in-itself is understood as the mere privation of that going-out. Henry quotes a commentator on Heidegger to the effect that an unfree being would be one so absolutely folded in on itself that it would be constitutionally incapable of being alongside the other. The unfree being, deprived of the possibility of going out of itself, is precisely a being; and the privation of freedom constraining it to stay within itself is called immanence. In this play of negative significations the content of the concepts drains away: the internal possibility of the structures they name is no longer even a problem, and the structures are not so much as described. On the ruin of these concepts is built a would-be philosophy of existence resting on the bare opposition of "existence" and "thing", an opposition whose emptiness lets it more or less coincide with the equally empty traditional opposition of subject and object. Or, if the opposition is not wholly empty, it marks the bare contrast between a being that goes outside itself and one that stays within, the in-itself. But since both possibilities are in fact understood from beings, they are as empty as their opposition. Since beings cannot go outside themselves, and since that possibility is grasped only negatively as what they lack, one cannot see how a being could ever claim it as its own. In man's "privilege" of *existing*, Henry says, the absurdity of the philosophy of existence is concentrated. And even if, by that singular privilege, man were united with an existence that, as the being-outside-itself of beings, is only indifferent and relationless exteriority, this would still not be the possibility of a surpassing — it would be nothing at all.

The concept of immanence no more finds its content in beings deprived of the power to surpass themselves than transcendence finds its content in their being-outside-themselves. The table is no more "in itself" than it is "outside itself". Thought that endows beings with an interiority obeys the same illusion as thought that sees in them the origin of a relation, that believes the table touches the wall. Freed from the aberrant significations conferred on them by a pseudo-genesis from an ontic origin they do not have, the concepts of transcendence and immanence cease to be opposed. Henry states the inversion sharply: it is not because the table remains in itself that it cannot touch the wall — on the contrary, it is *because it does not remain in itself* that it cannot surpass itself toward the wall, and that surpassing is in principle denied it. Because immanence is not a category of beings, transcendence does not belong to them either. Immanence is a pure ontological category, indeed the fundamental ontological category that makes surpassing itself possible.

Once these false ontic significations are set aside, transcendence and immanence can be grasped in their true relation, which is not opposition but grounding. This shows the vanity of critiques resting on the bare opposition of the two concepts. It is idle to challenge the philosophical value of immanence, and specifically to deny it any possible ontological sense, when the ground given for the challenge is the extension of transcendence to the whole phenomenological field of being. What that extension brings to light is not immanence's exclusion from the internal structure of the essence's ontological power but precisely its belonging to it. The *comprehension* of the pure ontological concepts of immanence and transcendence differs; their *extension* is identical. The extension of transcendence to the whole phenomenological field of being means the universality of immanence as the fundamental ontological structure of every possible manifestation. Because the extension is identical, the attempt to dissociate the realities forming their pure content, expelling each from the other's field of operation, is absurd. Grasping them in the identity of their extension is instead to penetrate their comprehension further and to seize the bond uniting them — a bond that is not exterior but lies in transcendence itself, if transcendence's essence is immanence. Understanding transcendence ontologically in its essence is identically understanding immanence within it. What comes to light there is what makes surpassing internally possible: its holding-near-itself, the remaining-in-itself of the movement of surpassing within the surpassing itself. Accordingly, wherever a relation exists, it exists first of all *in itself*. If man accomplishes a surpassing, if he can transcend himself toward the world, then it is false to say that man is never short of the world, man first. What remains and persists short of the world is, if not man himself, at least the reality that accomplishes the surpassing — and this remaining-short-of-the-world of the surpassing is its very reality. Only forgetting what constitutes transcendence's ultimate possibility can lead a problematic simply to deny the ontological significance of immanence.

The abstract moment of that denial, in which transcendence is stripped of its essence, is also the moment of an equally abstract affirmation in which the relation of transcendence is simply posited. The more immediate the positing, the more categorical its manner. Asserting the transcendence-relation outside any philosophical context that would indicate its internal possibility is not easily recognized as gratuitous, because the gratuitousness is itself immediately read as a mark of the real and as what grounds its reality. In the relation's *lack* of ground is found the character by which it is the ground, the absolute. When the absolute has no ground — when its positive internal possibility cannot be exhibited — its advent is only the more startling. The relation flashes forth like lightning; it is the simple Trait, *der reine Bezug*. This simplicity, which is the absence of all ground, marks the relation not merely as ground but as groundless ground. To be a groundless ground is then the essence of relation, the contingent nature of the absolute. In that contingency the absolute acquires the pathos it otherwise lacks. Henry's diagnosis is blunt: the problematic's ontological deficiency is the source of the existential prestige it wears. A commentator writes that existence is a sort of absolute without origin or destiny, Relation itself, at once irreplaceable and unjustifiable. So one sees an inability to justify the relation — to grasp what makes it possible — lead the problematic to absolutize it by making groundlessness the character and essence of the ground. The existential moment in which the absolute without origin or destiny surges up in the nakedness of its contingency is also the moment of realism. Realism is the hypostatizing of what is not reality but presupposes it; realism is abstraction. Nor does the abstract hypostatizing of the absolute in "Relation" make it the living relation that relates itself to what it relates to: adding a capital letter is no substitute for the ontological work that lays bare the concrete structure of reality. Reality is not the relation; it is presupposed by it, is the relation's being, what makes it possible. With the omission of transcendence's essence, the philosophy of being remains, despite appearances, at the level of the philosophy of consciousness, which declares that consciousness is precisely nothing but relation, referral, signification toward or for.

## **§ 34\. Consciousness of the world and consciousness without world**

With transcendence's essence determined as immanence, the transcendental relation of being-in-the-world is no longer merely asserted but grasped in its intrinsic possibility, which lies in the manifestation of the relation itself. Because the relation's original phenomenological possibility constitutes its very reality, determining the internal structure of that possibility is determining the relation's reality, grasping it in its true nature. And to grasp it so is to understand it in radical opposition to the being of the "world" and the phenomenality constituting it. Transcendence is not in the world. This means not merely that it does not occur within the world in the manner of a being, but — more decisive for understanding the nature of the "being-in" — that it does not occur *as that which is the world*. The not-being-in-the-world of being-in-the-world is its most proper possibility. That possibility, the ultimate phenomenological possibility for transcendence to be at all, lies entirely in the actual phenomenality of what is not the world, in the original immanent revelation of the movement itself. With that revelation, accomplished in radical independence of the world and its phenomenality, the phenomenological ground of the decisive opposition between the concepts of movement and objectivity is exhibited. Movement is essentially possible as non-objective — and possible here means real, since the possibility of movement is the phenomenological reality of its original manifestation. That movement is possible as non-objective means it always holds itself short of the world, outside the field of the horizon: although it is the movement of relating to the world, it is never *in* the world.

The reality of movement is the essence of imagination, and the essence of imagination is identically its manifestation, its "consciousness". Like the reality of movement, the consciousness of imagination does not reside in objectivity. To Husserl's question about the possibility of a consciousness without a world, the answer is given with the consciousness of imagination: it *is* a consciousness without world. But is imagination not the power to raise a world, and so consciousness of it? Henry insists on not confusing consciousness *of the world* with the consciousness *of imagination*. The world belongs to imagination as what imagination imagines in its act of transcendence, and in that sense imagination is a consciousness of the world; the world's belonging to imagination means, for the world, its manifestation as a phenomenological element — the manifestation of its nothingness. That manifestation occurs in imagination, more exactly in imagination's consciousness: because imagination is conscious, it is also conscious of what it imagines. But the world's belonging to imagination in no way means its belonging to the consciousness of imagination; from the essence of that consciousness the world is radically excluded. The exclusion follows from determining imagination's original mode of revelation as immanence. That the consciousness of imagination is a consciousness without world means that imagination's manifestation is not constituted by the phenomenality of the world. In imagination's manifestation resides not the world's phenomenality but what makes it possible, that in which it becomes actual. That the world is formed in the act of imagination means the world reaches actual phenomenality, becomes phenomenal, in that act — more exactly in the original revelation immanent to it and constitutive of its reality. That immanent revelation is the "consciousness of imagination", within which what imagination imagines, the world, also becomes phenomenal and conscious.

What is implied in "consciousness of the world" is therefore not the simple concept of phenomenality but its division. It is not merely that consciousness of the world is always also self-consciousness, as though consciousness, like the world, were held under its own concept, as though the concept of consciousness had for content not only the world but this consciousness too. For the concept of consciousness is empty so long as it is applied to both at once. What varies between the two cases is not only consciousness's content but the *structure of phenomenality*. This explains the reserved use Henry makes of the word "consciousness" throughout. One cannot even say that consciousness is accomplished in two different ways, as though it still somehow presided over both modes. It is phenomenality, consciousness itself, that differs — so that "consciousness" says nothing unless taken in the wholly general and empty sense in which it merely designates manifestation. And manifestation is always understood within monism's horizon, so consciousness is understood in general as consciousness of the world. What such an understanding passes over is not only the question of the internal structure of the phenomenality of self-consciousness — a structure in fact interpreted on the model of consciousness of the world — but the nature of consciousness of the world itself, along with its possibility. If the world becomes phenomenal in the original immanent revelation of the act of imagination, then consciousness of the world is actual only on the basis, within it, of a consciousness to which the world does not belong. Consciousness of the world is always also a consciousness without world.

"With" and "without world" are therefore not properties added to consciousness but structural determinations of consciousness's own phenomenality, and in their radical opposition the concept of consciousness divides. The phenomenality of the world is one thing, that of imagination another. Yet consciousness is one. There are not two consciousnesses without link, of which we could not say how they join, how consciousness of the world is at the same time, in the unity of one phenomenological event, self-consciousness. If self-consciousness and consciousness of the world do not arise separately as two juxtaposed essences, each closed in its own truth like a self-enclosed world of light without communication with the other, that is because consciousness of the world does not suffice to itself, is not an essence. Or rather it is one, is a self-subsisting actual manifestation, only insofar as it is also and indissolubly something else — and the problematic has shown what: consciousness of the world is identically the original dimension of revelation from which the world is absent and in which the world nonetheless becomes phenomenal, the worldless consciousness of imagination. Because the manifestation of the world as world becomes actual only in imagination's original immanent revelation, it is united to it. The unity of consciousness of the world with self-consciousness is its very possibility, and since that possibility is phenomenological, so is the unity. The possibility of consciousness of the world is consciousness itself as consciousness not of the world but of imagination, as consciousness without world. And in the possibility of consciousness of the world lies its essence, the essence of consciousness in general. Far from being an empty hypothetical possibility thrown up by chance before philosophical reflection, the possibility of a consciousness without world is the original ontological possibility of consciousness itself, and as such its essence.

Determining the essence of consciousness as consciousness without world has a rigorous phenomenological sense: it means the actual phenomenological reality of a revelation that does not have the form of the world, the existence of an original dimension of phenomenality where phenomenality does not become phenomenal in exteriority nor as the phenomenality of that exteriority. And in the phenomenality that does not become phenomenal in exteriority lies the phenomenological possibility of the phenomenality of exteriority itself. The question of the essence of phenomenality thus concentrates into the question of the phenomenological possibility of an actual, original dimension of revelation in which the phenomenality of the world itself becomes phenomenal *as a phenomenality that is not the world's*. The possibility of that revelation — where the phenomenological aspect of exteriority is formed and from which the form of exteriority is excluded — lies in the essence in which transcendence does not operate. The absence of a world is identically the absence of imagination: because the power to open a horizon and transcend itself toward it is not at work in the original essence of revelation, that essence does not take the form of the world, and the phenomenality originally becoming phenomenal in it is not that of exteriority. Consciousness is possible as consciousness without world insofar as it does not transcend itself toward the world, insofar as transcendence is not present in it. Yet this worldless consciousness is the "consciousness" of consciousness of the world, the consciousness of imagination. The phenomenological reality of the original dimension of revelation in which there is no world, because transcendence does not operate in it, is the phenomenological reality of transcendence itself. The problematic thus faces a double evidence: phenomenality originally becomes phenomenal in a sphere from which all transcendence is absent, and it is in the actual phenomenological reality of that transcendence-less sphere that transcendence itself becomes phenomenal and finds its reality. The reality of transcendence lies in the essence that does not transcend itself. And because its reality, understood phenomenologically, lies there, transcendence cannot claim to characterize phenomenality in its structure and possibility; it does not constitute its essence. Not every moment of the essence has the character of transcendence. Included in the phenomenological structure of the total being of transcendence's overall ontological process, as constituting that structure's ultimate phenomenological possibility, is the moment of the essence that does not have the character of transcendence, the moment that does not transcend itself — and that moment is where transcendence and the world alike originally become phenomenal. Determining the essence of phenomenality therefore requires exhibiting within it the moment where it does not transcend itself, and bringing the problematic before its present evidence: a sphere of existence without transcendence as the sphere of existence of transcendence itself.

With the grasp, within the transcendental relation of being-in-the-world, of the element that does not relate to the world and does not transcend itself, the movement of transcendence is not only grounded in its phenomenological possibility, its essence. Determining transcendence's essence as immanence is identically exhibiting what makes the internal coherence of the essence of manifestation possible.

## **§ 35\. The coherence of the internal structure of the essence**

What secures the coherence of the essence's internal structure was understood as what is most essential in it — but that understanding took place within monism's horizon and was already determined by it. Because the essence was interpreted as the act of going out of itself, the possibility of its internal coherence presented itself as the possibility of retaining and maintaining the horizon raised in transcendence, of receiving it. And because that reception was grasped as identical with the act of opposing, with transcendence itself, transcendence finally offered itself — as intuitive in nature — as securing by itself the coherence of the structure it unfolds.

Taking transcendence's unified structure to have its coherence in transcendence does not bring the problematic before a ground; it refers it back to that ground as to a problem. If the coherence of the structure transcendence unfolds resides in transcendence, then it is fundamentally dependent: it depends on the coherence of the internal structure of the act of objectivation taken in itself. For transcendence can retain the horizon it creates, can receive it in the very act of positing it before itself, only insofar as it can first retain *itself* in the originally coherent unity of its own structure. Something like the unity of an original coherence therefore belongs to the movement of transcendence as what makes it possible — and that originally coherent unity lies in the movement's holding itself near itself in its accomplishment. What makes that holding-near possible was understood as identical in essence with the movement's original revelation to itself; more precisely, what such an understanding exhibits is the internal structure of the movement's original mode of revelation in its ontological identity with, and as constituting, the movement's power to remain near itself. That power is thus identically the structure of its original mode of revelation. And in it lies the ground of the movement's unity with itself, hence its capacity to constitute a coherent structure at all. The originally coherent unity of the movement of transcendence, considered in its own structure, resides in immanence. Because it makes the act of objectivation possible, that unity is at the same time what makes possible the coherence of the structure the act engenders — the coherence and unity of the whole structure the essence unfolds in objectivation. The unity of that whole, the coherent unity of transcendence and horizon, therefore rests on the unity of transcendence itself as the act of creating and retaining the horizon. Here the results of schematism must be rejected again: specifically, the claim that the phenomenological unity of forming and receiving the horizon is the determinate and sufficient ground of the unity of the whole structure transcendence unfolds, and ultimately the unity of transcendence's own essence. The unity of spontaneity and receptivity with respect to the horizon has nothing to do with the unity grounding the internal coherence of the act of transcendence taken in itself. It designates only that the act which forms the horizon is essentially identical with the act which receives it. What is thought under that concept is one and the same act, the act of transcendence — not that act's internal possibility of remaining one in itself throughout its accomplishment. Because that internal possibility is neither thought nor grasped, what finally gets considered is not the act in itself but its relation to the horizon it creates. And because it concerns only that relation, the unity of spontaneity and receptivity turns out to be identically the unity of the total structure the act engenders, the unity of the essence with the pure milieu it imagines — not the internal unity of the essence itself.

The phrase "the coherence of the internal structure of the essence of manifestation" is therefore equivocal. Strictly, the essence's internal structure comprises only the essence's own reality; the synthetic totality of the whole structure constituted by transcendence contains, alongside the essence, the pure imaginary product of its activity. The subsistence of that whole is indeed a problem, and it is secured by the act of transcendence as the act of creating and retaining the horizon. So the unity of spontaneity and receptivity is the ground of the coherence of the whole structure transcendence freely raises. But the coherence of that whole is not the coherence of the essence in its internal structure; it presupposes it. The unity of the essence with its imaginary product refers back to the internal unity of the act of transcendence and to its original coherence as to a last ground. Schematism reverses the terms, offering the unity of the whole structure as the unity of the essence, as the originally coherent unity of transcendence itself. And the precondition of that reversal in the hierarchy of essences is exactly the confusion of the essence's internal structure with the whole structure that merely finds its ground in it. The coherence of the whole — improperly called the "unified structure of transcendence" — is thereby taken for the coherence of transcendence itself and for the unity of its internal structure. What sinks into oblivion under cover of the confusion is that structure's proper unity and what makes it possible: immanence as such, the essence of transcendence.

That the unity of spontaneity and receptivity, or of thought and intuition, cannot constitute the essential and original unity of ontological knowledge — the internal possibility of the essential unity of the pure veritative synthesis — is visible in how schematism accomplishes it: what is exhibited in thought and intuition as their common essence is not transcendence but precisely the whole structure transcendence unfolds. For the "essential and original" unity of the pure elements of knowledge is recognized by determining them in their essence as *representations*. Representation is the common essence that lets thought and intuition unite because it first constitutes the essence of each. And to be the essence of a thing means to make it possible. Representation is the essence of thought, constitutes its internal unity, because it makes thought possible by manifesting it; likewise for intuition. The internal unity of thought is therefore in it the unity of representation, which is each time the unity of transcendence and horizon. So under the improper concept of thought's "internal" unity, what is substituted is the unity of thought with what it thinks, that is, with what it represents. Likewise the concept of intuition's unity does not concern the moment of reality that intuition, taken in itself and in parallel with pure thought, designates within the essence; what the problematic actually has in view under the equally improper concept of intuition's "internal" unity is the unity of intuition with what it intuits — again the unity of representation as unity of transcendence and horizon. But insofar as intuition does not merely find its condition in representation but offers itself as what, in receiving the horizon, itself secures representation's unity and so its possibility, the concept of intuition's unity refers the problematic back to its proper sense. The unity of intuition no longer rests on the unity of representation: it grounds it. But how? What sense must the unity of intuition have if intuition is to ground representation and its unity? Is intuition one insofar as it unifies representation and so makes it possible in the coherence of its whole structure? Or is intuition — that is, transcendence itself — able to unify representation only insofar as it is itself one in the originally coherent unity of its own structure?

The concept of the unity of intuition therefore refers by necessity to what has been understood as *reality*. That is why it designates not only intuition's unity but equally thought's, the unity of imagination and of transcendence in general. Such a unity, as the internal, immanent unity of the essence, is the primordial unity, the unity of reality itself. It is on the ground of this unity — which constitutes in each of them the unity of their internal structure — that thought and intuition are one, not through the mediation of representation's unity, which itself presupposes as its possibility the internal unity of the act of transcendence. The internal unity of thought, that of intuition, and the internal unity of the act of transcendence in which representation finds its own unity are in truth one and the same unity, the unity of reality. It is on the plane of that reality, within the internal structure of the power of knowledge taken in itself, that the modes in which it is accomplished are originally united so as to produce together representation and its unity in the maintaining of the horizon. In other words, the power that makes intuition and thought possible by making them representations, and that originally reunites them in the unity proper to it, resides wholly in reality. That unity — theirs in the double sense of their internal unity and of the unity joining them — cannot be found in the structure of representation or as representation's unity, since it is on the contrary what makes representation possible.

Representation opens the transcendental horizon of being, and in opening and holding it open it originally unifies it; in representation's unity lies the ground of the unity of what is represented in it, the ground of the unity of the world taken in its pure concept. Henry closes the section by ordering three kinds of unity ontologically. First, the unity of the horizon. Because beings manifest themselves within that horizon they are reached not in dispersion and isolation but in the coherence of an already synthesized and unified complex. Unity accrues to beings only insofar as they manifest themselves; it resides in their manifestation itself. That is why a unity can be established among radically different beings belonging to different genera, essences, and regions: it lies in the unity of the field of intuition where, despite those differences, they can appear and be juxtaposed. Every unity is in principle phenomenological; the unity of phenomena belongs to them as phenomena. And that is also why the systematic determination of the concept of unity arises, and can only arise, on an ontological plane. But manifestation can unify only if it is itself one, only if it is actual. The horizon's power to bind what it encounters into an original synthesis refers to a synthetic power that constantly unifies the horizon itself — and for Kant that power is imagination, since all synthesis is produced by imagination. Imagination originally synthesizes and unifies the horizon insofar as it forms and receives it. So the unity of the horizon refers to the second kind: the unity of representation, as unity of the essence with what it represents, of transcendence with the horizon. And this in turn presupposes the originally immanent unity of the act of transcendence taken in itself — the third: the internal unity of the essence itself. Every question about the essence of unity, about the unity of thought and intuition, of spontaneity and receptivity, can be elaborated only on the basis of these distinctions and their rigorously determined ontological substructure.

## **§ 36\. The essential ontological signification of the concept of immanence: the immediate**

In its internal unity, as radically immanent and primordial unity, lies the fundamental possibility of the essence, its possibility of being itself. The essence is action; it is the becoming of exteriority, the power that produces it. How is the essence operative — what lets it be this action, unite itself with it, and do what the action does, if not precisely the action by which it unites itself with its action, the power by which it comes into possession of its own power? The action by which the essence unites itself with its action is its original action; the power by which it comes into possession of its own power is its fundamental power. What does that consist in? Where does the essence draw the force to unite with itself, so that in this strong reunion with itself it can be itself and can act? The problematic has answered: the ontological structure in which the essence's reunion with itself is accomplished is the original receptivity by which the essence receives itself in immanence.

That immanence refers to the internal ontological structure of the essence as what makes it possible, and so constitutes its essence — the essence of the essence — is what gives the concept its essential signification. That signification is lost when, under the concept of immanence and as its content, the mere *belonging of the essence to its determinations* is substituted for the essence's internal possibility and the question of determining it. In attending to the relation of modal inherence, thought loses sight of the essence's ultimate possibility; unable to go all the way to the radical ground of being and existence, it shifts attention to what finds its possibility in that ground and contents itself with registering the ground's presence in what it makes possible. The presence of the ground in what it grounds, the immanence of the essence to its determinations — this is what is henceforth thought under the concept of immanence and passes for the essence's "immanent character". The traditionally recognized sense of immanence, as determining the relation of an essence to its modes, thus covers over thought's impotence to grasp the essential sense in which the concept necessarily refers to the essence's internal ontological structure and to the problem of determining it.

In the absence of that determination, what is the philosophical interpretation of the relation binding the essence to its modes worth? What sense can be given to the essence's immanence in them, and how could such immanence make them possible and ground them? For the essence can make its own modes possible only insofar as it is itself possible. Classical philosophy satisfies itself cheaply with the immanence of the essence in natural consciousness — when it is not the far vaguer and wholly indeterminate immanence of "Spirit" or "Reason" in various "individuals". What result can it claim, what is actually thought as content, when the possibility of knowledge is sought nowhere but in the essence's immanence to the various modes in which knowledge is accomplished — other than a tautology in which that possibility is merely named?

Or does thought, with the concept of the relation of immanence, go beyond mere tautology? Henry suggests the idea secretly animating that elaboration, and concealed behind it, is the idea that serves ontology as guiding theme and ground: the idea of the possibility of the ground itself, of the essence's internal possibility. What is aimed at, at least confusedly, under the concept of the essence's presence in its modes, and grasped there as making the modes' action possible, is in reality what makes the *essence's own* action possible — its presence, the essence's unity with itself in the strong reunion where it is given to be what it is and to act. The essential ontological signification of immanence is the unnoticed content of thought that stops at the relation of inherence. For that reason it is not absent even from philosophies claiming to refuse immanence any ontological sense and to constitute themselves independently of it. The immanence of the essence in the actual content of experience — of real knowledge in natural knowledge, for instance — attests the impossibility for thought to forget entirely what it hides from itself under such a relation: the immanent revelation in which the essence originally gives itself to itself in the action by which it renders itself present and capable of acting. The obscurity, in Hegel as in Heidegger, of the status of natural knowledge and of the immanence of real knowledge within it belongs in truth to the unelaborated concept of that immanence, insofar as the concept designates not only, explicitly, the relation of the essence to its modes, but also, covertly, the essence's own structure — the internal structure of real knowledge and its ground. For the essence can act only if it is *there*; natural knowledge is possible only if the essence is present in it, immanent to it. But this possibility of being there belongs to the essence as its own: it is the possibility for the essence of presence to be itself present and so to be what it is, the essence of presence. Because the essence's power to be present and operative in natural knowledge rests on its own possibility, its action within natural knowledge must not merely be named but grasped in its internal ontological structure and its possibility. Henry compresses the point into a formula: the immanent essence is the essence of immanence.

Does saying that the essence arrives within itself — that its power to arrive in the light of exteriority is first the power to arrive within that arriving, to unite with it and so reunite with itself in the force of its internal unity — mean anything more than that such a power exists, that the essence must be present in order to act, or rather that it is present and therefore acts? Is the ontological content of immanence "in its essential signification" not constituted, just like what thought has in view in the relation of inherence, by the bare presupposition of the essence, in a tautology where the essence is merely acknowledged and named, where one says that it "is"? Henry answers by turning the question on the verb: but what does *being* mean? With the determination of the essence's fundamental possibility as its power to arrive within itself, what is described and grasped is the internal structure of the essence, the original structure of being itself. For only on the basis, within it, of the structure in which the essence originally receives itself in immanence can being unite with itself and so be what it is — can being *be*. Being is not something dead or ready-made, nothing simply given. Being obtains its being only through the work within it of the essence that makes it be in the original unity constituting it. For unity too is not something dead: it is precisely a work and an accomplishment. The manner in which this interior work of being is accomplished is what is represented by thought in possession of the fundamental ontological categories in which being's power to arrive originally within itself is defined.

Being's power to arrive originally within itself determines it as *the immediate*. Not the immediate of naive consciousness, which stops at the given and takes it as self-evident; nor that of a thought which, going back to the ontological condition of the given, that is, to being itself, then takes this condition in turn as something simply given and self-sufficient. The ontological condition of possibility of the given is indeed self-sufficient, if it is the condition — but that in virtue of which it is the condition, that by which it suffices to itself, is precisely what the problematic has to exhibit. It is this possibility, in virtue of which being suffices to itself and is the condition in an absolute sense, and which is identically its power to arrive originally within itself, that is thought under the concept of the immediate and determines it as the fundamental concept of ontology. The immediate is being itself as originally given to itself in immanence. And because this original self-donation, which properly constitutes being, is accomplished neither by chance nor by miracle but in immanence and as that immanence, the concept of the immediate does not stay indeterminate. The immediate is not a mere name for saying, absent any valid philosophical context and as a bare tautology, that being is; it designates being's internal possibility and refers to an essence, the fundamental essence in which that possibility finds its reality.

Determining the immediate ontologically sets aside the claim to grasp the condition of all presence in objectivation and to understand objectivation as the universal mediation in which everything that is finds its being. Everything that is does indeed find its being only through the mediation of the essence that makes it the gift of presence; every being, at least if we speak of it as a phenomenon, can be such only by obeying the strong law of that mediation, which therefore necessarily gives itself as *the* law. But the internal nature of that mediation is ontology's proper theme — and under its traditional presuppositions a confusion arises between two things both called "mediation": the necessary reference of beings to the pure formal ontological element in which they enter the phenomenal condition and by which they are mediated, and the internal development of that pure ontological element by which the element itself arrives in the light of the phenomenal condition, that is, in its own reality. Henry finds the confusion at work in Schelling, who, speaking of the I-monad understood as identically consciousness, that is, the essence of presence as such, holds that no objective opposite could ever arrive in it unless it were posited at the same time by the very act in which the monad posits itself. The essence's power to accomplish its work with respect to everything present, which thus finds its mediation in the essence, certainly presupposes that the essence has first accomplished its work with respect to itself — that the essence of presence has already rendered itself present to itself in the primitive and fundamental act by which it is realized, in the act by which, as Schelling says, it posits itself. But that act is understood as objectivation: the essence's self-positing is, for Schelling, a positing of the essence *before* itself. And precisely because it is, the act by which the essence posits itself turns out to be identically the act by which every objective opposite arrives in it, by which beings manifest themselves to it as objects. So the manifestation of beings not only presupposes the accomplishment of the essence's internal work in the action by which it arrives originally within itself; it is also shown to be identical in structure with that original internal action. Mediation then designates, on the basis of the identity of their internal ontological structure, both the action by which the essence renders beings manifest and the action by which it manifests itself. Because it designates both indifferently, mediation is not only the law of beings and of everything that is but the law of the essence, the law of being itself. Or rather, because the twofold action is only one, because its structure is everywhere the same, there is only one law and one action: objectivation is the universal law of everything that is and of being itself, the universal mediation.

What mediation lacks in its claim to universality is nothing less than the possibility of objectivation itself — its own possibility. For objectivation is possible only if the essence that objectivates itself arrives originally within itself as within that very objectivation, so as to be it and to accomplish what it accomplishes, the becoming of exteriority and its phenomenological arising. And that this original arriving of the essence within itself is not constituted by objectivation, that it cannot, as Hegel and Heidegger would have it, be objectivation's consequence, follows precisely from its being objectivation's condition.

The essence's original arriving within itself, which determines it as the immediate, cannot in any way be understood on the basis of an intellectual necessity or as a mere logical requirement — the requirement that the essence by which all presence is mediated cannot itself be mediated in turn and therefore constitutes the immediate. Such a determination of the immediate, to which mediation itself may lay claim, results from a one-sided decision of thought which, perceiving the necessity that the essence arrive originally within itself, declares that this is so and that such is its nature. Obeying the axiom that one must stop somewhere, thought merely takes its wishes for reality. Henry's rejoinder is that the immediate resides in reality, and it is there that it must be exhibited, as the fundamental structure constituting reality.

Exhibiting the immediate as constituting not a mere logical requirement but the very structure of reality and its essence is identically exhibiting the internal structure of immanence.

# Section III. The internal structure of immanence and the problem of its phenomenological determination: the invisible

## **§ 37\. The internal structure of immanence**

**Paragraph 1\.** It is by reference to transcendence and by the exclusion of transcendence outside its internal structure that immanence has been defined. The opening sentence locates the section within the architecture of the whole work: in the previous sections (especially §§32–36, the closing sequence of Section II), Henry has progressively developed the concept of *immanence* by way of contrast — immanence is what does not have the structure of transcendence (the horizonal-ekstatic structure of monism). The positive signification of such a definition has been shown with the bringing-to-light of the essential structural determinations it comports. Before pushing further the analysis of these determinations and the understanding of their decisive character for an adequate philosophical interpretation of the ultimate nature of the essence, it is important to remark *what already results, in a purely negative manner, from the exclusion*.

The methodological signal is precise: §37 begins by working out, in even sharper form, the *negative* implications of the exclusion of transcendence from the internal structure of immanence — in order to clear the philosophical ground for the positive thesis (the determination of immanence as life, as self-affection, as the *Parousia* of the absolute) that the section will articulate.

Where there is no transcendence, there is neither horizon nor world. The horizon of the world — far from being a universal structure of all manifestation and from constituting consequently the essence of manifestation — is on the contrary excluded from this essence considered in itself. Such an exclusion is identically that of every intramundane reality in general. *Here comes to the fore for the thought that wants to arrive at the essential the strange nature of the path it must follow if at least it wants to attain its goal.* To follow such a path, for thought, is *not* "to direct itself toward" but on the contrary "to turn away from" — and that in such a manner that, in this movement by which it turns away from what forms its natural object, thought *abandons not only this object* and the infinite richness of its multiple determinations, but more essentially and in a more decisive manner for the understanding of the indigence and destitution to which it devotes itself, *the very nature of the abode that was its own near things — that act of directing-itself-toward with which thought could however appear to confuse itself*. Thus to the loss of all that is, is added the loss (more essential) of being itself — at the same time as there is announced to thought, with the ontological character of the privation that strikes it, *its true distress*. For it is its own possibility — the possibility of thinking — that is withdrawn from thought when thought must turn away from the ontological milieu in which it finds itself illuminated by the truth. This is why this turning-away, prescribed to thought as the path — the abandonment of the existent in its ensemble — signifies, in the eyes of thought, only its own abandonment, measures its own impossibility.

The opening paragraphs articulate with great care the *philosophical asceticism* the section requires. To attain the essence of immanence (the goal of Section III), thought must *turn away* from the entire field of horizonal-transcendent manifestation — from the world, from intramundane existents, from the very act of directing-itself-toward (intentionality, transcendence) that has been thought's natural mode of operation. This turning-away is not merely an exclusion of objects; it is the abandonment of *being itself* in the monist sense (being as horizonal disclosure, as the field within which beings can appear). And since thought, in the philosophical tradition, has been defined precisely by its capacity for horizonal disclosure (intentionality, *Verstehen*, *theoria*), the abandonment of horizonal manifestation is the abandonment of thought's own self-conception. Thought encounters its "own impossibility" — it must turn away from what has constituted its very capacity for being thought.

The vocabulary of *indigence*, *destitution*, *distress*, *abandonment* is deliberately chosen to mark the gravity of the philosophical operation. This is not a technical maneuver but a structural-ontological reorientation that requires the philosopher to abandon the entire conceptual apparatus that has constituted Western philosophy from Plato through Heidegger. It is, in this respect, structurally analogous to what the medieval mystical tradition (Eckhart in particular, who will be analyzed at length in §§39–40) called the *Abgeschiedenheit* (detachment, releasement) — the soul's stripping-away of all its worldly attachments and conceptual representations in order to attain to the bare ground of God. Henry will explicitly invoke Eckhart in the next sections; the convergence is structural, not merely rhetorical.

**Paragraph 2\.** This abandonment however *is the abandonment of the essence*; it is in this extreme indigence (where nothing subsists of the world, and not even the world itself) that the essence holds itself *as in its possibility*. Indigence and distress, loss and abandonment, characterize the essence relatively to *that of which the essence finds itself deprived*. Of what then is the essence deprived? When the character of its privation has been understood and *that which it lacks* grasped itself as being-outside-itself of being — as exteriority and as alterity — it is of *this* (exteriority and alterity) that the essence finds itself deprived. *Being-other* is *other* than the essence. The foreign element where grow the rich determinations of existence — this is what is foreign to the essence. *The indigence of the essence resides in the fact that the essence encloses nothing other (rien d'autre).* It is because the essence encloses nothing other that the thought that turns toward the essence necessarily *turns away* from all that is other than the essence — from that very thing which is the *other*, from being finally understood as *alterity* and as *exteriority*. Because thought turns away from this pure milieu — from what manifests itself in this milieu and from what relates itself to this milieu — *the liberation of the essential pursues itself as a withdrawal*. This is why every approach to the essence immediately takes on the form of *épargne* (sparing, retraction, frugality); this is why every proximity (if at least it concerns the origin) will be "*économisante*" (economizing, sparing). *Sparing*, *economy* signify here, however, *rejection*, *abandonment*. This is why there is in this sparing — in the project of this economy — a certain courage: that not of a provisional renunciation but of *a poverty that makes itself and wills itself essential*. Essential is the poverty that lets-go (instead of joining itself to) the multiple configurations of being, the very form of its abode near the earth, the House and the Year. The very word in which all things are contained — the name and the appellation, what designates and what shows — to this also it is necessary to renounce in this poverty that is made of *silence*. *But what then remains?*

The vocabulary intensifies. The "essential poverty" is the methodological prerequisite for the discovery of immanence. The references — to the House and the Year (likely Hölderlinian reminiscences of the abode of the gods near the earth), to the renunciation of "name and appellation," to silence — situate the philosophical operation in the tradition of mystical theology and of Heidegger's late thought (the "Saying" that lets being come to language only by holding back from explicit naming). But Henry's purpose is precise and structural: to attain the immanent essence, philosophical thought must renounce the very structural orientation (transcendence, horizonal disclosure, language as designation) that has constituted it. The closing question — "What then remains?" — names the pivot of the section.

**Paragraph 3\.** What remains when, with alterity and exteriority, the milieu of being and all its determinations, its configurations, and the movement of thought toward it have been rejected or suppressed, is the *essence itself*. For *nothing is withdrawn from the essence*, which finds itself on the contrary *liberated and recognized in its integrity* when there is operated in thought the withdrawal of the transcendent being and of transcendence itself: nothing is withdrawn because the essence encloses nothing other, and the suppression of alterity is only the suppression of the foreign element with respect to the essence — of what covers the essence and dissimulates it from our eyes.

The pivotal answer to "what then remains?" is: *the essence itself*. The whole apparent loss is loss only with respect to what was foreign to the essence; with respect to the essence itself, *nothing is lost*. The essence is fully preserved, indeed *liberated*, by the abandonment of what was covering it. This is the structural-philosophical key to Section III: the immanent essence is not impoverished by the exclusion of transcendence; it is *made visible* (or rather, in Henry's vocabulary, *revealed in itself*) by this exclusion.

It is here the moment when *the negative determination of the internal structure of the essence* (from the exclusion outside it of all transcendence) *manifests its positive signification*. If the thought that devotes itself to the guarding of the essential accomplishes itself as a *withdrawal* and as a *rejection*, it is because, comporting itself in this way, it obeys *a prescription that is the prescription of the essence itself*. The withdrawal of the transcendent element does not have for simple effect to put the essence on display, without saying otherwise what the essence is — to set aside an obstacle before the gaze that wants to attain the essence. *It is in the essence itself that there is nothing transcendent; it is in the essence — in its internal nature — that the thought of exclusion penetrates.* This thought signifies not simply: everything that has to do with transcendent being, everything that goes off into exteriority is exterior and as such foreign to the essence — but more precisely: *in the essence itself, there is nothing exterior, nothing foreign*.

The shift from a methodological exclusion (we philosophers must turn away from the transcendent in order to grasp the essence) to a structural exclusion (within the essence itself, there is nothing transcendent) is decisive. The negative-methodological gesture *expresses* a positive-ontological structure: the essence's own internal structure is one in which transcendence has no place. This is the formal definition of *immanence*: the essence's structural condition of having nothing other than itself within itself, of containing no element of exteriority, no distance from itself, no doubling.

**Paragraph 4\.** Thus there present themselves anew to thought, to arise *in the repetition* with the plenitude of their concrete ontological positivity, the structural determinations that result from the exclusion and that are those of the essence. As in the essence nothing turns away and goes toward the outside — as the creative movement of exteriority is not present in it and has neither action nor effect there — *the essence does not divide itself*; it does not separate itself from itself; *no distance institutes itself between the essence and itself*. There is in the essence neither *opposition* nor *representation*. Because the act that posits-before is not included in the essence — because it (the act of positing-before) is not constitutive of the essence but finds itself on the contrary radically foreign to its nature — *nothing is posited in the essence before itself*. It is in this sense now that there is in the essence no opposition: there is in the essence nothing opposed.

The structural enumeration is now made explicit. The internal structure of immanence excludes:

* *opposition*: there is no opposed term within the essence's structure;  
* *representation*: there is no positing-before, no thematic re-presentation;  
* *distance*: there is no separation between the essence and itself;  
* *division*: the essence is not split, doubled, alienated;  
* *the creative movement of exteriority*: nothing of the essence "goes outside itself."

This is the formal-structural signature of immanence: an essence that *is itself, only itself, immediately, without distance*. Every attempt to think such an essence in terms of the categories of horizonal phenomenology will fail, because all those categories presuppose precisely what immanence excludes. A new conceptual vocabulary is required.

This is why the concept of *intuition* (with the help of which traditional philosophical thought has believed itself able to describe the immediate grasping of reality — more exactly, the very nature of this grasping considered as such) reveals itself fundamentally improper, because intuition implies the opposition (in intuition itself) of the *intuiting* and the *intuited*. Even if this opposition is finally understood as what must be surmounted, even suppressed (and that by intuition precisely in its accomplishment, insofar as intuition aims to "unite," to "confuse" itself with the intuited reality), opposition remains as the very *condition* of this act and of the teleology to which the act obeys: an *interest* directs the act, an interest that relates itself to a "reality" — not (despite appearances) by reason of this reality, but by reason of *the structure of every possible grasping in general*. This is why such a "reality" necessarily takes on the form of opposition — finds itself constituted by it. If, as Hegel will it, *"there is interest only there where there is opposition,"* it is because there exists in the essence neither interest nor anything similar — and least of all an interest with regard to itself. There exists in the essence no "reality" with which the essence could want to confuse itself, because there is in the essence nothing opposed.

The structural critique of *intuition* (the central concept of monist phenomenology, from Plato's *theoria* through Husserl's *kategoriale Anschauung*) is now made explicit. Even the supposedly "immediate" grasping of intuition operates within an opposition (intuiting subject ↔ intuited content) that the immanent essence does not contain. Intuition is structurally inadequate to immanence. The vocabulary of *interest*, *aim*, *relation*, *grasping* — all the structural terms of intentional phenomenology — are equally inadequate. Immanence requires a different conceptual vocabulary: not intuition but *self-affection*, not aim but *immediate self-presence*, not grasping but *self-experiencing*.

This is why also the essence wills nothing, proposes nothing to itself. *It is without project and without desire.* Because it wills nothing, because it has neither project nor desire, because there is in it nothing from which it is separated, all in it is also *repose*; the essence is, in this absence of trouble (with nothing that divides it), *the calm of its absolute simplicity*. For the calm that grows in the essence does not come from the essence having let outside of itself the perishable figures in which being destines itself to us in time and in death — no more from the essence having ceased to join itself to these figures. It is thus no doubt that the essence reposes when it no longer goes off outside itself, when, immobile, it no longer creates anything. The source of this repose, however, is not simple privation. *It is in itself that the essence reposes.* "In itself" does not signify only that, in the absence of every transcendence, the essence ceases to go off "outside itself," into exteriority. *"In itself" designates the place where the essence reposes, what remains to it, what is given to it*, when, in its perfect immobility, it no longer proposes and no longer gives itself anything other: *the essence itself*. "In itself" designates the place where the essence reposes *as constituted by the essence*. *It is because the place where the essence reposes is constituted by the essence itself, that the essence is itself, as such, the repose.*

The structural argument is now elegantly woven. The essence's "repose" is not the negative repose of a thing from which all activity has been removed. It is the *positive repose* of an essence whose entire being consists in being-with-itself, in having itself as its own content. The essence does not need anything other than itself; nothing other can be added to it; nothing can be taken from it. This is the *plenitude* of the essence — the structural condition of its being immediately, fully, and exhaustively *itself*.

**Paragraph 5\.** Because the place where the essence reposes is constituted by the essence itself, *there is in the repose of the essence nothing other than the essence*. The essence reposes in *solitude* and, because the repose constitutes its nature, the essence is itself, as such, *solitude*. What is the solitude that belongs to the essence as its very nature? No more than repose, the solitude of the essence is *not simple privation*. The essence does not remain alone *like a thing* when one has removed all the others. *When nothing other subsists, the essence remains alone with itself.* Solitude has a *content*. *What is contained in the solitude of the essence is the essence itself.* It is for this that the essence is solitude — because its content is constituted by it. But the essence is not in itself as a *dead* content but as that with which it is *immediately bound*, with which it has *relation*. This is what remains in the solitude of the essence: *the relation of the essence with itself as constitutive of this very essence and of its solitude*.

The concept of *solitude* (*solitude*) is here introduced in a structural-ontological sense. This is not the existential solitude of a person who has no companions; it is the *ontological solitude* of an essence whose entire content is itself. The essence is alone — not because it has been deprived of other things, but because *no other thing can be in it* (its very structure excludes alterity). This solitude is *full*, not empty: it is filled with the essence's own self-relation, its self-presence, its being-with-itself.

The structural point is that the immanent essence has a *content* — but this content is not some other thing that fills the essence; it is the essence's own *self-relation*. The essence relates to itself; this self-relation is what gives the essence its content; the content of the essence is the essence itself in its self-relation.

The solitude of the essence lets itself be understood from now on in *what it is*: it is the *unity* of the essence. This is why the understanding of the essence of this solitude counts as a *repetition* — is identically that of the signification recognized by the problematic for the concept of *unity* applied to the essence. As the unity of the essence has nothing to do with the simple exterior identity of a thing with itself such as it finds itself enounced in tautology, but resides on the contrary in the *interior work* by which the essence arrives in itself with the very act by which it gives itself to itself — what designates, in the same manner, the concept of the solitude of the essence is *the very structure of the essence in its internal ontological positivity*. What is implicated in this positivity as constituting it is *the relation of the essence with itself* — relation such that in it the essence *enjoys itself*, *has the experience of itself*, *reveals itself to itself in what it is, such as it is*. *That which has the experience of itself, that which enjoys itself and is nothing other than this pure enjoyment of itself, than this pure experience of self, is life. Solitude is the essence of life.*

Here the central positive concept of Henry's whole phenomenology is explicitly introduced: *life* (*la vie*). Life is not biological life; life is not historical life; life is the *ontological* concept of an essence that has the experience of itself, that enjoys itself, that is given to itself in the immediacy of its own self-relation. *Life is what experiences itself.* Life is what is given to itself in the immediate self-relation that constitutes the structure of immanence. The whole positive phenomenology of *L'Essence de la manifestation* — and of the entire Henrian corpus that follows — converges on this: the essence of manifestation, properly understood (against the monist tradition), is *life as immanent self-affection*.

The vocabulary is precise. *Jouir de soi* (to enjoy oneself) and *avoir l'expérience de soi* (to have the experience of oneself) are the structural terms by which Henry describes the immanent self-relation. These are not introspective acts (in which a subject reflectively observes itself); they are the structural condition of life itself, prior to all reflection, prior to all subject-object distinction. Life is the primitive auto-experience that constitutes the essence's being-with-itself.

**Paragraph 6\.** Because it is the essence of life, solitude is *not a moment* of life — not a determination intervening in life's history that would befall life by the consequences of circumstances or that life would be susceptible of giving itself freely; *it does not result from a choice* in connection with preoccupations of moral order, from an imperative. *Solitude is not a category of psychology or of ethics, but a fundamental ontological category*; it constitutes an absolutely universal structure, the very structure of the essence. That which has the experience of itself precisely, that which enjoys itself, *is not this or that*; it is the *essence*. For the essence alone relates itself originarily to itself in this relation that reveals it to itself in its reality. But the revelation-to-itself of the essence in its originary relation to itself *is the Parousia*. *The Parousia is the essence of life.* The *Parousia* which is the essence of life — this then is *the content of solitude*. Solitude is the solitude of the absolute, but of the absolute *in its absoluity*, in the profusion and in the enjoyment of its proper being.

The full identification is now made: *solitude \= unity \= self-relation \= self-experience \= self-enjoyment \= life \= Parousia of the absolute*. All these vocabulary items name the same structural reality: the immanent self-presence of the essence in itself. This is the positive determination of the structure that the negative analysis of the previous paragraphs had been preparing.

The polemical edge is also clear: *solitude is not a category of psychology or of ethics, but a fundamental ontological category*. Henry's "solitude" is not the psychological feeling of being alone, not the moral condition of withdrawal from society; it is the ontological-structural condition of the essence as such. Every existent (every consciousness, every life) is, in its essential being, *alone with itself* in this structural sense — alone with its own immediate self-presence. This is not a normative judgment about solitude as a way of life; it is a structural-ontological characterization.

**Paragraph 7\.** It is in this sense that *solitude is unity* — not the exterior unity of the isolated term but *the unity that reunites*: the unity of the essence which is *the reunion of the essence with itself*. The reunion of the essence with itself, however, is *nothing other than the essence itself*. This is why there is not properly speaking *a problem* of the unity of the essence. Such a unity proposes itself as a problem only inside the horizon of monism, when the structure of the essence is interpreted in such a manner that it is precisely a question of knowing how the essence can remain *one* — and that despite this structure (or at least, inside this structure) which is its own. *One*, on the contrary, is necessarily — and that by reason of what it is — *the essence that encloses nothing other*. But the unity of the essence (which encloses nothing other) does not establish itself simply on the foundation in itself of the rigorous ontological identity of form and content. *Unity designates the relation of the essence with itself*, the relation of form and content — relation such that it permits precisely their identity. This is why unity is, as has been said, *a work and an accomplishment*. Unity is what permits — that with the help of which the essence precisely enters into relation with a content, in such a manner also that this content is constituted by the essence. The nature of this relation (the manner in which the essence gives itself to itself) — this is what is designated under the concept of unity, and this also is the essence. But the essence is its own content. The manner in which the essence gives itself originarily to itself — in which it reveals itself — this is what is given originarily to itself, what reveals itself in the revelation of the essence and constitutes it. This is why the *content of revelation is revelation itself*; this is why it is the *Parousia itself* that renders itself present to itself in the *Parousia* — because revelation is in itself, because the *Parousia* is in its structure, *Unity*.

The structural characterization is now complete. The unity of the immanent essence is not a quantitative property (one rather than many); it is the *structural relation* of the essence with itself, which is at once the *form* of the essence (its mode of being-related-to-itself) and the *content* of the essence (what is related to in this relation, namely, the essence itself). Form and content coincide structurally because the essence's only content is its own self-relation, and the essence's only form is the form of self-relation. The essence is *self-revelation revealing itself*: the structure of revelation in which what is revealed is the very revealing.

**Paragraph 8\.** Because the content of revelation is revelation itself — because it is the *Parousia* itself that renders itself present to itself in the *Parousia* — the nature of the *Parousia* (the essence of presence) finds itself rigorously determined in its nature and in its characters: to the essence which gives itself to itself in unity, and as this very unity, *it belongs to give itself to itself in the totality of its reality*. That the essence give itself to itself in its reality results from the fact that it gives itself in unity: to the structure of unity nothing other, nothing exterior or foreign belongs. *The irreal element is by principle excluded from the essence*, which surpasses itself toward no transcendent content and which has, as such, *never to do with exteriority — that is, precisely with irreality as such*. It is with *itself*, on the contrary, with its own *reality*, not with any irreal content whatever, that the essence has to do in unity. To have to do with means to render oneself present, to give oneself, to receive. *Unity designates the originary mode of presence of the essence to itself.* It is this mode of presence, however, that finds itself designated habitually under the concept of "*proximity*" — concept whose ambiguous character lets itself be recognized once again. If by proximity one understands presence itself as such, there is place assuredly to speak of a *proximity of the essence* (which is also, in this case, the *essence of proximity*).

This proximity, however, has been seen to be understood inside the horizon of monism; more, it (proximity) designates — and that in an explicit manner — the understanding of the essence of presence inside this horizon: "proximity" means "presence" on the foundation of a certain *distance* and through the *mediation* of this distance — or rather identifies itself with this distance. Proximity so understood refers necessarily to *irreality*; it *is* irreality as such. Such a proximity can signify, with respect to the essence and to its reality, only an *unsurmountable distancing* — and that precisely because it is understood as a *mode of distancing* (or rather as identical with distancing): *the proximity of the essence is by principle impossible*. This is why the idea of an "*absolute proximity*" must again be called into question. It does not designate, in fact, the proximity of the absolute — a mode of presence for the absolute (in what it is, such as it is) — but, on a wholly other plane, *a privileged manner of giving itself for what gives itself always and necessarily however in an improper manner*: for the existent. The existent, it is true, does not give itself in this manner except by reason of its mode of givenness. It is the horizon, as has been seen, that is finite — that is, also, proximity, the irreality in which proximity grows. It is not the finitude of the horizon, however, that renders impossible the proximity of the absolute, but its *irreality*; it is the *mode* according to which proximity accomplishes itself. When this mode of proximity, however, ceases to grow in the milieu understood as proximity's own, the ontological characteristics that belong to proximity also vanish. *When it is a question of reality, there is no longer finitude.* From finitude there escapes by principle that which gives itself to itself in unity — that is, in reality: that the essence give itself to itself in its totality results precisely from the fact that it gives itself to itself in its reality, from the fact that the essence is *that which* gives itself to itself in reality and as this reality itself.

The polemic against the Heideggerian (and Derridean, prospectively) vocabulary of *proximity* is precise. The Heideggerian "proximity" (*Nähe*) — as elaborated in the late essays on language, on the thing, on the fourfold — is, on Henry's reading, a monist concept: it names a mode of presence that operates *through* distance, that is itself *a form of distance*. The "proximity" Henry seeks to name (the proximity of the essence to itself in immanence) is *not* this Heideggerian proximity; it is presence *without distance* — immediate self-presence. The very vocabulary of "proximity" risks importing the monist horizonal structure into the analysis of immanence; Henry uses the term cautiously and only with the structural correction.

**Paragraph 9\.** To the essence which, *as unity*, gives itself to itself in the *totality* of its reality, *nothing is lacking*; there is nothing in the essence that the essence is not yet — and for this reason, *the essence does not project itself toward anything*. The essence which projects itself toward nothing, to which nothing is lacking, could not await its accomplishment from anything else, and no more from itself; the essence has *already* accomplished itself; to the essence one cannot say "*become what you are*." To what cannot become anything other (and no more what it is), there manifestly lacks a *power* — the power-to-be in the precise sense of *being able to be otherwise*, of being able to be what one is not (or eventually what one is not yet).
