The "*not*" of "*not being*" or of "*not being yet*" is the condition of such a power, which appears as such — as essentially determined by this "not," essentially *finite*. The "not" which determines essentially the power-to-be in its possibility and in its finitude finds its ontological foundation in *irreality*. *Only that which holds itself in relation with irreality and lives in its light — that which relates itself to itself as to something irreal — can want to become what it represents to itself in this way*; can want the realization of what does not yet exist except in irreality, of *that self that is "not yet" real*. On this condition only can the essence *have to obey* the prescription of "becoming what it is" — on the condition of bearing within itself irreality, and that as a constitutive element of its very being.

This condition, which finds precisely its explicitation in the *ontological interpretation of the essence as Project and as Care, as power-to-be*, finds itself on the contrary radically excluded from what constitutes properly speaking the internal structure of the essence. This is why the essence considered in itself finds itself entirely deprived of the power here in question — of any power whatsoever relative to its proper being: *there where there is nothing irreal, there is also no possible realization*. The absence of any power whatsoever relative to its proper being is identically in the essence the absence of the "not" of "not being" or of "not being yet" — *the absence of all finitude*. Such an absence must then receive its true name — for it no longer signifies a privation but the *whole of reality*. *In non-power the essence finds its supreme power; its impotence is the impotence of plenitude.*

The polemic now takes on a precise Heideggerian focus. The Heideggerian doctrine of Dasein as *Sich-Vorweg-Sein* (being-ahead-of-itself, in *Sein und Zeit* §41), as essentially *Möglichkeit* (possibility), as essentially *Sorge* (Care), as defined by the Nietzschean injunction "*werde was du bist*" (become what you are) — this whole conception of the human being as essentially *projecting* itself toward what it is *not yet* — is, on Henry's reading, a conception that operates within the structure of *irreality*. Dasein "projects itself" toward possibilities only because these possibilities are *not yet real*; the "not yet" is the condition of the projecting; the projecting requires the irreality of what is not yet. So Heideggerian Dasein, structurally, lives in irreality: its very being is constituted by being-ahead-of-itself, by being-toward-the-not-yet.

But the immanent essence — life in Henry's sense — does *not* live in irreality. Life is not "ahead of itself"; life has no project, no Care; life is not "becoming what it is"; life *is* what it is, immediately, totally, in the plenitude of its self-presence. The injunction "become what you are" makes no sense to life; life has nothing to become because life is already, immediately, what it is.

The closing formula — *"in non-power the essence finds its supreme power; its impotence is the impotence of plenitude"* — captures the paradoxical structure with great precision. The essence "cannot" project itself, "cannot" become what it is not yet — but this "cannot" is not a deficiency; it is the structural mark of *plenitude*. The essence has no power to change itself because it is already, fully, what it is; this "impotence" is the mark of its perfection. The Heideggerian Dasein's powers (its projecting, its Care, its possibilities) are, on Henry's reading, signs of its *insufficiency* — its constitutive lack of full self-possession. The immanent essence's "non-power" is, by contrast, the sign of its *complete self-possession*.

**Paragraph 10\.** This *plenitude* of the essence — separated from all the determinations of the world and to which however nothing is lacking — this *richness of a reality without limit* that loses itself in its own profusion and entirely confuses itself with this profusion, *the experience of being in its nudity, in its simplicity, in its totality*, this experience without partition that *is being itself* — this is what the young Hegel represented to himself as the content of *religious consciousness*. Such a profusion, which is given to religious consciousness as that very thing which it is, religious consciousness lived in particular *in the symbol of water*. The liquid element knows *"no lacuna, no limitation, no diversity or determination."* This is why the experience of such an element is foreign to all distinction and to all finitude. *"The feeling of this plenitude is the least dispersed, the most simple…"* To give oneself the feeling of this plenitude, to enter into the element that contains it, to make precisely the experience of it — this is the wish that religious consciousness realizes in *baptism*: *"in the one who is immersed, there is only one feeling and the forgetting of the world, a solitude that has rejected everything from itself, that has torn itself away from everything, the suppression of all that existed until then, an exalting initiation…"*

The reference is to Hegel's early theological writings (the *Theologische Jugendschriften* — *The Spirit of Christianity and Its Fate*, in particular). The young Hegel — before the systematic dialectical-philosophical Hegel of the *Phenomenology* — had analyzed religious consciousness (especially the early Christian community, baptism, the Eucharist) as an experience of an absolute plenitude that escapes the categories of finite distinction. Henry retrieves these early Hegelian analyses precisely because they articulate, in a religious-experiential vocabulary, what Henry will articulate in a structural-ontological vocabulary: the immanent essence as the absolute plenitude of self-presence, beyond all distinction.

The experience of being in its simplicity and in its totality realizes itself otherwise, however, than in the representation of religious consciousness or in a determinate mode of its life; it realizes itself *in being itself* — in such a manner that this experience of being in its totality *constitutes being itself in its simplicity* and, as such, *an absolutely universal ontological structure independent of every understanding and every particular determination*. The experience-of-self of being in its totality determines being in its simplicity and constitutes being because being is precisely the *act of giving itself to itself*, and the structure of this act is such that, on the foundation in itself of this structure with which the act identifies itself, *being gives itself necessarily to itself in its reality* — that is, precisely *in its totality*. Such a structure (in conformity with which being gives itself to itself and with which being identifies itself) is nothing other, however, than *simplicity*. It is simplicity, in fact, that determines being as that which gives itself to itself in its reality and in its totality, in the totality of its reality. The simplicity of being — that is, in the absence of every distinction and of every finitude, *its omnipresence to itself* — results in being from the simplicity that constitutes it in its most intimate nature and determines it to be what it is, *the simple feeling of its plenitude*. Thus determined in itself by what it is as the simple experience-of-self in its totality, being offers itself to itself and gives itself to itself with the characters that confer on it a priori the structure of this experience — that is, its own structure.

The structural argument is elegant. *Being's omnipresence to itself* — the immanent self-relation that constitutes being's structure — is identical with *simplicity*. Being is simple because it has no internal distinction (no doubling, no opposition, no division); being is omnipresent to itself because it is *immediately given* to itself in the totality of its reality; being is its own simple feeling of plenitude because being is identical with this feeling. The structural identity *being \= simplicity \= omnipresence-to-self \= simple feeling of plenitude* is the central characterization of immanent life.

**Paragraph 11\.** In conformity with this structure, it appears that *there is in being, as positive phenomenological content constitutive of its effectivity, nothing more and nothing less than being itself* — nothing more and nothing less than this content in the effectivity of its phenomenality. Thus the reality of being exhausts itself in the originary experience that being has of itself, in such a manner that there is nothing beyond this experience and that in this experience being is wholly present to itself. The absence of a beyond does not signify, in what concerns the positive phenomenological content of this experience, *a limitation of this content* — more exactly, a limitation of being itself, its inscription inside the effective dimensions of this content — but, quite on the contrary, the *adequate character* of this content, the adequate character of phenomenality itself. The adequate character of the phenomenological content as such (when it is at least a question of the content here in question — that is, of the originary mode according to which phenomenality phenomenalizes itself), the absence of all finitude, not finitude — this is what is implicated in the absence of a beyond. It is with this restriction that it is fitting to understand, *not the empty identity of phenomenality in the tautology* (where it equally lets reality outside of itself), *but the rigorous coincidence of reality and appearance* — coincidence in which being finds its ultimate structure and (if you will) its privilege: *"chance,"* says Kafka, *"that the ground on which you stand cannot be wider than the two feet that cover it."* But this truth — that of truth itself in its originary and universal structure — is also *tragic*, because it signifies the *irremissible* and the *definitive*: the institution of an absolute world from which nothing can be subtracted, to which nothing can be added, where, without detour and without lie, things are what they are, being is what it is, in this perfect adequation that *is being itself*. This is why — it is the perfect character of this adequation and what this adequation signifies in general for the universal structure of being that Kafka has expressed again when he spoke of those *arrows exactly fitted to the wounds they have made*. *Privilege* or, in this world without rending, *rending of a wound*; *joy* or *suffering*; or rather (and that for essential reasons that will be exposed) *both at the same time* — such is in any case the structure of being in unity, *its indissoluble unity with itself in the adequate experience that constitutes it*.

The Kafka references are striking. They are taken from Kafka's *Reflections on Sin, Suffering, Hope, and the True Way* (the Zürau aphorisms). The first ("the ground on which you stand cannot be wider than the two feet that cover it") names the perfect adequation of being and appearance in the immanent essence: there is no surplus of being beyond what is given in the experience of being; the experience of being *is* being, exhaustively and adequately. The second (the arrows exactly fitted to the wounds they have made) names the same adequation in a tragic register: the wound (the suffering of life, given immediately to itself) is exactly fitted by what gives it (the arrow, the affecting of life by itself); life is, in the adequate experience that constitutes it, *both* the wounding and the wounded, *both* the affecting and the affected. There is no escape, no deferral, no distance between life's self-giving and life's reception of itself. This is the structural characterization of life's immanent self-affection.

The closing observation that joy *and* suffering are equally the structure of immanent life prepares the analyses of Section IV (where Henry will articulate the affective tonalities of life — joy, suffering, anguish — as the modal structures of immanent self-affection). Life is not a neutral self-experience; life is essentially *affected* — and the modes of this affection (joy, suffering) are the very modes of life's being-given-to-itself.

**Paragraph 12\.** The nature of the experience of being as *adequate experience*, as experience-of-self of being in the totality of its reality and in its unity with itself, the *indissoluble character* of this unity — they express *an impossibility inscribed in the essence as its very structure*. On what structure is grounded in the essence the impossibility here in question, and what does it signify first? Every impossibility implies *the absence of a power* in relation to which, on the contrary, something would be possible. What is impossible in the experience of being (and that in conformity with its structure) is the *non-adequation*, the *non-coincidence* of being with itself in the totality of its reality. What power is missing, when it is impossible for being not to coincide with itself, not to identify itself with itself in the absolute unity where, prisoner of itself and of its reality, it remains in itself? Manifestly *the power of going outside itself*, of *positing something other than its own reality* and of *escaping it* — that is, again, "*freedom*." *"Absolute being,"* said Fichte, *"is in this part of the form this freedom which is its own, outside itself."* *Freedom* — this is, quite on the contrary, the power of which absolute being finds itself deprived, in such a manner that there is in it no part, no "form" that is exterior to it — nothing it is not (or that it is not yet) in the actuality of its reality. The structure on which reposes the impossibility for being not to be wholly present to itself, the impossibility for being to break the link that attaches it to itself, to tear itself from itself and to exist outside itself, is *non-freedom*.

A new and decisive structural concept is introduced: *non-freedom* (*non-liberté*). This is one of Henry's most provocative theses. The immanent essence is *non-free* — it has no power to be other than what it is, no possibility of escaping itself, no capacity to project itself toward an outside. This is the structural counterpart, on the side of immanence, of the structural feature that on the side of monism appears as *freedom* (the power of horizonal projection, the going-outside-itself of transcendence). The Fichtean citation is from the *Anweisung zum seligen Leben* (already cited in §§9–11), where Fichte had analyzed absolute being's "freedom outside itself" as the structural feature of being's self-manifestation. Henry's reversal: this Fichtean "freedom" is precisely what the immanent essence does *not* have. The immanent essence is *non-free* in the structural sense — and this non-freedom is the mark of its plenitude, not its deficiency.

**Paragraph 13\.** What is implicated in the concept of non-freedom must however be specified — for everywhere there is an essence and laws of essence, there is a prescription, a rule, and precisely *the impossibility of overstepping this rule*. Non-freedom belongs in general to the essence as that very thing which constitutes it. And as the empire of essences extends over the totality of what is — as nothing is removed from its jurisdiction — one can say, without fear of being mistaken, *that everything obeys laws*, that *everything is determined*. Freedom itself, if at least it is possible for us to speak of it in a coherent manner, if it is not now this and now that, finds itself submitted in its nature to a structural determination with which, more, it identifies itself. It is a determination of this kind that has been encountered by the problematic when, precisely apropos of freedom, it has shown that the product of freedom takes on the form of a horizon, and that *necessarily*. Determined, the product of freedom is, because freedom itself is determined as necessarily linked to what it has produced and (in a more ultimate manner) by reason of *the very nature of this link*, that is, of its own nature. The structural determination of the horizon is however a determination that accomplishes itself *from freedom and through freedom*; it is freedom that constitutes the law of this determination and that expresses itself in this determination. This is why what is *bound* — because it is bound by freedom — is also *unbound*, develops itself in exteriority. *The necessity that determines the internal structure of being does not reduce in any way, on the contrary, to a simple necessity of eidetic order* (such as the one that belongs, for example, to the eidos of freedom); it is the *negation or absence of freedom* that this necessity expresses — in such a manner that it does not signify simply, *as non-freedom*, the necessity of a structure in general, but *the necessity of a determinate structure* — of that structure precisely which finds itself determined (and that in an essential manner) by the absence in it of all freedom and (in this rigorous sense) as *non-freedom*.

The structural distinction is made: there are two senses of "necessity." (i) *Eidetic necessity*: the necessity that belongs to every essence by virtue of its being an essence (every essence has its own structural laws, its own rules of identity). Even the eidos of *freedom* has its own eidetic necessity (the laws by which freedom operates as freedom). (ii) *Ontological non-freedom*: the necessity that characterizes a *particular* kind of structure — namely, the immanent essence — which has *no* freedom whatsoever, which is *non-free* in the strong sense. The immanent essence's necessity is not just any eidetic necessity; it is specifically the necessity of *non-freedom*, the necessity of a structure that excludes the going-outside-itself that would constitute freedom.

**Paragraph 14\.** Freedom has an ontological signification. To be free, for a pure ontological power (that is, for the pure power of arousing a manifestation), is to be capable of *positing something other than its own reality* — is to bear within itself a determinate power: the power precisely of positing something other than itself. The power of positing something other than itself is, as such, *creative*. Creation in no way signifies, from the ontological point of view, the position of an element radically other with respect to the ontological element itself, but only *the position of the element foreign to its reality (although produced by this reality)*. It is the *milieu of alterity* — not the existent — the *milieu of irreality and ideality* as pure ontological milieu — that finds itself produced by freedom *as creative*. As such, freedom comports assuredly, with regard to the existent itself, a certain power: that of rendering it manifest.

The structural argument continues. Freedom, on the monist conception, is *creative* in the precise sense that it *produces the milieu* (the horizon, the field of objectivity) within which beings can manifest themselves. Freedom does not literally create the existent (it does not bring beings into being from nothing); freedom creates the *transcendental opening* in which beings can appear. This is the Heideggerian-Kantian doctrine of transcendental imagination as the productive source of the horizon. Henry preserves this analysis but precisely to mark its boundary: this whole "creative freedom" operates *only* in the structure of monism — the structure that, on Henry's diagnosis, the immanent essence does not have.

No doubt such a power is limited, and that because the existent remains in itself fundamentally foreign to a light from which it never takes on but a borrowed luster (and from which it withdraws very quickly). This limit of its power, freedom — it is true — finds in itself, in such a manner that, as has been shown, *finitude does not concern primitively the existent or its relation to manifestation, but this manifestation itself as such* — insofar, more exactly, as it is produced by freedom. This is why finitude does not properly speaking *limit* the power of freedom but *qualifies* it properly in what it is, the power of instituting in irreality a dimension of encounter and approach for the existent — but first and (in truth) exclusively *this dimension itself in its proper phenomenological positivity*. It is with regard to this dimension and to the horizon opened by it that freedom reveals itself the holder of a power that it measures by this pure milieu. Because freedom creates this milieu, the milieu is submitted to freedom as that to which also freedom measures every thing. To submit to itself such a milieu — and that in the very act by which it binds itself to it — is the operation of freedom, its proper activity, what constitutes finally the ontological power itself as identical precisely with freedom. *How could such a power be on the contrary understood as non-freedom, how could it be susceptible of being deprived of that very thing which it is?*

The question is sharp. Freedom (in the monist sense) appears as the very essence of the ontological power of manifestation: how could *non-freedom* characterize the same essence? The answer requires the structural shift to immanence.

**Paragraph 15\.** Or rather, freedom (which creates the horizon whose opening is imputable to it and with respect to which freedom has mastery and power) — must it not be grasped in *what it is*? It is of the *internal structure of the power that constitutes the foundation and the essence of all manifestation* that it is a question. Such a power, considered in itself, does it not give itself from now on (and that *with evidence*) in its *radical independence with regard to the act that creates the horizon* — in its radical independence with regard to *freedom*? *Free* — freedom is, *in its relation to the horizon*, relation that constitutes precisely freedom itself. *Not in its relation to itself* — relation that is, as such, as radically independent of freedom, *the essence of non-freedom*. That the ontological power (which constitutes the foundation of all possible manifestation) lets itself be understood in itself as *determined by the essence of non-freedom* means: such a power, which dominates the horizon (aroused and assumed by it) of irreality, *no longer has with regard to itself and to its own reality any power, any possibility of positing itself, of arousing its being or of assuming it*. Here, in the internal structure of the originary essence of revelation, in the originary relation of being to itself, *cease all mastery, all faculty of acting or of operating, all that gives itself habitually as the foundation of a responsibility or of an imputability, as an origin or as a cause, all possibility of assuming and of taking attitude*.

The decisive structural distinction is now made. There are two relations that the ontological power has:

* (i) *Relation to the horizon*: in this relation, the ontological power is *free* — it creates the horizon, has mastery over it, can be said to "do" something. This is the structural site of all the classical concepts: freedom, mastery, action, responsibility, cause, decision, attitude.  
* (ii) *Relation to itself*: in this relation, the ontological power is *non-free* — it has no power over its own being, cannot create itself, cannot decide itself, cannot assume itself. This is the structural site of immanence: the relation of being to itself, in which being is *passively given to itself*, with no mastery over its own being.

The classical philosophical tradition has thought (i) and missed (ii). It has analyzed all the structures that pertain to freedom (creative imagination, transcendental constitution, projective Care, decision, etc.) without ever recognizing that beneath these structures lies a more fundamental structure of *passivity in the relation to oneself*. Henry's discovery (in this section) is precisely (ii): the structure of being's *self-relation* is non-free, passive, prior to all freedom, prior to all mastery.

The impossibility for being to take attitude with regard to itself, to put itself in question, does *not* result simply from the eidetic incompatibility of freedom and reality (the latter no doubt could not submit itself to the power of the irreal). If such an impossibility concerns not the simple exclusion of irreality but *the internal structure of reality itself* and its positive ontological determination, what does it signify in what concerns reality — what does it signify, for the ontological power considered in its fundamental relation to itself, *to no longer be able*?

**Paragraph 16\.** That which no longer has with regard to itself and to its own reality any power reveals itself to be in its most intimate nature *essentially passive*. *Passivity is the ontological structural determination of the originary essence of revelation* — that is, of being itself considered in its internal reality as fundamentally determined in itself by the essence of non-freedom. At the moment when the concept of *passivity* intervenes in the problematic to determine the internal structure of the originary essence of revelation (that is, of being itself in its reality), it is important to specify its signification, in order to recognize precisely the one that is fitting to it in this fundamental ontological usage. Passivity could not designate first (as Descartes wanted) *the action of a foreign reality*. *It is the relation of being with itself, with its own reality (not with a foreign reality), that finds itself described and subsumed under the concept of passivity*, if at least passivity must receive its fundamental ontological signification.

The Cartesian concept of *passion* (from *Les Passions de l'âme*) — passivity as the soul's being-acted-upon by foreign realities (the body, the external world, etc.) — is here put aside. Henry's *passivity* is structurally different: it is *self-passivity*, the passivity of being in relation to *itself*, not in relation to an external other. This is the structural feature that Cartesian and post-Cartesian philosophy missed.

Thus is set aside a *radically improper but traditional* understanding, in conformity with which passivity is heard necessarily inside its relation to *something other* that is in some way imposed on it (for example, *given* to it), and with respect to which passivity determines itself from now on (in the fact of being thus affected by something other) to be what it is, *passive*. That with respect to which passivity determines itself to be what it is, is interpreted at first no doubt — and for example in Descartes — as *the existent*; the action exerted on what proposes itself on the contrary as passive is at first assimilated to a *comportment of ontic order*. The existent however is no other than by *alterity*. *It is in its relation to alterity that passivity is understood as what it is.* The necessity in virtue of which the ontological milieu of alterity holds itself before passivity and imposes itself on it as that to which passivity is submitted is however nothing other than *freedom*. The true necessity concerns freedom — freedom itself as being what it is. Thus is defined *the nature of the link* that must be subsumed under the concept of passivity insofar as this latter shows itself capable of designating *the internal structure of the ontological power*: it is to *itself*, not to alterity, that the ontological power finds itself submitted in the passivity that determines it to be what it is. *The passivity that fundamentally determines the ontological power is, as passivity of being with regard to itself (not of something other), a passivity in unity.* How can such a passivity maintain itself in its concept? *How can what is given (and as such received) be that very thing which receives it?* To be oneself what one receives — and as such essentially *passive with regard to oneself* — such is however the essence of *life* and (when life designates revelation itself in its concrete effectivity, when passivity with regard to oneself is none other than *the experience of self*, that is, precisely this revelation itself) *the essence of spirit*. *"To spirit, to life,"* said the young Hegel, *"what they receive is not given; they become it by themselves; this passes into them in such a way that this is from now on a modification of themselves, their life."* What life receives (what spirit receives) is not, however, a modification of themselves. This is why, in truth, they do not *become* it; *they are it* — and that since always, because, since always, this is what they are — what they receive insofar precisely as *they are themselves what they receive*.

The structural pivot is the most concentrated philosophical formulation in §37: *to be oneself what one receives*. In immanence, the structure of *self-reception* is one in which the receiving and the received are *identical* — life *is* what it receives; the receiving of life by life is the very being of life. This is the structural answer to the problem of receptivity that Section II had posed (in §22): how can the essence be receptive in relation to itself? Answer: by *being* what it receives, by being identical with the receiving and the received in the immediate self-presence of immanent life.

The Hegelian citation (from the early *Spirit of Christianity*) is again deployed precisely. The young Hegel had already glimpsed this structural feature: spirit and life *are* what they receive, and what they receive *is* themselves. But the young Hegel mis-stated the structural relation as a *becoming* (life "becomes" what it receives, "receives" what it then is). Henry corrects: there is no becoming here; life is already, immediately, what it is — and what it is, is what it receives in the immediate self-affection that constitutes it.

**Paragraph 17\.** Insofar as life and spirit are themselves what they receive, the passivity that determines them — and which (as passivity with regard to itself or again as passivity in unity) constitutes their very being — has nothing to do with the passivity that characterizes the relation to *foreign being*. To the submission to being that gives itself as other in the element of alterity (a submission that constitutes however *freedom itself* and on which is grounded in consequence the possibility of taking-attitude and of thus assuming what is distinguished — objective being — in service, in fear, in defiance, or in the idea), is decisively opposed *what finds itself determined in itself by the absence of every choice* — what whose submission with regard to itself no longer signifies a possibility but on the contrary (and that in an unsurmountable manner, as well as a decisive one) *the impossibility of every possibility, the impossibility of every possibility in general*. What finds itself fundamentally determined in itself by the impossibility of every possibility with regard to itself, of every position-taking and every assumption concerning its own being, must be recognized as *what makes from the beginning the theme of the problematic* — and that insofar as the problematic wills and understands itself in its originary character, as having *the origin* for theme. For the origin is precisely *what has, with regard to itself, no power, no possibility of willing itself or of understanding itself, of surpassing itself or of dominating its being in any manner whatsoever and first by assuming it*.

The polemic is now turned sharply against the entire existentialist-phenomenological tradition. Heidegger's *Sein und Zeit* — and Sartre's *L'Être et le Néant* — make the assumption (*Übernahme*) of one's being the central existential structure (Heidegger's *Eigentlichkeit*, Sartre's project, choice, responsibility). The whole vocabulary of *taking-attitude*, *resoluteness*, *projecting*, *deciding*, *assuming* belongs to the structure of freedom — the structure of the *self-relation through the horizon*. But this structure is, on Henry's reading, *not* the originary structure; the originary structure (the immanent self-relation) excludes all this. The origin has no power to assume itself, to decide itself, to project itself; the origin is *what* it is, immediately, prior to all assumption, prior to all freedom.

The origin is what *escapes* — not as something hypothetical or mysterious, but in the sense of *what escapes a power*, of *what is removed from a power*. That the origin escape any power whatever concerning it — that it be removed from such power — means precisely that *it is the origin*; it means: it is *that from which a power is possible*, that from which power develops itself — in such a manner however that this power can never *return to it*, never *retake* it, and (a fortiori) never *posit it or create it*. Insofar as it is the "*that from which*" of a power, the origin is never the "*that on which*" of this power, but on the contrary (as has just been said) what escapes the power and withdraws from it, *its beyond*. Insofar as the "that from which" of a power is its "beyond," *the beyond of every power and of every possibility of power in general — the impossibility — it is from this (from the impossibility) that all possibility accomplishes itself*. That from which all possibility accomplishes itself, and which (as impossibility) holds itself beyond possibility, is *the irremissible*, is *the absolute*. The absolute is not such because it holds itself beyond every power; it is because it is the absolute (because such is its internal nature) that it holds itself in this beyond — beyond every power and every possibility of power in general. *What is the internal nature of the absolute? The internal nature of the absolute is passivity.* The absolute being is the being which (originarily and fundamentally passive vis-à-vis itself) has as such — and in consequence — *vis-à-vis itself no power*; is the being which is what it is — in such a manner that it cannot *not be* what it is, and that it cannot *"be"* it either, in the sense where being signifies still power, power-to-be, to assume. Being is what it is in the sense where being signifies *the originary immanent revelation of self in unity*.

The structural conclusion is now fully crystallized. The *origin* — what philosophy has from the start tried to think — is structurally what *cannot be assumed*. Every philosophy that thinks the origin as something that has to be *taken up*, *assumed*, *projected*, *decided*, *willed* misses the origin: such philosophies treat the origin as an object of possible action, when the origin is precisely *that from which* action becomes possible (and which is itself always already given, beyond all action). The origin is the *absolute* because it is the *irremissible* — the irrevocable, the unsurpassable, the not-to-be-modified. Its internal nature is *passivity* — the structural passivity of being-given-to-itself with no possibility of acting upon itself.

**Paragraph 18\.** That the internal structure of being resides in its originary passivity with regard to itself — and, as such, in *the essence of non-freedom* — is what reveals itself to every understanding that approaches the essential. Rare as such an understanding may be, it could not however not be produced in the history of human thought, at least under the form of *an experience*, even when the ultimate ontological structures that would serve as its foundation are not elaborated. The circumstances in which such an experience is produced can in themselves be illuminating. For if the irreducible structure of the essence arises in general in *free imagination*, how much must this be true also of *freedom itself* — insofar as freedom collides with necessity not only as with its contrary but as with its essence. That the unbreakable necessity of the link of being to itself in unity and in the originary passivity with regard to itself — that *non-freedom* — constitutes the essence of *freedom itself*, is what reveals itself to freedom *at the most extreme point of its exercise, in the most extreme will of its power and of its potency*. The moment of this discovery of its essence — of the discovery in itself of absolute necessity — gives itself to freedom from now on as the moment in which (in this extreme form of its power and of its will-to-power) freedom *pronounces the yes* — the *affirmation* no longer of itself but of *its essence, of necessity*, not as of what wounds it but constitutes on the contrary its most interior nature and the *permanent* in itself. *Thus one sees in Nietzsche the defiance invert itself and understand itself in the love of destiny — that is, also, in the love of self*. For destiny is not an exterior series of events constrained to be produced or to reproduce themselves in an inevitable manner, but the *internal structure of being* as originally and fundamentally constituted by the ultimate essence of non-freedom.

The Nietzschean reference is precise. *Amor fati* (the love of fate, especially in *Ecce Homo* and in late Nietzsche) — the affirmation of necessity, the embracing of one's destiny as one's own — has been read by many commentators (Heidegger, Deleuze, etc.) as the highest form of Nietzschean freedom (the will-to-power affirming itself in its full creative power). Henry reads this Nietzschean experience differently: at the highest point of the will-to-power, the will recognizes its own *non-freedom*; it recognizes that its very being is structurally given, irremissible, not subject to any free choice. The will-to-power's highest expression is *yes* — the affirmation of what is, not as what one chose but as what one *is*. This is the experiential approximation, in Nietzschean vocabulary, of the structure of immanent passivity that Henry has been articulating.

The whole reference is also a polemic against Heidegger's reading of Nietzsche (in the *Nietzsche* lectures of 1936–46). For Heidegger, Nietzsche is the consummation of Western metaphysics as the metaphysics of subjectivity (the will-to-power as the absolute self-positing of subjectivity). For Henry, Nietzsche's *amor fati* points precisely *beyond* the metaphysics of subjectivity — to the recognition of the structural non-freedom of being, to the immanent passivity of life with respect to itself.

**Paragraph 19\.** The understanding of an experience like Nietzsche's (which, *as experience of the internal structure of being*, results finally in *love and acquiescence*) must however take care not to misunderstand itself and its proper signification — and that at the very moment when it believes itself in possession of this signification. For if the ultimate structure of being grounds the phenomenon of yes and of acquiescence (and at the same time finds itself understood by it), the ultimate structure of being is *not* however *contained in* the phenomenon of yes and of acquiescence. To acquiesce, to say yes — or, in the same way, to refuse, to confront in defiance — are diverse manners *of taking attitude*, diverse modes of a power that is *that of freedom*. Insofar as acquiescement and consent are diverse manners of taking attitude (and as such modes of freedom), what they address themselves to (what they submit themselves to) is nothing other however than *what finds itself submitted to freedom and to its power*. Thus being becomes in the yes of consent the "*that on which*" that being never is of a power that being also never has. Thus the *ontological passivity* (which constitutes the internal structure of being as the structure of the originary relation of being to itself) is *confused* with the passivity that is only a mode of freedom and of the power of taking-attitude — with the passivity of which Kierkegaard could rightly say that *"there must always be in passivity enough activity for it to be able to keep its passivity."*

The structural distinction is now made with great precision. (i) *Existential passivity* (Kierkegaard's): the passivity that is itself a *mode* of activity, a *form of taking-attitude*. To "let oneself be passive" is itself an active stance, a decision, a posture; it requires "enough activity to keep its passivity." (ii) *Ontological passivity*: the passivity that is *prior to* all activity, that is the structural condition of every possible activity, that *cannot* be a mode of activity because it precedes the very distinction of activity and passivity. Henry's *ontological passivity* is the second; it is *not* what Kierkegaard, Nietzsche, or any existential philosopher could have grasped, because they were all working at the level of existential modes (of taking-attitude), not at the level of the originary structure that grounds all such modes.

Even Nietzsche's *amor fati* — the highest existential approximation of immanent passivity — is itself an *existential* yes, a mode of taking-attitude. It points toward, but does not coincide with, the *structural-ontological* passivity that is the actual essence of immanence. The phenomenologist must learn to distinguish the existential approximation from the structural reality.

No more than the acquiescence to what (in being) constitutes its most interior nature can be confused with this nature, no more could this structure be understood as *what reveals itself to such an acquiescement* — as if this acquiescence, *failing to coincide with this structure, did at least bear in itself (in the experience that it institutes and that constitutes it properly) the power of revealing this structure*. The most interior structure of being is *the internal structure of revelation insofar as it reveals itself interiorly to itself*: far from revealing this structure, the experience of acquiescence *presupposes* this structure on the contrary — as *what reveals it (the experience of acquiescence) originarily to itself*, insofar as this structure (the internal structure of revelation) reveals itself originarily to itself.

**Paragraph 20 (closing).** That the most interior structure of being (that is, being itself as originarily given to itself in the fundamental passivity of non-freedom — that is, again, *the internal structure of immanence*) constitutes precisely *the structure of revelation itself* and (as such) *the essence of the Logos* — this is what at least must be understood.

The closing sentence opens onto the program of the rest of Section III. What has been shown in §37 is the *structural identity* of three things:

* The *internal structure of immanence* (the immediate self-relation of being).  
* The *structure of revelation itself* (the manner in which the essence of manifestation reveals itself).  
* The *essence of the Logos* (the structure of the Word, the originary articulation of being).

This three-fold identity is the central thesis of Section III. Immanence is not a peripheral or marginal structure; immanence *is* revelation, immanence *is* the Logos. The whole of Section III will progressively articulate this identity in its various aspects: through the analysis of Eckhart (§39), of Fichte's late thought (§38), of the absolute situation (§§41–44), and of the radical critique of vision/representation/knowledge that gives the section its subtitle ("the invisible," §§45–51).

The reference to the *Logos* is theological-Johannine (recall §10's reference to John 1:1 and the Fichtean commentary on the Prologue of John). The *Logos* — the eternal Word that "was in the beginning" — is, on Henry's reading, structurally the immanent self-revelation of the absolute. The Logos is not a "word" in the sense of an exterior expression; the Logos is the *internal structure of revelation* by which the absolute reveals itself to itself. This will be the central thesis of Henry's later religious phenomenology (in *I Am the Truth*, *Words of Christ*); already here, at the foundational level of *L'Essence de la manifestation*, the structural identification is announced.

---

## **§ 38\. The internal structure of immanence and the problem of its understanding as revelation: Fichte**

**Paragraph 1\.** It is a question first to know whether, in the history of philosophical thought, what constitutes properly speaking *the internal structure of immanence* has ever been *truly understood*. Insofar however as such a structure has been *sensed* (or at least seemed to have been), it is remarkable that it has been interpreted most often — not to say almost always — *not* as constitutive precisely of the essence and of the possibility of *a revelation*, but as *excluding* revelation, in order to designate on the contrary what finds itself by principle *foreign* to the element of phenomenality, namely *the existent*. And it is thus that, at the very moment when its idea comes to the fore, immanence finds itself rejected outside the proper domain of ontology in order to receive on the contrary (as has been seen) *the signification of being an ontic category*.

The opening paragraph names the historical and philosophical predicament that §§38–40 will work through. The concept of *immanence* has been historically misunderstood: it has been interpreted as a property of *existents* (something is "immanent" insofar as it is just an inner property of an existent, with no reference to anything beyond) rather than as the structure of *revelation itself*. This misinterpretation has consigned immanence to the status of an *ontic* category (a category applicable to existents) instead of the *ontological* category that it properly is.

Now, it is not (if one reflects) the analysis of the existent that results in its thematic determination as immanent being — a determination, moreover, *absurd*, because (as has been seen) *the existent does not remain in itself any more than it goes outside itself*. *The thought of immanence intervenes in reality on an ontological plane*; it takes form and determines itself initially in its *opposition to the concept of transcendence*. This transcendence, however, being understood as the power in which phenomenality (identified with exteriority) acquires a foundation — immanence (from which such a power finds itself radically excluded) finds itself excluded in turn from this latter (that is, from the essence of phenomenality), and interpreted from now on as radically foreign to phenomenality — *as foreign not only to phenomenality itself in its effectivity but to its essence, to what there could be of non-phenomenal in the ontological element itself*.

The structural diagnosis is precise. The immanent has been excluded from phenomenality not because the existent (to which the term is wrongly applied) is non-phenomenal — but because *transcendence* (the ekstatic-horizonal structure) has been wrongly identified with *the essence of phenomenality as such*. Once this monist identification is made, immanence (as the negation of transcendence) appears as the negation of phenomenality itself — that is, as *non-phenomenal*. This is the structural error that has dogged the concept of immanence throughout the philosophical tradition.

And it is thus that the concept of immanence lets itself paradoxically be applied to the existent. It is from the existent (no doubt) that, in modern philosophy, *transcendence itself* is thought — and that for lack of being able to be thought from itself and from its foundation. Thought from the existent as that very thing of which the existent is deprived, transcendence offers thus to what serves it as an antithetical concept the possibility (and even the obligation) of designating *the existent itself*. Thus immanence signifies first *non-phenomenality*, secondarily what reveals itself characterized by non-phenomenality — and that in such a manner that the genesis of the pure ontological concepts (such as it accomplishes itself paradoxically from the existent) comes to corroborate this double signification.

**Paragraph 2\.** What is implicated in the content of the concept of immanence (such as it finds itself determined on a pure ontological plane and in a negative manner, in its opposition to that of transcendence) — *the idea of a subsistence and of a permanence in itself*, and that in what concerns being — does not let itself be so easily forgotten if the fact of remaining thus in itself in the primitive identity with self gives itself inevitably (at the very moment when immanence is grasped in its radical opposition to the traditional concept of phenomenality) as a properly *ontological* and at the same time *fundamental* character — as *constitutive* consequently of being itself. This is why, as soon as it is a question of grasping being in its most intimate and most essential structure, the idea of *immanence presents itself to the problematic*, and that despite its phenomenological incompatibility with the reigning concept of phenomenality. *Thus one sees the absolute be finally understood by Fichte not anymore as an arising and becoming of existence in alterity, as being-outside-itself of being, but on the contrary as the persistence and the maintenance of being in itself — and that under the form of love.* Love, says Fichte in the *Tenth Conference* \[of the *Anweisung zum seligen Leben*\], leans directly on itself, because *"it is directly the absolute supporting and maintaining itself."* And again: *"this love is nothing other than the maintenance of self by absolute being."*

The first major Fichtean thesis is now exhibited. In the *Anweisung zum seligen Leben* (1806) — Fichte's late religious-philosophical work, the *Way Toward the Blessed Life* — Fichte conceives the absolute not as the ekstatic *Tathandlung* of the early *Wissenschaftslehre* (in which the absolute "posits itself outside itself" in the I-Not-I structure), but as *love* — as the persistence and self-maintenance of being. The pivot is decisive: Fichte's late thought breaks with the going-outside-itself structure of his earlier work and articulates the absolute as *immanent self-maintenance*. This is, structurally, an approximation to the immanence Henry has been articulating in §37.

That the maintenance of self by absolute being signifies precisely the permanence and the persistence of absolute being in itself (in the sense of immanence) is seen in the fact that immediately after having posited love as this self-maintenance constitutive of absolute being, Fichte opposes love to *reflection* — not as one psychological modality opposed to another, but as a *universal structure* identified by him with the process of *division* and of *difference*. *"It is not,"* writes Fichte after the previously cited propositions, *"reflection — which by virtue of its essence divides itself and thus opposes itself to itself — it is love that is the source of all... reality."* Source of all reality, love is also (according to Fichte) the source of *beatitude*. And it is because love is understood as finding its structure in immanence (as that which is not separated from itself) that the search by men for beatitude must be said to be vain if it pursues itself *"in something other than what here already surrounds them so closely that it cannot be brought closer during all eternity."*

The Fichtean opposition love / reflection is, on Henry's reading, structurally the opposition immanence / transcendence. *Love* is the structure in which the absolute remains with itself, immediate to itself, undivided. *Reflection* is the structure of division — the structure in which the absolute is doubled, in which it goes outside itself in order to relate to itself through mediation. The whole problem of beatitude (the structural-religious problem of the *Anweisung*) is the problem of reaching the immediate self-presence that is operative *already*, that surrounds us *already* "more closely than it can be brought during all eternity." This is structurally an experiential approximation of the immanent *Parousia* that Henry articulates ontologically in §37.

**Paragraph 3\.** Not being separated from itself but remaining eternally one (in unity with itself), love gives itself necessarily from now on with the *fundamental ontological characters* that belong in general to *the structure of unity* — that is, *in reality* and consequently also *in its totality*: *"love is eternally gathered totally in itself... has in itself reality in its totality."* *"Also,"* pursues Fichte, *"the division of the divine life one into diverse individuals is in no way in love but solely in reflection."* This (reflection), consequently, reveals itself not only foreign to the internal structure of love (that is, also of *life*), but moreover *fundamentally incapable* of understanding it and of rendering it manifest in what it is. Reflection *transforms* love on the contrary, and that in such a manner that, far from finding itself revealed by this transformation, *what makes the essence of life and of love finds itself rather lost in reflection*: *"it is this content and this matter of love that the reflection of life transforms first into a solidified essence."*

The Fichtean development is precise. Love (the immanent self-maintenance of the absolute) carries within itself the structural marks of unity that §37 identified: totality, reality, gatheredness, simplicity. Reflection, by contrast, *fragments* love — divides it into individuals, opposes it to itself, transforms its living content into a "solidified essence" (a fixed thematic representation). Reflection does not *reveal* love; reflection *transforms* love into something other than what love is. This is structurally the same diagnostic Henry has been making throughout: the categories of monist phenomenality (representation, opposition, division) cannot capture the immanent essence; they distort it, reify it, lose it.

**Paragraph 4\.** With the opposition to reflection of a structure from which reflection finds itself radically excluded — and which can no longer be *understood* by reflection — *there comes to the fore in Fichte a new philosophy of existence in which existence no longer designates the simple opposition-to-self of being in exteriority, nor its foundation (namely, the surpassing of being itself), but on the contrary what could not be surpassed and which (not being able thus to surpass itself) can no longer return upon itself to posit itself, nor try to deduce or understand itself*. But the impossibility of surpassing oneself and of returning upon oneself is *that of the being which (originarily linked to itself in unity) cannot be without finding itself, and that as already given to itself*; it is *that of the origin and of immanent being*. *"Existence,"* writes Fichte, *"could not be without finding itself, conceiving itself, supposing itself..."* and he adds, in an essential proposition: *"by the absolute character of its existence, and from the fact that it is bound to this existence which is its own, every possibility is cut off for it of surpassing this existence, and of understanding itself, and of deducing itself again beyond this existence, ... it is already given..., without being able to explain how and why it is such."* The existence which (bound to itself) cannot surpass itself shows itself at the same blow *radically independent* with regard to what is produced in such a surpassing: with regard to the representation-of-self and to the concept; to existence primitively recognized as existence in exteriority, as objective existence: *"this existence itself,"* says Fichte, *"reposes and is grounded on itself, anteriorly to every notion that it has of itself, and insoluble for this notion that it has of itself."*

The Fichtean development of the new philosophy of existence is now articulated. The Fichte of the *Anweisung* has reached, by his own path, a structural insight into immanent existence: existence is *given to itself*, prior to all reflection, prior to all representation, prior to all conceptual self-understanding. Existence is *bound* to itself in such a way that it cannot surpass itself, cannot project itself, cannot turn back on itself to make itself an object of representation. The Fichtean formulations — "existence cannot be without finding itself, conceiving itself, supposing itself," "anteriorly to every notion that it has of itself," "insoluble for this notion" — articulate, in 1806, the structural conception of immanent existence that Henry will articulate ontologically. The Fichtean *Anweisung* is, on Henry's reading, the closest the philosophical tradition came to grasping the immanent essence — and the failures of Fichte's articulation will reveal, by contrast, the precise structural requirements that a true phenomenology of immanence must meet.

That existence (so understood in an essential manner as anterior to every notion it can have of itself, and as radically independent of this notion) constitutes precisely the very being of the absolute — this is what Fichte affirms unconditionally: *"Whence comes to it,"* he asks (apropos of existence), *"this being completely independent of all its being deriving from its notion of itself — and which on the contrary precedes this notion and renders it possible? ... This is the strong and living existence of the absolute itself, which alone is capable of being and of existing — and outside of which nothing is or exists truly."*

**Paragraph 5\.** The *radical modification* that the theory of existence undergoes when it concerns the existence of the absolute itself (that is, true existence — that which alone "is and exists truly") has been perceived by Fichte and even *explicitly* affirmed by him. This is why "*after having recognized in consciousness with all its diverse form (which we previously took for true existence) a simple existence of second hand and the simple manifestation of this existence — and recognized love in true and absolute existence,*" Fichte comes to modify in the same manner — and no less explicitly — *his theory of the Verb (Logos)*: that is, the interpretation he gives of the beginning of the Gospel of Saint John. *"In the beginning was the Verb"* no longer signifies: *in the beginning was the absolute in the conscious form of its existence — that is, in its exteriority with respect to itself*; but: *in the beginning was love — that is, again the absolute, but as that which remains in itself, as "eternally gathered totally in itself."* Existence no longer signifying — in what concerns the absolute — its exteriority with respect to itself, with respect to its originary and proper being, *there is no longer a difference between this latter, between being and existence — and that precisely because existence has ceased to be the difference*: *"the whole difference signaled... between being and existence, and the absence of relation between the one and the other, reveals itself here to exist only for us... but in no way as existing in itself and directly in divine existence."*

The Fichtean reinterpretation of the Johannine Prologue is significant. In the early *Wissenschaftslehre*, Fichte had read "In the beginning was the Word" as articulating the absolute's primitive going-outside-itself in the structure of consciousness (the Word \= the *form* of consciousness as the absolute's self-objectification). In the late *Anweisung*, Fichte reverses this reading: the Word is now the *immanent* love, the absolute remaining gathered in itself, prior to all going-outside-itself. The pivotal Johannine passage is now read in an *immanent* register: the *Logos* is not the absolute's self-exteriorization but the absolute's immanent self-presence.

And the identity here posited of being and of existence must be understood rigorously as characterizing in fact, in a *positive* manner, the internal structure of existence itself — in such a manner that it (the identity) no longer signifies, on the foundation of the understanding of this structure on the contrary as opposition and as difference, and of the simple affirmation of its immanence to being, *the exteriority of being, being-outside-itself*. This was precisely the *first* Fichtean philosophy of the Verb, in conformity with which the Verb found itself to be no doubt identical with the absolute, to be "in God" — in the sense, however, where "in" signified in reality "outside of," where the being-in-God of the Verb signified the being-outside-itself of God himself, the becoming of the absolute in exteriority, and that as the primitive becoming constitutive of the origin itself in its reality.

**Paragraph 6\.** At the very moment when it finds itself thus modified, in a manner as decisive as it is explicit, the philosophy of existence could not — without losing itself — totally forget the *fundamental ontological signification* from which it defines itself and which confers on it its place in the problematic. In conformity with such a signification, *existence means manifestation*. Of the true existence (which is that of the absolute itself, and to which the structure of alterity finds itself radically foreign) it is necessary to show *how it is in itself* and remains, despite this exclusion, *a manifestation*. That this be so — and that the existence-without-difference of the absolute be effectively a manifestation, be an experience — this is in Fichte *a presupposition*. This presupposition is visible in the fact that *love brings beatitude* — which constitutes the fundamental theme of Fichte's religious thought, and which reposes precisely on the new philosophy of existence. *Beatitude is an experience, a form of existence, or rather existence itself such as Fichte now understands it*, insofar as it is nothing other than "the absolute supporting and maintaining itself," nothing other than love. Love does not presuppose only — insofar as it gives beatitude — *conscious* existence; love's *power of revelation* with regard to the being of the absolute is explicitly affirmed: *"What gives the certitude of God if not love?"* — which is immediately characterized as "leaning solely on itself," and consequently as *radically opposed to "reflection,"* that is, to the old concept of existence. It is as such, as radically and explicitly opposed to reflection, that love is said to be not only the *source of all reality* but *"source of all certitude, of all truth."* This is why, *because absolute existence is identically the revelation of the absolute*, Fichte could from the *Third Conference* say of existence (insofar as it is precisely immanent — insofar as it "could not be without finding itself, conceiving itself, supposing itself") that *"it is of its essence to grasp itself."*

The structural pivot of Henry's reading of Fichte is now exhibited. Fichte, in his late immanent ontology, is committed to two propositions:

* (i) Absolute existence (love) is *immanent* — gathered in itself, with no division, no going-outside-itself.  
* (ii) Absolute existence (love) is *manifestation*, *revelation*, *certitude*, *truth* — it has the power of self-revelation.

The structural question: how can these two propositions hold together? If existence is immanent (excluding all reflection, all going-outside-itself, all representation), how can existence still be *manifestation* (which has been historically thought as requiring precisely going-outside-itself, representation, reflection)? Fichte *presupposes* the compatibility — but does not articulate the structural conditions under which an immanent existence could be a manifestation. This is the structural failure that Henry will diagnose in the next paragraphs, and which sets up the program of the rest of Section III: to articulate precisely the structural conditions under which the immanent essence is, as such, *the essence of revelation*.

**Paragraph 7\.** That to existence (insofar as it cannot be without finding itself as originarily and already given to itself, insofar as immanent) it belong to grasp itself and to be thus in itself *revelation* — this is what could not however be *simply presupposed*; this is what must be *grounded* on the contrary, and that *in an essence*. *The bringing-into-light of an originary mode of revelation as finding precisely its structure in immanence is alone susceptible of furnishing the ontological foundation* without which the phenomenological signification accorded to the new Fichtean concept of existence can only be at most a *presupposition* — and finally, not even that. Because such a bringing-into-light does not accomplish itself in Fichte, because the ontological work that should lead to it is neither undertaken nor even simply sketched, *the reigning and traditional concept of phenomenality* (whose rights have thus never been truly contested) inevitably resumes its power. And when it (existence) no longer bursts forth in exteriority but on the contrary confuses itself with the simplicity of primitive being, *existence falls back with primitive being into indetermination and into the night*.

The structural diagnosis is now explicit. Fichte presupposes that immanent existence is revelation; he does not show this. He does not *develop* an alternative phenomenology — an alternative concept of manifestation appropriate to immanence. He continues to operate, when he tries to articulate the *manifestation* of the absolute, with the inherited monist concept of manifestation (manifestation \= representation \= reflection \= going-outside-itself). And since this monist concept of manifestation is *precisely what immanence excludes*, the result is an inevitable contradiction: when Fichte tries to articulate how the immanent absolute is *manifest*, he must either smuggle in the monist categories he has just rejected, or he must accept that the immanent absolute is *not manifest* (falls into "indetermination and night"). Both options will be exhibited in the next paragraphs.

**Paragraph 8\.** Here Fichte's thought moves in *uncertainty*; the presupposition of primitive existence cannot maintain itself, as a constant presupposition, as an effective presupposition; inevitably the *contradictions* appear. What is an existence that does not divide itself in exteriority, that does not produce itself in representation? It is precisely an existence that offers of itself no "reproduction" — *an existence "without image."* It is remarkable that at the moment when it finds itself understood in this way by Fichte, *its phenomenological character becomes brusquely uncertain* or, better said, *finds itself called into question and finally denied*. *"At the inferior degrees of the spiritual life of man,"* says Fichte, *"divine being does not reveal itself as such to consciousness... at the central point of spiritual life... it discovers itself as such to consciousness... it enters into the form just demonstrated as the necessary form of existence and of consciousness — as an image and a reproduction, or as a notion that gives itself expressly for a simple notion, without in any way passing for the thing itself."* The existence of being in exteriority — that is, again, *the representation of the absolute* — does not coincide with the absolute; it is, according to the explicit affirmation of Fichte, only *a simple replica, a simple reproduction, "an image."* This (image), however, *constitutes the manifestation of absolute being* and determines as such "the central point of spiritual life." Without it, on the contrary, the absolute is not discovered, and the one who does not live in this image does not live in the presence of the absolute either — but holds himself for this reason "at the inferior degrees of spiritual life."

The Fichtean contradiction is now exhibited in its full sharpness. Fichte:

* (i) holds (in the new philosophy of existence) that immanent existence is radically opposed to reflection, image, representation; immanent existence is the *truth*, of which reflection is only a "second-hand" derivative;  
* (ii) holds (in his account of religious life) that the manifestation of the absolute occurs precisely *in* the image, in the representation, in the consciousness that grasps the absolute "as a simple notion"; without this image, the absolute is not manifest, and one remains at "inferior degrees of spiritual life."

These two positions are structurally incompatible. (i) says immanence is the locus of truth and revelation; (ii) says only the image-representation is the locus of revelation. Either:

* (a) the immanent essence is itself revelation (then no image is needed — but then Fichte's account of religious life is wrong); or  
* (b) revelation requires the image (then the immanent essence is *not* itself revelation — but then Fichte's whole new philosophy of existence collapses).

Fichte holds both incompatible theses. The result is that immanent existence ends up "without image" — and therefore, on the monist concept of manifestation that Fichte tacitly continues to operate with, *not manifest*. Immanent existence "falls into night."

**Paragraph 9\.** What is it however, at this stage, of the absolute? How can the absolute still determine, in the absence of every representation, every image, a "spiritual life"? *"Directly with its real and image-less existence, it has from all time entered into the real life of men, simply without being recognized — and continues also to penetrate it once it has been recognized, except that in addition it is also recognized in its image."* Thus the existence of the absolute (which, as image-less existence, as immanent existence, finds itself determined in an explicit manner as the element of *reality*) gives itself at the same time, in a manner no less explicit, as that which is *not "recognized,"* as that which *does not manifest itself*. The manifestation of this existence (that is, of the absolute itself) is no doubt possible — at least so it seems here — but this manifestation belongs to representation and is reserved to representation, in such a manner that it is produced only with representation. In other terms, *the manifestation of immanent existence is contingent with respect to it*; manifestation adds itself to existence in a *synthetic* manner, like representation — and that precisely *because the internal structure of immanence has not been recognized and understood as the very structure of revelation*. Because it has not been recognized and understood as the structure of revelation, the internal structure of immanence finds itself in itself (and as such) *delivered to night*. This is why, while thought (identified with the "imaged form") appears as the *only* mode of manifestation of the absolute — *"it is solely in pure thought that our union with God can be recognized"* — divine existence on the contrary gives itself, *independently of its reflection in alterity, as essentially hidden*. *"It is in itself,"* says Fichte, *"this divine immediate existence, that was life, the deepest foundation of every living, substantial existence — but remaining eternally hidden to the gaze."* And further, commenting on the word according to which *"no one has ever seen God,"* Fichte writes: *"divine essence is hidden in itself; it manifests itself only in the form of knowledge."*

The Fichtean position now reaches its self-contradictory completion. The immanent absolute is *real* but *hidden*; *fundamental* but *not manifest*; the *foundation of life* but *eternally hidden to the gaze*. The Johannine "no one has ever seen God" is read by Fichte as saying that the divine essence is structurally invisible *in itself* — visible only through the mediation of knowledge (= image, representation, reflection). So the immanent absolute, on Fichte's late ontology, is what theology has classically called the *Deus absconditus*: real, foundational, but structurally inaccessible. This is the structural failure: Fichte cannot articulate how the immanent absolute is, as such, *manifest*. He defaults to the position that the immanent absolute is *not* manifest in itself — but only mediately, through the image.

**Paragraph 10\.** Or rather, would it not be only *for us* — to our human gaze — that the absolute remains hidden? In such a manner that a knowledge that is only *ours* must then add itself to the absolute in an extrinsic manner, and that as a consequence of *our limitation*? The opposition to the absolute of existence (that is, again, of a knowledge that is opposed to it as such) could not, from now on, be considered as *interior* to the absolute itself — as an opposition concerning it or constituting it — but on the contrary as *the simple exterior addition* to its being (identical with its true existence) of an existence "of second hand," of *the knowledge proper to man*. It is because there is *"no separation between the absolute or God and knowledge in its deepest root"* that, as has been seen, *"the whole difference signaled... between being and existence... reveals itself to exist only for us, as a consequence of our limitation."* And it is only *with respect to this knowledge essentially finite which is ours* (and which is exterior to it) that the absolute can and must, from now on, be interpreted *as withdrawing from a light* which (because this light is not consubstantial with the absolute in the identity of a unique kindling) could not illuminate in the absolute its true nature. The possibility for this true nature to reveal itself in itself such as it is *remains*; it is simply *removed from the power of man and of his vision*. *"The eye of man,"* says Fichte, *"hides God from him."*

A second Fichtean strategy is now exhibited. Fichte sometimes seems to suggest: maybe the absolute *is* manifest in itself, but its manifestation is not accessible *to us* because *we* are limited; the absolute's hiddenness is only *relative* to our finite knowledge, not absolute. This would preserve the possibility of a self-revelation of the absolute "in itself," while attributing the apparent hiddenness to our finite limitations.

**Paragraph 11\.** The intervention of *man* — whose sense is thus to *reserve the possibility of a manifestation of absolute being itself*, more exactly, to leave open (inside the problematic) *the place for an ultimate ontological interpretation of the internal structure of immanence as revelation* — can it however receive and keep such a sense? *Is it not rather philosophically suspect?* For *man has by himself no power* — not even that of rendering a knowledge inadequate and "finite": every manifestation in general (whatever its characters, and precisely with all its characters) *grounds itself each time on a determinate ontological structure*. *It is of the eidetic analysis of this structure that it is a question.* If a manifestation does not have the power to reveal but, paradoxically, to hide the absolute (in what concerns at least its originary and proper being), such a manifestation and its foundation must be elucidated *in themselves* — abstraction made of every consideration of anthropological order. And likewise, if there exists a mode whose originary power expresses itself in the revelation of absolute being in itself and such as it is, *its elaboration and the determination of its structure constitute, evidently, the fundamental task of ontology*. To this task there belongs again, however (and that as integral part of its work), *the understanding of the relation that unites the two essential modes in conformity with which all possible manifestation in general accomplishes itself*: the one that hides the absolute and the one that reveals it. Precisely, the understanding of this relation has shown that *there is no finite knowledge that is not in its essence revelatory of the absolute*. If transcendence reposes in immanence, immanence is present (by its own work) everywhere there exists a relation — in man consequently, insofar as man has the possibility of relating himself to something in general. Should one say then that the immanent existence of the absolute (whose essence consists in the originary revelation of self) loses precisely this power of revealing itself when it is produced "in man"? Or again, precisely, that it (immanent existence) *is not produced in man* — and that, finally, *human existence is separated from absolute existence*? But this is, one has just seen, *an eidetic impossibility*, and as such an *absurdity*, if the immanent existence of the absolute is the essence of every possible existence in general. And how could Fichte have maintained in an absurd manner such a separation, he who affirms: *"to perceive the absolute unity of human existence and divine existence is certainly the deepest knowledge to which man can elevate himself"*? That to this knowledge of unity, however, man may elevate himself or not, this *unity exists* as a universal ontological structure and consequently as *unsurpassable*. It is this structure that constitutes in reality the foundation of all of Fichte's religious philosophy — of his conception of *the Christ* who knew how to recognize in himself the identity of his being and that of God (giving himself in this not as the exception or the paradox but as *the universal law* of every existence, which he calls only to recognize in itself this law as its proper destiny and the assured foundation of its salvation); of his interpretation of *truth*, which (as identical to the existence in man of the absolute) "exists," is "accessible to men," is *a good*; of his *horror*, finally — which kins him to the greatest religious thinkers and (for example) to *Kierkegaard* — for everything that misknows such a truth in what it is (as *the revelation of the absolute itself in its intimate being*), for every skepticism as for every relativism in general.

The structural argument is decisive. Henry refuses the anthropological evasion (Fichte's first strategy of attributing the absolute's hiddenness to our finite limitations). The immanent essence is the *universal* structure of existence; it is operative in *every* existence equally; there is no "human existence" that has a different structure from "absolute existence." The Fichtean affirmation of "the absolute unity of human existence and divine existence" is, for Henry, structurally correct — it expresses precisely the universal-ontological character of the immanent essence. The Christ is, on Fichte's reading (and Henry endorses), not an exception but the universal: every existence *is* in the immanent essence; the Christ knew this and recognized it; the religious task is to recognize what is universally already true.

But this means: the appeal to "human limitation" cannot save Fichte. If human existence is *not* separated from absolute existence (as Fichte himself affirms), then the immanent essence's hiddenness cannot be attributed to a limitation that is peculiarly ours; the hiddenness must be attributed to the immanent essence itself — that is, to a structural failure of Fichte's account, not to an empirical limitation of human knowers.

**Paragraph 12\.** Why then could Fichte not set aside the theses that are properly those of *skepticism and of relativism* — why does he say that *"we know nothing of this immediate divine life, for at the first contact of consciousness it transforms itself already into a dead world"* and again that *"always the form"* (that is, existence, manifestation as such) *"veils the essence from us"*?
