Why does his thought sink as inevitably *to the level of that of classical philosophy* and find itself constrained as classical philosophy to abandon finally the absolute and at the same time the essence of consciousness itself *to the fundamental indetermination of what escapes into the unconscious and into the night*? *Why, if not because the last conceptions of Fichte concerning manifestation itself, its structure and its possibility, were precisely the same as those of classical philosophy — the same as those of ontological monism in general?*

The closing diagnostic is now made explicit. Fichte's failure is not anthropological, not contingent, not the result of personal philosophical limits. Fichte's failure is *structural*: he continued to operate, in his account of *manifestation*, with the monist concept of manifestation (manifestation \= representation \= image \= reflection). And since this monist concept is precisely what *cannot* account for the manifestation of the immanent essence (which excludes all representation, image, reflection), Fichte was structurally unable to articulate how the immanent essence is, as such, *manifest*. He defaulted to the position that immanent existence is *not* manifest in itself — that it requires the supplement of "image" and "knowledge" to be manifest — that "always the form veils the essence from us." This is precisely the position of monist phenomenology, repeated unwittingly by the late Fichte despite his initial articulation of immanent existence.

**Paragraph 13\.** For it is *not man*, as has been seen, who can be held responsible for the dissimulation of the absolute and for its vanishing. That the absolute (such as Fichte precisely understands it as a primitive existence in immanence) does not manifest itself — *this holds to the absolute itself and to its nature*. More precisely: *to the fact that the internal structure of immanence is not grasped by Fichte as originarily revelatory of itself, as the structure of revelation*. For him, as for so many other thinkers, *there exists, in what concerns manifestation, only one power: that of monism* — to which existence (insofar as immanent) withdraws from now on necessarily, and that not by reason of a deficiency of this power (because the knowledge it arouses would be a deforming knowledge — precisely, it deforms nothing) but *because it is a knowledge of ideality, not of reality*. The reality of the absolute — this is what it was necessary to understand, *not only* (and that in a determining manner no doubt) *as constituted in its internal structure by immanence*, but *also* as a *phenomenological* reality, as the phenomenological reality of an absolute that ceases from now on to be that of which one can say everything one wants — in such a manner that everything one says of it (and for example the immanent character one attributes to it) becomes pure hypothesis on a being itself purely hypothetical. *The phenomenological reality of the absolute is nothing other however than its originary belonging to itself in immanence — than the mode according to which the absolute maintains itself and remains in itself.* This is why, on close inspection, *the understanding of the internal structure of immanence as revelation could not add itself to the simple understanding of this structure; it is identical to it*.

The decisive structural thesis is now made fully explicit. To understand the immanent essence is *eo ipso* to understand it as revelation; the two understandings are not separable. The immanent self-relation just *is* the originary self-revelation; the structure of immanence just *is* the structure of revelation. There is no further question of how immanence "manifests itself" or "becomes phenomenal" — immanence in its very structure is already phenomenality, because immanence is the *originary self-presence of being to itself*, and this self-presence is the most fundamental form of phenomenality.

This is the structural-philosophical breakthrough that Fichte missed and that Henry will articulate in the rest of Section III. The breakthrough requires recognizing that there are *two* fundamentally different concepts of phenomenality:

* (i) the *monist* concept: phenomenality \= representation \= image \= going-outside-itself \= horizon \= vision;  
* (ii) the *immanent* concept: phenomenality \= self-presence \= self-affection \= the immediate self-relation of life.

These are not species of a common genus; they are *radically heterogeneous* structures. The monist concept of phenomenality is *not* the *only* concept; there is the alternative immanent concept, which is in fact *more originary* (because it is the structure of revelation itself, prior to all representational manifestation).

**Paragraph 14 (closing).** Such an understanding (which is identically that of the internal structure of immanence and of the originary essence of revelation) is precisely what *was lacking to Fichte* to permit him to give an effective content to the fundamental intuitions of his religious thought — as it was to be lacking later (with, however, *infinitely more grave* consequences) to all *modern ontology*. Such an understanding has, in truth, *almost never met itself in history*, except however in *an exceptional thinker* whom one called formerly, with good reason, *a master*: *Eckhart*.

The closing sentence sets up §39 (which will be devoted entirely to Eckhart). Henry's thesis: the structural understanding of the internal structure of immanence as revelation has been almost completely missed by the philosophical tradition (Fichte's late thought is the closest approximation, and even it failed). The single great exception is *Meister Eckhart* — the medieval Rhineland mystic-philosopher (c. 1260–1328) — whose articulation of the structure of the divine essence and of the soul's relation to it is, on Henry's reading, structurally identical with the immanent phenomenology that Henry himself is articulating. The reference to Eckhart as "*magister*" (master) is the medieval-Latin honorific that Eckhart himself bore (Magister Eckhart, after his teaching position at the University of Paris) — and Henry adopts this honorific to mark Eckhart's exceptional status.

The closing reference to "all modern ontology" with "infinitely more grave consequences" is a sharp polemic, anticipating the critiques of Heidegger and Husserl that will run through the rest of Section III and beyond. Modern ontology — including Heideggerian fundamental ontology — has, on Henry's reading, repeated and even deepened the Fichtean failure: it has continued to think manifestation in monist terms, and has therefore continued to miss the structural possibility of an immanent phenomenology. The "more grave consequences" are the systematic destruction, in modern ontology, of the very vocabulary in which immanent phenomenology can be articulated — a destruction Henry's whole book aims to reverse.

---

## **§ 39\. Eckhart**

**Paragraph 1\.** The understanding of the ultimate ontological structures that constitute the essence of reality is not apparently the goal Eckhart proposes for himself. Only the *edification of souls* interests him, and the activity to which he consecrates himself to attain this is not of speculative order; it is *preaching*. Eckhart preaches to the soul its possible *union with God*. He teaches the soul what it must do to elevate itself to this union (in which it will find at the same time its salvation and beatitude). It is therefore not the internal structure of the absolute itself or God; it is *the relation of man to God* that constitutes the theme of Eckhart's thought and preaching. To relate oneself to God, however — to render the absolute manifest — is possible only by *the work of manifestation*, by the work of the absolute itself. This is why (as the problematic had necessarily recognized from the first moment of its effort to grasp and understand itself in its goal and in its means) the relation to the absolute *depends on the nature of the absolute and on its internal structure*, or rather *is identical with this nature*: *the existential union of man with God is possible only on the foundation of their ontological unity*. Such is precisely Eckhart's teaching: it is the absolute (in the effective accomplishment of its work) that constitutes (according to Eckhart) the essence of the soul — an essence that, as such, is not different from this work or (as Eckhart says) from *the operation of God*. *"When God made man,"* he declares, *"he operated in the soul his proper operation, equal to himself and continually operative. This operation was so great that it became nothing other than the soul; but the soul was nothing other than the operation of God."*

The opening paragraph establishes the structural-philosophical interpretation that will guide Henry's reading of Eckhart. Eckhart's apparent topic is *the soul's union with God* (the edifying-mystical theme of his preaching). But this apparent topic *is* in fact the topic of the internal structure of the absolute, because the soul's union with God is possible only on the basis of an *ontological unity* between the soul and God. So Eckhart's preaching, properly understood, is in fact *first philosophy* — fundamental ontology — disguised as religious edification. The Eckhartian formula "the operation of God in the soul \= the soul itself \= nothing other than the operation of God" articulates a structural identity that goes far beyond any traditional theological doctrine of creation. The soul is not a thing created by God's external act; the soul is *identical with* God's own internal operation, with the very essence of God.

**Paragraph 2\.** The identity here affirmed between the essence of the soul and the operation of God must be understood in its *radical signification*. For the operation with which the soul finds itself identified in its essence does *not in any way add itself* (as creation properly speaking would do) to the originary and intimate being of God himself; it constitutes nothing extrinsic with respect to God but identifies itself on the contrary with *his own ground*. This is why this operation of God is said to be "*equal to himself*" and again "*continually operative*" — because it is precisely *not an activity that would add itself for a time and in a contingent manner to the internal work that constitutes the essence of the absolute* but is nothing other than this work. The identification of the essence of the soul with the operation of God therefore signifies *its identification with the eternal essence of the absolute*; it signifies that *the essence of the soul is the very essence of God*. That the essence of the soul be the very essence of God is what Eckhart affirms unconditionally: *"it is,"* he says, *"the same thing that he is,"* *"it is itself the Kingdom of God,"* and that because *"the Ground of God and the Ground of the soul (is) but one and the same Ground."*

The Eckhartian doctrine of the *Seelengrund* (the ground of the soul) — one of the most controversial doctrines in the medieval mystical tradition, which led to Eckhart's posthumous condemnation in the bull *In agro dominico* (1329) — is here read in its full structural radicality. The "Ground of the soul" is not a faculty of the soul, not even the deepest faculty; it is the very *being* of the soul, which is *identical* with the *Ground of God*. This identity is not a similarity, not an analogy, not a participation; it is a structural-ontological *identity*: the same Ground is the Ground of God and the Ground of the soul.

**Paragraph 3\.** Because the Ground of the soul is constituted by God himself — because the soul finds in God its essence — *the soul does not proceed from God*; the soul has not been posited outside God or in God by an action which (adding itself to the eternal essence of God) would have added to him precisely *the soul*. *The soul has not been created.* Speaking in the name of man, Eckhart says: *"I am unborn"* and (in a general manner) rejects for man (insofar as man must be understood in his essence) *the condition of creature*. What does such a rejection signify — that is, also, the affirmation of a *radical independence of man with regard to all divine creation*, with regard to *God himself*? *The independence of man with regard to creation, with regard to God himself, signifies his identity with God.* This identity of essence Eckhart expresses not only in the affirmation of the independence of the soul with regard to God, but (in a more extreme manner) *in the affirmation of the dependence of God with regard to the soul*. *"The nature of God, his Essence, his Deity depend on the necessary operation that he effects in the soul."* And identifying himself with man considered in his essence (that is, precisely in his independence with regard to all creation), Eckhart affirms still more explicitly: *"here, I was the cause of myself and of all things. If I had willed it then, the entire world and I would not be... That God be God, of this I am a cause. If I were not, God would not be either."* The essence of the soul being God, in effect, the suppression of the essence of the soul (such as it is leisurely possible for us to operate it in eidetic imagination) *is the suppression of God himself*. This is why the signification of these radical theses — their truth — is well that which Eckhart himself expresses in the continuation of the text: *"that God and I are one."*

The Eckhartian sermons cited (especially Sermon 52, *Beati pauperes spiritu*, which contains the celebrated "I was the cause of myself") are the most controversial of the Eckhartian corpus — they were among the propositions cited in the condemnation. Henry reads them not as religious extravagance but as the *structural-ontological consequence* of the identity of Ground that Eckhart has articulated. If the Ground of the soul is the same as the Ground of God, then to remove the soul (eidetically, in thought) is to remove God; God depends on the soul as much as the soul depends on God; God is not a creator standing outside the creature but the very Ground of the creature, identical with the creature in its essence.

The Eckhartian "I am unborn" articulates the most radical ontological consequence: insofar as I am identified with the Ground (the immanent essence), I am *uncreated*, *eternal*, *prior to all creation*. The Eckhartian "I" (in its essence) is not the empirical-temporal I that was born and will die; it is the immanent essence that has always been and will always be. This is, on Henry's reading, structurally the same thesis as his own: the immanent essence is prior to all temporal-historical existence, prior to all "becoming," prior to all "projecting" — it is *what is*, in the eternal present of the *Parousia*.

**Paragraph 4\.** Can the ontological identity of the soul and God however be understood as *the essential content of Eckhart's thought* — is its affirmation susceptible only of being maintained — if (far from realizing itself in a necessary manner and being effective a priori) the union of man with God accomplishes itself on the contrary only *at the term of a progress* and under certain *conditions* that appear contingent and (as such) foreign to the structure of the essence? These conditions, explicitly named by Eckhart, are notably *love, poverty, humility*. Of love, it is true, Eckhart affirms with force — and this is not one of the least original and least profound aspects of his thought — *that love could not by itself accomplish or realize our union with God*. Commenting on the word of Saint John according to which "love unites," he corrects it in these terms: *"but love never transports into God; it does only consolidate what is already united. Love unites in no way, but it reinforces the links of what is united,"* and in conclusion: *"love unites in an operation, not in an essence."* This means that *the ontological unity of structure between the soul and God could not repose on love considered as an existential determination but finds itself on the contrary presupposed by love*.

Henry now anticipates and dispels what could appear as the natural objection: that Eckhart's mystical conditions (love, poverty, humility) are existential virtues to be cultivated, and therefore the union with God is not a structural-ontological identity but a contingent achievement. Henry shows that Eckhart himself blocks this reading. Love, *for Eckhart*, does *not* unite; love presupposes a unity that is already in place. The existential dimension is *consequent on*, not constitutive of, the ontological unity.

Love, it is true, designates also (in traditional religious thought) *the very essence of God* — no longer an operation, but *the operation of the absolute* such as it accomplishes itself in him in conformity with his structure and as that which he is. But when love receives this ontological signification, *its identification with the very being of God renders more evident, instead of calling into question, the identity of essence that exists between God and man*. It is because such an identity exists, in fact, that *in loving the soul, God loves himself* — and that in such a manner that there is in reality only *one love, one operation*, and that the love by which God loves the soul is nothing other (finally) than the love by which the soul loves God, nothing other than the love by which God loves himself. *"It is because he operates in the soul,"* says Eckhart, *"that God loves it as his work."* This operation (which Eckhart says in the same passage is identically love) is not "an operation" but *the very essence of the absolute* — that is, as he says again, *God himself*. And Eckhart adds: *"God loves himself... But in the love by which God loves himself, He also loves all creatures — not as creatures, but as they are God."*

The structural argument is now elegant. Even at the level of love, the Eckhartian doctrine is the doctrine of *immanent self-relation*: God's love of the soul is God's love of himself; the soul's love of God is also God's love of himself; there is *one* love, the immanent self-affection of the absolute. This is structurally the same thesis Henry will articulate as the *self-affection of life*: love (in the ontological sense) is the immediate self-relation of the absolute essence.

**Paragraph 5\.** What has just been said of love — can it be said however of *poverty, of humility*? Are these latter not visibly *determinate modes of existence* — determinate and at the same time *contingent*, in no way coinciding as such with the essence of existence? Such modes (which constitute only for existence determinations possible among others) — do they not give themselves however as *the condition* of union with God (a union that becomes itself, from now on, contingent and problematic, instead of being inscribed in the essence)? How does the union with God depend on poverty, on humility? Insofar as it (the union) realizes itself only in the man who *renounces* the world and himself in such a way as to *be no longer anything* — for it is only if he is no longer anything that there is place in him for the operation of God, that is, for God himself. *The radical stripping-away of man understood as the condition of the presence in him of God* — is this not the fundamental theme and at the same time the ultimate sense of Eckhart's "mysticism"? Insofar as this mysticism presupposes such a stripping-away as its condition (as a condition that must accomplish itself first in order that mysticism itself be possible), it (the mysticism) finds itself bound to a *duty*, suspended in its realization to *an ethics*. This is why Eckhart's religious thought takes on an *edifying form*; this is why it expresses itself in *preaching* — because it aims at *a transformation of existence* at the term of which only existence will be able to find itself truly united to God. *"Man must be empty,"* says Eckhart, *"... he must let God operate what pleases him and remain for his part entirely available."* The emptiness which man must thus let make itself in him must be *absolute* — in such a manner that what finds itself operated in him and himself are *no longer anything other than the operation of God, are no longer anything other than God*. If man is "stripped of all things" and "if there nonetheless remains in him a place where God can operate," it is that "he is not yet poor of the most intimate poverty... there is true poverty in spirit only when man is stripped to such a point... that God, if he wanted to operate in the soul, *would have to be himself the place of his operation*." And again: *"If God found man in this poverty, it is on himself that he would have to exercise his operation, and He would be himself the place of his operation."* It is therefore *poverty* — or, what comes back to the same, *humility* — that is the condition of union with God. *"The humble man and God make only one."* "It is here," says Eckhart again, "the kiss between the unity of God and the humble man." Because it is in the humble man only that the union with God realizes itself, of him alone finally can be affirmed *the extreme consequence of this union* (insofar as it signifies *unity*) — the *dependence of God with regard to man*: *"the humble man does not need to ask but he can command God."* Thus is clearly formulated the condition to which obeys the union and (because this condition is identified with determinate modes of existence) in such a manner that the union here in question (that is, finally, the unity between man and God) *can no longer be precisely understood as an ontological unity*.

The structural problem has now been sharpened. Eckhart's sermons articulate the union of soul and God as *conditional* on the soul's stripping-away (poverty, humility) — and this conditionality seems to undercut the structural-ontological identity Henry has been ascribing to him. If the union *depends* on existential conditions, then the union is not structural-ontological but contingent-existential.

**Paragraph 6\.** Or rather, *despite their determinateness — or rather, by reason of this very determinateness* — must humility and poverty not be interpreted on the contrary as *bearing in themselves an ontological signification*, their intervention in the problematic as belonging to the movement of a thought that aims at the essence and (precisely) at the determination of the essence and of its internal structure? Humility and poverty would then no longer contradict (insofar as they serve to establish between man and God the union and finally the unity) the ontological character of unity; they would help us much better to *grasp it*, to understand truly finally what it is fitting to understand under the concept of this unity. For if it lays claim for itself to such a character — an ontological character — *unity could not designate simply the union of man and God or its foundation*. Of what positive ontological signification could unity so understood prevail itself? That man be one with God because he finds in God his essence — this says neither what man is, nor what God is, because it says nothing of *this essence which constitutes at the same time the being of man and that of God himself*. To formulate such a unity (which expresses nothing other, in a sense, than the exterior identity of essence with itself in the tautology) is not assuredly without consequence: it is because the essence of man resides in God and finds itself constituted by him that *all of Eckhart's problematic — which gives itself as apparent theme man and the problem of his relations and finally of his union with God — reduces in reality to the determination of God, to the determination of the essence and of its internal structure*. Thus is profiled (behind the existential question of the destiny of man and his examination) *the fundamental eidetic analysis that aims at the very being of the absolute*.

Henry's interpretive pivot is now made explicit. Eckhart's apparent theme (man's union with God, the existential conditions for this union) is the *occasion* but not the *content* of his thought. The actual content — the structural-philosophical work that Eckhart's thought accomplishes — is the *determination of the internal structure of the essence (= the absolute)*. The existential conditions (poverty, humility) are *not* contingent existential supplements; they *are* (when read with structural eyes) the eidetic analysis of the immanent essence itself.

Such an analysis, in truth, does not profile itself only at the background, as if the considerations that precede it remained exterior to it. *The determinations that existence takes on in order that there realize itself in it its union with God — and which consist in the act by which existence rejects outside itself all that differs precisely from the intimate and originary being of God himself, that is, from the essence — act with regard to this essence as a destruction.* Such is the ontological signification that it is fitting to recognize for their intervention in the problematic and (at the same time) the reason for the central role they play in it: *because they accomplish the withdrawal of all that is not the essence, humility and poverty lay bare the structure of the essence*. Yet the sense of this destruction must be well understood. To lay bare the structure of the essence does not consist simply in removing what covers the essence; it is also *to penetrate into the essence, to make it appear in what it is*. Thus accomplishes itself the *ontological work* thought under the concepts of humility and of poverty: the signification of these is not only to liberate the essence; *they determine its internal structure*.

The structural-philosophical interpretation is now precise. Eckhart's existential conditions (poverty, humility) are, *eidetically interpreted*, structural moments of the immanent essence itself. Poverty is not just the soul's stripping-away of its possessions; *poverty is the structural feature of the immanent essence that has nothing other than itself within itself* (recall §37: "the indigence of the essence resides in the fact that the essence encloses nothing other"). Humility is not just the soul's submission; *humility is the structural feature of the immanent essence that has no power over itself, that is essentially passive with respect to itself* (recall §37 on non-freedom and passivity). The Eckhartian existential vocabulary is, on Henry's structural reading, *the appropriate vocabulary for the immanent essence* — far from contradicting the ontological identity of soul and God, it precisely articulates the structure of this identity.

**Paragraph 7\.** In humility and poverty, however, resides the principle of the union of the soul with God — what was primitively understood as *the unity*. If this unity cannot consist in the simple exterior affirmation of identity and concerns on the contrary (in the same right as humility and poverty, with which — as foundation of the union realized by them — it identifies itself) *the determination of the internal structure of the essence*, its ontological signification then must be shown — and that precisely as being *the same* as theirs. How does unity refer itself to the essence in such a manner that the signification it takes on for the determination of its internal structure reveals itself to be *ontologically the same* as what it is fitting to recognize for humility and poverty (themselves grasped in their radical ontological signification)?

The determination of the internal structure of the essence by *unity* has been understood by the problematic with the bringing-into-light of an *originary mode of receptivity* whose content is constituted by the very reality of the essence. The essence whose content is constituted by its own reality *encloses nothing other*. *"God,"* says Eckhart, *"is immanent to this pure essentiality of himself which encloses rigorously nothing other."* Thus the internal structure of the absolute is thought by Eckhart from the *exclusion outside it of alterity*. For it is by alterity (as has been seen) that all that is *other* reveals itself to be such. Alterity is not in fact an empty, purely logical category in which it is fitting to range in a formal manner all that is not the reality of the essence and reveals itself as such "other" than the reality; *alterity finds itself determined ontologically* — and that in a rigorous manner, as constitutive precisely of an ontological milieu, *as horizon and as world*. As that of alterity, the signification of *the exclusion* therefore finds itself itself determined. The exclusion is that of *the world* and (identically) of what manifests itself in the world. The content of what manifests itself in the world (insofar precisely as it manifests itself in the world and in the world's representation) constitutes each time what one calls *"an image"*. The "world" and all its "images" — this is precisely (according to Eckhart) what finds itself rejected outside the absolute, what must be excluded from the absolute, *if at least its internal structure must be understood*. *"If you wish to find the nature without veil,"* he says, *"it is necessary to break all the images; the more one advances in this work, the more one approaches the Essence."* The rejection of all images is identically that of *the pure milieu* where they are such — and which (as alterity) is also that of *exteriority*.

The Eckhartian doctrine of *Bildlosigkeit* (image-lessness) — the soul's required stripping-away of all images, all representations, all *species* (in the medieval epistemological sense) — is here read structurally. The "image" Eckhart asks the soul to break is not merely a mental image; it is the structural form of all *transcendent* manifestation — the world as the field of opposed objectivities, the horizon as the form of objectivity. The Eckhartian "imageless" essence is structurally what Henry has called the *immanent* essence: an essence that does not deploy itself in the form of a horizon, that has no opposed content, that is not the field of representational manifestation.

This is why (as Eckhart tirelessly affirms) *the liberation of the essence implies that thought turn away from all that is exterior*. *"God is in us,"* he says, *"but we are outside ourselves."* And, describing in a more explicit manner this movement of thought to turn away from all that is exterior (and notably from the *attributes* — which are the *transcendent determinations* of being), Eckhart understands it as the movement of *reason itself* to grasp itself in its proper essence and in its proper ground: *"Reason,"* he says, *"looks within..."* it *"penetrates to the interior; nothing exterior suffices to it, neither goodness, nor wisdom, nor truth... it bursts forth to the Ground from which Goodness and Truth gush forth; it grasps all things in principio, at the primitive source, where Goodness and Truth have their first origin even before receiving a name, even before they burst forth... Reason rejects these attributes, it goes forward, opens a passage to the Root..."*

The Eckhartian critique of the divine attributes (Goodness, Wisdom, Truth, Being, etc.) is structurally Henry's critique of all transcendent-representational determinations of the essence. The essence is not "good" or "wise" or "true" in the sense of bearing these attributes as predicates; the essence is the *Ground from which* such attributes flow forth, *prior to* their being named, *prior to* their differentiation. The Eckhartian via negativa (the negation of all attributes in order to reach the essence) is here read as the structural movement from transcendence to immanence — the movement to the immediate self-relation that precedes all attributive specification.

The rejection of all images and of all attributes is also that of the *"forms"* — it is, in a general manner, that of all that separates itself from the essence and finds itself posed outside it; *of the very act of positing exteriority and alterity, the rejection of all creation*. Thus is explicited (in its radical and at the same time decisive ontological signification) the necessity ceaselessly affirmed by Eckhart of *surpassing the plane of creature and of creation, the plane of the created*, in order to attain the essence and its opening — the necessity, as he says, of leaving "*all the created in order to attain to this Ground which is Abyss*." It is precisely because *"there is in the soul something that surpasses the created essence"* that the soul finds itself identical in its Ground to that of God himself, identical to the absolute. And that the surpassing of the created essence signifies that of the *exterior being* and of its *pure milieu* is what results from many passages and (for example) from the one where it is said (by opposition precisely to the plane of the creature) that *"there must be something more intimate and more elevated, something uncreated which escapes measures and form."*

The Eckhartian doctrine of the "Spark of the Soul" (*scintilla animae*, *vünkelîn der sêle*) — the uncreated something in the soul that is identical with the divine Ground — was the most controversial of all the Eckhartian doctrines. The condemnation by Pope John XXII targeted precisely the proposition "There is something in the soul which is uncreated and uncreatable; if the entire soul were such, it would be uncreated and uncreatable; this is the intellect." Henry restores the structural-philosophical meaning of this doctrine: the "uncreated something in the soul" is the *immanent essence*, which is structurally prior to all creation (= prior to all going-outside-itself, all positing of exteriority, all institution of the transcendent horizon). Every soul has, in its very being, this immanent essence — for it is the universal essence of all consciousness, the structure of the *Parousia* of being.

**Paragraph 8\.** Thus appears more and more clearly the manner in which Eckhart thinks the *approach and the liberation of the essential* from the rejection outside it of all that is not it — that is, first as a *withdrawal*. *"When an artist makes a statue,"* he says, *"he does not add to the wood; he takes something from it; he makes fall under his chisel all the exterior... and then can resplend what was hidden within."* And it is in this way that Eckhart understands the parable of the treasure buried in a field. The rejection outside the essence of the element other-than-it (ontologically interpreted and grasped as element of alterity and of exteriority) — such is, *behind the apparent existential signification of "the renunciation of the world,"* the *ontological* signification of such a renunciation, that is, also, of humility and of poverty: *they intervene in the development of an eidetic analysis and belong to it*. It is precisely because such is the ontological signification of their intervention in the problematic that humility and poverty render possible the union of man with God — *because they liberate in fact the essence of God, the essence of the absolute*.

The structural interpretation is now decisively confirmed. The Eckhartian "renunciation of the world" is not (or not only) a moral injunction; it is the *eidetic-structural* movement by which thought attains the immanent essence by stripping away the field of horizonal-transcendent manifestation. The Eckhartian artist who removes the wood to let the statue appear — this is the structural image of the eidetic phenomenologist (or the contemplative soul) who removes the layers of representational manifestation to let the immanent essence appear in its purity.

That they (humility and poverty) do not result, in consequence, in *a simple modification of human existence* (as existential determinations would do, properly speaking) but indeed in *the bringing-into-light in human existence of its essence* — that is, of the absolute — is what Eckhart affirms: *"here,"* he says, *"in this poverty, man retrieves the eternal being that he has been, that he is currently, and that he will remain eternally"* — that is, precisely the being of the absolute, *liberated in this poverty and by it*. This poverty always gives itself as that which permits *to retrieve what was already*, which signifies *to lay bare the essence* — and that in setting aside from the essence what covers it (and which is itself understood as the plane of creation and of "creatures"). These (the creatures) once set aside, *there discovers itself the originary region of the essence* — that where (says Eckhart again) *"I am what I was."*

The Eckhartian formulation "I am what I was" articulates the *atemporal* structure of the immanent essence. The immanent essence does not "become" what it is (in temporal succession); the immanent essence simply *is* what it has always been, in the eternal present of its self-presence. This is structurally the same point Henry made in §21 (against Hegel's becoming-of-the-absolute) and §37 (against Heideggerian Dasein's *Sich-Vorweg-Sein*).

Humility and poverty do not intervene only, however, in the eidetic analysis as a moment, as a preliminary condition permitting the unveiling of the essence but at the same time foreign to the nature of this essence. *The condition of the unveiling of the essence belongs necessarily to it as identical with it.* The ontological identity of the essence and of the determinations in which its manifestation accomplishes itself is recognized by Eckhart and explicitly affirmed by him: *"the virtue named humility,"* he says, *"is rooted in the Ground of the Deity where it is inserted in such a way as to have being only in the eternal unity and nowhere else."* How is such an identity possible — *how can the rejection outside the essence of the other element constitute, not simply the laying-bare of the essence (in the withdrawal of what covers it), but on the contrary its internal structure itself understood as unity*?

**Paragraph 9\.** Or rather, does it not suffice once more to the problematic to *recall its own results*? If — as the problematic has established — the exclusion does not set aside only an obstacle before the thought that wishes to attain the essential, if *it is in the essence that there is nothing other, nothing foreign* (and that because there is in it no opposition, no difference)? Such is also precisely the reiterated affirmation of Eckhart: *"no difference,"* he says, *"exists... in the nature of God."* What bears in itself, in its nature, no difference, no opposition (and consequently nothing other, nothing foreign) — this is precisely what constitutes *unity*. *"There is,"* says Eckhart, *"nothing foreign in unity."* Because unity constitutes the very nature of God (the nature of the absolute), it is *inside* the absolute — understood as unity — that there is neither opposition nor difference. Thus is determined "*the essence of primitive being in its simple unity, where there is no difference of any kind.*" Because it is *inside* the absolute itself (in its internal structure) that there is no difference, there could not be (everywhere there is present such a structure and operative the essence of the absolute, there where reality is constituted by it) *no difference either*, and consequently *no opposition, no distinction*. This is why Eckhart affirms that *God engenders man "without any distinction"* — because, as he says in the same proposition, *"all that God operates is unity"* — because there is in the originary reality of revelation (and consequently in man, where this reality accomplishes itself) *no difference precisely, no opposition, no distinction*. It is therefore of *the internal structure of the operation of God, that is, of his essence*, that it is a question; and it is because this essence is understood as unity that nothing distinct, nothing opposed, nothing created is produced in it. Far from implying the identification of the creature with the absolute, *it is on the contrary its exclusion outside the absolute that finds itself affirmed* (in a radical manner) *by Eckhart in the rejection of the distinction* and also of all difference. Such an exclusion is a constant theme of Eckhartian problematic, in which it intervenes not as antithesis (to correct what could be excessive in the identity of essence posed between man and God) but as *the strict corollary of this identity*. It is not *although* God engenders man "without any difference," it is *because* — *"the operation of the Father being unity"* — it is so, that it is true to say: *"there where the creature ends, there begins the Being of God."* To elevate oneself to the intelligence of this "because" — that is, also, to that of the *identity between the inclusion of man in God and the exclusion outside God of every creature* — *this is to understand Eckhart*, this is to understand the essence and all that has part in its manifestation (as manifestation-of-self) in its radical determination from the exclusion of every difference and of every distinction. This is to understand how and why (to speak as Eckhart) *"when man found himself still in the eternal manner of God, nothing other lived in him."* To those who *condemned* him (as if, dupe of his enthusiasm and perhaps also of his love, Eckhart had, in the supposed identification of the creature with God, somehow exaggerated the sentiments and ideas his "mystical" soul suggested to him), there lacked only one thing: *the understanding of his thought*.

The structural argument is now decisive. The Eckhartian thesis "the soul is identical with God" *and* the apparently opposite thesis "the creature must be utterly excluded from God" are not contradictory but *strictly equivalent*: both express the same structural fact that the immanent essence (the Ground of soul \= Ground of God) excludes alterity, distinction, the structure of "creature" (= the structure of being-other-than-God, being-posited-outside-God). When Eckhart says "I am identical with God," he is speaking of the immanent Ground (which is not creature, not other than God). When Eckhart says "the creature must be excluded from God," he is speaking of the same immanent Ground (which excludes the structure of creature-hood, the structure of being-other). The two formulations, far from being in tension, are the same thesis in two forms.

Henry's defense of Eckhart against his ecclesiastical condemnation is here both philosophical and pious. The condemnation rested on the misunderstanding that Eckhart was identifying the *creature* with God (which would be pantheism, the elevation of finite creature to divine status). Henry shows that Eckhart's actual thesis is the *exclusion* of the creature from the essence — the essence is *not* the creature but the Ground of the creature, which is identical with the Ground of God. Properly understood, Eckhart's thesis is not pantheism but the most radical articulation of the immanent essence as prior to all creator-creature distinction.

**Paragraph 10\.** The determination of the internal structure of the essence as unity from the exclusion outside it of difference finds its ontological foundation in what renders possible such an exclusion — in that of the *ontological process on which reposes all distinction and all difference* (a process thought by Eckhart as that of *creation*, no longer in the sense of the creature but of *what creates the creature and gives it birth in the world*; in the sense of *a power and an activity*, this latter explicitly recognized as such — as "activity," as "operation," or as "mediation"). That the unity of the essence reposes ultimately on the exclusion outside it of *the ontological process creator of exteriority* (of what Eckhart again calls the "*birth*") is what finds itself clearly enounced. *"God,"* he says, *"is unity in this natural union anterior to all birth."* That such a *birth* signifies the creative process of exteriority — the entry into the world grasped in its ontological possibility and in its foundation — results from the fact that it is put into relation with the *exterior images*, not with this or that one of them, but as that which renders them possible in general — precisely as their *foundation*. Because it grounds the possibility of exterior images in general, the birth so understood (in this ontological signification) receives the same antithetical concept as them — that which Eckhart qualifies (in his apparently existential language) as *"virginity"* or again *"purity."* These (insofar as, as unity, the internal structure of the essence leaves outside it exteriority and its foundation) designate (in the same right as humility and poverty) *this very structure of the essence* and (identically) the possibility of a state of union with the essence. This is why Eckhart writes: *"The person by whom Jesus was received could only be virgin, that is... free of all foreign images, as available as before her birth."* *To free oneself from all images*, to enter into this state which has just been understood as that of a union with the absolute, *to realize in fact the conditions that define the internal structure of the absolute*, is therefore to *reject the ontological process by which in general the existent phenomenalizes itself, and that as an "image"* — is to reject *what in monism gives itself as the presupposition of every possible manifestation and finds itself designated by monism under the general title of "mediation."* Thus is rendered clear (in the explicit rejection of mediation) the decisive importance of the problematic instituted by Eckhart, at the same time as there unveils itself without equivocation — at the term of his ethical preoccupations and as their truth — *its essential ontological character*: *"man,"* he says, *"must come out of all images... become absolutely foreign and dissimilar to all things, if he wishes... to receive filiation in the bosom of the Father. For all mediation is foreign to God."*

The decisive Eckhartian principle is now articulated: *all mediation is foreign to God*. The structural meaning is profound. Mediation is the structural form of monist phenomenology: in monism, the absolute manifests itself *through* the mediation of representations, images, going-outside-itself. The Eckhartian doctrine that "all mediation is foreign to God" articulates the structural fact that the immanent essence excludes mediation from its internal structure — the immanent essence is what it is *immediately*, without going through anything else, without representation, without image. This is structurally the same thesis Henry has been articulating: the immanent essence is prior to and excludes the entire structure of monist mediation.

**Paragraph 11\.** This *mediation* — which consists in the event where the existent finds its being — Eckhart most often designates (to underline its creative character) as *activity, as operation*. And it is by opposition to these (that is, in fact, to *transcendence itself*) that he thinks (to determine its internal structure) the absolute. Such a determination, accomplishing itself from the concept of transcendence and by the *exclusion* of transcendence from what in the absolute constitutes properly speaking its internal structure, brings into the problematic *the essential distinction instituted by Eckhart inside the ontological element itself between God and what he calls the Deity (Gottheit)*. This latter alone constitutes the *ontological reality* — and that precisely insofar as transcendence is *not operative* in it, does not operate in it, insofar as there is in it no *"operation."* *"The Deity does not operate,"* he says, *"... there is no operation in it; never has it cast its eyes on any operation whatever."* This absence at the heart of the Deity of "any operation whatever" is identically in the Deity that of *all activity*. *"In the pure Deity,"* says Eckhart, *"there is absolutely no more activity."* And that the activity (identified in its concept with that of operation) designates (as operation does) the *ontological foundation of the world where the existent informs itself* is what is shown by the immediate context in which it is said (always of the Deity) that it is the place "*where there are no longer either operations or forms.*" Such therefore is the essence of the Deity, the essence of God himself in his most intimate nature — what Eckhart calls again "*the divine Essentiality where,*" he says, *"God abstains from all activity."* God on the contrary, and his concept (instead of aiming in general at the ontological element) is then taken in a *restrictive* sense, designates the "*operation*" itself, *the creative act of the world, the origin of alterity and its foundation*: *"God operates,"* says Eckhart. It is in what precisely God differs from the Deity: *"God and the Deity differ as the operation and the Non-operation."* This reference of God so understood ontologically (and yet in a fashion conform to his traditional metaphysical function) as *the act of going outside himself of the absolute*, to the essence of creation and of what finds itself produced by creation, is explicit: *"before there were creatures,"* says Eckhart, *"God was not yet God, but He was what he was. When the creature was and received its nature of creature, God was not God in himself; he was God in the creature."* This is why: *"If God is called God, it is by the will of creatures."* And again, just as clearly: *"It is only when the soul became creature that it had a God"* — which means that the soul found itself submitted, from then on, to the *ontological power of exteriority*. It is because this (ontological power of exteriority) is excluded on the contrary from what constitutes the very essence of God, *because the foundation of alterity is foreign to his proper foundation, to the Deity*, that the Deity is *unity* — that, as Eckhart says, *"all that is in the Deity is Unity."*

The Eckhartian distinction between *Gott* (God) and *Gottheit* (Deity) is the most consequential conceptual distinction in Henry's reading. *Gott* (God) is the absolute *insofar as it operates, creates, manifests in the world, has relations to creatures*. This is the God of classical theology and of religious life. *Gottheit* (Deity) is the absolute *in itself, prior to all operation, prior to all creation, prior to all relation to creatures*. This is the *immanent* essence — what Eckhart calls the "Ground," the "Abyss," the "Desert."

Crucially, Eckhart's distinction is not the distinction between an inferior and a superior God; it is the distinction between *the same* absolute considered in two different aspects — under the aspect of operation (Gott) and under the aspect of immanent self-presence (Gottheit). The Deity is the originary structure; God is the secondary, derivative manifestation in the order of creation.

For Henry, this distinction is structurally identical with his own distinction between transcendence (the structure of monist manifestation) and immanence (the structure of the originary essence). Eckhart's *Gott* (God-as-operation) corresponds to the monist structure of horizonal-creative manifestation; Eckhart's *Gottheit* (immanent essence) corresponds to the structure Henry has been articulating as the immanent self-affection of life. The Eckhartian thesis "God depends on creatures for being called 'God'" articulates the structural fact that the *operative* essence (transcendent manifestation) is contingent on the field of alterity it produces; the *immanent* essence (the Deity) is not so contingent — it is what it is in its eternal self-presence, prior to and independent of all creation.

**Paragraph 12\.** What is it then that is in the Deity, of what is made the essence of God in such a manner that it lets itself be understood as Unity? Aiming no longer at God himself (heard in the restrictive sense of his concept) but, this time, at his essence, Eckhart says (in a fundamental proposition): *"All that is in God is God."* Thus is rendered to its proper ontological positivity the affirmation according to which there is in the absolute nothing other, nothing foreign. That the essence has a *content* belonging to it, and that this content be constituted by the essence itself — this is what confers an intelligibility to the fundamental ontological determinations under which Eckhart understands as *"solitude"* and as *"desert"* what forms the internal structure of this essence (that is, the very nature of the Deity). *The exclusion outside it of all the forms of being and of its configurations has for correlate the presence in it of their radical and ultimate foundation* — its own presence to itself as constitutive of such a foundation. What there is "*in the depths of the divine nature and of its solitude,*" this divine nature itself as absolute ontological reality, *explains why* "*the power*" that "*goes to the bottom... grasps God in his unity and in his solitude..., in his desert and in his proper ground.*" Because it is the proper ground of God, the Deity that constitutes the essence of this desert, the content of this solitude — the solitude and the determinations in which solitude realizes itself and which are identical to it (*humility and poverty, purity and virginity*) — therefore have precisely *a content*: namely, *the Deity itself*; they are, as such, *the experience of God* — that is, his own reality. This is why humility, for example, could be said to be rooted in the Ground of the Deity, inserted in the Deity, in such a way as to have being only in the Deity — because finally, having the Deity for content, *humility is identical to the Deity*.

The Eckhartian "solitude" and "desert" — vocabulary derived from the eremitic tradition (the desert fathers, the contemplative withdrawal from the world) — is here read structurally. The *Deity* (the immanent essence) is *solitary* and *desert-like* in the structural sense that it has nothing other than itself within itself, no determinations imported from outside, no figures, no images. But this "solitude" is not empty (recall §37: solitude has a content); it is *full* — full of the Deity's own self-presence, its own immediate self-relation, its own *jouir de soi*. The desert of the immanent essence is the desert of *the absolute reality* — a desert that contains everything that has any reality, because it contains the very source of all reality (the Deity itself).

**Paragraph 13\.** *The possibility for the Deity to constitute itself its own content, and to be thus (at the heart of its solitude and in the desert of its Ground) the absolute ontological reality, is however a problem*; its foundation resides (as the problematic has shown) *in unity heard no longer from the simple identity of form and content but precisely as that which renders possible such an identity* — as the originary mode in conformity with which this identity accomplishes itself: such is precisely *the Eckhartian concept of unity, which designates not the simple presence of the essence in itself but its fundamental power of arriving in itself, of receiving itself, and of reuniting itself thus with itself* — in such a manner that this unity of the essence with itself results in it from the *fundamental unity that constitutes it*. This fundamental unity (constitutive of the internal structure of the essence and of the possibility for it to be one, to reunite itself with itself, and at the same time to be itself its own content) is, in fact, *as an ontological power* that Eckhart thinks it, when he claims to subsume under the concept of unity and to determine by it the essence of the Deity. This is why such a unity is necessarily understood by him (as it had to be in turn by the problematic) as *a work and an accomplishment, as the very work of the essence*. *"He who wants to grasp in its entirety the interior work,"* he says, *"becomes foreign even to goodness, to truth, to all that, even if only in thought and by name alone, supports the appearance and shadow of distinction whatever it may be; he confides himself to the unity which is free of all diversity and all limitation, the unity where strips and loses itself all difference."* This active and ontologically founding character of unity, Eckhart expresses again when (speaking of the possibility for the soul to unite with the absolute) he declares (regarding the soul) that it is *"with the help of Equality that it succeeds in arriving at God"*; when finally (regarding this equality itself, that is, of unity) he says of its work that *"it accomplishes itself ceaselessly, night and day."*

The structural specification of *unity* is now made precise. Eckhart's *unity* is not merely the formal property of being one; it is *the active power of self-reception* by which the essence comes to itself, receives itself, reunites with itself. This is structurally the same conception of unity Henry has articulated in §37: unity as "work and accomplishment" — the originary structural work by which the essence is given to itself in the immediate self-presence of immanent life. For both Eckhart and Henry, unity is not a static feature but the *dynamic* (in the structural-ontological sense, not the temporal sense) self-relation by which the essence is itself.

**Paragraph 14\.** Thus determines itself in its essential ontological content what belongs properly to the thought of Eckhart: *the essence which subsists in the rejection outside it of the creative power of exteriority (and consequently of exteriority itself) is not the dead unity of the existent or its empty identity in the tautology*; it is, in its solitude and in the absence of all relation with the world, in the *"purity"* that characterizes this absence of relation, *the essence of the absolute itself, its originary and fundamental power of arriving in itself* — in such a manner however that, *in this arriving and by it, the essence remains in itself* in the ontological structural unity of its interior development and of its accomplishment. *"There is something in the soul,"* says Eckhart, *"that surpasses the created essence... It is a kinship of divine essence, a Unity in itself, without relation... with whatever it may be... A foreign country, desert too unnameable to be named... uncreated mystery within yourself..."* And characterizing again this unity in its absence of relation with the world as *"purity,"* he adds: *"It is in this Purity that God, the eternal Father, draws the plenitude and the Ground without ground of his total Deity. This Abyss, he engenders... but all in engendering, he remains in himself; but, all in remaining himself, he engenders... for he remains absolute Unity all in gushing forth in himself."*

The Eckhartian formulations here cited articulate the structural-ontological self-relation of the immanent essence with great precision. The Deity *engenders* itself (the Father engenders the Son in the immanent processions of the Trinity, in the traditional theological vocabulary), but in this engendering it *remains in itself*; it gushes forth in itself but remains absolute Unity. This is structurally Henry's *self-affection*: the immanent essence is given to itself, receives itself, "engenders" itself in the immediate self-relation that is its very being — but this self-relation is *internal*, has no exteriority, no going-outside-itself. The essence is at once the giving and the given, the engendering and the engendered, in the structural unity of immanent self-presence.

**Paragraph 15\.** Because (in the accomplishment of the interior work by which it realizes itself, and in conformity with the internal structure that determines it in its essence as unity) the absolute *"remains in itself,"* it lets itself be understood without equivocation as *immanence*. It is in the light of this fundamental ontological concept that there is thought (in a constant manner in the work of Eckhart) what constitutes the nature and the Ground of the essence. This is why (in the absence of all surpassing) the essence is understood on the contrary as *repose* — and that in a positive sense in conformity with which the essence reposes "*in itself*," because its content is constituted by it. *"It is a Unity reposing in itself,"* says Eckhart, *"and receiving nothing from outside."* It is this manner for the essence (while nothing affects it) of reposing on itself and of constituting thus itself the soil on which it stands that Eckhart expresses when (wishing to make understood what truly makes its most intimate nature) he designates it as the *Ground* precisely — *"the absolutely simple Ground"* — as the *"Bed,"* the *"Stream,"* the *"Source," "the deepest Source."* Here, at the heart of what is, there discovers itself further the *essential reason of the union* from and around which is developed the problematic instituted by Eckhart: *it is because "He is the one who operates in himself" that the soul (where God operates his operation) is identical with him — that "God and I are one in the operation."*

The structural identification with §37 is now complete. The Eckhartian repose, the essence's "remaining in itself," the Ground "reposing in itself receiving nothing from outside" — all of these structural-vocabulary items are precisely those Henry has been using in §37 to articulate the immanent essence. The convergence is not merely terminological; it is structural-philosophical. Eckhart and Henry are articulating the same structural reality.

**Paragraph 16\.** Because it operates in itself and reposes thus in itself, the essence *"wills nothing,"* it *"remains in its nudity without any need."* Such is the *calm* of the essence — that which grows in the soul while (cooperating with God — that is, renouncing all activity) the soul enters into this *state of poverty* that belongs properly to the essence and where it is said to will nothing, in this *nudity* where it has no need. Willing nothing and having (in the calm where it reposes) no need, the essence is, *in this poverty*, essentially *deprived* with regard to any power whatever to relate itself to *something other* — to something it would not have, or that would not yet be. *The horizon of irreality and the possibility of relating itself in the horizon to something irreal, the possibility of a lack in general — this is what is lacking to the essence in its poverty.* *"This secret Ground,"* says Eckhart, *"has neither past nor future; it awaits nothing that could be added to it, for it can neither gain nor lose..."* Such a "lack" understands itself from now on in *its true sense*, as belonging properly to *reality* — the absence of a horizon, like that of all finitude.

The Eckhartian "ground that awaits nothing" articulates the structural feature Henry has called *plenitude*: the essence is not waiting to become what it is not yet; the essence has no horizon of unrealized possibility; the essence has no *Sich-Vorweg-Sein*. In the structural sense, the essence "lacks" the horizon — but this "lack" is not a deficiency; it is the structural mark of the essence's being entirely real, entirely present to itself, with no surplus of possibility beyond what is actually given.

**Paragraph 17\.** Reality does not let itself be determined, however, in a negative manner and by the simple exclusion outside it of the finite power of the horizon. *Reality can only be what it is — reality — because the content of reality is given to it, and that in its totality.* Such is precisely reality: *the act of giving itself in unity the reality of its proper content* — the reality, and consequently the totality of this content. It is from the structure of this act that the power of alterity, alterity itself, irreality and finitude find themselves excluded. This is why such an act, interpreted in a negative manner, could not exhibit a finite content — why *"God cannot give little"* — and why on the contrary (determined in a positive manner in his internal structure as unity) *"he must give all at once"* and finds himself to be as such *constitutive of God himself*, whose "*gift is simple..., perfect, without division, without relation with time...*" And that this gift (which is the "*all*" of reality) constitutes *the essence of reality* and (as essentially determined in its structure by unity) *the essence of life* is what is affirmed when (speaking of this gift and of its absolute character) Eckhart says: *"of this I am as certain as of living."* Thus there are recognized, at the same time as its internal structure, *the ontological determinations that belong properly to reality* and in conformity with which reality gives itself necessarily *in its totality*. Thus is understood (from its essence and as belonging to its essence) *the adequate character of the experience of being* — the rigorous adaptation in this experience *of the form to the content* — in such a manner that nothing escapes from this content, that (as Eckhart says) *"what fills touches all the ends and lacks nowhere; it has width and length, height and depth."* The adequate character of this experience and its rigorous adaptation to a content constituted by it (the determination from the experience, and as identical to it, of reality) — this is what renders intelligible *the nature of reality, the manner in which it proposes itself to itself in its own profusion*: the *"plenitude"* and the *"sweetness"* of being. This plenitude and this sweetness Eckhart was not content to *name*; he grasped them *in the foundation*, from the most interior structure of reality (insofar as this reality constitutes itself, as unity, its own content). *"The joy of the Lord,"* he says, *"is the Lord himself."*

The structural argument now reaches one of its most beautiful formulations. The "joy of the Lord is the Lord himself" — the Lord's joy is not a relation of the Lord to *something other* (some object that brings joy); the Lord's joy is the immediate self-presence of the Lord to himself in his own reality. This is structurally the same point Henry made in §37: *that which experiences itself, that which enjoys itself, is life*. Joy (in the structural-ontological sense) is the *modality* of immanent self-affection; it is life's immediate self-presence in its own plenitude.

**Paragraph 18 (closing).** To the determination — such as it accomplishes itself from the foundation and from its most interior structure understood as unity — of what constitutes (with its proper phenomenological characters) the experience of being, its plenitude and its sweetness, *there lacks however the explicitation of a presupposition* in which finds itself contained (in truth) the *essential contribution* of Eckhart's thought: *the presupposition* according to which *unity precisely determines as such an experience* — the experience-of-self of being in the enjoyment-of-self — *the fundamental ontological presupposition in conformity with which the internal structure of immanence is that of revelation*.

The closing paragraph names what Eckhart accomplished and what (according to Henry) Eckhart did not yet make fully explicit. Eckhart articulated, in his preaching, the structure of the immanent essence with extraordinary precision (the unity, the solitude, the desert, the Ground, the absence of mediation, the rejection of images and forms, the identity of soul and Deity, the dependence of "God" on "creature," etc.). What Eckhart presupposed, but did not fully thematize, is *the equivalence* between this immanent structure and *the structure of revelation itself* — the structural identity that Henry articulated in §37 (and which §38 showed Fichte to have missed). Eckhart works as if it were obvious that the immanent essence is *eo ipso* the essence of revelation; he does not fully explicit the philosophical-structural reasons for this equivalence. Henry's whole project (and especially §40) is to make this equivalence explicit — to articulate the *fundamental ontological presupposition* of Eckhart's thought, which is precisely the structural identity Henry himself has been articulating as the central thesis of his work.

The closing reference to "the experience-of-self of being in the enjoyment-of-self" returns to the central vocabulary of §37: life as the immediate self-experience, the *jouir de soi* that is the structure of immanent essence. This is the "essential contribution" Eckhart makes — and that Henry's whole phenomenology will work to articulate philosophically. §40 will make this fundamental presupposition explicit.

---

## **§ 40\. The fundamental ontological presupposition of Eckhart's thought and the originary essence of the logos**

**Paragraph 1\.** The understanding of the internal structure of immanence as that of revelation — as constituting, in a more precise manner, the originary essence of revelation — is in Eckhart a *constant presupposition* of his thought, and at the same time the object of his most explicit affirmations. It is in an explicit fashion, indeed, that the essence which is to itself its proper content finds itself interpreted (on the ground in it of this identity) *not as the dead existent lost in its night*, but on the contrary as *Reason* — that is, as a power of intelligibility whose intelligible content is moreover constituted by this power itself, as a power of *revelation* consequently, and that precisely insofar as the essence remains in itself and relates itself to nothing other. Thus one sees that, immediately after having declared that the content of the essence he calls the Lord is constituted by the essence itself "and nothing other," Eckhart adds: *"and the Lord is the Reason — living, essential and existent — that understands itself, that is and lives absolutely only in itself."* Because it is and lives absolutely only in itself, the Reason that understands itself — that is, whose phenomenological power consists in the revelation-of-self — does not reveal itself, precisely, in a manner conform to the mode of manifestation that has been thought in these researches under the title of "understanding" (*compréhension*), but on the contrary *according to the structure of unity*. It is as fundamentally determined in it by unity that the understanding (which, according to Eckhart, affects the essence and belongs to it) must be heard — so that, accomplishing itself *without any mediation*, this understanding reveals the essence such as it is: not in the milieu of alterity but *in itself*, stripped of every foreign element. *"A unitary intelligence,"* says Eckhart, *"is so pure in itself that it understands without intermediary the divine Being in its Purity and its Nudity."* This necessity of hearing the essence of revelation that accomplishes itself *as unity* (in its radical opposition to the ontological process of objectivation) is visible in the critique instituted by Eckhart — in the name of unity precisely — against *intuition*, which finds in such a process its foundation: *"As long as we are still occupied with looking, we are not yet one with what we look at. As long as something is still the object of our intuition, we are not yet one in the One."* In the absence of every intuition, however — when the process that serves as its foundation does not accomplish itself — *a manifestation is produced*, which is the revelation of the essence itself in its reality. *"For,"* adds Eckhart, *"there where there is only the One, one sees only the One."*

The opening paragraph of §40 articulates the structural-philosophical thesis that §39 had approached but had not yet fully articulated: the structural identity between *immanence* and the *essence of revelation*. Eckhart's repeated affirmations that the Deity "understands itself" in unity, that "a unitary intelligence understands without intermediary the divine Being," that "there where there is only the One, one sees only the One" — these are not mere theological formulations but precise structural-ontological articulations of the fundamental thesis: the structure of immanence is *eo ipso* the structure of revelation. The immanent essence is not blind, not hidden, not merely present-to-itself in a silent way; the immanent essence is *luminous*, *revelatory*, *Reason*.

The critical point Eckhart makes (which Henry endorses and radicalizes) is that this immanent revelation is *not intuitive*. Intuition is structurally the monist-horizonal process: to intuit is to stand over against, to have the intuited as *object*, to be in the structural doubling of intuiter/intuited. Eckhart's "unitary intelligence" that understands without intermediary is *not* an intuiter in this sense; it is the immanent self-presence of the essence to itself, in which there is no separation of intuiter from intuited, no opposition of gaze from seen. The rejection of intuition is not a rejection of knowledge or revelation; it is the structural thesis that the deepest revelation is not intuitive but *immanent* — not the seeing of something placed over against, but the self-presence of the essence in the absence of all such opposition.

The quotation "there where there is only the One, one sees only the One" is one of Eckhart's most compressed formulations. Structurally: where there is no opposition, no structure of distance, no horizon, what "is seen" is the unity itself — that is, the immanent essence in its immediate self-presence. This is not a "seeing" in the intuitive sense (no opposition); it is a structural self-presencing that Henry will articulate as *self-affection*, *life's experience of itself*.

**Paragraph 2\.** What (on the ground in it of unity) constitutes itself its own content has been understood as *life*: because unity is as such the founder of a revelation, life too is, as constituted by unity, constitutive and founder of a revelation — life is *in itself* revelation. *"To know God alone, this is eternal life,"* says Eckhart — that is, life itself in its essence, insofar as it relates itself to itself in unity and not, in alterity, to a finite horizon. Because the finite horizon is *excluded* from the reality that is that of the essence and of life (as determined in them by unity), it is this reality — essentially infinite — that reveals itself in unity precisely and in its perfect adequation. This is why *"no one knows better what eternal life is than eternal life itself"* — why *"what is at the highest point, one knows equally at the highest point,"* why (finally) to *"a surabundant being"* corresponds *"a surabundant knowledge."* This knowledge could not however be considered as a particular modality of existence (a privileged modality, for example); it is *an ontological structure* that finds itself determined at once as unity and as revelation. It is this structure that constitutes this *"first Image in which all things are unity,"* where resides (according to Eckhart) the *"repose"* and which he calls again without equivocation *"God."* It is in this first Image that the experience of the absolute accomplishes itself — which, as adequate experience of its reality in unity, leaves outside itself all its transcendent determinations, in this originary ontological region where the soul *"can taste God before he becomes in any way Truth or knowability."* *"It is there,"* adds Eckhart, *"that the soul knows in the purest manner, that it assumes being in its perfect Equality."*

The thesis articulated here is the structural-philosophical pivot of the whole section. *Because unity is as such the founder of a revelation, life is in itself revelation.* This is the structural identity that §39 had approached through Eckhart's distinctions (Gott/Gottheit, solitude, desert, Ground) and that §40 now articulates with precision: immanent life, because it has the structure of unity (the structure of immediate self-presence without distance or mediation), is *itself* the originary essence of revelation. The revelation is not something that happens *to* life from outside; the revelation *is* life itself, in its immediate self-presence. To live is to be revealed; revelation is life's own self-relation.

The Eckhartian formulations are striking. "No one knows better what eternal life is than eternal life itself" — life is not known by some external cognitive faculty; life knows itself *as* itself, in the immediate self-presence that constitutes its being. This is not a tautology (life knows life) but a structural-ontological specification: the knowing and the known are not structurally distinguished; they are the same immanent self-relation. "Eternal life" here is the classical theological term for the life that is in God and in those who share God's life; Henry reads it structurally as the *ontological* life that has the structure of immanent self-revelation.

The taste vocabulary — "the soul can taste God before he becomes in any way Truth or knowability" — is significant. Tasting, in contrast to seeing (the paradigmatic intuitive sense), is *proximate*, *immediate*, *non-distantiated*. One does not taste at a distance; tasting is structurally intimate contact. Eckhart uses this vocabulary to characterize the pre-objectifying, pre-thematic encounter with the Deity that is structurally the immanent self-presence of life. Henry will return to the tasting-vocabulary in his mature phenomenology of life (especially in *I Am the Truth*) to characterize the non-intuitive, immanent self-experience of life.

**Paragraph 3\.** Thus is discovered — with the interpretation of the structure of unity as constitutive of *"the most pure knowledge,"* that is, of the originary essence of revelation — the *ultimate foundation of union*, placed by Eckhart at the center of his meditation: the union of the soul and God. What can such a union signify, indeed, if not *the manifestation to the soul of God himself in his unity with the soul*? The determination of the essence of the soul as constituted by that of the absolute remains a simple speculative affirmation, indeed, as long as this essence does not *manifest itself* in the soul as the soul's own. But this manifestation in the soul of the essence is the doing of the essence: *it is the essence in reality that manifests itself to itself*, in such a way that the union of the soul with God expresses nothing other than the *internal unity of the essence itself* — and does not become effective in manifestation except insofar as this unity finds itself to be as such constitutive of a manifestation, *insofar as the internal structure of immanence is that of revelation*. That the union is not effective except in manifestation — that is, insofar as its concept is recognized in its positive phenomenological signification — is what Eckhart affirms: *"If man is happy,"* he says, *"it is not because God is in him and is so close to him and because he has God, but because he knows how close God is to him, because he knows who God is."* The knowledge of God, where the phenomenological (that is, effective) signification of union is founded, is however the doing of God himself — in such a way that the self-revelation of the absolute (such as it accomplishes itself in unity) determines, in its unity with it and consequently as phenomenologically identical to it, the very essence of the soul. *"In the same act of knowledge in which God knows himself,"* says Eckhart, *"the soul receives its essence from God without mediation."*
