The Eckhartian doctrine of the *union of the soul with God* — which the mystical tradition had read as an experiential, ecstatic event attainable by the saintly person through prayer, contemplation, and grace — is here read structurally. The union is *not* primarily an experience to be attained; the union is the *structural fact* of the soul's essence being identically constituted with God's essence. The soul is not separated from God and then united with God by grace; the soul's very being is constituted in the immanent self-revelation of the absolute. What classical mysticism calls "union" is the *recognition* of this structural constitution — what Eckhart calls "knowing how close God is."

Crucially, Eckhart's formulation "*in the same act of knowledge in which God knows himself, the soul receives its essence from God without mediation*" articulates the structural identity Henry has been developing. There are not *two* acts — God's self-knowing and the soul's receiving of essence — related externally; there is *one* act of immanent self-revelation, in which the essence gives itself to itself, and this single act is at once God's self-knowing and the soul's constitution. The soul is not an addition to God or a recipient of God's self-communication; the soul *is* the structural receptivity of the immanent essence, the self-reception that is constitutive of the essence's immanent self-presence. This is the structural meaning of the Eckhartian thesis that the soul's essence is God's essence.

This is why — because the essence of the soul (its revelation) is constituted by that of God, by the originary revelation of the absolute to itself in unity — *nothing penetrates into the soul except in this absolute form of revelation constitutive of its essence*. *"Nothing penetrates to the heart of man except through all the sweetness of God"*; this is why *"it is in a divine fashion that all that happens to him takes form in him."* What penetrates into the soul however, in this absolute form of revelation (which constitutes its very essence and which, as fundamentally determined in it by unity, is the originary revelation of the absolute to itself), is precisely the absolute, God, *such as he is in himself, in his nudity*. This is why, as Eckhart says, man is a *theognost*, *"ein Gottwissender Mensch."* It is because he is such — a man who knows God — that God (according to Eckhart, who here reports the very words of the gospel of Saint John) addressed himself to him in these terms: *"I have not called you servants but I have called you my friends. The servant does not know the will of his master, but the friend knows all that his friend knows."* And it is because man is such also that all those who participate in his essence can say, as John again reports: *"You, you adore what you do not know; we, we adore what we know."*

The Johannine citations (John 15:15 on friends vs. servants; John 4:22 on knowing vs. ignorant adoration) are important. They articulate a distinction between *knowing* and *not-knowing* that is, for Eckhart, a structural-ontological distinction: those who share the immanent essence *know* the absolute (because the absolute is immanently revealed in them as their own essence), while those who stand in the ordinary relation of worshipper-to-transcendent-deity *do not know* (because they relate to the absolute only through the distantiating structure of transcendence). The Eckhartian-Johannine friendship of man with God is the structural fact that the immanent essence is shared; it is not a contingent relational fact. The "theognost" is not the learned theologian but the one whose very essence is the immanent self-revelation of the absolute.

**Paragraph 4\.** The interpretation of the structure of unity as constitutive of an *experience* does not only confer on the union of man with God its ultimate foundation; it *further determines in a rigorous manner the nature of this experience* — that is, the very essence of revelation. Because revelation accomplishes itself in unity, it arises and becomes effective *independently* of the ontological process of objectivation and of the phenomenality produced by that process; revelation manifests itself, and its manifestation is *not* that of a horizon nor of exteriority. *"The image,"* says Eckhart, *"is without image,"* and that *"because it is not seen in another image."* It is because the revelation of the essence is *not* the being-seen in the image of alterity that the soul — whose power of revelation reposes on that of the essence or rather is identical to it, as constituted by it — *"understands and knows"* (in this power precisely and by it) *"immediately and without image."* The image however — what is *"first purified and sifted in the air and the light, to arrive then under the form of image to my eye"* — this very form of the image manifests itself. Thus there is, alongside the originary revelation of the essence (such as it accomplishes itself *"without image"*), a phenomenality proper to image and such that in it "images" precisely are possible — and in general phenomena in the sense of phenomena of the world. *Thus is divided in the essential eidetic analysis the concept of phenomenality.* This division is the one instituted by Eckhart between what he calls *"the knowledge of the evening"* (which accomplishes itself under the form of *"images"* — that is, in exteriority — and finds itself thus grasping, and that in principle, the *"creature"* itself as such), and, on the other hand, *"the knowledge of the morning"* (whose structure is unity and encloses in itself, as such, nothing distinct nor represented, to which the creature can give itself only on the condition of being grasped — not in itself but in its being-identical to that of God — that is, precisely, on the condition of being grasped in Unity). *"When one knows creatures such as they are in themselves — what I will call a knowledge of the evening — one sees creation only in distinct images. But when one knows creatures in God — what I will call a knowledge of the morning — one sees the creature without the least distinction, without any of the images that represented it, and without resemblance to whatever it may be, in the Unity which is God himself."*

The Eckhartian distinction between *cognitio matutina* (morning knowledge) and *cognitio vespertina* (evening knowledge) — a medieval theological distinction traceable through Augustine and Aquinas — is here read in its full structural-ontological signification. Evening knowledge is the knowledge that operates in the horizonal-objectifying mode, grasping creatures "as they are in themselves" — that is, in their distinction, in their multiplicity, in their images. Morning knowledge is the knowledge that operates in the immanent-unitary mode, grasping creatures "in God" — that is, in the originary unity of the immanent essence, without distinction, without images, without separation.

The structural reading is precise. The two "knowledges" are *not* two subjective states or two epistemological capacities; they are *two structural modes of phenomenality*. "Evening" phenomenality is horizonal-monist: it has the structure of transcendence, of opposition, of image, of separation. "Morning" phenomenality is immanent-unitary: it has the structure of immediate self-presence, of unity, of non-mediation. The *division of the concept of phenomenality* that Henry thus finds in Eckhart is structurally identical with Henry's own division between monist and immanent manifestation — between the horizonal revelation-as-distance and the immanent revelation-as-self-affection. Eckhart and Henry are articulating the same structural division of phenomenality; their vocabularies differ but the structure is identical.

**Paragraph 5\.** It is this same distinction in the structure of ontological knowledge — between a manifestation accomplishing itself in unity and another in exteriority — that Eckhart expresses again in saying of man (with Scripture) *"that there is in us an exterior man and another, the interior man."* For, once set aside the existential signification that such a distinction first takes in the analysis, its ontological foundation appears at the same time as its true signification. The interior man is the noble man, *"noble because he is one and because in Unity he knows equally God and creature"*: it is the internal ontological structure of a *mode of manifestation* that finds itself thought — in such a way that the content of this manifestation is always constituted, in reality, by the essence itself. But the ontological signification, in virtue of which the distinction instituted by Eckhart between the interior and the exterior concerns the *power of manifestation considered in itself and its pure structure*, does not have to be induced by us as an ultimate foundation for the edifying themes that intervene in his problematic; it is explicitly affirmed by him: *"the soul has two eyes,"* he says, *"an interior eye and an exterior eye. The interior eye of the soul looks toward the essence and receives it directly from God; this is the work which is proper to it. The exterior eye… turns on the contrary toward the creatures and perceives them in images. But the man who enters into himself so as to perceive God in his own taste and in his own ground, that man is enfranchised from all created things and is withdrawn into himself as into a veritable fortress of Truth."*

The *interior man / exterior man* distinction (from Ephesians and Romans, via Origen and Augustine) is read here in its structural-ontological signification. The "interior" and "exterior" are not two subjective regions or two moral-spiritual states; they are two *structural modes* of the essence's self-manifestation. The "interior eye" is the structural receptivity by which the essence receives itself in immanent self-presence; the "exterior eye" is the structural intentionality by which consciousness aims at creatures in the horizonal mode. Eckhart's saying that the interior eye "receives the essence directly from God" articulates precisely the structure Henry has called immanent self-affection: the immediate, non-mediated, non-horizonal self-reception that is the structure of life.

**Paragraph 6\.** The revelation of the essence in unity does not, however, simply juxtapose itself to the manifestation of the horizon; it *founds* the manifestation of the horizon. This is why it does not suffice to say that *"other is the power by which the eye sees, and other the power by which it knows that it sees,"* but, in a more essential manner, that *"the power which produces in us the consciousness of our vision is more noble and higher than the power which produces vision itself."* Every given however has an equivalent right to that of any other given. The affirmation, concerning the pure givens themselves, of a higher dignity of one with regard to another remains speculative as long as it refers itself simply to the recognition of the *link of foundation* that unites them. Or else this recognition must accomplish itself otherwise and elsewhere than on the plane of speculation — with the bringing-to-light, *inside effective vision* and as its *originary phenomenological content*, of the originary phenomenological content *of the essence*. It is because the latter effectively constitutes the originary phenomenological content of vision that all that manifests itself in vision manifests itself originarily in this content of the essence and *belongs to it*. But the originary phenomenological content of vision is, as the originary phenomenological content of the essence, *Unity*. This is why Unity encloses in itself, in its phenomenological reality (which is that of the essence), *all phenomena* — why *"God has all things hidden in him, not in such a way that this or that is distinct, but all things make only one, in conformity with his Unity."* The unity of all phenomena in the ontological milieu where their manifestation is originarily revealed is a constant theme of Eckhart's thought: up there, he says, one knows things truly *"such as they are, all undivided and close to each other; the things that are here below far from each other are brought close up there, because all are there only in the present."* The ontological milieu where the unity of all phenomena accomplishes itself is however *not* the object of a metaphysical affirmation and does not constitute as such any *Hinterwelt* (behind-world); it is the milieu, *coextensive* with their manifestation, where this manifestation reveals itself and arrives originarily in effectivity. In the effectivity of this manifestation consequently — and everywhere that manifestation accomplishes itself — *is present the unity*, and that as an originary phenomenological content. The soul, insofar as it sees, *"possesses a power in which everything becomes one,"* and it is thus that (by essence — that is, in the effectivity of its phenomenological reality) it *"gathers what is dispersed and divided,"* *"comprehends with unity all diversity in itself."*

The structural thesis is now decisive and is articulated with great precision. Immanence does *not* stand alongside transcendence as two separate spheres; immanence *founds* transcendence. The unity of the immanent essence is the *originary phenomenological content* of every manifestation, including the horizonal manifestations of exteriority. Every appearance in the world — every intuition, every perception, every thought of an object — has *as its originary phenomenological content* the immanent unity of the essence. The horizonal-monist manifestation is not autonomous; it depends on the immanent-unitary manifestation as its condition of possibility, its foundation, its originary content.

This is the structural response to the problem posed at the close of Section II (the problem of the internal possibility of receptivity). The receptivity that monism required but could not ground within its own structure is grounded in the immanent self-reception of the essence. The horizonal structure of transcendence is *founded* on the immanent structure of self-affection. Transcendence is not originary; immanence is originary, and transcendence is a derivative-secondary mode that is made possible by the immanent self-reception.

The explicit rejection of the *Hinterwelt* (Nietzsche's term for the metaphysical "behind-world" projected by religious-metaphysical thinking) is important. Henry is *not* saying that immanence is a hidden metaphysical ground behind the phenomena; he is saying that immanence is *coextensive* with effective manifestation, operative *in* every phenomenon as its originary content. The immanent essence is not somewhere else; it is *here*, in every act of manifestation, as the originary phenomenological content that the act reveals. There is no "two-world" metaphysics in Henry's phenomenology; there is one phenomenality, differentiated structurally into two modes (immanent-originary and horizonal-derivative), where the immanent mode is operative *in* the horizonal mode as its foundation.

**Paragraph 7\.** Insofar as the revelation of the essence in unity does not simply juxtapose itself to the manifestation of the horizon but further founds *phenomenologically* the effectivity of the horizon, it constitutes precisely the *universal effective phenomenological foundation of every possible manifestation in general* — the *essence of the Logos*. Thus becomes intelligible in Eckhart — as the point where there gather and culminate the ultimate intuitions of his thought — *the theory of the Verb (Word, Logos)*. The Logos, understood by him in conformity with the religious tradition, is again called *the Son of God*. This signifies that the revelation, in its effective phenomenological accomplishment, is the *work of the absolute*. How does this work accomplish itself? How does revelation arise in effectivity? This is, as we have seen, *in unity*. For this reason such an arising — that of revelation in the effectivity of its originary phenomenality — is the act of *remaining in itself* of the absolute; such an act is the originary arising of revelation. Speaking of the Deity understood as Abyss (that is, of the originary revelation-of-self of the essence in unity), Eckhart says (in a text already cited and here restored in its entirety) that God *"engenders it in his only Son so that we too are the same Son. But all in engendering he remains in himself; but, all in remaining in himself, he engenders and manifests himself."* Thus is determined at once in its phenomenological character and in its structure what constitutes *the internal work of the absolute in its originary accomplishment*. This work, by reason of this character, lets itself be understood as the very essence of the Logos. *"What is the Word of God?"* says Eckhart. *"It is the operation of God."* Such a work, in conformity with its structure, with the structure of this operation (which constitutes the essence of the Logos), determines the Logos in its identity with the operation. Such is the ontological structural foundation that presides over the establishment of the relations existing between God and his Word, between the Father and the Son. Commenting on the saying of Saint John according to which *"the Word was in God,"* Eckhart adds: *"He was absolutely equal to him, he was in him without mediation, neither lower nor higher, but equal."* In what rigorous and radical sense these propositions must be heard, Eckhart takes care to indicate to us when (in another passage, ontologically more explicit) he rejects — as belonging still, in its reference to *"the eternal archetype,"* to the plane of transcendence — the concept of *equality* (which, as such, reveals itself finally improper to characterize the relations of the Son and the Father): *"in the archetype… the Son is equal to the Father. But in the Essence where they are one, they are not even 'equal' any more, for equality already supposes difference."*

The theological vocabulary is now operating at its full structural power. The Logos (Word, *Verbum*, *Logos*) — the central concept of Johannine Christology and of classical Trinitarian theology — is here articulated as the *essence of revelation itself* in its structural-ontological purity. Revelation, in its originary phenomenological accomplishment, *is* the Logos: the self-expressive, self-communicative, self-articulating power of the immanent essence. The "Father engendering the Son" is the classical Trinitarian formula for the immanent procession of the Word from the Father; Eckhart (and Henry) read this structurally as the immanent self-engendering of the essence — the immanent act by which the essence gives itself to itself in its own proper Word. "All in engendering, he remains in himself" — the procession is not a going-out-of-oneself (which would be transcendence); it is an *immanent* procession, an engendering that remains in itself.

The striking Eckhartian rejection of "equality" as an ultimate characterization of the Father-Son relation is structurally decisive. Equality presupposes difference (two things must first be distinct to be equal); but at the deepest level of the immanent essence, there is no difference, no duality, only unity. So "equality" belongs to a derivative-theological level (the level of *theologia* as speculative doctrine about relations within God); at the level of the immanent essence itself (the *Gottheit*), there is no distinction of Father and Son to be made equal. Henry endorses this structural thesis: at the level of immanent self-affection, there is no duality of self and self-revealed; there is only the immediate immanent self-presence in which the revelation *is* the essence revealed.

**Paragraph 8\.** It is with this ultimate ontological signification — as *radically exclusive of every relation of transcendence* — that must be heard the unity, affirmed by Eckhart, of the Father and the Son, of the essence and the Word. This is why such a unity has, despite the appearance, nothing to do with the unity which, for example, the young Hegel will recognize between Jesus and God, and whose existence he will affirm (against the Jewish mentality). Between Jesus and his Father — that is, as well between man and God — there is according to the young Hegel (beyond the frozen determinations of the understanding which irreducibly separate two natures) only *the homogeneity of life*. It is not the internal structure of this homogeneity (understood as revelation and precisely as Logos) that he pretends to characterize. The Logos, on the contrary, will not arise in the effectivity of the manifestation that constitutes its very essence except on the ground in it, not of unity but *precisely of difference*, and by the mediation of difference. This is why *"it is the Word which, pronounced, leaves alienated and empty the one who pronounces it, but is heard no less immediately"* in this very alienation. That the being-heard of the Word — that is, the Word itself, the being-heard of the essence — is *not* the being-alienated of the essence but its reality (the essence itself in the originary act by which it accomplishes revelation, pronounces the Word, and listens to it) is what the simplicity of essential language affirms unconditionally: *"what listens and what is heard is precisely the same thing in the eternal Word."* Because what is heard in the Word of the essence is the essence that pronounces the Word (that accomplishes the work of manifestation), it is this essence (which accomplishes this work) that manifests itself in the Word: *"all that the eternal Father teaches,"* says Eckhart, *"is his Essence, his Nature, and his total Deity."* What manifests itself however — the being-heard as such — is the Word. In the Word, then, manifests itself *all that manifests itself*: the essence that accomplishes the work of manifestation, the Father. This also is contained in the simplicity of the essential word, and it is why Eckhart adds: *"He reveals everything to us together in his only Son."*

The polemic here with the young Hegel's *Theologische Jugendschriften* (especially "The Spirit of Christianity and Its Fate") is significant. The young Hegel had articulated the Jesus-Father relation as the *homogeneity of life* — life as the shared substance of the divine and the human. Henry (via Eckhart) insists that mere "homogeneity of life" is insufficient; what must be articulated is the *internal structure* of life as the structure of immanent self-revelation (the Logos). The young Hegel's vocabulary of "life" hints at the right structural thesis but does not articulate it philosophically; Eckhart articulates the structural content that the young Hegel left implicit.

Even more pointedly, the mature Hegelian conception of the Logos (in the *Phenomenology* and the *Science of Logic*) makes the Logos arise *through difference and by the mediation of difference* — the word is spoken by the speaker and is heard as something different from the speaker, in the structure of alienation. Henry insists that this is the *horizonal-monist* conception of the Logos, which misses its essential structure. In the *immanent* Logos (Eckhart's Logos), what listens and what is heard are the same thing; there is no alienation, no mediation, no difference — only the immanent self-presencing of the essence in its own self-articulation. The essential Word is not the exterior word of everyday speech but the immanent Word in which the essence is given to itself.

This is a structural critique of the entire Hegelian philosophy of language. For Hegel, the Logos comes to itself through its self-alienation in otherness (externalization, sedimentation in the real, recuperation). For Eckhart-Henry, the Logos is *already* itself in its immanent self-presencing, without any alienation, without any need to externalize. The Hegelian Logos is structurally a monist-horizonal Logos; the Eckhartian-Henrian Logos is an immanent Logos. The two are different conceptions of the essence of language, of revelation, of meaning.

**Paragraph 9\.** The ultimate ontological signification of the theory of the Logos — the determination of the essence of effective revelation from unity and as constituted by unity — Eckhart has expressed rigorously *with the distinction of the three Verbs* (*three Words*). Independent of the manifestation that accomplishes itself outside of me or in me but always in representation, in a world, there holds itself in itself — *in unity* — the originary essence of the Logos, the foundation of all Reason. *"There is a Verb that has been pronounced,"* says Eckhart, *"for example: angel, man, or any creature whatever. But there is another Verb that is thought but remains unexpressed; that one I gather in myself at that precise level where representation is still possible. But there is still a third Verb, which remains unthought and unexpressed and never goes out but remains eternally in the one who says it; it is always grasped as on the point of going out and remains nevertheless in the Father. Reason directs, always operates inwardly. The more refined and spiritual a thing is, the more strongly it operates inwardly. Thus the stronger and more refined reason is, the more interior is the object known for it, and the narrower becomes its union with it…, even the beatitude of God reposes on the internal operation of reason, there where the eternal Word dwells in itself."*

The Eckhartian doctrine of the *three Verbs* is one of the most precise structural articulations in the whole tradition. The three words:

* The *first Verb* — the pronounced word, the spoken language, the word that has gone out into the world of representation (like "angel," "man," "creature"). This is the external, horizonal, creature-level language. This is the word of exteriority.  
* The *second Verb* — the thought-but-unexpressed word, the interior mental word that is still *representative* but has not yet been externalized in speech. This is Augustine's *verbum intus* (interior word) — the intentional aim of the mind that has not yet become language. Still within the horizon of representation, though interior.  
* The *third Verb* — the unthought, unexpressed word that never goes out but remains eternally in the one who says it. This is the immanent Word, the originary Logos, the structural self-articulation of the immanent essence in the absence of all externalization, representation, or mediation. This is the *essence* of the Logos.

The structural hierarchy is critical. The third Verb is the *foundation* of the first two; the second is *derivative* from the third (it is representation operating in the interior); the first is *further derivative* (it is externalization of the second into language). The whole domain of linguistic and representational meaning is founded on the immanent, unrepresented, never-externalized Word that is the structure of immanent essence. This third Verb is what Henry will articulate throughout the rest of the book as the essence of revelation — the immanent self-articulation of life in its own immediate self-presence.

The image of the third Verb as "always grasped as on the point of going out and remains nevertheless in the Father" is strikingly precise. The third Verb is *not* static (as if it were a mere silent presence); it is *dynamic* in the structural-ontological sense — it is the ongoing, continuous act of self-engendering, self-articulation, self-relation that is the very being of the immanent essence. The essence is not first present and then produces the Word; the essence *is* the self-producing of the Word in the immanence of its structural self-relation. The Father and the Son, in the immanence of the third Verb, are not two moments but one structural act of immanent self-revelation.

**Paragraph 10 (closing).** The ultimate ontological interpretation to which Eckhart has raised himself — of the internal structure of immanence as constitutive of the essence of the Logos — demands still to accomplish itself: (1) that *the elaboration of this structure be pushed further* so as to render apparent the totality of its ontological characters at the same time as the fundamental significative unity that these characters prescribe to it; (2) that *there become intelligible the reasons for which this structure, constitutive of the essence of the Logos, has precisely never been understood as such* — for which, in other terms, *there dissimulates itself, and that in an essential manner, revelation itself in the effectivity of its originary accomplishment*; (3) that *be shown finally and determined without equivocation what constitutes*, at the heart even of the act by which revelation "dissimulates itself," *the positive phenomenological content — the effectivity of this revelation*.

The closing paragraph announces with precision the program of the rest of the book. Three tasks are identified:

(1) *Further structural elaboration*: Henry must push further the analysis of immanence to bring out the totality of its ontological characters. This task is accomplished in §§41–44 (immanence and absolute situation, the essence of "Nichtigkeit," situation and temporality, the concept of situation in existentialism).

(2) *Diagnostic of the dissimulation*: Henry must explain why this structure, which is the most essential and originary, has *never* been understood in the philosophical tradition — why the philosophical tradition has systematically missed the immanent essence of revelation. This task is the great *polemical-diagnostic* project of §§45–49 (dissimulation and forgetting of the originary essence, critique of knowledge in religion, rationalism, Eckhart).

(3) *Positive exhibition of the phenomenological content*: Finally, Henry must show what the immanent revelation positively *is* — what its phenomenological content consists in, beyond its mere structural articulation. This task culminates in §§50–51 (the non-face of the essence, the visible and the invisible) and is fully developed in Section IV (the phenomenology of affective life).

The three-part program articulated here structures the entire remainder of the book. §40 thus functions as a *hinge* — the section that, having established the structural identity between immanence and revelation (through Eckhart), now projects the program by which this identity will be fully articulated and made philosophically rigorous.

---

## **§ 41\. Immanence and absolute situation**

**Paragraph 1\.** The elaboration of immanence in its internal structure has rendered manifest in it the *end of a power*. In the light of the idea of this end, immanence lets itself be understood as essentially affected by something like an *impotence*, by an *impossibility*. This impossibility could not however remain in the indeterminacy belonging to the generality of its concept. It does not concern — in conformity with the habitual sense of this concept — the simple privation of the power to do something (that is, of a possibility rooted originally, by its direction, in the irreal sphere of alterity). *It is with regard to itself that the essence reveals itself fundamentally impotent*; it is the relation of being with itself (not with something other) that the concept of impossibility comes to determine. What sort of impossibility affects being itself in its originary relation to self — that is, in its essence — becomes transparent if, on the other hand, possibility designates (in conformity with the specific signification that has been recognized to freedom in the framework of these researches) the *surpassing* (*dépassement*). The impossibility which determines the originary relation of being with self signifies, from then on, not simply and in general the impossibility of surpassing, but rather, *for being, the impossibility of surpassing itself*.

The opening paragraph introduces the section's central concept — *situation* — by approaching it through a structural analysis of *impossibility*. The impossibility at stake is not privation of a power to do something external; it is the impossibility internal to the essence's self-relation. The essence cannot surpass itself — that is, it cannot get outside itself, cannot take up a distanced perspective on itself, cannot place itself in a position of freedom with regard to itself. This structural impossibility, far from being a defect, is the very signature of immanence. The whole section will develop this impossibility into the positive structural concept of *situation* (the being-situated of the essence in itself).

The connection with Heidegger's vocabulary is carefully managed. In *Sein und Zeit* §§29–31, *Situation* is a central concept for Dasein — Dasein is always in a situation, always found in a thrown condition from which it must project itself. Henry will argue that Heidegger's *Situation* is a derivative-existential concept that presupposes, but does not articulate, the *absolute situation* (*situation absolue*) that is the immanent essence itself. The absolute situation is not one that Dasein finds itself in among other possibilities; it is the structural situatedness of the essence in its own being, from which no exit is possible.

**Paragraph 2\.** The impossibility for being of surpassing itself lets itself be heard in turn in two manners — and first as *impossibility of "going out of oneself."* Such a "going out" however designates habitually nothing other than *transcendence* — and, as the act of going "out of oneself," the arising of alterity precisely, the relation to the other. That the impossibility of surpassing oneself (thus reduced to the simple impossibility of a surpassing in general) be susceptible, as such, of characterizing the relation of being with self — this can only be in a *purely negative manner*, by the simple exclusion (outside the structure of this relation) of alterity. *The relation of being with itself*, considered in itself and not in an exterior manner (from its pure opposition to the relation of alterity), can find the condition necessary to a determination of what properly constitutes its nature only insofar as *being gives itself to itself, as self, as the term of this relation*. It is therefore *with regard to the self of being* that must be heard — not indeed the surpassing, but precisely the impossibility of surpassing, or if one prefers, its essence.

The argument now proceeds precisely. There are two ways to hear "impossibility of surpassing oneself":

* (i) *Negatively*, as the absence of transcendence — the simple exclusion of the going-out-to-alterity. This is the definition of immanence merely by contrast to transcendence. But this negative definition tells us nothing positive about the self-relation.  
* (ii) *Positively*, as the internal structure of the relation of being with itself, in which being *gives itself to itself* as the term of this relation. This is the positive definition: the essence has itself *as self*, and the impossibility of surpassing is the structural-positive feature of this having-of-self.

The positive definition requires that we understand "self" (*soi*) — that is, the structural self-givenness of being in the immanence of its self-relation. This is where the section pivots: from the negative characterization (immanence as not-transcendence) to the positive structural analysis (immanence as the concrete self-having of being).

Thus is discovered the *second manner* of hearing the impossibility for being of surpassing itself — the one in conformity with which being constitutes itself, *as "self,"* the term of a relation which can find itself determined then (in an essential fashion) as "relation of being with self." That in this essential relation with self being cannot surpass itself means: by reason of what it is (and what determines it in its internal structure as being, precisely, what it is), it *cannot separate itself from itself*, *cannot withdraw from itself*, *cannot come back to this side of what it is*, cannot finally open a dimension of retreat by virtue of which it would have the opportunity precisely to escape itself, to detach itself from self, to tear itself from itself and from its essence. Thus finds itself determined (with regard to its relation to self) the impossibility for being of surpassing itself as the impossibility for being of *separating itself from what constitutes its own being* — in such a way that this impossibility does not only take form and sense in its explicit reference to the relation of being to self, but *further constitutes itself the self of being* — the fundamental and ultimate possibility for concretizing in it something like an *ipseity*.

The final clause is critical: the impossibility of self-separation *is* the self of being — the structural positive fact of the essence's attachment to itself is what constitutes the essence as *an ipseity* (a *this-ness*, a "self" in the strong sense). The ipseity of the essence is not the result of some prior self-positing (as in Fichte) or of some reflexive appropriation (as in Hegel); the ipseity is the very structure of immanent self-presence — the fact that the essence cannot get away from itself is what makes it a "self" in the ontologically primary sense.

**Paragraph 3\.** But this last remark is premature. It suffices that be shown here the necessity — for the interpretation of being from the impossibility of surpassing — to maintain itself in the originary direction prescribed by the question of the relation to self, inside which only the phenomenon of this impossibility is susceptible of receiving its positive sense. However (as has been seen), the relation of being to self is *not* such (essentially determined by the impossibility for it of separating itself from self in surpassing) *because* surpassing (that is, the essence of transcendence) is in principle absent from it; it is on the contrary the *internal positivity of this originary relation* that makes the *exclusion* appear in the relation as its *result*. What impossibility signifies appears therefore finally as being able to be understood only from this *positivity of the originary relation of being with self and of what founds this positivity* — from the coherence of the essence in the originary unity that belongs to it and constitutes it. *Impossibility means, consequently: unity, necessity of this unity, link, link that cannot be untied, and in this sense precisely, "impossibility."* Because the impossibility for being of surpassing itself results from the force with which it coheres originarily with itself in the primordial unity, it is this unity — the internal structure of the essence — that is here thought by the problematic. And that it be thought in the light of the concept of impossibility attests precisely the *at once ultimate and originary, insurmountable and unsurpassable character of this unity* — and thereby determines the unity in its specific ontological positivity and in what it is. *It is one and the same understanding that institutes itself through these positive or negative determinations*, and the impossibility for being of surpassing itself (of withdrawing to this side of its being and of escaping it) signifies identically its *irremissible attachment to self*, the irreducible character of the link that enchains it to itself in the originary relation that constitutes it.

The structural-philosophical thesis is now precise: the impossibility of surpassing is the *negative* expression of the *positive* structural fact — unity, coherence, irremissible self-attachment. Immanence is the structural-positive coherence of the essence with itself; the impossibility of self-surpassing is this coherence seen from its negative side. The vocabulary of *irremissibility* (already deployed in §37) is central: the essence cannot be remitted, cannot be let go of, cannot be relinquished. The essence has itself with a structural necessity that admits no exception, no exit, no escape.

**Paragraph 4\.** Where does the determination of being in the light of the concept of impossibility lead, if this determination is not the simple repetition (by eidetic analysis) of the fundamental ontological characters constituting the internal structure of the essence as immanence? In what, more exactly, does such a repetition show itself fecund? How does it manifest its necessity? *What is it then* — to be linked and riveted to itself by the irremissible self-attachment of what constitutes itself (in the originary unity) its own content and identifies itself with this content? *The evidence of the progress realized in the repetition of the structural ontological determinations of the essence (which has been understood as that of immanence) stands then before us: what — in conformity with the originary link that attaches it to itself — can neither cut itself from itself nor survey its being, what is not susceptible of contemplating itself from the exterior nor of taking at any moment (with regard to itself) a free point of view, is what is situated.* The structural ontological determination of immanence furnishes its transcendental foundation to *the concept of situation*, which (as such — as essentially determined by what in being constitutes its internal structure and its foundation) is, in this ultimate and "fundamental" sense, *an ontological concept*.

The structural concept is now articulated: *situation* (*la situation*) is the ontological name for the structural being-itself of the essence in the irremissibility of its immanent self-relation. To be situated is not (primarily) to be in this or that empirical-existential place; to be situated is to be *structurally unable to survey oneself from outside*, to be riveted to oneself in the structural immanence from which no exit is possible. This is the *absolute situation* — not a situation among other possible situations but the structural situation *as such*, the structural being-riveted-to-itself of the essence. Every empirical-existential situation presupposes this structural absolute situation as its ontological foundation.

**Paragraph 5\.** Determinations such as "impossibility of surveying one's own being and of considering it from the exterior," "impossibility of finding oneself placed outside oneself, and consequently of taking on oneself an exterior point of view," "impossibility of cutting oneself from self, of withdrawing to this side of one's being and, somehow, of undoing it" — these belong no doubt to being-in-situation and define it habitually (in the eyes of precritical consciousness as well as of reflection). Reflection has tried to express philosophically these diverse impossibilities in diverse manners, which could not find in the framework of this analysis their exposition nor even a simple recall. Let it suffice to indicate here, by way of examples: (i) the general critique directed more specially against classical philosophy, concerning the pretension of arriving at an absolute truth (that is, at a truth that would be solidary with no particular point of view and would not find in such a point of view the condition of its necessarily progressive development in the obtaining of universality); (ii) the idea that universality can accomplish itself and be understood only as the arising of a new signification from pre-existing significations that determine existence-in-situation; (iii) the affirmation of the insurmountable and insuppressible character of existence-in-situation and the correlative rejection of any "point of view of Sirius" (that is, of the possibility precisely of surmounting this situation and the point of view that belongs to it and constitutes it); (iv) the bringing-into-evidence, finally, of the insubstitutable and "unique" character of each situation and each existence, and of what results each time for this existence — the necessity of reaching others only laterally (from oneself and inside one's own point of view), the impossibility of ever dominating the ensemble of possible situations or of living this ensemble precisely as an ensemble of possibilities among which one could choose (as from above and in the transparency of a kind of total intelligibility) the one one prefers and that suits one.

Henry surveys the diverse philosophical articulations of situation in contemporary philosophy:

* The critique of absolute truth as situation-free (directed against classical rationalism) is associated especially with Nietzsche's perspectivism, Dilthey's historicism, and Merleau-Ponty's phenomenology of perception.  
* The genesis of universality from particular significations is associated with the Husserlian late-*Krisis* analyses, Merleau-Ponty's *Phenomenology of Perception*, and the broader existential-phenomenological tradition.  
* The rejection of the "*point de vue de Sirius*" (a French philosophical idiom for the view from nowhere, the absolute external perspective — the term is associated with Renouvier but is widely used in French existential philosophy) is associated with Sartre and Merleau-Ponty.  
* The uniqueness of each existence in its situation is a central thesis of Sartre's *L'Être et le Néant* and of Kierkegaard's category of the "single individual."

All these are existential-phenomenological articulations of what Henry is identifying as a structural-ontological fact. The task is to show that these articulations have been made without their ontological foundation being explicit.

In all these theses, at their root and as what they formulate, are found the determinations that have been recognized to be those of being-in-situation, and (further on) a same impossibility that confers on them their unity (perceived or hidden). *As long however as the ontological origin of this impossibility has not been itself unveiled*, the determinations that express it and their presumptive unity remain uncertain with regard to themselves and their foundation. In such uncertainty (which signifies the non-apperception of the originary link that unites them to being insofar as they constitute its structure and belong to it) such determinations *float in the air*, give themselves as extrinsic with regard to being. Being-in-situation becomes something contingent with regard to being — and further, this contingency is understood as that of the situation. The determinations that express situation and constitute it come therefore to add themselves, in a synthetic manner, to what originally does not contain them. This synthetic addition of an ensemble of extrinsic determinations was already visible in the classical philosophy of the body. What signifies the intervention of the body in the problematic of truth and of existence, indeed, if not that such an addition gives itself as responsible for the limitation that comes to affect being in a decisive though totally mysterious manner. The very idea of limitation can be understood only from the presupposition (explicit or not) of an *intervention exterior to the originary that constrains it*. This is why the persistence of this idea (and its maintenance inside the philosophies that pretend to determine the concept of situation from the ontological element itself and its essence) *renders suspect their attempt* — and, more, the result of which they believe themselves assured. For, if it accomplishes itself effectively from such an element and in it, *the originary arising of the situation implies no idea of limit or of constraint imposed on being, but signifies on the contrary (concerning being) its own expansion and the liberation of its essence*.

The structural argument is now critical: the existential-philosophical tradition has articulated the features of situation but has not grounded them ontologically. Without ontological grounding, situation appears as *extrinsic* to being — as a contingent condition imposed on an otherwise "free" being by external constraints (classically: the body, the flesh, the historical circumstance). This is the "classical philosophy of the body" that makes the body responsible for a mysterious "limitation" of being. Henry rejects this picture: situation is not an external limitation imposed on being; situation is the *essential* structural feature of the essence in its immanent self-relation. Far from limiting being, situation is the very *expansion* and *liberation* of being in its proper essence — being's achievement of its own ipseity in the immanent self-presence.

**Paragraph 6\.** The determination of the essence of situation from being cannot in any case be simply affirmed; it must recognize itself in this: that *the nature of the determinations that together characterize being-in-situation is identically that of being itself* — in such a way that the bringing-into-evidence of being renders account of the impossibility these determinations all express equally, and which constitutes their essence while at the same time founding their unity. On what condition however does the nature of being render account of the impossibility expressed in the determinations of being-in-situation? On the condition of being itself determined by this impossibility, *by the impossibility for being of surpassing itself*. The pretension of assigning a transcendental origin to the concept of situation (in its determination from the internal structure of the pure ontological element) presupposes the constitution of this structure as immanence and its uncovering by the problematic. The work of the problematic alone permits — in the final analysis — that there be linked in the originary and fundamental unity of the essence (instead of being left to their freedom) the characters under which being-in-situation is habitually thought. And the pursuit of this work in the direction prescribed by such a result gives itself necessarily from then on as determining *conjointly* immanence and situation, and as *the deepening of their correlative concepts*: because immanence encloses in itself (as being precisely its own) the structural ontological determinations that determine the essence of situation, immanence does not only found situation; immanence receives in return from situation (and from the thematic elucidation of situation's concept) an increased light on what constitutes in immanence its most intimate and most essential nature.

The structural-methodological point is precise. Situation and immanence are not two separate topics that happen to illuminate each other; they are two faces of the *same* structural reality. Immanence is the essence's immediate self-presence in the impossibility of surpassing itself; situation is the being-riveted of the essence in the irremissibility of this self-presence. The deepening of one concept is *eo ipso* the deepening of the other. The analysis will therefore proceed by *conjoint* articulation.

**Paragraph 7\.** In the light of what constitutes in immanence its most intimate and most essential nature — that is, finally, *the essence of non-freedom* (where the impossibility for being of surpassing itself finds its ultimate ontological origin, and consequently the concept of situation finds its radical and ultimate foundation) — situation does not only receive the positive determination of being *the insurmountable and irremissible self-attachment of being* (and, as such, of identifying itself with being); situation further manifests in this a *negative determination* — which, to be such, is no less decisive concerning the problem of its elucidation by philosophical thought and the latter's effort to resolve it. Insofar as it finds its foundation in the essence (where resides originarily the impossibility that determines it), *the concept of situation does not only reveal itself foreign to the idea of freedom; it manifests with regard to freedom and to what freedom each time renders possible an incompatibility of eidetic order*. In conformity with this incompatibility, it appears that it is *precisely because freedom is excluded from the structure that determines its reality* that being as such is situated. In freedom, however, resides the origin of the world — and, with the arising of the world, the possibility of *taking attitude* (*prendre attitude*). The diverse modalities according to which such a possibility realizes itself indicate each time (inside the world and in the milieu opened by the world) what is at stake in the act of relating oneself to, and they express themselves in an effective comportment such as "accepting" or "refusing," "choosing," "taking on oneself," "suffering," "assuming," etc. To each of these comportments corresponds a *"view"* (not theoretical but linked in the comportment to what renders it possible), and on this view is founded in turn the possibility of taking a point of view. This possibility does not accomplish itself either, originarily, in a theoretical manner, but precisely under the form of these comportments — where the *affective tonality of existence* determines itself. That such comportments be possible only by freedom and inside the originary sphere of existence where there historicalizes itself and takes form something like the ontological concrete possibility of a situation and a being-in-situation: *situation is precisely what cannot be chosen, what one cannot "accept" or "refuse."*

The structural-critical thesis is now fully drawn. The whole existentialist vocabulary of comportment — "accepting," "refusing," "choosing," "taking on oneself," "assuming," all the terms of Sartrean and Heideggerian existential analytic — belongs to the *transcendent* level, the level of freedom opening up a world within which attitudes can be taken. But the *absolute situation* is precisely that which makes all these comportments possible without being itself one of them. The absolute situation cannot be accepted or refused, cannot be chosen or rejected, cannot be assumed or evaded — because it *is* the structural condition of any act of acceptance, refusal, choice, rejection, assumption, or evasion.

This positions a powerful critique of the whole existentialist-Heideggerian framework. The structural situation — the essence's being-riveted to itself in immanent self-presence — is foreign to the entire vocabulary of existential comportment. To apply existential-comportmental vocabulary to the absolute situation is a category error: the absolute situation is not something Dasein is in; it is the structural condition of Dasein being a Dasein at all.

**Paragraph 8\.** To the interminable and habitually pathetic dissertations which prescribe precisely this necessary "acceptance" by man of a situation which one gives at the same time however as the product of his freedom, the eidetic analysis opposes the evidence of its results. Still, this impossibility of choosing (inscribed in the essence of situation as what determines it) must in no way be understood *as if it were a matter of a limit imposed on freedom and encountered by it in the exercise of its power*. This is why the discussion does not aim at the impossibility (universally admitted and accepted as self-evident) of *refusing* a situation, but rather at the impossibility (no less generally refused) of *accepting* it. *These two impossibilities however make only one*: the originary impossibility in which the essence finds itself of taking attitude with regard to itself — the impossibility of freedom as impossibility *constituted not by freedom itself but by its essence*, as *non-constituted* impossibility. That it not be constituted and cannot be so designates the impossibility that determines the essence of situation as *radically foreign* to what pertains to freedom, to the possibility of some comportment in general. This is why such an impossibility is not itself a comportment and does not take birth in a comportment; it is rather *the non-comportment* and, manifesting in this the insurmountable force of what *originarily situates* (of what situates comportment itself), *the essence of non-freedom*.

The critique is pointed. Existentialist authors (Sartre especially) are fond of insisting that man must "accept" his situation — accept his freedom, his responsibility, his factual being. But this "acceptance" talk is doubly incoherent: (i) it treats situation as if it were something Dasein could either accept or refuse (whereas situation is the structural condition that precedes all acceptance and refusal); (ii) it treats situation as the *product* of Dasein's freedom (whereas situation is precisely what is *not* constituted by freedom). The impossibility of acceptance and the impossibility of refusal are one and the same impossibility — the impossibility of the essence taking up any attitude whatsoever toward itself, because the essence *is* the condition of attitude-taking.

The concept of *non-comportment* (*le non-comportement*) and *non-freedom* (*la non-liberté*) are precise structural concepts. Non-comportment is not a *deficient* comportment; it is what is *prior to* the possibility of comportment. Non-freedom is not a deprived freedom; it is the *structural condition* prior to the possibility of freedom — the condition from which freedom is released into its proper element of transcendence. The vocabulary of negation ("non-") is structurally significant: it marks the *radical difference in kind* between the immanent essence and the transcendent-existential comportments it makes possible.

**Paragraph 9\.** For the originary ontological determination of the concept of situation (in its radical opposition to freedom) concerns precisely and first *freedom itself*. Freedom cannot accomplish its work — be the free surpassing that advances toward a world — except insofar as it *remains in itself* and *maintains itself in itself as what it is*. Remaining in itself and maintaining itself in itself, it is *as such* (as what it is each time and has to be) that it exists and can be the free surpassing that it is. Transcendence has a *self*; transcendence is the transcendence of its self. It is from this self alone and *as* this self that transcendence exists — in such a way that this self is never what transcendence transcends but rather *what transcends*, what it is and has to be in order to be what it is. How does transcendence have, as that very which it never transcends, a "self"? How does transcendence maintain itself inside its own surpassing in order to be this surpassing and have to be it? With the liberation of what (in the essence) constitutes its internal structure, the problematic does not only give an answer to these fundamental questions; it says, further on, what is at stake in this self of transcendence and what it signifies for it "to be as what it is and has to be." Such determinations remain obscure and in fact non-understood as long as thought is tempted to interpret them *from surpassing* (that is, from transcendence itself). What else do they then express, indeed, other than simple tautology — but in a bizarre and uselessly complicated manner? Or else, does transcendence not give itself in these determinations (in the absence of every other foundation) *as the sole origin from which it has, precisely, to be what it is* — and, as such, to assume (in what then constitutes its most insurmountable abandonment) the mode of existence that is each time its own? Or else again — and on the contrary — does the fundamental ontological determination of transcendence from being-self and as *being-left-to-self* come not from transcendence but precisely from *what leaves transcendence invincibly to itself in the impossibility for it of surpassing itself*? From this impossibility alone, and from the essence that contains it, are heard and illuminated (in their radical opposition to those of tautology) the structural ontological determinations that *vow transcendence to the existence that is its own* and make the *being-left-to-self* of surpassing so that it may be the surpassing it is. At the same time is lifted *the equivocation* that concerns (in the philosophy of transcendence) the being of transcendence insofar precisely as transcendence "has to be" — an equivocation that subsists on the contrary as long as the origin of such a determination (and of the prescription addressed by it to freedom) has not been itself drawn into clarity. *That freedom has to be what it is comes not from freedom but from its fundamental anti-essence. In the essence of this anti-essence resides (along with the impossibility for freedom of surpassing itself, an impossibility which delivers freedom to itself) what results — the being-in-situation of transcendence and of what it produces.*

The structural critique of Heidegger's *Sein und Zeit* is now explicit. Heidegger had articulated Dasein as characterized by *Jemeinigkeit* (mineness) and by *Zu-sein* (having-to-be) — Dasein is always *mine*, always *has to be* its being. But, Henry argues, Heidegger could not properly account for these determinations within the philosophy of transcendence alone. If we try to explain "mineness" and "having-to-be" from transcendence itself, we get only tautologies. The proper ground of Dasein's mineness and having-to-be is in what Henry calls the *anti-essence* (*anti-essence*) of freedom — that is, the *non-freedom* which is the structural essence of immanence, the structure that leaves freedom to itself by making it impossible for freedom to surpass itself.

The term *anti-essence* is carefully chosen. Immanence is the "anti-essence" of transcendence not in the sense of being against or contrary to transcendence, but in the sense of being the *other* essential structure — the essence that is *not* the essence of transcendence but is its ontological ground. Just as "non-freedom" is the structural condition of freedom (without which freedom would have no ground), "anti-essence" is the structural condition of the monist essence (transcendence) — the condition on which transcendence is possible as the surpassing that it is.

**Paragraph 10\.** This indeed is what signifies, for transcendence, to have a self, to be the transcendence of its self. *Transcendence is not what it is — left to itself, on the ground of its proper essence, in its abandonment to itself — but as determined independently of itself, on the contrary, and by what constitutes precisely its anti-essence*, that transcendence is such and further takes on (in this determination) the ultimate ontological characters that define it as what it is: the being-self of what cannot separate itself from self, the being-situated of what (in this unity constitutive of the self) cannot surpass itself nor escape its "condition." Not being able to escape its condition, nor to dismiss this condition, surpassing is (for this reason alone) what it is: it is *on the ground in it of its anti-essence* that it realizes its essence. That it realizes its essence does not mean simply: it accomplishes itself according to a certain structure (which is precisely its own, the structure of transcendence); it means: *it accomplishes itself in such a way that at no moment can it retake what it accomplishes* — its surpassing and what this surpassing produces, the distancing and the being-distanced — at no moment can it retake this nor escape its law, this law which is its own, which is its essence, because it situates itself inside this law (inside this surpassing which always distances what it can never rejoin). That it be this surpassing which always distances what it can never rejoin — this can be, in the final analysis, only because *surpassing is always the surpassing and can never escape it*. With the bringing-to-light of what constitutes the ultimate foundation of this "never" and this "always," the problematic gives itself the transcendental elements from which becomes intelligible something like *the unsurpassable character of surpassing*. Such a character — not surpassing — constitutes being-situated in general (the being-situated of surpassing itself, consequently). *It is only because as being-situated it is constituted by such a character that surpassing gives itself precisely and lets itself be heard as what cannot be surpassed*. This is why *"Dasein cannot vanquish its distancing from the Zuhanden,"* not only because (as Heidegger says) *"it is essentially distancing, that is, spatial,"* but for this more ultimate reason (and explicated by the problematic) that *Dasein realizes in itself the essence of its distancing* — because, on the ground in it of its anti-essence, *transcendence cannot be transcended*.

The argument is now structurally decisive. The *unsurpassability* of surpassing is not a feature of surpassing in itself (that would be a tautology); it is a feature imposed on surpassing by the *absolute situation* — by the immanent essence in which surpassing is grounded. Surpassing is always the surpassing; it cannot escape itself — not because it lacks the power to escape (for surpassing is the power of escape par excellence), but because it is situated *in* the immanent essence in which all surpassing is grounded. This unsurpassability of surpassing *is* the being-situated of transcendence; it is the trace of immanence within transcendence.

The Heidegger citation is from *Sein und Zeit* §23 — "Dasein cannot vanquish its distancing from the Zuhanden." Heidegger had explained this by Dasein's essential spatiality. Henry offers the deeper structural explanation: Dasein cannot vanquish its distancing because Dasein *realizes in itself the essence of its distancing* — Dasein *is* the being-situated of the immanent essence in the mode of existential-transcendent distantiation. So Heidegger was right about the phenomenon but wrong about its grounding; he grounded it in spatiality, whereas it is actually grounded in the immanent absolute situation that is the anti-essence of transcendence.

**Paragraph 11\.** That transcendence cannot be transcended — that is, as well, that one can neither escape it nor subtract oneself from its action — determines transcendence as *that whose work always accomplishes itself*, the arising of exteriority as *the irrevocable destiny of being*. In such an arising however *there take form and historicalize themselves the possibility and the effectivity of a view and a point of view*. It is the *irrevocable character* of the view/point-of-view, consequently, that finds itself prescribed by transcendence insofar as it cannot be transcended — insofar as it is situated. Has not however the originary ontological determination of being-in-situation made appear (as constitutive of its essence and its possibility) *not* the arising of a view precisely, nor the development and persistence in the view of a point of view, but on the contrary *the impossibility of a point of view*? The impossibility of taking a point of view, the originary impossibility for being of relating itself to itself (inside a comportment and by a comportment) — do these take place in the essence and can they do so if the essence lets itself be determined on the other hand (and that precisely as situated) as the tireless and insurmountable accomplishment of exteriority? Or does not the tireless and insurmountable character of this accomplishment result from the impossibility for this accomplishment of taking attitude with regard to itself? Further, is it not identical to this impossibility? Here there order and organize themselves among themselves the structural ontological determinations from which the problematic finds itself constrained to think what constitutes the essence of a situation and being-situated in general: *insurmountability of point of view and impossibility of taking one are solidary and determined among themselves as transcendence and immanence*. Or more exactly: if insurmountability is as such the impossibility of taking a point of view, insurmountability comes to the point of view as its most proper character only insofar as the point of view itself shows itself capable of manifesting in itself such an impossibility (that is, its own negation) — *insofar as transcendence lets itself be determined in its essence as immanence*.

The structural synthesis is now complete. There are two structural phenomena of situation:

* (a) *Insurmountability of the point of view* (at the level of transcendence): one cannot escape one's perspective, one's factual condition, one's historical situatedness. This is what existential-phenomenological philosophy has articulated.  
* (b) *Impossibility of taking a point of view* (at the level of immanence): the essence cannot get outside itself to take a distanced view on itself; it is structurally incapable of self-surpassing.

These two are *one and the same* phenomenon, seen from the two sides of the structural articulation transcendence/immanence. The point of view is insurmountable *because* the essence that founds the point of view is incapable of self-surpassing. The immanent impossibility grounds the transcendent unsurpassability. And conversely, the transcendent unsurpassability is the phenomenological manifestation of the immanent impossibility.

**Paragraph 12\.** The ontological determinations that belong to being-in-situation may appear singular or contradictory to naïve consciousness, even philosophical, but they nevertheless *feed the representations* by which naïve consciousness spontaneously tries to render accessible to itself what constitutes its own situation. It is thus that situation often finds itself interpreted and understood from the idea of a *center* — a center which determines a perspective and (preventing this perspective from being confused with all others) makes precisely that the perspective is situated. In this representation of a center — which comes to specify each time perspectives and points of view — there comes to the fore also the idea of *impossibility* as essential precisely to this specification and constituting it. Such an impossibility is that, for the point of view, of *changing*. It is on the ground in it of this impossibility that the point of view (insofar as it designates not a simple way of seeing but existence itself) is not precisely susceptible of being exchanged with others, gives itself as *"unique"* and *"irreducible."* In what however does such an impossibility consist, and how does it come to what we call each time a "perspective," a "point of view," as its most proper character? These are not such (incapable of changing and, consequently, of being exchanged) except insofar as they develop *from a "fixed point"* — from a "center." But how to understand, in turn, the "fixity" of this "point" (from which the perspective develops, a fixity that determines the point precisely as "center")? A point is said to be fixed when it cannot displace itself in space (nor occupy inside space another position than its own), when it *cannot go out of itself*. Although it can only be understood in its essential relation to exteriority, *the idea of center defines itself by the negation of exteriority and of what produces it*. Thus the point that serves, for example, as center to a circle gives itself immediately as implying by necessity around it the existence of a space (essentially oriented with regard to the point), but no less immediately as *what negates this space* — this "around" to which (as center) the point never belongs. The center represents in exteriority *what negates* exteriority. But the exteriority of space presupposes the *pure* exteriority and represents it in turn; the negation of exteriority must be heard, as space's negation, in a *transcendental* sense. The ultimate ontological structures that give its form and its sense to the habitual representation of the characters of being-in-situation are discovered then with evidence to the problematic: *as representation in the exteriority of space of what negates exteriority, the representation of being-in-situation is that, by naïve consciousness, of immanence*.

The geometrical-phenomenological analysis is exquisite. The everyday notion of "center" (a fixed point at the center of a perspective, around which the space of the perspective organizes itself) is, on Henry's reading, naïve consciousness's spatialized-representational rendering of the structural-ontological *immanence*. The center is "fixed" — unable to go out of itself — *within* space, but in such a way that it negates the exteriority that surrounds it: the center is the *negation in space of space itself*, the non-exteriority that marks space. Translated back to the transcendental-ontological level, this is precisely immanence: the non-exteriority that is operative *in* exteriority as exteriority's grounding non-exteriority.

So everyday representation, in its use of the concept of "center," unknowingly articulates the structural-ontological immanence. The philosophical task is not to invent a new structure but to properly thematize the structure already operative in everyday representation.

**Paragraph 13 (closing).** The originary ontological determination of the essence of situation as immanence *inevitably refers* the analysis to a consideration of historical order. It is in contemporary philosophy of existence, indeed, that (for the first time no doubt, and that in relation with the concern of grasping existence in its concrete character) the concept of situation finds itself elucidated for itself and constitutes, in this title, the explicit theme of the problematic. That such a philosophy develops exclusively inside the field opened by the idea of transcendence and remains on the contrary blind to what constitutes the ultimate possibility of this idea (that is, as well, to the essence that determines this idea as originarily situated) — this renders visible already and at the same time inevitable the failure to which this philosophy prepares itself. The bringing-into-evidence of this failure, its understanding from the profound motive that determines it, constitute at the same stroke (with regard to the theses here advanced by the problematic) a *verification* — and, if this verification is truly one, *a repetition of their essential ontological content*.

The closing paragraph announces the program of §§42–44: a structural-historical critique of contemporary philosophy of existence (especially Heidegger and Sartre), which articulated the concept of situation without being able to ground it in the immanent essence, and which consequently failed to resolve the structural problems it raised. The critique will serve as *verification* of Henry's thesis — because a correct structural thesis should explain both the insights and the failures of prior philosophical attempts at the same phenomena.

---

## **§ 42\. The ontological determination of the essence of situation as immanence and the fundamental ambiguity of "Nichtigkeit"**

**Paragraph 1\.** As soon as it makes the explicit theme of a problematic, the concept of situation lets itself be heard in its *pure ontological signification*. The understanding of this signification implies the rejection of the *realism* that confides to the existent, and considers as belonging to the existent, the character in virtue of which the existent shows itself always in a certain situation. It is true that the phenomenology of naïve perception manifests without delay its hesitations in the movement by which it finds itself inevitably referred (as soon as it interrogates itself on what makes the situation of an object) *outside* of the object. Thus one saw already Aristotle renounce grasping the essence of place *inside* the thing in order to think it on the contrary as its *limit*. To be situated implies indeed a relation between what is situated and a milieu inside which it is situated — a milieu generally understood as *space*. To be situated therefore means to find oneself in space, to occupy a certain position inside space. But space is not indifferent; it is not first an objective space. The objective determination of space and of the positions it encloses implies a modification of the ambient preoccupation and the transformation of the view it comports in that of theoretical discovery. *Situation is not primitively that of the given realities but that of tools*; as such, situation refers necessarily to *Care* (*Souci*, *Sorge*). Care, in conformity with what it preoccupies itself with, determines each time a situation; it is Care that "*decides of the proximity… of the tool… in the ambient world.*" Deciding of the proximity of what it preoccupies itself with, it is its own situation that Care decides at the same stroke. *"My body,"* says Merleau-Ponty, *"is where there is something to do."* Thus existence understands itself from what it projects — in such a way that, understanding itself thus, existence also determines in this its situation.

The opening paragraph surveys the existential-philosophical determination of situation, beginning with Aristotle (on place as limit — *Physics* IV, where Aristotle defines *topos* not as the space internal to a thing but as the limiting surface of the surrounding body) and proceeding through Heidegger (Care, the tool, the ambient world, the decision of proximity — *Sein und Zeit* §§15–18, §22, §23) and Merleau-Ponty (the body's spatiality — *Phénoménologie de la perception*, Second Part). The common thesis: situation is not an objective spatial fact but a *pragmatic-existential* determination — I am situated by and through my involvement with tasks, tools, projects. The Merleau-Pontian formula "my body is where there is something to do" crystallizes this: the body's *there* is constituted by the practical orientation of its concerns, not by geometric position.

**Paragraph 2\.** The existential determination of the concept of situation however has nothing originary; precisely it betrays its indigence as soon as one approaches *what makes the origin of every situation*. Such an origin is discovered *in anxiety* (*l'angoisse*). In anxiety what formed each time the object of preoccupation sinks into indifference, while there reveals itself *the nothingness of the world*. *"The world thus opened can no longer liberate the existent except in the character of the non-situation."* No longer preoccupying itself with the existent (which for Care no longer means anything), Care cannot henceforth understand itself from the existent: Care "*finds nothing from which it could understand itself.*"

The Heideggerian-Kierkegaardian doctrine of *anxiety* (*Angst*) — developed in Heidegger's 1929 inaugural lecture *Was ist Metaphysik?* and in *Sein und Zeit* §40 — is here invoked. In anxiety, the preoccupations and projections of everyday care break down: the tools become useless, the projects lose their grip, the world "sinks into indifference." What is revealed is the *nothingness* (*das Nichts*) of the world — the *non-situation* that underlies every situation. The Heideggerian argument: the pragmatic-existential situation is not originary; it breaks down in anxiety, and what anxiety reveals is closer to the originary structure.

Henry's point: this Heideggerian observation, in the moment of breakdown, approaches a deeper structural truth but does not yet articulate it. The "non-situation" revealed in anxiety is not merely the negation of the pragmatic situation; it is the *structural-ontological* ground that is revealed when the existential-pragmatic structures are suspended.
