But Heidegger still interprets this "non-situation" within the framework of transcendence (the world is suspended, but Dasein's being-in-the-world is what is thereby uncovered). Henry will argue that the proper interpretation requires the structural-ontological immanence that Heidegger did not articulate.

**Paragraph 3\.** The collapse of the existential concept of situation puts us however in the presence of its *ontological foundation*. The world that shows itself in anxiety does not only manifest in anxiety the *absurd* character of quotidian preoccupation; *as* world and *as* being-in-the-world, world renders quotidian preoccupation each time *possible*. Far from finding itself resolved by the consideration of what determines a situation from the existential point of view, the problem of situation concentrates itself on the contrary on *the condition of possibility of such a determination* — on world and being-in-the-world as such.

The structural step is precise: when the pragmatic-existential concept of situation breaks down (in anxiety), what is revealed is *being-in-the-world as such* (the structural condition of every pragmatic situation). So the problem of situation, rightly posed, is not "what makes this or that particular situation particular?" but "what makes being-in-the-world itself — the structural condition of every situation — *itself* situated?" The question concerns the *absolute situation* of being-in-the-world.

**Paragraph 4\.** What however means, for the problem of situation, to concentrate itself on the world and on being-in-the-world? Does the taking-into-consideration of these (whose necessity has been established by the problematic) designate these as *the ultimate origin of the concept of situation*, as the very power that originarily situates and from which every situation must understand itself as being possible only by it? Disposing around itself a world, transcendence opens the place and distances the regions inside which it lets each time arrive what it understands itself from and situates itself from. The world from which and in which is susceptible of instituting itself something like a situation does not however float freely in the air in the indeterminacy of what is unattached; nor does the power that founds the world. *It is not freedom that originarily situates; freedom is itself situated.* To concentrate on being-in-the-world does not mean for the problematic of situation: to understand situation from the world and from what founds the world, but rather (more originarily) *to determine the situation of being-in-the-world itself as such*.

The structural pivot is decisive. The task is not to ask "how does being-in-the-world situate other things?" (which would keep us within the transcendent-existential register); the task is to ask "what situates being-in-the-world itself?" That is: what is the structural condition that makes being-in-the-world *itself* a situated structure? This question takes us *beyond* the philosophy of transcendence to the immanent ground that situates transcendence.

**Paragraph 5\.** The task of determining the situation of being-in-the-world is left, in the philosophy of transcendence, to *transcendence itself* (that is, to being-in-the-world itself). How does transcendence found itself its own situation? How does transcendence enter of itself into this determinate situation that is its own? To this question — which is not imposed on the philosophy of transcendence in virtue of an exterior dialectic — the philosophy of transcendence tries to respond. *The task of founding, from transcendence itself, its proper situation* constitutes in fact one of its ultimate aims, even if most often hidden. Such an aim becomes apparent however — and lets itself be recognized — in the attempt made by the philosophy of transcendence to determine what it is *really* about with the being of transcendence insofar as transcendence must be understood as a *foundation*. As such precisely, transcendence appears as *situated*. How does the fact of being a foundation signify identically, for transcendence, being situated — in such a way that transcendence constitutes as such (insofar as it is in general a foundation) the foundation of its own situation?

Henry now enters into an extended structural exegesis of Heidegger's *Vom Wesen des Grundes* (*On the Essence of Ground*, 1929\) — one of Heidegger's most important early essays, which develops the relation between Dasein's transcendence and the phenomenon of ground (*Grund*, foundation). The dense language that follows is a careful reading of that text.

To found, to be a foundation, does not mean simply "*to let a world reign*." The world, precisely, extends its reign over the ensemble of the existent only insofar as the transcendence which projects the world finds itself *in the midst of the world*. Finding itself in the midst of the world (and that insofar as it projects the world — as being-in-the-world consequently), transcendence *feels* itself in the midst of the world and of the existent; it is *invested* by the world and, as Heidegger says again, *"attuned to the tone of this existent which penetrates it."* Insofar as it is invested by the existent, attuned to its tone, transcendence finds in the existent a "foundation": *"it has taken its base in the existent."* To found, to be a foundation, is therefore for transcendence *to found itself*. What means this *new manner* of founding which belongs however to the foundation itself as such (that is, to transcendence)? What comes about for transcendence insofar as — in the project (that is, as well in virtue of its very nature) — it does not "give" only but *"takes itself a foundation"*?

The structural claim from Heidegger: transcendence has two moments — the *projective* moment (giving a world, letting it reign as horizon of meaning) and the *receptive* moment (finding itself *in* the world, invested by it, attuned to its tonality). These two moments together constitute transcendence as *foundation*: it founds by projecting, but it itself is also founded (in another sense) by being invested in the world it projects. This is Heidegger's attempt to give transcendence a *grounding* within itself — to account for how transcendence both founds and is founded.

**Paragraph 6\.** To take a foundation, to take base in the existent, to feel and find itself in the midst of the existent — this is *to be situated*. In the investment of transcendence by the world resides what makes each time its situation. But the investment by the world is identical with the project of the world and results from it. *"The Dasein could not be… penetrated by the tonality of the existent, nor consequently be surrounded by it, taken by it, crossed by its rhythm… if this investment by the existent were not accompanied by the flowering of a world."* And again: *"if the Dasein is invested by the existent, this is no less uniquely as being-in-the-world."* This is why — because the investment by the world reposes on the project of the world — transcendence *"experiences its situation in a project"*; this is why it is said again that *"although feeling itself in the midst of the existent and although penetrated by the existent's tonality, it is as a free power-to-be that the Dasein finds itself thrown among the existent."* Because the investment reposes on the project (or more exactly, is included in the project as what determines it, as what determines the act of founding in its integrity), it is true to say then that *"the Dasein founds, 'institutes' the world uniquely insofar as itself 'founds itself' in the midst of the existent."* Thus the being-in-situation of transcendence does not finally add itself to the reality of its project; being-in-situation belongs on the contrary (in the same title as the project) to *the act of founding considered in the coherence of its ensemble-structure* — that is, to transcendence itself.

The Heideggerian thesis from *Vom Wesen des Grundes* is now exhibited in full. Transcendence's situation is internal to transcendence itself: the investment-by-the-world is a structural moment of transcendence (not something added to it from outside), because the investment reposes on the project that is transcendence's own act. Dasein is situated by being invested in the world it itself projects; the projecting and the being-invested are two aspects of one structural act of transcendence.

**Paragraph 7\.** The belonging to transcendence of what constitutes each time its situation does not only determine transcendence (insofar as it acts as a foundation) as the foundation of its own situation; it says further, more profoundly, *what situation is*. For transcendence does not find itself simply invested by the world and (as thrown into the world) inexorably linked to the existent that it undergoes. It does not undergo the existent, precisely — and does not feel itself veritably in the midst of the existent; its investment is not effective — except insofar as the investment accomplishes itself *as a privation* (*comme une privation*). By reason of privation — and because what gives itself to be felt in the project implies *the withdrawal of certain possibilities* — transcendence is not only (in its impotence) thrown into the world; it further comprehends in the world *the finitude of its destiny*. Because the effective investment by the existent finds in this finitude the origin of its proper finitude, the being-in-situation of transcendence also finds itself determined by this finitude. But the transcendental finitude of the horizon signifies identically *death*. That its project render death visible to it determines the transcendence of Dasein as what situates it not in a general and still indeterminate manner but *in and by the relation to what signifies each time its proper death*. It is therefore as *being-toward-death* (*être-pour-la-mort*) — toward *its* death — that finds itself determined the *In-der-Welt-Sein* as such (that is, as well, transcendence itself). Such a determination (which belongs to transcendence in virtue of what it is) brings transcendence into its situation and renders visible to it *the particular and concrete truth* of this situation. Because this truth is not occasional and does not concern only a moment (for example the last) of Dasein's history but its structure — because transcendence carries it in itself as its proper law and as what it produces — does not what makes not only its situation but (each time) the concrete and particular character of its situation, belong to it in virtue of what it is?

The Heideggerian doctrine of being-toward-death (*Sein-zum-Tode*, *Sein und Zeit* §§46–53) is here integrated into the structural-schematic exposition. Death, in Heidegger, is the horizon that makes Dasein's finitude concrete: every existential possibility is a possibility-toward-death, a possibility that takes its determinacy from the ultimate finitude of the one projecting it. So not only is transcendence thrown into a world, it is thrown into a *particular* world that is particularized by the horizon of Dasein's proper death. Being-toward-death specifies Dasein's situation and gives this situation its concrete character.

This is the high point of Heidegger's attempt to found Dasein's situation from Dasein's transcendence itself. Henry will now show that this attempt fails — that Dasein cannot, in fact, found its own situation from transcendence, but presupposes a structural-immanent ground that transcendence does not articulate.

**Paragraph 8\.** The pretension of transcendence to constitute itself the internal possibility and the foundation of its situation (and at the same time the specificity of this situation) appears *illusory* as soon as — interrogating itself in a more radical manner on what makes veritably the essence and the foundation of a situation (the essence and the situation of the foundation itself) — the philosophy of transcendence sees erect before it the structural ontological determinations that are *foreign to its presuppositions*. Insofar as it projects the world that invests it and thus finds itself in the midst of the world (in the world), transcendence gives itself each time a situation. This situation is nothing other, finally, than *being-in-the-world itself* as such; it is the Dasein insofar as the being of Dasein finds itself understood ontologically as transcendence. To be situated, however, does not mean simply to find oneself in a certain situation. Or rather: it is *the foundation of this "finding oneself"* that must be exhibited and grasped. *Why does transcendence find itself in the situation that is its own* — that is, in the Dasein — since the Dasein constitutes, as such, the possibility and the essence of a situation and being-situated in general? Does the foundation of this "finding oneself" (which brings transcendence into the Dasein) reside in transcendence itself — that is, in freedom? *"Has Dasein… freely decided, and will it be able to decide on this — namely, whether it wishes or does not wish to come into Dasein?"*

The critical question is posed with precision. Dasein (as being-in-the-world, as transcendence) is the structure of being-situated. But why does *Dasein itself come to be Dasein*? Why does transcendence find itself in the structural condition of being-in-the-world? Is this something Dasein chooses, or is it imposed on Dasein from outside its own freedom? The Heideggerian answer, Henry will show, is that Dasein does *not* choose its coming-into-Dasein; it is thrown into Dasein. But this means that the *ground* of Dasein's being-situated is *not* in Dasein's freedom/transcendence; the ground lies elsewhere — in something that is foreign to transcendence. This is the critical breakthrough.

**Paragraph 9\.** To this fundamental question — where is explicitly posed the problem of whether transcendence constitutes veritably itself the foundation of its proper situation, whether it brings itself into this situation — the philosophy of transcendence has responded. Thrown into the world in view of which it exists and which belongs to it, transcendence does not only undergo the world but (more fundamentally) *the originary act by which it temporalizes itself in the world*. *"It is as a free power-to-be,"* said Heidegger, *"that the Dasein finds itself thrown among the existent. That it be in potency a 'self' and that it be so in fact proportionately each time to its freedom, that transcendence temporalizes itself as proto-historical act — all this is not in the power of this freedom itself."* That the act by which transcendence temporalizes itself in a world *not be in the power of freedom* (that is, of transcendence itself) — this is however what *originarily situates* transcendence. *"But,"* continues the text we are commenting on, *"such an impotence — the fact that Dasein finds itself thrown, abandoned — is not simply the result of the encroachment of the existent on the Dasein; this impotence determines the being of man as such."* Thus one sees the being-in-situation of transcendence — its abandonment in the *Geworfenheit* (thrownness) — explicitly referred to *the impotence which characterizes originarily transcendence insofar as transcendence does not have the power to bring itself into its situation*. Because this impotence of transcendence must be heard in this way (with this originary signification) — because the impotence "is not simply the result of the encroachment of the existent" (that is, of the investment by the world identical with its project) — the situation it determines, and which finds itself constituted by it, does *not* reside either in such an investment (that is, in Dasein as such — in being-in-the-world itself as such). Thus finds itself completely modified (inside the philosophy of transcendence and by the philosophy of transcendence) the concept of situation — which Dasein (that is, as well, transcendence) shows itself now incapable of founding. Such a modification of the concept of situation signifies, in a more precise manner, *its dédoublement* (*doubling*, *splitting*): in investment, transcendence founds each time *a situation*, not *the fact for it of finding itself in this situation*. In this fact, however, resides the essence of situation — *not in the situation itself, but in the fact of finding oneself thus in the situation, in the fact for transcendence of coming into the Dasein*, in such a way however that this coming does not depend on transcendence but is on the contrary imposed on it as what finds not in it its foundation. Thus arises before the problematic of transcendence (in the light of what constitutes veritably, in the *dédoublement* of its concept, the essence of situation) *the evidence that condemns this problematic*: *to be situated means, for transcendence, not to be the foundation of its situation*.

The structural argument now reaches its critical result. The Heideggerian philosophy of transcendence cannot, on its own, account for the being-situated of transcendence. The question "why does transcendence find itself in a situation?" cannot be answered from transcendence itself — and Heidegger himself, despite his project of grounding situation in transcendence, recognizes this when he says (in *Vom Wesen des Grundes*) that the temporalization of transcendence "is not in the power of freedom itself," that "impotence determines the being of man as such." This acknowledgement is an implicit recognition that the ground of transcendence's situatedness is *beyond* transcendence.

The concept of situation therefore splits (*se dédouble*) into two:

* (i) *A situation* — the particular pragmatic-worldly condition transcendence projects (which transcendence can indeed be said to found);  
* (ii) *The fact of finding oneself in a situation* — the structural being-situated of transcendence *as such*, which transcendence does *not* found but is on the contrary imposed on transcendence from its own anti-essence.

The "essence of situation" lies in (ii), not in (i). Heidegger tried to ground situation in transcendence but succeeded only at the level of (i); the essential ground (at the level of (ii)) remains unthematized in Heidegger's philosophy of transcendence.

**Paragraph 10\.** That transcendence never is itself the foundation of its situation — and that first (and in a general manner) the problem of this situation and of what founds it refers (in virtue of its essential character) to that of the foundation — all this is contained also in *Sein und Zeit*, and in a way all the more manifest in that the pretension of resorbing *Befindlichkeit* (the fact of finding oneself, feeling-oneself-situated) into the founding activity of transcendence constitutes there *neither* the unique theme *nor* the explicit preoccupation of the problematic. As soon as it is a question of determining the being-in-situation of Dasein, it is to transcendence no doubt (that is, to Dasein itself) that appeal is made. Dasein appears, on the ground in it of transcendence, as a power-to-be that (because it projects and chooses its own possibilities) finds itself as such *delivered to itself* — insofar as it belongs to Dasein alone to decide each time of its being. Having neither anything nor anyone to turn to, but deciding each time itself of what it is and can be, *Dasein is, in its existence, the foundation of its power-to-be*. Because it is this foundation — and because to be this foundation means to be delivered to oneself in order to decide each time (without recourse but only from oneself) what one is and has to be — because, in its abandonment to itself, Dasein exists and can exist only as this foundation (near which it is dismissed, in order to be as self the being of the foundation), *Dasein is situated*. The being-in-situation of Dasein (its abandonment in the *Geworfenheit*) is therefore what belongs to Dasein insofar as it is (in the project, as power-to-be consequently, and as transcendence) *the foundation of what it is each time*. Because being-in-situation belongs to Dasein insofar as it is itself the foundation of its power-to-be, is Dasein not also itself (as such, as transcendence) the foundation of its situation?

The question is set up to be negated. The Heideggerian text of *Sein und Zeit* does indeed seem at times to suggest that Dasein founds its own situation (because Dasein is the foundation of its own power-to-be, and situation-belongs-to-Dasein in this founding). But, as Henry will now show, the deeper Heideggerian analysis (through the concept of *Nichtigkeit*, nullity) undermines this apparent conclusion and reveals that Dasein is *not* the foundation of its own being (though it is the foundation of its power-to-be).

**Paragraph 11\.** What however means, for Dasein, to be the foundation of its power-to-be — to be a foundation? Let us give the word here to Heidegger himself: *"To be a foundation means never… to be master of one's most proper being."* Thus Dasein is the foundation of its power-to-be (and consequently of what it is each time) *only insofar as it can never render itself master of what ultimately constitutes it itself*. *"The Self,"* says Heidegger, *"which has as such to posit the foundation of itself can never render itself master of this foundation."* Never to render oneself master of one's most proper being — does this not signify, indeed, *not to be its foundation, never to be its foundation*? *"Dasein,"* says Heidegger, *"is not as self the foundation of its being."* But how can Dasein be the foundation of what it is each time and at the same time not be as self the foundation of its being — be *and* not be the foundation of its being? How are such contradictory determinations susceptible nonetheless of uniting in Dasein — and, further, of composing together what constitutes each time its situation? Can the concept of situation maintain itself — and for this preserve its unity — if it refers so manifestly to opposed ontological determinations? Unless, in conformity with the essential results of the problematic, *it splits itself* (*se dédouble*) *and lets appear (in this splitting and by it) the elementary ontological structures that truly found it*. But if the being-delivered-to-itself of Dasein (which determines Dasein as the foundation of its power-to-be — or again, as *"an existent whose being has to assume the being-foundation"*) constitutes as such (in the abandonment this being-delivered signifies each time) Dasein's being-situated, how does the *inverse determination* — the fact for Dasein of never being the foundation of its being — refer itself, in turn, to the concept of situation? And that *as what founds this concept originarily*?

Let us give the word again here to Heidegger: *"In existing Dasein is dé-jeté (thrown-out), not brought from itself into its Da."* The essence of situation — ontologically grasped and interpreted by Heidegger as *"Geworfenheit"* — resides in the fact for Dasein *not to bring itself into its Da* (that is, never to be the foundation of what it is). Such a determination alone confers on Dasein (along with its originary situation) the characters that existentially determine this situation and make it appear precisely as what it is. That Dasein (which *"is in existing the foundation of its power-to-be"*) *"has not itself posited the foundation — this reposes in its heaviness, which makes Stimmung (mood, affective tonality) appear to Dasein as a burden."*

The structural argument is now precise. Heidegger's own vocabulary has two registers:

* (i) Dasein is the *foundation of its power-to-be* — it is delivered to itself, chooses its possibilities, decides what it is and has to be. This is the *existential* register: Dasein as free projection.  
* (ii) Dasein is *not the foundation of its being* — it is thrown into Dasein, did not bring itself to its own Da, cannot master its originary being. This is the *ontological* register: Dasein's structural thrownness.

Heidegger's own texts go back and forth between these two registers. What Henry now articulates is the structural-ontological primacy of (ii) over (i): the thrownness is the deeper structural fact, which grounds the existential freedom. Dasein can be the foundation of its *power-to-be* only because it is *not* the foundation of its *being* — that is, because it is thrown into the condition of being-Dasein from a source foreign to Dasein's freedom. This thrownness *is* the being-situated of Dasein; it is the immanent ground that situates Dasein's transcendence.

**Paragraph 12\.** Thus ontologically grasped and interpreted (in the light of the originary phenomenon that determines it as what it is), does the *Geworfenheit* not differ — and that in virtue of a radical structural opposition — from the simple abandonment-to-oneself that affects Dasein insofar precisely as Dasein *"is in existing the foundation of its power-to-be"* — abandonment primitively understood as the *Geworfenheit* itself? That such an understanding not be totally improper — and must be set aside only in its pretension to originariness; further, that such an understanding be possible at all — results from this: that the *being-foundation* does not simply oppose itself (in Dasein) to what determines Dasein on the contrary (in authentic *Geworfenheit*) as originarily situated; rather, the being-foundation finds in this originary determination of its authentic situation (in the *not-being-foundation-of-self* of its being) its own foundation. Thus is discovered (among the essential ontological structures where the concept of situation draws its concrete effectivity) their true relation as a relation of *not only opposition but of foundation*: it is *because Dasein is not the foundation of its being* that it is delivered to itself in order to be (as this being of which it is not the foundation) *the foundation of its power-to-be*. It is in the light of this "*because*" that must be heard (as what renders possible, in the preservation of unity, the concept of situation) the relation in Dasein between the being-foundation and the not-being-foundation of its being — the "*however*" of their opposition. *"The Self,"* says Heidegger (in a proposition already cited but here restored in its integrity), *"which has as such to posit the foundation of itself can never render itself master of this foundation, and however has in existing to assume the being-foundation."* That the abandonment-to-itself of Dasein (which determines Dasein to assume the being-foundation in existing) *reposes on the not-being-foundation-of-self of its being* designates the structure of this determination as *the originary essence of the Geworfenheit*.

The critical structural relation is now articulated. Dasein's being-abandoned-to-its-freedom (its capacity to be the foundation of its power-to-be) *is grounded in* Dasein's not-being-foundation-of-its-being (its thrownness, its absolute situation). The "however" (*jedoch*) in Heidegger's text — "the self… can never render itself master… *and however* has in existing to assume the being-foundation" — marks a structural *foundation-relation*, not a mere opposition. The existential freedom (foundation of power-to-be) *rests on* the ontological thrownness (not-foundation of being). Transcendence's own foundation is in the immanent absolute situation.

**Paragraph 13\.** Thus understands it Heidegger. To the *not-being-foundation-of-self* which determines the being of Dasein belongs essentially a *"nicht"* ("not"), which constitutes the *Geworfenheit* as such. *"This 'not…,'"* says Heidegger, *"belongs to the existential sense of the Geworfenheit."* Insofar as (as foundation of its power-to-be) Dasein is not the foundation of its being, it appears thus *essentially affected* by this "not…" or (as Heidegger says again) by a *Nichtigkeit* (nullity, not-ness). *"Being foundation,"* declares the author of *Sein und Zeit*, *"Dasein is itself a Nichtigkeit of itself."* The effective ontological determination of the *Geworfenheit* demands however that there be drawn into clarity the essence of this *Nichtigkeit* which constitutes the *Geworfenheit*. The question concerning the essence of *Nichtigkeit* lets itself be formulated — in conformity with what has just been said — in the following manner: what does it mean for Dasein *not to be the foundation of its being* and, first, in a general manner, *not to be a foundation*? Such an apparently negative determination must be understood, manifestly, in its opposition to the corresponding positive determination. How therefore, in what, is Dasein — and can Dasein be — a foundation? *As transcendence* — and that all the more clearly since transcendence constitutes its being and at the same time the essence of foundation. Thus arises in eidetic evidence the possibility here sought as the essence of *Nichtigkeit* and (identically) of the *Geworfenheit* — the possibility for Dasein of not being the foundation of itself: *not to be this foundation means not to find oneself determined in one's being as transcendence*.

The structural specification is critical. The *Nichtigkeit* that affects Dasein (according to Heidegger) is the "not…" that belongs to Dasein's not-being-foundation-of-its-being. To be a foundation, for Dasein, is to be transcendence (which is the active power of projective founding). So *not* to be a foundation means: *not to find oneself determined in one's being as transcendence*. The *Nichtigkeit* of *Geworfenheit* is therefore: *the not-being-transcendence of Dasein*. This is the structural-ontological meaning of Heidegger's *Nichtigkeit*.

But this "not-being-transcendence" is precisely what Henry calls *immanence* — not as a sheer absence of transcendence, but as the *positive* structural condition that is other than transcendence. The *Nichtigkeit* — which Heidegger introduces as a negative "not" — is in fact the *immanent absolute situation*, which is a positive structural reality, not a mere absence.

**Paragraph 14\.** Such a determination — the non-determination of the being of Dasein by transcendence — cannot however remain simply negative if it contains the concrete ontological positivity of being-in-situation (and, more precisely, the being-in-situation of Dasein itself). Of Dasein, however, it constitutes not only the situation but identically Dasein's very being — if Dasein reveals itself situated as such and if moreover Dasein is something other than nothing. Thus Heidegger hears it: *"Nichtigkeit in no way means not to be given, not to exist (nicht bestehen) but signifies a 'not…' which constitutes this being of Dasein, its Geworfenheit."* And again: *"existential Nichtigkeit has in no way the character of a privation, of a lack…"* *In what however consists the ontological positivity of the Nichtigkeit?* To what does the determination that constitutes it (in the same title as the *Geworfenheit*) refer — the *not-being-foundation* which means *"not to find oneself determined in one's being as transcendence"*? To what does *Nichtigkeit* refer, to what effective structure, in such a way that *Nichtigkeit* does not signify a simple privation, a lack, but on the contrary lets appear in itself an essence? Where does this essence reside? These fundamental questions find their answer in the eidetic work of elucidation where the sense of being is elaborated: *the concrete ontological positivity of the essential structural determination that Nichtigkeit lets appear in itself resides in immanence*. For this reason *Nichtigkeit* reveals itself identical with the *Geworfenheit* and founds the *Geworfenheit* — because immanence carries in itself as its very structure *the essence of situation*.

The structural conclusion is fully articulated. The Heideggerian *Nichtigkeit* (which Heidegger himself insists is *not* a mere privation but has *positive* structural content) finds its positive content in what Henry has articulated as *immanence*. The "not-being-transcendence" is not a mere absence of transcendence; it is the positive structural reality of the immanent essence in its absolute situation. Heidegger's *Nichtigkeit* converges with Henry's immanence — they are two vocabularies for the same structural reality.

This is the positive result of the §. The critique of the philosophy of transcendence — the demonstration that transcendence cannot ground its own being-situated — opens onto the recognition that *immanence is the essence of situation*. The absolute situation that grounds every situation is the immanent self-presence of the essence in the irremissibility of its self-relation.

**Paragraph 15\.** Because the ontological positivity of the *Nichtigkeit* resides in immanence, what makes this positivity (and identically the essence of situation) does *not* let itself be recognized with the help of the presuppositions which are those of Heidegger's philosophy. This is why, inside Heidegger's philosophy, *the signification of Nichtigkeit finds itself necessarily travestied*. This travesty accomplishes itself in *two fashions*. Insofar as Dasein is in its existence the foundation of its power-to-be, it understands itself from the possibilities that it projects — in such a way that this project accomplishes itself also (as one has seen) as *a withdrawal*. *"Being able to be,"* says Heidegger, *"the Dasein holds itself in one or the other possibility; it is constantly not the other and has been deprived of the other in its existential project."* That Dasein *not be* in the possibility of which it finds itself thus deprived (insofar as it holds itself in its project inside an effective possibility) — this determines Dasein as *essentially* nichtig. The *Nichtigkeit* so understood refers to *the finitude that affects the project of possibilities in its effective accomplishment* — that is, to *freedom itself*. *"Freedom,"* Heidegger says, *"is only in the choice of a possibility — that is, in the fact of assuming the non-choice… of the other."* The *Nichtigkeit* that refers to the finitude of freedom (that is, to transcendence itself considered in its founding activity) has however *nothing to do* with the *Nichtigkeit* that designates the simple suppression of this activity — the *impotence of transcendence to found itself*. Thus reveals itself the *fundamental ambiguity* of the Heideggerian *Nichtigkeit* — according to whether it translates the finite mode in conformity with which (projecting itself from itself toward its possibilities) Dasein finds itself determined as the *being-foundation*, or, on the contrary, the "not…" that affects this being-foundation essentially insofar as the being-foundation is *never itself the foundation of its being*.

The first Heideggerian confusion is now diagnosed. Heidegger uses "Nichtigkeit" in *two* different senses:

* (i) *Nichtigkeit of projection*: the projective finitude of freedom — Dasein, in choosing one possibility, does not choose the others, and is "null" with regard to the un-chosen possibilities. This is a *Nichtigkeit internal to transcendence*.  
* (ii) *Nichtigkeit of Geworfenheit*: the structural not-being-foundation of Dasein's being — Dasein is thrown, cannot master its own origin, is not in its being the ground of its being. This is a *Nichtigkeit of what is other than transcendence*.

These two are fundamentally different structural phenomena, and Heidegger confuses them by using the same term. The confusion masks the structural difference between transcendent-projective finitude and immanent-structural being-situated.

**Paragraph 16\.** It is in the light of these two fundamentally different significations (finally confused by Heidegger — and as the very expression of this confusion) that it is fitting to read the following text: *"the project is not only (as thrown) determined by the Nichtigkeit of the being-foundation, but as project itself it is essentially nichtig."* *On the Nichtigkeit that determines originarily the being-foundation insofar as it is never itself the foundation of its being — not on the simple nichtig character of the project — reposes however what makes each time the possibility and the essence of a situation, the essence of the Geworfenheit itself.* This is why the *Nichtigkeit* of the *Geworfenheit* differs totally from that which belongs to the project as such (that is, to the founding act of transcendence). Thus appears in turn the equivocation contained in this other proposition: *"in the structure of the Geworfenheit as well as in that of the project is essentially a Nichtigkeit."* Because the *Nichtigkeit* — understood as constituting at once the structure of the *Geworfenheit* and that of the project — remains as such in total ontological indeterminacy and further is fundamentally ambiguous, *indeterminate as well and totally ambiguous are the existential themes that pretend to found themselves on Nichtigkeit* — and, more specially, the *formal existential determination of guilt as being-foundation of a Nichtigkeit*. The affirmation of the guilt of Dasein refers ultimately however to the ontological structure of Dasein, and it is *the ambiguity of this structure* (that is, of the *Nichtigkeit* itself) that renders finally unusable on the philosophical plane the affirmation given as essential according to which *"Care itself is in its essence crossed through and through by Nichtigkeit."*

The diagnostic is now sharp. Because Heidegger's *Nichtigkeit* is ambiguous (conflating the projective finitude of transcendence with the structural ground that is other than transcendence), the existential-existenziell analyses built on it (guilt, conscience, care) suffer from the same ambiguity and are philosophically unusable as they stand. The Heideggerian existential analysis of Dasein in *Sein und Zeit* §§54–60 (conscience, call, debt/guilt) rests on an unclarified concept of *Nichtigkeit*, and this unclarification vitiates the analysis. Only by drawing out the structural distinction between projective-finitude and structural-immanent-ground can one make these existential themes philosophically usable — but doing so requires displacing them from the framework of transcendence to the framework of immanence.

**Paragraph 17 (closing).** Of the *Nichtigkeit* considered in general — whose concept includes also in itself (in its fundamental ontological indeterminacy) the *not-being-foundation-of-self* where the being of Dasein draws the effective possibility of its situation — Heidegger has attempted a *general interpretation*, not referred to the finitude of the project. Such an interpretation however constitutes nothing other than *a second manner of travestying the originary ontological signification of the Nichtigkeit*. Of *Nichtigkeit* understood as determining in general the being of Dasein (and, consequently, as the foundation of its guilt), Heidegger himself ascertains the *uncertain* character: *"the ontological sense of the Nichtheit (nothingness) of this existential Nichtigkeit remains obscure."* To what does this obscurity hold? *"This holds,"* he says, *"of the ontological essence of the 'not…' in general."* It is because such an essence remains uncleared-up that the ontology and the dialectic which make constant use of negation without founding it (and without even making of it a problem) remain in fact *blind to their fundamental presupposition* — to what makes the origin of the *nicht* and of *Nichtigkeit*. How to lift this obscurity — the obscurity of *Nichtigkeit* itself? *By "a thematic clarification of the sense of being in general."* The thematic clarification of the sense of being (identical precisely to that of nothingness) is accomplished however in Heideggerianism *by the discovery of transcendence and its essence*. Thus the *Nichtigkeit* — whose ultimate philosophical signification consists in *putting into question the ontological power of transcendence with regard to its proper being* (that is, the possibility for transcendence to constitute a veritable foundation) — finds itself finally *referring back to transcendence itself, as to this foundation*. In such a referring-back and by it, *the philosophy of transcendence returns to the presuppositions which are its own and holds itself there* — in such a way however that *the essential phenomenon near which the philosophy of transcendence finds itself brought by its progress finds itself from then on lost*.

The critical-diagnostic result is devastating. Heidegger himself recognizes the obscurity of *Nichtigkeit* and proposes to resolve it by "thematic clarification of the sense of being in general" (the program of fundamental ontology). But this clarification, as Heidegger carries it out, is done *by the discovery of transcendence* — that is, by developing further the philosophy of transcendence. But this is structurally to *repeat* the error that generated the obscurity in the first place: the *Nichtigkeit* can only be clarified by recognizing its ground in *immanence* (which is non-transcendent), not by further articulating transcendence. Heidegger's attempt to clarify *Nichtigkeit* by developing transcendence is therefore self-defeating: it returns to the presuppositions that generated the obscurity, and the essential phenomenon (the immanent ground of situation) is lost.

This is one of the most pointed critiques of Heidegger in the whole book. Heidegger's fundamental ontology, in its own terms, is structurally incapable of grounding the phenomenon of *Nichtigkeit* that Heidegger himself identified as central. The grounding requires precisely what Heidegger's framework excludes — the articulation of an *immanent* ontology other than the ontology of transcendence. This is what Henry's work undertakes to do, on Heidegger's behalf (one might say), articulating what Heidegger could not articulate within his own framework.

---

## **§ 43\. Situation and temporality. The ontological heterogeneity of their originary structures and its interpretation in the philosophy of transcendence: the idea of contingency and the fall of Dasein**

**Paragraph 1\.** Heidegger has tried to determine further — inside the presuppositions that are his own — the essence of situation. The effective and concrete accomplishment of transcendence in Dasein does not only imply the project of possibilities. Of these possibilities it has been said that it is from them that Dasein *understands itself*. What signifies, for Dasein, to understand itself from the possibilities toward which it projects itself? Not simply to project itself (precisely) toward such possibilities, but *to return on itself from them* — in such a way that it is only in this returning and by this returning that Dasein discovers itself to itself and understands itself such as it is. Such a discovery by Dasein (returning on itself from the possibilities it projects) of what it is in this project is the discovery of *its situation*. The spatial situation of Dasein, for example, has nothing to do with the simple fact for a given reality of finding itself there where it is in space; nothing to do either with the being-in-situation of a tool as the latter is determined from a region. Dasein's spatial situation presupposes on the contrary *the discovery* of the region — that of a space that Dasein disposes and puts in place, from which *"it determines each time its own place, in such a way that it returns from the space put in place onto the place it has occupied."* Because it is only from the space put in place in the transcendence of the opened horizon that Dasein returns to its place in order to determine it and understand it, *"Dasein in conformity with its spatiality is never first here but there; it is from this there that it returns on its here, and that only in such a way again that it explains its being concerning itself for… from the Zuhanden which is there."* Such a *return on self* (from the object of its concern) by Dasein concerning itself determines in general Dasein's situation and constitutes the structure of this situation.

The opening paragraph articulates the Heideggerian doctrine of situation with precision. Situation is not objective-spatial placement; situation is the structural *return on oneself from one's projected possibilities*. Dasein discovers its situation not by looking at itself where it is (as an object would be looked at) but by projecting forward and then returning from the projection to itself. This is the basic structure of existential self-understanding: Dasein understands itself from what it is not yet (its projected possibilities) and thereby discovers what it is (its situation). The reference is to *Sein und Zeit* §22 (on Dasein's spatiality) and §65 (on care and temporality).

**Paragraph 2\.** Such a structure becomes visible notably in the case of the existential determinations that concentrate Dasein on its proper situation. Thus is it in *fear* — which does not reduce itself to the intuition of a threatening object nor to the simple expectation of the object as a future evil. The apprehension experienced before this future evil is such and can consequently be felt as *fear* only insofar as Dasein does not only project itself in expectation toward the threatening term that approaches, but *returns further on itself from this term* — to understand itself (from then on, in its submission with regard to the term) in the light of the danger it itself incurs in its proper existence. It is because *"the expecting of fear lets the redoubtable term return backwards on the factical power-to-be concerning itself"* that the fear experienced by Dasein concerns Dasein — is not only a "fear-before" but a "fear-for" — and, as fear-for-self of Dasein thus threatened, discovers Dasein to itself in the effectivity of a concrete situation. That this situation always results from the movement by which Dasein returns backwards on itself from what it projects before itself (and discovers itself in favor of this returning) is seen also in *anxiety*. It is because (holding itself face-to-face with death and coming to be broken on death) Dasein finds itself rejected in anxiety onto its factical existence, that Dasein perceives in anxiety (in favor of the affective tonality anxiety realizes) the *ineluctable character of its condition* and lets itself be grasped (in the light of this ineluctability) in its truth *as being-toward-death*.

The Heideggerian analyses of fear (*Furcht*, *Sein und Zeit* §30) and anxiety (*Angst*, §40) are presented as exemplifying the structural return-on-self. Fear is not a mere registering of a threatening object; fear is *fear-for* (the self) that returns from the anticipated threat onto one's own endangered being. Anxiety is not registration of a future event; anxiety is the structural return onto one's own factical existence from the horizon of death. In both cases, the situation is grasped through a *return* — the existential self-understanding via the affective tonality (*Stimmung*) that breaks through the everyday preoccupations.

**Paragraph 3\.** That a situation (that of Dasein itself, not of some object) find the structure that constitutes it, and take form in the act by which Dasein returns on itself from what it projects, poses the question of what is at stake — more precisely — in this act, and implies that there be elucidated the nature of *that from which* this act accomplishes itself, as well as *that onto which* it "returns." That from which the act of Dasein returning on itself accomplishes itself is never *an existent*, even if (in fear, for example) it seems to be so: the threatening term that approaches, before which Dasein experiences fear, is such and can approach only insofar as there has been opened for Dasein the horizon in which this term manifests itself as what arrives — *the horizon of the future*. It is from this horizon (in reality) that Dasein returns on itself — in such a way that, in this return backwards (as it accomplishes itself from the future), Dasein discovers itself as already being, as the existent that (insofar as it is) is *already been*. That onto which Dasein returns (from the horizon it projects of the future) is Dasein itself as *past* — not in the sense of what *is no longer* (a reality which is no longer given), but in the sense of *what, being still, was already*. The act of returning (from the future Dasein projects) onto the being-been of this act (that is, of Dasein itself) is *temporality*. It is as temporality — as modes of temporality and of its temporalization — that fear and anxiety find themselves grasped by Heidegger and described by him, insofar as they let appear in themselves (as what they themselves discover) *the abandonment of Dasein in the Geworfenheit, Dasein's situation*. The concrete character of this situation (the fact that it signifies precisely the abandonment of Dasein, its dereliction) does not result simply, however, from the accomplishment of temporality. The accomplishment of temporality rather must be understood not as the simple return of the future onto the past, but from *the most originary determination* of these ekstases — from the finite horizon of death and from what (relating itself to death) is already (from its birth consequently) delivered to it. The being-having-been as *delivered to death from its birth*, the being that carries in itself co-originarily birth and death (not as what is no longer or what is not yet "real" but as what arises tirelessly from the accomplishment of temporality and as this accomplishment itself) is as such (as essentially determined in itself by temporality — as transcendence and as Dasein) *situated*.

The structural argument mobilizes the Heideggerian doctrine of ecstatic temporality (*Sein und Zeit* §§65–69). Temporality, for Heidegger, is the structural unity of three ecstases (future, having-been, present) — and Dasein's being is constituted by this temporality. The future is primary (Dasein projects itself toward its possibilities); the having-been is revealed by returning from the future projections to the present state; the present is the situated moment of decision. Dasein's situation is revealed in the return from future-projections to having-been; and the whole is grounded in being-toward-death, which gives the temporality its finite and concrete character.

**Paragraph 4\.** The situation of Dasein, however, does not confuse itself with temporality; *it takes birth in temporality*. In the project of the future there is nothing other than death. It is only in the act of returning on itself from death that Dasein understands itself in its abandonment (as being delivered to death). Because this self-understanding of Dasein in its dereliction accomplishes itself in such an act (as a return backwards), it arises *in the ekstasis of the past*, takes its form, and presupposes this ekstasis. This is why the concept of situation appears originally linked to the past — because the *Geworfenheit* of existence discovers itself inside the past, in the ekstasis of its horizon. *"In the Befindlichkeit Dasein is surprised as the existent that being still was already — that is, that it is constantly been. The first existential sense of facticity reposes in the Gewesenheit."* *Gewesenheit* (having-been) however is not to be confused with the past (*Vergangenheit*); it *discovers itself in the past*. *"The already-being,"* says Heidegger, *"is open in the horizon of the past."* In the constitutive structure of being-in-situation (here thought in the light of the link uniting dereliction and past), it is therefore fitting to distinguish, on the one hand, *the pure horizon of the past* (whose ekstasis temporalizes itself co-originarily with that of the future, and from the future), and, on the other hand, *what manifests itself inside this horizon*: Dasein itself as being already there, as being-having-been. This being-having-been reduces itself so little to the pure ontological content of the horizon opened by temporality in the ekstasis of the past that *it manifests itself in this ekstasis as what was already — as anterior consequently to the opening of this horizon*. Far from the ekstatic understanding-discovery that returns backwards being able to found Dasein's being-thrown (its situation), this understanding-discovery *discovers Dasein's situation as what does not depend on it nor on the ontological act of its freedom*.

The structural breakthrough is precise. Within the ekstatic horizon of the past (opened by Dasein's temporalizing activity), what *appears* is a content that is *anterior to* the ekstatic opening — namely, Dasein as *already-been*. The ekstasis opens a horizon, but what the horizon reveals is something not itself constituted by the ekstasis. The *Gewesenheit* (having-been) is *given to* the temporal ekstasis of the past; it is not *produced by* the temporalizing activity. This means that Dasein's thrownness — Dasein's being-situated — is not a product of temporalization but is *revealed by* temporalization as already-there, as having-been-before-the-revealing. The situation is prior to the temporal act that reveals it.

**Paragraph 5\.** What signifies the anteriority (discovered in the ekstasis of the past) of being-having-been with regard to the opening of this ekstasis lets itself then be recognized: *anteriority means independence*. What this independence signifies is in turn clear for us. The independence of what discovers itself in the ekstasis of the past (relatively to this discovery as it accomplishes itself in the originary temporalization of temporality — that is, as well, in transcendence itself) is *that of immanence*. For this reason the content of such a discovery reveals itself *originally situated independently of this discovery itself* — because its structure is, as immanence, that of situation. For as much however as the being (to which the ontological determination of situation belongs by reason of its very structure, originarily consequently) discovers itself in the ekstasis of the past, it discovers itself there precisely *as situated by reason of what it is, as "already" situated*. *The ultimate ontological signification of this "already" alone permits that there be rendered intelligible the link that can exist between the originary concept of situation and the past.* This "already" alone renders necessary and founds the distinction instituted between *past properly speaking* ("Vergangenheit") and *being-having-been* ("Gewesenheit") — while at the same time it designates being-having-been as what discovers itself to the past *in its radical heterogeneity* with regard to the past (that is, to the temporal mode of its own discovery). In the incapacity of past properly speaking to reduce to itself what escapes it (the being-having-been where there manifests itself in time what is foreign to time) *resides its "depth." In the depth of the past is hidden the origin of being.* It is in the light of the origin of being only (of what constitutes the ontological structure of being as being-situated) that must be heard those propositions where Heidegger thinks he determines (and that as essential) the link uniting the *Befindlichkeit* to the past: *"The act of bringing before the fact (das Dass) of its own dereliction — whether it be authentically by discovering or inauthentically by hiding — becomes existentially possible only if the being of Dasein is (in conformity with its sense) constantly been. The act of bringing before the thrown existent one is oneself does not only create the being-been (das Gewesen), but its ekstasis alone renders possible the finding-oneself in the mode of finding-oneself in situation."* That such a link be inessential, and that the explicit signification of the propositions stating it in fact *be reversed*, results from the fact that the ekstasis of the past creates only *the horizon* of the past — and consequently the mode (insofar as this mode accomplishes itself temporally) of the discovery of the *Befindlichkeit*, *not the internal structure of the Befindlichkeit insofar as it resides originarily in immanence*.

The structural-philosophical conclusion is decisive. Heidegger's "already" (that Dasein's being is *already* been, *already* situated) has an ontological signification that Heidegger himself did not properly thematize. The "already" is not a temporal modifier (past tense); the "already" is the structural mark of *immanence*, of the absolute-ontological situatedness that is *prior to* temporality and is merely *revealed* within temporality. The "already" of Dasein's situatedness is the immanent anti-essence, the ontological ground of transcendence's situatedness.

The distinction *Vergangenheit / Gewesenheit* (past / having-been) in Heidegger is a subtle structural one. Henry endorses the distinction but reads it more radically: the *Gewesenheit* is not just a different temporal-ecstatic mode from *Vergangenheit*; the *Gewesenheit* is the *immanent* ground that reveals *itself* within the temporal ekstasis of the past but is not itself a temporal mode. The "depth" of the past is the depth of the immanent origin that manifests itself in time but is not of time.

**Paragraph 6\.** That the internal structure of situation resides originarily in immanence — the philosophy of transcendence lets appear in itself when (as has been seen) the philosophy of transcendence finds itself constrained to determine *the foundation of being-situated* from the idea of a foundation that (as transcendence precisely) is *not the foundation of itself* — from the idea of the *Nichtigkeit*. Because the abandonment of existence to itself (constitutive of its situation) resides in the essence of this originary *Nichtigkeit*, it shows itself as such radically foreign to everything that takes on the structure or the form of an ekstasis — to the arising of the past in the first temporalization of transcendence, consequently. This is why the affirmation by which Heidegger pretends to characterize what constitutes Dasein's facticity as a *hidden state* (*Verschlossenheit*) — and according to which it "*co-determines the ekstatic character of the abandonment of existence to the nichtig foundation of itself*" — *must be rejected*. The *eidetic incompatibility* of the temporal ekstasis and of the proper "*nichtig*" foundation of the ekstasis (of what finds itself determined as "*Nichtigkeit*" by this incompatibility itself) also renders *unintelligible* (incapable in any case of exhibiting in itself the originary essence of the *Geworfenheit*) the idea given however by Heidegger as decisive for the understanding of the *Geworfenheit*: an *"ekstatically temporal relation of Dasein to the thrown foundation of itself."* *Far from being able to found itself on temporality, the originary ontological concept of being-in-situation finds itself on the contrary broken by temporality.*

The structural incompatibility is now named. The *Nichtigkeit* (the immanent not-being-foundation-of-itself of transcendence) is by its very nature *foreign* to the structure of ekstasis — because the ekstasis is the structure of transcendence, and the *Nichtigkeit* is precisely the structural ground that is other than transcendence. So Heidegger's formulation of an "ekstatically temporal relation of Dasein to the thrown foundation of itself" is *incoherent*: it tries to combine what is structurally incompatible (ekstasis \+ immanent ground). The attempt to ground situation in temporality is therefore misguided; temporality *reveals* situation (as we saw in §5) but cannot *ground* situation. Situation is grounded in immanence, not in temporality.

This is a significant critique. Temporality was (for Heidegger) the fundamental sense of being ("*Zeit* und *Sein*") — and being-situated was to be grounded in ecstatic temporality. Henry contests: temporality is itself the form of transcendence; situation is rather the structural being of the immanent ground that *transcends* temporality (in the sense of being structurally prior to it). The situation is not temporal; the situation is the immanent ground of temporality.

**Paragraph 7\.** Thus one sees, with the intervention of temporality in the definition of the originary concept of situation, the problematic constrained to *infringe* the prescriptions that define together (at the same time as the fundamental ontological characters of situation) the essence of situation. Among these prescriptions, the most essential (the one that constitutes the foundation of all the others) has been recognized as *the impossibility for existence of taking attitude with regard to itself*, concerning at least its real, originary, and proper being. In the act of returning backwards on itself, however, opens the dimension inside which moves (as identical to it) such a possibility — that for Dasein of taking attitude precisely and (in the light of this ekstasis) of *"assuming"* what the ekstasis discovers to it (the *Geworfenheit* that belongs to it and constitutes it). Thus one sees (despite the evidences arising in the eidetic analysis and despite their apodicticity) the *free* determinations of existence intervene in the definition of being-in-situation and further be understood *as belonging to being-in-situation*. The *call of "Gewissen"* (conscience), for example — is it anything other than a call to freedom, if (in the event by which it finds itself returning back beyond the fault onto the originary being-guilty that Dasein itself is) Dasein does not only discover its situation but finds itself further *invited* to retake this situation as its own in order to *"assume"* fully in this situation the fallen being that it is. Speaking of this call (as it lets itself be understood in its essential connection with the primitive arising of temporality), Heidegger characterizes it (with regard to Dasein and for Dasein) as a *"call forward into the possibility of assuming oneself in existing the fallen existent that one is, backwards in the Geworfenheit, in order to understand the Geworfenheit as the nichtig foundation that one has to retake in existence."* That the possibility of thus freely assuming (in determinate acts of existence) the thrown foundation of existence realize itself precisely in freedom and by freedom (in the form of its originary ontological accomplishment as temporality) Heidegger indicates clearly: *"Only an existent that in its being is essentially futural — such that (free for its death) it can, by breaking on death, let itself be rejected onto its factical Da — that is, only an existent that (as futural) is co-originarily having-been — can (transmitting to itself the possibility it inherits) assume its own dereliction and, in the Augenblick (moment), be for 'its time.'"* Thus there introduces itself in an equivocal fashion in Heidegger the concept of *repetition* (*Wiederholung*) as repetition of what presents itself first under the form of a *transcendent* reality in the ekstasis of the past. What presents itself first under the form of a transcendent reality in the ekstasis of the past is however nothing other than the *thrown being of Dasein, its dereliction* — which Dasein must then (transmitting to itself what it is "in an immediate fashion" — Heidegger says — but in fact "by temporal ekstasis") *take on, assume, accept* — whereas nothing more *repugns* to the originary internal structure of the *Geworfenheit* (that is, of situation itself) than the freedom included in such acts as what renders them possible. The *juxtaposition of these heterogeneous ontological determinations* is visible in the philosophy of *destiny* (*Schicksal*). For Dasein cannot in destiny "*choose*" the possibility it "*inherits*" (and consequently understand itself in destiny's "*impotent super-power*," *"in the super-power of its project… on the debt that commits it properly"*) except insofar as there is added to the dereliction in the *Geworfenheit* the power of Dasein precisely to return on the *Geworfenheit* and to retake it in the freedom of the project. Thus Dasein — of whom it is said however that *"it never returns on this side of its dereliction"* — finds itself returning precisely on its dereliction (beyond and on this side, in the ekstasis of the horizon where it gathers it) — as if the hyper-power of this act by which Dasein "*assumes*" dereliction came to compose, with the impotence that ontologically determines the essence of situation, the structure of situation at the same time as its originary opening in *the consciousness of destiny*.

The critique now becomes sharp. Heidegger's doctrine of authentic existence — of Dasein's "assuming" its thrownness in resolute decision (*Entschlossenheit*), in the call of conscience (*Gewissensruf*), in destiny (*Schicksal*, *Sein und Zeit* §74) — requires that Dasein have the *freedom* to take up, accept, or retake its own thrown being. But the thrown being is precisely that in which Dasein *cannot* take attitude toward itself; the *Geworfenheit* is structurally *foreign to freedom*. So the Heideggerian doctrine of authenticity is structurally incoherent: it requires that Dasein freely assume what is structurally foreign to Dasein's freedom. Heidegger has juxtaposed heterogeneous structures (immanent non-freedom \+ existential freedom) without resolving the structural tension.

The doctrine of *repetition* (*Wiederholung*) in Heidegger (the taking-up of one's thrown possibilities in a fresh decision) is here noted as the precise locus of this confusion. Dasein is supposed to *repeat* what it already is (its thrown past) in a new free act; but a truly thrown being cannot be repeated by an act of freedom because it is precisely what is prior to freedom.

**Paragraph 8\.** With the eidetic incompatibility of the determinations that compose this destiny, the problematic is referred to the *doubling* (*dédoublement*) — brought to light by it — *of the concept of situation*. It is not the *originary reality* of situation but *its understanding* that finds itself defined in what constitutes precisely the ultimate ontological structure of every possible act of understanding: in the ekstatic bursting-forth of temporality (where transcendence accomplishes itself concretely). Because (in the act of returning backwards from the finite horizon of the future onto the thrown being of Dasein) it is not the essence of this thrown being (as originarily delivered to itself) that finds itself defined, but rather the *ontological understanding* of this essence — and because such an understanding is founded on freedom — such an understanding is susceptible, for this reason, of accomplishing itself *in diverse manners, corresponding each to a particular determination of existence*. In conformity with this modalization inscribed in its very structure, the understanding of the thrown being of Dasein realizes itself each time in a determinate act of existence — in such a way that in this act of understanding oneself existentially, existence can render manifest to itself *but also hide from itself* what constitutes properly its situation. This is why the discovery of this situation in its truth accomplishes itself finally inside a *particular and at the same time privileged* existential determination. It is in the *resolute decision* (not in the simple tireless accomplishment of temporality) by which Dasein projects forward toward death that Dasein grasps itself as already delivered to death in the insurmountable abandonment of the being-having-been. It is inside this decision and the *Stimmung* that prepares and renders it possible that the problematic has in fact placed itself in order to describe the truth (which reveals itself only in decision and *Stimmung*) of situation. Thus the horizon from which the understanding return backwards is produced was already (as in the anticipatory projection of decision) grasped as *that of death* — in such a way that it is only from death that the being-having-been can discover itself in the essential finitude of its dereliction. *"The anticipatory projection of the last and most proper possibility,"* says Heidegger, *"is the understanding return onto the most proper being-been ('Gewesen')."* That the being-been (the thrown being of Dasein constitutive of Dasein's situation) discover itself only in resolute decision and by resolute decision, Heidegger affirms explicitly: *"Situation has its foundation in Entschlossenheit"*; *"Situation is the Da opened in Entschlossenheit."* And, in a more categorical manner still: *"There is no situation except in and by Entschlossenheit."* In this *Entschlossenheit* therefore discovers itself (at the same time as what makes the effective and concrete situation of Dasein, and as this situation itself) *the truth of existence*. *"With the phenomenon of Entschlossenheit we are led before the truth… of existence."*

The critical-diagnostic step is now taken. The Heideggerian doctrine of resolute decision (*Entschlossenheit*, *Sein und Zeit* §§60, 62\) is the locus where the philosophy of transcendence claims to discover the *truth* of situation. But, Henry argues, this is precisely the locus where the *understanding* of situation is conflated with its *reality*. Situation itself (the immanent structural fact of being-situated) does not depend on *Entschlossenheit* — it is operative whether or not Dasein achieves resolute decision, for it is the immanent ground of Dasein's being. What depends on *Entschlossenheit* is the *ontological understanding* of situation — and this ontological understanding is one particular existential mode among others. So Heidegger has confused the *understanding of situation* (which is modal, existential, free) with the *reality of situation* (which is structural, immanent, non-free).

To every truth belongs (as appropriating to itself what is discovered in truth) a *being-certain* (*Gewisssein*) that is co-originary with truth. Because situation cannot be evaluated as a given reality, the certitude that belongs to the truth of its discovery has nothing to do with the certitude bearing on a state of things; it implies precisely an *act of existence* and maintains itself only in this act and by this act — for as much precisely as such an act maintains itself, for as much as resolute decision accomplishes itself as *"authentic decision for the repetition of itself."* Thus one sees a specific mode of existence constituting (at the same time as the authenticity of existence) the *essence* of its situation — in such a way that this situation can be possibilized only inside such a mode (outside of which, on the contrary, there is no place for situation) — in such a way that "*to the Man* (They-self)," for example, "*situation is essentially closed.*" Thus *the essence of situation* (whose ontological structure is defined by its radical independence with regard to all that existence can do or be — whatever existence does, precisely, it is situated) finds itself on the contrary depending on the *authenticity* of existence.

The structural inversion is flagrant. Situation — whose essence is its *independence* from existential modes (because it is the immanent ground of every existential mode) — ends up in Heidegger *depending* on the existential mode of authenticity (*Entschlossenheit*). This is the structural inversion that Henry's diagnosis reveals: Heidegger has inverted the grounding relation between immanent situation and existential mode, making the immanent depend on the existential when it should be the other way round.

**Paragraph 9\.** With the intervention of existential themes in the determination of the concept of situation, the philosophy of transcendence does not however abandon itself to *subjectivism*; it keeps to the phenomenon whose structure it wants to grasp an *ontological ground*. Authenticity and inauthenticity do not simply juxtapose themselves, indeed, as equivalent determinations of existence; their relation is one of *foundation*. It is the objective reality of situation that discovers itself in *Entschlossenheit*; it is this same reality that inauthentic existence flees, in such a way that situation further determines inauthenticity (and the dissimulation inauthenticity contains) as that which renders both possible. All the modes of existence attest equally its dereliction. Dereliction resides in the very structure of existence *as* universal ontological structure. Such a structure is that of *temporality* — which (from the finite horizon it projects) returns on itself to discover itself (linked to this horizon) in the essential finitude of its situation, in such a way that temporality constitutes situation at once as what discovers situation and as what is discovered in situation. That existence can (after this) look in the face or hide from itself what it is (as existence) does not prevent but *presupposes* the ontological rooting of its situation in its very structure. Thus (the passage from the ontological plane to the existential plane not being able to be imputed to it as an objection) the philosophy of transcendence is in a position to pretend to *an ontological definition of being-in-situation as temporality*. Accordingly, the philosophy of transcendence *misses* being-in-situation, and that *all the more gravely* in that its failure is produced *on the ontological plane itself* — *if the originary structure of situation is defined by its radical independence with regard to temporality*.

The structural point is now decisive. Heidegger does not (reductively) make situation *merely* existential; he grounds the existential possibilities in the ontological structure of temporality. So his failure is not (narrowly) a sliding from ontology into mere subjectivism; his failure is more grave — it is a failure *at the ontological level itself*. He grounds situation in temporality (which is an ontological structure) when situation should be grounded in immanence (which is structurally independent of temporality). This is an *ontological* failure, not a mere categorial confusion.

**Paragraph 10\.** This independence of situation from temporality — the philosophy of transcendence has *recognized*, but (lacking the capacity to understand this independence from the originary ontological determination of being-in-situation) *it interprets this independence as that of the existent*. It is as an *existent*, indeed, that Dasein arises insofar as it returns on itself in the ekstasis of the past, insofar as it is *the surpassed*. *"What is surpassed,"* says Heidegger, *"is precisely and uniquely the existent itself, and in fact every existent that can find itself unveiled to Dasein or become unveiled to it; consequently also and precisely this existent which Dasein itself is by its existence."* Thus accomplishes itself (in the ekstatic relation of Dasein to itself) *an essential fall* (*une chute essentielle*) — such that what such a relation primitively designates finds itself understood in the relation *as the "that upon which"* of the relation and *as an existent*. In the accomplishment of this ekstatic relation (that is, of originary temporality), there takes birth however — and constitutes itself, according to Heidegger — *the effective possibility of situation*: situation finds itself *liberated* at the same time as the existent, and as situation *of this existent itself*. It is as existent that Dasein is situated; it is as such that Dasein gives itself in the act by which it returns backwards on itself — as *anterior* to this act, and consequently as radically independent with regard to its own manifestation in the ekstasis of the past. Insofar as (as being-situated) Dasein appears and gives itself always in reality as *"already"* situated, Dasein (because this determination falls to Dasein by the fact that it is an *existent*) refers inevitably the problematic to the consideration of the existent and of its relation with being. For it is the existent itself that shows itself as such foreign to the light of being — in such a way that the existent enters the light of being and manifests itself only as *other than being, as anterior to being's action, in its irreducible opposition to what composes (as transcendence and as world) the reign of manifestation*. Thus operates (in an avowed fashion or not) the understanding of being-in-situation from its independence and from what founds this independence. *The ontic-ontological heterogeneity of the existent with regard to temporality covers over the ontological heterogeneity of temporality and of what (insofar as temporality is not itself its proper foundation) founds and situates temporality* — and *is substituted for* this ontological heterogeneity.

The critical-diagnostic step now reaches its sharpest formulation. Heidegger has recognized an *independence* at the heart of being-situated — the structural fact that Dasein is "already" situated, independent of any act of its own. But Heidegger, unable to articulate this independence as *immanence*, interprets it as the independence of *the existent* (*das Seiende*) with respect to being (*das Sein*). So the structural-ontological problem (immanence vs. transcendence) is converted into the *ontic-ontological* problem (existent vs. being). The existent, with its brute thereness that is foreign to the light of being, becomes the stand-in for immanence.

This conversion produces a *fall* (*chute*) — the fall of Dasein from its proper ontological status into the status of an "existent." In Heidegger's analysis of Dasein's thrownness, Dasein appears *as an existent* (something given, something thrown there, something with brute facticity). This is structurally a *category mistake*: Dasein is not an existent (like a chair or a rock); Dasein is structured by transcendence. But the thrownness is interpreted through the category of existent, because the philosophy of transcendence lacks the resources to articulate immanence properly.

**Paragraph 11\.** This substitution — the confusion it institutes between *the ontological impotence of transcendence with regard to itself* and *the metaphysical impotence of transcendence with regard to the existent* (the fact that transcendence is not "creative") — the necessity in which the problematic finds itself (to accomplish such a substitution precisely, and to treat the impotence of transcendence with regard to itself as impotence with regard to the existent) of including the existent in Dasein (that is, as well, of letting transcendence fall to the rank of an existent) — all this accomplishes itself and becomes visible when (speaking of man considered in his existence) Heidegger says of him that *"ordained to the existent that he is not, he is neither fundamentally master of the existent that he himself is."* That such a confusion be neither accidental nor deprived of consequences — that it hold to the ontological deficiency of the ultimate horizons of the philosophy of transcendence and be found again consequently in every thought that moves inside these horizons — one sees in the affirmation formulated by Sartre: *"the pour-soi grasps itself in anguish, that is, as a being which is foundation neither of its being, nor of the being of the other, nor of the en-soi's that form the world…"*

The structural diagnostic is extended to Sartre. Sartre's famous analysis in *L'Être et le Néant* (Part Two, Chapter One) of the *pour-soi* as not-being-foundation *of its being* is here read as the same structural confusion Heidegger commits.
