The "*pour-soi is not the foundation of its being*" (Sartre) is grammatically the same proposition as "Dasein is not the foundation of its being" (Heidegger); but both philosophers, lacking the resources of immanent ontology, collapse this proposition into the proposition "the *pour-soi* is not the foundation of the *en-soi*" (that is, of the brute existent) — and so transform the structural-immanent not-being-foundation into the ontic-metaphysical relation between consciousness and existent. This is the structural sliding from immanence-diagnosis into ontic contingency.

What does not find its foundation in transcendence — what escapes transcendence's power and does not hold from transcendence its "reason" — is *contingent*; and (because the act of transcendence remains ontologically founding) manifests itself *as such*. Thus the existent manifests itself (in its radical independence with regard to its own manifestation) with the *essential characteristic of contingency*. This contingency affects Dasein itself insofar as (in the act by which it returns on itself and manifests itself) Dasein manifests itself *as an existent*. In the radical independence of the existent-Dasein with regard to the act by which it returns on itself (with regard to temporality) resides however the foundation of its situation. *Contingency crosses the essence of situation as its most proper determination.* Thus intervene the existential themes that find themselves inevitably developed by the problematic as soon as it interrogates itself on what constitutes precisely the being-situated of Dasein itself (the situation of man). That man — that Dasein — does not find (as existent) its foundation in transcendence (understood however as the sole foundation) determines the insurmountable character of his abandonment; and (because the idea of this absence of foundation — the idea of contingency — inevitably carries with itself an appreciation of axiological order) such an abandonment (the very fact for man of being situated) signifies from then on (in an ethical and metaphysical perspective at once) his *own guilt*.

The structural-philosophical diagnostic is now complete. The *contingency* of the existent (that the existent has no foundation in transcendence) becomes the fundamental characterization of being-situated. And because contingency is taken (in the philosophical tradition from Leibniz through Sartre) as having an *axiological* valence — the contingent is the *unjustified*, the *unredeemed*, the *without-reason* — the situation of Dasein takes on an ethical-metaphysical coloring of *guilt*. Dasein is guilty of being the contingent existent it is. This is the Heideggerian-Sartrean doctrine of existential guilt — the doctrine that man, in his very factical existence, is burdened with an unredeemable guilt.

**Paragraph 12\.** Thus determines itself further the concept of situation from that of *contingency* — that is, more precisely, from *the heterogeneity of the existent with regard to transcendence* (understood as a foundation). It is because the founding activity of transcendence cannot absorb in itself the existent that transcendence liberates, that (in the act by which it returns on itself) Dasein manifests itself *as something absurd* — with the contingency that co-determines (as their very essence) the structural determinations constitutive of its situation: facticity, *Gewesenheit*, *Geworfenheit*. This is why Dasein *"finds itself always only as thrown fact,"* why it is true to say (in this sense) that *"the act of bringing before the thrown existent one is oneself… creates the being-been (Gewesen)."* It is because the relation of Dasein to the thrown foundation of itself is understood as *ekstatically temporal* that this foundation appears precisely as *thrown*. It is because Dasein returns on this side of its dereliction that dereliction (in reality) is what it is — that the essence of situation lets itself be grasped as *contingency*. *Under the concept of contingency is hidden however the originary ontological determination of being-in-situation: the not-being-foundation of transcendence with regard not to the existent but to itself.* That transcendence not be itself the foundation of its being and consequently cannot confer on this being a reason (something like a legitimation) — this determines the being of transcendence as "*contingent*." *Such a contingency signifies the reign of anti-essence.* It is in the light of this originary signification that must be heard the multiple affirmations to which the philosophy of existence finds itself constrained — and according to which existence is not its own foundation. It is this same affirmation that (when freedom is understood as the foundation — *Grund*) brings the problematic to describe this foundation on the contrary (from what is in it most essential) as *the non-foundation and as the abyss* (*Abgrund*). But because what constitutes the essence of non-foundation (the essence of foundation) is not grasped in the positivity of its proper ontological structure, this essence finds itself interpreted finally (under the cover of the concept of contingency, and in favor of its ambiguity) from the simple opposition of being and existent — from the *contingency of the existent*. "*The fact that the pour-soi is not its own foundation*" reduces itself thus to "*the necessity*" for it "*of existing as a contingent being engaged among contingent beings*" — and determines the pour-soi as linked to a body which (though described "*as it is on the plane of the pour-soi*") gives itself as the *mysterious presence of the en-soi at the heart of the pour-soi*, as *"the en-soi surpassed by the pour-soi néantisant and regrasping the pour-soi in this very surpassing."*

The Sartrean doctrine of the body — as the "mysterious presence" of the *en-soi* within the *pour-soi* — is here identified as the direct consequence of the same structural confusion. The body in Sartre has precisely the role that the immanent ground should have: it is the non-transcendent foundation of the transcendent consciousness. But because Sartre lacks the immanent ontology, he interprets this foundation through the ontic category of the *en-soi* (brute existent), producing the famously paradoxical Sartrean body: the body that is "transcended" by the *pour-soi* and yet is the ground of the *pour-soi*'s situatedness. This is the same structural confusion Heidegger commits: the immanent ground of transcendence is interpreted as the brute existent within transcendence.

**Paragraph 13 (closing).** What happens however when the originary structure of being as being-situated (the not-being-foundation-of-self of transcendence) finds itself confused (under the title of contingency) with the irreducible character of the existent? What element does the problematic then dispose of to determine the essence of situation? *The question of this ontological determination — of the determination of the situation of transcendence itself — is not even posed.* Such a determination produces itself rather in a confused manner (in favor of the fall that has been described), so that it is *the insertion of transcendence into Dasein understood as an existent* that clothes transcendence with the characters of being-situated: these characters belong to the existent itself as such. *It is the being-thrown of the existent that Dasein is that confers on Dasein its dereliction.* Thus is completely *forgotten* the ontological signification of the problematic that aims at the essence of situation. Thus accomplishes itself in an absurd fashion the determination of situation — if the existent holds its situation only from transcendence, if the concept of situation concerns not the existent itself but the existent's *place*, if *"the fact of having a situation is the ontological determination of the being of this existent, not an ontic proposition about this existent."*

The closing paragraph names with precision the fatal structural consequence. The philosophy of transcendence, by conflating the immanent-ontological non-foundation with the ontic contingency of the existent, has produced a hopelessly confused concept of situation in which:

* (i) The ontological question (why is transcendence situated?) is *forgotten*;  
* (ii) The concept of situation is applied to the *existent* (as the ontological determination of its being);  
* (iii) But the existent, in its being-situated, derives its situation from transcendence (which projects the place in which the existent is situated);  
* (iv) So the existent's situation is ontologically dependent on transcendence, while at the same time the immanent ground of transcendence's own situatedness is conflated with the existent's contingency.

The result is an absurd circle: transcendence founds the existent's situation, while the existent (conflated with immanence) is supposed to ground transcendence's situation. The Heideggerian-Sartrean concept of being-situated is internally incoherent. Only by returning to the proper immanent-ontological grounding — which §42 identified as the structural truth concealed in Heidegger's *Nichtigkeit* — can the concept of situation be properly articulated.

---

## **§ 44\. The concept of situation in existentialism. The failure of ontology and realism: "nature and freedom"**

**Paragraph 1\.** In pretending to determine the essence of situation from *the existent* — and that for lack of being able to do so from *transcendence itself* (from what, more exactly, delivering transcendence to itself, constitutes it as originarily situated) — the problematic moves *in a circle*. Because of the two elements at its disposal (transcendence and the existent) neither encloses in itself the internal possibility of being-situated, the problematic finds itself referred from one to the other. The idea that comes to the fore then — of a *"dialectical"* concept of situation, of the interpretation of situation as dialectic of freedom and nature — illuminates singularly the impotence from which this idea proceeds. Thus one sees in Sartre, on the one hand, situation being primitively defined *from freedom*: it is only in the light of the end projected by freedom that existence discovers each time *its* situation — in such a way that existence bears the full responsibility of what it is, that everything arrives by man, and that *"there is no inhuman situation."* Freedom however (for as much as it does not find itself described in a purely psychological manner, and the problematic wants on the contrary to assign it an ontological foundation in the nothingness of transcendence) shows itself as such *identical to a power of tearing-away and surpassing* by which man (considering every thing and himself *"in the light of a non-being"*) finds himself always *beyond* what is — separated, in this exile that is his very freedom. Freedom, far from being able to found the situation of man, determines man on the contrary *as an impersonal and empty subjectivity* — separated from all content, without possible insertion into the real. Hence, on the other hand, *the problem proper to existentialism*: after man has been understood as this power of "*escape*" and of "*disengagement*" (*dégagement*), the problem of his necessary *"engagement"* in the world — and, more generally, the affirmation (for example) that *"the human condition… cannot… be dismissed."* Such a proposition however could not be simply affirmed; and (because the philosophy of existence shows itself incapable of giving it a foundation in the internal structure of subjectivity as constitutive structure — as immanence) the philosophy of existence has no other means than *to link, despite their heterogeneity* (despite the ontological negating power that defines freedom as precisely what is not the existent) the existent and freedom — in such a way that each term (finding itself linked to the other) receives in this link and by it *something like the ersatz of a situation*.

The opening paragraph stages the critical diagnosis of existentialism (Sartre, with Jaspers and Merleau-Ponty to follow). The structural problem is clear: existentialism defines situation from freedom alone (the projected end illuminates the situation), but freedom is structurally an impersonal power of tearing-away and surpassing — it cannot by itself situate anything. So existentialism must *link* freedom to what is other than freedom (the given, the existent, the contingent, the body, nature) in order to produce the ersatz of a situation. But this linkage is arbitrary because it rests on neither of the two terms being by itself capable of producing the structural reality of situatedness. Immanence — which alone could ground situation — is foreign to existentialist ontology.

Precisely freedom (or again, existence, the pour-soi) — being nothing other than what is not the existent, the en-soi (Sartre says) — sees its being exhausted in this negation; it does not cease to carry in itself what it does not cease to negate in order to be what it is: the nothing *"which is nothing except because it is not the en-soi."* This is why (because *"the term origin of internal negation is the en-soi, the thing that is there,"* because linked to the en-soi the pour-soi is *"crushed on what it denies"*) — what the pour-soi denies, *"the surpassed en-soi, remains and haunts it as its originary contingency"* — the pour-soi *"cannot prevent itself from being at distance from itself what it is,"* that is, *"this contingency, this heaviness at distance… that it never is but… has to be as heaviness surpassed and conserved in the surpassing."* Because such a heaviness (which signifies identically *"facticity,"* *"past"*) finds itself conserved in the surpassing — because it remains in the surpassing and attaches itself to it as its originary contingency — this heaviness *situates* the surpassing precisely, and determines the surpassing by this link (even though the heaviness itself is determined, as contingency, as this individuated and situated *there-being* only *by* the surpassing). Thus draws itself the circle in which *the brute given* and *freedom* situate and determine each other *reciprocally*. *"The facticity of my place,"* says Sartre, *"is revealed to me only in and by the free choice that I make of my end… But, reciprocally, facticity is the only reality that freedom can discover — the only one that freedom can néantize by positing an end… For if the end can illuminate the situation, it is because the end is constituted as projected modification of this situation."* And in a more manifest manner still: *"it is by its very surpassing of the given toward its ends that freedom makes the given exist as this given — but at the same time… freedom chooses itself as this surpassing-here of the given."* Thus one must define situation as *"illuminated by ends which themselves are projected"* — and one would have to add "*situated*" — *"only from the there-being that they illuminate"*; and say again that *"the end illuminates the given"* — and one would have to add "*situates the given*" — *"only because the end is chosen as surpassing of this given."* But there is no better way to get out of a circle than to *realize* it — and that in the most extreme confusion: *"situation,"* says Sartre, *"common product of the contingency of the en-soi and of freedom, is an ambiguous phenomenon in which it is impossible for the pour-soi to discern the contribution of freedom from that of the brute existent."*

The Sartrean texts from *L'Être et le Néant* (Part Four, Chapter One on situation — especially the analyses of "My Place," "My Body," "My Past," "My Neighbor") are scrutinized. The structural diagnosis: Sartre produces a *circular* definition of situation — situation is what surpassing discovers as given, while the given is what the surpassing individuates as this situation. Each term borrows from the other the structural determination that neither has in itself. The final Sartrean admission — that "it is impossible to discern the contribution of freedom from that of the brute existent" — is the philosophical capitulation in the face of a structural confusion.

**Paragraph 2\.** Such uncertainty (which sees the most different realities subsumed in turn under the same concepts — each term conferring the determination of being-situated on the opposed term only insofar as it holds this determination itself from the opposed term) is found again *in Jaspers's philosophy* — where the essence of situation is explicitly described as *a dialectic of nature and freedom*; while the union of these heterogeneous elements cannot raise an objection since it gives itself precisely as a *"paradox"* — and since it suffices, all in all, to consider reality as constituted by paradoxes of this kind in order to find in each of them *an evident proof of its truth*. Thus man's situation understands itself easily from his *historicity*, which consists in "*the union of existence and empirical being*" — that is, again, in that "*of freedom and necessity, of possibility without resistance and of the irrefutable given — of time,*" finally, "*and of eternity.*" *It is the most naïve realism, in fact, that finds itself at the origin of these conceptions* — where the situation of man is finally interpreted from his insertion in the milieu of *objective being*. What is to be remarked concerning such a union (also described as "*synthesis of the world insofar as the world affects freedom, and of freedom insofar as it assumes the world*") is that — for lack of being able to be understood as the very essence of freedom — the necessity that constrains freedom and determines it as originarily situated sees itself finally interpreted (from this insertion of man as objective being in the context of the objective world) *as the necessity of things* — in such a way that its relation with freedom becomes *exterior*, that necessity can no longer be (indeed) anything but assumed by freedom, that necessity pre-exists freedom, and that *the structure of situation (far from resulting from the action of freedom) shows itself in fact foreign to freedom — resides in the very nature of things*. *As always, the failure of ontology leaves the field free to realism.*

The critique of Jaspers (*Philosophie*, 1932; *Von der Wahrheit*, 1947\) is concise but devastating. Jaspers openly makes situation a *dialectic of nature and freedom*, relying on the rhetorical device of the "paradox" to cover over the philosophical incoherence. Jaspers's historicity — the union of existence and empirical being, freedom and necessity, time and eternity — is, Henry diagnoses, simply naïve realism dressed up in paradoxes: man is in a situation because man is an objective being in an objective world. The "paradox" is the philosophical failure to articulate what situation really is ontologically.

The closing proposition — "*as always, the failure of ontology leaves the field free to realism*" — is a sharp structural thesis. Whenever ontology fails to ground a phenomenon in proper ontological structures, realism (the positing of brute mind-independent objects as the source of the phenomenon) fills the void. Situation is grounded in "nature" (a brute realm of objective being) because ontology has failed to ground situation in immanence.

**Paragraph 3\.** To this failure (and to this realism consequently) testifies the interpretation of the phenomenon of being-in-situation proposed in turn by M. Merleau-Ponty. One finds, to tell the truth, in the *Phénoménologie de la Perception* something like the *presentiment of a philosophy of immanence* — which comes to the fore precisely concerning the problem that occupies us, that of situation. Such a problem is introduced from a *critique of intellectualism and of classical philosophy* — more precisely, of reflection — when it is shown concerning reflection that it *"never carries itself outside every situation,"* that *"the analysis of perception does not make disappear the fact of perception, the ecceity of the perceived, the inherence of perceptive consciousness in a temporality and in a locality."* *"Radical reflection,"* it is said more precisely, *"is consciousness of its proper dependence with regard to an unreflected life which is its initial, constant, and final situation."* If unreflected life defines the situation of reflection (and that because unreflected life constitutes reflection's internal structure, because reflection itself is a mode of life), it matters to determine what constitutes this situation (that of life — and consequently also of reflection). Life (existence) is however nothing other, for Merleau-Ponty, than *transcendence*. The nature of transcendence, however, does not find itself elucidated in and for itself — in such a way that transcendence could appear as by itself constitutive of a situation. Rather, this elucidation accomplishes itself in a negative manner — from the simple opposition (to thought, that is, as well, to reflection) of *a more ancient existence*, which gives itself in this opposition as *deprived* of the power of intelligibility that belongs to reflexive consciousness as such and characterizes it — and (because no other mode of manifestation finds itself defined in its proper ontological positivity) as deprived finally of *all light*, as something *"blind."* Because it is thus understood as something blind — because its phenomenological and consequently ontological status becomes *totally uncertain* — existence *degrades*: it appears as a mysterious force situated *below* the consciousness-I, a kind of *natural substrate* constituted by an ensemble of anonymous functions. The presupposition borrowed from Heidegger (according to which these anonymous functions can accomplish themselves only on the ground in them of the transcendence which links them to the world) becomes *without object* when this transcendence no longer signifies identically the effective arising of phenomenality. This is why such a link loses finally its *transcendental* character and becomes veritably *"natural"*: its accomplishment in the functions of the body confuses itself with that of an *ontic process*. *It is the insertion of consciousness into an empirical nature that — in conformity with the presuppositions of realism — determines man and situates him.* The definition of a world in which the ego has no part gives itself paradoxically as constitutive of the situation of the ego — while (as the problematic of ipseity will bring into evidence, but as in fact every thought faithful to the teachings of phenomenological intuition can understand) *the situation of the ego resides necessarily in its very structure and is identical to it*.

The Merleau-Ponty critique is the most nuanced of the three. Henry credits Merleau-Ponty with a genuine "presentiment" of a philosophy of immanence — the opening moves of *Phénoménologie de la perception* correctly critique the intellectualism-reflection tradition and correctly diagnose reflection's dependence on a prior unreflected life. But Merleau-Ponty fails to articulate this unreflected life as *immanence* in the proper structural-ontological sense. Because Merleau-Ponty retains the Heideggerian framework of transcendence as the principle of phenomenality, the "unreflected life" can only be characterized *negatively* — as what is not reflection, as what is prior to reflective intelligibility. And since no positive alternative mode of phenomenality has been articulated, the unreflected life becomes a mysterious "blind" force below consciousness.

The result is the well-known Merleau-Pontyan anonymous body, the lived body as anonymous substrate of perception. This body, which should have been the locus of *immanent* self-affection, instead becomes a mysterious natural substrate — a sort of *natural* unconscious, a force foreign to consciousness that nonetheless grounds consciousness. Merleau-Ponty thus repeats the structural confusion Sartre commits (interpreting immanence as a brute natural given within consciousness) though in a more subtle register — via the anonymity and the "flesh" that will be central to the later work.

It is in the light of these remarks that it is fitting to appreciate the following text — the ambiguity and indetermination inscribed in it. *"There is therefore,"* writes Merleau-Ponty, *"another subject below me, for whom a world exists before I am there and who marked my place there. This captive or natural spirit is my body — not the momentary body which is the instrument of my personal choices and fixes itself on this or that world, but the system of anonymous 'functions' which envelop every particular fixation in a general project."* Because *"this blind adhesion to the world,"* what is for the subject *"the fact of his birth,"* *"a communication with the world older than thought,"* oppose themselves simply to thought (which concentrates on the contrary in itself the principle of phenomenality), *"they congest consciousness and are opaque to reflection,"* determine *"the vital experience of vertigo and nausea which is consciousness… of our contingency."* Thus one sees there falling back *into the dualism of the one and the other* a thought whose most remarkable design was however to escape this dualism. It is finally — *as a mysterious incarnation, the insertion of spirituality into what has no name* — that constitutes the proper of man's situation and condition, as this proposition attests again: *"if the so-called instincts of man do not exist apart from the spiritual dialectic, correlatively this dialectic is not conceived outside the concrete situations in which it is incarnated."*

The critique is pointed. Merleau-Ponty, despite his intention to overcome the dualism of consciousness and brute thing, *falls back* into this dualism when it comes to the grounding of situation. The "natural spirit" that is the body, the "blind adhesion to the world," the "communication older than thought" — all these are characterized by opposition to consciousness-reflection, and Merleau-Ponty lacks the ontological resources to give them positive content other than through the vocabulary of brute natural facts. The body becomes a "captive or natural spirit" — a mysterious something that mediates between consciousness and nature — and this is, structurally, the mysterious incarnation of the transcendence-in-the-existent, another instance of the structural confusion §43 diagnosed.

**Paragraph 4 (closing).** The concept of situation has *an ontological signification*. This means that it can be understood only from *pure phenomenality* as by itself constitutive of the possibility and the effectivity of a situation — as identical to the essence of situation. This is why (after having shown how the existential situation of the existent-Dasein determines itself — how *"the 'here' of a 'here-I' is always understood from the 'there' of a Zuhanden"* toward which preoccupation projects itself) Heidegger adds: *"'here' and 'there' are only possible in a Da — that is, if there exists an existent that has opened spatiality as the being of the Da."* But this spatiality must be heard in turn in a *transcendental* sense; it implies that *"this existent carries in its most proper being the character of not-being-hidden ('den Charakter der Unverschlossenheit'). The expression 'Da,'"* continues Heidegger, *"signifies this essential opening."* It is because temporality constitutes (according to Heidegger) the originary mode according to which this essential opening accomplishes itself that temporality confers its ontological possibility on the concept of situation and founds the structure of situation. *"Ekstatic temporality illuminates the Da originarily."* The design of conserving *pure* the content of the concept of situation implies however that the there-being (*l'être-là*) be grasped in *what founds it ultimately*. Such a grasp of what (giving the there-being originarily to itself) constitutes it precisely as *the originary there-being* and as *the foundation of every conceivable there-being*, alone permits that there be avoided *the fall* of the concept of situation — its interpretation from the determinations that the existent borrows from being itself. *Why does this fall produce itself? Why must the analysis of being-situated end in confusion — if not because the constitutive structure of being-situated, the originary essence of revelation, remains hidden?* Here the problematic encounters *the second question* it had posed in its attempt to determine this originary structure: *the question concerning the reasons for which revelation itself in the effectivity of its originary accomplishment dissimulates itself*.

The closing paragraph restates the structural-philosophical thesis and pivots to the next large project. Situation has an ontological signification: it can only be properly understood from pure phenomenality itself (that is, from the proper structure of revelation). Heidegger himself recognized this when he said that the "here-there" structure presupposes a *Da* whose being is *Unverschlossenheit* (not-hiddenness, openness) — and when he identified ekstatic temporality as the illumination of the *Da*. But the philosophy of transcendence, lacking the immanent-ontological ground, ends in the "fall" that §43 diagnosed: the concept of situation is interpreted through the categories of the existent, and the ontological question is forgotten.

The "*second question*" now named — why does revelation itself dissimulate itself in its originary accomplishment? — is the diagnostic question §40 had projected as the second part of the three-part program. The transition from §44 to §45 is therefore the transition from the structural elaboration of immanence (Part One of the program, §§37–44) to the diagnostic of dissimulation (Part Two, §§45–49). §45 will begin with the fundamental structural question: why does the immanent essence of revelation systematically conceal itself in the philosophical tradition's attempts to articulate revelation?

## **§ 45\. The dissimulation of the originary essence of revelation and its forgetting**

**Paragraph 1\.** The reasons for which the essence of revelation dissimulates itself in its originary accomplishment have been *evoked by the problematic and already understood by it* — since these reasons find their origin in a set of presuppositions with which in reality they confuse themselves. Such presuppositions constitute what has been called *monism*. To the thought that conceives for phenomenality no form of realization other than the manifestation of a transcendent horizon — that is, *objectivity* — there necessarily escapes and slips away what constitutes however the foundation of this very horizon. The *inaptitude* of this thought to grasp the originary mode according to which phenomenality phenomenalizes itself cannot be simply noted, however, nor understood as a *"prejudice."* If this prejudice (supposing that one can speak in philosophy of "prejudice" and that, among all those one denounces so easily, the only one that deserves to be retained does not consist precisely in believing that there are prejudices) extends its power over the ensemble of the development of philosophical thought, that is because its origin — what makes precisely that it is *not* a prejudice — must be shown. One has likewise been able to see the problematic strive to circumscribe not only *what makes the insufficiency of monism* but, further, *that from which this insufficiency results or its motive*. Was the bringing into evidence of this motive not contained in the remark according to which the impotence of the problematic that moves within the horizon of monism to edify a phenomenology of the foundation and to give a content to the idea of the formal structure of *"Selbständigkeit"* reposes on the impotence of this foundation *to produce itself in the light of phenomenality*? Thus the dissimulation of the essence was referred, not to an incomprehensible failing of thought, but *to this essence itself*, to the ontological structure of reality. This is why, besides, what at first was only a set of living thoughts essentially different in their procedures and aims can appear retrospectively as *the unity of a tradition affected with one and the same insufficiency* — because there is of this insufficiency a reason, and that in the nature of things, in the nature of reason itself.

The opening paragraph states the thesis that will govern the entire diagnostic that follows. The dissimulation of revelation's originary essence is not an accidental historical failing of particular thinkers but a structural-ontological necessity rooted in the nature of reality itself. Henry had already prepared this thesis earlier (the reference to the impotence of the *Selbständigkeit* to produce itself in the light of phenomenality points back to the diagnostic of Heideggerian transcendence in §§42–43): whenever thought operates within monism — that is, within the presupposition that phenomenality has only *one* mode of realization, horizonal manifestation — the proper ground of phenomenality, immanent self-revelation, *cannot* appear within it. This is not because thinkers have been negligent but because the very structure of monism excludes immanence from what it can thematize. And — this is the decisive step — Henry refuses to call this exclusion a "prejudice." A prejudice, on the classical model, is something one could in principle identify and correct through further reflection. But the exclusion at issue is not corrigible from within; it follows from the structural orientation of thought toward the outside. This is why a tradition of thinkers working in essentially different ways (Kant, Schelling, Husserl, Heidegger, Sartre, Merleau-Ponty) nonetheless exhibits *one and the same insufficiency*: not because they share a prejudice but because they share a structural orientation whose blind spot is structurally inevitable. The "reason" for this insufficiency is in "the nature of things" — and, crucially, in "the nature of *reason* itself." The Ionian fire has its own structural way of concealing what makes it possible.

**Paragraph 2\.** This recognition — in the essence — of a *foundation of its own dissimulation* (that is, of the essence as this foundation) the problematic that institutes a general critique of monism nonetheless accomplished by placing itself *inside* monism and the perspective that is its own. Thus the transcendence to which phenomenality (identified to horizon) refers itself slipped away abruptly *before* a thought henceforth grappling with *"the unknown."* The comprehension of this unknown and of the dialectical movement where it loses itself — of what constitutes properly speaking *the destiny of monism* — remained nonetheless *negative*: transcendence slips away because it does not itself assure the possibility of its own manifestation — such was its content. The pretension to recognize *in the foundation itself* (and that as identical to it) the reason for its own dissimulation signified nothing other, finally, than the non-recognition in it of the power capable of revealing it originarily. This pretension opened the way, for this reason, to a *research and a positive determination of this power* — that is, precisely, *of the real being of the foundation*. Such a determination is the work accomplished by the problematic. *The essence of transcendence resides in immanence.* In the *positivity* of immanence (not in the simple fact for transcendence of not itself assuring its own manifestation) must be sought — if there is one — *the reason of dissimulation*, and that in such a manner that the bringing into evidence of this reason (identical to the essence) belongs to the elucidation of the essence and of its internal structure.

The second paragraph marks a sharp methodological turning point. Earlier stages of the investigation had already identified a "dissimulation" at work in the monistic tradition, but they did so *from within* monism: the point was that transcendence fails to produce its own manifestation, and so withdraws into "the unknown." But this was merely a *negative* characterization — a way of marking the absence of immanent self-manifestation without yet possessing the positive concept that would explain this absence. Now, having established the positive structure of immanence in §§37–41, Henry can reverse the direction of the analysis. Dissimulation is not to be explained as the *failure* of transcendence to manifest itself; it is to be explained as the *positive structural property* of immanence itself. The essence *actively* does not enter into the horizon of objectivity; this non-entry is not a defect but a structural feature. And because this non-entry is structural, it must itself belong to the account of immanence's internal constitution. The diagnostic of dissimulation is therefore not an external critique of monism but a further positive elaboration of the essence — a point at which the polemical diagnostic and the constructive phenomenology coincide.

**Paragraph 3\.** How does dissimulation find its reason in the positivity of the essence and is identical to it? What makes, in the internal structure of immanence, that immanence slips away? Or rather — does it not belong to immanence (conformably to the most important eidetic results obtained by the problematic) *not to go out of itself in exteriority* but to *retain itself in itself* on the contrary? In this act of retaining itself in itself (that is, likewise, in its originary essence) is included the reason for which immanence precisely *does not advance itself into exteriority* and does not show itself in exteriority as this exteriority itself nor as the phenomenality that constitutes it. The *non-belonging* of the essence to exteriority and to its proper phenomenality, the fact that it does not show itself in this exteriority — that is what determines its dissimulation. Because this non-belonging — the non-manifestation of the essence in the manifestation of the horizon and in the world — is *included in its structure* (in the act of the essence of retaining itself originarily in itself), dissimulation not only concerns the essence, *it is its work*. For this reason also it is neither accidental nor provisional and cannot be *overcome*. *The idea of a manifestation of the essence in the world is in principle absurd.* Dissimulation is inscribed in the essence *as what it is*; it happens to the essence through its own will. This is why, too, dissimulation *necessarily* produces itself and *does not cease producing itself* in the essence. Thus there is *in the essence an event* that founds its dissimulation at the same time as it explains the nature and the object of dissimulation. What dissimulates itself is *the essence itself*. The nature of this dissimulation is *the non-manifestation in the world*, and this non-manifestation in turn defines the nature of an *absence* which finds itself henceforth understood — for it is explained from a *presence* and on the ground of this presence. Absence is the absence *of the originary essence of presence* — absence willed and prescribed by it.

The third paragraph provides the structural derivation of dissimulation from the internal constitution of immanence. The argument is remarkably tight. §37 had established that the internal structure of immanence consists precisely in *not going out of itself* into exteriority — immanence is what retains itself in itself, in the absolute proximity of self-affection. But this very structural property *is* the reason for dissimulation: immanence is by its internal structure *incapable* of entering the horizon of exteriority; if it entered this horizon, it would by definition no longer be immanence but transcendence. The dissimulation of immanence from the world is therefore not an accidental concealment that could in principle be overcome through better methods of inquiry; it is an ontological necessity inscribed in immanence's constitution. And — this is the decisive Henry-ian move — dissimulation is not merely negative. It is, as Henry says, an *event* within the essence, the essence's *own work*. Immanence positively "wills" its non-manifestation in the world; the withdrawal is not defect but active retention. This positivity of withdrawal is what makes absence comprehensible: absence is not the bare lack of presence but the *absence of a specific presence* that has by its own structure taken itself out of the field. The sentence "the idea of a manifestation of the essence in the world is in principle absurd" is the strongest formulation of the thesis — no methodology, no phenomenological refinement, no improved intuition will ever bring immanence to show itself as a phenomenon of the world, because its constitution structurally precludes this. This thesis will govern everything that follows: the entire second part of Section III is the working out of this structural dissimulation through its various historical and philosophical modalities.

**Paragraph 4\.** That the originary essence of presence retains itself outside the world and finds itself in principle absent from the world — that is what makes its *modesty* (*pudeur*). This modesty, for this reason — because it roots itself in the internal structure of the essence and is identical to this essence — is not a fortuitous determination susceptible of coming to existence at a given moment of its history (a psychological determination, for example). It is rather *the very ground of every conceivable existence*, its internal possibility, its essence. *"It is,"* says Hölderlin, *"in huts that the human being dwells."* That this dwelling in which *"he envelops himself in a modest garment"* is essential to such a being and defines his humanity results precisely from the fact that it cannot be changed for another — results, more ultimately, from what institutes this dwelling as *a gift that does not cease to form itself*, from the essence. For if the concrete determinations of existence present all the vicissitudes of a history (if they show themselves susceptible of growing and, it seems, of disappearing — each time indicating a cause of their becoming) they are possible in reality only *from the structures of the essence and through them*. In modesty, man experiences his difference from the exterior and foreign being, and takes consciousness of it. That this consciousness becomes sharper and exasperates itself when it assists impotent (in the sentiment of death for example, or in desire) at the determinations of its objective being and their proper movement — or that it remains on the contrary latent as this secret trembling that does not cease to affect existence — this consciousness in any case *reposes on the essence*; its possibility is *the negation* (which does not cease accomplishing itself in immanence) *of exteriority*, the *refusal* of exteriority. Because such a refusal is that of the essence and depends as such on no particular will, it does not admit either (as its reverse) the opposite determination. Being-outside-self in objectivity may well solicit existence and define the τέλος (explicit or not) of its project — but the failure of this project (as of every comportment aiming at the exhibition of the essence and its spreading-out in the world) *is prescribed by the essence and by what constitutes in it the ultimate possibility of its being-itself*, its modesty.

The fourth paragraph develops the concept of *pudeur* — an almost untranslatable French word that can mean modesty, chastity, reserve, shame, decency, self-containment. Henry takes it in a very specific ontological sense: *pudeur* is the essence's structural self-retention from exhibition in the world. What is crucial is that Henry refuses any *psychological* interpretation of modesty. Modesty is not a feeling one might or might not have depending on upbringing; it is the structural orientation of the essence itself, prior to and grounding every psychological state. The Hölderlin quotation — *"It is in huts that the human being dwells"* — is loaded. It comes from late Hölderlin and captures the sense that human being is constitutively *sheltered*, dwelling in a reserve that cannot be traded for open exposure. The "modest garment" is not a covering one might choose to remove; it is the very condition of being human, the essence's gift of self-hiddenness to the existent. Henry's vocabulary — *pudeur*, *refus*, *négation de l'extériorité* — is operating at the ontological register: these are structural properties of immanence, not moral or psychological attributes. The trembling the human experiences facing death or in desire is not the occasion of *pudeur* but its *manifestation* in consciousness; the trembling itself rests on the essence's prior structural refusal of exteriorization. The last sentence states the radical thesis: every comportment that would aim at the *exhibition* of the essence in the world, every attempt to bring immanence out into visibility, *is in advance prescribed to failure* by the very structure of what it aims at. The essence is structurally unexhibitable.

**Paragraph 5\.** Because, in its modesty, the essence retains itself outside the world and does not appear in the world, *the essence remains hidden*. *Being-hidden* characterizes the essence and belongs to it in virtue of its internal structure, essentially affects this structure — namely, precisely, *immanence as such*. But immanence constitutes the most interior nature of the absolute, the absolute itself, its essence. This is why the absolute allows itself to be understood from *this hidden state* and as what maintains itself in hidden state — why *"no one has ever seen God,"* why God is finally *the "hidden God" (Deus absconditus)*. Thus one finds — for the propositions that at first translate the insufficiency of the problematic — an *ontological foundation* henceforth capable of conferring on them an acceptable sense. Thus must be understood, inside this ontological foundation, the aforementioned affirmations according to which the divine existence gives itself — independently of its reflection in alterity — as *essentially hidden*, according to which *"the divine essence is hidden in itself."* For this being-hidden is a *name of immanence*, and its concept concerns, consequently, the ensemble of characters that constitute immanence and belong to it. If, for example, *"the Geworfenheit… remains hidden,"* if *"this hidden state is not a simple non-knowing but constitutes the facticity of Dasein,"* that is because the being of Dasein *resides positively in immanence* and finds itself as such situated and, at the same time, in this state where it dissimulates itself — Dasein and what constitutes the insurmountable character of its originary situation. But immanence does not only found each time a situation — *it is the essence of life*. This is why life is what one never sees and escapes perpetually from our gaze — why (as was said again) *"it is in life, this immediate divine existence, that was life, the most profound foundation and every living, substantial existence — but remaining eternally hidden from the gaze."*

The fifth paragraph gathers a series of formulas in which Henry articulates the *ontological* sense of the theological and philosophical language of hiddenness. The *Deus absconditus* of Lutheran theology (and of the apophatic tradition more broadly, reaching back through Eckhart and Dionysius to the Platonic and biblical sources) is not a contingent theological trope but the tradition's most precise formulation of what Henry has identified as the internal structure of immanence. The Johannine "*No one has ever seen God*" (John 1:18) receives its proper ontological interpretation: God-as-absolute is identical to immanence, and immanence by its internal structure does not appear in the field of vision. The reference to the "divine essence hidden in itself" likely draws on Eckhart's *Gottheit* and on the mystical tradition's insistence that God's essential being is inaccessible to every created intellect. But Henry's key move is to re-read Heidegger's *Geworfenheit* through this lens: the hiddenness of thrownness in *Sein und Zeit* (the Dasein does not know *whence* or *whither* of its being-thrown) is not a psychological opacity but the positive mark of Dasein's immanent structure. When Heidegger says that the "hidden state" of thrownness "constitutes the facticity of Dasein," he is, *malgré lui*, testifying to the immanent-ontological structure that §42 had diagnosed as the missing ground of Dasein's situation. And this connects to the passage's culminating thesis: immanence is not only the ground of each particular situation, it is *the essence of life*. Life — in the strictly ontological sense Henry has given this term throughout (life \= the self-affective structure of immanent self-revelation) — is what perpetually escapes the gaze precisely because the gaze operates in exteriority while life is constituted by the refusal of exteriority.

**Paragraph 6\.** Because the essence remains hidden in itself and escapes perpetually from the gaze — because the essence is as such *dissimulation* — *it falls into forgetting*. The nature of this forgetting must be elucidated. Of forgetting in general, it is fitting first of all to recognize its *positive character*. Forgetting is not nothing; it has an object. This is what makes it differ from a simply negative phenomenon — from a pure absence, from a nothing. What is forgotten may certainly no longer exist (as in the case of an object that has been destroyed). Whatever the importance of this object — whether an insignificant thing or on the contrary, for example, a civilization that has disappeared without leaving traces — its belonging to a world, the ensemble of the relations of universe it sustained and in a certain way still sustains with the totality of what is, its necessity in a word, confers on it an *ideal existence* that makes possible, at least in principle, its re-memoration in memory. It is in its reference to memory precisely that forgetting is first of all and most often understood. Does its positivity not find its expression in the fact that it is susceptible of mutating into its contrary — into "the corresponding memory"? But the forgotten reality does not necessarily belong to the past; its presentation to consciousness does not necessarily accomplish itself within a mode of thinking such as memory. What we forget of essential — is it not, in a certain way, *what is always there*? And if it is always there — if this essential-being consists precisely in the fact that it is *the universal and always present essence of presence*, the essence of every possible and conceivable being-there — *how can we forget it?* *By not thinking of it.* This is what constitutes the nature of forgetting. Forgetting is only in principle possible on the ground of the presence of something *to which one is not thinking*, and as *this act of not thinking of it*. Forgetting is the *fact of thought* — and, when it is a matter of this fundamental ontological forgetting here in question (forgetting of pure presence), the fact for thought of not thinking this essence which, however, makes it possible and finds itself as such always present.

The sixth paragraph inaugurates the second main concept of §45 — forgetting (*oubli*) — and its distinction from simple absence. The analysis is methodical. Henry first establishes the positivity of forgetting: forgetting is not nothing; it has an object that in some way persists (ideally, through its relations to other things, through its "necessity") and that can in principle be recovered through memory. But this classical model of forgetting — forgetting as applicable to past things recoverable through *souvenir* — is inadequate for the phenomenon Henry is after. The forgetting of immanence is not the forgetting of a past event; it is the forgetting of *what is always there*. Immanence is the universal and ever-present essence of presence; its forgetting cannot therefore be a temporal forgetting of something that has receded into the past. How, then, can we forget what is always there? *By not thinking it.* This simple answer is ontologically decisive. Forgetting in the fundamental sense is not a withdrawal of the forgotten object from presence but a *structural orientation of thought away from what is persistently present*. Thought forgets by being turned elsewhere — by having its intentional direction set toward exteriority. The essence is not lost; thought is turned the wrong way. Forgetting is thus, precisely, the *fact of thought* — not an accidental lapse but a structural property of thought as such, insofar as thought is constitutively oriented toward exteriority and therefore constitutively turned away from the immanent essence that makes it possible.

**Paragraph 7\.** Which thought does not think the essence that makes it possible? Is this not that of *natural consciousness* which devotes itself to the *existent* (*étant*)? Because such a consciousness defines a determinate mode of existence and constitutes this mode, it is to this mode manifestly that the forgetting of the essence refers — and the formation of this consciousness presupposes free existence and appears contingent. Or rather: if *"this forgetting is neither fortuitous nor temporary — if it does not cease forming itself and forms itself necessarily,"* that is because the mode of being that sustains it has a *specific pre-eminence* in existence and, as a fallen mode of existence, determines existence from the beginning of its history and, most often, up to its end. The possibility of other modes, however, remains open, and it realizes itself for example in *philosophical knowledge*. That this knowledge acts as a *"Remembrance"* (*Re-mémorial*) and that in it the intelligence of being is torn finally from the forgetting where natural consciousness maintains it — that this forgetting attests precisely, in its connection with Remembrance (which defines the fundamental act of ontology as always possible), *its positivity* — does this not show that the thought which turns away from the essence, because this turning-away is its deed, *can still open itself to this essence*?

The seventh paragraph raises the question of the relation between forgetting and ontology-as-*Remembrance*. This is of course the Heideggerian problem — the forgetting of being (*Seinsvergessenheit*) and its overcoming through the ontological recollection (*Wiederholung*) that defines the fundamental act of ontology. Henry's move is characteristically dialectical. First, he concedes a level at which the Heideggerian answer is correct: the forgetting of the essence may be attributed to *natural consciousness* in its everyday absorption in the existent, and this forgetting can be in principle overcome through the philosophical-ontological recollection that tears intelligence from its absorption in the existent and returns it to its proper object (being, or — in Henry's terms — the essence of manifestation). At this level, forgetting is a contingent property of one mode of existence (the everyday, absorbed mode), and Remembrance is a genuine alternative mode that is always possible. But Henry is only setting this answer up in order to knock it down — the next paragraph will argue that the Heideggerian Remembrance does *not* in fact overcome the forgetting of the essence but rather *deepens* it, because the Remembrance itself operates within the horizon of transcendence and thereby misses immanence just as systematically as natural consciousness does.

**Paragraph 8\.** Or does not the forgetting of the essence characterize on the contrary *every thought as such*? Does it not belong to the very nature of thought as what, in a certain way, *cannot be overcome*? It is in this sense then that forgetting is the fact of thought — as what depends not on a particular determination of thought (on a direction thought freely gives itself) but on *what thought is*, on *this originary direction that is prescribed to it as its own* — insofar as thought is *from all time and by nature the thought of exteriority*. For it is not thematism that misses the essence. To thematism doubtless it belongs to aim or not at the condition of its own possibility. And it can happen, moreover, that this condition escapes thematism, even when thematism explicitly directs itself toward this condition — if, as has been said, the horizon does not let itself be thematized. But it is not in *forgetting* of the horizon, then, that thought lives. Thought, on the contrary, experiences the horizon in the very act by which it slips away and finally escapes thought — *as the mystery that thought preserves*; the horizon is the important thing, the object of thought's solicitude. Thought knows only that what it has at its disposal, it does not have explicitly at its disposal. But pure *exteriority* is the milieu in which thought moves — if not (and in a certain way cannot ever) be properly speaking its *"object."* To thought that moves in general in exteriority — as well as to thought which (in the Remembrance it believes authentic of being) gives itself explicitly for theme the object of ontology — this very exteriority escapes necessarily on the contrary, and there slips away in principle the *most ultimate* condition of exteriority. This is why and how forgetting is the fact of thought — why and how it is forgetting *of the essence*: because thought directs itself toward exteriority, outside of which retains itself (by reason of its very structure) the originary essence of pure presence — immanence.

The eighth paragraph delivers the crucial radicalization. The Heideggerian answer (§7) treated forgetting as a property of a *mode* of existence that could be overcome by another mode, philosophical Remembrance. But Henry now argues that forgetting is a property of *thought as such* — of every thought, however directed, however philosophical. The reason is structural: thought is by its nature turned toward exteriority. Thematism — the act of thinking that takes something as its explicit theme — can take any object; it can even take the horizon of its own possibility as theme (this is what Heidegger's fundamental ontology attempts). But the horizon itself *cannot* be thematized — and here Henry quietly accepts the Heideggerian point that thought experiences the horizon not as an object but as what withdraws in the very act by which objects are given. The horizon, in Heidegger, is experienced as "the mystery thought preserves." But — and this is Henry's decisive move — even this properly Heideggerian relation to the horizon-as-not-thematizable *still moves within exteriority*. The horizon is not a thing in the world, but it is the *exteriority-structure* of the world, the milieu of exterior-being. And therefore the *condition* of this horizon itself — that is, the immanent essence that grounds the possibility of horizonal manifestation — still systematically escapes thought, *even* thought that has taken the horizon as its theme. The Heideggerian Remembrance, which aims to recover being from its forgetting in natural consciousness, does not thereby recover *the essence of manifestation*; it rediscovers the horizon while remaining blind to what makes the horizon possible. Forgetting is therefore not a contingent property of everyday existence overcome by philosophy but a structural property of every thought whatever, because every thought is by nature directed outward and immanence by its nature is retained inward.

**Paragraph 9\.** Because thought directs itself toward exteriority (outside of which retains itself, by reason of its very structure, immanence), the forgetting of the essence in which thought lives is not susceptible, for this reason, of transforming itself into the opposite determination. This determination instead — this *re-memoration* that one opposes to forgetting — because it does not cease (on the ground in it of thought) directing itself, *consciously this time*, toward the exteriority of the milieu it thinks, misses *yet more inevitably* the condition it searches for of its own possibility. Thus one sees — at the very moment when it claims to vanquish the forgetting of the essence which illuminates it and believes it can, moreover, with *being-beyond-the-essence as being-beyond every thematic grasp* (as *transcendence of the horizon*) give itself the theory of this forgetting — thought *falling back into a deeper forgetting*. In the insurmountable character of this forgetting resides *the powerful origin of monism*. *Ontological monism is the theory of thought.* That it surpasses thought toward its conditions — toward intuition and, finally, the ekstatic transcendence of a horizon — does this not show precisely that it does not cease moving in reality in the direction prescribed by thought and by its aim? This is why the research that monism institutes remains submitted to the *immanent teleology that governs every object-consciousness*. Because Remembrance-of-being accomplishes itself in thought and aims through thought at its object, it repeats in reality, with regard to originary immanence, the forgetting of naïve consciousness and carries this forgetting to the absolute. Thus in thought, the forgetting of the essence cannot change itself into its contrary — since this contrary, rather, *is identical to it*.

The ninth paragraph draws the most devastating consequence of the preceding analysis. Not only does philosophical Remembrance (the Heideggerian *Wiederholung*) fail to overcome forgetting; it *intensifies* forgetting. The reason is as follows. Natural consciousness forgets immanence passively, by being absorbed in the existent. Philosophical Remembrance attempts to overcome this forgetting by *explicitly turning toward* the conditions of the manifestation of the existent — that is, by thematizing the horizon itself, the transcendence that grounds being-in-the-world. But this very explicit turn reinforces the orientation toward exteriority: the philosopher now *consciously* and *methodically* directs attention outward, toward the horizon, and the immanent-ontological condition that grounds this horizon itself is therefore *more completely* missed than it was by naïve absorption. Naïve consciousness at least did not have a theory that excluded immanence; philosophical monism possesses such a theory and wields it methodically. The Heideggerian fundamental ontology, insofar as it identifies being with horizonal transcendence and makes the horizon's ecstatic structure the theme of thought, *carries to the absolute* the forgetting of immanence that natural consciousness merely practices unreflectively. Henry's formula is stark: *ontological monism is the theory of thought*. It is thought's self-theorization — thought articulating the structural principles of its own outward-directed operation and taking this articulation as first philosophy. But precisely because this self-theorization remains within the teleology of thought (remains directed outward), it systematically misses the immanent essence that grounds thought itself. Philosophy, on this diagnosis, is not the cure for forgetting but its highest expression.

**Paragraph 10\.** Where resides the positivity of forgetting, if it cannot mutate into the opposite determination? To what does it refer, to what reality — if it is something rather than nothing and if it must be understood, effectively, as a forgetting? *The originary essence of pure presence* is what determines forgetting as such. How, however, does such a forgetting belong to thought? How can it be imputed to thought as *its* forgetting? For one cannot forget, it seems, except what one has some relation with. In what does this relation consist? What links thought to the essence in such a way that thought can be said — in the mis-recognition of this link — to "forget" the essence? Or rather, *is the essence not that of thought itself* — the originary unity with itself of the act that aims at the object, its final possibility, its substance, and its *life*? *What thought forgets when it misses the essence that retains itself outside exteriority — is itself.* Thus is discovered (after what there is of fatal in forgetting) its *positive* and *essential* character — how finally forgetting is that of thought and is veritably imputable to it as its own, *because it is its deed* — because, more gravely and in a manner determining for all that thought understands or represents to itself concerning itself, forgetting is for thought the forgetting of its own essence, *the forgetting of self*.

The tenth paragraph delivers the core thesis of the entire analysis. Forgetting is imputable to thought because what thought forgets is *thought's own essence*. This is the reason forgetting is not bare absence: there is a *real relation* between thought and the immanent essence — namely, the relation of *constitution*, since the immanent essence is what grounds thought's very possibility (thought exists only as a modality of the life of the subject, and the life of the subject is immanent self-affection). Thought forgets this immanent essence *not as one forgets a stranger but as one forgets oneself* — forgets the constitutive ground of one's own being. This *self-forgetting* is what makes the forgetting of the essence so profound: it is not only that thought misses the essence; thought misses what *it* most intimately is. This is why every self-representation thought gives of itself within the regime of monism is structurally distorted: thought describes itself as intentional outward movement, as transcendence, as ekstatic projection — all of which are real but derivative modalities — while missing its own immanent-life essence. Every ontology of thought that operates within monism is, at bottom, a systematic misdescription of thought by itself. The diagnosis here anticipates later Henry (especially *Généalogie de la psychanalyse* and the late trilogy on Christianity), where the "forgetting of life" is the specifically modern form of the forgetting of the essence.

**Paragraph 11\.** The determination of what — on the foundation of the essential forgetting that is its own — thought represents to itself concerning itself and its relation to the essence (that is, finally, concerning the essence) — the determination of *philosophy understood as fundamental ontology* — is the following. Because thought that aims at exteriority misses in principle the essence that retains itself outside exteriority, thought *negates* the essence. The relation to exteriority in which thought moves — transcendence — that is its sufficient foundation, the essence outside of which there is nothing. What essential determination other than this movement toward the outside which is its own could thought recognize and name? Where is this "interior" of which some speak? We search and strain toward this interior in vain — we grasp nothing of the kind. Always the world is there, and we find only exteriority and our own opening to it. Thus must the naïve representations be rejected of a knowledge first closed in the subject and constrained in consequence to "come out" of its so-called interior sphere to attain, outside this sphere, the object. *"The more one affirms categorically that knowledge is first of all and properly 'interior,' that it has absolutely nothing of the mode of being of a physical and psychical existent — the more one believes oneself to advance without presupposition in the question… of knowledge and the elucidation of the relation between subject and object."* But — abstraction made from the difficulties relating to the question of knowing how the knowing subject can go out of its interior sphere and (*"risking the leap"*) attain an *"other and exterior"* sphere, up to the object — *"on what positively signifies the interior of the immanence in which knowledge is first of all enclosed, and on the manner in which the being-character of this 'being-in-the-interior' of knowledge is founded in the mode of being of the subject, silence reigns."* In reality *"in the act of directing oneself toward… and grasping, Dasein does not in a certain way go out preliminarily of its interior sphere, in which it would first be closed, but it is (conformably to its primary mode of being) always already 'outside'…"* — and that not only in perception properly speaking but as well in simple thought, in representation, or in memory. *"Even forgetting of something — in which apparently every being-relation with what was formerly known has been erased — must be grasped as a modification of the originary Being-in; in the same way every illusion and every error."* Thus is rejected by thought — conformably to the τέλος that animates thought and structurally determines the direction of its aim — *the very concept of immanence*, every possibility for the essence to retain itself originarily in itself and to compose thus (in this act of retaining itself originarily in itself) something like *an interiority*. *"There is no sphere of immanence, no domain where my consciousness is at home… no intimacy of consciousness"* — and that because consciousness, in vision for example, *"does not possess itself and on the contrary escapes into the thing seen."* Such is (understood by thought) the universal structure of existence — so that even the body (on the ground in it of this structure) *"never falls back totally on itself,"* so that *"corporeal existence never reposes in itself."*

The eleventh paragraph works through a long series of Heideggerian and Merleau-Pontyan passages to exhibit the concrete form taken by thought's self-forgetting when it constitutes itself as fundamental ontology. The quoted passages from Heidegger's *Sein und Zeit* §13 are exemplary. Heidegger is there attacking the Cartesian picture of knowledge as an interior sphere that must somehow "go out" to reach an exterior object. Heidegger's alternative is the well-known analysis of being-in-the-world: Dasein is "always already outside," already in the midst of entities, and the Cartesian picture of an interior sphere is a derivative and confused representation. Now Henry does not deny Heidegger's critique at the level at which Heidegger conducts it: the Cartesian picture of knowledge-as-interior-sphere *is* indeed crude and confused. But Heidegger's critique *throws out the baby with the bathwater*: in rejecting the Cartesian misrepresentation of interiority, Heidegger also rejects the very *concept* of immanence, of a structural interiority that would not be the closed sphere of Cartesian epistemology but the self-retaining self-affection of the essence. The result is that Heidegger's ontology can only thematize existence as being-outside, as already-there-in-the-world. Everything becomes a modification of *In-sein*, including forgetting, illusion, and error. And Merleau-Ponty continues this trajectory: "no sphere of immanence," "no intimacy of consciousness," consciousness "escapes into the thing seen," even the body "never reposes in itself." Henry diagnoses this as the *systematic* outworking of thought's self-forgetting: having identified phenomenality with horizonal transcendence, fundamental ontology *must* deny structural interiority because it has no place for what could constitute such an interiority. The silence that reigns about what immanence "positively signifies," which Heidegger complains of in pre-phenomenological philosophy, is the very silence fundamental ontology itself produces — because fundamental ontology has no resources for articulating what immanence is positively.

**Paragraph 12\.** But thought carries in itself the essence that it negates. Because this essence constitutes thought's *life* — this originary immanent life that is thought's in the very act by which it turns toward the outside — the negation that thought formulates when (identifying itself to such an act) it thinks this act and thinks itself in the light of the τέλος that determines this act in exteriority, loses its assurance and becomes *ambiguous*. And that not only because for us the content of its negation remains enigmatic as to its origin (so that the problem of its origin is inevitably posed and the simple denunciation of the "prejudice" of the preliminary interiority of the subject of knowledge remains in truth *blind* with regard to what it denounces — maintains itself thus on a pre-philosophical plane and loses finally all signification). For thought — for thought which (conformably to the τέλος of intentionality) sinks into the knowledge of the object — the interiority of the object is not first of all (despite this constant direction it gives itself and which belongs to it in principle) the *inadequate idea* in the light of which it misunderstands itself: this "prejudice," rather, *is its own*; it is *what thought spontaneously says about itself in the truth of natural language*. At the moment of the negation of immanence by philosophical consciousness there pre-exists the moment of *its immediate affirmation in life*. In whatever fashion life figures this immanence to itself — that the representations it gives itself of immanence find inevitably their content in the thought of the existent and belong to this thought, that life understands itself for example as a "box" — *it is itself that life expresses thus spontaneously*, and the absolute interiority of originary immanence that constitutes properly its essence is what life formulates confusedly. This is why such representations have for them *the force of their transcendental origin*; they break a path up to philosophical consciousness, maintain themselves there, and finally juxtapose themselves to the theoretical negation of the essence that nourishes them. Immanence is nothing — in such a manner however that this nothing becomes insensibly something and, in the final account, *the name of an essence*.

The twelfth paragraph introduces the decisive counter-movement. Having diagnosed fundamental ontology's systematic exclusion of immanence, Henry now argues that ontology's very *negation* of immanence structurally testifies to the immanence it negates. The argument is subtle. Thought's negation of immanence is not free-floating; it is spontaneously *accompanied* by an affirmation of immanence — an affirmation that shows up in the spontaneous "prejudices" of natural language about the interiority of subjects, the self-presence of consciousness, the intimacy of the mental. Heidegger dismisses these as *Vorurteile* to be overcome by fundamental ontology, but Henry's point is that these so-called prejudices are not accidental confusions; they are *transcendentally motivated expressions* of the essence in the medium of thought. When natural language (and the philosophy that honors it) says that knowledge is "interior" or that consciousness "possesses itself" or that the self has an "intimacy," these expressions admittedly use the vocabulary of the existent (the "box," the spatial metaphor of containment, etc.) and so are not ontologically adequate to immanence. But they are *testimonial*: they show that immanence presses into expression even where the only available vocabulary is inadequate to it. And this is why fundamental ontology's theoretical negation of immanence *cannot simply win the day*: the negation is always haunted by the pre-philosophical affirmation that comes up from below, from "life" itself, and that the ontology must continually keep suppressing. The result is *ambiguity*: ontology says "immanence is nothing" and yet immanence "becomes insensibly something" — becomes the name of the essence even in the very philosophical texts that had claimed to abolish it.

**Paragraph 13\.** Thus one sees — after immanence has been negated as a fiction (moreover, inexplicable), after it has been said that there is no sphere of immanence, no possession of consciousness by itself, no intimacy of this consciousness nor domain where it is at home — *the interiority of consciousness reintroducing itself into the problematic* and being implicitly admitted by it. *"It is of course essential to consciousness to grasp itself,"* it is affirmed of vision (that is, in fact, of perceptive consciousness and of every consciousness in general) — *"and if it did not do so it would not be vision of anything."* This self-grasping of vision in consciousness as self-grasping of consciousness, this something *"essential"* that gives to the pseudo-concept of immanence *a singularly positive content*, does not remain however (contrary to what the problematic had first affirmed in a first moment of its analysis) totally undetermined: its ontological elaboration pursues itself on the contrary, and that conformably to the prescriptions that are those of the essence. This is why the text we are commenting on always adds concerning vision: *"but it is essential to consciousness to grasp itself in a kind of ambiguity and obscurity."* That such determinations do not affect simply a thought that contradicts itself and becomes uncertain as soon as it finds itself in presence of the ultimate foundation (and which cannot be indefinitely eluded) of every possible consciousness — that they belong *to the essence* and can as such serve to define the essence — one sees in the fact that they are not cited only as unexplained determinations of consciousness but find again *in consciousness, in the essence, a reason*. *It is because the foundation of exteriority retains itself outside exteriority and does not manifest itself in it that the consciousness where this foundation resides is said "obscure" — and, precisely, does not show itself.* This is why consciousness is not easy to grasp — in itself nor in the structural modalities by which it is supposed to constitute the world — why it remains something ambiguous. *"It is not easy to put motor intentionality in the nude,"* says Merleau-Ponty — *"it hides itself behind the objective world it contributes to constitute."* *"Everything that in some manner is there for me… hides from me my transcendental subjectivity,"* affirms more generally a commentator on Husserl. And, always in the same sense, speaking of *"the truth immanent to the given,"* another commentator will say of it that it is *"given in an originary evidence whose form of immediacy dissimulates the movement that has engendered it."*

The thirteenth paragraph tracks the re-entry of immanence into the Merleau-Pontyan and Husserlian problematic, after its explicit denial. The paradox is pointed. The same thinkers who deny that there is "a sphere of immanence" must nonetheless admit that consciousness is "essential to itself to grasp itself" — for without such self-grasping consciousness would have no unity and would not be consciousness of anything. This forced concession reopens precisely the structural function Henry has been articulating: a self-relation of the essence that cannot be reduced to the outward relation to an object. Merleau-Ponty adds that this self-grasping is "in a kind of ambiguity and obscurity" — and here Henry finds the most striking testimony: the "obscurity" of consciousness's self-grasping is not a defect or a provisional cognitive limitation but *the positive ontological mark* of immanence itself.
