Immanence is "obscure" *because* it does not manifest itself in the light of exteriority, *because* it retains itself outside the horizon where things show themselves. The Husserlian vocabulary of "hidden motor intentionality" and "transcendental subjectivity hiding behind the objective world" receives its proper ontological interpretation through Henry's immanence-dissimulation thesis: these talkings about what "hides itself behind" are the tradition's inadequate but inevitable attempts to articulate the structural self-retention of immanence.

**Paragraph 14\.** It is not only because *"the intentionality that produces them remains in them in the implicit state"* that the "productions" proper to the positive sciences remain naïve, inexplicit as to the ontological sense constitutive of their being. Or rather, it is to the origin of this "implicit state" that it is fitting to go back, if one wishes truly to dissipate but first to understand the naïve character of the sciences, which is ultimately founded in *the hidden structure of the constitutive power itself* and of the specific intentionalities through which it expresses itself. Thus is elucidated, from the non-manifestation in the given of the donating intuition, the habitual mis-recognition of this donation. Thus is understood finally, *not as what is nothing but as this very thing* (as the condition of objectivity, the obscure element that retains itself outside objectivity). Because the obscure element is the condition of objectivity, *"the obscurity of the hall necessary to the clarity of the spectacle"* and, finally, the condition and the essence of every possible presence, it is as such — as its condition — *"what there is of opaque in my present,"* and that in whatever manner the present accomplishes itself, everywhere and always, so that *"to think thought,"* for example, *"is never to eliminate — it is only to push higher the opacity of thought for itself."*

The fourteenth paragraph extends the diagnosis to positive science. Husserlian phenomenology had observed that the positive sciences operate with an "implicit intentionality" that is not thematized — scientific productions rest on constitutive acts that the scientists do not thematize, and this is the source of scientific "naïveté." But Husserl's response to this naïveté — transcendental phenomenology as the thematization of constitutive intentionality — does not suffice, Henry argues, because the implicit character of scientific intentionality itself derives from a deeper source: *the hidden structure of the constitutive power itself*. The constitutive power is not hidden because it has not yet been thematized; it is hidden because it *is immanence*, and immanence by its structure does not show itself in objectivity. Hence the Merleau-Ponty formula: "to think thought is never to eliminate, it is only to push higher the opacity of thought for itself." No phenomenological reflection can bring thought's immanent constitutive operation into the light of objectivity, because this operation structurally does not take place in the light of objectivity. The opacity is not epistemic but ontological — not "thought hasn't yet thought itself through" but "thought cannot as such be laid bare in the medium of exteriority, because its being is precisely the refusal of exteriority." This is why Henry's reading of "the obscurity of the hall necessary to the clarity of the spectacle" is ontological rather than metaphorical: the dark auditorium is not a pedagogical image of how intentionality operates unnoticed; it is the structural condition of immanence, which makes the light of horizonal manifestation possible precisely by retaining itself in its own non-manifestation.

**Paragraph 15\.** Because there is in it something opaque and because its own essence dissimulates itself, thought falls into forgetting. Because thought cannot however (and for this reason, in the very act by which it thinks itself) totally eliminate but only push higher its own opacity for itself, thought does not simply fall (to tell the truth) into this forgetting — but (and that conformably to the positivity that belongs to the concept of this forgetting and makes it possible in general) *lives it as such, as the forgetting by itself of its own essence*. Thus appears this forgetting in the heart itself of the thought that accomplishes it. *"The essence of consciousness is to forget its own phenomena."* That these phenomena find themselves interpreted or not as simple psychological events (as specific intentional determinations in any case) matters little here: it is on the ground in it of *its own essence* that consciousness forgets them as that very thing which it is. How does such a forgetting accomplish itself? That consciousness which aims at exteriority misses the essence that retains itself outside this exteriority and cannot in principle hold this essence in its aim, that on the object of this aim consciousness flees from itself in such a way that its knowledge is only ignorance of self — all this has been said. That it is thus however — that is now the *affirmation of object-thought*, the *self-negation of the negation of immanence*. *"My act of perception occupies me… enough that I cannot, while I effectively perceive the table, perceive myself perceiving it."* Speaking of sensible beings that surround me (this paper under my hand, these trees under my eyes), Merleau-Ponty says again that *"my consciousness flees from itself and is unaware of itself in them."* *The definition of existence as self-escapement implies what it negates; immanence is its conscious presupposition.*

The fifteenth paragraph drives to the paradox at the heart of Merleau-Pontyan phenomenology: the very concept of "self-escapement" (*échappement à soi*) presupposes what it seems to deny. If consciousness "flees from itself" in its absorption in the object, then *there is a self to flee from* — there is an immanent structural self-relation whose fleeing is precisely what absorption-in-the-object consists in. Merleau-Ponty wants to use "self-escapement" as a way of dispensing with immanence (consciousness has no interiority; it is always already outside, in the world); but the very phrase contains its own refutation. Henry presses this: self-escapement \= affirmation-through-negation of immanence, the negation of immanence is itself negated by the presupposition inherent in the analytic category used to effect the first negation. Merleau-Ponty's phrase "the essence of consciousness is to forget its own phenomena" thus becomes, against its author's intention, a formula for *exactly what Henry has been arguing*: consciousness (which Henry identifies with thought's outward orientation, the teleology of transcendence) structurally forgets its own phenomena — that is, its own immanent life — because it is structurally oriented away from them. But in the very act of saying so, Merleau-Ponty presupposes the immanent essence of consciousness that makes such forgetting-of-self intelligible.

**Paragraph 16\.** Because, according to the philosophy of existence, consciousness forgets its own phenomena, *"it can recall them."* The idea in existence (and in the philosophy that existence inevitably gives of itself) of a *Remembrance* possible or necessary attests in existence the positivity of its forgetting — *the reality of what it negates*. Thus one sees birth and development in object-thought — at the heart itself of its movement toward the object and of the grasp it accomplishes — the sentiment that this grasp (and that because of this direction that is its own) is not exhaustive: *something in it is lost, something essential that is to be recovered*. That the loss of the essence in object-thought results from its direction (and not from the finitude of a content surrounded by horizons), the character of the Remembrance where on the contrary the possibility of an ontology takes body and historializes itself concretely for the first time in Western philosophy, attests. It is not to the teleology of thought nor to its project of a systematic explicitation of the *cogitatum* in the successive unveiling of the horizons it implies that the ἐποχή in reality obeys: the ἐποχή is the ἐποχή *of the world*, its bracketing (*mise hors circuit*) — and that with the radical signification of concerning *this world as such*, exteriority itself and the movement toward it of intentionality, *the teleology, precisely, immanent to intentionality*. That this radical signification of the ἐποχή escapes it and does not show itself either in the results at which it arrives — that in the examination of constitutive problems, thought holds itself in an exclusive manner to the movement of consciousness toward the world, and that the explicitation of this world and of its typical structures pursues itself conformably to the τέλος of intentionality and according to the mode of unveiling that belongs to this τέλος and characterizes it, that the Remembrance still moves in the forgetting of the essence — the essence in any case determines Remembrance and makes it possible. Thus becomes transparent the question that the ἐποχή poses to itself about itself, the question of its possibility and of its origin. Because this possibility resides ultimately in *the originary immanence of transcendental life*, the thought that searches for this possibility in the world does not find it. To the phenomenologist who interrogates himself on what he does, the reduction — because it does not let appear its origin in thought and as a *"motive"* — appears henceforth without foundation; it is, according to the famous word of Fink, *"unmotivated."* That it produces itself however and that, what is more, the phenomenologist poses precisely at its subject the question of its possibility and of its origin, that he cannot respond otherwise than by saying that the reduction *"supposes itself"* or, in a still more significant manner, that *"its veritable motives reside in the depths of transcendental subjectivity"* — not in *"man"* but in *"the transcendental ego that we truly are without knowing it"* — that Remembrance carries in itself and for itself (as the certain signs of its positivity) those of the forgetting it accomplishes — is all this not illuminating?

The sixteenth paragraph extends the analysis to Husserl's ἐποχή and phenomenological reduction. Husserlian transcendental phenomenology poses to itself, through Fink and others, the question of the *motivation* of the reduction: why does the phenomenologist perform this astonishing act of suspending the world? The answer, Husserl and Fink admit, cannot be given from within the natural attitude (since that would circumvent the reduction), nor from within the reduced attitude (since that already presupposes what it is supposed to motivate). Fink's formula is that the reduction is "unmotivated" (*unmotivierte*). Husserl's own deepest answer is that the reduction's motivation lies "in the depths of transcendental subjectivity," in "the transcendental ego that we truly are without knowing it." Henry reads this with great interpretive sympathy: Husserl's inability to find a motivation for the reduction *within thought* (within the teleology of the intentional consciousness of the world) and his identification of the motivating source as a subjectivity "we truly are without knowing it" is testimony — half-recognized by Husserl himself — that the condition of the reduction resides not in the intentional structure of world-directed consciousness but in *the originary immanence of transcendental life*. The reduction is a Remembrance — an attempt to recall the forgotten essence — and its very possibility attests to the positivity of what is being forgotten. Husserl's text is therefore, in Henry's reading, a major piece of testimony *for* the immanent-phenomenological ontology Henry is articulating, even though Husserl himself did not fully grasp the testimony he was providing.

**Paragraph 17\.** Thus one sees — with the intervention (within the philosophy of existence itself) of the *concept of forgetting* and the bringing to light of its positive signification (as the idea of a Remembrance still attests) — *immanence* no longer only negated by this philosophy, but on the contrary *presupposed* by it (and that as what makes possible this forgetting and determines it, as what hides itself). The phenomenological positive determination of immanence explains the status of existence *within the philosophy that takes existence for theme* and its *"obscurity"* — the obscurity of existence itself. That such an obscurity is that of the essence and constitutes its most remarkable phenomenological character — that this character, moreover, finds itself understood in its *explicit opposition to the light of exteriority* (identified to that of consciousness) — becomes transparent to the thought that, precisely, thinks every thing from the essence. *"He who perceives,"* says Merleau-Ponty, *"is not deployed before himself as a consciousness must be."* That which is not deployed before self, that *"which remains always on this side of our perception,"* is not nothing however: it is the existence that makes possible every knowledge as its foundation — this *"latent knowing,"* *"pre-conscious,"* *"habitual,"* *"this implicit or sedimented science,"* that we constantly use without ever putting in question, that is our permanent *"acquired"* (*acquis*), an *"historical thickness,"* a *"tradition."* Because the obscurity of these determinations is that of the essence, they concern existence *under its most profound form, the body*. It is the immanence of the originary body that makes of it this *"latent knowing"* and determines it phenomenologically (in its radical opposition to consciousness — which signifies exteriority) as something obscure, *"ungraspable,"* as what is *"neglected,"* *"passed in silence."* It is the immanence of the originary body, consequently, that makes Merleau-Ponty (as Descartes) say of the body that it obscures the mind — and (because it founds in general perception) that this *"obscurity gains the whole perceived world."* That this obscurity remains most often misunderstood as to its radical and ultimate ontological foundation — that it is nothing other than the obscurity of an uncertain thought and lets itself introduce then (into the new and absolutely original sphere of existence it nonetheless indicates) foreign determinations — and, for example, in the case of the body, the figures of extension and the processes that accomplish themselves in it in the third person — that this obscurity finds itself confused with the zone of shadow that affects every object-consciousness and that the body (whose originary mode of revelation it constitutes) becomes in turn a marginal phenomenon of this consciousness (the simple accompaniment of the perceptive act, its repercussion and its wake in sensibility) — it is the principial immanence of the essence that is at the bottom of this obscurity; it is this immanence that nourishes the confusions this obscurity raises in thought.

The seventeenth paragraph extends the diagnosis to Merleau-Ponty's philosophy of the body and of the latent knowing. Merleau-Ponty's rich analyses — the "latent knowing," the "habitual body," the "pre-conscious," the "sedimented science" — all identify a pre-objective and pre-reflective dimension of existence whose phenomenological character is *obscurity*. Merleau-Ponty sees clearly that this dimension is not nothing, that it is the foundation of every explicit knowledge, and that it has an original mode of givenness that cannot be assimilated to the thematic clarity of object-consciousness. But because Merleau-Ponty does not possess the structural-ontological concept of immanence, he can only describe this dimension *negatively* — as "not-deployed-before-self," "latent," "pre-conscious," etc. — and when he tries to give the body ontological weight, he oscillates: the body is sometimes the bearer of the originary latent knowing, but sometimes it becomes merely the "accompaniment" of object-perception, a "repercussion in sensibility," slipping back toward a derivative and psychological status. Henry's diagnosis is that Merleau-Ponty's oscillation testifies to what he is groping toward: the body as originary locus of *immanent self-affection*, which in Henry's own later work (*Philosophie et phénoménologie du corps*, 1965, and the long discussions of Maine de Biran) will be articulated explicitly. The Cartesian-Merleau-Pontyan association of body-with-obscurity is not a mistake about the body's cognitive value but an unwitting testimony to the body's ontological character: the body obscures the mind, as Descartes said, because the body's mode of revelation is immanent self-affection, which structurally cannot manifest itself in the light of exteriority that characterizes thought.

**Paragraph 18\.** The *presentiment* of immanence — at the heart of its very negation and forgetting — does not allow itself to be recognized only within contemporary theses on existence; *classical philosophy carries it in itself throughout the ensemble of its development*. To the determination of reality from the objectivity where reality phenomenally concretizes itself, there juxtaposes itself the idea of what on the contrary *does not manifest itself in objectivity*. Such an element — in principle non-objective — is nonetheless *not nothing* but rather *the condition of objectivity itself*. That it retains itself outside objectivity in the very act by which it founds objectivity, determines positively the *"obscurity"* of the mind, gives sense to the repeated propositions according to which the mind is *"the ungraspable,"* *"the unknowable,"* *"the un-co-ordinatable,"* and, according to the word of Alain, an *"eternal absent."* The traditional concept of the mind can only be understood from that of immanence — as its at once blind and inevitable formulation. Thus one sees — in the *System of Transcendental Idealism* (where the fundamental theses of classical philosophy concentrate themselves in an ensemble) — Schelling identify phenomenality with objectivity as such and, at the same time, posit (as the condition of this objectivity, as the absolute) *the "non-objective."* For objectivity presupposes its *"production."* Because this production is not itself objective, it is *"unconscious."* That it exists nonetheless — and that as the absolute, that *non-phenomenality is the name of the essence* — Schelling preoccupies himself with showing, or rather (by reason of this non-phenomenality of the principle of phenomenality) with *demonstrating*. Such a demonstration accomplishes itself in the following manner. The accord manifested in experience between our ideas and reality presupposes *the production of reality by the mind*. What we call reality, however — is it not what does not depend on us and seems to us foreign to our activity, anterior to its exercise? That is because the creative activity of objective reality, its production precisely, is *unconscious*. This is why its products astonish us — why they seem to us to be there before us without our intervention: because our intervention is not conscious. *The unconscious of production is the foundation of reality.* But this thesis — which forms the principal content of the *System of Idealism* — demands, if it is to be understood in its ultimate ontological signification, a *more radical interpretation*. It is because *it retains itself outside exteriority* that the essence can open itself to exteriority; it is because it *does not show itself in exteriority* that it is the *condition* of exteriority. To open oneself to exteriority is however the *originary act of intuition*. Because in opening itself to exteriority this originary act does not show itself in exteriority, does not show itself — *it is not known*. Thus are explained (because what is not before-us in the light finds itself — and that as the condition of this light — *on this side of it, in the night* — that is, finally, from the ontological interpretation of the essence of transcendence as immanence) the fundamental theses of Schelling: the idea that intuition in itself, *"the non-objective… escapes consciousness."* This is why — as it is said explicitly — *"the self cannot have an intuition and have at the same time the intuition of itself as having intuition,"* why *"the self, in having intuition, does not know that it has intuition."*

The eighteenth paragraph turns to Schelling, reading the *System of Transcendental Idealism* (1800) as the most concentrated expression of the classical philosophical presentiment of immanence. Schelling's fundamental problem is the agreement between thought and reality: since reality appears to us as independent of our activity, how can we explain its agreement with our ideas? Schelling's answer is that reality is in fact produced by the mind, but this production is *unconscious* — we do not experience ourselves as producing the world; the world appears as given because the productive activity underlying its appearance is not objective, not conscious. Henry reads this as a major piece of testimony for the immanence-thesis. Schelling identifies phenomenality with objectivity (thus remaining within monism at the level of his theory of phenomenality), but then is forced to posit, as the condition of this objectivity, something *non-objective*, *non-phenomenal* — the unconscious productive power of the mind. This "unconscious" is Schelling's name for what Henry calls immanence: the non-objective, non-phenomenal, structural self-activity that underlies and makes possible the field of objective phenomena. Schelling cannot quite say this in Henry's vocabulary — he lacks the phenomenological-ontological distinction between two modes of phenomenality — and so he is forced to characterize the productive ground *negatively*, as unconscious, non-objective, non-phenomenal. But the structural function is identical. The two Schellingian formulas — "the non-objective escapes consciousness," "the self in having intuition does not know that it has intuition" — are, in Henry's reading, exact formulations of the immanence of intuition to itself in a mode that is not a mode of objective thematization.

**Paragraph 19\.** Because the self, in having intuition, does not know that it has intuition — because this intuition is unconscious — it forgets itself and is *lost in the object*. The self-forgetting of intuition in the object to which it opens itself *calls for and renders necessary its remembrance*. The goal of transcendental philosophy is precisely to give back to consciousness its act of intuition that primitively escapes consciousness. As that of its forgetting, the idea of a *Remembrance* of the essence is present in Schelling. How such a Remembrance accomplishes itself, why it fails and inevitably repeats the forgetting from which it proceeds — the problematic that has shown this now understands. To the idea of Remembrance is linked in general in classical philosophy the idea of *method*. That method takes the form of reflexive analysis and can thus only project (by means of induction) the conditions of the object — that is, as well, the essence itself — into a *Hinterwelt*, that this essence reduces itself to this ensemble of conditions \= x (in such a manner that nothing in reality authorizes one to conceive as mind and to call by this name an unconscious capable of receiving in it any determination whatever — and, for example, the power to create the world), that in the favor of this confusion and in its delirium the subject-constructor-of-the-universe imagines himself also to be its author, that we need on the contrary at once more certainty and more humility, that the sense of this humility leads thought (conscious of its impotence) to reduce the condition it searches of the possibility of experience to an ensemble of purely *"logical" "functions"* — and to lose thus (no longer by identifying it to the act of a super-existent, but by stripping it of all reality and in the void of the unreal) *ontological reality*, so that of this reality finally subsists only a *transcendental mythology* constituted at the hazard of hypotheses or of subjective preferences — none of all this matters here. What matters is the ultimate origin that these developments find *in the nature of things*, in the essence that retains itself outside exteriority and yet (because it is the condition of exteriority) does not let itself be so easily forgotten. That classical philosophy is conscious of the forgetting in which it moves and at least conceives the essence as what escapes it — *that is doubtless the most interesting, the most essential character of philosophy* (whether it is that of the *"mind"* or of *"existence"*). By such a character, in effect, traditional or contemporary reflection attaches itself to the essence, and if it does not arrive at the *positive ontological determination* of its internal structure as immanence, it can appear at least in many of its developments as *the presentiment of this immanence*.

The nineteenth paragraph completes the diagnosis of Schellingian Remembrance and extends a generous judgment to classical philosophy as a whole. The move is important. Henry is not accusing the entire philosophical tradition of simple blindness; he is identifying classical philosophy's recurrent formulation of an "obscure," "unconscious," "non-objective" condition of objectivity — the "eternal absent," the "ungraspable," the "unknowable mind" — as the *transcendentally motivated presentiment of immanence* in the medium of thought oriented toward exteriority. The philosophical tradition cannot articulate immanence positively because its phenomenological vocabulary is governed by the teleology of outward-directed consciousness; but it does the next-best thing by recording the structural necessity of a non-objective condition that eludes objective thematization. Schelling, Kant (with the logical-functional reduction of transcendental conditions to an x), reflexive analysis, and German Idealism more generally — all are, for Henry, *presentiments* of the immanent essence they cannot explicitly articulate. The classical critique of rationalism (at which this paragraph now arrives) is the highest concentrated expression of this presentiment: philosophy's recognition that the essence is what escapes rational-objective grasp is philosophy's deepest self-knowledge, even though it falls short of the positive determination of immanence's structure.

**Paragraph 20\.** In the history of Western thought, however, such a presentiment does not remain only implicit: the essential philosophical content that it approaches in ambiguity finds its *explicit formulation in the critique of knowledge*.

The brief closing paragraph of §45 is pivotal in the architecture of Section III. It announces the next phase of the diagnostic. Until now, Henry has been tracing the presentiment of immanence through its *implicit* and ambiguous formulations in contemporary (Heidegger, Merleau-Ponty) and classical (Schelling) philosophy. But there is, he claims, a point in the Western tradition where the presentiment of immanence becomes *explicit* — where the tradition's deepest insight into the non-objectivity of the essence finds a direct and unambiguous philosophical articulation. This is the *critique of knowledge* — the movement in Western thought that identifies the essence of the mind or of the absolute as what *cannot* be grasped by knowledge, what exceeds the subject-object structure, what is foreclosed from rational thematization. This critique of knowledge is the domain of negative theology, of certain strands of mysticism (Eckhart again), of Kantian limits of reason, of Pascalian *ordre du cœur*, of Bergsonian intuition against analysis — all the traditions in which what is most real is posited as beyond the grasp of discursive knowledge. §46 and §47 will undertake the analysis of this critique of knowledge: §46 will treat it in the register of religion (the essence of religion as the critique of objectifying knowledge), §47 in the register of rationalism itself (the auto-critique of reason as the recognition of its own insufficiency with regard to the absolute). These sections work out the final part of the diagnostic of dissimulation before the concluding positive exhibition (§50: *the non-face of the essence*; §51: *visible and invisible*).

---

## **§ 46\. The critique of knowledge. The essence of religion**

**Paragraph 1\.** By *critique of knowledge* one does not understand here (as one does traditionally since Kant) the determination of the *positive* conditions of the knowledge of the object. It is only the *possibility* for such a knowledge — thus defined in its positivity — *to attain the essence, the "absolute"* — that is in question. Such a possibility constitutes besides, in Kant himself, the object of an explicit problematic. This problematic develops itself parallelly to the determination of the positive conditions of knowledge, in strict solidarity with this determination, in such a manner however that its originality conserves itself and finds itself marked with force by *the intervention of the concept of finitude*. One finds in modern ontology, it is true, a *positive* interpretation of finitude insofar as finitude itself enters into the definition of knowledge and of its conditions. Already in Kant, the finitude of knowledge appears identical to its effectivity if the horizon of time (which constitutes the originary exteriority of the world) determines — and that in an essential manner — the phenomenological process in its effective accomplishment, that is, the very nature of every possible experience. That such an experience is not according to Kant the experience of the absolute — that in contemporary ontology the effectivity of pure manifestation does not likewise exhaust the whole of reality and leaves on the contrary outside itself the originary essence of reality — does not this show that *finitude does not simply nor first of all designate the positive mode according to which every knowledge accomplishes itself* (a determination belonging to its effectivity and capable of serving to define it), but rather *its limit* — the inevitable reference of this knowledge to what invincibly escapes it? Because the originary essence of reality escapes it, knowledge is *finite* — in such a manner that the concept of this finitude recovers a *negative* signification. The attempt to reabsorb this negative signification into the positivity of historical experience *fails*, its motive even testifies against it. The critique of knowledge does not reduce itself to the determination of the internal structure of knowledge — of its nature and its possibility; it is not either the bringing into evidence of the necessarily progressive and indefinite character of its work of elucidation, but designates on the contrary this work as *principially incapable of concerning reality nor the essence that constitutes reality*.

The opening paragraph sharply redefines what Henry means by "critique of knowledge." This is not the Kantian sense in which critique determines the positive a priori conditions of possible experience; it is the classical sense — running from medieval negative theology through certain strands of mystical, Pascalian, Kierkegaardian, and Nietzschean thought — in which critique *limits* knowledge by showing that the absolute is not accessible to knowledge's operations. Henry notes that the modern (especially Heideggerian) interpretation of Kantian finitude tries to positivize finitude — finitude becomes the positive mode in which manifestation accomplishes itself (in time, through horizons, etc.). Henry rejects this positivization: the very fact that contemporary ontology still has to locate the "originary essence of reality" *outside* the effectivity of phenomenal manifestation means that finitude still functions, structurally, as a *limit* — as the mark of knowledge's principial inadequacy to what most matters. The critique of knowledge, on this reading, is not the articulation of the conditions *under which* knowledge can advance but the articulation of why knowledge is *constitutively incapable* of attaining the ontological ground.

**Paragraph 2\.** By *knowledge* one does not understand (when it is a matter of a general critique aiming at its nature and its possibility — or, as is the case here, at its principial impotence with regard to reality and to the problem of its determination) a *particular* act of the mind, an act of grasp explicitly directed on something. Such an act presupposes in general (besides the passive pre-donation that furnishes it with the impressional content on which it directs itself to determine it) *the milieu where this pre-donation itself is susceptible of accomplishing itself — the originary ontological milieu of pure knowledge*. On this milieu is founded every "act" of the mind, every active grasp having the knowledge of determinate objectivities for goal and constituting them. The progress of this concrete and active knowledge does not depend only in consequence on the effort of the mind nor on the importance of its effective work; its originary determination resides in the pure milieu where it effectuates itself. The determination of knowledge by this milieu and conformably to the eidetic properties prescribed by it, is *double*. Because the milieu where every act of knowledge moves is a domain of encounter constituted by *pure exteriority* (outside of which retains itself on the contrary the originary essence of reality), its *principial inaptitude to grasp this essence* is the *first ontological structural determination of knowledge*. That such a determination does not characterize this or that act of grasp considered in its particularity, in its relation to the freedom of the mind or to the specificity of its content — that its incapacity to grasp the originary essence of reality concerns *knowledge itself*, its structure and its possibility, every possible act of grasp consequently — *that is precisely the ontological foundation of the "critique of knowledge" understood in its radical signification*, its motive and what it unveils. Knowledge must be critiqued because the absolute *keeps away from it every approach accomplishing itself in the milieu where knowledge moves — that is, by knowledge itself*. In the constitutive act of its essence by which it keeps away from it every approach (every possible grasp accomplishing itself in the milieu where knowledge moves) resides *the inaccessible character of the absolute*, as a *non-provisional but insurmountable character*. The absolute, however, is not nothing — it is *the essence of life*. This is why *"the divine life subsists in the only place where it can be — inaccessible to the intellect,"* why every determination belonging to the intellect (every knowledge, every thought) is not *grasp* but *loss of being* — and that not in fact but in principle (*en droit*). *"The more a thing is knowable,"* says Nietzsche in an essential proposition (often cited and yet misunderstood in its radical and ultimate ontological foundation), *"the more it distances itself from being."*

The second paragraph establishes the structural thesis. Knowledge is not fundamentally a collection of acts; it is a *milieu* — a specific ontological dimension within which acts of knowing take place. That milieu is pure exteriority (*pure extériorité*), the ecstatic open of horizonal transcendence. Every act of knowing, whatever its content or aim, necessarily moves in this milieu because the milieu is what *constitutes* the field within which any knowing can occur. But precisely because this milieu is exteriority, and because the essence of reality is by its structure *retained outside* exteriority, the milieu of knowing is structurally *inaccessible* to the essence. Knowledge's inability to grasp the absolute is therefore not a failure of particular cognitive acts but a structural feature of knowledge itself. The Nietzschean aphorism, "*The more a thing is knowable, the more it distances itself from being*," receives here its ontological grounding: knowability is a mode of exteriorization, and exteriorization is precisely what removes something from the immanent essence of being. The medieval-mystical formula "*the divine life subsists in the only place where it can be — inaccessible to the intellect*" is Henry's shorthand for the structural thesis — *inaccessibility to the intellect* is not a contingent theological claim but an ontological determination of the absolute.

**Paragraph 3\.** The milieu where knowledge moves — in which knowledge does not approach being but rather *distances itself from being* — is *objectivity*. As soon as a thought has to do with life, as soon as it produces itself from its essence — from this essence of life which is also thought's — it no longer recognizes in objectivity the means of attaining what matters most to it, to itself. Knowledge is no longer for this thought a means of *knowing*; the absolute milieu of exteriority no longer constitutes *an access* but its contrary — no longer a *path* but what *interdicts every access* and *bars every path*, a partition and a wall. This is why *in the spiritual world where life relates to life, mind to mind, where the absolute relates to itself, there is no place for objective knowledge* — which could only produce itself in the spiritual world as a *"fault"* (*faille*), which could only destroy the spiritual world. *"Between mind and mind there is not this fault of objectivity."* That the originary essence of life does not manifest itself in objectivity, and that objectivity cannot in consequence unite us to this essence but only separate us from it — separate from self everything that is living — *the young Hegel* had still had the intuition when (apropos of the first religious community formed by Christ and his disciples, and speaking of Christ's disappearance) he shows in the suppression of Christ's *objective being* not precisely the suppression but the *condition* of Christ's relation with his disciples: *"when he had distanced himself,"* Hegel says, *"there fell also this objectivity, this partition between them and God."*

The third paragraph turns the abstract structural thesis into the concrete phenomenological thesis about the nature of objectivity as wall. When thought takes itself seriously in its relation to the essence of life (to immanence), it discovers that the objectivity-milieu is not a means of access but an obstacle — a *partition between it and what it seeks*. The young Hegel's reading of the disappearance of Jesus (this is from the so-called "*Spirit of Christianity and Its Fate*," 1798–1799) is the paradigmatic case. The historical death and physical disappearance of Christ is, on the young Hegel's reading, the *condition* of the community's spiritual union with him: as long as Christ was physically present as an objective being, his very objectivity was a barrier between the disciples and the divine life they were to share with him. Only when the objectivity fell away could the purely spiritual, immanent relation of life-to-life be constituted. Henry reads this as a major instance of the classical philosophical presentiment of the immanence-thesis: the recognition that the spiritual milieu, the milieu of life, is structurally *not* the milieu of objectivity, and that the two are indeed in structural conflict.

**Paragraph 4\.** The ontological milieu of knowledge does not only determine knowledge as principially incapable of attaining the essence — the essence of reality and of life — it also confers on the mode of its effective accomplishment a *defined structure*. Because the transcendence of temporality constitutes the originary exteriority, what shows itself in this exteriority surrounds itself with *horizons*, is taken in the unfolding of the phenomenological process, gives itself with the essential characteristic of *"passing."* The intentional explicitation of the *cogitatum* leans on the effective content of experience and prolongs this content. If in this explicitation the mind turns itself actively toward what happens to it, the fashion in which this active grasp accomplishes itself is each time determined by the mode of presentation of the given and obeys this mode. The knowledge of which it is question with the philosophical project of a critique explicitly oriented toward knowledge and toward its possibility does not let itself be identified to the ensemble of concrete acts of grasp in which the mind determines the given, nor to their simple description — but the milieu where knowledge moves nonetheless prescribes it to accomplish itself *in* such acts and *through* them. Accomplishing itself in the acts of grasp that model themselves on the phenomenological unfolding of our experiences, the knowledge of the given does not cease *stretching itself toward its horizons*; it takes on the form of *discursion*. With the coming into the field of the present evidence of the given of contents primitively implied by it, knowledge progresses — in such a manner however that (in the continuous arising of horizons) new configurations and new contents do not cease to propose themselves to knowledge's work of elucidation. For all these reasons, knowledge pursues itself necessarily as a *research* (*recherche*): such is the *second structural determination* prescribed to it by the ontological milieu where it moves.

The fourth paragraph unfolds the second structural determination of knowledge: knowledge is constitutively *research*. Because knowledge operates in the temporal-horizonal milieu of exteriority, and because in this milieu content is given discursively (successively, against horizons that keep opening up), knowledge cannot be a single completed grasp but must be an indefinitely extended process of elucidation. Every act of grasping opens new horizons that invite further acts of grasping; knowledge cannot terminate in itself but is structurally a pursuit. This is not a defect to be overcome; it is the structural form of any knowledge whatever that operates in temporal-horizonal exteriority. The point is Husserlian at the descriptive level (Husserl's analyses of horizon-structure and the endless task of the *explication* of the *cogitatum*), but Henry gives it an ontological twist: the discursive-progressive character of knowledge is the *second* consequence of knowledge's operating in the exteriority-milieu; the first was its principial inability to reach the essence.

**Paragraph 5\.** Conformably to the first determination, however, this research is *vain* and (no less necessarily) the essence of the real — which subtends in reality its systematic project of elucidation and which it ultimately aims at in this project — *escapes* it. Here must be understood the word that arises *outside every explicit or thematically constituted philosophical context*, with all the more force however, and in *the simplicity of originary language*: *"He who searches does not find."* Because the essence it ultimately aims at retains itself outside the ontological milieu where its research is produced, knowledge *does not find* the essence. Because it does not find the essence, it *researches*. In the structure of reality resides (besides the motive of its failure) *the origin of knowledge*. This knowledge however — because it does not find what it searches for — pursues its research further. In the concrete mode according to which this research pursues itself, the failure against which it strikes does not find itself simply repeated. Turning itself each time toward something else, toward the explicitation of the new horizons that propose themselves to it, advancing always further on the path of exteriority, knowledge does not cease *distancing itself from what it searches for* (and which it believes on the contrary to approach). To follow a path in such a manner that, believing to approach the goal, one does not cease distancing oneself from it, is properly *to go astray* (*s'égarer*). *Every knowing research has, with regard to its ultimate goal, the character of a going-astray* or — because "turning-toward" signifies in reality for it "turning-away-from" — *the character of a turning-away*. This is why *"life"* (insofar as it is this research) *"is a perpetual turning-away that does not even permit one to realize what it turns away from"* — that is, from itself. This is why (because this essence of life is not destroyed but only missed in knowledge) *"there is a goal but no path"*; this is why finally (speaking of life) Kafka says, still more explicitly: *"He who strives particularly to attain it is suspect of striving against it."*

The fifth paragraph brings together three figures — the originary-language formula, the Kafka aphorisms (*"there is a goal but no path"* from the *Betrachtungen über Sünde, Leid, Hoffnung und den wahren Weg*, as well as the suspect-striver line), and Henry's structural analysis — into the diagnosis of the constitutive self-defeat of knowing research. The formal structure is: knowledge aims at the essence, but because it operates in exteriority and the essence is in immanence, knowledge must seek the essence outside the immanence in which alone the essence resides. Every concrete cognitive act therefore moves *away from* the essence in the very act by which it believes it is *moving toward* the essence. This is not contingent failure that might be corrected by better method; it is structural. To follow a path believing to approach a goal while distancing oneself from it is *égarement* — going-astray. And Kafka's aphorism states the structural paradox exactly: the one who strives most intensely to attain life is precisely the one most suspect of striving against it, because striving-to-attain is itself the structural move that removes one from the immanent life one is trying to attain. Life is not something at the end of a path; it is what one already is in the mode of self-affection, and the attempt to make it a goal of knowing research is the attempt to thrust it into the exteriority where it cannot be.

**Paragraph 6\.** The whole novelistic work of Kafka recounts — with infinite humor and drollery — the peripeteias of such a research (whether it is that of reflection or takes on the contrary the form of a "real" comportment): its failures, how it rebounds and (conscious of going astray) attempts to grasp itself again, to assure itself of itself — and, in this return on self, distances itself still a bit more from this self it searches, persists in its error and goes astray more beautifully. Thus is explained — from the *eidetic incompatibility of being and knowledge* — the *antinomy* that is at the center of such a work, *the inversion* it describes, *the contradictions* that result from it. The idea that there are *two worlds*, that everything that takes place in one is without relation with reality (without importance in the other), that *means go against the goal searched for*, serve only to mask this goal — that is, as well (in the principial direction where every action and every thought lose themselves) to mask this goal's *absence*, the absence of being and of life — *the reversal of values, the inversion of perspectives* — express and comment this incompatibility. This incompatibility is not only *recognized*; it is understood *in its foundation*, grasped *in its structure*. That the essence (which remains in itself) of life does not let itself be encountered in the milieu toward which the act of knowledge directs itself (in the ontological dimension of division and of alterity) — that is what Kafka explicitly expresses: *"truth is indivisible — it cannot therefore know itself; whoever wants to know it must be a lie."* Because the act of knowledge (which divides, and gives itself in alterity an unreal object) misses the essence which is (in the act itself, first of all) that of being and of life — what the act of knowledge determines does not carry the character of reality, does not manifest the truth of reality. The exposition in nothingness is not that of being, and its language is not *veridical*; in this language rather is dissimulated what it claims to say. *"Confession and lie are identical. To be able to confess, one lies. What one is, one cannot express — since precisely one is that; one can only communicate what one is not — that is, the lie."* Because the language of knowledge does not manifest the truth of being, because life is not present in the milieu where every thought progresses, the research here attains only a *dead essence and frozen determinations*. The unhappy consciousness is not only the sensible consciousness; it is not to the sensible consciousness precisely but *to every knowledge, to every thought*, that the interrogation addresses itself which is that of the essence itself, its most essential word: *"Why do you search among the dead him who is living?"*

The sixth paragraph reads Kafka's entire literary work as a sustained phenomenological diagnosis of the eidetic incompatibility of being and knowledge. Kafka's protagonists — K. in *The Castle*, Joseph K. in *The Trial*, the man from the country in "Before the Law," and countless more — are figures of the knowing-researching subject who, in the very structural form of their search, are removed from what they seek. The more methodically K. tries to reach the Castle, the more he is kept away from it; the more Joseph K. tries to understand his trial, the more he is woven into the guilt that renders him unable to understand. This is not bad luck but structural necessity, and Kafka's *humor* is the humor of someone who has seen the structural paradox with crystalline clarity — the infinite peripeteias of self-defeating search are, from a sufficiently elevated point of view, cosmic comedy. The two Kafka aphorisms Henry quotes (*"truth is indivisible,"* *"confession and lie are identical"*) state the structural position in epigram form: truth \= immanence, indivisible self-presence; the act of knowing \= division, alterity, exposure-in-nothingness. Therefore knowing cannot grasp truth, and the language of knowing cannot speak truth — can only speak what-one-is-not, the lie. The closing Gospel formula (*"Why do you search among the dead him who is living?"* — Luke 24:5, spoken to the women at the empty tomb) is appropriated as the structural interrogation of all knowledge: the essence of life is not to be found among the "dead" — the objectified, the frozen, the exteriorized — and every knowledge that seeks life there is looking in the wrong dimension.

**Paragraph 7\.** *The structural opposition of being and knowledge is the central intuition of religion.* The conviction that characterizes religion is the *immediate consciousness of being*, which expresses itself no less immediately in the sentiment that this essential element (from which religion lives and which also constitutes the essence of all life) does not let itself be encountered on the path followed by knowledge and cannot be grasped by knowledge. From this *double intuition* and from its *originary unity* are explained the different forms religion may take and in which religion equally expresses itself. The retreat of the absolute outside the field of every possible knowledge explains and founds its *theoretical negation* — determines the philosophical content of *atheism*. When atheism does not allow itself to be reduced to its naïve formulation (to the simple systematization of the theses of natural consciousness — which claims to hold firmly to objective determinations, to what one can see and touch) — its *truth* appears in the *refusal* to search in these objective determinations (and in the milieu where they manifest themselves) anything other than what they are in effect: the determinations of the world. That in such a refusal — and through this refusal — the originary essence of being and of life finds itself not negated but on the contrary *preserved* (with the maintenance outside the world of the ontological dimension where this essence accomplishes itself), the term of this atheism become conscious of self — that to which it invites us — indicates clearly. The rejection of the concept of God is that of *a transcendent absolute* (exterior to life) — is the rejection of *exteriority* as incapable of enclosing in itself the essence of life. The invitation expressly made to consciousness *no longer to lose itself in the unreality of the milieu where it alienates its essence* — the correlative abandonment of the representations in which this alienation accomplishes itself (that is, precisely, of the concept of God), the *return to life* and to the originary sphere of existence where its concrete possibility resides — define this atheism, constitute the moments of an eidetic analysis where the originary structure of being finds itself recognized and posited. Thus one sees in *Niels Lyhne*, Jacobsen explicitly understand and describe atheism as *the refusal to substitute for the immanent reality of life a world of dream or of hope* whose only effect is to turn us away from immanent life and to prevent us from living it *in its splendor*. It is not the reality of life nor its absoluteness — it is the pretension of finding life *in the unreality of representation* — that finds itself put in question by atheism. If *"it can be useful to avoid the name of God,"* that is therefore not (as Hegel thinks) because it is a matter precisely of a *name* (which *"is not immediately and at the same time concept"*), but on the contrary by reason of the *very structure of the concept and its movement*.

The seventh paragraph delivers an astonishing and deliberately provocative reading of atheism. Henry argues that atheism — when it is not the naïve positivism that merely stays with the world of visible things but is the sophisticated philosophical atheism that refuses the concept of God — is in fact a *positive expression* of the immanence-thesis. Why? Because the concept of God, when it is the concept of a *transcendent* absolute residing in the horizon of objectivity, is precisely the concept that must be rejected if the essence of life is to be preserved *as* immanence. The transcendent-objective God is the most extreme case of the *alienation* of life into exteriority — the projection of the immanent essence into a world beyond the world, a *Hinterwelt* of the sort Nietzsche diagnosed. Atheism, rightly understood, is the recognition that the essence of life cannot be found in this projected beyond and must be recovered as immanent. The reference to J. P. Jacobsen's novel *Niels Lyhne* (1880) is telling — this is a Danish naturalist novel whose protagonist is an atheist who refuses the religious consolations of his culture but does so precisely in the name of a more intense engagement with the splendor of immanent life, not in the name of a deflating materialism. Jacobsen (whom Rilke cherished) is for Henry the literary exemplar of *philosophical* atheism as positive articulation of immanence. The implicit critique of Hegel is also important: Hegel (in the *Phenomenology*'s discussion of religion, and elsewhere) suggested that one might avoid the name of God because a name is not a concept. Henry disagrees: the useful avoidance of the name "God" is not because names lack conceptual content but because the concept of God, when interpreted as transcendent absolute, is itself the source of the alienation of life.

**Paragraph 8\.** That *in the being which remains in itself* resides on the contrary (and finds itself constituted, in its irreducibility to the milieu of this movement) *the reality of the essence and of life* — this reality identically makes the experience of it, makes the experience of its proper reality, *in religion*. *Faith is the internal experience of life and of its essence*; its traditional opposition to knowledge expresses philosophically *the ontological structural heterogeneity of being and knowledge*. This is why (as religious consciousness understands or rather spontaneously *lives*) the belief by which it defines itself is not a *flight* outside reality but *the immediate apprehension of this reality* — the originary experience of being, constitutive of being itself and of its structure. *"To believe,"* says Kafka, *"signifies: to liberate in oneself the indestructible — or more exactly, to liberate oneself — or more exactly: to be indestructible — or more exactly: to be."* *The ontological identity of being and belief* (*Glauben ist Sein*) is the constant theme of every authentic religious thought — which lives this identity and expresses it as well *as the correlative heterogeneity of being and knowledge*. That being withdraws from knowledge no longer determines the theoretical negation of being in thought but rather *the comprehension of its internal structure*. Such a structure accounts for the impossibility that principially affects the very project of a *knowing grasp* of the absolute — that is, as well, every *teaching* concerning the absolute and accomplishing itself by way of knowledge. *"God,"* said the young Hegel, *"cannot be object of study or of teaching — for he is life and can only be understood by life."* The impossibility that principially affects the project of a knowing grasp of the absolute calls in existence and renders *legitimate* the determination to hold oneself *apart* from such a project — gives its metaphysical and religious signification to *the state of ignorance*. *"The ignorance of Socrates,"* Kierkegaard was to say (and that not by accident), *"was a kind of fear and worship of God."* It was not only, to tell the truth, like the transposition into Greece of the Judaic idea of the fear of God, but went back again to the origin of this idea — to *the act of the essence of retaining itself in itself*. This is why (because it values finally as the recognition and the preservation of the absolute itself and of its internal structure) *Socratic ignorance lets itself be understood as essentially ambiguous, identical rather to its contrary* — why *"the divinity has recognized in Socrates the greatest of knowings."*

The eighth paragraph delivers the positive formulation: faith is not an epistemic state (believing something without adequate evidence) but an *ontological* state — the internal experience of life and its essence, that is, the immanent self-affection of life that Henry has throughout called the structure of immanence. The Kafka aphorism *"To believe signifies… to be indestructible… to be"* states the thesis exactly: faith in its most essential sense is *being-in-immanent-life*, self-liberation into the indestructible immanent self-affection of life itself. This is why the Lutheran-Kierkegaardian opposition of faith and knowledge is not the counter-rational irrationalism of fideism but the correct philosophical registration of the ontological heterogeneity between immanence (the milieu of life) and exteriority (the milieu of knowing). The young Hegel formula — "*God cannot be object of study or of teaching, for he is life and can only be understood by life*" — puts the thesis classically: the relation to the absolute is not a cognitive relation but a *life-to-life* relation, a being-in-immanent-life. The Socratic ignorance ("*I know that I know nothing*") is now read through this lens: Socrates' ignorance is not an epistemic modesty or a confession of limits of reason but the positive *philosophical* recognition that the absolute withdraws from the knowing grasp — a recognition that, as Kierkegaard saw, has the structural form of a *fear and worship*, a holding-oneself-back from attempting to capture what structurally withdraws. Hence Socratic ignorance is "ambiguous, identical to its contrary" — it is the highest knowing precisely because it is the recognition of the absolute's structural non-knowability.

**Paragraph 9\.** Socrates, it is true, *posed questions*. Is not every interrogation like an invitation to knowledge — or rather its first step, the arising in a certain direction and within a defined framework, of the horizon where something must be able to show itself and be grasped? At his questions, however, Socrates (as is known) *did not expect an answer* — if it were not to make appear immediately their illusory character. The dialectic as he understands it does not aim at the progressive constitution of a *knowing* (*savoir*) but rather at the *non-knowing* (*non-savoir*) and ends in it. This non-knowing constitutes the essence of the *trouble* inherent in every question, in knowledge itself insofar as the essence necessarily escapes it. This dissimulation of what it searches for, the knowledge that interrogates may well experience as an exterior or provisional determination — but it belongs to knowledge in reality and arises at the same time as knowledge. The trouble in which knowledge lives this dissimulation does not therefore precede its own question nor result from it as a consequence: it is *produced* by the question and is *identical* to it. *"If no one asks me what time is,"* says Saint Augustine, *"I know it; if someone asks me I do not know it."*

The ninth paragraph deepens the analysis of Socratic interrogation. Socrates poses questions, but Socratic questioning is not the initiation of a knowing-research that aims at a positive answer; it is the *dialectical movement toward non-knowing*, which constitutes the essence of the trouble inherent in every knowing-question. The famous Augustinian *aporia* about time (*Confessions* XI, 14\) receives a characteristically Henry-ian reading: Augustine's difficulty is not a contingent cognitive failure to articulate a concept of time he grasps implicitly; it is the structural *trouble* that arises whenever knowing is turned toward what is most immediate, most immanent, most intimately lived. Time, as the form of the life of the soul, is not something the soul can set at a distance as an object — and therefore when interrogated about it, the soul finds itself unable to produce an objective definition. What the soul lives it cannot say; what it can say it does not live. This is the structural opposition of being and knowledge in its most intimate register.

**Paragraph 10\.** The failure of speculative knowing in its pretension to grasp the being of the absolute — that is, the essence of the divine — gives its philosophical signification to *the distinction instituted by Fichte* (apropos of the divine precisely) between the *"historical"* and the *"metaphysical"* element of the phenomenon. That *the primitive fact of Christianity* — the being-founded-in-God of Jesus, his divine essence — does not let itself be included in a metaphysics, that it is not *"the necessary consequence of a higher and more general law and cannot be deduced from it"*, that it does not admit beyond itself the transcendence of a horizon of comprehension from which it would be explicable — this does *not* result from a provisional failing of knowledge but from the nature of knowledge and from the ontological milieu where it moves — results from the nature of *this fact itself* as *foundationally foreign to such a milieu*. Such foreignness determines what there is of *"historical"* in Jesus, and this *historicity* of the primitive fact of Christianity signifies in turn nothing other than *the definition of its essence as immanence*. From this essence only and from its internal structure is illuminated the rejection of every possible knowledge concerning it. This is why (as Fichte notes) Jesus *"explains absolutely nothing of the world by means of his religious principle, and deduces nothing from this principle,"* why (as concerns his proper being) Jesus *pushes aside the very possibility of a speculative knowledge*. Only his *historical existence* — the *interior experience of God*, that is, God himself as constitutive of this existence and consequently of Jesus's being — counts in his eyes. Because *in the internal structure of this originary experience, transcendence is not included* — to what reveals itself in this experience one cannot come from a horizon, and Jesus's being cannot be understood. *"For Jesus,"* says Fichte with infinite profundity, *"such a transcendence was pure impossibility; for to this effect it would have been necessary for him in his personality to distinguish himself from God, to pose himself apart, to be astonished before himself as before a curious phenomenon, and to take it as a task to resolve the enigma of the possibility of an individual such as him."* The interdiction expressly formulated by Jesus and ceaselessly opposed by him to those who want to establish a distinction between him and his Father — the correlative impossibility of knowing him in the milieu of exteriority — are explained thus from the historical character of his existence and from the structure prescribed to this existence by this character.

The tenth paragraph reads late Fichte (the *Anweisung zum seligen Leben*, 1806, already discussed in §38 as the site of Fichte's partial breakthrough toward immanence) on the "historical" and "metaphysical" elements of the Christian phenomenon. Fichte distinguishes in the religious phenomenon (Jesus) a "historical" element (the brute fact of Jesus's being-grounded-in-God, his *being*) from a "metaphysical" element (the conceptual deductions that could follow from this fact). Fichte's striking thesis is that the historical element *cannot* be deduced from any higher principle and does not itself explain anything about the world — Jesus "deduces nothing from his religious principle." Henry reads this precisely: the "historical" character of the primitive fact is Fichte's name for its *immanence*, its resistance to inclusion in the horizon of speculative-metaphysical transcendence. Jesus, on Fichte's reading, stands in an immediate relation of immanent self-identity with the Father — a relation that structurally excludes the self-distinction, the setting-oneself-apart-as-object, that would be required for any speculative knowing of this relation. Fichte's formulation — "*for Jesus, such a transcendence was pure impossibility*" — is exactly the philosophical registration of the thesis that the Christ-God-relation is constituted in immanent self-affection and therefore structurally excludes objectifying reflection. The *je suis* of Jesus ("I and the Father are one") is not a conceptual claim but the immediate self-articulation of immanent life, and it is this structural character that makes the later theological attempts to conceptually comprehend the Incarnation structurally impossible: one is trying to objectify what by its structure cannot be objectified.

**Paragraph 11\.** This is why (speaking of this existence of Jesus and of what it was for him) Fichte can say again that *"he did not know it under the form of general concept — in the manner in which the speculative philosopher knows it and seeks to define it; for he did not draw from concept but purely and simply from his self-consciousness. He considered it historically."* It is because (by reason of the structure of his existence) Jesus could *not* propose this existence to a knowledge — that his teaching had to be what it is: not precisely the *exterior* communication of a *knowledge* but *the transmission of his existence itself* — and that in the ontological milieu which is his own, *in the originarily immanent sphere of existence which is the essence of life*: *"The only initiation he could give to his disciples was: to become similar to him."*

The final paragraph of §46 delivers the structural consequence for the nature of Christian teaching. Because the being of Jesus is constituted in immanence and cannot be propositionalized in a knowing, his teaching cannot have the form of a doctrine transmitted from one subject to another. Teaching in the ordinary sense presupposes the exteriority-milieu — the teacher and learner face the same content in the horizon of objectivity; the content passes from one mind to the other through its objective mediation. But the "content" of Jesus's teaching is not a content in this sense; it is his own immanent mode of life-in-God. And therefore the transmission of this teaching can only take the form of the *transmission of his existence itself* — a transmission that accomplishes itself not in the milieu of objectivity but in the immanent sphere of life. The Gospel formula Fichte quotes (*"to become similar to him"*) is the structural designation of this non-objective transmission: discipleship is not the adoption of a set of doctrines but the entry into a *form of immanent life* similar to the teacher's. And this is why Christianity, when it degenerates into a system of propositions and doctrines, is a falsification of its own original structure. What Henry will in his late work call "Christianity" in the strong sense (especially in *C'est moi la vérité*, 1996, and *Paroles du Christ*, 2002\) is precisely this immanent transmission of life — a phenomenological ontology of Christian truth as the truth of immanent life. The seeds of that late project are already here in 1963: Christianity is the privileged historical articulation of the immanence-thesis, because Christ is the one who lived and taught not the knowing of a transcendent God but the immanent communion of life-with-life.

---

## **§ 47\. The critique of knowledge within rationalism**

**Paragraph 1\.** *The eidetic incompatibility of being considered in its internal structure and of knowledge* does not only constitute one of the fundamental intuitions of religion. Its *belonging to the reality it defines* renders it *perceptible and operative* at the heart even of thoughts which claim on the contrary to *found on knowledge itself* and on its systematic development a sufficient and adequate approach to being. The manifestation of this incompatibility is, *in the heart of rationalism*, the contradiction to which rationalism finds itself inevitably led, *its interior transformation into its contrary*. The more categorical the identification of the experience of being with the act of knowledge, the more explicit the comprehension of knowledge from the projection of a horizon and as a grasp accomplishing itself in a horizon — the more inevitable also the moment when, striking against the reality it precisely cannot apprehend in its knowledge, thought finds itself constrained to *renounce* knowledge and the direction prescribed by knowledge. This *overturning of positions* is visible for example in the book consecrated by Jean Laporte to Descartes — and precisely to his "rationalism." After having affirmed that every knowledge consists in "seeing" — that is, in "taking consciousness of the objects present to it" — one must *avow* that reality does not let itself be recognized nor grasped in an apprehension of this sort. The *unreality of the milieu* where knowledge moves puts in question the validity of the criteria by which knowledge had attempted to seat its ontological signification. *"Clarity and distinction are not marks of reality but of possibility."* Likewise, when (after having determined the essence of the soul as *thought* — that is, in fact, after having identified and confused it with knowledge itself and finally with the unreality of its milieu) Cartesianism wishes to add to this essence the *element of reality* and gives itself — with the taking into consideration of the theme of the *substantial union* — as a *problematic of concrete existence*, the fundamental ontological presuppositions by which Cartesianism is primitively defined as a rationalism *become inoperative* and must be *dismissed*. If the conceptual apparatus of knowledge (the eidetic determination of the positive modes of its accomplishment) is no longer of any help to the thought that wishes to attain the *internal structure of existence* and to *make the experience* of it — if "*he who wants to perceive clearly his union with the body must turn away… from a knowledge of this sort*" (from knowledge by clear and distinct idea — that is, in fact, from every knowledge) — if "*to well conceive the substantial union one must experience it in oneself without philosophizing… one must live it*" — if the path by which one arrives at the conception of this union "*contrasts strangely with the ordinary path of scientific or metaphysical conceptions*" and implies *renouncing the professional orientation of the philosopher* — *that is because there is no transcendence of reality* and, for this reason, *the dialectical overturning of rationalism has accomplished itself*.

The opening paragraph launches the critique of rationalism from within. The Laporte book is the 1945 *Le rationalisme de Descartes* (published in that year, a classic of the French Cartesian scholarship). Henry reads Laporte's study as a symptomatic text — one in which a sympathetic scholar of Cartesianism is forced, by the internal logic of his reading, to acknowledge that Cartesian rationalism *breaks against* reality. Clarity and distinction, the canonical criteria of Cartesian knowledge, turn out to be criteria of the *possible* and not of the *real*. When Descartes comes to the problem of the substantial union of soul and body (the problem of the *sixth Meditation* and, more especially, of the correspondence with Elisabeth), he is forced to admit that this union is *not* knowable by clear and distinct idea — that it must be *lived* rather than thought, *experienced* rather than known. This is, on Henry's reading, the *dialectical self-overturning* of rationalism: from within rationalism's own articulation, rationalism is compelled to renounce knowledge as the means of access to real existence and to invoke instead a non-conceptual, non-objectifying mode of experience. The critique of knowledge appears not as external opposition to rationalism but as rationalism's own internal logic, pressing against its own limits.

**Paragraph 2\.** To the comprehension of Cartesian rationalism (that is, to every act of comprehension as such) escapes in general *the real* — not only the concrete existence thought under the title of the "union" but its determinations as *interior determinations of being*: *will and action*. The impossibility (lived by Descartes and expressed by him as implying the provisional character of morality) of giving to action an assured foundation assumed and furnished by knowledge itself, does not depend on the unfinished state of knowledge — on the necessity for man of acting before there ends the (never-exhaustive) exploration of the concrete historical situation each time his. With the theme of *urgency* rationalism believes to promote or to maintain in the domain of ethics the validity of its own criteria, and limits itself to noting that "circumstances" render their application difficult or only partial and progressive. But when it is a matter of defining what properly constitutes this domain of ethics — when thought comes to strike against the problem of the *interior determination of action itself* — the eidetic analysis of action lets appear at the same time *its originary rooting in being* and *its structural opposition to the sphere of knowledge*. Such is the signification of the Cartesian problematic of *will*. That the nature of will does not let itself be reduced to that of the understanding, that will escapes every possible grasp accomplishing itself on the mode of evidence — and of confused thought as well — that is precisely what determines will not as a lesser reality but as *the originary essence* of reality. Because it constitutes the originary essence of reality, will does not only oppose itself to knowledge *as what always and inevitably holds itself beyond knowledge's act of apprehension*; it still constitutes *what there is of real in this act of apprehension*. Thus one sees knowledge find its own foundation in what by principle refuses itself to the ideality of the milieu that knowledge develops — in this act of the *"I think"* ultimately understood and interpreted as an *"I can"*. Thus manifests itself again — at the heart even of the horizon drawn by its own presuppositions — the *failure* of the presuppositions in virtue of which thought believes itself to grasp being immediately on the plane of knowledge. *Voluntarism does not simply oppose itself to intellectualism; it is its consequence.* It is comforting to think that the interpretation of Cartesianism (as of every authentic thought) does not obey only the subjective preferences of commentators and specialists but repeats (as in spite of itself) *the prescriptions of the essence*. After having attempted (following Descartes) to seat the character of human action on that of knowledge and on the finitude of knowledge in its necessarily temporal accomplishment, Jaspers comes to the essential — to *the identification of will and being*. It is because being principially escapes knowledge that action takes on the form of *audacity and risk*, in such a manner that the apparent gratuity of the decision in its abrupt arising does not signify the arbitrariness of what is without foundation but determines the being of decision *in its foundational opacity to the phenomenality of the world*.

The second paragraph extends the critique of rationalism from the Cartesian problem of the substantial union to the Cartesian problem of the will. The Cartesian "provisional morality" (from *Discours de la méthode* Part III) is usually read as a temporary expedient — one needs rules for action while the full edifice of knowledge is still under construction. But Henry argues this reading misses what is structurally at stake. The will is *not reducible* to the understanding; it is not a mode of cognitive grasp but a mode of *being*. And precisely because will is being's own internal determination, it *cannot* be captured by cognitive grasp, not even in principle; the provisionality of Cartesian morality is therefore not a temporary stage of knowledge-construction but a *structural* feature of the relation between knowledge and will. The second key move is the interpretation of the Cartesian *cogito* as *"I can"* rather than *"I think."* This is a thesis Henry will develop at length in *Philosophie et phénoménologie du corps* (1965), drawing on Maine de Biran: the ego's most fundamental self-affection is not as a thinking subject confronting representations but as a striving-active power, an "I can" that lives itself in immanent effort and willing. The late references to Jaspers (*audacity, risk, abruptness of decision*) take Jaspers's existential vocabulary and read it as a philosophical registration of the irreducibility of will-as-being to knowledge-as-representation. Voluntarism (the philosophical thesis that will is ontologically primary) is thus not the opposite of intellectualism but its internal development: when intellectualism strikes against reality and finds that reality escapes it, intellectualism *itself* is compelled to posit will as the ground it cannot reach.

**Paragraph 3\.** The whole philosophy of Jaspers attests the *irreducible opposition of being and knowledge*.
