It is in the light of this opposition, and by it, as *foundationally foreign* consequently to what makes the clarity of thought or of reason, that existence (which constitutes here the principal theme of the problematic) finds itself precisely defined. Whence the institution in Jaspers of *a critique of knowledge* whose philosophical signification is to make appear at the heart itself of knowing and of its development what necessarily escapes it. What escapes knowing (and that necessarily) — what holds itself beyond the ontological milieu where knowing moves, beyond every objectivity and every possible representation — is called *transcendence*. This transcendence values as a determination of real being and concerns for this reason *existence itself*, which is secretly linked to it. Because (as concerns at least its real being) existence does not let itself be grasped in a representation nor reduced to objective being — or, as Jaspers often says, to *empirical being* — existence remains affected by an *essential obscurity* and, in its ineffable intimacy, *refuses itself to knowing*. For this reason also — because the determinations it gives itself are those of being and produce themselves from being — existence (as has been seen) *assumes* these determinations in risk, and its accomplishment in these determinations takes on each time the form of a *"leap."* This is why again the project of constituting *a psychology of existence* (of its various determinations as of its fundamental attitudes — a psychology of *Weltanschauungen*, for example) limits itself necessarily to the description of *simple possibilities*, while the actualization of these possibilities in a singular existence — what makes the effective reality of this existence — escapes necessarily both the design of objective knowing and its realization.

The third paragraph turns to Karl Jaspers's philosophy as the most thoroughly articulated version of the rationalism-that-overcomes-itself. Jaspers's position (in the three-volume *Philosophie* of 1932 and in *Psychologie der Weltanschauungen* of 1919\) is that existence cannot be grasped by knowledge — that the attempt to produce a knowing of existence generates only objective determinations that systematically miss what makes existence real. Hence the Jaspersian vocabulary of *Existenz* (as distinguished from *Dasein* in Jaspers's own special sense — empirical being), the "leap" (*Sprung*), the "encompassing" (*Umgreifendes*), the "ciphers" (*Chiffren*) — all vocabulary designed to articulate what escapes objectifying knowledge. Henry notes that Jaspers's project of a *Psychologie der Weltanschauungen* is structurally doomed: a psychology of existence can only describe *possible* attitudes and determinations; it cannot reach the actuality of existence, which lies in the leap that cannot be objectified. Jaspers's term for what escapes knowing is *transcendence* — and here a dangerous ambiguity emerges, which the next paragraph will unfold.

**Paragraph 4\.** Because, in its transcendence, *reality retains itself beyond every possible representation*, consciousness can open itself to reality only if, in turn, consciousness *surpasses representation* and orients itself deliberately *beyond the world and objectivity*. This effort of consciousness to surpass itself every objectivity as such and every representation is the *act of transcending*, which manifests itself precisely as this effort, as an *élan* and an *impulsion*. These become visible in turn in Reason and in the movement by which Reason does not cease (as Kant had recognized) *to project itself beyond the productions of the understanding and of its thought*, in faith and — in a general manner — in all the determinations of existence that accomplish themselves in Reason from its originary reality, that is, finally, from *transcendence*. It is this transcendence of reality and the correlative necessity for consciousness (which does not want to renounce this reality) to accomplish the act of transcending that determine *the failure of ontology* — that is, of an objective representation of being and of its grasp as totality. The bursting-apart of this totality and its impossible coming-to-pass, the recoil-to-infinity of the objectives of knowing, the failure of knowledge, attest at the heart of knowledge and *for* knowledge the reality of what at once subtends knowledge and remains foundationally foreign to it.

The fourth paragraph introduces the critical ambiguity at the heart of Jaspers's system. Jaspers correctly identifies that reality escapes representation, and correctly identifies that consciousness must *transcend* representation to reach reality. But he names this act of transcending "transcendence" — and this name encodes a structural confusion. Henry's entire Section III has been arguing that reality's retention outside representation is *immanence*, not transcendence. The act of "surpassing" the milieu of representation, if it is to reach reality, must go *inward* (toward the immanent self-affection that constitutes the subject) rather than *outward* (toward a transcendent horizon beyond the world). Jaspers, however, thinks of the transcending as a movement *beyond* the world, toward an absolute that lies *farther than* the horizon of objects. This move lands Jaspers in the familiar paradox: to think the beyond-the-horizon, he must think it *as something accessible in some horizon*, because thought itself operates only in horizons. The "failure of ontology" Jaspers diagnoses is real but is misread: ontology fails because it tries to represent immanence in the medium of exteriority, not because reality lies somewhere beyond the last horizon of exteriority.

**Paragraph 5\.** How does reality manifest itself to knowledge — the reality of what remains foundationally foreign to it? The impotence of knowledge to produce itself as a whole and as an achieved system, the movement of consciousness that carries it invincibly beyond the objectivities constituted by the understanding, what makes the reality of this movement (and similarly of every effort, every élan, every impulsion, the reality of existence itself and what determines it, the act of transcending and transcendence) — all this cannot be *simply affirmed*. If the philosophy of existence is something other than an arbitrary metaphysics, it has need, for the reality by which it claims to define itself, of *an assured foundation*. This foundation can only consist in *the determination of the phenomenological status of this reality*. But the critique of knowledge sketched by Jaspers develops itself inside what constitutes the *ultimate horizon* of knowledge — the horizon of rationalism, as well as of the doctrines opposed to it (of empiricism for example). The question that has just been encountered develops itself henceforth and lets itself be formulated in a rigorous manner: *how does there manifest itself, in the ontological milieu of representation, what principially refuses itself to the phenomenality of this milieu and "necessarily escapes" this milieu?*

The fifth paragraph poses the structural question that will drive the rest of the critique. Jaspersian philosophy of existence invokes transcendence, the act of transcending, the leap, the reality of existence that escapes knowing — but it invokes these as *simply affirmed* without grounding them phenomenologically. The question Jaspers cannot avoid but also cannot answer is: what is the *phenomenological status* of transcendence? How does transcendence, which by Jaspers's own account escapes representation, *show itself* to the thinker who invokes it? The question is genuinely sharp. If transcendence manifests itself in any mode, it manifests itself either in representation (in which case it has not escaped representation) or not in representation (in which case how is the philosopher aware of it?). Jaspers's position thus faces a structural dilemma: either transcendence is genuinely outside representation and cannot be spoken of (which would end the philosophy of existence as philosophy), or transcendence shows itself in some mode after all (which would mean it is not really what Jaspers claims). Henry's question to Jaspers is phenomenological and rigorous — what is the phenomenality of transcendence?

**Paragraph 6\.** *The contradiction included in this question cannot in any way constitute the principle of its solution.* When one has said and repeated that "metaphysical thought" proposes for itself precisely as object *to think what can no longer be thought* — and (renouncing for this the use of the categories which are its own — that is, finally, its very structure and its proper form) to grasp (in this act of formally transcending itself) *the insurmountable character of its failure* — that the comprehension of this failure (and, what is more, the will not to escape it but to sink further into it and, in a certain way, to dedicate oneself to it) is identically, however, that *of being itself as principially escaping every effort of apprehension* — that, consequently, *"in this failure of knowing, it is being itself that comes to my encounter"* and that thus the *"passion of failure is the supreme lucidity"* — *it is fitting to give to these developments* and to the "steep dialectic" they define *some support in reality*. If, as Jaspers himself affirms, *"the non-being (revealed by failure) of every being which is accessible to us — is the being of transcendence"* — it must be said, if this non-being is not entirely *nothing*, what phenomenologically this non-being (identical to absolute being) *is*.

The sixth paragraph drives the critique. The Jaspersian move — "metaphysical thought is thought that thinks what cannot be thought; the failure of thought is the advent of being; the passion of failure is supreme lucidity" — sounds philosophically noble but is, on close inspection, logically incoherent unless one can give *some phenomenological content* to the "being" that is supposedly revealed by the failure. If the non-being revealed by failure is genuinely nothing, then nothing is revealed, and the whole apparatus of *existence-encountering-being-in-its-failure* collapses. If the non-being revealed by failure is something — if it has any phenomenological status whatever — then it must be described, and the description must either identify it with some mode of phenomenality (in which case we need a positive theory of what that mode is) or identify it as lying outside all phenomenality (in which case we cannot talk about it). Jaspers does not resolve this dilemma; he performs a sublime-sounding philosophical gesture that leaves the structural question unanswered.

**Paragraph 7\.** The *immanence of transcendence* (and by this must be understood transcendence's *representation* in the world as being-given to thought and as object) is, according to Jaspers, its only possible manifestation. Likewise it is for existence, which cannot manifest itself (also) except under the form of *empirical being*. To the principial incapacity in which empirical being finds itself to exhibit in itself, in its representation, what by nature refuses itself to representation, Jaspers thinks he escapes with his *theory of the "cipher."* The objective entity constitutes the unique phenomenological given, the sole possible content for thought — in such a manner however that, in *authentic existence*, the objective entity gives itself to authentic existence with the essential signification of *referring to something other*, of being an *"appearance"* as *"appearance of…"* (*"Erscheinung"*). That "appearance" is, in the cipher, "appearance of" — that it gives itself in the cipher with the signification of referring to something other, namely to *being itself as irreducible precisely to this appearance* (that is, to pure representation as such) — this is now what requires an explanation. *Far from being able to determine the originary structure of being in its radical ontological heterogeneity with respect to representation, the signification that representation takes on in the cipher presupposes on the contrary such a determination — the effectivity of the originary phenomenological content of absolute being, as its condition.* With his philosophy of the cipher, Jaspers supposes resolved the problem of the being of transcendence such as he understands it — and that of the very possibility of its affirmation.

The seventh paragraph delivers the central critique of Jaspers's theory of ciphers. The cipher (*Chiffre*) is Jaspers's technical term for an objective phenomenon that, beyond its ordinary objective content, gives itself *as appearance of* transcendent being. A cipher is, on Jaspers's account, a phenomenon whose ordinary appearance carries the additional signification of pointing beyond itself to what cannot appear — this is how Jaspers thinks he solves the dilemma posed by paragraph 5\. Appearances can refer beyond themselves; so transcendent being can be "manifested" *through* appearances even though transcendent being itself does not appear. Henry's critique is devastating: the signification of "appearance of" — the referring-beyond-itself of the cipher — already presupposes the determination of the very thing it is supposed to produce. For an appearance to *be* an appearance of being, being must already be determined in its being, in its phenomenological structure. Jaspers wants to derive being from the cipher; but he can only do so if he presupposes that being is already available to ground the cipher's reference. The "theory of ciphers" is thus circular: it presupposes what it claims to explain.

**Paragraph 8\.** Either the signification that appearance has of surpassing itself must *belong to appearance*, must *enter into appearance's effective phenomenological content* — and the surpassing itself must manifest itself *as such*. The manifestation of the surpassing, the being-beyond-the-entity as *effective* being, is *the phenomenological content of pure objectivity*, the manifestation of transcendence as *transcendence of the horizon* — that is, *representation* precisely. Far from escaping representation, the thought that (to accomplish the surpassing) leans on the effective and concrete character of the surpassing *moves in representation* — *is the thought of the world*. The transcendence of Reason with respect to the understanding signifies nothing other than *this transcendence of the originary world*. Thus one sees again Jaspers attempt to seat the signification that appearance has of referring to what retains itself in principle outside it on the *disappearance* of the entity. Such a disappearance is however nothing other than *time*, which constitutes precisely the originary ontological structure of representation and its horizon. What manifests itself in representation (and, conformably to representation's law, disappears) cannot therefore lead *beyond* representation. This mute expression by which every thing becomes cipher — the foundational strangeness into which things enter — it does not belong to the philosopher freely to interpret. If the frightening silence of the Earth sometimes seems to us to be a speech, the nature of this speech and what it enunciates are *known* to us. This is why such a language says nothing more than what it says — it is *the language of things*, *their manifestation*.

The eighth paragraph deepens the critique. If the cipher's referring-beyond-itself is to be non-circular, it must itself be a phenomenon — the referring-beyond must *show itself* in the cipher's content. But what would it mean for a referring-beyond to show itself? Either this showing is itself an event of representation (in which case the cipher's reference-beyond is just a further object of representation, not an escape from representation), or the reference-beyond is somehow a feature of the cipher that does *not* reduce to representation (in which case we need a positive account of this non-representational feature, which Jaspers does not provide). The "transcendence of Reason" (the Kantian idea that Reason surpasses the limits of Understanding) is, on Henry's reading, still a movement *within* the world of representation — Reason's transcending is the horizon-structure of the world, not a movement to a different ontological dimension. When Jaspers appeals to the *disappearance* of entities (their finitude, their fading) as the basis for the cipher's reference-beyond, he is appealing to *temporality* — but temporality is precisely the structure of representation itself, the horizon that constitutes objectivity. Temporal disappearance thus takes place *inside* representation and cannot serve to transport us *outside* representation. The eloquent romantic topos — that the silence of the Earth sometimes speaks to us, that things become ciphers of the divine — is, for Henry, a poetic conceit without phenomenological grounding. Things say what things say; their "language" is the language of their manifestation as things, not a communication of transcendent being.

**Paragraph 9\.** To this manifestation in any case Jaspers opposes only *the unknown*. If the absolute being of which he speaks escapes representation (that is, according to the author of *Philosophie*, every possible manifestation in general), that is because it shares with the existent that the world manifests obscurely *at least one character* (in truth essential): its foundational heterogeneity with respect to the ontological element of pure manifestation. Because it accomplishes itself within a horizon that is ultimately the same as that of rationalism, the critique of rationalism *loses all ontological signification*. Far from putting in question the pretension to universality of a determinate form of manifestation, and from being able to concern consequently the specifically ontological problem of *the internal structure of pure phenomenality as such*, Jaspers's critique *debouches on what has no name* and which Jaspers calls (in a totally illegitimate manner) *being*, the absolute. Such a "being," conceived in reality *in the image of worldly determinations* and borrowing from them the characters they seem to manifest — *force, unconsciousness, irrationality* — is most often only a kind of *super-existent*. Voluntarism, for example, accomplishes itself with the simple metaphysical promotion of natural powers; the prestigious concept of action that voluntarism believes it can oppose (as Goethe's Faust does) to the originary Verb, remains of course *without any status*, and the problem of this status is neither posed nor even perceived. Thus deprived of all ontological signification, the critique of rationalism finds its *naïve culmination* in an elementary *irrationalism*. This irrationalism, it is true, has been explicitly refused by Jaspers. But the subjective preferences of philosophers and their intentions are without power before the interior logic of the system. That existence must be elucidated but that it can only be elucidated *in an indirect manner* by a light to which existence remains foundationally foreign in its originary and proper "being" — does not tear but *rejects irremediably* existence into the night of brute determinations. The praise of intellectualism, the appeal to the unique Western philosophy, *do not temper but found an irrationalism of chaos*.

The closing paragraph delivers the verdict on Jaspers and, more broadly, on all critique of rationalism that operates within the rationalist horizon. Because Jaspers's critique does not overcome the ontological monism of rationalism (he still identifies phenomenality with objective manifestation), his critique can only reach *beyond* this monism by positing an *unknown* that shares with the world one crucial feature — heterogeneity with respect to the true ontological element of pure manifestation (which, on Henry's analysis, is immanence). But an unknown defined solely by heterogeneity to representation is, structurally, not an ontologically distinct dimension — it is only a boundary-concept, a *residual* of what representation cannot handle. And so, despite all Jaspers's careful elaboration, the "absolute being" of Jaspers turns out to be a kind of *super-existent* — a more powerful, more mysterious version of worldly being, characterized by worldly-borrowed features (force, unconsciousness, irrationality). This is, Henry argues, the fate of every "irrationalism" that attempts to critique rationalism from within rationalism's own horizon: it can only oppose to rationalism a chaos — the brute underside of rational determinations, which has precisely the same structure as rational determinations but with the signs reversed. Goethe's Faust opposing *In the beginning was the Act* to *In the beginning was the Verb* is, on this diagnosis, a merely *inverted* rationalism, not a genuine overcoming. The appeal to voluntarism, action, force, life-beyond-knowledge — all these, when they remain within the rationalist horizon, are only the night-side of rationalism, the super-existent that reason has not managed to grasp. The genuine overcoming of rationalism would require — and this is the thesis Henry has been preparing since §45 — the articulation of a *different* ontological dimension, the dimension of *immanence*, which is not the unknown-beyond-representation but the immanent self-affection of life. Without this articulation, every critique of rationalism is only rationalism's inverted shadow.

---

## **§ 48\. The ontological signification of the critique of rationalism**

**Paragraph 1\.** Otherwise significant, otherwise important in the history of philosophical thought and of its development, is the critique of rationalism that reveals itself capable — not of simply opposing to rationalism the *abscons* character of what remains in itself foreign to the light of phenomenality — but of *putting in question the structure of phenomenality such as rationalism understands it*, that is, precisely, the ontological horizon that is ultimately its own. Now it is remarkable that such a critique produced itself *in modern philosophy* — and that at the moment even when rationalism was finding its full development and, for the first time perhaps, an explicit ontological foundation. Is it by chance that it is precisely in *Malebranche* — where exteriority is posed without equivocation as the condition of the intelligibility of phenomena, that is, as constitutive of their pure phenomenality — that, brutally, *the concept of phenomenality divides itself and lets appear a foundationally other mode of its realization*? Knowledge, transcendentally understood from *extension* — that is, precisely, from the originary spatiality of pure exteriority as such — finds itself immediately attained in its pretension to universality. *Something escapes knowledge that is not the existent and that however is not nothing* — something whose effectivity is constituted by *phenomenality itself and the ontologically pure mode according to which it phenomenalizes itself*. The central affirmation of Malebranche's philosophy — *the affirmation according to which the soul cannot be known* — must indeed be understood. It signifies in no way (if we want to recognize it however and to grasp it in its decisive ontological range) that *the substance of the soul remains unknown to us, finds itself situated beyond every possible manifestation* as principially incapable of entering into the phenomenological content of manifestation and incapable either of being figured by manifestation as by a model. This last point deserves to be deepened.

The opening paragraph sets up the paradigm shift. Where §47 showed the critique of rationalism *from within rationalism's own horizon* (Jaspers) ending in a sterile irrationalism-of-chaos, §48 turns to a different kind of critique — one that does not merely oppose a non-cognitive unknown to cognition but actually *puts in question the horizon of rationalism itself*. The astonishing claim Henry makes is that this genuine critique appeared precisely at the moment when rationalism was at its zenith — in Malebranche, one of the very architects of the rationalist program. What Malebranche's famous thesis *"we have no idea of the soul"* articulates, rightly understood, is not that the soul is an unknowable substance beyond phenomenality but that there are *two modes of phenomenality*, and that the soul phenomenalizes itself in a mode *different from* the extension-based mode that constitutes the object-pole of knowledge. This is the crucial insight Henry will develop: Malebranche is the first modern philosopher to *divide* the concept of phenomenality, to acknowledge that there is a mode of manifestation proper to the soul that does not reduce to the extension-based mode of objective manifestation.

**Paragraph 2\.** The idea that a *metaphysical reality* (that of a substance in-itself inaccessible) finds itself linked however *to the manifestation of an effective phenomenological content* — in such a manner that the configurations and the structures which this phenomenological content lets appear in it correspond to the configurations and the originary structures of the substance itself and, more, *determine* it — is present in Malebranche. It is precisely because it shows itself identical to *the essence of pure phenomenality* and that its determinations are as such *"intelligible"* — that extension must be understood as the essential *"attribute"* of a corresponding substance whose knowledge it founds or rather constitutes. To this extended substance (that is, to created matter), Malebranche juxtaposes, it is true, that of *the soul*, to which there no longer corresponds however (at least for us) *any intelligible attribute, any "archetype."* It is in this sense, assuredly, that the soul cannot be known — in the sense that the essential properties that determine its metaphysical substance are *not represented for us in the milieu of exteriority* and *cannot be*. This impossibility (for the essential properties that determine the metaphysical substance of the soul to be represented in the milieu of exteriority and to find in it thus the phenomenality constitutive of their intelligibility) Malebranche expresses in saying *that we have no "idea" of the soul*. *"Idea"* does not primitively designate in Malebranche the *particular* conception of a determinate relation nor its specific ideal content — but, precisely, *this ideality itself, the milieu where such a relation is susceptible of manifesting itself* — the conception grasped in its universal ontological possibility *as identical to the transcendental spatiality of the pure world, to "extension."* The idea is justly a determination of this spatiality. This is why again, for Malebranche, every knowledge is as such *a knowledge by idea* and finds in the idea (and in the effectivity of the milieu that the idea determines each time) its own effectivity. It is precisely because we have no idea of the soul — and that thus a knowledge of the soul is rigorously impossible — that (to attempt nonetheless to seat such a knowledge and to give to the very idea of a psychology something like a foundation) Malebranche was constrained to *have recourse to a detour*. The project of reconstructing the unknown substance of the soul *parallelly* to that of extension — that is, from the phenomenological content where extension is accessible to us — the effort therefore to reconstitute (conformably to that of extension) an intelligible archetype of the soul, to *deduce* the properties that must belong to the metaphysical reality of the soul itself and constitute its substance — this strange path followed by thought (and which defines however the method even of psychology) — all this reposes on the central affirmation cited above and *results from it*.

The second paragraph works out Malebranche's structural thesis about extension and idea. In Malebranche's framework, "idea" is not just any concept but specifically a determination of intelligible extension — the ideal ontological milieu where relations between objective natures can be articulated and known. Extension is for Malebranche the essence of pure phenomenality as it applies to the known object; idea is the specific mode of givenness within this extension-based milieu. This is why Malebranche says the soul has no idea: the soul does not fit within the extension-based milieu of objective knowledge. The "detour" Malebranche was forced to take — reconstructing psychology by analogy with the extension-based knowledge of matter — is what produces his famously awkward psychological writings. But the detour is a symptom of the fact that Malebranche recognized the soul's heterogeneity to the milieu of extension without yet being able to articulate the alternative milieu positively. The remarkable thing, for Henry's purposes, is that Malebranche *at least recognized the heterogeneity* and articulated it structurally, giving modern philosophy its first rigorous formulation of the thesis that the soul is not knowable in the mode of ideas-in-extension.

**Paragraph 3\.** Is the signification of this central affirmation preserved however with the bringing into evidence of its consequences concerning psychology — with the attempt, more exactly, to maintain psychology on a *rational* basis, whereas precisely such a basis here totally fails? Does not this attempt show on the contrary that, far from taking consciousness of its necessary limits, rationalism intends with Malebranche to maintain the validity of its own presuppositions *there even where reality no longer lets itself be enclosed within the horizon* that these presuppositions trace? The affirmation according to which we have no idea of the soul remains in any case purely *negative* when it limits itself to noting the absence of every assignable phenomenological foundation for the edification and the development of a rational knowledge in a determinate domain of being — and the correlative necessity of compensating this absence by an expedient. *Such is not precisely the originary signification of this affirmation in Malebranche.* This affirmation does not intervene inside a problematic explicitly oriented toward the question of the possibility of a rational knowledge of the metaphysical reality of the soul understood and defined as a substance in-itself unknown and unknowable; it takes birth *in the description of the phenomenological modalities of consciousness* — that is, of the soul primitively identified with consciousness — *and it is the positivity of this effective manifestation that serves as its substrate*.

The third paragraph delivers Henry's crucial interpretive move. The Malebranchean thesis "we have no idea of the soul" has usually been read as the premise of a negative epistemological argument — the soul is metaphysically inaccessible, and psychology must therefore proceed by analogical reconstruction. But Henry argues that this is *not* the original function of the thesis in Malebranche's text. The thesis emerges within a *descriptive* context — a phenomenological description of the modalities of consciousness — and it functions *positively*, as the articulation of a different mode of manifestation, not negatively as the denial of cognitive access to a metaphysical substance. Malebranche's later psychology, reconstructive and analogical, departs from the original phenomenological intuition. The positive content Malebranche was groping for is the articulation of *another mode of manifestation* — a mode that does not proceed through ideas-in-extension — and it is *this* positive articulation that constitutes Malebranche's decisive contribution.

**Paragraph 4\.** Yet the nature of this manifestation must be understood, for it is of this manifestation that it is a matter here — not of a plurality of determinate phenomena. The *irrationality of the psychological modifications* signifies in no way their principial insubordination to a pure legality of a priori type — the impossibility for example of establishing between them rational relations, the obligation placed on the mind to passively register their content without being able ever to claim to really understand them or to deduce them. Or rather, it is *the origin of this insubordination* that must be elucidated, for no more than he first dreams of explaining it from the simple absence of an archetype does Malebranche content himself with noting it. The unforeseeable character of the course followed by the interior modifications of our soul, the contingency of the history they compose together, express still only *the fact* of their insubordination. The *eidos* of this insubordination resides in each of these modifications in the positivity of their common essence, in *the internal structure of their pure phenomenality*. The effective manifestation that serves as substrate to the critique of rationalism is constituted by the "phenomena of the soul" considered, not in their particularity or in their multiplicity, *but precisely in their pure manifestation identical to the soul itself*. The soul no longer designates the metaphysical reality of a substance \= x but *the effective manifestation of a sphere of existence defined and constituted by this manifestation, the originary essence of phenomenological consciousness*. It is as a determination of *this* (and of the phenomenality that constitutes it — as an eidetic determination of the internal structure of this phenomenality itself) that values the decisive problematic here instituted by Malebranche. That we have no idea of the soul — this means: the soul, the essence of a revelation whose effectivity reveals itself foundational for existence, *phenomenalizes itself without being apperceived in intelligible extension nor proposing itself there as a content*.

The fourth paragraph gives the positive structural formulation. What Malebranche is describing is not a domain of "irrational" phenomena that happen to not fit the rational mold; he is describing a *different structure of phenomenality*. The modifications of the soul (sensations, emotions, volitions, memories) do not manifest themselves in the milieu of extension-based ideality; they manifest themselves in a different milieu — the milieu of immanent self-affection. The "soul" in Malebranche's decisive moments is not a metaphysical substance \= x but *the effective manifestation of a sphere of existence* — a sphere that is constituted by its very mode of manifestation. This is an extraordinarily precise formulation of what Henry himself calls immanent self-revelation. The soul is, for Malebranche in his most rigorous phenomenological moments, *nothing other than* this mode of manifestation; it is not something that manifests but a certain *structure of manifesting* that constitutes a sphere of existence. The thesis "we have no idea of the soul" becomes, on this reading, *the soul phenomenalizes itself in a mode other than idea-in-extension* — a mode that is not accessible to objectifying knowledge but that is no less a genuine (indeed, more originary) mode of phenomenality.

**Paragraph 5\.** Such is the rigorous ontological signification of the essential opposition Malebranche establishes *between consciousness and knowledge*. That the element opposed to knowledge finds itself precisely to be *consciousness* — not the x of a mysterious substance — that this consciousness is understood according to the specific phenomenological mode of its proper effectivity, and that, more, *this effectivity constitutes and defines, in its specificity, originary existence* — one sees in the fact that the eidetic determination of the soul from its structural heterogeneity with respect to idea intervenes precisely in *a discussion of the cogito* and as *a decisive element for the interpretation of the cogito*. What Malebranche reproaches Descartes with is justly *to confound* the phenomenality that in the cogito reveals itself originarily foundational for existence (as being identical to it) with the phenomenality that constitutes the substrate of every knowledge — with the phenomenality of pure exteriority as such. Not only does Descartes commit such a confusion, but he carries this confusion in a certain way to its extreme point when — not content with assimilating the *je pense* to a knowledge — he claims to see in the *je pense* the first *fact* and, what is more, *the prototype* of knowledge. In such a claim is assuredly included (as its properly philosophical foundation) the idea that *every real being reposes on its proper apparition* — is defined by its apparition and by the concrete mode conformably to which this apparition accomplishes itself. Precisely, the mode according to which accomplishes itself *the originary revelation of existence in the cogito* has nothing to do with the mode that constitutes the milieu of knowledge as Descartes understands it. *The rejection of knowledge outside the internal structure of the phenomenality that delimits the concrete sphere of originary existence* — that therefore is what implies (conformably to its philosophical foundation) *the universal rationalism identical to philosophy itself* and *defined by the extension of the Logos to the totality of the fundamental ontological dimensions that belong to and constitute it*. It is nothing less than the project or in any case the possibility of the instauration of such a universal rationalism that comes to light in the critique directed by Malebranche against the cogito of Descartes. This is why the signification of this critique must not be limited. That the cogito is not an *ideal liaison of simple natures*, that it does not present in it the configurations and the concatenations that are those of knowledge, nor can it be reduced to them — *does not result from the simple opposition* (to the unity of the originary intuition that the cogito is supposed to express) *of the necessarily discursive character of the thought where this intuition finds its explicitation*. It is the *mode of manifestation* that belongs to the cogito and defines it — *that* does not let itself be identified with that of a simple nature, to that of intuition itself consequently.

The fifth paragraph is the pivotal structural claim of §48. Malebranche's critique of Descartes concerns not the *content* of the Cartesian cogito but its *phenomenological mode*. Descartes treats the cogito as the first piece of knowledge, the paradigm of intuitive clear-and-distinct grasping; Malebranche sees that the phenomenological mode of the cogito — the way the cogito manifests itself to itself — is *not* the mode of clear-and-distinct idea but something structurally different. The cogito does not present itself in the mode of an idea-in-extension that is grasped as an object; it reveals itself in the mode of an immanent self-affection that is the *being* of the subject, not the *object* of a knowing grasp. This is why Descartes was wrong to identify the *je pense* as both *first fact* and *prototype of knowledge*: the *je pense* is indeed the first fact (the foundational phenomenality of the subject), but it is emphatically *not* a case of knowledge, because its mode of manifestation is not the knowing-objectifying mode. Descartes confused the two modes; Malebranche separated them. And this separation, Henry argues, is the seed of what he calls *universal rationalism* — a rationalism extended to include both modes of phenomenality, including the immanent mode that the knowing-rationalism of Descartes had missed. Henry is here identifying his own philosophical project as the completion of what Malebranche began: the rigorous articulation of the two modes of phenomenality and the extension of the Logos to the immanent mode that has been hitherto excluded.

**Paragraph 6\.** The *structural ontological foundation* of this ultimate opposition is present in the philosophy of Malebranche: *if we have no idea of the soul, it is because the soul is not separated from itself*. It is on the ground of its internal structure, consequently — because this internal structure *excludes the very possibility of a separation* — that the soul manifests its *foundational opacity to every grasp accomplishing itself in the milieu of knowledge and through knowledge*. This is why the cogito had to find itself rejected by Malebranche outside the sphere of necessary truths of mathematical type, outside the sphere of ideas and of what constitutes in general the intellectual order of knowledge — *not precisely because of the specifically "intellectual" character of these latter*, but *by reason of the structure itself of the phenomenological milieu that serves them as foundation*. For this reason again, the sphere of originary existence defined by the cogito had to constitute *a "world" apart*, foundationally foreign to that of knowledge and irreducible to the latter. That *logical necessity* is *banished from this "psychological world"* — where there is *neither separation nor alterity*, where ideality *has no place* — that is a simple consequence. The *insurmountable* character of this banishment refers to the *eidos* where it is rooted — *to the structure of the originary Logos identical to the cogito itself*.

The sixth paragraph delivers the ontological grounding. The reason Malebranche's soul has no idea is not a contingent epistemological limitation; it is a structural ontological feature of the soul itself. The soul is *not separated from itself* — its mode of being is the immanent self-affection, the self-coincidence of self with self that §37 had identified as the structural core of immanence. Because the soul is not separated from itself, it cannot be given in the separated-and-other mode of idea-in-extension; it can only be given in the mode of immediate self-coincidence. This is a remarkably precise registration of the structural distinction Henry has been elaborating throughout Section III. The *"world apart"* that Malebranche identifies as the domain of psychology (*le monde psychologique*) is structurally the immanent sphere; its resistance to logical-mathematical necessity is not a defect but a structural feature of a sphere where there is *neither separation nor alterity*. Without separation, there is no idea (since idea presupposes an ideal distance between the knowing and the known); without alterity, there is no logical relation in the ordinary sense (since logic operates on distinct terms). The "Logos originel identique au cogito lui-même" is, in Henry's vocabulary, exactly the Logos of immanence — the self-revelation of the essence in its immanent self-affection, which is a Logos but a Logos structurally different from the Logos of discursive-objective knowing.

**Paragraph 7\.** That Malebranche, after this, saw in this consequence (in the impossibility of establishing between the modifications of existence ideal connections of mathematical type) only *its negative aspect* — that is true. Such an impossibility signifies in his eyes the impossibility of every knowledge, and that *rightly*, if by knowledge one understands (with him) the establishment — on the ground of intelligible extension and between its determinations, between simple natures — of connections of this kind and their concatenation. At the moment even when he puts in question the phenomenological milieu of exteriority in its pretension to constitute the nature and the essence of every possible manifestation, *Malebranche remains dupe of the prejudice* that consists in considering as alone rational the enunciations that found themselves on the phenomenality of such a milieu and on the configurations that belong to it properly. *The bursting of rationalism toward its universal accomplishment goes hand in hand with the maintenance of its traditional concept* — such as this concept finds itself elaborated within the horizon of monism. Thus one sees — after he has understood it from the structure itself of originary existence — Malebranche deplore the absence of every idea relative to this existence, *interpret this absence as the end and not the beginning of a research*, as closing a path instead of opening it — and preoccupy himself then with remedying it in the manner that has been said. The cogito considered in itself *no longer leads, henceforth, to much*, and finds itself abandoned — in such a manner that its abandonment by the Cartesians corresponds *paradoxically* to the moment when one of them discovers (without however elucidating it fully) *its decisive signification*. At least Malebranche maintains firmly — and that as constituting the absolutely original ontological dimension where the concrete modalities of our existence and this existence itself develop themselves — the *phenomenological reflectivity* of what manifests itself *otherwise than in the form of extension*. *The effectivity of this sui generis manifestation places its content outside the reach of critique* and confers thus (whether one wants it or not) on the propositions that enunciate it something like *an absolute rationality*. This is why (as Malebranche recognized) one cannot put in question what the *"sens intime"* (inner sense) teaches us of our existence and of its modifications — why, more, the inner sense defines *the only path of access* to the modifications of existence *because it constitutes precisely their essence, the unique possible mode of their revelation*. What teaches us something about something and unveils it as it is — is what one calls a *knowledge*. That this knowledge (under pretext that it does not accomplish itself in extension nor by the mediation of ideas) be said imperfect, non-veritable — does not take anything from the phenomenological content of the phenomenon it constitutes by itself, *attests only the impotence of thought to equal its proper discovery*.

The closing paragraph delivers the nuanced verdict. Malebranche took the decisive step (articulating the two modes of phenomenality) but did not take the further step (positively elaborating the immanent mode as a rationality in its own right). He saw the immanent mode as an *absence* — as the lack of ideas that afflicts psychology — rather than as a *positive mode of revelation* that constitutes a different rationality. This is the point at which Malebranche's *cogito*\-breakthrough was partially reversed within Cartesianism itself: the Cartesian school abandoned the cogito (*"the cogito no longer leads to much"*) precisely at the moment when one of its interpreters had discovered its decisive ontological signification. But even this partial reversal could not eliminate the achievement. Malebranche's firm insistence that there is a *phenomenological reflectivity* of what manifests itself *otherwise than in the form of extension* — and that this sui generis manifestation is *absolutely rational* because it constitutes its own essence — is the precious core of his critique. The Malebranchean *sens intime* — the inner sense that teaches us of our own existence and its modifications — is, in Henry's reading, nothing other than the immanent self-affection of life. When Malebranche says that the inner sense is not just a path of access to our modifications but *constitutes their essence*, he is articulating exactly the thesis that the mode of manifestation *is* the being of what manifests itself in immanence. This is what the rationalist tradition took to be an "imperfect" or "non-veritable" knowledge; for Henry, it is a *more originary* knowledge — the Logos of immanence as the self-revelation of life.

---

## **§ 49\. Ontological signification of the critique of knowledge in Eckhart**

**Paragraph 1\.** The extension of the Logos to the totality of its fundamental ontological dimensions and its blossoming in the exhaustive concept of phenomenality — this is on the contrary what characterized the thought of Eckhart. This is why the critique of knowledge receives in the latter its radical signification, which consists not only in the bringing into evidence of a phenomenological dimension in itself foreign to exteriority but further in the determination of this originary dimension and its internal structure. It is from this internal structure — from the internal structure of being itself — that there finds itself understood the impossibility for knowledge of attaining being. Still this comprehension does not accomplish itself in some way by chance — in the abrupt surging-up of an intuition unconnected to the system and subsisting without profit at its margin. The elucidation of the internal structure of the revelation constitutive of being and of its reality is the explicit and central theme of the problematic instituted by Eckhart. To the essential content of this problematic attaches itself consequently, inasmuch as it roots itself in the very nature of the Logos, the critique of knowledge. The propositions in which such a critique finds its explicit formulation thus never constitute simple affirmations but are constantly *founded*. Because the mode of this foundation is phenomenological — because their truth is apperceived in the structure of the originary Logos constitutive of absolute being — the enunciations that together compose the critique of knowledge manifest among themselves the unity that is that of this structure, determine the successive moments of a single analysis that is that of being. It is within this ontological work of elucidation and as belonging to it that the critique of knowledge finally accomplishes itself in Eckhart. Thus is explained its *systematic character*. The fundamental intuitions of religion find themselves again in it, no longer in the dispersion of their historical surging-up but veritably understood, grasped in an internal vision of being and constituting it. This is why the theoretical exposition of this critique includes in itself as the *motif* of this critique — or rather as its very content — the ontological structural determinations of reality elaborated by Eckhart and in a general manner by the problematic, and repeats them. For this reason, the critique of knowledge as it accomplishes itself in Eckhart can here only be retraced *in its great lines*.

The opening paragraph establishes the framework and the decisive contrast with the preceding sections. Where Malebranche (§48) took the decisive step of *dividing* the concept of phenomenality but stopped short of positive elaboration, and where rationalism within its own horizon (§47) ended in the irrationalism of chaos, Eckhart *completes* the task: he extends the Logos to *the totality of its fundamental ontological dimensions* — that is, he develops the immanent mode of phenomenality not merely as a negative limit to knowledge but as a *positive structure with its own internal articulation*. This is what Henry means by the "exhaustive concept of phenomenality": phenomenality is no longer restricted to the extension-based milieu of objective knowing (as in classical rationalism) nor reduced to the ontological horizon of *Seinsverständnis* (as in Heidegger) but is articulated in both its horizonal-ekstatic dimension and its immanent-affective dimension, with the immanent dimension grasped as foundational. Because of this, Eckhart's critique of knowledge is not a mere assertion (as religious intuitions often remain) but a *rigorously phenomenologically founded* critique. The propositions that constitute it are *founded* in the sense that they are grounded in the *internal structure of the originary Logos*; and because they are so grounded, they form a systematic unity rather than a collection of disparate insights. This is the decisive achievement of Eckhart over all merely religious or moral formulations: the critique of knowledge becomes an *ontological* analysis, an analysis of being itself. Henry's methodological signal — that the exposition can only be "retraced in its great lines" — is a fidelity-claim: the critique cannot be adequately rendered in paraphrase because its force depends on the internal coherence of Eckhart's whole ontological elaboration. Henry will therefore move through the main articulations, quoting decisively where needed.

**Paragraph 2\.** The essential structural determination of being, brought into evidence in the theory of the Logos, has the following signification: the experience of being, identical to being itself, is possible only on the ground of unity and through it. In the structure of this unity consequently and in its maintenance resides the internal possibility of being, its *essence*. Such a possibility finds itself excluded on the contrary, and that by principle, from the ontological milieu that is that of knowledge. Thus is founded, for this latter, in the very structure of being, the impossibility of arriving at it. Such an impossibility expresses nothing other than *the irreducible opposition of two phenomenological essences*: it is because the phenomenality that constitutes its reality has nothing to do with that which defines the milieu of knowledge that being cannot show itself in the latter. Because the phenomenality constitutive of being and that of knowledge have nothing in common between them — because they differ in their nature, in what makes their phenomenality itself — the effectivity of the one implies each time in it, in the surging-up of its manifest content, the non-effectivity of the other. The irreducible opposition of phenomenological essences has this ultimate signification. Conformably to this, because the manifestation of one essence determines in it the non-manifestation of its phenomenological *anti-essence*, every apparition is identically — with regard to the pure originary given-ones that structure fundamentally reality and define it — *a disappearance*. This is why knowledge cannot develop the milieu in which becomes visible what it attains — such a milieu cannot become visible in itself without making vanish outside its light what remains, in its essential phenomenological content, irreducible to this light. In its positive development, knowledge each time accomplishes *the work of hiding*. Nothing of what it produces — neither the objectivities it liberates, nor the ideal milieu in which are moved the multiple determinations of transcendent being — composes an approach to the essential, constitutes to whatever degree (even in the form of a *"simple appearance"*) a manifestation of the absolute. "*The least created image that presents itself in you in whatever manner is just as great as God… because it bars to divine totality the way that leads to you. It is precisely, Eckhart adds, at the moment when the image enters into you that God must yield the place with all his divinity.*"

The second paragraph establishes the structural-ontological foundation of Eckhart's critique by re-deploying the central thesis of §37 (the essence of revelation is unity, self-coincidence, the structure of immanence) and §46 (the phenomenality of knowledge is the milieu of exteriority). Eckhart's critique of knowledge is not a skeptical thesis about cognitive limits but an *ontological* thesis about the *eidetic incompatibility of two modes of phenomenality*. The milieu of knowledge is the milieu of exteriority — a medium structured by distance, alterity, and representational projection; the milieu of being-in-its-essence is the milieu of immanence — a medium structured by unity, self-coincidence, and self-affection. These two structures are not merely different but *eidetically opposed*: the manifestation of one implies the non-manifestation of the other. This is an extraordinarily strong structural claim: it is not that knowledge is merely *inadequate* to being but that *every positive achievement of knowledge is simultaneously a concealment of being*. Henry's formula — *every apparition is identically a disappearance* — is the structural heart of the critique. To manifest something in the milieu of exteriority is to manifest it *as other, as distant, as object*; but the being whose essence is immanent self-coincidence cannot be manifested as other without being thereby falsified. The Eckhartian image (which Henry quotes) expresses this with stark precision: the *least created image* — even the smallest representational content, the most apparently harmless cognitive mediator — *bars the way* to the divine. It is not that images are inadequate representations of God that could be improved upon; it is that every image as such, precisely by being an image (a content in the milieu of exteriority), prevents the immanent reception of the divine essence. "At the moment when the image enters into you, God must yield the place with all his divinity" — the entry of the representational content *is* the disappearance of the immanent essence. This is the structural reason why Eckhart's critique does not admit of any degree: one cannot approach the absolute "more" or "less" through refined cognitive means; the refinement is itself the flight.

**Paragraph 3\.** The phenomenological signification of these propositions — their reference to the eidetic structures of pure phenomenality — appears without equivocation when, speaking of everything which (outside us or in us) constitutes a first layer of transcendence, a *"knowledge"* — and, for example, of joy, of fear, of assurance and of all the determinations of existence precisely inasmuch as they are *known*, inasmuch as they are *"only an intermediary"* — Eckhart, inspiring himself from Boethius, declares: "*while you regard these things and they regard you, you do not see God*." It is because the phenomenality of God (constitutive of his being, and identically of the possibility of arriving at him) is not the exteriority in which knowing moves — it is because, as Eckhart repeats in a proposition borrowed this time from Saint Paul, "*God dwells in a light to which there is no access*" — that he precisely withdraws from every knowledge and "*dies to the soul*" when the soul "*turns toward external things*." It is this incompatibility of the essential phenomenological structures that Eckhart again expresses when, concerning *"the truth"* (understood by him as the originary essence of revelation in its opposition to the ideal milieu of knowledge), he says simply: "*truth is an interior thing and one cannot find it in its external manifestations*." It is because (on the ground of the incompatibility of their essential phenomenological structures) truth cannot be found in its "external manifestations" — cannot manifest itself in the milieu of knowledge — that every research accomplishing itself in this milieu inevitably *misses* it, misses the absolute itself (phenomenologically interpreted and understood as the essence of this originary truth). Speaking of this latter (that is, of God), Eckhart says: "*The more one seeks you, the less one finds you*" — and, addressing himself to man: "*You must seek him in such a way as never to find him; if you do not seek him, you find him.*"

The third paragraph illustrates the structural thesis through a specific phenomenological register — the register of the *affective modalities* of existence (joy, fear, assurance). The point is subtle and decisive: Eckhart's critique does not concern only the representation of a transcendent God as object of contemplation; it concerns *every* mode of manifestation that proceeds through the structure of exteriority, including the reflective consciousness of one's own affective states. Joy as *lived* is immanent self-affection; joy *as known* (as an intermediary, as an object of reflective consciousness) already introduces the structure of exteriority and therefore already falsifies. The Boethian formula Eckhart quotes — "while you regard these things and they regard you, you do not see God" — articulates the structural point: the regarding-and-being-regarded is the relation of subject-and-object in the milieu of exteriority; in this structure, the immanent essence cannot appear. The Pauline reference (*"God dwells in a light to which there is no access"*, 1 Tim 6:16) is read by Eckhart not as an assertion of divine transcendence in the sense of spatial distance but as a *structural* claim: the light of the divine essence is not the light of objectifying knowing; there is no cognitive access-route because the structure of access would itself be the falsification. When the soul "turns toward external things," God "dies to the soul" — not because God withdraws in some spatial sense but because the soul, by turning outward, *places itself in a structure where the immanent divine essence cannot be received*. The Eckhartian paradoxes about seeking and finding ("the more one seeks, the less one finds"; "seek him in such a way as never to find him; if you do not seek him, you find him") are not mystical mystifications but rigorous articulations of the structural opposition: *seeking* is already in the structure of exteriority (the sought is other than the seeker, at a distance, to be traversed); the immanent essence can only be given where this structure is abandoned. This is why the positive side of the paradox is "if you do not seek him, you find him" — the cessation of the outward-seeking movement *is* the reception of the immanent essence which was never absent but only covered over by the seeking structure itself.

**Paragraph 4\.** Thus is founded, in the milieu in which develops the research that characterizes every knowledge as such, the *failure* of knowledge. What, in the structure of this milieu, founds such a failure presaged and intuitively affirmed by religious thought — Eckhart gives us to understand. Commenting on the prayer made to Moses by the Jews (to transmit to them the words they could not themselves hear from the divinity): "*they held themselves at a distance*, says Eckhart, *and it is precisely because of this that they could not hear God*." The impossibility of arriving at God — of "hearing him" — an impossibility still visible in the failure of every *perception*, thus resides in the very structure of the milieu opened by phenomenological distance and constituted by it: in *objectivity*. The signification that this objectivity clothes — of constituting not a way but an *obstacle* for the one who wants to join the essence — Eckhart affirms it also when (before the young Hegel) he takes up the word of Christ to his disciples — "not only to his disciples of that time but to all those who would still become his disciples and would want to follow him toward the highest perfection" — "*it is good for you that I go away*." Precisely because it does not concern only his disciples of that time, the disappearance of Christ does not accomplish itself as a simple historical event; it finds at once its foundation and its signification in the ontological structure of the Word itself, that is, in God. The latter, if at least the problematic aims in him at his originary essence (the essence of the Logos), could not strictly speaking disappear from the world for this reason that *he has never shown himself there*. Because the impossibility for God of manifesting himself in the world roots itself in him — in the originary essence of his Deity — it is the preservation of this Deity (the preservation of his own essence) that Christ pursues in the invitation addressed to the disciples not to attach themselves *"with dilection"* to his own person, more exactly (as Eckhart says) to "*his human form*" — that is, to his objective appearance — in the interdiction that is made to them of confusing this appearance with his proper being.

The fourth paragraph develops the critique into the register of *biblical hermeneutics* — Eckhart's reading of the Sinai episode (Exodus 20\) and the Johannine discourse on the departure of Christ (John 16:7). Both readings are presented as ontological rather than merely exegetical: the biblical texts, when read through Eckhart's phenomenological structural categories, turn out to articulate the structural thesis of the immanent essence's withdrawal from the milieu of exteriority. The Sinai reading is precise: the Israelites "held themselves at a distance," and *because of* this distance — because of the structure of distance as such — they could not hear God. This is not about moral timidity or lack of faith; it is about the structure of *objectivity* itself. The milieu of objectivity is precisely the milieu opened by distance and constituted by it; in this milieu, the divine essence cannot be present, because presence in this milieu is presence-as-object, which is precisely what the divine essence cannot be. The striking gloss Henry adds — that this impossibility is visible even in the failure of *perception* — is a subtle structural claim: perception as such is the paradigm of the distance-structure, the archetype of the subject-object relation; every perceptual act, even the most vivid and immediate, occurs within the structure of exteriority and therefore falls under the same critique. The Johannine reading (John 16:7 — "it is expedient for you that I go away") is even more striking. Eckhart reads Christ's farewell discourse not as a contingent historical prediction of the Ascension but as an *ontological statement about the Logos itself*. The "disappearance" of Christ is not a temporal event; it is the structural withdrawal of the immanent essence from every representational content. "He has never shown himself there" — this is the rigorous claim: the Christ as manifested in the milieu of exteriority (the "human form") is precisely *not* the Christ as essence of the Logos. The Christ-event, properly understood, *includes as its internal moment* the withdrawal from its own appearance, the refusal to allow the disciples to fix the immanent essence in a representational content. The anticipation of the young Hegel (whose *Spirit of Christianity* develops a similar reading of the *necessity* of Christ's departure) is a genealogical observation: this ontological reading of Christ's departure is not an Eckhartian eccentricity but a philosophically important line of interpretation that surfaces again in German Idealism.

**Paragraph 5\.** The eidetic incompatibility of the latter \[the essence\] and the former \[the human form\] does not determine only the immediate attitude of Jesus; it founds in Eckhart the critique he directs against *the concept of God*. Because the originary essence of the Logos is not the phenomenality of knowledge, everything that phenomenalizes itself in this phenomenality — *God himself insofar as he is known* — reveals itself to be *without relation to this originary essence*, without relation to the Deity. This is why "*the well-established design of God is that the soul lose God*," because "*as long as the soul still has a God, knows a God, has the notion of a God, it is still far from God*." Here surges up in its transparency the singular affirmation according to which "*we must free ourselves from God himself*." If nothing suffices to Reason — "*not even God in person*" — if God "*cannot suffice me with everything that he is as God*" — it is that the mode according to which he phenomenalizes himself in knowledge (and which determines his *concept*) lets escape the originary essence of the Deity, which constitutes identically however the very essence of the soul. This is why the soul cannot pacify itself in God, does not find itself again in him — "*this is why I pray God to free me from God; for my essential being is above God*." That these prescriptions and the ethic they apparently compose root themselves in the eidetic structures of pure phenomenality — that, thought in the light of these structures, the imperative they formulate first expresses nothing other than the rejection of the transcendent God who is not the essence — Eckhart affirms it simply: "*We must in no way grasp God outside of ourselves nor suppose him outside of us; we must on the contrary consider him as our own good, as a reality that belongs to us.*" This is why again, "*we must not… work… for God… nor for any good exterior to us, but uniquely for the love of what is our own essence and our own life*" and which resides in us. That the essence does not reside outside us but in our own life — and that because it is the very essence of this life that is ours — what Niels was to presage later in his manner, all this is said here and founded. The philosophical content of atheism is present in Eckhart, understood by him in its truth — starting from the *structural heterogeneity of the fundamental phenomenological dimensions* elaborated in the problematic of the Logos and as the expression of this heterogeneity.

The fifth paragraph is the most structurally radical moment of Eckhart's critique: the critique extends not only to creaturely objects of knowledge, not only to the human form of Christ, but to *the concept of God itself*. This is Eckhart's notorious "atheism" — the prayer to be freed from God ("*bitten Gott, daß er uns quitt mache Gottes*"), the claim that the soul's essential being is "above God." The apparent paradox of a Christian mystic praying to be freed from God is resolved, Henry shows, as soon as one grasps the structural distinction Eckhart operates throughout. "God" as concept — "God" as phenomenalizing himself in the milieu of knowledge, as posited by thought, as an object of reverent attention or theological reasoning — this "God" is *transcendent* in the phenomenological sense: he is in the milieu of exteriority, at a distance from the soul, given as an object (however sublime). But the essence of the Deity (*Gottheit*) — the originary immanent essence of the Logos — is not this object; it is the immanent self-revelation that is identical with the essence of the soul itself. So Eckhart's prayer "free me from God" means: free me from the objectifying concept of God that stands in the way of the immanent reception of the Deity itself. "My essential being is above God" means: my essential being is in the immanent essence of the Deity, which is "above" the representational concept "God" in the same way that the immanent essence is "above" every object of knowledge (not spatially above, but structurally more originary). This reading rescues Eckhart from the charge of blasphemy: what he rejects is not the divine but the *conceptual-representational mediation* of the divine, in the name of the more originary immanent presence of the divine essence. Henry then extends this to articulate the *philosophical content of atheism*. The atheistic intuition — that the God of theology is an anthropomorphic projection, that the transcendent God concept is a fiction — is, Henry argues, *rightly understood* a rigorous ontological thesis: the *transcendent* God concept is indeed inadequate; there is indeed no such transcendent being; what there is, is the *immanent essence of life itself*, which the transcendent God concept has been an attempt to capture but has rather covered over. The reference to "Niels" is to Jens Peter Jacobsen's novel *Niels Lyhne* (already invoked in §46): Niels's atheism is not the rejection of the divine essence but precisely the rejection of the transcendent God concept in favor of a more immediate presence-of-life. This is the *positive* content of atheism, which Eckhart had already articulated in its truth six centuries before Jacobsen.

**Paragraph 6\.** This \[structural heterogeneity\] — the impossibility of eidetic order that it opposes to the pretension of grasping the originary essence of the Deity in the dimension of exteriority, of *knowing* it — finds its most rigorous and most explicit formulation in the *theory of the eternal archetype*, which designates precisely the first manifestation of God in the milieu of alterity and implies as such the affection of the mind by this alterity as by a transcendent reality. For this reason precisely, a radical opposition institutes itself between the essence and its archetype: far from being able to consist in this archetype, the revelation of the essence presupposes on the contrary its *suppression* and its *annihilation*. This is why (as Eckhart says in an essential proposition borrowed from Saint Denys): "*the greatest pleasure of the mind resides in the nothingness of its archetype*." In the nothingness of its archetype — when every transcendence ceases — the essence finds again its unity, accomplishes itself. The greatest pleasure of the mind is its *possibility*. Because the accomplishment of the mind resides in unity, nothing transcendent then subsists; the essence itself is, by reason of this possibility of its accomplishment, no longer anything transcendent. "*God is someone whose nothingness fills the whole world, and his something is nowhere.*" Because the essence itself is, in its accomplishment, no longer anything transcendent, "*it is there*" — in this accomplishment of its essence — "*that God disappears*." The disappearance of God is, in the nothingness of every knowledge, that of his archetype. "*Since then God no longer exists for the mind, this eternal archetype is no longer present either to the mind.*"

The sixth paragraph articulates the most rigorous formulation of Eckhart's critique through the concept of the *eternal archetype* (*urbilde, ewig bild*). The archetype doctrine concerns the "first manifestation" of God in the milieu of alterity — the first representational content by which God enters the intelligible order, the primary image through which the mind apprehends the divine. In a classical metaphysical framework (one thinks of Neoplatonism, or of Bonaventure), this archetype is the *positive* mediation: the soul ascends to God through the eternal archetype. Eckhart reverses this: the archetype is precisely *that from which the soul must be freed*. Between the essence and its archetype there is *radical opposition* — not an opposition of inferior and superior within a common milieu, but an opposition of *structurally incompatible modes of phenomenality*. The archetype is still within the structure of alterity, of image, of representational mediation; the immanent essence is outside this structure. Therefore the revelation of the essence does not consist in contemplating the archetype *ever more perfectly* but requires the *annihilation* of the archetype. The Dionysian quotation Eckhart invokes — "the greatest pleasure of the mind resides in the nothingness of its archetype" — registers this structural reversal: the mind's *accomplishment* (its coming to its essence, its realization of its own immanent ground) is not the attainment of the archetype but precisely the *dissolution* of the archetype into nothingness. Henry's gloss unfolds the structural logic: because the accomplishment of the mind is *unity* (the immanent self-coincidence of the essence with itself), *nothing transcendent* can remain in this accomplishment; every transcendent content, including the archetype, must fall away. "God is someone whose nothingness fills the whole world and whose something is nowhere" — this is the structural formulation: what in God is representational (the "something") *has no place* in the immanent accomplishment; what accomplishes is the "nothingness" which is not privation but the very mode of the immanent essence (its not-being-anything-transcendent). "It is there that God disappears" — the disappearance of God is the disappearance of the transcendent-representational God; the "there" of this disappearance is the immanent essence's accomplishment. This is the most rigorous ontological formulation of the Eckhartian *Gelassenheit* (letting-go, releasement): the releasement of even the eternal archetype is the precondition of the immanent essence's presence to itself.

**Paragraph 7\.** It is in the light of these fundamental propositions that there must be understood the moral prescriptions or the observations of psychological order that confer on the doctrine its practical aspect. If "*it is not a question of thinking of God in a constant and regular fashion*," it is not because "*for our nature this would be an impossible or very difficult design*" but because — God not being in his reality anything transcendent — this reality could in no case be attained by thought. "*What one must have*, says Eckhart, *is a God in substance who is above thought*." The irreducible eidetic heterogeneity recognized between the reality of God and the transcendent manifestation of his concept expresses itself in the *character of dependence* that affects this manifestation inasmuch as its effectivity remains each time subordinated to a specific act of the mind. "*When thought disappears*, says Eckhart, *God disappears equally*." To the contingency of his manifestation in the milieu of thought — contingency prescribed by the structure of this milieu and linked to the free determinations of the mind — there opposes itself irreducibly (in its radical independence with respect to such determinations) the originary being of God, the untiring accomplishment of his essence in the first work of the Logos, and the permanence of this accomplishment. It is this permanence of the originary essence of God — his ontological *indifference* to the process of knowledge (to its progresses and its levels) — that the existential and religious themes that dominate the preaching of Eckhart in fact express: the imputation to free existence and to its sole freedom of the distance in which it holds itself with respect to God; its indissoluble unity with God on the contrary on the plane of reality. "*Man can turn himself away from God*, says Eckhart; *as far as man goes away, God remains there and awaits him*." And again: "*Whether man is near or far, God himself never goes away. He remains always in the neighborhood; and if he cannot dwell in us*" — that is, in our thought — "*he never goes farther than the other side of the door*."

The seventh paragraph addresses the *practical dimension* of Eckhart's doctrine — the moral prescriptions and psychological observations that might seem to belong to a different register but that Henry shows to be direct consequences of the structural-ontological critique. The first example concerns the prescription not to "think of God constantly": this is *not* a concession to human weakness but a structural *recommendation* grounded in the heterogeneity thesis. Since God is not a transcendent object of thought, constant thinking-about-God would be a structural error — it would be constantly occupying oneself with the transcendent concept of God at the expense of the immanent essence. What Eckhart recommends instead is a "God in substance who is above thought" — the immanent essence that is received not by thinking-about but by *being*. The more general principle Henry extracts is the *contingency* of God's appearance in thought: God-as-thought-of is subordinated to specific mental acts (one must be thinking about God for God-as-concept to be present to the mind); this is contingent, intermittent, dependent on the will of the thinker. But God-as-essence is not contingent in this way — the originary essence is continuously accomplishing itself in its immanent self-revelation, *independently* of whether any specific mental act of thinking-about-God occurs. This is why Eckhart can say (with what might otherwise seem contradictory): whenever thought of God disappears, God-as-concept disappears; but God-as-essence never disappears, because God-as-essence is the immanent accomplishment of the Logos itself.
