The invisible is a moment within a process, not a positive mode with its own structure. This is precisely what Henry has denied in §50 and will continue to dismantle. The critique is double: (a) the tradition has misunderstood what the invisible is; (b) phenomenology, in its self-understanding as "rendering the invisible visible," has set itself a teleologically confused task. If the invisible is a structurally distinct mode of phenomenality, then the phenomenological task cannot be to render it visible (which would be to destroy it as what it is); the task must rather be to articulate the invisible *in its own mode* — which is the task Henry has set himself in the present work.

**Paragraph 4\.** Or rather: *does not the ontological determination of the concept of the invisible (and its elaboration by the problematic) render principially absurd the insertion of this latter (as an opposed element) in the dialectical unity of the process* — the idea of its possible passage into the "visible"? In the positivity of its proper phenomenological content, does not the invisible rather constitute in itself *an essence* — does not this latter find (in the effectivity of this content and in the specificity of its phenomenological structure) the determination of *Selbständigkeit*? But, conformably to the laws that regulate the domain of pure a priori possibilities to which it belongs, no essence can (with respect at least to its essential properties and precisely to its structure) "*transform itself*." If a transformation is possible inside the essence and as the play of the determinations permitted by it, *the transformation of the essence itself has no signification, not even "dialectical"* — it is its pure and simple *suppression* (such as it is permitted to us to operate, at least on the plane of fiction). Thus the invisible — if it is not the nothingness of what is nothing at all and must not either become nothing, if it designates on the contrary the effectivity of an originary dimension of phenomenality and its structure, its internal possibility — *could not "transform itself"* (for example into its "contrary"). Likewise it is for the transcendental essence of the world. Moreover these two essences (conformably to the structure that they each time exhibit in the reflectivity of their pure phenomenality and as constituting this latter) have nothing similar and cannot consequently enter into the common genus of a more general essence nor be subsumed by it.

The fourth paragraph delivers the decisive structural argument that the invisible cannot enter into dialectical opposition with the visible. The argument uses the Husserlian notion of *Selbständigkeit* (self-standing, essential independence, the property of a region that constitutes an autonomous essence with its own laws). The invisible, in its positive phenomenological effectivity (as elaborated in §§37-50), is an essence with its own *Selbständigkeit*. As an essence with its own structural integrity, it cannot *transform itself* into its contrary — because essences do not transform; their structural features are a priori. What can transform are the determinations *within* an essence (the way a perception can become a memory, both remaining within the essence of conscious lived experience). But the essence itself cannot change; to "change" an essence is to suppress it and replace it with a different essence. Therefore, if the invisible is an essence with its own structural integrity, it cannot pass into the visible as its dialectical other; the passage would be not a transformation within an essence but a suppression of one essence and the surging of another — which is not a dialectical process but a structural discontinuity. This argument rigorously grounds Henry's thesis. The second structural point — that the invisible and the visible cannot be subsumed under a more general essence — is equally important: the two modes of phenomenality are not species of a single genus "phenomenality"; they are radically heterogeneous essences whose "phenomenality" is not a common predicate but two distinct modes whose commonality exists only at the level of the word, not at the level of structure.

**Paragraph 5\.** Because their essences have between them nothing similar — because they differ on the contrary in the irreducible heterogeneity of their structures — the invisible and the visible *could not transform themselves one into the other*; no passage, no time links them — but they subsist *one apart from the other*, each in the positivity of its proper effectivity. Thus must be heard (in the light of this essential structural heterogeneity) their opposition: *not as an opposition between two opposites* (such as it institutes itself in the tie) but precisely as *the opposition of what has no tie* — as *an opposition in absolute difference*. Such an opposition (in absolute difference) is that of *indifference*. It is in the indifference of this difference that, finally, the invisible opposes itself to the visible — in such a manner that *it does not turn itself toward the visible to confront it in a combat, to refuse itself to it at the end of a struggle and inside of this latter* — but remains rather *in itself* and (entirely occupied with self) *ignores it and cannot know it*. Thus determines itself (from the exteriority of what is without relation, and as the expression of this latter) the impossibility for the invisible *to "become visible."* Such an impossibility, *as impossibility to accomplish the passage*, has in itself no less force than that which results from the passage itself and constitutes itself in it (in the tension of contraries) — but, because it reposes on the eidetic heterogeneity of the ultimate ontological structures, it is *insurmountable and definitive*.

The fifth paragraph delivers the positive structural formulation. The relation between visible and invisible is not dialectical opposition (which presupposes the tie and the homogeneous essence) but *absolute difference* — which is the same as *indifference*. The invisible does not confront the visible, does not struggle against it, does not refuse itself to it; the invisible *ignores* the visible, is not aware of it, does not know it, because the invisible is *entirely occupied with itself* in the mode of its own immanent self-affection. This is an extraordinary claim: the immanent essence does not even *notice* the visible world, does not set itself in opposition to it, does not negate it; the immanent essence simply subsists in its own mode, and the visible world arises as a secondary-derivative mode that does not touch the immanent essence. The Heideggerian *Unverborgenheit* or Hegelian dialectical negativity both presuppose that the hidden is in tension with the unhidden, negotiating a combat for coming-to-visibility. Henry's essence does not negotiate; it is simply *there*, in its immanent self-living, untroubled by and oblivious to the sphere of the visible. The impossibility for the invisible to "become visible" is therefore not a dialectical impossibility (the resistance of an invisible that stakes its being in *not* becoming visible) but a structural impossibility (there is no passage in principle, because the two essences are structurally heterogeneous). This impossibility is "insurmountable and definitive" — it cannot be overcome by any future phenomenological development, because it is not an impediment to progress but a structural feature of the distinction of the two modes.

**Paragraph 6\.** *The comprehension of the invisible in its insurmountable, non-dialectical opposition to what is visible and to its element accomplishes itself for the first time in Christianity* — where it finds its concrete historical realization. With the apparition of the latter uncovers itself indeed (as constituted by the invisible precisely and by the effectivity of the phenomenality which belongs to it in its own) *a new and infinite dimension of existence* such that everything that proposes itself in the world and manifests itself in it as "phenomenon" reveals itself henceforth *to be without relation with it, nor with what it contains of the essential*. That indeed is the signification of the critique directed by Christianity against the "world" and its determinations — that of promoting (in its radical heterogeneity with respect to this latter understood first as a pure ontological milieu) the effectivity and the reality of the irrepresentable essence of being and of life. This is why such a critique does not accomplish itself first in *the moral perspective* under which one habitually envisages it (and which it was able to provoke afterwards, when the concept of the "world" takes in Christianity itself a more particular and new determination) — it finds on the contrary its *primitive essential content* in the mere recognition (on the plane of the ontological structures of the real) of what had been up to then constantly misrecognized in this latter. This is why again the opposition of life in its invisible reality to the reigning concept of phenomenality (such as it expresses itself in the comprehension of *destiny* as the universal law of all things) is not — if one considers in it the power of protestation and of refusal that inhabits it and the revolutionary force that it manifested historically — *the fact of the invisible itself* but rather of a thought in struggle with the ancient world. That *indifference* on the contrary characterizes in the real the opposition of the structures that divide it — the division in it of the open world of the city (where accomplishes itself and recognizes itself in struggle the spirituality of men) and of the invisible (where shut themselves up on the contrary the originary consciousness of life and its sacred essence) — this is what renders clear the famous word: *"Render to Caesar what belongs to Caesar and to God what belongs to God."* The Christian antinomy (such as it finds its most striking expression in the paradoxical propositions of the Sermon on the Mount, and under all its forms) — does it express anything other than this *indifference of life with respect to what passes habitually for its concrete forms* — anything other than *the liberty with which it lets move the determinations of being in representation*? It is the *absence of relation between two worlds* that comes to light in it — in such a manner that what manifests itself in one, in the world precisely, does not concern the reality of life nor its originary accomplishment in the invisible — in such a manner that "what appears is the contrary of what resides in the ground." Such a "contrary" indeed is not that of dialectical opposition, of which it takes the form only to underline in it (and as its secret foundation) *the ontological structural heterogeneity of the ultimate dimensions of phenomenality* — the possibility for what phenomenalizes itself here as sadness, denudation, etc., to reveal itself *elsewhere* to be joy, possession, beatitude.

The sixth paragraph mobilizes Christianity as the historical discovery of the non-dialectical opposition of invisible and visible. Henry's thesis: Christianity, in its primary and fundamental content, is not a moral teaching but an *ontological* discovery — the recognition that the invisible (the sphere of life, the essence, the absolute) stands in *absence of relation* with the world (the sphere of objective manifestation, the visible). The Christian critique of the "world" is therefore misunderstood when it is read morally (as if the world were corrupt and should be rejected in favor of virtue); it must be read ontologically (the world is the sphere of irreality, of the non-essential, and the essential is elsewhere, in the invisible). The famous logion "render to Caesar what is Caesar's" is read by Henry as articulating *indifference* — the two spheres (political-temporal, sacred-eternal) do not negotiate or oppose in a single process; they subsist side by side in complete absence of relation. The Sermon on the Mount, in all its paradoxes ("blessed are the poor… blessed are those who mourn… blessed are the meek"), articulates the same structural thesis: what manifests itself in the world as denudation, sadness, powerlessness is *elsewhere* (in the invisible mode) joy, possession, beatitude. This is not dialectical inversion (as if poverty *became* richness through some process); it is the assertion that the two sphere-descriptions apply to different essences, the worldly and the invisible, without passage. The "contrary" that appears in the Gospel ("what appears is the contrary of what resides in the ground") is not dialectical contrary but the structural difference of two modes. Revolutionary Christianity, moral Christianity, political Christianity — these are subsequent deformations; the primitive ontological content of the Gospel is the recognition of the two modes.

**Paragraph 7\.** With the ambiguity inherent in the concept of *appearance* — and such that this latter designates sometimes the "mere appearance" and sometimes reality itself — is not the relation maintained (in spite of their formal ontological heterogeneity) between the phenomenological determinations that compose together the totality of the given — in such a manner that what manifests itself *here* shows itself not only foreign to what appears *there* but still and precisely constitutes *its "contrary"*? Does not the concept of this latter imply in it that of *opposition* (as dialectical and living opposition)? Is not an opposition of this kind present in Christianity if it is anything other than a description of essences or their theory — and concretizes itself on the contrary *in the interior tension of an existence engaged with the advent of one reign in the rejection of the other*? The opposition of the invisible to the world — of the true kingdom to what passes — has however *nothing to do originarily with the fundamental determinations of an ethics*. The axiological signification that it takes on and that determines it without doubt in this respect as an "opposition," *founds itself in ontology and only in it*. Such a signification is the following: *what reveals itself in the invisible and under the form of this latter (in its phenomenological and ontological identity with it) is reality*. The world on the contrary is the ontological milieu of *irreality*. The opposition of the visible and the invisible, far from implying their insertion in the dialectical unity of a single process, expresses on the contrary — as opposition of the real and the unreal — *the radical ontological heterogeneity of their essences* and finds in it its foundation.

The seventh paragraph anticipates and addresses the predictable objection: but doesn't Christianity insist on a *real struggle* between two reigns — the Kingdom of God and the Kingdom of the world — and doesn't this struggle imply a dialectical opposition? Henry's reply: the apparent opposition is axiological (the world is rejected, the Kingdom is pursued), but this axiological opposition *founds itself in ontology*. The Kingdom is real; the world is unreal. *This* is the distinction, and it is not dialectical. The real (the invisible, the essence, life) does not struggle with the unreal (the world, the transcendent representation) in a drama whose outcome is uncertain; the real is *simply* real, and the unreal is *simply* unreal, and the existential tension that the Christian experiences is the tension of recognizing this distinction, of *awakening* to the real by letting go of one's attachment to the unreal. The language of "struggle" and "rejection" is therefore existential-descriptive, not ontologically-structural. The structural thesis remains: the invisible and the visible are ontologically heterogeneous, and their difference is the difference of real and unreal. This thesis — that the world is ontologically unreal — is one of Henry's most radical and most difficult claims. It does not mean that the world does not exist (in the sense that there is no experience of the world) but that the world is not a *mode of reality* in the sense in which the invisible essence is a mode of reality. Reality, in its strict ontological sense, is the self-affection of life; the world is a derivative-secondary mode that does not constitute reality but only its phenomenal reflection.

**Paragraph 8\.** It is precisely because their opposition takes on this *radical ontological signification*, because they differ between them as *what is real and what is not*, that the invisible and the visible cannot transform themselves one into the other. For nothing real can become unreal, and nothing that is unreal obtains by itself (on the ground of a modification of its proper being) the being of reality. Thus determines itself (with the discovery of the invisible as constituting — in the effectivity of its originary phenomenality — *the ontological milieu of reality and its essence*) *the essence of Christianity*. It is because the bringing-to-discovery of the invisible (such as it accomplishes itself in Christianity) is that of *reality in its opposition to the milieu of irreality ontologically grasped and interpreted as that of the "world,"* that such an opposition *has nothing to do with that which determines in general ethics* — Christian ethics, for example — *with the metaphysical or moral opposition of Good and Evil*. For — and this in Christianity precisely — *evil is not less real than good*, and this is why *it is eternal like it*.

The eighth paragraph delivers what may be the book's most provocative ontological-theological thesis. The essence of Christianity — the doctrinal core, the philosophical content — is the *ontological* distinction of invisible-as-real and visible-as-unreal. This distinction is fundamentally different from the ethical distinction of Good and Evil. Good and Evil are *both real* — they are both modes of the invisible essence, both participate in reality. The Christian ontology does *not* consist in the identification of reality with the good and unreality with evil; it consists in the identification of reality with the immanent essence (whether good or evil in its axiological determinations) and unreality with the transcendent milieu (the world, the sphere of representation). This is why evil in Christianity is *eternal* — it is not a privation of being (as in the Augustinian-Thomistic *privatio boni* tradition) but a *real* mode of the essence, with the same ontological weight as the good. The demonic, in Henry's reading, is not less real than the divine; hell is not less real than heaven; both are modes of the invisible essence, both participating in the ontological milieu of reality, both eternal in their reality. What is unreal is the world — the sphere of transcendent representation, the sphere of phenomenal visibility. This reading has profound theological consequences that Henry does not spell out (the problem of evil becomes ontologically peculiar; the eternity of hell is given an unusual grounding; the distinction of the economic and immanent trinity takes an unexpected turn). But the structural point is made: Christian ontology is not an ethical-metaphysical ontology of good-vs-evil but a *phenomenological* ontology of real-vs-unreal.

**Paragraph 9\.** Because the discovery of the invisible as constituting the originary essence of revelation and its effectivity is that of reality, the critique directed against Christianity by the young Hegel (and so often taken up after him) — *the idea that (the Kingdom of God as he understood it having no place on earth) Jesus (unable to live in it but only to carry it in his heart) transferred it to heaven and, seeking in this latter a refuge against the world, thus constituted in ideality a disappointed life* — *is simply absurd*. For it is precisely the *ideality of the world* that Jesus rejects — *not as what is null or bad in itself but as the inessential* — while he indicates on the contrary *the place where resides and accomplishes itself, in the invisible, the essence of reality and of life*. Because the essence of reality and of life resides and accomplishes itself in the invisible, *one cannot indeed find it in the world* — nothing of what exhibits itself in the latter can contain it nor render it manifest. This is why the pretension to recognize the essence of the sacred in what one can see and in its light *turns short* — in the latter other values substitute themselves for reality, and *the Greek god is not true*. Still the Christ does not share with this latter (even in the very short instant of a history) the determination of objective being and its appearance — and is it not exact to say that, if in Greek religion (where the god dwells in the phenomenal and maintains himself in it) "the phenomenon" for this reason "constitutes the supreme aspect, and in a general manner the whole of the divine — in Christian religion" on the contrary "the apparition is considered only as a moment of the divine"? For the divine designates in Christianity *the reality of the originary Logos in its non-provisional effectivity* — in its *irreducible ontological opposition to what is thought since always as "appearance."*

The ninth paragraph takes up the young Hegel's famous critique of Christianity (from *The Spirit of Christianity and Its Fate* and *The Positivity of the Christian Religion*, 1795–1799). Hegel had argued: Jesus could not realize the Kingdom of God on earth (because his religious vision was too pure, too interior, too disappointed), so he transferred the Kingdom to heaven and thereby created an otherworldly ideality that constitutes a kind of *disappointed life* — a life that has retreated from the world into an inner ideality, which is the source of Christianity's alienation from the world and from worldly spirit. Hegel's mature philosophy (in the *Phenomenology of Spirit* and elsewhere) will develop this diagnosis: Christianity is the religion of the "unhappy consciousness" that has not yet reconciled itself with actuality; the dialectical task is to overcome this unhappy division through the realization of spirit in the world. Henry's counter: Hegel has completely misread Christianity. What Jesus rejects is not *the world* (as a real thing that he renounces because he cannot have it) but *the ideality of the world* (the pretension of the visible-objective-transcendent milieu to constitute reality). Jesus is not a disappointed idealist who flees to heaven; he is the ontologist who has recognized that reality is elsewhere — in the invisible, in the immanent essence — and that the world is the inessential. The Hegelian reading fails because it presupposes precisely what Henry has denied: that reality is continuous with the world and that any "beyond" must be either a world-to-come or an idealized-refuge. Henry's Christianity breaks with the visible-as-real framework altogether. The contrast with Greek religion is phenomenologically sharp: in Greek religion, the god *dwells in the phenomenal*, is given in the world-milieu (in statues, in temples, in visible cultic manifestations); in Christianity, the apparition (of the incarnate Logos) is only a *moment* of the divine, not the whole of it; the divine itself is the *invisible Logos*, which cannot be reduced to its worldly appearance. The Greek god is not true because the Greek god is merely the visible-appearing, which is ontologically unreal.

**Paragraph 10\.** Because reality (conformably to the structure in it of phenomenality) *cannot take place in the world* nor take in this latter the form of the "appearance," the problematic that provides itself with the ontological dimension absolutely fundamental and originary — where life finds in the invisible the effectivity of its essence — *does not only escape the "objections" that mere common sense cannot fail to direct against it — it further traces their horizon and their frame*. These objections — the ironic interest that they manifest first with respect to this "superior reality," foreign to our world and so marvellously "transcendent" — express themselves finally in a too-natural demand: that of *letting us see a little in what consists such a reality* that thought declares itself ready to admire, on the condition however that one will show it to it. For one cannot admit on the faith of enthusiasm the existence of who-knows-what mystical intuition nor the content foreign to our world of its novelistic ecstasy — and only what is susceptible of exhibiting its object in *this experience which is manifestly ours* can be taken into consideration by science and claim for itself the rigor of a rational knowledge. It is not a matter here — let us remark — of the naive and still prephilosophical question of a consciousness that holds to the existent. Such a demand is rather *that of ontological thought itself* — which (in demanding a "proof") aims at reality, the becoming of effective phenomenality and its possibility. That this latter does not confuse itself with the object of natural consciousness — and must be understood on the contrary as what is not the existent — *has no effect in drawing it out of the prescriptions that define reality*. Thus one sees (and this in the very heart of daily life) pure consciousness show — *as a supreme proof that can at need be given in death* — its difference from natural being. Thus has the essence accepted to submit itself too to the hard law of reality, *in such a manner as to be seen and heard*. And if it does not pertain to it finally to produce itself thus in the day of presence — if it refuses itself rather to its light — it is *in the relation to this latter and as its refusal precisely* that the non-phenomenality which ultimately determines it finds itself to be *thought* — *so true it is that the problematic shows itself decidedly incapable of grasping the most originary essence of truth otherwise than inside its dialectical opposition to objectivity* — that is, *in its unity with it*.

The tenth paragraph takes up the predictable objection from "common sense" (which Henry notes is in fact the objection of ontological thought itself): show me this "invisible reality" you claim; let me see it, touch it, verify it in my experience. Henry's response is subtle. He does *not* say that the invisible reality exists in some super-transcendent beyond that is unknowable and must be taken on faith; he rejects that gesture as equally confused. He says instead that the demand for "proof" — the demand for exhibition in the mode of our experience, in the milieu of visibility — is itself structured by the monistic presupposition that reality is confined to the visible-mode. The objection shows that ontological thought itself (the thought that purports to inquire into reality and its conditions) is unable to escape the visible-mode framework; it can think the immanent essence only *in relation to* the visible — either as what is given in the visible or as what refuses itself to the visible. Even the notion of a "refusal" is structured by the visible-mode: the immanent essence is thought as that-which-would-not-come-to-visibility, as the negation or refusal of visibility. But this is still a monistic thinking; it has not escaped the framework of ontological monism. The reference to "pure consciousness" exhibiting itself in death is illuminating: the tradition (Plato, Seneca, the Stoics) has often appealed to the example of death as the moment where consciousness shows its difference from the natural being — but this appeal operates within the monistic framework, as if consciousness had to *prove* itself in the mode of the visible (by giving itself as a publicly-demonstrable phenomenon, even if only in the extremity of death). The "essence has accepted to submit itself to the hard law of reality, in such a manner as to be seen and heard" — this is the tradition's concession to ontological monism, its attempt to make the essence phenomenal-visible at least in certain privileged moments. Henry rejects this concession: the essence does not need to be seen and heard; the essence is *itself* reality, in its own mode, without needing to exhibit itself in the mode of the visible.

**Paragraph 11\.** But *the objectivity that confers its rigor on scientific knowledge and defines it* has principially nothing to do with that which ontology understands in its foundation as the transcendence of the world — it designates rather *the theoretical exigence by which defines itself such a knowledge as that of recognizing reality under all its forms*. What thought misses (in its pretension to objectivity when it gives itself on the contrary an ontological interpretation of this latter and understands it thus structurally as the condition of the object) is *nothing less than what escapes this condition* — not only (to tell the truth) a form of reality but *reality itself*. It is the essence of life that is lost, while philosophy — in accord in this with simple common sense — insists on demanding a *proof* (in the sense in which it understands it) — thus doing nothing but repeating the presuppositions which are since always its own and which mask for it *the essential*. Thus one sees in Kant (where the conditions of phenomenality are explicitly understood as objectivity) the problematic show itself *incapable of determining the being of the originary consciousness of the ego* — of its concrete life — as, in a general manner, of everything that has relation to the essence — and, in its pretended rejection of speculation, *recur on the contrary to this latter* to reconstruct as it can (by the detour precisely of a speculative morality) *the reign of reality* that it presages mysteriously behind appearance. Still this reality (because it is the product of a speculative construction) gives itself finally as *a back-world* — as that very thing to which "the sons of the earth" claimed to understand nothing. Thus turns short the irony of the half-clever — in such a manner that it does not only recognize the existence of what it first denies but *denatures it*. For *the invisible is nothing that is beyond the visible, nothing "transcendent"* — it is the originary essence of life such that (accomplishing itself in a sphere of radical immanence) *it never rises in transcendence and cannot either show itself in it*.

The eleventh paragraph distinguishes two senses of "objectivity": (a) the theoretical exigence of recognizing reality under all its forms (a legitimate sense, which would include the immanent essence in its reality); and (b) the ontological construal of objectivity as the condition of the object, which restricts reality to what can be given in the milieu of objective manifestation. Ontology has habitually slid from (a) to (b), restricting the theoretical exigence of objectivity (an exigence any phenomenology should satisfy — to acknowledge reality wherever it is found) to an ontological restriction (reality is only what appears as object). Kant is the paradigmatic case. The Kantian identification of the conditions of phenomenality with the conditions of objectivity is, for Henry, the structural origin of the modern exclusion of the immanent essence from ontology. Kant, unable to grasp the ego in its originary consciousness (because this ego does not appear as an object), has to recur to speculative morality (the postulates of practical reason: God, freedom, immortality) to reconstruct the "reign of reality" that he feels must exist behind the world of appearance. But because this reconstruction is speculative — not phenomenological — the reality he reconstructs is a *back-world* (*Hinterwelt*, an arrière-monde, a world behind the world). This is the Nietzschean critique of Kantianism turned against Kant: the noumenal realm of practical reason is a metaphysical fiction, a back-world that is not the real-real but only a speculative substitute. Nietzsche's "sons of the earth" — who refuse the back-worlds — are right in their refusal but wrong in their conclusion (that there is nothing beyond the visible). Henry's counter-thesis: the invisible is *not* a back-world, not a transcendent beyond, not a speculative construction; it is *this very life, in its immanence*, which does not rise in transcendence (and therefore is not a beyond) but is the very reality that we *are*. The back-world is a symptom of the failure to grasp immanence; when immanence is grasped, the back-world vanishes, because the immanent essence is found *not behind the world but in the very reality of our living*.

**Paragraph 12\.** Because (accomplishing itself in a sphere of radical immanence) the originary essence of life never rises in transcendence and cannot either show itself in it, *nothing transcendent precisely* — no entity, no objective determination — *contains it nor exhibits it*. This incapacity of the objective determination to exhibit (as what it is) the originary essence of life is what confers on it its most proper character — *the abandonment in which it holds itself* — and (in its being-foreign to the essence) its insurmountable *forsakenness*. It is in this abandonment of the entity — in its forsakenness and what it has of the insurmountable — that *takes birth the sadness of the thought that thinks it*. Such a sadness is that of *the life that does not recognize itself in what one presents to it* — it is this sadness that runs through Greece and manifests in it (in the extraordinary deployment of the values that relate to the existent, or rather to its dwelling, in the splendor of the day) *the presaging that it has of what it does not know*. For the Night does not show itself in the day — but, in it, *it hides itself more profoundly than in itself*. Such a presaging — that of not being the essence and of not being able either to manifest it — does not the entity that manifests itself in the light manifest it when *it negates itself and takes in tragedy the form of the mask*? For this latter only figures in appearance the tragic hero but rather *the impotence of every figure as such* — the essence itself of tragedy. *The mask expresses nothing* — in this resides its infinite expressive power. It says that, there at least where rises and flashes its naked presence (in the space that it petrifies), *there is nothing to say, nothing that concerns the essence*. What it covers and hides from our sight is not precisely this or that. This too-daily form, it does not reject for another, more heroic — and the face that it turns toward us is no longer entirely a visage. In it rather *freezes everything that composes a physiognomy and confers on it what we call its life* — the expression of the features, their mobility. In the immobility of the mask — in its terrifying fixity — announces itself what precisely does not manifest itself in it and cannot either manifest itself in it — *the element radically other in its fundamental strangeness to everything that takes the form of being-there — the non-visage*. The terror is precisely the sentiment of the unknown — it is this "innate fear" that man feels "when he apperceives that a signification hides itself under a form which does not express (as sensible) this signification — and which consequently attracts and repels, awakening presagings…"

The twelfth paragraph — one of Henry's most beautifully rendered and least often discussed — develops the phenomenology of Greek tragedy as an anticipation of the invisible. The entity in the world cannot exhibit the essence; it stands in abandonment and forsakenness, as what is foreign to the essence. This abandonment is the source of *sadness* — not a psychological mood but an ontological register, the sadness of life that does not recognize itself in the entity that is presented to it. This sadness, Henry claims, runs through the whole of Greek civilization — which was the civilization par excellence of the splendor of the day, of the deployment of the visible-values of the existent in its beautiful manifestness. Greek sadness is not merely a cultural or psychological trait; it is the presaging, within the civilization most devoted to the visible, of what the visible could not contain: the Night, which hides itself in the day more profoundly than in itself. The phenomenological analysis of the tragic mask is extraordinary. Henry reads the mask not as a portrait of the hero's face but as the structural articulation of the impotence of visibility. The mask does not show the hero's face; it shows *the failure of any face* to be the essence. It expresses nothing because what it could express (the essence) is not expressible in the mode of visible features. Its "infinite expressive power" consists precisely in this: it announces that here, at the most intense moment of visibility (the theater of the tragic presence), there is *nothing to say* — nothing that concerns the essence. The mask is therefore not a mask-in-the-ordinary-sense (a concealment of a face behind it) but the *structural figure of the non-visage*: the face that is no face, the countenance that is no countenance, the visible-form that declares the essence to be non-visible. The mask's immobility petrifies the physiognomy and freezes the life that would ordinarily move in the features — and in this petrification, it *announces* the essence that does not and cannot manifest itself in such features. The quotation at the end (which Henry attributes indirectly, drawing on Hegel's *Lectures on Aesthetics* regarding the symbolic) articulates the terror of the unknown that attaches to the mask: the signification hides under a form that does not express it sensibly, and this produces attraction and repulsion, the awakening of presagings.

**Paragraph 13\.** The presaging of what hides itself under the mask (and which this latter does not manifest otherwise than in designating it as *the element radically other and which precisely hides itself under it*) — it is life however that experiences it — *in it, in the consciousness that it has of itself, founds itself the signification that appearance has of being only an appearance*. This is why this latter (the form) is not only what repels but still *what attracts* — why it "awakens presagings." Such an awakening is that of life — *what it presages behind appearance is itself*. Because the signification that appearance has of being only an appearance reposes on life and on the originary consciousness that it has of itself, *such a signification* (the presaging that the form is nothing and hides the essence) *is present everywhere this latter is present* — everywhere life (not recognizing itself in appearance) *seeks itself behind it*. Thus penetrates the Hellenic world *the principle that will destroy it*. For one does not explain here — at the whim of a subjective preference — the anterior by what came after it — but only *what was for a moment the world of men by what is and was always the acting and eternally living essence of life*. It alone explains and founds *the ambiguity of the sensible* — of which it was given to the Greeks to experience more intensely the splendor and the decline. That appearance does not cease to grip us — and that the eternally-visible always proposes itself to us as what attracts and repels — that the most extreme determination that it takes on in the mask be in a certain way always its own and its most habitual manifestation, *the very essence of this latter* — the attitude that (for example) we take before our body (before this body that one sees and can touch) — does it not show it sufficiently? For *everywhere what appears lets appear in it as its underside or gives to guess, there where it seems to us that hollows itself out (as a fissure in the being without words) the path toward the interiority of what is living, rises desire* — and what we call *sexuality* is only our manner of perceiving in terror *the ambiguity of what no longer reduces itself entirely to itself*. More visible in Greece — where precisely its foundation held itself hidden and was not recognized — *an obscure sexuality runs through the world and pierces it*. But because the entity cannot finally resolve the signification that attaches itself to it (and whose origin however is elsewhere) — cannot manifest what it hides — *the failure of sexuality says enough* (in the vain repetition of the project that determines it most often in men) *the impotence of the world to exhibit in it what principally escapes it* — *the irreducible and non-dialectical opposition of the visible and the invisible*.

The thirteenth paragraph delivers one of the most remarkable phenomenological analyses in the entire book: the reading of sexuality and desire as the ambiguous phenomenal registration of the invisible. The argument: the presaging of the invisible behind the visible form is rooted in life's non-recognition of itself in the appearance; the appearance attracts (because it seems to promise that life will find itself in it) and repels (because life does not find itself in it, does not recognize the appearance as itself). Greece is the civilization that most intensely experienced both the splendor of the visible and the sadness of its decline — the ambiguity of the sensible. Greek tragedy is the tragic register of this ambiguity; Greek sexuality is another register. Henry's crucial move: sexuality is not primarily a biological drive or a psychological urge but *the phenomenological modality in which the body (which one sees and can touch) presents itself as harboring an interiority that is not itself the visible body*. The visible body "lets appear in it as its underside" (or "gives to guess") an interiority — and precisely in this gap between the visible surface and the presaged interiority, *desire arises*. Sexuality is "our manner of perceiving in terror the ambiguity of what no longer reduces itself entirely to itself." This is a structural-phenomenological definition of remarkable precision. Sexuality is not about the other body as an object of pursuit; it is about the recognition that the other body is not exhausted by its visible manifestation, that an interiority is presaged behind the visible form, that life seeks itself in what appears to harbor a life. The project that determines sexuality "most often in men" — the repetitive attempt to resolve the ambiguity through the pursuit of bodily union — *fails*, and this failure is not contingent but structural: the entity (the visible body of the other) cannot manifest what it hides (the interiority of the living life), because the interiority is immanent and the entity is in the visible-mode. The "failure of sexuality" is therefore phenomenologically the confirmation of the structural thesis of the section: the visible cannot manifest the invisible; the two are non-dialectically opposed. Greek sexuality, pervasive and intense, is an "obscure sexuality" because its foundation (the invisible essence sought through the visible form) was not yet recognized as such; the Greek eros was the phenomenological registration of the invisible through the only mode the Greeks knew (the visible), and its perpetual inadequacy pointed toward a recognition that only Christianity would finally articulate.

**Paragraph 14\.** With the positive ontological determination of the concept of the invisible — *has the problematic responded to the third question that it posed to itself about the ultimate essence of revelation and of its originary accomplishment* — that of knowing *what constitutes (at the very heart of the act by which it dissimulates itself) the positive phenomenological content, the effectivity of this revelation*? Is it indeed to a manifest content that such a concept refers? Is its signification truly phenomenological? Does it comprise anything other than *the formal and empty negation of this world (finally) which is ours — and of the manifestation that constitutes it*? Does not the invisible consist — as the non-essence — *in the mere arbitrary realization of this negation*?

The closing paragraph of Section III ends, strikingly, not with a positive statement but with *a series of critical questions*. This is a crucial rhetorical-philosophical move. Henry has developed, across §§37–51, the positive doctrine of the invisible as the mode of immanent self-affection. But he recognizes — with the intellectual integrity that the work demands — that the whole positive development is susceptible to a radical objection: perhaps the "invisible" is not a positive phenomenological content at all but *the mere formal negation of visibility*, and therefore the elaborate architecture of the immanent essence is a system of mere negations, of what-is-not, with no positive content of its own. This objection takes the form: if one cannot point to or exhibit the invisible in any phenomenal way, then the concept of the "invisible" is merely the logical-formal negation of the concept of the "visible," and Henry's elaborate structural descriptions (self-affection, jouissance de soi, unity, parousia, pudeur, night, etc.) may all be re-readable as merely negative determinations (not-separated, not-representational, not-visible, not-exhibited, etc.). In which case the invisible would be the "non-essence" — the arbitrary realization of a formal negation, a philosophical ghost that has no positive phenomenological content but only the content provided by the negated visibility. This objection is precisely the objection that any thinker in the monistic tradition would raise against Henry's project. And Henry is honest enough to pose it as the closing question of Section III. The response — the positive phenomenological content of the invisible, articulated in its own mode — is the work that Section IV will undertake. Section III has cleared the ground negatively (by dismantling the monistic framework) and structurally (by showing that the invisible is a distinct mode with its own Selbständigkeit); Section IV will attempt the positive articulation, showing that the immanent essence has a positive phenomenological content — the content of *affectivity*, of *suffering-and-enjoyment*, of *life in its immanent self-affection* — and that this content is not a mere negation of visibility but a structure with its own positive determinations. The closing question of §51 is therefore the bridge to Section IV, where the book's most original phenomenological contribution — the phenomenology of affective self-affection — will be elaborated.

## 

# Section IV. Fundamental ontological interpretation of the original essence of revelation as affectivity

## **§ 52 — Fundamental ontological interpretation of the original essence of revelation as affectivity: affectivity and ipseity**

Henry opens by recapitulating the result of Sections I–III and then converting it into a regress. Beings show up only inside a horizon that must itself be phenomenologically effective; whatever manifests itself can therefore affect us. He cites Heidegger's formula that all affection is a manifestation in which an already given being announces itself (Kant-book, 244\) — the formula concedes exactly what Henry needs, since if the manifestation of a being requires the manifestation of a horizon, then every ontic affection rests on an ontological one. The correction that follows is aimed at the ordinary concept of affection, which reduces affection to whatever excites us. Henry is careful to say where the reduction goes wrong: not in overlooking that the persisting excitant needs the syntheses of internal time-consciousness to be constituted as the identical datum of the affection, but in missing what those syntheses signify. Retaining an affecting thing that comes at us out of the future presupposes that the future is already open, and with it a pure present and a pure past in which the thing can stand and exert its pressure. Husserl's nature as the ground of all that goes by the name of experience (*Erfahrung und Urteil*, 53), the field in which primitive sense-data organize themselves passively by association and time, is a ground only because time first deploys the horizon of a pure world. What touches us reaches us through that world. The conclusion inverts the ordinary picture: the world is not the medium in which affection occurs but the affecting agency itself, and the pressure we ascribe to things is the world's. The passivity of natural consciousness toward the excitant conceals the ontological passivity of pure consciousness toward the three-dimensional horizon of time it never stops raising and undergoing. Every affection is therefore in essence pure affection, in which the subject is affected outside experience — that is, independently of beings.

The second unit compresses Heidegger's Kant-book into a single chain in order to expose its terminus. Opposition (the letting-stand-over-against) makes possible the manifestation of what is as manifest, and so what affects is never the being itself but the object, whose possibility lies in being-opposed, in the world. But opposition succeeds only if the being-opposed that imagination forms is also received and retained by imagination; time is precisely imagination's power to receive by intuiting what it sets over against itself. In receiving the term of opposition intuitively, time renders it sensible and thereby phenomenologically effective. The power to render sensible — the power of sensing — thus lies in time as identical with transcendental imagination, and constitutes inner sense. Because inner sense names the projection of the horizon by which, in receiving it, essence affects itself, it is also the form of all self-solicitation, the act in which essence offers itself what it intuits. The essence of sensibility is contained in the structure of that act, and each particular sense functions only on its basis, since receiving an already given being presupposes that the horizon is perceptible and has been transposed sensibly into intuition. Empirical sensibility, whose forms look pre-inscribed in nature, is therefore conditioned by pure sensibility, whose essence is inner sense. Henry has reconstructed the Kant-book faithfully in order to make its final term stand out as a term — inner sense, not an absolute beginning.

Inner sense then requires a foundation of its own, and the third unit takes the decisive step. If sensing something consists in forming a sensible horizon, the act that forms the horizon must itself be exhibited in its reality, or the claim remains metaphysical assertion. The act that forms the horizon receives itself before it receives or forms anything, and this original self-reception secures its ultimate possibility. With that, the problem of receptivity migrates: it no longer concerns the opposed being but the very possibility of opposition and the act's holding of itself close to itself. Henry piles the descriptions up — the act's self-adherence, transcendence receiving itself, discovering and seizing its own being, cohering with itself in the unity that lets it be and act — and then names the whole: the original affection of transcendence not by the world but by the act that forms the world, that is, by itself. This auto-affection, transcendence's being-already-affected before it affects itself as time, conditions all ontological affection by the world and all affection by beings, and conditions inner sense. The move breaks out of ontological monism because the founding term is no longer anything opposed.

Precisely because it conditions inner sense, auto-affection cannot be identified with it — the point Henry had already isolated in § 31 under the heading of the ambiguity of the concept. The word does not name the ekstasis in which the time of affection solicits itself and is affected by the horizon of pure time; it names the structure that ekstasis presupposes, where no ekstasis occurs and transcendence is absent. That structure is immanence. In it lies essence's fundamental possibility of affecting itself without the mediation of a sense — for a sense always means affection by something foreign — so that the content of its affection, as immanent content, is constituted by essence and by its own reality. Readers who assimilate Henry's auto-affection to Heidegger's time as pure self-affection collapse exactly the distinction this unit exists to draw.

Henry then raises the objection that governs the transition to the whole of Section IV, and answers it with the book's central thesis. Does the description of immanence's internal structure remain formal? Are the properties it uncovers, and the a priori regulations governing their linkage, anything more than ideal and abstract, if the necessity to which essence is subordinated — the necessity of obtaining oneself in advance in the phenomenon of original affection — is merely a necessity that is understood? Does the ultimate condition of inner sense come down to a "it must be that," the eidetic analysis reducing to the demands of reflective thought? The alternative Henry poses is to read in auto-affection what it is rather than deducing it. The simplest experience, the one instituted before ekstasis and within it, the immediate experience of self, the original feeling essence has of itself — that can be recognized. What feels itself without the intermediary of a sense is in its essence affectivity. Affectivity is the essence of auto-affection, its concrete rather than speculative possibility, immanence grasped no longer in the ideality of its structure but in its phenomenological effectuation; it is the way essence receives itself and feels itself, so that the self-feeling presupposed by essence and constituting it turns up within affectivity as effective self-feeling, that is, as feeling. And that is the essence of feeling: not something that feels itself, this or that feeling, but the very fact of feeling oneself taken in itself, in its phenomenological effectuation, in its reality. Feeling is therefore not distinct from essence: affectivity is the original essence of revelation. The answer to the charge of formalism is not a further argument but a change of register — from structure eidetically prescribed to structure phenomenologically effectuated — and it is on this that everything after § 52 depends.

The consequence is the heterogeneity of affectivity and sensibility. Henry fixes the terms: sensibility is the power to sense something insofar as the affection runs through a sense and ultimately through inner sense; affectivity is the form of essence in which essence is affected not by something else but by itself, so that this original affection as self-feeling constitutes and defines it. The tradition has confused the two from the beginning; they are structurally heterogeneous. The heterogeneity can be stated exactly: reception of being in the sensibilized horizon of transcendence — reception of it as other, which is what sensibility is — is in principle absent from whatever constitutes the possibility of feeling. No feeling is either the act of sensing as performed in a sense or the content of that act, whether that content be empirical or pure. Since feeling is never the content of a sense, feeling is never and can never be felt.

Because it cannot be felt, it cannot be perceived either. Every perception, even a pure one and so independent of our sense organs, presupposes at least the schematism of the understanding, that is, the mediation of a sensible horizon. So there is no point in distinguishing an empirical perception of feeling from a pure perception that would obey rigorous a priori regulations on a par with the functions of reason and would deliver a pure feeling, non-empirical and independent of any organic or psycho-organic disposition of the natural subject. Whatever can take the form of a feeling escapes perception as such, because perception presupposes inner sense and the ekstatic development of a horizon. The construction Henry is refusing is Scheler's a priori of feeling, and behind it Kant's *Achtung* as a pure feeling produced by reason — the latter the express theme of § 58\.

The next unit dismantles the grammar in which feeling is ordinarily reported. Since feeling is never the act of sensing structured by inner sense, affectivity taken as a power of sensing — more exactly, of undergoing something and being affected by it — has nothing to do with sense or with what founds sense, nothing to do with transcendence. So "I feel a great love in me" or "a deep boredom" is thoroughly equivocal, because there is no power of feeling distinct from the love or the boredom and charged with receiving them as an opposed or alien content. It is the love, the boredom, feeling itself, that receives and undergoes itself; that capacity to receive and undergo itself, to be affected by itself, is what makes it affective and makes it a feeling. Neither the form of sense nor the content that form determines — nothing that makes the sensible sensible — recurs in the affectivity of the affective. A "sensible feeling" is strictly empty, ontologically an absurdity; affectivity as such is never sensible. And because it is never sensible, feeling can be what it is: not the feeling of something else. By nature it is never that, for just as feeling cannot be felt, feeling itself cannot feel anything other than itself. It is always and necessarily the feeling of self. The property belongs to the essence of feeling and constitutes it: feeling is itself what undergoes and what is undergone, itself the power to be affected and what affects it. This is no synthetic or contingent determination added to it — feeling is not something that additionally has the property of undergoing itself; rather the self-feeling living in it constitutes, in the effectivity of its phenomenological effectuation, what it is. The refusal of any intentional structure in affectivity is the direct target of § 54\.

From here Henry reaches ipseity. What feels itself in such a way that it is not something that feels but the very fact of so feeling itself, so that its "something" is constituted by that self-feeling, self-undergoing, being-affected-by-self — that is the being and the possibility of the Self. What is given to a Self originally and exclusively, as constituting its own reality, is itself; and not as a dead content in the unconscious tautology of a thing identical with itself, but as what it undergoes and what affects it. The identity of the affecting and the affected is realized in the Self, and finds its possibility — real, not theoretical, the effectivity of its phenomenological effectuation — in affectivity. Affectivity is what puts each thing in relation to itself and thereby opposes it to every other, in the absolute sufficiency of its radical interiority. Affectivity is the essence of ipseity. The contrast with the logical tautology A \= A is not decorative: it is the distinction Henry will use in the last units of the section to dispose of the transcendental subject.

Two polemical consequences follow. First, since affectivity is the essence of ipseity, every feeling is as such a feeling of self and so a feeling of the Self, letting it be, revealing it, constituting its being. No feeling can therefore be set above another with respect to this power, as though only certain fundamental feelings — beatitude, say, or despair — had it by virtue of some particular determination of their being or their depth, and could alone be called metaphysical feelings of the Self. The phrase is Scheler's (*Formalismus*, 351), and the note fixes the target. It is never a feeling's particular content, the affective tonality that differentiates and isolates it, that makes it the feeling of an ego; the ego is precisely never the particular content of a particular feeling. Particular content coincides with the feeling itself, determining it here as hatred and there as love, as beatitude, sadness, despair. But a feeling is not the feeling of an ego qua hatred or qua love. A Self belongs to each of these affective determinations — belongs to it because the feeling is each time necessarily a feeling of self, not on account of its particular character but on account of its affective character. The self-feeling that lives in it is what makes it possible, what makes possible the identity of the feeling and its content: its essence, affectivity as such. Henry's argument here cuts at Scheler's stratification of feeling and, by anticipation, at Heidegger's privileging of fundamental attunements — a thesis he will make explicit in § 70\.

Second, no feeling can be nearer to or further from the ego than another, none more truly its own and none merely at its surface, "superficial" or "deep." Feeling is never bound to the ego by a tighter or looser relation, and cannot reach it as something external that touches it more or less and then, as the novelists say, insinuates itself and contaminates it partly or wholly — not if feeling itself constitutes, as self-feeling, the ipseity of that ego. For the same reason the ego's liberation cannot depend on the particular affective tonality in which it occurs, as though the ego could count as authentic or inauthentic, as true being-a-self or as fallen, according to that tonality and the mode of existence it attests. Still less can that liberation and its history through variously ranked forms of existence depend on the nature of the object in whose presence the feeling arises, since ipseity as affectivity has nothing to do with objectivity or with the power that produces it. The passage disposes of the *eigentlich/uneigentlich* distinction of *Sein und Zeit* at a stroke: if ipseity is constituted affectively and not by a mode of comportment, no comportment can make a self more or less its own. As to the psychologists' observation that feeling belongs to the ego more intimately than other psychic states such as representations, the eidetic prescription is stated flatly: every representation, and more generally every possible determination of existence, encloses an ego and belongs to it insofar as it is affective and to the degree that it is. This licenses the founding of representation in affectivity that §§ 66–67 will carry out.

The last three units close the argument by showing that inner sense cannot ground ipseity but presupposes it. The project of grounding ipseity in inner sense arises only because inner sense — that is, time — has itself been construed as the original form of all self-affection. But essence does not affect itself by itself in inner sense; it affects itself as time by the unreal content in which it alienates itself. In inner sense the Self of essence is not presented to it, and the possibility of feeling itself is not realized in time.

Alternatively, the interpretation of time as self-affection rests on time's positing the very content by which it is affected. But the origin of the content of an affection cannot substitute for that affection's phenomenological reality, and in ipseity the ego shows itself in itself, not in the alien appearance said to proceed from it. Nor can that origin simply be located in sense itself, that is, in essence: the claim that inner sense gets everything from itself remains speculative. It says that in sense the subject affects itself, being both what posits the content of its affection and what receives it. Insofar as the subject is not that content, its being stays mysterious. Insofar as it is construed as what both posits and receives the content, the Self at the origin of the affection means only the tautology of what posits and receives — the purely logical tautology of the logical subject. Such a tautology expresses a formal identity without founding it, and has nothing to do with the ipseity of essence; at most it presupposes it. The ipseity of essence, its auto-affection in the immanence of pure affectivity, is the subject's being-a-self as effective, concrete Self, the original Self of affection which as such makes every affection possible, including sensible affection. It is this Self, not the logical subject, that forms opposition; it is to a Self that opposition opposes what it opposes and to a Self that the opposed being offers itself; and it is this Self that receives what only a Self can receive, making every opposition and every reception possible together with their identity. Inner sense presupposes the essence of ipseity as what makes its own structure possible.

Henry closes by naming what inner sense was supposed to supply and cannot. With inner sense the analysis believes it has secured the identity, constitutive of the Self, of the affecting and the affected. But in sense the affecting is being-other, and as such does not coincide with what it affects. That identity is not contained in what sense yields; it withholds itself entirely outside sense and outside the phenomenological content of the affection sense produces. It resides in essence itself, which is the original affecting and equally the originally affected — affected not in a sense but by itself. The identity of affecting and affected is affectivity, and only as such, as essence's auto-affection in its radical immanence, is it essence's Self, its ipseity.

## **§ 53 — Affectivity as original ontological passivity and the effectivity of its essence in "suffering"**

The section takes up immanence's internal structure under the description reached at the end of Section III: passivity of being with respect to itself, original ontological passivity. That structure determines what being ultimately is — bound to itself, without power to break the bond, without any power at all over its own being, unable to posit it, will it, understand it, or get ahead of it in any way, and therefore unfree and essentially passive with respect to itself, cohering with itself in the absolute unity of the adequate experience that constitutes it. But this structure can no more be merely posited as an ideal structure, a condition prescribed by analysis, than immanence itself could. What is realized in it is no abstraction but being's experience of itself, which as adequate experience, as being's self-revelation in itself and as it is, constitutes being. Such an experience, performed in conformity with the structure that makes it possible, necessarily takes on in that structure the form in which it is rendered phenomenologically effective and concrete, imposes itself on us, bears witness to itself in the force of its own phenomenality, and cannot be contested. Being's experience of itself as originally passive with respect to itself is its passion. This is the prototype and essence of every possible passion; every passion is the passion of being, is founded in it and constitutes it. The essence of passion lies in affectivity. Affectivity is the revelation of being as being reveals itself to itself in its original passivity with respect to itself, in its passion.

Henry then places this result historically, and the placement is a critique. Uncovering affectivity as the essence of original ontological passivity establishes an essential connection between affectivity and the concept of passivity through which the being of the ground is first interpreted, a connection expressed in the determination of affectivity's being as passion. That connection surfaces at a crucial moment in philosophy, and is immediately falsified. Descartes files all the affects under the common rubric of passion, and so looks for their essence in passivity — but he has no adequate, ontological concept of passivity. For him passivity does not name the internal structure of being, such that its phenomenological realization in affectivity could concern being and constitute the absolute. On the contrary, Cartesian being or substance is radically foreign to affection, since taken in itself, by itself alone and apart from its attributes, it does not affect us (*Principia* I, 52; AT VIII, 25). What Descartes thinks under the title of passivity is the action of one reality on another, passivity naming the state of the reality that undergoes the action and is modified by it. The ultimate possibility of such an action never becomes a problem, because the alterity of the other being that presses on the passive existent is never considered. What is at issue is an ontic process on the model of natural causality, in which one being determines another, and which deserves to be called action when referred to the first term and passion when referred to the second. On that model Cartesianism conceives the bond between mind and body, the determination of the former by the latter, and out of that determination it makes affectivity arise as what qualifies the mind insofar as the mind is passive toward the body, that is, undergoes its action.

Passivity so understood therefore has nothing to do with affectivity as affectivity offers itself. In asserting an action of the body on the mind and the mind's consequent passivity, Descartes advances a theory of the origin of affectivity that is both unintelligible and, being a theory of origin, useless — an origin external to affectivity and to the phenomenological content of its real being. The third-person process that provokes the affective modification of thought from outside, and with it, on Descartes's account, the emergence of affectivity itself, remains foreign to the structure of essence from which affectivity draws its internal possibility. Yet it is that structure — affectivity's internal structure and its phenomenological effectivity — that the concept of passivity aims at and claims to determine. The concept therefore has to reject the naive formulations in which things act on one another, has to reject every ontic signification, and equally has to reject the ontological signification presupposed by the ontic one, according to which passivity has always been understood exclusively as passivity toward being-other in the upsurge of alterity. Henry is not merely correcting Descartes: he is claiming that the tradition's ontological concept of passivity is as inadequate as its ontic one, because both index passivity to alterity.

Rightly understood, the concept of passivity is the very thought of affectivity and takes on a concrete sense: every feeling is essentially passive with respect to itself, so that in this absolute passivity toward itself and its own being it is delivered over to itself irremediably in order to be what it is. To be delivered over to oneself irremediably in order to be what one is can only mean to undergo oneself, to suffer one's own being, to experience oneself in an undergoing stronger than any freedom, than any power of escape or wrenching away — to feel oneself as one is in the absolute identity of the feeling and what it feels. That original passivity of being toward itself in the self-feeling identical with the essence of feeling, the inner being of feeling and its phenomenological effectivity, is what the concept of passion expresses in general — not the mere extrinsic determination of a being left ontologically unelaborated. Further, the idea of such an extrinsic determination, of thought becoming affective under the body's action according to laws of external causality, the idea of passivity in the third person, is only natural consciousness's naive formulation, made with the means it has and borrowed from the usual content of its representation, of the original ontological passivity inscribed in affectivity's internal phenomenological structure. The various doctrines that profess the alienation of man, the determination of his conscious being by a foreign and stronger reality on the model of a natural process, presuppose the idea of passivity and, more deeply, only symbolize in their own way the fundamental experience of passivity as passivity of being toward itself. They originate in affectivity. Henry thus turns the standard aetiology around: theories of alienation do not explain affectivity but are themselves derivative expressions of it.

Because affectivity is originally passive with respect to itself, its being is marked essentially by an "already." Feeling feels itself, undergoes itself, is given to itself in such a way that in this being-given-to-itself it appears to itself not as given but as always already given to itself. The "already" needs precise elucidation, since it bears on the ultimate ground of everything. Feeling does not discover itself as already given to itself in a gaze, for instance, to which it would offer itself as a content prior to or independent of the gaze's aim. The "already" of feeling's being-given does not concern feeling's past, nothing that would lie there in advance for a power that discovers it. It concerns that power itself, its being already given to itself as soon as it is exercised — the original passivity of essence toward itself in the unity of its auto-affection. The "already" bears on feeling's phenomenological effectivity and determines it. That feeling is always already given to itself means: as soon as it is, on the basis of the self-feeling that constitutes it, it has always already felt itself, always already been given to itself, so that it has a content and appears to itself as overflowed by that content, although the content is identical with it. Better: it is because the content is identical with it, because on the basis of its identity with itself feeling has always already felt itself and carries what it is as what accompanies it invincibly and cannot be shaken off, that it undergoes itself as surpassed by itself and by its own reality. Feeling's identity with itself binds it to its content, so that it is subjected to it and bears it, and, in the absence of any relation, relates to it only within a suffering, and as this suffering, which ultimately determines it and constitutes in it the essence of affectivity. The "already" thus marks the difference between Henry's immanence and any form of retention: what is always already given is not a past content but the power itself.

The self-suffering of feeling in its original ontological passivity toward itself is what must be thought if the essence of affectivity is to be explained. In suffering, feeling's thickness takes form, its real being, decidedly irreducible to the empty tautology of identity that philosophy — when it tries to think identity not as an ultimate condition at which one must simply stop but as effective, in the effectivity of phenomenality — represents as pure transparency, the translucency of consciousness. Feeling's transparency is not a windowpane's, letting one see something else, everything, and in itself nothing. Through its own transparency feeling plunges into the reality of its effectivity. Feeling's surpassing thus takes place within its immanence, the surpassing of the feeling toward what it feels — yet in surpassing itself this way, the feeling surpasses itself toward nothing, does not surpass itself at all: it is feeling's being-seized by its own reality. The absence of surpassing is in feeling what surpasses it, its identity with itself. Such a surpassing, the surpassing of identity accomplished within identity, gives feeling its content, opens it to that content, binds it indissolubly to a content that is itself, and loads it forever with the weight of its own being. What is thus loaded with itself in order to be itself forever is what alone deserves the name of a Self. In the Self is accomplished the motionless movement in which it receives what it is as a substantial and heavy content, seizes it, arrives at itself, undergoes its own profusion. The Self is the surpassing of the Self as identical with itself. The interpretation of ipseity as affectivity acquires its ultimate ontological sense only with the interpretation of affectivity as finding its essence in suffering. With the original passivity of being toward itself as realized in suffering, there is accomplished — as a surpassing of immanence identical with immanence — the Self's surpassing toward what it is, its obtaining of its own being, and identically the surpassing within identity of feeling toward its own content, its upsurge in itself in the profusion of its inner richness, the becoming of its effective being and its consistency. Henry needs this paradoxical language of a surpassing without distance because he must give immanence an internal dynamism without reintroducing an ekstasis; the "motionless movement" is the price of that.

Because feeling's becoming, its obtaining of its own content, its upsurge in itself, is accomplished in the identity of absolute passivity and as that passivity, feeling is delivered over to what it undergoes and to itself in such a way that it can neither contest nor refuse nor assume nor accept what it is. In suffering, feeling's powerlessness announces itself as identical with its essence. That powerlessness has nothing to do with what is ordinarily called a feeling of powerlessness. The latter always occurs in the presence of something; the powerlessness it expresses concerns its relation to an object — powerlessness to modify or suppress it, impossibility of escaping a situation whose conditions are given independently of the subject and imposed on him. Referring to a given situation and depending on it, such a feeling can be transformed. Let the course of things change and subordinate itself to the subject's wishes instead of constraining him, and a new tonality arises, a feeling of power or of joy. The possibility of transformation into the opposite modality is inscribed in the feeling of powerlessness and belongs to its concept as an at least ideal possibility, imaginary but effective as such: the prisoner can always dream his escape. The powerlessness that announces itself in suffering is instead feeling's powerlessness with respect to itself, its powerlessness to break the bond attaching it to itself, the bond of identity in which its content is given to it as what it is. It concerns feeling's internal structure, the suffering in it as self-suffering; it is an eidetic determination. As such it concerns every feeling, cannot be reduced to a particular tonality and cannot turn into another. It cannot be lifted or cancelled in favour of a contrary determination; its negation in imagination is the negation of the essence of affectivity itself and of what affectivity founds. Such a negation therefore cannot be thought at all; only the external suppression of essence can be, and since essence founds the being of the Self each time, that suppression offers itself concretely in the idea of suicide. Suicide reveals in its very concept the ego's powerlessness to rid itself of itself as constitutive of its being, a powerlessness that can be lifted only by the ego's external destruction — as Alexander, unable to undo the Gordian knot, cut it with his sword. But that powerlessness is itself founded in the original powerlessness of suffering, which, thought further, determines feeling's being negatively as deprived of all power over what matters most to it, its own being. The power feeling essentially lacks is the power to hold its being at a distance, to escape it at least in a gaze, the power of distance as such: freedom. And this is indeed what characterizes feeling's being — the impossibility of freeing itself from itself, of arranging behind itself a fallback position into which it might withdraw and, so withdrawing, escape whatever is oppressive in its being.
