The eidetic prescription is that no dimension of retreat can be unfolded, so that there is nothing between feeling and itself, no possible recoil; backed against its being and adhering to it point by point, feeling is delivered over to it in complete powerlessness, in the passivity of suffering. Feeling is the gift that cannot be refused, the coming of what cannot be turned aside. Suicide functions here as a limit-concept proving the thesis rather than as a topic in its own right: it is the only form in which the negation of ipseity can even be represented, and it must destroy the ego from outside because it cannot reach the bond from within.

The reversal follows immediately, and it is the section's decisive move. Precisely because in the passivity of suffering feeling is given to itself and cannot refuse what is given, cannot flee itself or escape its content but is delivered over to it and riveted to it, adhering at every point in the perfect adherence of identity and in complete powerlessness — precisely in that passivity feeling arrives at itself, becomes what it is, arises in itself in the enjoyment of its own being. That is what the passivity of suffering means and accomplishes: the effectivity of what is given. In it feeling seizes its content, undergoes it, undergoes itself, experiences itself, enjoys itself; and in this enjoyment as pure self-enjoyment constitutive of its being, it arrives at that being and posits itself in it effectively. In the powerlessness of suffering the power of feeling appears. Feeling's power is its springing forth, its being-seized-by-itself, its adherence to what it is, the absolute unity in which it coheres with itself — and in that coherence and adherence, in the absolute self-identity of what is seized by itself, in its being-a-Self and as what constitutes it, the kindling of its being, being undergoing itself and, in undergoing itself, illuminating itself, arising, being revelation. Feeling's power is feeling itself, self-feeling as it is accomplished in its effective possibility as suffering. That power does not stand opposed to feeling's powerlessness as one determination to another: it is identical with it and resides in it. *Souffrir* and *jouir* are thus not two affective tonalities but the two faces of one structure — a pairing that will govern the whole treatment of fundamental tonalities in § 70\.

Feeling is the original force. In it is established the upbuilding gathering of what is, without which nothing would be. Only in feeling and through it does what comes to itself come to itself, and, coming to itself, meeting and uniting with itself, emerge into the sufficiency of being-with-itself and so have the power to be. The vocabulary of gathering (*Versammlung*) is borrowed from Heidegger and reassigned: it names not the gathering of the *logos* in the open but the coincidence of being with itself in the absence of any opening.

Since feeling's power resides in its powerlessness and is identical with it, the upbuilding gathering takes place within powerlessness, in the passivity of suffering. That gathering therefore performs no action and gathers nothing that was first separated, as though it had to be accomplished in struggle, in the tearing of a being separated from itself, and as that tearing itself. Because the upbuilding gathering of being — the emergence of the absolute in the absoluteness of being-with-itself, its revelation in presence and its effectivity — answers to no struggle, to no effort of the absolute to seize itself, and no more to the effort of any knowledge, ignores the tearing of opposition and does not presuppose it, but is the absolute passivity of suffering, there is in feeling a certain gentleness. The gentleness of feeling is its quiet force, the silent coming of what comes to itself, is with itself, undergoes itself. In everything that comes, wherever from and wherever to, whatever it be, there is the silent coming of what first comes to itself: the gentleness of being coming to itself in feeling. Such gentleness, in which being comes to itself effortlessly, penetrates everything that is. Take the feeling of effort. What is given in it is the inner tension of an existence confronting the being-opposed and in that confrontation giving it to itself — effort; but in the way effort is given to itself, in the feeling of effort, there is no effort. The being of effort, realized in feeling, is its original passivity toward itself, its being-given to itself in suffering as self-suffering: its gentleness. The example is well chosen, since effort is the paradigm case in Maine de Biran of a self given through resistance; Henry keeps Biran's phenomenon and removes the resistance from its foundation.

The same holds for the feeling of action, for all action, for everything that is. Action is operation. But the being of action is not the operation, not the action itself, and no more the various determinations in which actions express themselves, the varied modes of their unfolding or realization. The being of action is non-action, its original ontological passivity toward itself. Every action is undergone — not by something else, not by the thing on which it is exercised or by the subject who exercises it, but by itself. Or rather, that is what it means to be the subject of an action: to be the action itself insofar as it originally undergoes itself in its ontological passivity toward itself. To be a subject means to undergo, means to be. The being of the subject is being itself. The being of the subject is subjectivity. Subjectivity, constitutive of being and identical with it, is being-with-itself, being's arriving at itself as accomplished in the original passivity of suffering. The essence of subjectivity is affectivity. The chain from "to undergo" to "to be" is the pivot on which Henry converts subjectivity from a regional topic into ontology proper, and it prepares the treatment of action in §§ 68–69.

What silently arrives at itself and gathers itself in the omnipotence of being-a-Self, and coheres with itself in the powerlessness of being delivered over to itself by its original passivity toward itself; what, in the omnipotence of that powerlessness, undergoes what it is and, in the gentleness of its own coming to itself, feels itself and trembles inwardly in the inner trembling of its own revelation to itself — that is life. What life is in its ultimate possibility and its concreteness becomes transparent here: all life is by essence affective, and affectivity is the essence of life. The formula is the destination of the whole book, and the reader should register that it has been reached by an ontological route, not by any appeal to biological life.

Henry immediately blocks two misreadings of it. Interpreting the ultimate ground of all reality as finding its being in life does not mean the analysis forgets its own design and substitutes for the eidetic structural determinations of being properties borrowed from beings, naively promoted in the pre-philosophical conceptualizations of vitalism or biologism. Nor does interpreting the essence of life as affectivity obey any romanticism, any particular and "subjective" vision dependent on a determinate attitude — withdrawal, say, or flight — of an existence unable to face its concrete tasks and seeking illusory compensations in itself and in "feeling," a refuge against the world. To live means to be, as the Greeks already saw and as Nietzsche and Heidegger in turn recognized; so what is at issue in bringing feeling into relation with life is not a particular and arbitrarily chosen mode of realizing life but the internal structure of everything that is. Understood in its internal structure, that is, in its emergence, being is inseparable from affection and finds its own radical and ultimate possibility, its essence, in affectivity.

The section closes by turning against Heidegger's late thought. The analysis's task is ultimately expressed in the question of the phenomenological determination of the being of the ground. Thought in the light of that question, and of the demand for reality it expresses, being has been understood in its structural phenomenological heterogeneity to the open milieu of knowledge — as life, as the invisible. But the mere assertion of the invisible's internal phenomenality, of the invisible as constituting the very essence of revelation and as coextensive and cointensive with revelation's original effectivity, does not make the invisible evident so long as, grasped in opposition to the reign of the visible, it still presents itself as a negative concept, and so long as the non-dialectical character of the opposition from which it is thought is itself merely asserted. Hence the natural wish, quoted from Heidegger, that instead of abstract and floating considerations on unconcealment and concealment one might be given intuitive information about where the thing named properly has its place. Heidegger's reply is that this question comes too late, since one cannot assign a place to what is the condition of every place, to that in which, in the sense of a dwelling, every possible "where" of having-a-place reposes.

Henry accepts the form of the objection and turns it against Heidegger. The absolute that founds every possible manifestation founds it insofar as it manifests itself, and precisely in that self-manifestation. The essence of phenomenality does not lie beyond its effective appearing but constitutes it; reality is not exempt from the conditions that define it. What is floating is rather the account according to which being turns away from us, holding itself back, withdrawing, keeping itself in reserve. If withdrawing is here holding-in-reserve and thereby coming to pass, one must say what the being of that withdrawing is, what makes it an event, an *Ereignis*. If being affected by the real can isolate man from what concerns him, from what approaches him enigmatically, then this approach of the enigmatic, the affection by the invisible, is the problem. Philosophy walks on its head, claiming to found the ground on what the ground founds, when its only way of finally circumscribing being as the enigmatic is to appeal to man's movement toward what escapes him — the appeal Henry documents by Heidegger's commentary on Hölderlin's line that we are a sign without meaning. Being is enigmatic and invisible not insofar as it escapes us and withdraws far from us, but insofar as it affects us. The invisible is being understood as affection, as original affection, as its first effectivity and the essence of all effectivity; phenomenality itself, absolute and irrecusable, as it originally reveals itself to itself, is affectivity. The whole disagreement with Heidegger comes to a point here: withdrawal cannot be the last word about phenomenality, because withdrawal is itself a phenomenon and must be given somewhere, and the only place it can be given is in an affection that does not withdraw.

## **§ 54 — Ontological interpretation of affectivity as the foundation of affection: the problem of "intentional affectivity"**

Affectivity, in which immanence is grasped no longer in the ideality of its structure but in its concrete phenomenological effectuation, has been understood as immanence, in its ontological heterogeneity to the form of sense. But immanence is the condition of transcendence, the reality of the act that sets a horizon over against itself; affectivity is therefore the condition of sensibility. Sensing a sensible content and receiving it is possible only on the basis of the self-feeling that delivers the act of sensing to itself and gives it the reality of what it is — possible, that is, only as affective. Affectivity is not a condition in the sense of something reflective analysis extracts, a logical condition; it constitutes the effectivity of the act of sensing taken in itself, its own phenomenality, the experience of sensing, identical with it and constitutive of its reality. Only as affective in its essence does sensing deploy the structure of inner sense. As affective, as self-feeling, as a Self, the act of sensing — the act of opposition — opposes what it senses to a Self, to the Self it itself is, and is affected by it as an affected Self, in the way that only a Self can be affected by the sensible content of its affection. Only what takes the form of a Self, and only on that condition, can sense: the ego alone senses. The thesis that sensible affection occurs in a sphere foreign to ipseity, ipseity being confined to clear thought and assigned to the I-think of intellectualist consciousness without any reason given for the assignment or the restriction — the thesis that "one senses" — is ontologically absurd. Henry's note names Merleau-Ponty (*Phénoménologie de la perception*, 249, 277\) as the author of the impersonal formula, and the objection is exact: an anonymous sensing has no principle of individuation, since only an ipseity constituted affectively can be the one to whom a content is given.

The confusion of affectivity with sensibility can now be both explained and refused, and Henry does both at once. It is refused because affectivity, realized concretely in suffering, excludes the structure of sense from itself; it is explained — indeed founded — because the structure of sense and the act that deploys it are possible only on the basis of that act's original coherence with itself in suffering. The eidetic law governing the ultimate domain of the ground reads in two clauses that must not be run together: affectivity is never sensible; sensibility is constantly affective. The asymmetry is the whole point, and the prejudice Henry has been attacking since Section I arises from reading the second clause backwards into the first.

Because it is constantly affective, sensibility can be what it is: not the theoretical representation, the cold contemplation of the reality it grasps, but that reality's apprehension in sensing and in the form of sensing. The tonality proper to sensing does not come from the specificity of the sensible datum in its irreducible qualitative diversity, in the *quid proprium* of its materiality. Such a datum is still only the empirical content of sensibility and offers itself to sensibility only insofar as sensibility's pure power is exercised. Tonality concerns that power and claims to characterize it. What, then, is that power, sensing taken in itself, if it is determined in its being by a tonality of its own and is thereby irreducible to the pure gaze of theoretical knowledge? The power of sense is the projection and reception of the horizon; and because reception is entrusted to intuition and can be accomplished only by it, the act of sense is not the pure act of thinking but the act of intuiting what, as received in intuition, necessarily offers itself as a sensible content, albeit a pure one. Henry's note here glosses Heidegger's claim that the essence of sensibility lies in the finitude of intuition (Kant-book, 87), and extends it: Heidegger means empirical sensibility, bound to receive a being it did not create, but pure sensibility, in which empirical sensibility is founded, must also receive its content intuitively.

Intuition, however — as the circularity of the schematism problematic already showed — is only a name for receptivity. The content the schematism transposes sensibly, in order to give itself its effective appearance, is only the being-there-in-front as being-extended-in-front; the sensible character of that content means nothing more than its phenomenality as the phenomenality of the being-extended-in-front, nothing more than the effectivity of its appearing. And in that appearing there is nothing that constitutes the tonality of sensing. Should tonality then be sought on the side of sense and its power to sense rather than in its content? But when the name of that power is intuition — reception of the being-extended-in-front, the letting-extend-in-front of the being-extended-in-front, its upsurge into phenomenality and that phenomenality itself — then tonality is precisely not there, not in a power of sensing identified with what it senses and thought as that content's emergence. The alternative is to take into account the reality of that power, the act of sensing grasped in itself as self-feeling. The tonality of the act of sensing is its self-feeling, its affectivity. Affectivity alone allows sensibility to be what it is: an existence, the thickness of a life gathered into itself and undergoing itself while it is affected, suffering and bearing what affects it — not the cold apprehension of what affects it or its indifferent contemplation. And coldness of apprehension and indifference of contemplation, the theoretical gaze included, are themselves affective tonalities, belong to sensibility and determine it; they are the concrete modalities in which the act of sensing, taken in the reality of its essence as affective, is each time accomplished. The move disarms the standard objection in advance: there is no affectively neutral case, because neutrality is itself a tonality.

The affective character of sensibility is therefore its essential character. It determines the act in which sense gives itself its content as an act that is never a slack-jawed staring at a pure object, never deprived of tonality, but always affected by tonality and constituted by it. It is essential because it is not superimposed on sensibility's exercise as a variable or passing colouring, or even as an ever-present accompaniment, but makes that exercise possible. Opposition can occur, and the world can affect and touch us, because the power of opposition that opens the world to us and is affected by it affects itself originally. The world is not first given to us and only then, perhaps, apt to move us or leave us indifferent; it can be given to us only as what touches and moves us, and this because the affection of transcendence by the world is conditioned by auto-affection. Sensibility is transcendence itself as affective in its essence. The essence of sensibility lies in affectivity.

Sensibility is accordingly not a particular faculty determining in the being that exercises it a specific form of life as against other possible modes — intelligent or active life, say. It names the essence of the relation to the world, and so every possible relation to the world, whatever its mode: practical, theoretical, or "sensible" in the narrow sense of what occurs through bodily organs and belongs to them. And because sensibility names and constitutes the essence of the relation to the world, being-in-the-world taken in itself, abstracting from the kind of reality it puts us in relation with, is determined out of the essence of sensibility in it as essentially affected each time by a tonality. Every relation is affective and can occur only as such. What occurs in the relation is our being placed in the presence of transcendent being and our accord with it taken as a whole, our accord with the totality of beings. That this accord, in which every particular comportment toward beings is antecedently founded, goes mostly unnoticed and forgotten within the very comportment it founds takes nothing away from its reality — from the secret trembling that runs through our relation to the world and determines it everywhere and always as essentially affective. Henry is here taking over Heidegger's *Befindlichkeit* as disclosure of the whole and its characteristic self-concealment, in order to found it elsewhere.

What founds our accord with the totality of beings has been interpreted, following contemporary ontology, as the understanding of being. Since understanding is accomplished in and through sense, the eidetic analysis of sensibility is identically the analysis of understanding, and its propositions hold for it. All understanding is affective; every act of understanding has its tonality, variable no doubt, but bound to it and unavoidable. Wherever the opening of the horizon of being is presupposed — in every comportment, action, perception, cognition, representation — whatever presents itself as deprived of tonality, as an absence of *Stimmung*, is in fact only a particular tonality: the impassivity of a gaze, the coldness of speculative knowledge, the indifference of a contemplation are affective determinations among others. The interpretation of understanding as affective posits an essential bond, such that wherever the being-extended-in-front arises as the very possibility of an object in general and of objectivity, it arises necessarily as affected and determined by a tonality. All the modalities that involve and relate to the object, all the modalities of representative life, are indissolubly modalities of affective life. But why understanding is affective must remain clear. Ontological understanding of being and affectivity do not go together as co-original components of the event in which phenomenality arises, and do not constitute that event on the same footing or equally. The bond uniting them is therefore no mere juxtaposition, no assemblage of properties whose simultaneity one merely records before including them in one and the same absolute under the title of *Gleichursprünglichkeit*. This is the explicit break with *Sein und Zeit*: Heidegger's equiprimordiality of *Befindlichkeit* and *Verstehen* is exactly the thesis Henry denies, because their bond is one of foundation. Affectivity has already done its work when the world rises; to everything that offers itself in the world and presupposes it, affectivity is bound constrainingly, as what makes it possible in its ground.

Henry tests the thesis on Husserl's treatment of evidence. Is evidence a feeling? Husserl says no, and rejects the theory that a judicative act, remaining identical in all the rest of its psychological essence, could sometimes carry an affective colouring and sometimes lack it — appearing now as evident, now as non-evident (*Ideen I*, 71). That theory distorts the phenomenon: evidence is not a subjective tonality winning our assent, calling to us like a mystical voice from a better world, but a special mode of positing (*Ideen I*, 484), consisting in this, that the statement expressing the judgement's meaning is on one occasion fitted point by point to an intuition, yielding a clear evidence of a state of affairs, while on the other occasion a wholly different phenomenon underlies the statement, a non-intuitive consciousness of the state of affairs (*Ideen I*, 72). Henry accepts the refutation and turns it. Every positing act, in whatever mode it is accomplished, including the case where thought gives itself the intuitive fulfilment of the meaning it intends, is in itself — in its original self-affection, as self-feeling — an affective phenomenon. The affectivity of evidence certainly does not accrue to a judgement whose content and positional mode remain otherwise unchanged, as a monotonous tonality joined to it here and absent there: the bond between affectivity and representation is not synthetic and so not contingent. Because it is a bond of foundation, the relation obtaining each time between the positional act and the tonality that inevitably affects it becomes intelligible. The affective tonality of an act of presentification in judgement is that act's very reality; far from being contingent with respect to it or indifferent to the positional mode it effects, the tonality varies as the act varies and is identical with it. The tonality of a presentification accomplished in evidence is rigorously determined, eidetically bound to the positional mode governing that presentification, and so essentially different from the tonality bound to a presentification whose positional mode differs. If eidetic laws govern the relations between positional acts that have the special constitution of evidence and those that lack it (*Ideen I*, 485), then eidetic laws govern the relations between the affective tonalities eidetically bound to those acts as well. Henry has, in effect, annexed Husserl's eidetics of positional modality and made it deliver an eidetics of tonality.

The eidetic correlations between acts' affective tonalities and their noetic-noematic structure are not confined to evidence or to judgement; they are universal and concern every possible intentional act. Our feelings are neither more nor less contingent than our thoughts. Just as thoughts exhibit absolutely determinate typical structures they obey, so do feelings in their bond with those thoughts and, through them, with things. Each of us feels a landscape, a work of art, a moment of history, everything that happens to him, differently and subjectively — yet these ways of living are subject to the laws of perception, imagination, memory. The tonalities bound to acts of perception, imagination, and memory, and inevitably determining them, are not contingent with respect to those acts: they are their reality and the modes of their realization. We do not undergo just anything in the presence of just anything. The feelings things provoke in us are the consciousness of their constitution. The last formula is the strongest concession Henry makes to intentional analysis, and it is a concession only in appearance: constitution is legible in tonality because tonality is the reality of the constituting act, not because tonality is directed at the object.

If understanding is affective, then every tonality inherent in an act of understanding and bound to it as its very reality is, as such, understanding. That is the thesis Henry now confronts. It denies that affectivity consists in subjective modifications or qualities, in themselves opaque, irrational, inexpressible, incapable of surpassing themselves toward a meaning or reaching one, deprived of sense, whose bond with our representations could only be external and contingent and so give rise to association, transference, sublimation — to purely mechanical phenomena. Because affectivity is itself understanding, it presents itself from the start as a significant phenomenon, deploying the horizon of understanding within which it aims at the object and relates to it, so that this aiming, the very possibility of intending an object and relating to something else, belongs to it and defines it. So arises in modern philosophy, given out as one of its most important discoveries, the thesis that affectivity is intentional. Affectivity is not a thing; it is consciousness, and as such consciousness of something. Every affective determination, like any other psychic fact, exhibits this essential character of intentionality. What would a love without an object be? How would one delimit a hatred that was not hatred of Peter or Paul, of some social group, some trait of character, some attitude lived precisely as hateful? Because a feeling is never a brute fact but means something, surpasses itself toward it and understands it, feeling is as such intelligible, and there is room for a new philosophy of affectivity which, instead of explaining the play of our emotions causally by physiological or psychological mechanism, will seek their sense and their aim, taking them as one takes a finalized and organized structure. Henry states the intentionalist case at full strength — it is the case of Brentano, Husserl, Scheler, and Sartre, and it is what makes phenomenological psychology of the emotions possible — before dismantling it.

The dismantling turns on a single question: how can affectivity be understanding, capable of grasping and living transcendent significations, if nothing is more repugnant to its essence than transcendence, if the deployment of a horizon of understanding is what is most foreign to it? Taken in itself, affectivity understands nothing. It is rather the impossibility of all understanding, the non-development of ekstasis, and only in that impossibility is it what it is: the absolute immanence of life in its original passivity toward itself, suffering, and precisely as such, affectivity. Believing it had seized affectivity's most important character in intentionality, modern philosophy missed its essence and lost it. Besides, taken as intentional, affectivity shares that character with all other psychic facts — and there are psychic facts that are not affective. The essential, the psychological essence, would then be constituted by intentionality; in the stricter language of ontology, transcendence would be the foundation of all psychic phenomena and would determine them all equally, affective phenomena included. The truth is the reverse: affectivity is the universal foundation of all phenomena and determines them all originally as affective. The affectivity of phenomena resides in the auto-affection of the transcendence that deploys the horizon. Affectivity is not the grasping of the horizon but the reality of the act that grasps; not understanding, but its ultimate possibility and its ground. Affectivity is not understanding in the way that understanding is affective; the two propositions are not equivalent formulations of the ultimate eidetic structure of the ground but stand in a relation of foundation. Affectivity is understanding only because understanding is affective and to the degree that it is. The asymmetry repeats, at the level of intentionality, the asymmetry stated earlier at the level of sensibility, and it is what separates Henry's position from every phenomenology of the emotions, however anti-mechanistic.

Because understanding is affective, what it understands is affective too: the world itself and its horizon. "Affective world" must not be taken as the psychologists take it, as a determinate region of reality or existence peculiar to each of us, some secret inner garden where imagination, freely projecting its desires, would rest and live apart from the world. It is the world itself, this external and "real" world, the world of things and objects, that is affective. "The world," precisely — not the things or objects populating it. Here too the psychological explanation must be set aside, the one that takes things to be affective in themselves or at least affectively coloured by the projection onto them of the subject's desires and interests. For it is not things or objects, not beings, that are affective. Or, if one prefers, it is the object — not in the naive, pre-critical sense psychology still gives it, but the object as such, the being taken insofar as it manifests itself. Affectivity is bound to manifestation and belongs to it; it concerns the very upsurge of the object and its possibility, the world in its pure worldhood. It is a determination of the being of beings, not an ontic property. In what sense and how is the world affective? Insofar as it is understood by understanding, insofar as the reality of the act that understands is affectivity.

Heidegger, in what Henry grants is the deepest movement of Western thought and one whose source lies in Greece, interpreted manifestation as the image, as the pure place in which and by whose prior manifestation everything that manifests itself manifests itself. But the image is possible only on the basis of reality. The reality of the image is the non-image: affectivity. The image is affective. The compression here is deliberate — three sentences dispose of the entire ontology of the horizon by locating its reality outside itself.

Henry then illustrates and immediately corrects the illustration. Proust writes that the memory of an image is only the regret of a certain moment, and that houses, roads, and avenues are as fleeting as the years (*Du côté de chez Swann*, I, 427). But the affectivity of the image is not to be sought in its representative content or in that content's link to a particular event. Our images' tonality is indeed determined in accord with our history, yet their power to touch and move us must be thought in itself, as a pure possibility of a priori order. The affectivity of the image is its internal possibility, is the possibility of being itself and its essence. The correction is characteristic: Henry takes the literary evidence for the affective charge of memory and refuses the empirical explanation of it, since what is to be explained is the very capacity of an image to bear any charge at all.

## **§ 55 — Ontological determination of affection by affectivity**

Since affectivity founds affection, it determines it, and the ordinary relation — the one thought establishes in agreement with common sense between what affects us and the feeling we undergo — is thereby inverted. Feeling does not simply result from affection as its inevitable and assured effect; it is superordinate to affection as what regulates it and on which affection depends. There is of course a standing correlation between the manifold excitations that beset us and the successive modalities composing the history of an existence, which it undergoes in connection with those excitations and as their effect. But the link is not mechanical, not the link of cause and effect. It is the object, not the being, that affects us — the object, that is, that toward which existence surpasses itself and which it constitutes — so that the feeling existence undergoes in the presence of that object is the very reality of the act constituting it. Alongside the noetic-noematic correlations, or rather as their real and so affective expression, there are established eidetic correlations uniting existence's affective tonalities with its affection by objects. The passive syntheses governing the relation of existence to what affects it — in perception, for instance — mean the determination of feeling and its modalities by what affects, and their subordination to the process of affection, while the possibility of active synthesis, as the possibility of the inverse determination, remains open and always to some degree effective.

That determination of affectivity by affection does not merely occur; it must also be possible, and its possibility is the possibility of affection itself, is affectivity. What happens does not determine affectivity; affectivity makes possible the coming of what comes and determines it, determines what happens as affective. Superordinate to the determination of existence's tonalities out of what affects and according to the modalities of its constitution stands, as its foundation, the structural ontological determination of affection by affectivity. That determination states that everything exciting or touching us, everything received, can be such only insofar as something like a tonality forms in the receptivity that receives it and as that receptivity itself, as its concrete and effective phenomenological reality. Everything that reaches us and becomes real in us does so in and through the affectivity of that tonality, in and through the affectivity of the absolute. Hence the tonality of this reaching must itself be understood: it is not in the first place the variable and contingent modality existence takes on in its dependence on foreign being, but a property of essence and indeed its universal structure — the universal structure of affection as finding its essence in affectivity.

Affectivity is not the abstract condition of affection; it is the event in which everything that comes, comes and gathers, the coming as such, as original coming, and its phenomenological effectivity. The tonality existence takes on, described as "variable and contingent," is inseparable from that coming; it designates the particular mode in which the coming is each time accomplished. It is a modality of essence, drawing its substance from essence and belonging to it, and therefore explicable out of essence and receiving from essence its first and last determination. The structural ontological determination of affection by affectivity does not merely make the existential determination of tonalities by what affects possible; it determines it, so that the existential determination proves illusory and its sense must be inverted. The course and nature of the tonalities that determine an affected existence originate, within that very affection and within the constitutive passive synthesis, in essence, and arise out of it. Tonalities depend on essence, that is, on their own innermost being; determined by what comes, they are, as constituting each time the very reality and the concrete phenomenological possibility of that coming, co-determined by it — that is, by their own reality and by the absolute of life in them. Henry is not denying the phenomenon of situational feeling; he is reassigning the direction of determination inside it.

Tonalities depend on essence as on what depends on nothing, what arises outside any relation to anything whatever, in the sufficiency of its own being. That sufficiency is feeling's own, as foreign in itself to any affection by foreign being, as being itself in its original ontological passivity toward itself. The name of this sufficiency is autonomy. Autonomy is the essence of life, identical with affectivity: it is the fact that life feels itself, has and is the feeling of itself. And precisely because life is in its essence autonomy, it "depends on circumstances," which is to say it can be affected. A stone is affected by nothing, and so is any body whatever, however complex its internal organization, even a biological organization endowing it as a living body with a nervous system. Only what hollows itself out in itself as a self, the absolute entity that is self-feeling, the essence of affectivity, is and can be affected. Every dependence presupposes an absolute independence, the original autonomy of being as being-a-Self, and of life. This autonomy is not freedom in the customary sense, nor even the ontological freedom that unnoticed underlies it, but its contrary: the original passivity of being toward itself and its self-sufficiency, the essence of non-freedom. The paradox is exact and load-bearing — autonomy here means being unable to get free of oneself, and it is that inability which makes affectability possible at all.

Since life depends on circumstances only on the basis of its absolute independence as absolute dependence of its being on itself, what that dependence on circumstances is becomes transparent. Tonality is the way life undergoes itself, a mode of suffering, the self-suffering of the absolute, such that this self-suffering depends on the absolute itself and is identical with it as the mode in which the absolute is each time realized and accomplished, and as its history. The inner becoming of the absolute and the mode in which that becoming is accomplished is what regulates every affection, its law, its essence, its reality. The reality of affection, the auto-affection of the affected being, is the reality of the absolute and its history: it is tonality. Tonality does not proceed from affection by foreign being; it is affection's reality as the reality of the absolute itself, realized each time in the absolute, out of it, and as what it is.

The relation between feeling and the conditions supposed to provoke it can therefore be understood for what it is: an expression of feeling's independence of those conditions within its absolute dependence on itself. That absolute self-dependence, feeling's original ontological passivity toward its own being, is what constitutes it and makes it possible — suffering as such and the essence of affectivity in it. On the basis of what it is, therefore, feeling forms itself, arises and persists, in absolute dependence on itself and so in absolute independence of foreign being. Such independence, in which feeling's reality attests itself and in which what deserves to be called its "spontaneity" becomes manifest, shows up in every authentic feeling as its most proper character. Superficial talk attaches to every determination of life some external event supposed to account for it — some action, some social, historical, individual, or collective condition making up the milieu in which life is lived, the world to which life is inevitably bound, if not by blind mechanical relations then by the play of intentional ones. To the philosophical gaze it appears instead that the tonalities in which existence expresses itself in turn, and which together compose the course of its history, spring from existence itself, "inexplicably" — that is, without reference to the conditions one claims to assign to their upsurge, and without finding in those conditions a sufficient reason, since the sufficient reason lies in feeling alone, in the mode in which the absolute is each time accomplished in and out of itself. Despair, as Scheler saw forcefully, shows itself wherever there is genuine despair as fundamentally indifferent to the circumstances surrounding it or in which it arose; it cannot be modified by them, and one cannot act on it, provoke it, or suppress it by acting on them, by trying to bend their course in a direction favourable to the subject's aspirations. Nor can the subject act on his own feeling, which thus appears, in absolute independence of every condition foreign to its own nature, as capable of being given only where the play of transcendent correlations and their power ceases — where, in Scheler's words, no possible conduct of ours could be thought able to modify the feeling (*Formalismus*, 351). The same holds for beatitude, which cannot depend in existence on the alternation of joys and sorrows, on what events bring, but rests on itself with such force that nothing apparently opposed to it, not even adversity or the caprices of fortune, can alter its serene tonality. And just as the obstacles it apparently meets in the world cannot put an end to it, so what favours beatitude, or seems to, cannot in fact produce it; the project of eliciting it by modifying the objective conditions into which it should insert itself naturally, as their effect, is vain. Like despair, and for the same reasons, beatitude cannot be produced. The techniques by which men transform the world and arrange it to suit themselves can do a great deal, and nothing whatever where beatitude is concerned; the attempt to provoke it nonetheless issues only in the multiplication of means to that end, and the senseless proliferation of new happiness-techniques in the modern world manifests only their total impotence. The diagnosis of modernity is not an aside: it follows directly from the thesis that tonality is the reality of the absolute and not the effect of a state of affairs, which is why no rearrangement of states of affairs can reach it.

Henry then turns Scheler's own observation against Scheler's restriction of it. Beatitude and despair are far from being the only tonalities capable of arising in existence and determining it without reference to the world of its affection; Scheler was wrong to call them the only feelings one cannot even conceive as produced or merited by our conduct or by the course of circumstances. If, as the eidetic analysis has established, feeling's independence of affection — indeed its determination of every possible affection — belongs to it by virtue of what it is, then the self-upsurge out of itself must be affirmed of every tonality whatever, as determining what affects it and as identical with the reality of that affection. That our tonalities appear to depend on life's vicissitudes and to be regulated by them; and still more, the project always detectable in such cases of leading the kind of existence in which, turning toward the event, we offer ourselves to it and ask it to bring us the pleasure or joy we do not find in ourselves; the decision to entrust ourselves to what happens and, so to speak, to let it pass through us in order to be what it is; availability, curiosity, trust in the course of sensations and impressions; the organization of that course, whether in the piecemeal attempts of individuals or in the coherent effort of a civilization to satisfy needs, desires, and tendencies, and still more those it itself arouses; aestheticism, hedonism, utilitarianism and their actualization each time in a singular existence — all of this, which has its roots in the emptiness of existence, that is, in its tonality, is far from being able to determine that tonality: it is identical with it and results from it. Thus the autonomy of affectivity, and its determination of all affection, attests itself within dependence on foreign being and all the more within it.

Two positions must accordingly be rejected. Fichte's thesis that feeling depends on chance (*Anweisung zum seligen Leben*, 109–110), and that feeling therefore cannot let us grasp and enjoy life or establish our relation to the absolute — that possibility being left to what alone can subsist by itself and so endure, self-consciousness identified with knowledge and thought — falls with the demonstration of affectivity's autonomy. And with it fall the very differently inspired doctrines that nonetheless share with Fichte, and with nearly all philosophies of feeling, the conception of feeling's absolute contingency, its dependence on the event and on affection generally, and that believe they can found on that dependence, now understood as an essential character of affectivity, a positive knowledge of feeling's genesis, development, and principal properties. Chief among them are the functional theories of self-styled scientific psychology, which claim to illuminate feeling from its function and role, namely to adapt us to things and to institute between the living being and the universe an equilibrium essential to the maintenance and development of any life. Given this adaptive character and the objective orientation it confers, it is "normal" that feeling, adapting to a thousand diverse objects, aroused by them and varying with them, should change ceaselessly, so finding in its own nature the reason for the contingent and changing character that seems to define it. Contrary determinations — stability, subjectivity — are then explained by a disturbance of that essential function, a defunctionalization, a maladaptation in which feeling, detached from its environment and henceforth foreign to its fluctuations, ceases to change accordingly and persists instead, following a fixation, a regression, or some trauma, as a pathological and anachronistic feeling, fit for analysis and destined at best to be dissolved by it. Passion, in which feeling asserts itself in defiance of a historically defined situation and its shifting demands, counts as a typical case of maladaptation, which however can be understood only from adaptation itself, as its negative determination or limit-case, since a feeling's pathological duration is only the persistence of what was once functionally founded. The theory Henry has in view is Pradines's, and he reproduces it accurately before showing where it inverts the order of foundation.

What is characteristic of so-called positive research is its habitual failure to know the essence of the phenomenon it studies, which leads it to ascribe a number of characters to that phenomenon without being able to rank or found them, to enumerate them gratuitously and haphazardly, and consequently to argue about them indefinitely. Thus "subjectivity" turns up at one moment, in the derangement of passion, as a property of affectivity and so as an accidental determination of it, bound to it contingently and precisely by way of a derangement — whereas affectivity constitutes the very possibility of subjectivity and its essence, and is identical with it. Thus one sees the analysis orient itself absurdly toward the function of feeling and its role in the general economy of the psyche, trying to account for feeling from the phenomenon of adaptation, explaining the emotions by an abrupt rupture of adaptation and so again out of adaptation, pursuing every kind of analysis in that direction before ever asking what feeling as such is, and never asking. As for adaptation itself, if it is to play the part of an explanatory principle within a problematic of affectivity, one must first consider what makes adaptation possible and serves as its foundation, namely affection. To explain affectivity by adaptation is to explain it by affection, to take the condition for the conditioned and so to walk on one's head — in agreement, admittedly, with common sense, for the more superficial a thought is and the more it inverts the true order of things, the wider the audience it is assured. If something is to be thought under the title of adaptation, it is the relation to external being, a relation indissolubly bound to affectivity as to the essence that excludes it from itself yet founds and ontologically determines it.

The structural ontological determination of affection by affectivity contains the principle of a general critique of mechanism, that is, of the idea that the affected depends rigorously on what affects it. Where affection is concerned, mechanism cannot mean some third-person process analogous to the relations of interdependence obtaining among beings. Affection itself cannot be reduced, as it constantly is in the positive sciences and in psychology insofar as psychology conforms to their methods in order to earn the title of rigorous science, to a process of that kind, to a law of beings and the determination of beings by themselves. Because affection is not that, and because its concept must be pulled out of the ambiguity on which the whole pseudo-positivity of objective psychology rests, mechanism as applied to affection no longer designates the determination of one being by another but the inner and living relation of the affected being to what affects it as object. Interpreted in the light of mechanism so understood — a kind of psychological mechanism — the relation of what affects and what is affected presents itself as the rigorous determination of the affected being's inner being by what affects it, by the object whose passive synthesis it constitutes. That such determination is never rigorous, and that the inner being of the affected is never reducible to the mere effect of what affects it, follows from its being on the contrary the condition of what affects it. What is called the spontaneity of the living being, and set in that capacity against "mechanism," is only an improper name, the worldly expression of what constitutes the nature of affection: not the action of a being, but the ontological event that makes such action possible. Because affectivity constitutes the original structure of that event and its reality — the reality of the being's action itself, understood in its phenomenological effectivity and its possibility as action on us — that action finds its origin and its reality where it makes itself felt, where ipseity is hollowed out, in ourselves and in essence, and finds in essence the origin and sense of the determination it each time accomplishes.

These are the structural ontological foundations governing the essential relation of life and external being, that is, affection, and only from them can that relation be understood. Founded in affection and made possible by it, the relation of life and external being shows itself as irreducible to the mere passive production, in the affected being, of what it undergoes following external excitations; it implies on the contrary the determination by the affected being and by its being-a-self of the tonality that is each time its own, the determination of feeling by feeling itself and by the essence of affectivity in it. The relation of life and external being, a being's history understood as the correlation of what befalls it and what it is, is what is called its destiny. If destiny cannot be reduced to what happens in us without us — and in truth nothing of the sort ever happens — and if destiny is the ensemble of events which, unsought, are nonetheless undergone by us when they befall us as being in conformity with what we are (Scheler, *Wesen und Formen der Sympathie*, 289), then this manifestation of life's spontaneity must not simply be translated into psychological terms. Its origin must be sought elsewhere: not in the subject's history or in the particular content of his prior experiences, but in what constitutes the ontological structure of every possible experience, in the structure of affection itself and in its essence. Anything like a destiny can ultimately be understood only from the destiny of the absolute itself and as its history. Henry thereby annexes a Schelerian topic to the doctrine of § 53: destiny is not a pattern discernible in a life but the *historial* of self-suffering, and its conformity to what we are is analytic rather than remarkable.

The universal ontological structure of affection is that of sensibility itself. That this structure — finding its ultimate possibility and the reality of its concreteness in the affectivity of essence and in its absolute autonomy, that is, in what constitutes the essence of ipseity — necessarily determines and founds everything that affects us and can be sensed by us: this is what founds the "spontaneity" of sensing. Henry closes the section by giving an apodictic ground to a thesis Lagneau had asserted intuitively (*Célèbres leçons et fragments*, 182). Lagneau's argument is that there could be no way of feeling that counted as the true one for us in given circumstances, since that would require either that our sensible nature not change or that its development follow a rigorous law — in which case sensible nature would be wholly a resultant of its relation to the external world, and there would be no spontaneity in us and so no sensible nature at all. To say that we are individuals is to say that in these individuals there is a sensible nature in which something does not result from the action of the environment; were everything in sensible nature necessitated by the external world, we would not feel at all. Henry's point in quoting it is that Lagneau had the conclusion without the ground: the impossibility of a "correct" way of feeling is not a residual indeterminacy left over by causal explanation but follows from tonality's being the reality of the absolute.

## **§ 56 — Affectivity and sensations**

Since affectivity founds and determines affection, it cannot be reduced to what finds in affection the condition of its own possibility, namely sensation, nor be confused with it. The prejudice denounced throughout these researches does not consist in simply identifying affectivity with sensibility, but in interpreting affectivity as the result of whatever affects our sensibility — sensibility itself then being understood not as the pure ontological power making every affection possible but as what occurs within that power and "really" affects us each time, that is, as the sum of our sensations. Empirical sensibility serves as the basis both for common sense's account of affectivity and for the accounts offered by "positive" research. Feeling certainly does not reduce to sensation and cannot be contained in it: sensation passes and feeling lasts, sensation is simple and feeling complex, sensation superficial and feeling always of a certain depth. But the sensation called simple and fleeting, the isolated sensation, is an abstraction never realized, not even under the abstract conditions of the laboratory. What is real at each instant is the whole of our sensations — not their sum but what they compose together, melting into one another: the affective tonality of existence and the modalities through which existence successively passes and in which it never stops transforming itself. Henry concedes the descriptive distinction between feeling and sensation, and immediately withdraws the atomism that alone made it a real distinction.

The whole of our sensations, their being-together, the common sense in which everything sensibility produces is unified in a tonality that continually differentiates and modalizes itself without ceasing to be one, is what is called coenesthesia. Coenesthesia is not a separate dimension made up of certain specific so-called internal sensations, brought to light by psychology at one moment of its history — by the French *idéologues*, more precisely — and juxtaposed within sensibility to the content furnished by the five traditional senses. Representative sensibility belongs to coenesthesia too, and not merely because the sensations it procures are inevitably bound to the internal sensations attending the exercise of the corresponding organs. Every sensation, representative ones included, contains an element irreducible to representation proper: a subjective impressional content, impossible to analyse or describe, which can only be undergone and felt, homogeneous with that of any other sensation, internal or not, and therefore capable not merely of being linked to it by the external bond of association but of merging with it in the consubstantial unity of one and the same tonality. The general feeling we have at every moment of our being, the feeling of existence, is thus thinkable from coenesthesia and as its result.

That the tonality which never ceases to affect existence results from coenesthesia does not mean it differs in nature from it. Since "result" here means to depend on the ensemble of sensations simultaneously or successively undergone, as what they produce and as the unity in which they all merge, it means that tonality is identical with coenesthesia. That is why feeling can be understood as "sensory" or "sensible," always complex, made of multiple elements indiscernible yet fused within it; and why affectivity is in the end assimilable to real or empirical sensibility in the richness of its concrete effectivity. That is why too, since it merges with the impressional content of sensation and with what that content holds of the qualitatively ineffable, affectivity can be grasped only within sensation, and its study must orient itself — as positive psychology in fact does — toward simple tonalities such as pleasure and pain, the agreeable and disagreeable, in order to find in them the bases of affectivity and its first determinations, from which the formation of more complex feelings can then be traced, the affectivity of the complex remaining homogeneous with that of its elements. Henry is not reporting an error but deriving it: given the identification of tonality with coenesthesia, the sensualist research programme follows with necessity, which is why refuting it piecemeal has never worked.

Psychologists do not always identify these primitive tonalities with sensation, and the question of what elements constitute affectivity's basis generates endless dispute — whether pain is a sensation, whether it is homogeneous with pleasure, whether affective life has a single source or must be understood as a dichotomy. But the very fact that the difference between affectivity's fundamental elements and sensation proper constitutes a problem, and that positive psychology must answer it by resorting to criteria external to the region of being to which these phenomena belong — considering the arrangement of the organs to which they are referred, asking whether there are specific algesic nerve endings, whether the same holds for pleasure, what physiological organization underlies internal sensations, whether the division in normal sensibility between agreeable and disagreeable depends on that organization or only on its functional modalities — attests the primary homogeneity of all these impressions and their phenomenological indissociability with respect to what makes each of them affective. The argument is neat: the recourse to organic criteria is an admission that the phenomenological criterion has failed, and the failure is evidence for the homogeneity, not against it.

Relating the impressional and affective content of sensibility to the body as the object of physiology does not put that homogeneity in question but underlines it: to the unity of being is added, confirming or even founding it, the unity of explanation. That such explanation — of immanent being by a cause transcendent to its effective content and fundamentally foreign to it — should claim its rights for affectivity as for sensibility, or rather should attest the common origin of whatever is at once affective and sensible, qualitatively specific, in the impressional content and tonalities of subjective existence, is shown well enough by the philosophy of affectivity, which through its whole history and across apparent doctrinal opposition maintains that there are no feelings without an accompanying set of bodily phenomena — a formula Henry takes from Sartre's *L'imaginaire* (177), and the choice of source is pointed, since it shows an existential phenomenology committed to the same premise as the physiologists.

That affectivity is neither identical with sensation nor its effect follows from its being sensation's condition, and here lies the paralogism of every sensualist theory of affectivity: it takes sensation *in abstracto*, as something isolated and self-sufficient. "Isolated" no longer means taken outside the concrete phenomenological context in which it shows up as a modalization of the general feeling of existence, modifying that feeling but still more and always already modified by it. The problem concerns rather the ontological sufficiency of sensation and of the total impressional content into which it merges. Sensation, the whole of sensation, has by itself no sufficiency whatever: neither the qualitative specificity of a sensation's impressional content nor the specificity of the overall tonality into which it merges constitutes and founds its reality, the effectivity of its concrete phenomenological being. Where does the reality of sensation lie? Sensation is real insofar as it is felt. Its reality lies in the being-felt taken as such and, further back, in the essence in which being-felt finds its own possibility and the effectivity of its effectuation: in affectivity.

Affectivity is not an external condition of sensation, a form inside which sensation would be given and would manifest itself as a content. Sensation is not a content, since a content of sensibility presupposes a power charged with receiving it and rendering it manifest — sensibility, and so affectivity itself. That sensation is real insofar as it is felt means that original sensation is not what affects us, not the being that sense gives itself in opposition; it is the affection itself, the being-affected such that, in being affected by what affects it, it is first affected by itself. Original sensation affects and feels itself, presupposes the ontological dimension of auto-affection, and forms and arises within it. This is how affectivity is the condition of sensation: by constituting its very reality and the substance of its concrete phenomenological being. Every possible sensation is therefore affective, and the affectivity of sensation is necessary a priori, belonging to it not as one eidetic character among others but as its essence and its substance. As such, sensation is living, carries in it the inner trembling of life, forms where life forms, vibrates in and with life, and determines life as one of its modalities and tonalities. And with that the absurdity weighing on the concept of "external sensation" is lifted — as if anything external or transcendent could by itself constitute a sensation, could carry in itself the inner being of what is living, the self-undergoing which alone can undergo anything as a mode of its own self-undergoing.

Sensation is "external" only by its signification, in its reference to what it is a sensation of. Precisely because it is accomplished in sense, as a mode of sensing and of the transcendence within sensing, every sensation is by nature the sensation of something, and what it is the sensation of is the excitant. The excitant is not an unknown term determinable only by scientific progress and acting on a sense organ that would itself be foreign to sensible experience; it is the object of that experience, and only as such does it affect us. Insofar as sensation refers to an object it is representative — which does not mean that it thinks that object, represents it in an act of knowledge, or that the object is the determinable object of the understanding. Because the object of sensation is received by it in sensing, it is felt, "affective" in the sense established. And this ontological determination concerns not only the object of sensation but equally the productions of thought, objects of every kind; it is a structural ontological determination of transcendent being, since thought itself takes its support in sense and occurs within it, in the ontological milieu of affection that conditions all experience of objects.

Sensation accordingly has two contents: an immanent, affective one — the content of being-affected, what life undergoes when it undergoes itself in the particular determination affection produces in it — and a transcendent one, the excitant, as given to it in and through sensing. That in sensation proper this sensing occurs through bodily organs determines only the specificity of the corresponding impressional content, which must itself be understood in both senses, and which each time finds the ontological condition of its "sensibility" and of its "affectivity" in the ontological structure of affection, in the structure of inner sense and in that of affectivity. Transcendent and immanent must here be taken radically: transcendent designates everything that is not life itself in its absolute subjectivity — not only the transcendent significations aimed at by objective intentionalities but equally the adumbrations of things, their subjective appearances, the silhouettes and the data Husserl's terminology calls immanent, out of which things are constituted. The redefinition matters: what Husserl counts as *reell* immanence falls, for Henry, wholly on the side of transcendence, and readers who assimilate the two immanences lose the entire argument. Because sensation always has two contents in this sense, the sensibility of which it is a mode is necessarily both affective and representative: the intuiting of a sensible and affective content in an act tonally determined by that content and co-determined by the essence of affectivity within it.

This dissolves the illusion peculiar to the genetic standpoint, by which positive psychology claims to exceed the supposedly narrow frame of a phenomenology confined to lived data — the illusion that affective and representative sensibility are two successive phases within one process of evolution. In that process affective sensibility appears first, its essence left in total ontological obscurity: lacking the concept of auto-affection, it is understood as an affection whose affective character has no foundation at all, and is besides confused with a third-person process, with a set of reflexogenic reactions to simple stimulations — with automatism. Because it is not only that, and because, following the double use of signs customary in the positive sciences, it surreptitiously recovers the fundamental ontological signification by which it designates the original upsurge of something and its manifestation, affection reappears on the psychological plane as the conscious counterpart of the accompanying neuromotor stimulation, and so in this first phase is that stimulation itself together with its instantaneous reaction: a quasi-mechanical shock charged with consciousness, with that confused form of consciousness called affectivity. On Pradines's account, which Henry follows closely here, the initial excitation occurs in heavily affective point-blank discharges in which things affect us without yet giving any image, in which the affected and the affecting are as one, the former knowing the latter in intimate communion, as when an object dissolves into us in the unconscious current of vegetative life.

So arises the picture of an original affection that excludes all distance between affecting and affected and is besides instantaneous — a punctual affection in which what affects us does so by immediate contact, by a shock like that between two contiguous realities. Confused, because it identifies the upsurge of the affecting with a blind contact between two beings, and unthinkable, because in such contact there is precisely no affection at all, the picture nonetheless lets something be glimpsed. With the idea of suppressing all distance between affecting and affected — however inadequately that idea is figured with elements borrowed from an elementary realism, as "immediate contact" — another structure is intimated than that of affection, one that founds affection along with its affectivity; and it is that structure which marks sensibility in its original form as affective sensibility. Representative sensibility then succeeds it, arising when the affected being stops undergoing what affects it in immediate contact or mingling with it in quasi-mystical fusion, turns against it, and holds it at a distance, reached now only by delayed excitations that, growing less affective and more capable of delay, signify ever greater distances of the excitant through ever longer anticipations. The excitant is then no longer undergone directly but only represented in a degraded symbol of its action — its quality — while it is itself set in space at a certain distance, as an object. Primitive affective impressions that stir us give way to impressions that leave us unmoved because merely represented, a substitution expressing the living being's effort to put itself out of reach and secure around itself an inoffensive field, the field of representation. Representation therefore does not merely succeed the primitive reign of affectivity; it is destined to end it, so that an inverse relation holds between them, affectivity diminishing progressively as representation develops, with sensation proper as the exemplary case of an impression in which the progressive compression of the affective element has made the representative element stand out.

The idea of an inverse relation between affectivity and representation, and of their successive appearance within one temporal process, can only look absurd to a thought that grasps them as ontological structures, sees their contemporaneity in essence, and sees the founding relation uniting them. Philosophy does not have to choose between genesis and description — the latter today given out as phenomenological, though it is most often only an external inventory of ungrounded characters which genesis then takes over in turn and enumerates in whatever order suits it. Philosophy is the eidetic intuition of the ontological structure of reality, and as such prescribes to all phenomena, sensation included, the essential characters belonging to them of necessity insofar as they must and can be real phenomena. For sensation this prescription defines the place where it gives itself to be felt and is undergone as constituting its reality: the self-undergoing of life in the absolute immanence of its affectivity. The dismissal of the genetic-versus-descriptive alternative is not incidental — Henry's charge is that a phenomenology reduced to inventory invites the genetic account it cannot then resist, and that only an eidetics of the ontological structure closes the gap.

## **§ 57 — Affectivity as the universal form of all possible experience in general and as the form of that form. The pure concept of affectivity**

That the total being of sensation — its unreal representative content and equally its reality as immanent affective reality in the sphere of absolute subjectivity — should then be constituted, retained in retention, and so profiled as a transcendent unity, "immanent" in Husserl's terminology, within the flux of internal time-consciousness, in no way affects the ontological status of original sensation; it merely prevents thought from grasping it. For it is this constituted sensation that thought inevitably has before its gaze when it turns toward sensation to seize it, and this constituted sensation that already intervenes in immediate experience, since the representative content of a sensation always contains in itself the representation of its immanent subjective being, that is, of its affectivity. Philosophy's error is not that it confuses affectivity with coenesthesia; it is that it cannot grasp coenesthesia's original being, the originally immanent being of the impression as finding its reality in the self-suffering of the being that suffers it — cannot grasp the essence of affectivity itself. The degradation of the concept of original sensation and that of the concept of affectivity happen at one stroke and for one reason. This diagnosis is worth marking, because it explains why the historical survey that follows finds the same failure in thinkers who otherwise share nothing: the constituted sensation is what is always available to reflection, and only a doctrine of auto-affection can go behind it.

Lachelier shows the degradation. He had grasped the original being of sensation as identical with its being-felt, that is, with its affectivity, and grasped affectivity as constitutive of the subject's being-given-to-itself, that is, of its subjectivity: it is by what is affective in sensation that sensation belongs to the subject and the subject is given to itself. But lacking the fundamental ontological categories that would articulate the intuition, the author of *Psychologie et métaphysique* proves at once unable to hold it or preserve its decisive import. The original being of the impression is confused with its constituted being, with its insertion into the lived body; sensations become simply our organic affections; and it is by being bound to those affections and rooted in our viscera that sensible things are said to be given to us and to exist for us. The being-given of the thing is then no longer grasped in the affectivity of sensation, that is, in the subject's original auto-affection, but absurdly in a connection established between two transcendent realities, between the thing and the organic world to which it is "bound" on a naive realist picture. Inserted into that organic world and constituting coenesthesia, now explicitly understood as a first stratum of transcendence, sensation becomes nothing but something transcendent; its original being, affectivity, is lost, and affectivity is grasped as a transcendent content, external to the subject and to what constitutes ipseity in it. Lachelier's own question betrays the collapse: are our sensations ourselves, and does saying that we enjoy a pleasure and suffer a pain not confess that we are something distinct from them? Once the impression has been transposed into the body, the self must be sought elsewhere than in what it undergoes, and the intuition Lachelier began from is spent.

Classical philosophy in its decline, and the thoughts that take themselves to oppose it, exhibit the same fall of sensation's original being and the same forgetting of the ontological power of donation belonging to it insofar as that being is identical with affectivity. It is this power to accomplish the original ontological work of donation that is confusedly thought under the concept of coenesthesia whenever that concept designates not merely a specific dimension of sensibility but its universal foundation, namely the being-given of every sensation as such. Bénézé gives the concept that founding role when he holds that there is visual sensation only because there is coenesthesic sensation of the visual apparatus, and that what is merely peripheral in visual sensation would without that support be an insufficient datum to claim existence; and when, discussing vision in the dark — which involves the suppression of the peripheral while the coenesthesic subsists — he insists that such vision can be defined by a negation only as regards the peripheral, being coenesthesically positive, as much the presence of the living eye as the absence of light. The example is well chosen for Henry's purposes, since it isolates a positive givenness that survives the withdrawal of every object.

But the presence of the living — the auto-affection of sensation constitutive of its original being-given, present as such in every sensation, in visual sensation just as much as in the coenesthesic sensation of the visual apparatus, provided one does not arbitrarily reduce the former to its representative content — is exactly what goes unthought. The fundamental ontological phenomenon of auto-affection, instead of being grasped in its structure and intrinsic possibility, is spirited away, since the idea expressing it — the privilege of immediacy by which, in sensations of this kind, the thing known is also that by which it is known — is referred to an external cause and explained by it, being ascribed solely to a physiological arrangement. And that arrangement does not even concern auto-affection or aim any longer to found it: it furnishes the matter of consciousness without sufficing to constitute consciousness itself. Sensation, instead of carrying in itself, as living sensation in its original immanence, the possibility of being-given, becomes merely the matter of knowledge, something transcendent that presupposes outside itself the possibility of knowledge and experience in general.

The same happens in Sartre, where coenesthesia first appears on the plane of unreflected existence and seems to belong to it. In a reading consciousness accompanied by an ocular pain, the pain is in no way an object and does not refer to an objective body; only for reflection can it appear as such and be known and named as pain in the eyes. In itself the pain is not different from the reading consciousness: it is its very being, the translucent matter of consciousness. It exists beyond all attention and all knowledge, since it slips into each act of attention and knowledge and is that act itself. Pain is the texture of consciousness, the ineffable of its very existence, what consciousness cannot separate itself from, so that the project of escaping it inevitably fails, the ineffable one wants to flee being recovered at the heart of the wrenching-away and being the very being of the flight that would flee it. Henry lets the analysis stand at full strength — it comes closer than anything in Lachelier or Bénézé to identifying the reality of the impression with an inner self-undergoing.

But in Sartre pain constitutes only consciousness's in-itself, its being-there, its attachment to the world, its contingency; it is what consciousness is only insofar as consciousness is not what it is. Pain is being; consciousness is nothingness. Pain is what it is, and is given, only because the nothingness nihilates it. Being-given belongs neither to pain itself nor to what constitutes its essence, the essence of affectivity in it; it is the work of a power external to affectivity, and that power is exteriority as such. After identifying the being of pain with that of non-thetic consciousness, Sartre must distinguish them and institute between them an interval which is exteriority: on the plane of pure being, pain can be existed non-thetically by consciousness only if it is surpassed, painful consciousness being internal negation of the world and at the same time existing its pain — itself — as a wrenching-away from itself.
