Painful sensation and its affectivity thereby sink into the transcendent and appear there as a content: not, admittedly, as the object of a free and indifferent contemplation, not as a psychic object, since the reading consciousness remains invincibly bound to its pain — but the bond is a bond of transcendence. Consciousness exists its pain in the sense that existing means surpassing, so that pain is the texture of consciousness precisely insofar as consciousness surpasses that texture toward its own possibilities and toward the world.

Such is the status of coenesthesia, and so of the body itself, of what Sartre also calls contingency and facticity: a presence haunting consciousness as what it cannot rid itself of, the inevitable term from which it rises toward the world and builds its projects — a presence that is such only by the distance at which consciousness holds it, consciousness being itself identical with that distance. Coenesthesia is that contingency, that weight held at a distance by the for-itself, which the for-itself never is but has to be as a weight surpassed and preserved in the very surpassing; it is facticity. And precisely because a distance is necessarily instituted, identical with the for-itself itself, between the for-itself and the coenesthesia signifying the original contingency of its existence, it is possible and indeed inevitable for consciousness to take up an attitude toward the bodily existence that pervades it, to live it in one way or another, to overcome its fatigue or pain or abandon itself to them in a project whose sense can each time be deciphered and traced by regressive analysis back to the fundamental project. Lived in a project, always in some manner assumed, the affectivity inherent in coenesthesia is, in existentialism as in classical philosophy, a transcendent content that finds outside itself, in the exteriority of transcendence, the ontological condition of its possibility. That the most anti-substantialist philosophy of the period lands in the same place as Lachelier is the point of the survey: nihilation does the work exteriority did, and the result is identical.

This is the crucial moment in any problematic of affectivity: the moment when what constitutes the condition of all affection and all experience is instead included within the content of experience and thereby subordinated to what it was supposed to condition. What constitutes the condition of all affection and all experience, of everything capable of being given to us — the being-given itself taken as such, in its intrinsic possibility and its own reality — is what is called a Form, the transcendental element of the real and what is ontological in it. Affectivity is precisely that: the universal form of all possible experience in general, the ontological and transcendental dimension founding the reality of everything that is.

The concept of form is not simple. It includes first the structure of pure affection as affection of essence by the horizon it projects. But if form designates the structure of affection, form must itself be possible, and its own possibility — the ultimate ontological possibility of everything that is — is the form in which form is given to itself as form: auto-affection. Affectivity is the form of the form, the essence of the essence. In this way form is affective, not as the mere form of objects, not as the ontological condition of their possibility, but insofar as that form of objects is itself possible. The analysis therefore cannot rest content with stating the fact that form is affective, since affectivity is not a character of form, an enigmatic property joined to it and accompanying it as something opaque whose presence one merely records. Affectivity is in form what makes form possible, the self-undergoing that renders it originally present to itself and capable of acting — its innermost form, what is most intelligible in it and the ultimate principle of all intelligibility, its essence. The doubling of the concept of form is the section's hinge, and everything that follows tests historical positions against it.

When affectivity is not grasped on the transcendental plane itself as this pure ontological possibility of what is and as a form, and still less as the innermost possibility of that possibility and the form of that form; when instead, identified with coenesthesia understood not in its original being — which lies precisely in the transcendental element of pure affectivity — but as the constituted whole of our sensations and so as a transcendent content, affectivity presents itself and is interpreted as a content of that kind, then philosophy enters the confusion in which we still find it today, and what constitutes at once the essence of affectivity and that of form, the essence of being itself, is irremediably lost.

Two consequences follow, one for affectivity and one for form. Affectivity is then no longer the form or its essence but a content among many of conscious life, mediated by form and presupposing it, foreign to the essence of conscious life, to pure consciousness and pure phenomenality as such — something opaque, heterogeneous to spirit, more or less assimilable to the specific, contingent, variable, irrational impressional content of some sensation, or rather simply identical with it. Contingent, variable, irrational, affectivity is then nothing universal or necessary, nothing that could be prescribed a priori to experience by its own structure; and if experience should everywhere and always exhibit an affective character, that would still be only an unforeseeable fact, a determination learned like all the others composing experience's matter. And because it belongs to that matter, to the empirical content of our experience, affectivity is not merely contingent, variable, and irrational: it shares that content's status, offers itself as a transcendent content, and can appear only in that form. This is the absurdity dominating the history of the philosophy of affectivity, since the essence of affectivity — the self-undergoing constitutive of a sphere of radical immanence and of life in its living interiority — obviously cannot really be found as effective self-givenness, as feeling of self, in the insensible and blind content of a transcendent entity, nor belong to it. Henry's note concedes the only thing that can be conceded: affectivity's essence can be *represented* in such a content, which is quite another matter, and the point is developed in §§ 66–67.

As for form, precisely because affectivity is placed outside it as a content foreign to what is properly ontological in it, form is nothing affective, and the purity of the transcendental element means the inaffectivity of form. Bénézé states it flatly: the transcendental form is entirely foreign to affectivity. Experience then presents itself as the in itself inaffective, atonal manifestation of an infinitely diverse content to which affectivity belongs like any other content, affective states receiving the framing of this non-sensible form on the same footing as intellectual and active ones. This inaffective and atonal character of pure manifestation is what determines it as a knowing, as an impersonal empty gaze, a pure light illuminating everything and indifferent to what it illuminates — objectivity as such, with the existential and axiological significations attaching to that concept. The effort visible in contemporary philosophy to define the ontological event of the relation to the world outside pure theory, which becomes merely one of its modalities, remains vain so long as the innermost possibility of form, the form of the form, is never thematized and grasped in itself. For only in that way is the relation affective, on the basis in it of its anti-essence, which is affectivity. When affectivity is not referred to this innermost possibility of everything that is, the affectivity of form — form now grasped as the mere form of objects, as transcendence — becomes incomprehensible, can only be recorded as an enigmatic fact, and philosophy, complacently describing what it cannot grasp the essence of, is nothing more than literature. The jab lands on Heidegger and on existential phenomenology together: the attempt to make the world-relation more than theoretical succeeds descriptively and fails at the level of foundation.

Alternatively, if affectivity does not originate in the essence of form yet manifests itself in form as an undeniable apparent character, it must accrue to form accidentally under an external influence, as a synthetic and parasitic addition, an alteration of form's original ontological purity. That is Descartes's situation. Affectivity does not constitute the form of our knowledge or the essence of thought in Cartesianism; it presupposes them, since the affective and sensible modifications of the soul, run together, offer themselves in the effectivity of the manifest only insofar as they are received by the understanding, and since the soul itself is conceived only by the pure understanding (letter to Elisabeth, AT III, 691). What characterizes pure thought is on the contrary its radical heterogeneity to whatever is affective in sensibility and in feeling, the heterogeneity of form to the essence of affectivity and its fundamental opposition to it. Descartes understands form as the understanding, as the objective grasp not only of simple natures but of everything that offers itself as an object and can, on that condition of the form of objectivity, be something for us. Hence sensibility and affectivity envelop representative elements as the very condition of their effectivity in the being-given. Considered *in abstracto*, as the mere condition of objective knowledge and finally as objectivity itself, form is indeed nothing affective. From this abstraction — form considered in its relation to what it makes possible rather than in its own inner possibility — arise the ideal and the fiction of a pure knowledge, a pure thought foreign to affectivity and to everything carrying life's interest, a pure and disinterested theory.

Having conceived a pure knowledge and a pure thought in this way, Cartesianism then collides with the fact of the affectivity of form, and does so in the irrecusable evidence of the cogito, which makes manifest the existence of affective and sensible lived experiences: to sense is still to think (AT VII, 29). Affectivity no longer belongs to the content of knowledge; it appears on the plane of form and concerns pure thought as such. Failing to refer that fact to form's inner and ultimate possibility, Cartesianism refers it instead to the influence of a reality foreign to form but bound to it and altering its originally pure nature: the body is that reality heterogeneous to pure thought which, acting on it, makes it affective. So the affectivity of form, made manifest in the cogito on the plane of pure thought and precisely as the affectivity of that thought, is at once acknowledged by Descartes and denied, since it is held to arise not from the nature of thought or from form as such but only from thought's determination by a reality at once external and foreign to it. Such a theory, whose transparent aim is to maintain the denial in spite of the evidence, runs up against an impossibility of principle. The determination of thought by an external reality cannot be accomplished as a causal or blind third-person process; because it is thought's determination, it manifests itself in thought, is lived by thought, and the passivity it implies is undergone as such. Determination of thought necessarily means affection. But affectivity is the ultimate possibility and the essence of every possible affection. Far from being able to found affectivity, the affection of thought by a foreign reality presupposes the affectivity of that thought as its condition. The refutation is internal: the very mechanism Descartes invokes to externalize affectivity is itself an affection and so already requires what it was meant to explain.

In Malebranche, by contrast, affectivity appears as constitutive of form itself — something quite unusual not only within Cartesianism but within the history of philosophy. The decisive ontological significance Malebranche accords affectivity is that affectivity constitutes the original dimension of existence brought to light in the cogito and identical with it, with the essence of pure consciousness and with the soul itself: the original and fundamental dimension of phenomenality in its irreducible opposition to that of the idea, to the phenomenality of the transcendental spatiality of the pure world, of extension. And affectivity does not merely oppose the pure ideality of extension; it founds it. The idea finds the sufficient ontological condition of its existence in the pure spatiality of intelligible extension only insofar as one considers in it nothing but its representative content, its objective reality, as Malebranche says — whose phenomenality, that is, whose reality, turns out to be constituted by that of extension and identical with it. Malebranche does identify the idea with that representative content, and it is as so reduced, considered as a pure determination and a mode of intelligible extension, that the idea stands opposed to the soul and is irreducible to it.

But considered as a mode of extension, and although extension confers on it the positivity of its inner rationality and the rigour by which it imposes itself on the mind, the idea is still an abstraction: it becomes real only insofar as it is received. The being-received of the idea is its form, identical with thought itself, and affectivity is that form. Since the idea presupposes that form and since its real being, like sensation's, consists in its being-given-to-itself, in being felt, the idea is affective just as sensation is. Likewise the understanding is affective at bottom, since its bottom consists in the self-givenness of the power that represents to itself the objective content of the idea, in the understanding's own being-given-to-itself. That self-givenness, whether of understanding, idea, or sensation, is the essence of thought, of the soul, of consciousness — the essence of form. That form, that being-given-to-itself taken as such, that auto-affection, resides in affectivity: this is Malebranche's brilliant presentiment. Thought, consciousness, and soul are for him not merely affective but constituted by affectivity as constitutive of form. That is what the claim that the soul does not know itself by an idea ought to mean, and means because, not being separated from itself, the soul feels itself.

But the persistence of the Cartesian presuppositions reserving intelligibility to objective knowledge and finally to extension, together with Malebranche's own religious presuppositions and his aberrant interpretation of the human soul's finitude and intrinsic obscurity, keep his thought from remaining faithful to its initial and central intuition. The soul's constitutive self-feeling, its affectivity, is no longer understood as an ontological power but, in the light of that finitude and obscurity, as something opaque, a mere fact, an empirical content which far from founding the intelligibility of the real is irreducible to it. The idea's inevitable reception by the soul, its necessary belonging to a form itself obscure and unintelligible, to an affective understanding, thereby becomes incomprehensible. Malebranche is accordingly at pains to minimize form's affective character, distinguishing from feeling proper — with everything heavy, obscure, and properly affective about it — the mere inner feeling, which in the end is only a word for consciousness and whose affectivity is nil. Contamination by affectivity and its intrinsic irrationality, by the confusion it carries and that is not provisional but insurmountable and in a sense essential, must be kept away from the pure idea, which is for that very reason said only to touch the soul lightly. The founding interiority of form, the very concept of form, is thereby eliminated and replaced by the crudely realist picture of a contact, a real if minimal intrusion of the idea into the soul and of the modification it produces there — a modification which is just as much, and more, a modification of the idea by the soul, an alteration of the principle of all intelligibility. The ontological interpretation of affectivity is lost, and affectivity is nothing but an empirical content once more. The pattern repeats the diagnosis given at the outset of the section: what is lost is always the original being of the impression, and it is lost as soon as intelligibility is conceded in advance to objective knowledge.

An analysis that can preserve the radical ontological significance of the concept of affectivity must still make one further proposition its own: interpreting affectivity as constituting not a determinate content of experience but its form, as universal and pure form and moreover as the form of that form and its innermost possibility, does not banish the idea of content from the rigorously ontological plane, from form itself. Affectivity precisely has a content. It designates the essence whose own character is to feel and undergo itself, so that in this self-undergoing it gives itself to itself as it is, in its reality. On the basis of this essence, every feeling is by nature what it is, the feeling of self. To be the feeling of self means to have a content, and not just any content: to have for content what one is oneself, one's own reality. That is what form is, insofar as its own form is constituted by affectivity: the feeling of self. Form is to itself its own content. And precisely for that reason form is possible, because, given to itself in order to be what it is, only so is it able to act.

For the same reason form is not empty, and the classical opposition between the empty form of knowledge and a content necessarily foreign to that form loses its rights. Monism's interpretation of the form of experience can certainly, when it operates on an ontological plane as it does in Heidegger, credit form with a content of its own, pure and itself ontological. But the pure horizon transcendence develops does not constitute transcendence's real content. So that development, form considered in its relation to what it makes possible, is not itself possible so long as its original being — and with it the possibility of acting — is not given to it in the original being-given that constitutes it. Only in affectivity, and insofar as it is constituted by affectivity, does form find its real content, as immanent content.

Only the ontological interpretation of affectivity as the universal and ultimate possibility of experience and as its form makes it possible to understand the relation of experience to its content as a pure ontological content constituted by form itself and identical with form's reality. That sets aside the classical conception of a content heterogeneous in principle to form and as such non-ontological; it sets aside the Heideggerian conception of a pure ontological content that is nonetheless unreal and so still foreign to the reality of form; and it sets aside Malebranche's as well, whose most remarkable feature is the recognition of affectivity's content — that is, form's content — as identical in its radical immanence with form itself and with form's reality. For it does characterize all our feelings that they belong to the soul, and belong not only by their form, that is, as felt by it, but by their content, which is nothing transcendent or objective in any degree, nothing foreign to the soul's reality but constituted by it. This is just what sets feeling against the idea, whose form alone resides in the soul and is identical with it while its content lies outside, as a representative content, an objective reality not merely external to the soul's but wholly independent of it. Yet here the following becomes evident: considered in its form, as a pure modification of the soul, the idea has a content identical with the soul and constituted by the soul's own reality, an original, radically immanent content necessarily belonging to it. This belongs of necessity to form insofar as form is ultimately possible, insofar as it is constituted by affectivity: a content identical with its own reality. And this is what makes the reality of the ontological element of experience, of pure ontological possibility taken as such — that it is never an empty form, never the pure medium of transparency through which one reaches something else, but what, through its own transparency, first arrives at itself: feeling, affectivity.

The idea, being itself necessarily form, does not escape this ultimate prescription of the essence of form: as such it is affective and is constituted in its original being as feeling of self. And just as the idea necessarily has, as affective, an original immanent content — which Malebranche does not see — so sensation, contrary to what he asserts, and precisely because it is accomplished in sense and so carries in it the ontological structure of affection, has a transcendent content and is always and necessarily a representative sensation. To include sensation entirely within the soul, to treat it wholly as a modality of the soul, is to insert into the originally immanent flux of absolute life elements ontologically heterogeneous to it, and at the same time to reserve arbitrarily to the objective reality of the idea, to the Cartesian simple nature, a privilege of exteriority that belongs just as much to the image or to sensation. Considered as affective, in its reality, sensation is indeed nothing transcendent or objective — but the same holds for the idea. This is what affectivity consists in: the radical immanence of the content as identical with its form, with affectivity itself. Interpreting affectivity ontologically as the universal form of experience, as its ultimate inner possibility, and likewise its content as a pure ontological content identical with form and with form's reality, yields a pure concept of affectivity and rules out understanding affectivity from the being of empirical sensibility, rules out assimilating it to a specific, determinate, itself empirical content. Sensation is of course affective, and affective in its specificity. But the affectivity of a sensation means nothing more than its being-given-to-itself; it is in sensation sensation's own form, pure and in itself non-empirical, the fundamental transcendental form of the auto-affection constitutive of the reality of sensation as of every possible reality. It is as pure, as accomplishing the work of original donation in the self-donation of everything that is, that affectivity is present in sensation as its pure ontological possibility, constitutive of and identical with its reality; and in the same way it is present in the idea, in imagination, and in all the determinations of life, since it constitutes the essence of life. For this too characterizes form insofar as it is constituted by affectivity: it is not an empty structure presupposed by everything and equally presupposing everything in order that there be reality, not an abstraction that by itself is still nothing, but life itself and its essence. The ontological interpretation of affectivity and the dissociation it institutes between the concept of affectivity and that of empirical sensibility call into question the presuppositions on which the whole classical philosophy of affectivity rests — presuppositions contained and summarized in remarkable fashion in the Kantian theory of respect. The critique of that theory therefore carries a general significance and serves at the same time as a repetition of the fundamental evidences established here.
